  2. Actuator resolution as data. Buttplug's StepCount/StepRange records a control's real granularity. We bury min/max in per-command parameters but never say "this is the device's actual resolution." Folds into P7.
  3. Named endpoint roles. Buttplug names characteristics by role (tx, rx, whitelist, firmware). We name them by human string, which is friendlier but not machine-routable. A minor optional role enum is noted in P7.

Everything else Buttplug does — handler dispatch, a merged user-config layer — is either already covered (protocol_handler) or a consumer concern, not a spec concern.

docs.title: Recommended now
docs.text: Low risk, high value, purely additive — existing specs keep validating unchanged.

docs.title: P1 — A reproducible checksum descriptor
docs.text:
Problem. A checksum in a spec is only useful if an implementer can reproduce it, and today many can't be reproduced from the file. framing.checksum is enum: [crc32, xor, sum] — it cannot say which bytes are covered, and "crc32" does not pin the polynomial or reflection. bus.checksum is better (it has a scope string) but still can't parameterize a CRC. So specs describe checksums in prose, and "CRC-16" is ambiguous across ~20 real functions.

Evidence. 18 device specs carry checksum/CRC logic. The NIIMBOT D110 documents both an XOR checksum and a CRC32 firmware-upgrade variant entirely in prose. The Bafang BBS02 sums different byte ranges on read vs write — the asymmetry that most often causes a first implementation's writes to be silently rejected.

Proposal. A shared $defs/checksum used by both framing and bus:

checksum:
  algorithm: "crc16"          # xor | sum8 | sum8-mod256 | crc8 | crc16 | crc32 | custom
  catalogue: "CRC-16/MODBUS"  # optional: a CRC RevEng catalogue name
  params:                     # optional: full parameters when not using a catalogue name
    width: 16
    poly: 0x8005
    init: 0xFFFF
    refin: true
    refout: true
    xorout: 0x0000
  scope: "bytes 2..n-3, i.e. command through last data byte; excludes header and trailer"
  check: "0x4B37"             # known-good CRC of the ASCII string \"123456789\", per the catalogue

Cite the CRC RevEng catalogue for names and the check convention. The check value is the important part: it turns "my CRC is wrong and I don't know why" into a one-line unit test.

Compatibility. Additive. The existing enum-only form stays valid; params, catalogue, scope and check are all optional. No consumer breaks.

Effort. Small schema change; back-fill is opportunistic, spec by spec.

docs.title: P2 — Mark SIG-standard services and characteristics
docs.text:
Problem. Standard GATT characteristics are re-documented, by hand, in every spec that uses them — and their format is often just omitted, left to the reader's knowledge of the GATT Specification Supplement. A consumer cannot tell "this is standard Battery Level 0x2A19, decode as uint8 percent" from a vendor characteristic that happens to look similar.

Evidence. 9 specs reference 0x180A/0x180F and the standard characteristics under them. In xiaomi-lywsd03mmc.yaml the Battery Level (0x2A19) and the Device Information strings (0x2A29/0x2A24/0x2A26) are genuinely exposed GATT characteristics listed with properties: [read] and no format — their decode is left to the reader's knowledge of the GSS rather than stated. (The same spec's 0x2A6E entry is deliberately not cited here: it is a passive-beacon placeholder whose decode already lives in payload_formats, which is P6's territory, not P2's — marking it standard: true would wrongly point a consumer at a GATT read that does not exist.)

Proposal. An optional boolean on services and characteristics:

- uuid: "00002a19-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb"
  name: "Battery Level"
  properties: ["read"]
  standard: true    # SIG-defined; decode per the GSS, resolve name from Assigned Numbers

standard: true means: this is not ours, its authoritative decode is the GSS, and a consumer may resolve its name and format from the Bluetooth numbers database rather than trusting local prose. See Standards Worth Citing for the list of standards involved and the Base-UUID shorthand rule.

Compatibility. Additive boolean, default false. Existing specs unchanged.

Effort. Small. Pairs naturally with a CI check that a standard: true characteristic's UUID actually is SIG-assigned.

docs.title: P3 — Endianness on BLE format fields
docs.text:
Status: landed. endianness is on BLE format items in schema.json, with the same enum and the same little default as the bus field it mirrors, and test_device_specs.py pins the two declarations to each other so they cannot drift. The mobile decoder honours it. The six fields that were already stating the key — five in xiaomi-miflora, one in pax-vape — now mean something; before, they were writing into a key nothing defined, tolerated by a permissive schema and dropped by every parser. Kept here as the worked reasoning; the rest of this section is written as it was proposed.

Problem. A multi-byte value read from a BLE characteristic has no byte order in the schema. bus.fields carry endianness (default little); the BLE format items — offset/length/name/type — do not. A uint16 temperature is therefore ambiguous, and specs resolve it in prose.

Evidence. The bus block already has the field (schema.json field endianness, default little). The BLE format array does not. The Xiaomi PVVX payload's int16 little-endian temperature is documented only in a parse_rules string, not in the format block that ought to carry it.

Proposal. Add the same optional field to BLE format items:

format:
  - offset: 0
    length: 2
    name: "temperature"
    type: "int16"
    endianness: "little"   # little (default) | big
    scale: 0.01

Default little matches BLE convention and every current implicit assumption, so nothing changes for existing specs.

Compatibility. Additive with a safe default. Aligns BLE with bus.

Effort. Trivial. This is the cleanest correctness fix in the list.

docs.title: High value, needs consumer coordination
docs.text: Additive to the schema, but only useful once the Rust/HA consumers honour them, so land them in step with the consumer.

docs.title: P4 — Bit-field decoding in format
docs.text:
Problem. Status and flag bytes pack several values into one byte. The schema decodes at byte granularity only (the bus block has a bitfield type but no bit offset or mask; BLE format has neither), so bit-packing is explained in prose.

Evidence. The ATC beacon's battery byte is "bits 6–0 = battery %, bit 7 = trigger flag" — currently a parse_rules string. This pattern recurs in status notifications across the LED and sensor specs.

Proposal. Optional bit addressing on a format field:

- offset: 2
  name: "battery_percent"
  type: "uint8"
  bit_offset: 0
  bit_length: 7
- offset: 2
  name: "trigger_flag"
  type: "bool"
  bit_offset: 7
  bit_length: 1

Compatibility. Additive; absent bits mean "whole field", as today. Rust decoder needs the masking logic before specs rely on it.

Effort. Small schema, moderate consumer work.

docs.title: P5 — Symmetric command responses on BLE
docs.text:
Problem. A BLE command documents the bytes written but not the reply, even though request/response over a notify characteristic is everywhere — printers, locks, challenge-response auth. The OBD side already models this: obd.requests carry expected_response. BLE commands have no equivalent, so correlation is prose.

Evidence. obd.requests[].expected_response exists in the schema; BLE commands have no response field. The Ember Mug's first-writer claim, the NIIMBOT print-status replies and every challenge-response device document their responses only in notes.

Proposal. Optional response fields on a BLE command, mirroring OBD:

commands:
  get_status:
    description: "Request printer status"
    value: [0x1A, 0x01]
    response_characteristic: "0000ff02-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb"
    expected_response: "5A ?? ?? AA"   # ?? = variable byte, same convention as obd/bus

Compatibility. Additive. Brings BLE to parity with a pattern the schema already blesses elsewhere.

Effort. Small schema; consumers that only write are unaffected.

docs.title: P6 — First-class advertisement / beacon payloads
docs.text:
Problem. Passive sensors broadcast their state in the advertisement and are read without ever connecting. The schema can match on advertisement data (discovery.manufacturer_data) but has nowhere to say "the temperature comes from these bytes of the service data," so these devices are modelled with a workaround.

Evidence. xiaomi-lywsd03mmc.yaml lists a format-less characteristic under Environmental Sensing with a notes disclaimer: "Not used as a GATT service — data is obtained from passive BLE scanning of the advertisement payload." Govee and SwitchBot specs have the same shape.

Proposal. An optional top-level advertisement block, and an entity binding that points at it:

advertisement:
  service_data:
    uuid: "0000fcd2-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb"   # BTHome v2's own SIG-allocated service-data UUID
    format: "bthome-v2"        # a named open format (see standards page) …
  # … or a custom layout under the device's own service-data UUID: the ATC/PVVX
  #   formats live on 0x181A, not 0xFCD2, and would give an explicit field layout
  #   here reusing the format/payload_formats machinery
entities:
  - platform: "sensor"
    name: "Temperature"
    state_source: "advertisement"   # vs a GATT characteristic

Naming BTHome v2 as a format lets the pvvx-firmware devices skip re-documenting a payload that is already an open standard.

Compatibility. Additive. Removes a standing workaround rather than adding a new convention on top of it.

Effort. Moderate; worth it because passive sensors are a large, growing slice of the registry.

docs.title: P10 — Multi-byte command parameters that encode one number
docs.text:
Problem. $defs/number_semantics made a numeric value's meaning machine-readable, and deliberately kept the transform linear so a command parameter can be encoded by inverting it. That works when one parameter carries the whole number. It does not when a device splits the number across several byte-wide parameters, which is the normal shape for any 16-bit value sent over a byte-oriented template. Nothing in the schema says those parameters belong together, or which end is which, so a consumer that wants to set the value has to be told in prose — and prose is exactly what the number-semantics work removed everywhere else.

Evidence. ember-mug.yaml's set_target_temp is the worked case:

template: ["{temp_low}", "{temp_high}"]
parameters:
  temp_low:
    type: uint8
    description: >
      Low byte of the little-endian uint16 target in centi-°C. The pair
      encodes round(target_c * 100): 56.5 C -> 5650 -> temp_low 0x12,
      temp_high 0x16.

Everything a client needs is in that sentence and none of it is in a field. The matching format block one level up is fully machine-readable (target_temp_raw, uint16, scale: 0.01), so the mug's target temperature can be read generically and written only by hand — the asymmetry number-semantics set out to fix. The same shape recurs wherever a template is a byte list: ibbq-meat-thermo.yaml's set_target_temp splits two probe thresholds across four bytes (low_lo/low_hi/high_lo/high_hi), and idotmatrix.yaml's set_password splits one value across three.

A consumer is already blocked on this, which is what distinguishes it from the other proposals in this section: the Flutter+Rust app resolves a number entity's setpoint to a sendable command only when exactly one parameter is un-defaulted, and deliberately refuses the Ember case rather than guess a byte order. Guessing wrong writes 0x1216 instead of 0x1612 — 46.6 °C asked for, 56.5 °C delivered, on a heater.

Proposal. An optional encodes block on a command, declaring that some of its parameters jointly carry one number:

set_target_temp:
  description: "Set target temperature"
  template: ["{temp_low}", "{temp_high}"]
  parameters:
    temp_low:  { type: uint8 }
    temp_high: { type: uint8 }
  encodes:
    # Significance order, least-significant FIRST. The list is the byte
    # order, so there is no separate `byte_order` key to disagree with it.
    parameters: ["temp_low", "temp_high"]
    type: "uint16"     # width and signedness of the assembled value
    unit: "C"          # ...plus the rest of $defs/number_semantics
    scale: 0.01

Encoding is then fully determined, in the same terms the schema already uses:

raw   = round((value - value_offset) / scale)      # number_semantics, inverted
byte0 = raw        & 0xFF   -> parameters[0]
byte1 = (raw >> 8) & 0xFF   -> parameters[1]
...

Listing the parameters in significance order rather than adding a byte_order enum is the deliberate choice: a list and an enum can contradict each other, and the contradiction is silent and catastrophic. One ordered list cannot. encodes.parameters is also independent of template order, so a device that interleaves the bytes with other protocol filler still describes itself correctly.

Reusing $defs/number_semantics on the block means unit, scale, value_offset and values all mean exactly what they already mean elsewhere; encodes adds only parameters and type.

Compatibility. Additive and inert. No existing spec has an encodes block, so nothing changes until one is written; a consumer that ignores it behaves exactly as today. Validation should require that every name in encodes.parameters is a declared parameter of the same command, that each is an integer type, and that their widths sum to the width of encodes.type — all checkable at load time, which turns a whole class of silent wrong-temperature bugs into a spec error.

Effort. Small schema, small validator. The consumer work is real but bounded: assemble on encode, and the existing format block already handles the decode direction. Backfilling ember-mug, ibbq-meat-thermo and idotmatrix would move three known devices from prose to reproducible.

docs.title: P11 — Plural local_name_prefix
docs.text:
Status: landed. local_name_prefixes is in schema.json, and the mobile matcher reads the singular and plural keys together, so a match on any one of them carries the weight a local_name_prefix match always did. Kept here as the worked reasoning; the rest of this section is written as it was proposed.

Problem. device.identification.local_name_prefix holds exactly one string, but a device family that ships under several rebadged names has several. There is nowhere to put the rest, so the ones that do not fit are unmatched at scan time — the cheapest, earliest identification signal, missing for exactly the families most likely to be mislabelled.

Evidence. inkbird-bbq-thermometer advertises under eight names (BG-BT1X, IBBQ-4BW, BBQ-4BW, IBT-4XS, IBT-2X, IBT-24S, IBT-26S, Inkbird@) with no shared prefix. Its spec carries local_name_prefixes: — plural, and not a schema key, so identification sweeps it into extensions and no consumer reads it. All eight names are in the discovery block, which consumers do not execute, so today the family has no working name signal at all. admore hits the same wall from the other side, declaring local_name_dfu and local_name_armband* as separate extension keys.

Proposal. Accept either form on the same key, the way mac_prefixes accepts either a bare string or a map:

identification:
  local_name_prefix: "Ember"              # unchanged, still valid
  # or
  local_name_prefixes: ["IBT-", "IBBQ-", "BG-BT1X", "Inkbird@"]

A match on any one of them means what a match on the single prefix means today, so the confidence rules do not change.

Compatibility. Additive. Consumers reading only local_name_prefix keep working; specs using the plural form gain matching they do not have now.

Effort. Small schema, small consumer work — the matcher already loops over service_uuids and mac_prefixes the same way.

docs.title: P12 — Executable HTTP commands, paired credentials, and hub children
docs.text:
Status: landed. method on commands, the credential:/instance: schemes on parameter source, and instances: on entities are in schema.json; the hue-bridge spec exercises all three and the mobile consumer executes them. Kept here as the worked reasoning; the rest of this section is written as it was proposed.

Problem. The commands: block made a role map executable for exactly one transport. transport: http was in the enum from the start, but an http command carried only path — no method — and a REST-shaped API answers GET and PUT on the same path with different operations, so the file could not say which one a command performs. Two further gaps sat behind that one. First, real HTTP paths carry values the spec cannot know: a per-client credential issued at pairing time (every Hue call after the link-button handshake embeds the issued username in the path), and the identifier of whichever child a hub command addresses. source could only say state:<command>.<field>, which covers neither. Second, an entity binds to exactly one reading, but a hub is one network presence fronting a population — which lights sit behind a Hue bridge is the owner's business, not the spec's, so no fixed list of entities can describe one.

Evidence. hue-bridge.yaml: discovery, identification, pairing and endpoints live-verified against hardware, and every byte of it declarative. The mobile app finds the bridge, badges it, and has nothing to offer — the protocol is documented and none of it is executable, which is precisely the gap commands: closed for SOAP.

Proposal. Three additive pieces of vocabulary:

commands:
  light_turn_on:
    transport: "http"
    method: "PUT"                              # new: the missing half of the address
    path: "/api/{username}/lights/{id}/state"  # placeholders now substitute from parameters
    arguments: { on: true }
    parameters:
      username: { type: "string", source: "credential:username" }  # new scheme
      id:       { type: "string", source: "instance:id" }          # new scheme

entities:
  - platform: "light"
    name: "Hue Light"
    instances: { keyed_by: "id", label_path: "name" }   # new: entity as per-child template
    state_command: "Lights"
    state_mapping: { is_on: "state.on", brightness: "state.bri" }

method pairs with path the way service pairs with action. credential:<name> names a per-device secret the client stored when it paired; instance:<key> names the current child's id. Both inherit source's contract: no default, and a renderer with no value must fail the send visibly — an unpaired client erroring at credential:username is the correct behaviour. instances: declares the entity a template: the state_command reply is a JSON object keyed by child id, enumeration and state in one request, with state_mapping paths resolving inside each child's object.

Compatibility. Additive. SOAP specs are untouched; existing consumers that predate the keys see an http command with no method (declarative, as ever) and an instanced entity whose paths resolve nothing from the response root — the correct degraded behaviour for a hub they do not understand.

Effort. Small schema; the consumer work is the real half (an HTTP renderer beside the SOAP one, credential storage, instance enumeration) and landed with it. Deferred at the time: a headers: vocabulary. Hue's CLIP v2 API moves the credential from the path into an hue-application-key header, and other devices will want Authorization:. That piece has since landed as headers on the command object, following the arguments substitution model exactly (AUTH: "{auth_token}" filled from a credential: parameter); Vizio's SmartCast and Sony's JSON-RPC reads are the first users, and the same key is what a v2 Hue spec would use.

docs.title: P13 — Power as a stateful control, and the toggle problem
docs.text:
Status: spec half landed. Eight TV specs carry the Power switch (Panasonic excluded, as proposed), Philips gained set_power_standby, and the toggle role is documented in the spec-format guide. The consumer half — a toggle role in the mobile app's role tables and the read-state-then-toggle rule — is in flight downstream. The rest of this section is written as it was proposed.

Problem. A consumer cannot turn a TV off from these specs without guessing. All nine category: tv specs express power as a stateless button, and the schema enforces that shape: the button contract in entities.items.allOf[0] requires exactly the press role and forbids every state binding. That is right for a remote key — a keypress is honestly stateless — but it leaves no role meaning "make this device off", so a consumer wanting one has to match on command names.

Command names will not carry that weight. The same idea is spelled press_power_off (Roku, Sony, Vizio, Philips), power_off (LG), press_power (Samsung, Panasonic, Hisense, Android TV), press_standby (Philips) and press_power_toggle (Vizio) — and the last three are toggles, so a consumer that globs *power* will turn a sleeping TV on. Worse, the toggle/discrete distinction exists today only in prose: panasonic-viera.yaml marks it in a YAML comment (# -- Power. NRC_POWER is a TOGGLE, not discrete on/off.) and vizio-smartcast.yaml in an entity notes: string. Neither is machine-readable, so nothing in the file distinguishes the two operations.

Evidence. lg-webos.yaml already proves the fix is expressible today: its Mute control is a switch entity binding turn_on/turn_off with a state_topic, on a Wi-Fi device, with no schema change. Power is the same shape and simply was never written that way. Meanwhile the mobile consumer's bulk operations resolve strictly by entity action role — deliberately, so that destructive verbs are unreachable from a fan-out by construction rather than by blacklist — which means TVs are currently excluded from bulk control entirely, not by policy but for want of a role to bind.

Proposal. Give each TV spec a platform: "switch", name: "Power" entity alongside its existing remote buttons. The buttons stay: a remote's power key is still a keypress, and removing it would break every remote UI.

  - platform: "switch"
    name: "Power"
    icon: "mdi:power"
    commands:
      turn_on: "press_power_on"      # only where network power-on really works
      turn_off: "press_power_off"    # only where a discrete off exists
      toggle: "press_power"          # new role, for the toggle-only sets
    state_endpoint: "/sony/system"   # where the device reports power at all
    state_command: "getPowerStatus"

toggle is the one new role, and it is what makes the distinction machine-readable: a command bound to toggle is declared to flip state, so a consumer knows it must establish the current state before sending. Each spec binds only the roles its hardware honestly supports:

Spec turn_off turn_on toggle Power state readable roku-ecp press_power_off press_power_on (warm standby only) — no sony-bravia press_power_off press_power_on press_power yes — Power Status vizio-smartcast press_power_off press_power_on press_power_toggle yes — Power Mode philips-jointspace press_power_off press_power_on press_standby yes — Power State, v6 only lg-webos power_off — — no samsung-tizen-tv press_power † — — no hisense-vidaa — — press_power yes — TV State android-tv-remote — — press_power yes — Power State panasonic-viera no switch entity — see below no

† Samsung's KEY_POWER is nominally a toggle, but the spec records that the network stack is down in standby, so no network client can reach an off set. The toggle is therefore discrete-off in practice, and binding it as turn_off with that reasoning in notes: is the honest description rather than a convenient one. This is a verified protocol signal, not an assumption — which is exactly what separates it from Panasonic.

Panasonic is deliberately excluded. It is the one set that is toggle-only and reachable while off: panasonic-viera.yaml states that power-on over the network works from network standby ("Powered On By Apps" / "Networked Standby"), with Wake-on-LAN needed only when that is disabled or on several older plasma models. So a Viera in standby will receive NRC_POWER-ONOFF and turn on. It also reports no power state, so a consumer can never establish that it is safe to send. Giving it a Power switch would ship a control that is either inoperable under the rule below or actively harmful in a bulk off; it keeps its remote button and nothing else until it gains a readable state or a discrete off.

turn_on is deliberately unbound for LG, Samsung and Hisense: those specs state that no network command can wake a standby set, because the network stack is down. Note this is "cannot wake over the network", which is a different claim from Panasonic's "has no discrete on command" — Panasonic can wake, it just cannot be told which direction to go. Wake-on-LAN, the documented route for the first group, has no declarative representation in the schema — out of scope here, and worth its own proposal rather than a field smuggled in beside commands.

Bind Philips' discrete off, which is documented but unreachable. philips-jointspace.yaml catalogues "Set Power State" under http_endpoints and never exposes it as a command, so no consumer can invoke it:

  set_power_standby:
    transport: "http"
    method: "POST"
    path: "/{api_version}/powerstate"
    arguments: { powerstate: "Standby" }

Genuinely cheap — a flat scalar body, the same shape Vizio's and Philips' own existing HTTP commands already render through arguments — and it gives Philips an off that does not depend on a key code being accepted.

Sony's equivalent is not cheap, and this proposal should not pretend it is. sony-bravia.yaml documents setPowerStatus, but every Sony REST call is a JSON-RPC envelope — {"method": …, "params": [ … ], "id": N, "version": "1.x"}, where the spec states params is always an array. arguments cannot express that: the schema constrains its values to ["string", "number", "boolean"], so an array containing an object has nowhere to live. body: does not rescue it either — the schema defines body as the counterpart of arguments for SOAP and path for HTTP, i.e. for a JSON-over-socket protocol (tcp-json), not for HTTP.

So binding Sony's REST off depends on a prior extension: literal or nested body values for transport: http. That is a vocabulary gap of its own and belongs in its own proposal — the same call P12 made when it deferred a headers: vocabulary rather than widening its scope. Sony loses nothing in the meantime: its press_power_off IRCC command already works over SOAP, and that is what the table above binds.

A note the consumer contract needs. On a toggle-only set the Power switch resolves only toggle, so a consumer predating the role sees a switch with no resolvable actions. docs/api/spec-format.md should state that a control which resolves no roles must be hidden, not rendered dead — otherwise this proposal ships a non-functional toggle to older clients.

A failed read is not the same as "off", and the contract must not conflate them. A state read can fail from packet loss, a stale address, an auth failure, or an endpoint that was never there — philips-jointspace.yaml explicitly documents 403/404 as endpoint-not-present, which says nothing about power at all. Two separate rules, then:

  • Infer standby only from a verified, protocol-specific signal. Some specs supply one: a Sony in standby answers control calls with the error string "not power-on", which its spec says "a client should read as 'off', not 'broken'"; Vizio documents its state endpoint as unreachable rather than wrong while the set is asleep. Where such a signal is documented, a consumer may act on it.
  • Otherwise the state is unknown, and must be surfaced as unavailable — never as off. Unknown still means "do not send the toggle", because declining to act is the safe default for a bulk off. But that is a rule about the toggle decision only: it must not suppress ordinary retries or hide a recoverable network or configuration fault behind a confident-looking "off".

Compatibility. Additive. The button contract is untouched, every existing button entity keeps working, and a consumer that does not know toggle degrades to "this TV offers no bulk power control" — which is exactly today's behaviour, so nothing regresses. The switch is also shaped to map cleanly onto a Home Assistant media_player/switch with assumed_state: true where no state is readable, keeping that consumer's route open.

Effort. Small per spec — one entity each, plus one new command for Philips. Sony's REST off is explicitly not in scope, for want of an HTTP nested-body vocabulary. The real half is consumer work: a toggle role in the mobile app's role tables, and the read-state-then-toggle rule that makes it safe. As with P12, the schema change is not the interesting part.

docs.title: P14 — Disambiguating a shared discovery service type
docs.text:
Status: landed. $defs/mdns_txt_match, identification.mdns_txt_match and discovery.methods[].mdns.{txt_match,platform_fallback} are in schema.json; ratgdo and the new esphome-device are the two halves of the worked example, and scripts/test_esphome_spec.py holds the family to it. Kept here as the worked reasoning; the rest of this section is written as it was proposed.

Problem. identification.mdns_service_type is a single string, matched by itself. That is fine for _ankivector._tcp and wrong for a service type that belongs to a firmware platform rather than a product. A consumer resolving a service type to a spec has no way to prefer one claimant over another, so the whole platform gets labelled with whichever spec the matcher reached first.

Evidence. ratgdo was the only spec claiming _esphomelib._tcp, which is the service type of ESPHome itself. Every ESPHome node on the LAN — sensors, plugs, bluetooth proxies — rendered as a garage-door opener, offering /cover/door controls for entities those nodes do not have. The same shape is sitting in the registry unexploded: lifx-z, rachio-controller and lutron-caseta-smart-bridge all claim _hap._tcp, and wled-controller and purpleair-sensor both claim _http._tcp. Each says the right thing in prose notes and none of it is machine-readable.

Proposal. Two additive keys, and a resolution rule that needs no new ordering field:

identification:
  mdns_service_type: "_esphomelib._tcp.local."
  mdns_txt_match:                    # ANDed conditions; narrows type -> product
    - key: "project_name"
      match: "prefix"                # exact | prefix | contains | regex
      value: "ratgdo."               #       | present | absent (no value)
discovery:
  methods:
    - type: "mdns"
      mdns:
        service_type: "_esphomelib._tcp.local."
        platform_fallback: true      # the catch-all, on the platform's own spec

A consumer takes the claimant with the most satisfied conditions; a spec with no conditions loses to one that has them, and platform_fallback marks the spec that is meant to catch the remainder. The fallback spec declares no entities — it cannot know them — and documents how to enumerate instead.

The two keys are exclusive. txt_match is a precondition; platform_fallback is what a consumer reaches for when no precondition was met. A method carrying both has no single reading, and read the wrong way it rebuilds the bug one service type over — an ESPHome spec that is also the catch-all for _http._tcp claims every printer on the link that fails its TXT condition. Enforced across the catalogue by test_no_method_is_both_narrowed_and_a_fallback.

A claim in identification counts even with no discovery behind it. identification is the block the scanner reads, so a spec naming a platform service type there and nowhere else over-matches exactly as badly while presenting nothing for a reviewer to object to. The regression suite derives claimants from both blocks and fails either divergence.

Compatibility. Additive. A consumer reading only mdns_service_type behaves exactly as it does today; one reading mdns_txt_match stops mislabelling whole platforms. No existing spec changes meaning.

Effort. Small schema, small consumer work (one filter step before the service-type lookup). The open follow-up is evidence, not design: the _hap._tcp and _http._tcp claimants above each need a matcher written from an actual TXT dump — HomeKit's md (model) and ci (accessory category) are the obvious candidates — and inventing those values rather than observing them would be worse than the prose we have.

docs.title: P15 — A second address for the same invocation
docs.text:
Status: landed. commands[].path_fallback and entities[].state_topic_fallback are in schema.json and exercised by ratgdo. Kept here as the worked reasoning.

Problem. A spec states one path per command. That is right until a firmware family renames the thing the path addresses, at which point the file is correct for one half of the fleet and a 404 for the other, and there is nowhere to put the second address.

Evidence. ESPHome addressed entities by slugified object_id up to 2025.12 (/cover/door/open), accepted both forms from 2026.1.0 through 2026.6, and from 2026.7 accepts only the percent-encoded entity name (/cover/Door/open). (The JSON identifier moved one release later, at 2026.8 — a separate boundary.) ratgdo boards in service today span the whole range. Whichever form the spec stated alone, it broke working hardware — and prose saying "older firmware uses the other one" reaches no consumer, because consumers execute the bindings.

Proposal. One optional sibling key each, named for the <role>_fallback pattern the schema already uses in state_mapping and for fallback_characteristic on BLE:

commands:
  door_open:
    path: "/cover/Door/open"
    path_fallback: "/cover/door/open"

The contract is deliberately narrow: try path, and fall back only on an unambiguous "no such entity" answer (HTTP 404) — never a timeout, never a 5xx, never a blind second send. A door that opens twice because the first request was slow is a worse outcome than the 404 this exists to survive.

Compatibility. Additive and ignorable: a consumer that never reads the key behaves exactly as it does today, correct for current firmware. Consumers that do read it keep older hardware working.

Effort. Small. The judgement is in the 404-only rule, not the plumbing.

docs.title: P16 — Scope a surface to the discovery method that proves it
docs.text:
Problem. A spec's protocol_handler, http_endpoints and entities are unconditional: whatever method discovered the device, the whole surface applies. That is right for a product spec and wrong for a platform spec that claims several service types of unequal capability. The generic printer spec claims _ipp._tcp, _ipps._tcp, _pdl-datastream._tcp and _printer._tcp as fallbacks, and reads status over IPP; a printer that advertises only the raw-socket or LPD type has no IPP resource to ask, yet a consumer reading the spec by key offers it the status entities and the ipp_status handler, and gets connection refused or a 404 for its trouble. The restriction lives in prose and in a protocol_details key (ipp_status.requires_service_types), where only a consumer that knows to look will find it.

Evidence. ipp-network-printer today. The same shape waits in any spec that pairs a rich service type with a poorer one for the same hardware: a device advertising both _hap._tcp and a vendor type, where only the vendor type carries the local API.

Proposal. One additive key, requires_discovery, on each entry of entities and http_endpoints, and a top-level sibling for the handler, because protocol_handler is a plain string and can carry no key of its own:

protocol_handler: "ipp_status"
protocol_handler_requires_discovery:  # same shape as below
  - service_type: "_ipp._tcp.local."
  - service_type: "_ipps._tcp.local."
entities:
  - platform: "sensor"
    name: "Printer State"
    requires_discovery:               # any of; absent = any method
      - service_type: "_ipp._tcp.local."
      - service_type: "_ipps._tcp.local."
http_endpoints:
  - method: "POST"
    path: "/{rp}"
    requires_discovery: [...]

A consumer that matched the device through a method not listed hides the entity, endpoint or handler, as it hides an entity whose variants exclude the unit. The IPP spec's protocol_details.ipp_status.requires_service_types is the interim form: its two values would move into these keys, in the object shape above.

Compatibility. Additive. A consumer that ignores the key behaves as today (the surface is offered everywhere); one that reads it stops offering a status it cannot fetch. No existing spec changes meaning.

Effort. Small schema; small consumer work (the method that matched is already known at resolution time, so it is one filter at render time).

docs.title: P17 — A home for Bluetooth Classic
docs.text:
Status: landed (2026-09-27). device.protocol: bluetooth_classic, device.transport: rfcomm | l2cap | hid, the bt_classic_inquiry discovery method, the bt_classic_pairing setup method, rfcomm on commands[].transport and on a DFU transport, and the top-level bluetooth_classic block are in schema.json; quin-pillcalendar is the first spec written against them and brother-ql-1110nwb, obd2-bluetooth-adapter and obdlink-mx-plus were migrated off their workarounds. Kept here as the worked reasoning.

Problem. device.protocol named every link the catalogue speaks except one. A BR/EDR device — an SPP printer, a Classic ELM327 dongle, a headset with a vendor RFCOMM control channel, a pill box that is found over BLE and talked to over SPP — had nowhere to go. The three that existed were filed as ble or wifi with a paragraph of apology ("recorded as a ble_scan method because the schema has no bt_classic_inquiry type"; "under ble_direct for want of a bt_classic setup type"), and the 2026-09 missing-devices survey parked four whole families and two research notes on the gap.

Evidence. The Quin PillCalendar decompile (2026-09-27): an unfiltered BLE scan filtered by name prefix, then createInsecureRfcommSocketToServiceRecord with the SPP UUID to the same address, a raw byte stream with no length field and no checksum, and per-command fixed reply lengths. Not one of those facts had a declared key. The mobile Rust Protocol enum already preserves unknown values verbatim rather than failing the parse, so the value could be added without breaking the one consumer that reads it.

Proposal, as landed. Name the link, then give a client the four things it needs in the order it needs them: find it (bt_classic_inquiry, or a ble_scan on a dual-mode unit, with bluetooth_classic.ble_role saying what the BLE side is for); pair or not (device.pairing, bt_classic_pairing); open the right socket (bluetooth_classic.profiles[], each with its SDP UUID, channel and — the consequential bit — secure, the flag the vendor app opens the socket with); then read a stream with no edges (bluetooth_classic.serial.framing, and a per-command response with prefix and length, because a protocol without a length field is splittable only that way). Commands ride the top-level commands block with transport: rfcomm and the BLE value/template/parameters envelope, so one encoder serves both radios. Two conventions are enforced beside the schema: a Classic spec answers the iPhone question with a corebluetooth host_compatibility verdict, and its control profile states secure.

Second pass, same day. Three adversarial reviewers — the engineer who would implement the RFCOMM transport, a spec author writing the pill box, a Bose headset and an ELM327 dongle against it, and the schema maintainer — found 45 defects before any consumer did. The ones that changed the shape: there was nowhere to declare frames the device sends unprompted, so the pill box's low-battery push would have desynchronised every client (serial.unsolicited); nothing said how a reply maps to its command (correlation, max_in_flight); a length-prefixed stream could not say where its length was; terminators were escaped strings that validated two ways and the ELM327 prompt had no key (line_terminator, prompt, command_terminator, all hex); a Classic handshake could not be written because initialization demanded a GATT characteristic (steps now name a command); one device.pairing block was describing two radios (bluetooth_classic.pairing); the documented iPhone verdict failed validation four ways (symptom: no_transport, cause: {missing_api}, workaround: vendor_mfi, link, and an iobluetooth stack for macOS); and the inquiry matchers were OR-combined, so name + SPP UUID matched every serial module (they now narrow).

Compatibility. Additive for the catalogue: every existing spec validates unchanged, and the three migrated ones changed only the keys they had been apologising for. The mobile app's parser loads every new key (unknown values are preserved, not rejected), but its BLE scan matcher does not yet check device.protocol or ble_role, so a Classic spec that also matches a BLE advertisement is offered as a BLE device until it does. On iOS the RFCOMM half never will work, which the host_compatibility verdict states per spec rather than leaving to a footnote.

Effort. Schema and docs: done. Consumer: an Android/Linux RFCOMM transport in the mobile app, which is the second half of this change.

docs.title: P7 — A normalized capability vocabulary
docs.text:
Problem. There is no machine-readable answer to "what can this device do?" that is independent of its bytes. entities maps to Home Assistant platforms and features enumerates three upload types, but a consumer that wants "every device with a dimmable output" must special-case each spec.

Proposal (the Buttplug idea, kept as an optional layer). A small controlled vocabulary describing capabilities, sitting on top of the byte-level spec, never replacing it:

capabilities:
  - type: "actuator"
    kind: "dimmer"            # dimmer | switch | color | rotate | oscillate | vibrate | position | temperature
    resolution: { min: 0, max: 100, steps: 100 }   # Buttplug's StepRange, as data
    maps_to: "set_brightness"                        # the command that drives it
  - type: "sensor"
    kind: "battery"           # battery | temperature | humidity | pressure | rssi | button | weight
    maps_to: "0000181a-...-battery_percent"

This is what would let a generic client or a cross-device search work without per-device code — Buttplug's central win — while keeping our byte-level ground truth intact. It also subsumes P3-era range metadata and could carry an optional endpoint role for the machine-routing Buttplug gets from tx/rx.

Partially landed since this was written. The schema now has $defs/number_semantics — unit, an invertible linear scale/value_offset transform, values code tables, and unit_source/unit_reference/ unit_values for devices whose wire unit follows a device setting (C-vs-F on the Inkbird iBBQ) — shared by BLE command parameters, BLE format fields, bus fields and payload_formats fields; number entities carry min/max/step (Buttplug's StepRange, as data). That covers this proposal's resolution/range half. The capability vocabulary — actuator / sensor kinds independent of the bytes — remains open and still deserves its design pass.

Compatibility. Fully additive and ignorable. The risk is scope, not breakage: a controlled vocabulary has to be curated or it rots into free text. Start with the handful of kinds the registry actually has and grow it deliberately.

Effort. Larger, and worth a design pass of its own before any schema change.

docs.title: P8 — Resolve the advanced / command_class name collision
docs.text:
Problem. "advanced" already means two different things, and CLEANROOM_RULES flags it as an open decision: on BLE commands advanced is a consequence signal, while obd.requests[].command_class: basic | advanced is an adapter-capability signal.

Proposal. Rename the OBD field command_class → adapter_class (it really is about the adapter), keeping command_class as a deprecated alias for one minor version so nothing breaks immediately. Then advanced means "consequence" everywhere, with no gloss required.

Compatibility. Needs an alias window; the validator and index generator accept both during it.

Effort. Small, but touches the OBD specs and the consumer — do it deliberately.

docs.title: P9 — Version the schema with SemVer
docs.text:
Problem. Schema changes are tracked only in prose (the CHANGELOG) and an implicit schema_version in the generated index. schema.json's $id is not versioned, and there is no stated compatibility policy — so a consumer cannot pin a version or reason about whether an update is safe. Buttplug versions its config format explicitly (v3 → v4) for exactly this reason.

Proposal. Adopt SemVer 2.0.0 for the schema: embed the version in $id (…/device-spec.schema.v1.json) and optionally a top-level spec_version, and write the policy down — additive field = minor; a new required field, a removed field, or a narrowed enum = major. Keep the JSON Schema 2020-12 dialect.

Compatibility. Process change, not a breaking one. Makes every future change on this page classifiable.

Effort. Small, and it is the change that makes the rest safe to make.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
# Proposal Value Risk Verdict P1 Reproducible checksum descriptor High Low Recommended now P2 Mark SIG-standard GATT entries High Low Recommended now P3 Endianness on BLE format Medium Very low Landed P4 Bit-field decoding Medium Low With consumer P5 Symmetric BLE command responses High Low With consumer P6 First-class advertisement payloads High Medium With consumer P10 Multi-byte command parameters High Low With consumer — one is blocked today P11 Plural local_name_prefix Medium Very low Landed P12 Executable HTTP commands + hub children High Low Landed P13 Power as a stateful control + toggle role High Low With consumer P14 Disambiguating a shared discovery service type High Very low Landed P15 A second address for the same invocation Medium Very low Landed P16 Scope a surface to the discovery method that proves it Medium Very low With consumer — the IPP printer spec needs it today P17 A home for Bluetooth Classic High Low Landed P7 Normalized capability vocabulary High Medium Needs a design pass P8 Rename command_class → adapter_class Low Low Governance P9 SemVer the schema Medium Low Governance — enables the rest

The through-line: P1, P2 and P6 all push in the same direction — put the standard-shaped parts of a protocol (checksums, SIG characteristics, open beacon formats) in terms of published standards instead of local prose, so more of every spec is reproducible from the file. That is the same lever test_wemo_spec.py already pulls, applied to the parts of a spec that are currently prose-only.

P10 is the same lever pointed at the write direction. Number semantics made reading a value reproducible from the file; a device that splits that value across byte parameters is still readable and no longer writable without prose, which is the one place the asymmetry now shows.

docs.title: Not everything here was liberated
docs.text:
Almost every entry above is a reconstruction — somebody worked the protocol out from captures, firmware or an app teardown. A few are not, and specs say which they are in device.openness:

Status Means open_by_design Published protocol; third-party clients are the point. Read upstream, not us documented_api Official interface exists, product otherwise closed. Part cited, part reconstructed undocumented Nothing published. Our best reconstruction — the default here, and the usual case hostile Vendor actively fights third-party clients. Documented anyway; expect breakage

WLED is the worked open_by_design example, and it is here partly to keep the distinction honest: a registry framed around liberating documentation should be able to say when there was nothing to liberate. See Reading a Device Spec for the field.

docs.title: 94Fifty Smart Sensor Basketball
docs.text: Status: Spec Available Protocol: Bluetooth Classic RFCOMM (vendor SDP service; BLE used only to find the ball) Manufacturer: InfoMotion Sports Technologies Inc. Manufacturer Status: Shutdown

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The 94Fifty was the first consumer smart basketball. It is regulation size, with a sensor puck suspended inside: a nine-axis motion sensor, a magnetometer, a small microcontroller, a Bluetooth radio, a lithium-polymer cell and a Qi charging coil. The ball does its own work. It recognises dribbles and shots on board and sends finished numbers to the phone: shot arc, backspin, release time, dribble counts, streaks and dribble force. The vendor's app was a display and coaching shell around those numbers.

InfoMotion Sports Technologies filed for Chapter 11. The website, the account service and the app are gone. The only build that survives is version 1.4 of the Android app (December 2014), from a third-party mirror. None of the ball's function depends on the dead server. Drills, metrics, the ball's clock and firmware update all run over the local Bluetooth link.

The Android app finds the ball with a short BLE scan for a vendor service UUID. It then talks to it over Bluetooth Classic: an insecure RFCOMM socket to a vendor SDP record, opened to the address the scan returned. There is no GATT in the Android path. The protocol is a small binary request/reply protocol with HDLC-style 0x7e framing, a CRC-32 on every packet, and unsolicited records streamed during a drill.

Everything here comes from static analysis of that Android app, whose protocol layer is unobfuscated, plus the user guide and test report filed with the FCC grant. No ball has been driven from this spec and no traffic has been captured, so every byte is reported. One HCI snoop session would confirm most of it; see Capturing a session.

Scope: both hardware revisions (hw1, hw2) speaking protocol v1, as the Android app v1.4 drives them. Not covered: the SmartNet instrumented net and the shooting-machine integration (the only trace of either in the protocol is a SmartNet-detected flag in shot records), the dead cloud service, firmware image contents, and the factory and FCC test modes, which are named but not specified.

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/94fifty-basketball.yaml. Where this page and the spec disagree, the spec wins.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model 94Fifty Smart Sensor Basketball; FCC test model TBBX001 Hardware revisions hw1 and hw2, reported in the system-info reply. The app treats them as protocol-identical; the revision only selects the firmware image. Sensors The app's hardware self-test checks an InvenSense MPU-9150 nine-axis IMU and a Honeywell HMC5983 magnetometer. Launch press quoted nine sensors and 6,000 data points per second in total. MCU Unknown part. The bundled firmware images are not Cortex-M; their layout points to a 16-bit MCU. Radio controller (hypothesis) The ball's radio test-mode requests use the same modulation, test-pattern and ACL packet-type values as TI's CC256x vendor-specific tester commands. With the 16-bit host images, that suggests a CC256x-class dual-mode controller beside a separate host MCU. This has not been seen on a board. Radio Dual-mode Bluetooth 4.0. Launch-era coverage names a Texas Instruments part; the FCC photo markings are illegible. BLE advertising (used only to find the ball) plus BR/EDR RFCOMM (all control). The app assumes one address for both. Power 3.7 V 240 mAh lithium-polymer cell; Qi charging pad (about 3 h from empty) Range Earlier research notes say about 30 m. No primary source was found for that figure; the FCC report gives 1.38 mW conducted into a -0.5 dBi chip antenna. FCC ID 2AARZ-TBBX001 (DTS, 2402-2480 MHz, granted 2013-09-30). The grantee holds no other grant, so the SmartNet and the charging pad are not filed under this code. Vendor app 94Fifty Basketball, Android package com.spectrumdt.ist, last version 1.4. An iOS app existed and was not examined. Firmware The Android app bundles hw1 OEM 0.73, hw2 OEM 0.130 and hw2 manufacture 0.106 as its newest images

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method none. Activate once on the pad, wake by bouncing, scan, open the socket. Advertised name Classic inquiry name starts IST-. What the ball advertises over BLE is not recorded; the app matches its BLE service UUID instead. Passphrase protection not_applicable (no network, no credentials) Confidence medium (activation and wake from the user guide, the connect sequence from the app's code; none of it run)

A client's first contact is the same as the vendor app's:

  1. First use only: activate the ball. Balls ship in Travel Mode, a locked state with the radio off. Plug in the Qi pad (its blue light blinks once), then set the ball on it with the ball logo over the pad logo. The light turns solid blue when activation is done.
  2. Wake it. Bounce the ball four or more times in a row. It sleeps again after a period of inactivity. How long it stays connectable without a connection is not established.
  3. Scan BLE for an advertisement that carries the 128-bit service UUID b69bc590-59d9-4920-9552-defcc31651fe, and keep the address. The vendor app scans in 5 s windows. A host that cannot scan BLE can use a Classic inquiry instead and keep devices whose name starts IST-.
  4. Open an insecure RFCOMM socket to the SDP service 32e5fcfc-52ee-41b0-827a-f18929716fef at that address. The app tries twice, 250 ms apart. The RFCOMM channel number is resolved through SDP and is not recorded.
  5. Send system info and wait up to 5 s for the reply (type 0x8001). The app sends nothing else until this arrives. There is no login, no key exchange and no clock sync.

On Linux the same steps are sdptool browse aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff to find the channel, then rfcomm connect 0 aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff <channel> or a raw AF_BLUETOOTH RFCOMM socket.

Factory reset: none is known, and none is needed to change hands. The user guide documents no reset, and the app sends no reset-to-defaults command. Power-control mode 1 is a reboot, not a reset. The ball holds no bond and no credential. Its clock, stored name and any stored records are overwritten or ignored by the next client.

Rebinding: nothing to rebind. A new phone wakes the ball, scans and connects. The vendor app kept renames and history in its own storage and its cloud, not on the ball.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none (insecure RFCOMM socket) Bonding none PIN source n/a One central at a time Unknown (the app keeps one socket; whether the ball takes a second is untested) One bond at a time n/a: nothing bonds Confidence medium (static analysis of the vendor app)

Entering pairing mode: there is no pairing mode, but there is a wake step, and the spec records it under device.pairing.enter_pairing_mode because it gates everything the same way. Bounce the ball four or more times in a row. A ball in Travel Mode will not wake this way; it needs a few seconds on the charging pad first.

Unpairing: nothing to unpair. No bond is created on either side.

Recovery: close the vendor app, or turn off Bluetooth on the phone running it, before connecting from anything else. Before switching to a new ball the vendor app sends the old one power-control "disconnect", so a client taking over from it can do the same. Do not open a secure socket. That makes the host start a pairing, and nobody knows whether the ball would complete it or what PIN it would want.

The app's diagnostic connection test has a switch between secure and insecure sockets, so its developers tried both. The shipped connect path uses the insecure one.

docs.title: Bluetooth Classic profiles
docs.text: Property Value Control profile Vendor RFCOMM service, SDP UUID 32e5fcfc-52ee-41b0-827a-f18929716fef (not SPP) Socket insecure (no bond) Dual-mode Yes. BLE advertises service b69bc590-59d9-4920-9552-defcc31651fe; the Android app uses BLE only to find the ball. ble_role is unknown because the iOS app may have used GATT. Same address for both assumed, not confirmed. iOS reachable Not over this spec: CoreBluetooth has no RFCOMM, and nothing suggests MFi. The user guide lists iOS devices "that support Bluetooth 4.0", which points to a GATT surface the iOS app used and nobody has recorded. Stream binary, 0x7e-delimited frames with byte stuffing and a CRC-32; frames up to 2048 bytes

docs.title: Frame format
docs.text:
wire      7e | packet, with 7d and 7e escaped | 7e
request   type u16 | token u16 | payload           | crc32 u32
reply     type u16 | token u16 | error u16 | payload | crc32 u32
  • Escaping: a packet byte 0x7d or 0x7e is sent as 0x7d followed by the byte XOR 0x20, so 7d becomes 7d 5d and 7e becomes 7d 5e. No other byte is escaped. Everything below, offsets included, is about the de-stuffed packet with the flags removed. Offset 0 is the high byte of the type.
  • Byte order: big-endian throughout.
  • Length: every packet, CRC included, is a multiple of 4 bytes and at least 8. A request payload is therefore a multiple of 4 and a reply payload is 2 more than a multiple of 4. That is why most replies have 2 zero bytes of padding at offset 6. A reply with a non-zero error carries a 2-byte zero payload, 12 bytes in all.
  • Replies: the reply type is the request type with bit 15 set (0x0005 → 0x8005), and the reply echoes the request's token.
  • Tokens: the requester picks the token. Token 0 marks an unsolicited frame (live records, stream data). The app uses 1 for its opening system info and otherwise the low 15 bits of the clock in ms, never 0.
  • CRC: CRC-32/BZIP2 over every packet byte before it, computed before stuffing and appended big-endian. Parameters: polynomial 0x04c11db7, init 0xffffffff, not reflected in or out, final XOR 0xffffffff, check value 0xfc891918 for ASCII 123456789. This is not the zlib/Ethernet CRC-32 (which gives 0xcbf43926 on the same string); a client that reaches for zlib.crc32 gets every frame rejected.
  • Receiving: split on 0x7e, undo the escapes, drop empty frames. Drop a frame on 7d 7d or 7d 7e, on more than 2048 buffered bytes, on a length under 8 or not a multiple of 4, or on a CRC mismatch. The app drops unknown types silently.

A quick check of an implementation, using the spec's test vectors:

Frame Meaning 7e 00 01 00 01 3d e2 93 b4 7e system info, token 1 7e 00 05 00 7d 5e e2 7b 81 f2 7e status with token 0x007e: the token's 7e is escaped 7e 00 05 00 0b 15 0a f7 7d 5e 7e status with token 0x000b: the CRC's last byte 7e is escaped 7e 80 05 00 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 0f 3c 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 1c 5e 47 2d 7e status reply: idle, 3900 mV

docs.title: Opcodes
docs.text:
Starts are 0x01xx, ends 0x02xx, stored-record fetches 0x03xx, test modes 0x04xx, data frames 0x83xx. Replies are request | 0x8000.

Request Reply Name In the spec 0x0001 0x8001 system info get_system_info 0x0002 0x8002 firmware segment advanced, role only 0x0003 0x8003 firmware finalize advanced, role only 0x0004 0x8004 power control: mode u16, delay u16 ms power_off, power_reset, power_disconnect, power_travel_mode, power_disable_bluetooth 0x0005 0x8005 status get_status 0x0006 / 0x0007 0x8006 / 0x8007 get / set clock get_rtc; setting is parameterised 0x0008 0x8008 abort activity or stream abort_activity 0x0009 / 0x000a 0x8009 / 0x800a bandwidth test start / end advanced, role only 0x000b / 0x000c 0x800b / 0x800c get / set ball name get_ball_name; setting is parameterised 0x000d 0x800d hardware self-test get_hardware_diag 0x0055 0x8055 echo (dummy payload) named only 0x0101 / 0x0201 0x8101 / 0x8201 raw sensor stream start / end, data 0x8301 diagnostic 0x0102 / 0x0202 0x8102 / 0x8202 orientation stream start / end, data 0x8302 diagnostic 0x0120 / 0x0220 0x8120 / 0x8220 dribbling activity start / end, records 0x8320 start_dribbling_drill, end_dribbling_activity 0x0121 / 0x0221 0x8121 / 0x8221 shooting activity start / end, records 0x8321 start_shooting_drill_pass, start_shooting_drill_solo, end_shooting_activity 0x0320 / 0x0321 0x8320 / 0x8321 fetch a stored dribbling / shooting record parameterised 0x0401-0x0406 0x8401-0x8406 factory and FCC test modes advanced, named only — 0x8080 bandwidth-test data advanced

Earlier notes on this ball listed decimal 512 as the raw-stream start. There is no opcode 0x0200: raw stream starts at 0x0101 (257) and ends at 0x0201 (513).

The echo opcode 0x0055 is defined by the app's protocol library but never sent, and nothing in the app uses it as a keepalive. The keepalive the app actually uses is a status request every 3 s, and only on its diagnostic raw-stream and bandwidth-test screens.

docs.title: Fixed commands
docs.text:
Each is a complete frame with token 0x0001, flags and CRC included, so it can be written to the socket as-is:

Command Frame get_system_info 7e 00 01 00 01 3d e2 93 b4 7e get_status 7e 00 05 00 01 3a 80 21 a8 7e get_rtc 7e 00 06 00 01 38 e9 d4 21 7e get_ball_name 7e 00 0b 00 01 30 96 ae 82 7e get_hardware_diag 7e 00 0d 00 01 34 45 45 90 7e (reply can take several seconds; the app waits 15 s) abort_activity 7e 00 08 00 01 32 ff 5b 0b 7e end_dribbling_activity 7e 02 20 00 01 bb 35 87 0a 7e end_shooting_activity 7e 02 21 00 01 ba ed 2b 8d 7e power_off 7e 00 04 00 01 00 00 00 00 e6 6a 9e d8 7e power_reset 7e 00 04 00 01 00 01 00 00 e7 b2 32 5f 7e power_disconnect 7e 00 04 00 01 00 03 00 00 e4 03 6b 51 7e power_travel_mode (advanced) 7e 00 04 00 01 00 02 00 00 e5 db c7 d6 7e power_disable_bluetooth (advanced) 7e 00 04 00 01 00 04 00 00 e1 08 2c c4 7e

Power-control modes: 0 off (sleeps until bounced), 1 reboot, 2 Travel Mode (radio off and locked until the ball sits on its pad), 3 drop the link and stay awake, 4 Bluetooth off. Travel Mode is advanced because a ball without its pad stays unusable. Bluetooth-off is advanced because only the factory validator uses it and nobody knows how the ball comes back from it. The app never waits for the 0x8004 reply. Whether it arrives before the link drops is unknown.

The three drill starts are in the spec as fixed frames: start_dribbling_drill and the two shooting starts (see below).

docs.title: Requests that take a value
docs.text:
These need a CRC computed over caller data, which the schema's command encoder cannot express yet. The spec documents them byte by byte, with worked frames, under protocol_details.parameterised_requests:

Request Packet (de-stuffed) Worked frame (token 0x1234) set clock 0x0007 00 07 token, UTC seconds u32, CRC (12 bytes) 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z: 7e 00 07 12 34 69 55 b9 00 c7 85 c9 90 7e set ball name 0x000c 00 0c token, name 48 bytes UTF-8 NUL-padded, CRC (56 bytes) "Court 1": 7e 00 0c 12 34 43 6f 75 72 74 20 31 + 41 × 00 + c8 e1 b3 73 7e fetch stored record 0x0320 / 0x0321 type, token, activity id u32, record id u16, 00 00, CRC (16 bytes) shooting record 0 of activity 1: 7e 03 21 12 34 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 00 c8 7b e0 2d 7e start activity 0x0120 / 0x0121 see Starting an activity —

The Android app never sends set ball name, the stored-record fetches or the echo. Its rename feature changes only its own record and its cloud copy, and allows 1-20 ASCII characters. Whether the ball keeps records after an activity ends, or across a power cycle, is not established.

docs.title: Starting an activity
docs.text:
The common start payload is 20 bytes, all big-endian:

Offset Length Field Notes 4 4 user id always 0 from the app 8 4 start time always 0 from the app 12 2 padding 00 00 14 2 notify method bit 0: the limit counts events (1) or ms (0). Bit 1: a record every N events (1) or every N ms (0). 16 4 activity limit ms or events, minimum 100 ms or 1 event 20 4 notify interval ms or events, minimum 100 ms or 1 event

Dribbling (0x0120) adds DSP algorithm u16 (0) and dribble window u16 (5): a 32-byte packet. Shooting (0x0121) adds player height u16 in inches, shot distance u16 in inches, shooting algorithm u16 and 2 bytes of padding: a 36-byte packet. The app sends the player's height, or 70 in when it is unknown. Its distances are 165 (free throw), 180 (15 ft), 216 (18 ft), 240 (20 ft) and 276 (23 ft). Algorithm 1 is for a shot taken off a chest pass and 2 is solo. The protocol library also names them "with magnetometer" and "without magnetometer". Values 3 and up are debug values.

The app's presets, which the spec carries as fixed frames:

Command Settings start_dribbling_drill time limit and time trigger, 600 000 ms, a record every 200 ms, algorithm 0, window 5 start_shooting_drill_pass event limit and event trigger, 20 shots, a record every shot, 70 in, 180 in, algorithm 1 start_shooting_drill_solo as above with algorithm 2

The start reply (0x8120 / 0x8121) carries an error and then, at offset 8, the activity id (u32), which every record repeats. Start errors the app handles: 2 system busy, 8 low battery, 9 invalid state. The end reply (0x8220 / 0x8221) carries the highest record id at offset 6.

For a shot to register, the user guide says it must follow a chest pass to the shooter. For a solo shot, spin the ball into the air, catch it and shoot without letting it bounce.

docs.title: Live records
docs.text:
During an activity the ball sends one record per notify interval with token 0. The last one has is_last set, and the app ends the activity on it without using its metrics. The app de-duplicates on the record id.

Shooting record 0x8321 (64 bytes):

Offset Length Field Type Scaling 6 2 is_last u16 non-zero: activity over 8 4 activity id u32 from the start reply 12 2 record id u16 shot number 16 / 20 / 24 4 each samples to first shot / last shot / buffer end u32 sample rate unknown 28 2 shot made i16 negative missed, 0 undetermined, positive made 32 / 36 4 each samples to release / to rim u32 40 2 release time u16 ms; the app grades 850 ms or less as quick 42 2 average release time u16 ms 44 2 shot arc u16 binary angle: degrees = raw × 360 / 65536 (0x2000 is 45°) 46 2 average shot arc u16 as above 48 2 shot spin i16 the app shows raw / 24.6 as rpm; sign convention unknown 50 2 average shot spin i16 as above 52 2 launch height u16 unit unknown 54 2 SmartNet detected u16 non-zero: true 56 2 shot distance u16 unit unknown, probably inches

Bytes 14-15, 30-31 and 58-59 are padding; 60-63 are the CRC. Without the SmartNet accessory, most shots are expected to read "undetermined".

Dribbling record 0x8320 (56 bytes):

Offset Length Field Type Scaling 6 2 is_last u16 non-zero: activity over 8 4 activity id u32 12 2 record id u16 16 / 20 / 24 4 each samples to first dribble / last dribble / buffer end u32 28 4 samples in control u32 feeds the app's control percentage 32 4 total dribbles u32 tenths: the app shows raw / 10 36 2 best streak u16 tenths 38 2 current streak u16 tenths 40 2 average streak u16 probably tenths; the app prints it raw 42 2 average dribble speed u16 unit unknown 44 2 dribble intensity (moving average) u16 the app shows raw / 1024 as G 46 2 dribble intensity (activity average) u16 as above 48 2 streak restart count u16 increments when a streak breaks

Bytes 14-15 and 50-51 are padding; 52-55 are the CRC. The app's ball-control percentage formula is in protocol_details.control_percentage.

docs.title: Status and system info
docs.text:
Status reply 0x8005 (24 bytes): offset 8 and 9 each hold an activity code (0 idle, 1 raw stream, 2 orientation stream, 3 bandwidth test, 32 dribbling, 33 shooting). The app treats the byte at offset 9 as the current activity. Battery voltage is a u16 at offset 10 in mV. Offsets 12 and 16 are u32 link byte counters the app ignores. The app's battery gauge maps voltage to a percentage through a piecewise curve, given in protocol_details.battery_percentage. Its battery icon turns yellow at 30 % and red at 15 %.

System info reply 0x8001 (28 bytes):

Offset Length Field Notes 8 2 release type 1 OEM, 2 Debug, 3 Manufacture 10 / 12 / 14 2 each protocol / bootloader / firmware version high byte major, low byte minor: 00 82 is 0.130 16 4 hardware revision u32: 1 hw1, 2 hw2 20 4 serial number u32; the app prints it in decimal

An older 24-byte form (protocol revision 3 and below) has no release type: the versions sit at 6, 8 and 10, the hardware revision at 12, the serial at 16. Tell the two apart by length.

Hardware self-test reply 0x800d (12 bytes): a u16 at offset 6 with a bit set per failed check: 0x01 bounce, 0x02 IMU bus, 0x04 IMU self-test, 0x08 magnetometer, 0x10 power-off check. 0 means all passed. 0x7fff is the app's own "diagnostics unavailable" value. The app substitutes it when no reply arrives and shows a reply carrying it the same way. Whether a ball ever sends it is unknown. Read the whole word before testing bits, so that 0x7fff is never taken as five failures. Only the app's device-validator screens run the self-test.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 no error 1 unknown packet type 2 system busy (retry) 3 in progress (the firmware updater treats it as success) 4 firmware segment out of sequence 5 firmware image corrupted 6 invalid packet size 7 invalid packet field 8 low battery 9 invalid state 10 invalid activity id 11 invalid record id 12 activity not running 13 scoring engine failed 14 out of resources 65535 unspecified failure (the app maps any unlisted value here)

docs.title: Diagnostic streams
docs.text: The raw sensor stream (0x0101, data 0x8301, 1344-byte frames carrying 1324 sample bytes) and the orientation stream (0x0102, data 0x8302, 28-byte frames carrying 8 bytes) exist for the app's diagnostic screens. The app treats the data as opaque and writes it to a file, so neither layout is known. The end replies carry a notification count at offset 6.

docs.title: Firmware update
docs.text:
The ball takes new firmware over the same RFCOMM link, from the running firmware, with no separate bootloader entry. The spec gives the exchange's role only and marks both opcodes advanced. It gives no flashing bytes.

  • A firmware-segment request (0x0002) carries a sequence number counting from 0, a length and up to 1012 image bytes. The ball answers 0x8002. "System busy" means send the same segment again after 50 ms. The app allows 2 s per reply.
  • A firmware-finalize request (0x0003) commits the image. Then the app reboots the ball with power-control mode 1.
  • The images are raw binaries of about 150-250 kB, one per hardware revision and release type, bundled in the app. The ball has an "image corrupted" error, so it checks something. Whether that is a signature is not known, and nor is what an interrupted update leaves behind.

docs.title: Factory and FCC test modes
docs.text: Opcodes 0x0401-0x0406 put the radio into certification and production test modes: an FCC test mode (modulation, pattern, channel, power), an RF signalling test, a set-maximum-output-power command, an FCC TX/RX mode, and BLE directed and undirected advertising tests. The bandwidth test (0x0009, 0x000a, data 0x8080) floods the link. The spec names these as advanced and gives no payloads. They leave normal operation, may transmit outside the grant, and nothing documents the way back.

docs.title: Why a 94Fifty might misbehave
docs.text: Findings from the vendor app and user guide. None has been reproduced on a ball.

docs.title: 1. It won't show up after bouncing
docs.text: The user guide gives three causes, in this order. The battery is flat: charge it on the pad for at least an hour. The ball is in Travel Mode: a few seconds on the pad releases it. It hasn't woken yet: keep bouncing until it connects. A client should also allow for the ball's sleep timer. The ball sleeps after inactivity, and nobody has measured how long it stays connectable.

docs.title: 2. It has to be bounced again after every session
docs.text: When the vendor app disconnects it sends power-control off, not "disconnect", so the ball goes to sleep. A client that wants the ball to stay awake for the next connection should send power_disconnect (mode 3) instead, or just close the socket.

docs.title: 3. The vendor app reflashes the ball without asking, downgrades included
docs.text:
By default the Android app compares the ball's firmware with the one OEM image it bundles for that hardware revision (hw1 0.73, hw2 0.130). If the two differ in either direction, it goes straight from its ball-connection screen into flashing, with no prompt. A ball running newer firmware than the app's image (for example one updated by a later iOS build) is downgraded the first time the Android app v1.4 connects to it. A ball whose firmware major version is 72 is exempt. If you care about the firmware on your ball, check its version with get_system_info from your own client first. Don't connect the old app to a ball whose firmware you have not recorded.

The policy can be switched off. Type diag in the sign-in email field to open the diagnostic screen, then open its settings page. It has a firmware validation mode selector with four choices: fixed version (the default described above), upgrade only, downgrade only and disabled. Choose disabled, or upgrade only, before the app connects to the ball. The release build exposes this selector, and nothing on this path needs an account.

docs.title: 4. The app won't sign in
docs.text:
Accounts lived on the dead server. The login screen has a guest path ("Just Visiting" in the user guide) that runs drills entirely offline, and typing diag in the sign-in email field opens the app's diagnostic screen without an account. The app targets Android 4-era APIs, and nobody has confirmed it still runs on a current phone.

The app has four device-validator screens. They are production-line tests (battery, streams, a short dribbling activity, the hardware self-test, firmware and the power modes), not an authenticity check, and they never run in the consumer flow. They open only from the diagnostic screen's test list, or at launch if the diagnostic settings put the app in factory mode. Leave that mode alone. Nothing in normal use depends on them.

docs.title: 5. A ball name set in the app doesn't follow the ball
docs.text: The Android app never writes the name to the ball. It keeps the name in its own storage and its cloud record, which is now gone. The ball has a 48-byte name slot (get_ball_name / set ball name) that the Android app never touches, so it holds whatever an iOS or factory tool last wrote, possibly nothing.

docs.title: 6. An iPhone can't reach it with this spec
docs.text: CoreBluetooth has no RFCOMM API. The vendor's iOS app almost certainly used a BLE GATT surface on the same ball, and nobody has recorded that GATT table. Until someone does, an iPhone can find the ball but cannot drive it.

docs.title: 7. The FCC grant covers only the LE radio
docs.text: The grant is DTS only, and the report lists 40 channels 2 MHz apart, the LE channel plan. Yet the Android app can only have reached the ball over BR/EDR, because RFCOMM does not run over LE. The app's own radio test modes include BR/EDR modulations, frequency hopping and ACL packet types up to 3-DH5, so the radio can do BR/EDR whatever the filing says. An inquiry scan or an HCI snoop log would settle it in minutes. Until then, the BR/EDR side rests entirely on the app's code.

docs.title: Capturing a session
docs.text: The cheapest confirmation is Android's Bluetooth HCI snoop log (Developer options) while the vendor app connects to a ball, runs one dribbling drill and one shooting drill, and disconnects. In Wireshark the btrfcomm filter shows the payloads in the clear. One such session confirms the SDP record, the framing, the CRC, the handshake and both record layouts, and gives the BLE advertised name and whether the BR/EDR and BLE addresses match. Keep your own ball's address and serial number out of anything you commit.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
How a factory-fresh device is provisioned, and how confident we are in it. See Initial Device Setup for the patterns, and mirror this into device.setup in the machine-readable spec.

Property Value Setup required Yes / No (most BLE devices: No) Method softap_http / softap_soap / ble_provisioning / ble_direct / bt_classic_pairing / wired / device_ui / button_pairing / cloud_account Setup AP / advertised name e.g. Wemo.*, Vector-XXXX Passphrase protection plaintext / device_encrypted / tls / not_applicable Confidence high (ran it) / medium (public source) / low (inferred)

Factory reset: which button, held how long, in what power state, and the LED or screen signal that confirms it. Note what the reset clears and what survives. Mirror it into device.setup.factory_reset.procedures in the machine-readable spec, and mark a procedure you have not run verified: false with a basis saying where it came from.

Rebinding to a new network: in place, remotely triggered, or physical reset only. If the old network has to still be up, say so — that changes what a user must do before replacing a router.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Whether a client has to pair or bond before the control surface answers — a different question from provisioning, and the one that decides whether a "connect and go" implementation works. See Pairing, Bonding and Unpairing, and mirror this into device.pairing. Required on every device spec; "nothing pairs" is the common BLE answer and worth stating. On Wi-Fi/LAN, describe how a client is authorised by the device — link button, on-screen PIN, a key fetched from the vendor cloud, an admin login — or say the API is open and the network is the only gate.

Property Value Pairing required Yes / No / Unknown Security mode none / just_works / passkey_entry / numeric_comparison / out_of_band / legacy_pin / network_join / app_layer Bonding none / optional / required (does the device store it?) PIN source fixed_default / printed_label / device_screen / vendor_app / derived / user_chosen One central at a time Yes / No / Unknown One bond at a time Yes / No / Unknown — a new client replaces the old Confidence high (ran it) / medium (public source) / low (inferred)

Entering pairing mode: the button and how long, the signal that says the device is now pairable, and how long the window stays open. If the device is always pairable, say so.

Unpairing: how to drop a bond without a factory reset, or state plainly that there is no such route — that answer tells a user what adopting a second-hand unit will cost them.

Recovery: what a user must do when something else is holding the device — close the vendor app, forget it in the OS Bluetooth settings, power-cycle it.
