docs.title: Anker soundcore Earbuds, Headphones and Speakers
docs.text: Status: Spec Available Protocol: Bluetooth Classic, RFCOMM to a per-model vendor UUID or SPP (BLE for discovery; a GATT tunnel on some models) Manufacturer: Anker Innovations Limited (soundcore brand) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Anker's soundcore range covers true-wireless earbuds (Liberty, Life, Space), over-ear headphones (Life Q, Space Q) and portable speakers (Motion and others). The soundcore app changes settings the hardware keeps itself: noise cancelling, transparency or normal mode, the equaliser, button mapping, auto power-off, voice prompts and firmware. Audio is ordinary A2DP and HFP and needs no app at all.

The reason to document it anyway is the app. Recent versions ask for an account, show full-screen advertising before the device screen and bundle an AI assistant, and store reviews say so at length. The device needs none of that. Its control channel is an unauthenticated RFCOMM socket speaking a small framed binary protocol, which two open-source clients already implement: OpenSCQ30 and SoundcoreManager.

The protocol is a family keyed by the SKU (A3947, A3116, ...), not one command set. The frame is shared, but command IDs mean different things on different models, and the state reply has a different layout on each. This page and the spec describe the shared frame, a table mapping 60-odd SKUs to their control channel, and three models in full:

Model Evidence Liberty 4 NC (A3947), earbuds Public HCI capture of the vendor app (SoundcoreManager #162): frames, checksums and SDP records confirmed Motion+ (A3116), speaker Public HCI capture of the vendor app (OpenSCQ30 #215): frames, the missing checksum and SDP records confirmed Life Q30 / Life Tune (A3028 / A3029), headphones OpenSCQ30 and SoundcoreManager only: reported

For any other model, take its command set from OpenSCQ30's per-model module (lib/src/devices/soundcore/<sku>.rs) before sending it anything.

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/anker-soundcore.yaml. Where this page and the spec disagree, the spec wins.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Liberty 4 NC Motion+ Life Q30 / Life Tune SKU A3947 A3116 A3028 / A3029 Type True-wireless earbuds, adaptive ANC, LDAC, charging case with a button 30 W portable speaker, aptX, AUX in, TWS pairing with a second Motion+ Over-ear ANC headphones, NFC pairing FCC ID 2AOKB-A3947 (granted 2023-03-28) 2AOKB-A3116 2AOKB-A3028 (granted 2020-08-12; both models) Chipset Bestechnic (BES), going by its SDP records TOTA and BESOTA Qualcomm/CSR, going by its SDP record CSR GAIA and aptX support Unknown Classic name soundcore Liberty 4 NC (captured) Soundcore Motion+ (manual) Soundcore Life Q30 / Soundcore Life Tune Control channel vendor UUID 0cf12d31-fac3-4553-bd80-d6832e7b3947, channel 15 in the capture vendor UUID 0cf12d31-fac3-4553-bd80-d6832e7b3116, channel 1 in the capture SPP 00001101-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb (vendor app's table) Checksum byte yes no yes Captured firmware 04.88 (both buds) 80.01 n/a Observed OUI E8:EE:CC (Fantasia Trading LLC, Anker's US company) 7C:96:D2 (Fihonest Communication) n/a

The grantee on all three FCC IDs is Anker Innovations Limited (grantee code 2AOKB), 2402-2480 MHz. One unit each was seen, so the OUIs are weak signals. The A3947's BLE advertisements come from a random address with no OUI at all.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes: ordinary Bluetooth pairing from the host's settings Method bt_classic_pairing Advertised name soundcore … (current products) / Soundcore … (older) Passphrase protection not_applicable (no network, no credentials) Confidence medium (FCC-filed manuals; pairing not observed in the captures)

The vendor app provisions nothing. It lists bonded devices, recognises the model, and opens the control socket. Its account is for the vendor cloud, which the device never contacts. A client does the same:

  1. Pair the device from the phone or computer's Bluetooth settings (see Pairing for each model's button).
  2. Browse SDP and pick the control record. Take the vendor UUID 0cf12d31-fac3-4553-bd80-d6832e7b<sku> if it is there; otherwise take SPP 00001101-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb. This is OpenSCQ30's rule, and it matters: on a Liberty 4 NC the record with the SPP class is Bestechnic's test service TOTA (channel 12), not the control channel.
  3. Open an insecure RFCOMM socket to it. The vendor Android app always uses the insecure constructor; the link is already bonded for audio.
  4. Send the model's state request and read the reply by its length field.

There is no handshake and no authentication in either capture.

Factory reset

Model Procedure Source Liberty 4 NC (A3947) Earbuds in the case, lid open. Hold the case button all the way down for 10 s until the LEDs flash white rapidly three times. Quick guide, FCC exhibit, panel 13 Life Q30 / Life Tune (A3028 / A3029) Hold power + volume up together for 5 s. Manuals, FCC exhibits Motion+ (A3116) None documented. The manual only says to remove the speaker from the phone's Bluetooth list and pair again. Vendor manual (2020-11)

None of these has been tried by this project, and the manuals do not say what a reset clears.

Rebinding to a new phone: pair it like any other host. The earbuds and headphones remember more than one host. The Motion+ reconnects to the last host at power-on and re-enters pairing mode from its Bluetooth button. Nothing in the control protocol is tied to a phone or an account.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required Yes (it is an audio device; both open clients list only bonded devices) Security mode just_works (inferred: no display or keypad; not observed) Bonding required PIN source none One central at a time Unknown for the control channel; the vendor app held it for its whole session in both captures One bond at a time No: dual connection / dual pairing in the manuals Confidence medium

Entering pairing mode (from the manuals, not tried):

  • Liberty 4 NC (A3947): opening the case the first time powers the buds on and makes them pairable. Manually: buds in the case, lid open, hold the case button for 3 s until the LEDs flash white rapidly. To add a second host, wear both buds and hold both touchpads for 3 s at the same time.
  • Life Q30 / Life Tune (A3028 / A3029): from off, hold power for 5 s until the LED flashes blue. After the first host connects, press power twice to pair a second. Android phones can also tap the right ear cup (NFC).
  • Motion+ (A3116): at power-on it reconnects to the last host or becomes pairable. Press the Bluetooth button to re-enter pairing mode; the indicator fades blue in and out while pairable and is solid blue once connected.

Unpairing: no button or command removes one host from the device's list. Forget the device on the host. The factory reset presumably clears the device side too, but the manuals do not say so.

Recovery: close the vendor app, or turn off Bluetooth on its phone, before connecting from another client. If the device will not show up, remove it from the host's Bluetooth list and pair again.

docs.title: Bluetooth Classic profiles
docs.text:
Property Value Control profile vendor RFCOMM UUID 0cf12d31-fac3-4553-bd80-d6832e7b<sku> on most models; SPP 00001101-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb on older earbuds and headphones Socket insecure (the vendor app never opens a secure one); the link is bonded for audio anyway Dual-mode Yes. BLE role: secondary control on some models (SoundcoreManager's GATT tunnel), discovery elsewhere iOS reachable Not over RFCOMM (CoreBluetooth has none). The vendor iOS app probably uses the BLE GATT tunnel; not examined

SDP records seen in the captures:

Record A3947 A3116 Role vendor 0cf12d31-fac3-4553-bd80-d6832e7b<sku> "Spp1", channel 15 "CSR GAIA", channel 1 Control: every soundcore frame SPP 00001101-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb "TOTA", channel 12 none BES test service. Not the control channel 66666666-6666-6666-6666-666666666666 "BESOTA", channel 13 none BES firmware update (out of scope) df21fe2c-2515-4fdb-8886-f12c4d67927c "RFCOMM COM", channel 17 none Google Fast Pair Message Stream (opened by Android, not the app) HFP / HSP channels 3 / 1 channels 12 / 11 Telephony A2DP sink, AVRCP L2CAP 25, 23 L2CAP 25, 23 Audio

The Motion+ has no record with the SPP class, so a client that opens "the serial port" by 00001101-… finds nothing on it. Its control record is named "CSR GAIA" (the slot a Qualcomm/CSR SoC reserves for its GAIA protocol) but carries soundcore frames, not GAIA.

docs.title: Frame format
docs.text:
phone -> device:  08 ee 00 00 00 | c1 c2 | len_lo len_hi | payload... | [sum]
device -> phone:  09 ff 00 00 01 | c1 c2 | len_lo len_hi | payload... | [sum]
Field Offset Size Notes Direction 0 5 08 ee 00 00 00 out, 09 ff 00 00 01 in Command 5 2 A reply repeats the command it answers Length 7 2 u16 little-endian, counts the whole frame, header to last byte Payload 9 len − 9 (− 1) Per command, per model Checksum last 1 Sum of every preceding byte mod 256. Absent on the Motion+ (A3116).

Split the stream by the length field; that works with or without a checksum. A set is acknowledged with an empty-payload frame carrying the same command. The vendor app sent one frame at a time and waited for its answer.

Worked examples, all captured:

08 ee 00 00 00 01 01 0a 00 02            A3947 state request: 08+ee+01+01+0a = 0x102 -> 02
09 ff 00 00 01 06 81 0a 00 9a            A3947 acknowledgement of a sound-mode set
08 ee 00 00 00 01 01 09 00               A3116 state request: 9 bytes, no checksum
09 ff 00 00 01 01 10 0a 00 01            A3116 voice-prompt reply (on): payload 01, no checksum

OpenSCQ30 treats the checksum as a per-model setting, and the Motion+ is the only model it knows of without one. A client meeting an unknown model can check the first reply: if its last byte is the sum of the others, the model uses checksums.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Liberty 4 NC (A3947), checksummed:

Command Frame Reply Status State 08 ee 00 00 00 01 01 0a 00 02 09 ff 00 00 01 01 01, 169 bytes on firmware 04.88 confirmed LDAC query 08 ee 00 00 00 01 7f 0a 00 80 … 01 7f 0b 00 <ldac> <sum> confirmed exchange; meaning from OpenSCQ30 Sound modes 08 ee 00 00 00 06 81 11 00 + 7 bytes + sum empty ack confirmed

The seven sound-mode bytes are, in order: ambient mode (0 noise cancelling, 1 transparency, 2 normal); ANC strengths (high nibble manual 0-5, low nibble adaptive 0-5); transparency (0 full, 1 vocal); NC mode (0 manual, 1 adaptive, 2 transportation); wind noise (bit 0 suppression); environment detection (0/1); transportation type (0 plane, 1 train, 2 bus, 3 car). The same seven bytes sit at offsets 135-141 of the state reply. To change one, read the state and send the other six back unchanged, as the vendor app did:

08 ee 00 00 00 06 81 11 00 02 50 00 01 00 00 00 e1   normal       (captured)
08 ee 00 00 00 06 81 11 00 01 50 00 01 00 00 00 e0   transparency (captured)
08 ee 00 00 00 06 81 11 00 00 50 00 01 00 00 00 df   noise cancel (captured)

State reply fields (offsets from the first byte of the frame): 9 host earbud, 10 buds linked, 11-12 battery left/right (0-5 steps, not percent), 13-14 charging left/right, 15-19 and 20-24 firmware left/right (ASCII NN.NN), 25-40 serial number (ASCII), 46-47 EQ preset (u16 LE), 48-67 EQ bands, 135-141 sound modes, 148 case battery (0-5), 163-164 auto power-off. The offsets past the serial number come from OpenSCQ30's A3947 parser, and every one decoded sensibly on the captured frame. The case battery read 2 while the same unit's Fast Pair report said 40 %.

Motion+ (A3116), no checksum:

Command Frame Reply Status State 08 ee 00 00 00 01 01 09 00 45 bytes: 9 charging, 10 battery (0-5), 11 volume (0-16), 13 auto-off, 14-18 firmware, 19-34 serial, 35 EQ preset, 36-44 EQ bands confirmed Voice prompt? 08 ee 00 00 00 01 10 09 00 … 01 10 0a 00 <0/1> confirmed Voice prompt on/off 08 ee 00 00 00 01 90 0a 00 <0/1> ack confirmed Volume 08 ee 00 00 00 01 81 0a 00 <0-16> ack confirmed Auto power-off 08 ee 00 00 00 01 83 0a 00 <1-4> (5/10/30/60 min) ack, then push 01 05 <value> confirmed EQ preset 08 ee 00 00 00 02 81 0a 00 <p>: 0 BassUp, 1 BassOff, 2 Voice, 3 Heavy, 4 Classic, 5 Original, ff custom ack, then push 02 01 <p> confirmed Custom EQ 08 ee 00 00 00 02 83 12 00 + 9 bands (dB + 6; 80 Hz … 12 kHz) ack confirmed Power off 08 ee 00 00 00 01 85 09 00 link drops reported 05 01 08 ee 00 00 00 05 01 09 00 41 bytes, 16 × u16 LE, meaning unknown confirmed exchange

Life Q30 / Life Tune (A3028 / A3029), checksummed, all from OpenSCQ30:

Command Frame Notes State 08 ee 00 00 00 01 01 0a 00 02 70 bytes on older firmware: 9 battery, 10 charging, 11-12 EQ preset, 13-20 bands, 44-47 sound modes, 48-52 firmware, 53-68 serial; newer firmware appends fields Sound modes 08 ee 00 00 00 06 81 0e 00 + 4 bytes + sum ambient (0 NC, 1 transparency, 2 normal), NC mode (0 transport, 1 outdoor, 2 indoor), transparency, custom strength Equaliser 08 ee 00 00 00 02 81 14 00 + preset (u16 LE) + 8 bands + sum band byte = gain in tenths of a dB + 120; preset fe fe = custom

Commands mean different things on different models. 01 81 is volume on the Motion+ and auto play/pause on earbuds; 01 83 is auto power-off on the Motion+ and touch tones on earbuds; 01 05 is a Motion+ push but the serial/firmware reply on earbuds. Never send a command to a model it was not documented for.

docs.title: Unsolicited frames
docs.text: Prefix Model Payload 09 ff 00 00 01 02 01 A3116 EQ preset, after every preset set (confirmed) 09 ff 00 00 01 01 05 A3116 Auto power-off value, after every set (confirmed; meaning inferred from the echo) 09 ff 00 00 01 01 03 all Battery levels (reported) 09 ff 00 00 01 01 04 all Charging flags (reported) 09 ff 00 00 01 06 01 earbuds, headphones Sound modes changed on the device (reported)

docs.title: BLE
docs.text:
Many models advertise over BLE so the app can find them without an inquiry. The advertisement carries a model code as a service UUID and the device's BR/EDR address in its manufacturer data. A client reads that address and opens RFCOMM to it, not to the advertiser's address:

A3947 (captured) Older models (vendor app, reported) Service UUID 32-bit, raw 01 4e f5 da = daf54e01-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 128-bit 01XXf5da-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, XX per model (12 for most earbuds, 0a for the Motion+) Manufacturer data 8 bytes: BR/EDR address MSB first, then 00 00. No company ID 7 bytes: BR/EDR address LSB first, then one byte Also Google Fast Pair service data (0xfe2c)

Some models also tunnel the same frames over a GATT service. SoundcoreManager drives the A3951, A3027, A3028, A3029 and A3935 that way (from Windows), picking the first non-generic service with a notify+read and a write+write-without-response characteristic. That layout is not documented here.

docs.title: Model table
docs.text:
protocol_details.model_table in the spec maps each SKU the vendor app (an older 2.9.9 build) knew to its control channel and BLE code. In short:

  • Vendor UUID (0cf12d31-fac3-4553-bd80-d6832e7b<code>): all the speakers (Soundcore 3, Mini 3, Motion+, Motion Boom, Flare, Rave, Trance, Select, Icon+, Infini Pro, Boost …), PowerConf, Frames, and newer earbuds (Life A1, Life Note 3/3S/3i, Life P3/P3i, Life Dot 3i, Life A3i, Liberty Neo 2, Liberty 3 Pro, Life Q20+, Life 2 Neo). The Liberty 4 NC, too new for that build, follows the same rule (captured).
  • SPP: Life Q30, Q35, Tune and Tune Pro; Liberty 2, 2 Pro, 2 Pro+; Liberty Air 2 and Air 2 Pro; Life A2 NC; Life Dot 2 NC.

Some speakers also have a per-model OTA UUID with 7c in place of 7b. OpenSCQ30's list of 38 supported SKUs is in the spec too. It covers models the table lacks, such as the Space Q45 (A3040) and Space A40 (A3936).

docs.title: Fast Pair (A3947)
docs.text: Android itself opens Google's Fast Pair Message Stream on the Liberty 4 NC, next to the soundcore channel. In the capture it carried the model ID D1E4E3, the BLE address, and a battery report for left, right and case in percent (bit 7 = charging). A client that only wants battery percentages can read them there without the vendor protocol.

docs.title: Firmware update
docs.text: Out of scope, and deliberately not examined: a failed transfer can leave earbuds unbootable. What is known: the A3947 publishes a BES OTA channel (BESOTA, captured) and the app bundles a BES updater. The app also bundles a Qualcomm GAIA BR/EDR service that may serve the Motion+ (unverified), and some speakers have per-model 7c OTA UUIDs. Images come from the vendor cloud.

docs.title: Controls a client can offer
docs.text:
Model Controls A3947 Battery (left, right, case, 0-5), charging, sound mode, NC mode, firmware A3116 Battery (0-5), charging, volume (0-16), EQ preset, auto power-off, voice prompts, power off, firmware A3028 / A3029 Battery (0-5), charging, sound mode, NC mode, firmware

EQ curves are declared as commands but not bound to a control, because no entity type holds an eight- or nine-band curve.

docs.title: Troubleshooting: what the evidence says about common complaints
"The app says not connected, but the earbuds are playing"
docs.text: A recurring review, including for the Liberty 4 NC. Audio (A2DP) and control (the RFCOMM channel) are separate links, so one can be up while the other is down. On the Liberty 4 NC the record with the SPP class is the wrong one (TOTA, channel 12), and only one client may be able to hold the control channel. Try: close every other soundcore client, including the vendor app's background service, then reconnect. A client of your own should open the vendor UUID, not SPP.

docs.title: A Motion+ that no third-party client can connect to
docs.text: The Motion+ has no SPP-class SDP record: its only serial record is the vendor UUID, named "CSR GAIA". A client that asks for 00001101-… gets nothing. OpenSCQ30 now pins the vendor UUID for this model, and its changelog lists several Motion+ connection fixes. The Motion+ also sends and expects frames without a checksum, so a parser that insists on one rejects every reply.

docs.title: "Gaming mode shows as on but does nothing" (Liberty 4 NC)
docs.text: Reported in a 2026-09 review. OpenSCQ30 handles gaming mode on the A3947 with a model-specific module. Not examined here.

docs.title: Forced account, ads, AI
docs.text: Nothing on the device side needs any of it: both captured sessions are unauthenticated byte frames on a local socket. OpenSCQ30 (Android, Linux, Windows) covers most models without an account.

docs.title: Capturing a model not covered here
docs.text:
1. On Android, enable Developer options → Enable Bluetooth HCI snoop log, toggle Bluetooth, then use each control once in the vendor app (Android's guide).
  2. Pull btsnoop_hci.log from adb bugreport and filter btrfcomm in Wireshark. Payloads starting 08 ee and 09 ff are this protocol.
  3. Your unit's address and serial number belong in your notes only. On the Liberty 4 NC seen here, the serial number is 3947 followed by the unit's own BR/EDR address byte-reversed (a unit at aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff would read 3947FFEEDDCCBBAA), so treat the state reply as identifying.

From Linux, a first look:

sdptool browse aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff    # find the 0cf12d31-…-d6832e7b<sku> record and its channel

import socket
ADDR, CHANNEL = "aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff", 15      # channel from sdptool (15 on the captured A3947)
CHECKSUM = True                              # False for the Motion+ (A3116)

def frame(cmd, payload=b""):
    n = 9 + len(payload) + (1 if CHECKSUM else 0)
    b = bytes([0x08, 0xee, 0, 0, 0]) + bytes(cmd) + n.to_bytes(2, "little") + payload
    return b + bytes([sum(b) & 0xff]) if CHECKSUM else b

s = socket.socket(socket.AF_BLUETOOTH, socket.SOCK_STREAM, socket.BTPROTO_RFCOMM)
s.connect((ADDR, CHANNEL))
s.send(frame([0x01, 0x01]))                  # state request
buf = b""
while len(buf) < 9 or len(buf) < int.from_bytes(buf[7:9], "little"):
    buf += s.recv(1024)
print(buf.hex(" "))                          # 09 ff 00 00 01 01 01 …

docs.title: Anova Precision Cooker (original, Bluetooth)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Anova Applied Electronics Manufacturer Status: Active (app subscription-gated for new accounts since 2024-08-21)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The original Anova Precision Cooker is a sous-vide immersion circulator sold in two models. The 2014 800 W Bluetooth unit is the A2 generation. The 900 W Bluetooth + Wi-Fi unit is the A3 generation. Both speak the same phone-direct BLE protocol. It needs no account and no cloud. Commands are plain ASCII strings ending in a carriage return, and they go to one HM-10-style serial characteristic.

The protocol is worth writing down because of how the vendor app changed. Anova made its app a subscription for accounts created after 2024-08-21. It also announced that Bluetooth control of these cookers would end in 2025, then cancelled that plan on 2025-01-16 (see Missing Devices). A second-hand cooker on a new account still hits the paywall. The local protocol avoids both problems.

Anova has since published a developer page and an MIT-licensed reference client for this cooker. The community had already worked the protocol out: neilpa/circulate in 2014 and Aldaviva/SousVide in 2024. The vendor pages leave out reply formats, status strings and ranges. The spec therefore cites Anova where it can and uses the community sources for the rest.

Out of scope:

  • the 900 W model's Wi-Fi and cloud path
  • the Precision Cooker Nano, which uses a framed binary protocol on service 0e140000-0af1-4582-a242-773e63054c68
  • the first Precision Cooker Mini, which uses JSON + Base64
  • the 2022-and-later Precision Cooker 3.0, Pro 3.0, Mini and Lite
  • the Precision Oven

None of this has been driven against hardware by this project.

This starts a heater remotely

Every temperature on this protocol is in whichever unit the cooker is currently set to. Suppose a client means 60 °C but the cooker is set to °F: the cooker aims for 15.6 °C, and nothing on the wire flags the mistake. Re-read the unit every poll cycle, because anyone can toggle it at the cooker. Before a remote start, check that the cooker is clamped in a pot and the water sits between its MIN and MAX marks.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number 800 W Bluetooth: A2 generation (also referred to as A2.2; SousVide calls its unit a Precision Cooker 1.0). 900 W Bluetooth + Wi-Fi: A3 generation Chipset Not identified. The 0000ffe0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb / 0000ffe1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb layout is the one TI CC254x "HM-10"-style UART modules use, and one community unit's address carries the TI OUI 84:eb:18 (hypothesis) Radio BLE (GATT server). The 900 W model adds 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi Heater / pump 800 W (120 V or 220 V), 8.2 L/min (vendor manual, 800 W model) Temperature Room temperature to 99 °C, stability ±0.01 °C (vendor manual). Over BLE the cooker accepts 5.0–99.9 °C / 41.0–211.8 °F (circulate) FCC ID 800 W: not found. 900 W: the 2015 manual says it contains FCC ID AZY-HF-LPB100, a modular Wi-Fi radio grant (product code matches the High-Flying HF-LPB100). The later FCC IDs 2APBOAN300/425/525/625 are the excluded 2022-and-later generation

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name Local name Anova (match the name, never the shared 0000ffe0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb UUID alone) Passphrase protection not_applicable (the 900 W model's Wi-Fi onboarding is out of scope and undocumented) Confidence medium (two open implementations and the vendor docs agree; not replayed here)

To connect:

  1. Plug the cooker in.
  2. Scan for Anova and connect.
  3. If the host asks for a PIN, enter 0000.
  4. Enable notifications on 0000ffe1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb.
  5. Send read unit. The cooker answers c or f.
  6. Optionally send get id card. A reply that starts anova f56- means the 900 W Wi-Fi model.

Factory reset: none is documented. The cooker stores a pairing, a temperature unit, a calibration offset and, on the 900 W model, Wi-Fi credentials. Pressing the Bluetooth symbol clears the pairing (vendor manual). Writing cal 0.0 restores the factory calibration offset. No procedure is known that clears everything at once. That is a finding from reading the operating manual and Anova's developer pages end to end, not a test.

Rebinding to a new network: not applicable on the BLE path. To move the cooker to a new phone, forget it on the old one, press the cooker's Bluetooth symbol, and pair again.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required Unknown Security mode legacy_pin (PIN 0000, entered as passkey 000000 on an LE link) Bonding optional PIN source fixed_default — 0000 One central at a time Unknown (likely, as with HM-10-style modules) One bond at a time Unknown Confidence low (the sources disagree)

The sources disagree on whether pairing is needed:

  • Aldaviva/SousVide pairs the cooker in the operating system's Bluetooth settings with PIN 0000.
  • Anova's own Bleak reference client connects without asking for a bond, and so does pycirculate's bluepy connection.

Most likely the cooker answers on an unbonded link and keeps a bond when a host starts one. Nobody has confirmed that.

Entering pairing mode: press the Bluetooth symbol on the control panel. According to SousVide, the indicator turns blue and blinks. The vendor manual warns that this breaks any existing pairing. Anova's reference client says the cooker is also connectable right after power-up.

Unpairing: press the Bluetooth symbol, which breaks the cooker's existing pairing, then forget the cooker in the old host's settings. No factory reset is needed.

Recovery: close the vendor app and any other client. If the cooker still will not pair, the vendor manual says to switch it off for 10 seconds and power it back on. On Windows 11, set Bluetooth devices discovery to Advanced or the cooker stays hidden.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 0000ffe0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Serial service The only vendor service. The UUID is shared by every HM-10-style module, so it does not identify the cooker 0000ffe1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Command/reply Write requests without response. Replies arrive as notifications on the same characteristic

docs.title: Framing and client rules
docs.text:
• Requests are ASCII strings ending in CR (0x0d). Each one is 20 bytes or less. Send one at a time.
  • Replies are ASCII strings ending in CR. A reply longer than 20 bytes is split across notifications; power interrupt error + CR is 22 bytes, for example. Accumulate until a CR arrives, then strip CR, NUL and whitespace. Anova's own rule ends a reply at a notification shorter than 20 bytes or one ending in 0x00. Keep that rule only as a fallback, because on its own it never completes a reply that exactly fills 20 bytes.
  • No request IDs, no unsolicited traffic. Serialise every request, wait for its reply or a timeout (Anova suggests 15 s), and poll for everything. SousVide polls read temp, read set temp and status once a second.
  • Unknown command: the reply is Invalid Command. Treat it as the answer to the request in flight.
  • Units: every temperature, in both directions, uses the unit read unit reports. The calibration offset is the one exception and is always °C.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
The table gives the command and the reply it gets. Every request ends with CR.

Request Reply Notes read unit c / f Governs every temperature set unit c / set unit f the new letter Same as holding Start/Stop for 3 s on the cooker read temp e.g. 73.4 Water temperature, current unit, 0.1 resolution read set temp e.g. 145.0 Setpoint, current unit set temp <n> the value with one decimal, e.g. 135.0 Does not start heating. Range 5.0–99.9 °C / 41.0–211.8 °F (circulate) status stopped, running, low water, heater error, power interrupt error Only stopped is idle. The running string is circulate's and unconfirmed start start Echoes even if the cooker does not start, so confirm with status stop stop set timer <minutes> the minutes Whole minutes. Anova's reference client sends 0 for no timer. Loads the timer but does not start it start time none, or start time Sources disagree. Wait a bounded time and discard any echo stop time stop time read timer <minutes> running / <minutes> stopped circulate's format get id card begins anova f56- on the 900 W model The rest is a per-unit ID, so don't publish it clear alarm not documented 900 W model only version not documented 900 W model only read cal e.g. 0.0 Calibration offset, always °C cal <offset> echo −9.9 to 9.9 °C. Declared advanced: a wrong offset silently shifts every cook

docs.title: Worked example: set the setpoint
docs.text:
Every byte below is ASCII. The number is decimal text in the cooker's current unit, with one fractional digit, never a binary value.

Request (write without response to 0000ffe1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb):

Offset Length Bytes Description 0 9 73 65 74 20 74 65 6d 70 20 set temp (with the trailing space) 9 4 35 37 2e 35 57.5, in whatever unit read unit reported 13 1 0d CR terminator

Response (one notification, since it is under 20 bytes):

Offset Length Bytes Description 0 4 35 37 2e 35 The accepted setpoint echoed with one decimal 4 1 0d CR terminator

To start a cook, Anova's reference client sends these in order:

  1. set temp
  2. stop time
  3. set timer
  4. start
  5. start time, if the timer is above 0

circulate also documents more commands: multi-step programs, set led, set name, the date and history commands, and set password. The spec lists them under protocol_details without declaring them, and says why for each.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Readings look shifted by one command. The client lost request/reply alignment, usually because of a late start time echo or a reply that arrived after a timeout. To resync, stop sending, drain notifications, send read unit, and wait for c/f. SousVide's client never waits for a start time reply, so if the cooker does echo it, every later reply is off by one.
  • Client hangs after one command. The cooker answered Invalid Command, for example to version on the 800 W model, and the client dropped it. SousVide's C# client does exactly this, and it waits with no timeout.
  • Temperatures suddenly wrong mid-session. Someone toggled °C/°F at the cooker. SousVide reads the unit only once, when it connects.
  • Timer restarts after a reconnect, or starts before the bath is hot. Store reviews report this about the vendor app. The vendor start sequence starts the timer together with the cook, and re-running it on reconnect resets the countdown. On reconnect, read status and read timer. Send start time only once read temp reaches the setpoint if you want the timer to count from temperature.
  • Setpoint jumps to about 1 °C after "calibrating". pycirculate's calibration helper sends set temp <factor> instead of cal <factor>.
  • Can't reconnect after changing phones. A stale pairing is holding the cooker. Press the Bluetooth symbol, forget the cooker on the old phone, and pair again with 0000.

docs.title: Apple AirPort Extreme / Time Capsule / Express (ACP)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (unverified) Protocol: LAN (Bonjour _airport._tcp, ACP on TCP 5009) Manufacturer: Apple Manufacturer Status: Unsupported. Apple discontinued the line in April 2018.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Apple's AirPort base stations are the AirPort Extreme, the AirPort Time Capsule (an Extreme with a built-in disk) and the AirPort Express. They are managed with ACP on TCP 5009, a protocol Apple never published. This spec lets any client read a base station's status, change its settings and restart it, all locally. Two open-source implementations are the sources: node-acp (TypeScript, with SRP) and airpyrt-tools (Python, archived).

Security: legacy ACP puts the admin password into every request header in an easily reversed form. Authenticate with SRP, which also encrypts the session, and keep "setup over WAN" (property waNM) off so port 5009 cannot be reached from the internet.

Caution: writing a property, even through the same path that renames the unit, can change Wi-Fi, WAN or DHCP settings and drop every device on the network, including the client that made the write. Read and save a value before you change it.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Models AirPort Extreme (802.11n, 802.11ac), AirPort Time Capsule, AirPort Express 802.11n Product id (syAP) 115 = Express 802.11n (2nd gen), 120 = Extreme 802.11ac; others not in the sources Last firmware named by the community tooling 7.9.1 (802.11ac Extreme / Time Capsule), 7.8.1 (Express) Radio Wi-Fi access point and router; Ethernet WAN/LAN

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No. The spec manages a unit that already has a base station password Method wired: discover, connect to TCP 5009, then authenticate Discovery Bonjour _airport._tcp.local.. node-acp reports that the TXT data arrives as one entry, waMA=<mac>,raMA=…,raM2=…,raNm=…,raCh=…,rCh2=…,raSt=…,raNA=…,syFl=…,syAP=…,syVs=…,srcv=…,bjSd=… Credentials The base station password (user name is always admin for SRP) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (community code, not run here)

First-time setup of a factory-fresh unit is out of scope. The sources do not cover it.

Factory reset: these are the 802.11n and 802.11ac procedures from Apple's archived support article. The reset button is recessed, so press it with a pen tip.

  • Soft reset: with the unit powered, hold the button about 1 s. The status light flashes amber. For the next five minutes the password is cleared and access control is off, so you can set a new password. If nothing is changed, the old settings come back.
  • Hard reset: with the unit powered, hold the button about 5 s, until the light flashes amber rapidly. The unit becomes unconfigured, but it keeps the last configuration so you can restore it.
  • Factory default: unplug the unit, hold the button while you plug it back in, and keep holding for about 6 s. This erases the saved configurations and profiles. Apple ties this procedure to firmware 7.9.1 on the 802.11ac models.

None of these resets erases a Time Capsule's disk or an attached USB disk.

Rebinding to a new network: nothing to redo. A base station that acts as the router normally keeps its address. One that is bridged behind another router gets a new address by DHCP, and a client finds it again through Bonjour.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text: Property Value Pairing required Yes: the base station password, proved again on every connection. Nothing is issued, and changing the password revokes every client Security mode app_layer (SRP-6a, or the legacy password key) Bonding none PIN source user_chosen Confidence medium

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
Every message starts with a 128-byte big-endian header:

Offset Length Field 0 4 Magic acpp 4 4 Version, 0x00030001 8 4 Header checksum: Adler-32 of the header with this field zeroed 12 4 Body checksum: Adler-32 of the body (1 when there is no body) 16 4 Body size, or -1 when there is no body 20 4 Flags (4 on get-property and authenticate, 0 elsewhere; meaning unknown) 24 4 Unused, 0 28 4 Command id 32 4 Error code 36 12 Zero 48 32 Key field 80 48 Zero

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Id Name Use 0x14 GET_PROPERTY Read properties 0x15 SET_PROPERTY Write properties; writing acRB = 0 reboots 0x18 MONITOR Start a stream of pushed status frames 0x19 RPC Named functions, each with a plist of inputs 0x1A AUTHENTICATE SRP exchange 0x1B GET_FEATURES Feature plist; needs no password 0x01, 0x03, 0x05, 0x06, 0x16 Echo, flashing, perform Not covered here

Properties have four-character names, such as syNm (name), syVs (firmware), syAP (product id), syUT (uptime), raNm (Wi-Fi network), waIP (WAN address) and logm (log). Each property travels as an element: the name, 4 bytes of flags, a 4-byte size, then the value. A read sends each wanted name with a 4-byte zero value. The reply lists the elements and ends with a marker of all zeros (00000000 00000000 00000004 00000000). If an element has flag bit 0 set, its value is an error code instead, for example -10 when the property is not available. Structured values, and the bodies of AUTHENTICATE, GET_FEATURES, MONITOR and RPC, use Apple's compact CFB0 plist format.

Authentication:

  • Legacy: the key field holds the password, NUL-padded to 32 bytes and XORed with a fixed keystream. Byte i of the keystream is ((i + 0x55) & 0xFF) ^ static_key[i % 16]. AUTHENTICATE and GET_FEATURES always send the keystream itself, which is the result for an empty password.
  • SRP: SRP-6a with SHA-1 and the 1536-bit group, as user admin. Stage 1 sends {state: 1, username: admin} and gets back the salt, B, g and N. Stage 3 sends {iv, publicKey: A, state: 3, response: M1} and gets back {response: M2, iv}. After that, both directions use AES-128-CTR. Each direction's key is PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 of the SRP key with its own fixed salt (5 iterations for client to server, 7 for server to client), and its starting counter is that side's IV. The key field is then zero.

Firmware flashing exists (0x03, 0x05 and 0x06). Both community projects can also decrypt firmware images. This spec deliberately leaves both out.

scripts/test_apple_airport_acp_spec.py rebuilds every example message in the spec from these rules, using an invented password. That includes the Adler-32 checksums, the legacy key and an example of the PBKDF2 session-key derivation. The rules were also checked against node-acp's unit-test vectors.

See device-specs/devices/apple-airport-acp.yaml for the full spec.

docs.title: Aqara Hub family (M1S Gen 2 / M2 / AC Partner P3)
docs.text: Status: Protocol recovered from the Aqara Home app (v4.2.1, SecNeo-packed — payload dumped from a rooted Android device); provisioning crypto verified against the vendor library on-device; not replayed against hub hardware Protocol: WiFi/LAN (mDNS + UDP multicast discovery, encrypted UDP 10008 provisioning) — steady-state control is cloud-relayed Manufacturer: Lumi United (Aqara) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Aqara's Wi-Fi hubs bridge the vendor's Zigbee and BLE sensors to the LAN and cloud; some models add an IR blaster (M2, AC Partner P3) or a speaker and RGB night light (M1S Gen 2). This entry exists because the vendor app is packed (SecNeo/Bangcle) and its local surface had never been documented; the full analysis is in the machine-readable spec (device-specs/devices/aqara-hub.yaml).

The headline finding cuts both ways:

  • Local: discovery and Wi-Fi onboarding. Hubs answer mDNS _aqara._tcp.local. and a UDP multicast whois probe, and accept Wi-Fi credentials as AES-128-CBC-encrypted JSON on UDP port 10008. The crypto parameters are app-wide constants and are recovered and verified (below).
  • Not local: everything after onboarding. The current app contains no LAN command channel for hubs at all — control (arm/disarm, light, IR, Zigbee child state) and event delivery are relayed through Aqara's cloud. Onboarding also needs the cloud: the payload embeds a cloud-issued bindKey. See Cloud dependency.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Models covered Hub M1S Gen 2 (HM1S-G02), Hub M2 (Ethernet + IR), AC Partner P3 (IR) Radio Wi-Fi 802.11b/g/n 2.4 GHz + Zigbee 3.0; BLE (commissioning/locks) Setup AP lumi-gateway-<model><suffix>, Aqara Hub * (open) Setup-AP address 192.x.y.1 (the /24 gateway of the lease it hands you); UDP 10008

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes — Wi-Fi join and cloud account binding Method softap_udp (primary), softap_http / ble_provisioning / wired-Ethernet variants Setup AP lumi-gateway-* / Aqara Hub *, open Passphrase protection device_encrypted (AES-128-CBC, app-wide key — recovered) Confidence medium (recovered from app code; crypto oracle-verified; no hub hardware replayed)

The onboarding exchange, recovered from the app:

  1. Join the hub's setup AP. The hub is at 192.x.y.1, UDP port 10008.
  2. Send one datagram: JSON {"cid":" ","ssid":"…","passwd":"…","lang":"…","bindKey":"…","country_domain":"…","timeZone":"GMT±8"} encrypted with AES-128-CBC (PKCS7, fixed IV — parameters in the spec's aqara_lan_protocol.crypto).
  3. Hub replies with encrypted JSON (iotError/errorMessage on failure); the client closes with an encrypted {"ack":1}.
  4. The hub joins the home Wi-Fi and advertises _aqara._tcp on the LAN.

Variants by model: plaintext JSON over TCP 10000 ({"ssid","password", "bindKey"}), an HTTPS POST while on the setup AP (default-looking endpoint https://192.168.5.1:4567/ is a placeholder in the binary — unverified), BLE "Magic Pair" commissioning (service 0000fcb9-…), and standard Matter commissioning (BLE 0xFFF6 / _matterc._udp) on Matter-capable models. Ethernet models (M2) skip the AP: find the hub with the multicast probe and push the same encrypted payload to its LAN address.

Factory reset: hold the hub button ~10 s until the yellow LED flashes — this resets the network only and keeps Zigbee child bindings (the router-replacement move). On the M1S Gen 2, pressing the button 10 times restores factory defaults (bindings cleared). Both per vendor documentation, neither replayed here (verified: false in the spec).

Rebinding to a new network: in place via the 10 s network reset; no full factory reset needed.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No local client pairing: discovery and the Wi-Fi handoff answer anyone. The cloud-issued bindKey is account binding, which is part of setup Security mode none on the documented LAN surface; control is cloud-only One client at a time N/A on LAN; account-bound in cloud

Local control routes outside this spec have their own gates: a HomeKit setup code on supported models, a Matter pairing code from the Aqara app, or the per-hub developer-mode key on older Xiaomi-era firmware. None of them is verified here.

Zigbee sensors pair to the hub (standard Zigbee joining while the hub is in pairing mode), not to the phone. Aqara's BLE locks are a separate, fully mapped local GATT surface (ECDH P-256 + AES-CCM session after a cloud-assisted binding) — summarized in the spec's protocol_details.ble_lock_family for a future dedicated entry.

docs.title: Cloud dependency
docs.text:
Steady-state control in app v4.2.1 is cloud-only: authenticated HTTPS REST resource-writes (subjectId/dataKey/value) for control and cloud push for events. Onboarding fetches the bindKey, region and position IDs from the same REST API. If Aqara's cloud disappears:

  • already-provisioned hubs keep answering discovery (mDNS/multicast) but expose no documented local control;
  • adopting a reset hub is blocked on the bindKey unless testing shows hubs accept an arbitrary one (see remaining_unknowns in the spec).

Older hub firmware had a developer-mode LAN control protocol (multicast 224.0.0.50, ports 54321/9898) used by third-party projects such as the Home Assistant AqaraGateway integration; it has no trace in the current app and was not verified by this project.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text: Mechanism Detail mDNS _aqara._tcp.local.; TXT md=model, id=did, pv=true when already provisioned UDP multicast 230.0.0.1:10008; send plaintext {"command":"whois","address":"<your IP>","port":"<your port>"} Reply JSON array of {"command":"iam","address":"<ip>:<port>","model":"…","name":"…","registered":"yes|no"}

docs.title: Provisioning crypto (verified)

docs.title: Aranet4 CO2 Sensor
docs.text: Status: Complete (protocol fully documented from cross-checked prior art; live unit observed, GATT not yet driven — old firmware requires bonding) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: SAF Tehnika JSC Manufacturer Status: Active — fully local by design; cloud is an optional paid add-on

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Aranet4 is a battery-powered e-ink CO2 / temperature / humidity / pressure sensor with an exemplary local story: with firmware ≥ v1.2.0 and the "Smart Home integrations" toggle enabled, it broadcasts every measurement in BLE advertisements — no connection, no pairing, read by any passive scanner (this is exactly how Home Assistant integrates it). GATT adds current readings, full history download and settings. The same advertisement/GATT skeleton covers the Aranet2, Aranet Radiation and Aranet Radon.

A real unit ("Aranet4 19385") was observed live 2026-08-14: it broadcast the short 7-byte header-only payload decoding to firmware v0.4.14 — pre-v1.2.0, so no measurements in adverts, and it dropped every unbonded GATT connection during service discovery, exactly as the pairing rules predict. Full verification needs the pairing PIN from its e-ink display (human present) or a firmware update.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Sensor Senseair Sunrise NDIR CO2 (per teardowns) Radio Nordic BLE SoC, random static address; Nordic Secure DFU 0xFE59 present Battery 2×AA, ~1–2 years Advertised name Aranet4 NNNNN

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text: Property Value Setup required No (passive) / one-time toggle for broadcast measurements Method ble_direct; bonding (passkey shown on e-ink display) for history/settings and for everything on firmware < v1.2.0 Passphrase protection not_applicable (standard BLE passkey bonding) Confidence high (reference implementation ships in Home Assistant; official SAF Tehnika Homey app cross-checked)

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
• Advertisement (manufacturer ID 0x0702): 7-byte short (header only) or 22-byte long payload — CO2 u16@8, temp ×0.05 u16@10, pressure ×0.1 u16@12, humidity u8@14, battery u8@15, status color u8@16, interval u16@17, ago u16@19. Family devices (Aranet2/Radiation/Radon) use 24-byte payloads with a leading type byte.
  • GATT: vendor service f0cd1400-… (fw < v1.2.0) or 0xFCE0 (fw ≥ v1.2.0). Current readings f0cd3001 (13 B), command char f0cd1402 (history requests 0x82/0x61, interval 0x90, integrations toggle 0x91), history V1 notify f0cd2003 / V2 poll-read f0cd2005.
  • Sentinels: CO2/pressure bit15, temperature bit14 ⇒ invalid (seen during calibration).

See device-specs/devices/aranet4.yaml for byte-exact layouts, the history protocol and the family differences.

docs.title: Artiphon Orba 2
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (capture-verified upstream; untested here) Protocol: BLE-MIDI and proprietary SysEx Manufacturer: Artiphon, Inc. Manufacturer Status: Shutdown — liquidated in 2025

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Orba 2 is a handheld instrument and looper whose performance and configuration paths work without Artiphon's app or cloud. Standard MIDI carries playing data; a proprietary SysEx command layer carries transport, tempo, key/scale, quantization and mix settings. The same SysEx works over USB-MIDI and BLE-MIDI.

This document covers Orba 2 only. The public protocol source's live hardware and captures are Orba 2, not Orba 1. Do not infer compatibility with Orba 3, Chorda or INSTRUMENT 1. The recovered Orba 2 companion package is com.artiphon.kestrel; the older Orba 1 app is a different target.

An immediate alternative is Orba Console, a browser controller using Web Bluetooth or Web MIDI with no account.

docs.title: Initial Setup and Pairing
docs.text:
No account or provisioning is required. Wake the Orba and close any other central, then connect to the device whose advertised name is exactly Artiphon Orba 2 and which carries the BLE-MIDI service. Neither signal is enough alone: the BLE-MIDI service is on every BLE-MIDI product, and this spec has destructive erase commands. The name read after connecting can differ from the advertised one, so match on the advertisement. A unit advertising another name is not matched automatically; the user picks it. The device holds one BLE central at a time.

Property Value Setup required No Pairing / bonding None required Service 03b80e5a-ede8-4b33-a751-6ce34ec4c700 MIDI I/O 7772e5db-3868-4112-a1a9-f2669d106bf3, write + notify Factory reset Unknown; erase-song is not a factory reset

Enable MIDI notifications and serialize every write of a command.

docs.title: SysEx framing
docs.text:
The command payload is 02 for GET or 03 for SET, then a domain and a 16-bit big-endian register address, followed by any values. Wrap it as:

82 01 <message-id> <payload-length:u16be> <payload> <crc:u16be>

CRC-16 uses reflected polynomial A001, initial zero, over 82 through the last payload byte. Repack the packet from 8-bit to 7-bit LSB-first, prefix 00, and delimit with F0 and F7.

BLE-MIDI splits that stream into ordered writes, normally at 20 bytes:

first:        80 80 <up to 18 stream bytes>
continuation: 80 <up to 19 stream bytes>
end:          80 80 F7

Incoming notifications require the mirror reassembly through F7; a single notification is not necessarily a complete reply. Message ids correlate responses. Do not blind-scan registers: invalid reads can fault and reboot the instrument.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Command Payload Select part 03 01 00 03 <0 Lead / 1 Chord / 2 Bass / 3 Drum> Record / overdub 03 07 00 02 01 Play / resume 03 07 00 02 05 Pause, preserving the loop 03 07 00 02 06 Tempo 03 07 00 07 <BPM x100:u16be> Scale 03 03 00 13 <index> Battery request 02 03 00 0f

Quantization is per part at 07@0003 through 07@0006: 0 as played, 1 snap to grid, 2 Orba groove. Scale indexes 0–10 are Major, Natural Minor, Harmonic Minor, Melodic Minor, Major Pentatonic, Minor Pentatonic, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian and Locrian respectively.

Per-part FX lives at 02@50xx: part bases Lead 00, Chord 08, Bass 10, Drum 18, offsets volume +0, pan +1, reverb +2, delay +3. Values 0–255 map to 0–100%. The trailing 00 01 04 is required; without it the Orba can acknowledge but ignore a write. Changing a preset resets that part's FX.

Erase-active-loop (…02), erase-song (…03) and fresh-record (…04) are advanced, destructive operations, not ordinary transport stop commands. Preset selection uses a 129-byte filename and a separate commit; it is not exposed as an ordinary command here.

docs.title: Verification and open questions
docs.text:
The canonical public specification reports replaying 31 captured writes and acceptance of synthesized writes by a live Orba 2. This project has not run the hardware. scripts/test_artiphon_orba_2_spec.py independently rebuilds short and fragmented reference vectors, including the mandatory FX trailer.

Open: the exact metronome enum, battery reply semantics, preset-file workflow, and compatibility with every other Artiphon model.

See device-specs/devices/artiphon-orba-2.yaml for the machine-readable spec.

docs.title: Astral Hoops Atomic V (AF Series)
docs.text: Status: In Progress Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Astral Hoops Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Astral Hoops Atomic V line — LED hula hoops, wands and fans — are programmable flow props driven by the vendor's Astral app (com.astral.astral). The props speak a clean ASCII protocol over a standard transparent-UART BLE module, need no account and no cloud, and even their firmware updates are public downloads — an unusually friendly target for local control. The full machine-readable protocol is in device-specs/devices/astral-hoops.yaml.

Everything the app does works locally: mode and colour control, per-prop settings, custom POV pattern upload, and firmware OTA all run over the BLE connection. The app's only network use is fetching firmware images and pattern packs from public HTTPS URLs.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Models Atomic V Hoop / Wand / Fan (AF series) MCU Microchip/Atmel SAM D21 (ARM Cortex-M0+) Radio BLE via Microchip/ISSC transparent-UART module Firmware Public: a5.ver = 5.2.5 (beta 5.3.0), raw flash image af5.bin FCC ID Unknown

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Advertised name Atomic + 5-character unit ID (AtomicNNNNN) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (from app analysis; not yet exercised against hardware here)

Power the prop on, scan for the Atomic name prefix, and connect from inside your app — there is no pairing, PIN, or account. After connecting, enable notifications on the RX characteristic and walk the settings query chain (#GS, #GT, #GD, #GA, #GO, #GE, #GL, #GN) to learn the prop's configuration.

Factory reset: there is no physical reset procedure known; resets are BLE commands. #WIPE clears your customizations (the prop answers OK); #FORMAT reformats pattern storage, after which the factory patterns must be re-uploaded through the normal image upload flow. Neither affects the BLE identity or the unit ID.

Rebinding to a new controller: just connect from the new phone — nothing binds the prop to a controller. The prop holds one BLE connection at a time, so disconnect (or power-cycle) the old phone first; a phone that keeps auto-reconnecting will hold the link.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 49535343-fe7d-4ae5-8fa9-9fafd205e455 Astral Service ISSC transparent UART 49535343-1e4d-4bd9-ba61-23c647249616 TX Phone → device (write) 49535343-8841-43f4-a8d4-ecbe34729bb3 RX Device → phone (notify)

Transparent UART: plain ASCII bytes both ways, no framing. The app never negotiates an MTU — split long writes into 16-byte GATT writes with ~10 ms spacing.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
App → device commands are #-prefixed ASCII strings. The most useful:

Command Description #GM Query current mode (replies &M…) #GV Query firmware version #GS/#GT/#GD/#GA/#GO/#GE/#GL/#GN Settings query chain: sleep seconds, POV stabilization, LED count, battery type, prop type, LED type, battery level, product ID #SM2=<mode>;1=<item>; Set display mode and menu item #SM3=<speed>;4=<hue>; Set custom speed and hue #SO<i> / #SE<i> / #SA<i> Set prop type / LED type / battery type index #SD<hi><lo> Set LED count (2 raw big-endian bytes on fw ≥ 5.2; 1 byte older) #SS<n> Set auto-sleep seconds (0 = off) #ST0 / #ST1 POV stabilization off / on #V + byte(46+slot) Preview stored pattern slot #D Begin pattern image upload (expect OK) #WIPE / #FORMAT Clear customizations / reformat pattern storage #B + MCURESET Enter firmware-update bootloader (expect BL)

Device → phone messages on RX are &-prefixed status records (&M mode, &L battery 0-7, &S sleep, &B brightness, &T POV stabilization, &D LED count, &A/&O/&E type indices, &N product ID, &V version), pushed spontaneously on state change and in reply to the #G* queries, plus simple ACKs: OK, BL, and single-byte 0x06 ACK / 0x18 CAN on the XMODEM path.

docs.title: Pattern upload
docs.text:
Custom POV patterns persist on the prop in numbered slots:

  1. Send #D, wait for OK.
  2. Send a 10-byte header: [width, height, 3, 0,0,0,0,0,0,0] (3 = RGB888).
  3. Send gamma-corrected RGB888 pixel data in 20-byte chunks, waiting for OK after each.
  4. Send one final byte = the pattern slot to save into, expecting OK.

#FORMAT erases pattern storage; the factory art is then restored by re-uploading images the same way. Free pattern packs are hosted at extras.astralhoops.com/patterns/.

docs.title: Firmware OTA
docs.text: The vendor publishes firmware openly: a5.ver (plain text version) and af5.bin (raw flash image for offset 0x2000; beta: a5beta.ver / af5beta.bin). Updating means entering the custom SAM D21 bootloader (#B, MCURESET → BL), verifying the chip ID, erasing the app region, writing the image word-by-word staged through RAM, and resetting. The exact command sequence is documented in the device spec's firmware_update feature. This path can brick the prop if interrupted — it is documented for owners reflashing their own hardware, and has not yet been replayed against a live unit by this project.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
• Exact #GV/&V reply layout (string vs 0x05-led binary triplet) — needs a live capture.
  • &M payload semantics and the mode/item index tables (they live in app UI resources).
  • Whether the XMODEM block path in the bootloader is still used, or legacy.
  • Exact gamma-correction table used for pattern upload (a standard LED gamma ramp is a close approximation; capture for bit-exact colours).

docs.text:
• [x] APK static analysis (jadx)
  • [x] Live fetch of the public firmware/version endpoints
  • [ ] HCI snoop of connect + settings chain + pattern upload (pending)

docs.title: Aurora LED Shoes
docs.text: Status: Complete (protocol mapped from app analysis; live capture pending for details) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: jtkj (app developer; shoe hardware OEM unknown) Manufacturer Status: Unsupported

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Aurora LED Shoes are Bluetooth-controlled light-up rave shoes driven by the "Aurora LED Shoes" app (com.jtkj.auroraled, v1.0.1 analyzed). The protocol is about as simple as BLE control gets: one service, one characteristic, and a handful of 1–4 byte opcode-first packets with no handshake, no pairing, no checksum, no encryption, no OTA and no vendor backend. Everything the app does can be reproduced locally — these shoes have no cloud dependency at all.

One phone can drive many shoes at once: the app holds several connections and broadcasts every command to all of them, so a pair (or a whole dance floor) stays in sync.

Same developer as CoolLED1248 — different protocol

The app developer (jtkj) also ships CoolLED1248 (com.jtkj.led1248). The apps share a BLE wrapper library and coding style, but the GATT profiles and opcodes are different (CoolLED1248 is the 0xFFE5/0xFFE9 family). The two are not interchangeable.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number Unknown (generic "FS"-named BLE module) Chipset Unidentified — 0xFFF0/0xFFF1 is the classic cheap BLE-UART-bridge profile Radio BLE FCC ID Unknown

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
No provisioning of any kind. The shoes advertise as soon as they are powered on and accept a connection from any central — no account, no pairing PIN, no credentials.

Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name Name prefix FS + advertised service 0xFFF0 (the app's scanner requires both) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence high (from app code); live scan still pending

Factory reset: there is nothing to reset — the shoe stores no credentials or bonds. Power-cycling drops the current connection, which is the actual fix for the most common failure mode: the shoe still being connected to another phone (only one central can hold the link).

Rebinding to a new controller: just connect from the new phone. The catch is the old phone: the vendor app caches previously-connected MAC addresses and auto-reconnects to them, so close the app (or unpair/forget at the OS level) on the old phone before expecting the new one to connect.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 0000fff0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Control Service Sole service 0000fff1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Control Write + notify; all commands and the state reply

Commands are raw opcode-first packets of 1–4 bytes, one write (write-without-response) per command. No header, length field, checksum or encryption.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Bytes Description Music color 01 RR GG BB Set displayed color live (app feeds this from phone-mic FFT; any color source works) Solid color 03 RR GG BB Set static RGB color Power toggle 04 Flip on/off Set power 05 VV 01 = on, 00 = off Set speed 10 VV Pattern speed — lower = faster (inverted slider); exact range unconfirmed Slow color change 07 04 NN NN: 00 blue, 01 green, 02 red, 03 cyan, 04 purple, 05 yellow, 06 white, 20 seven-color, 30 red+green, 40 red+blue, 50 green+blue Flash 07 05 NN NN: 00 blue, 01 green, 02 red, 03 cyan, 04 purple, 05 yellow, 06 white, 10 seven-color Shining presets 07 … Ten fixed presets: 07 06 01 00, 07 01 08, 07 01 13, 07 03 01 00, 07 09 00, 07 09 01, 07 0A 01, 07 0A 02, 07 01 01, 07 02 00 — visual semantics unmapped State query F0 Reply on notify: F0 FLAG SPEED (FLAG 00/01 = power, SPEED = speed echo). Defined in the app but only logged — possibly unused

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: The only device→app frame is the 3-byte F0 FLAG SPEED reply to the state query, delivered as a notification on 0xFFF1 (enable via CCC 0x2902; the app does this ~500 ms after connect). There is no handshake or authentication sequence — you can write commands immediately after connecting.

docs.title: Music mode
docs.text: All signal processing happens on the phone: the app runs an FFT over microphone input (35 bins, picks peaks per 11-bin third, maps to RGB) and streams 01 RR GG BB writes. The shoe simply displays the last colour it received, so a replacement app can drive "music mode" from any audio pipeline — or any other live colour source.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
• Exact on-wire range and direction of the speed byte (10 VV): the app computes it as an inverted slider value with a default of 120, but the slider maximum wasn't recoverable from the decompiled code. Needs a live capture.
  • Which visual effect each of the ten 07 … shining presets produces.
  • Whether the F0 state query is actually sent in normal app use, and whether state notifications also arrive unsolicited.
  • Full advertised device name (beyond the FS prefix) and MAC OUI — needs a hardware scan.

docs.text:
• [x] APK static analysis (jadx) — com.jtkj.auroraled v1.0.1, unobfuscated, complete command table recovered
  • [ ] HCI snoop / live capture (pending — speed range, shining presets, state query, advertised name)

docs.title: AUTOBABA LED Backpack
docs.text: Status: Minimally verified (queries, brightness, static and animated upload) Protocol: BLE; Wi-Fi on some related LOY SPACE products Manufacturer: LOY SPACE / popled.cn (active)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A programmable full-color LED backpack using the LOY SPACE protocol family, also seen in NYAN GEAR and other panels. The detailed spec is device-specs/devices/autobaba-led-backpack.yaml.

On 2026-11-07 this project used the documented protocol on one 64×64 unit. It completed a device-information query, a reversible brightness test, a read-only telecontrol query, and static plus eight-frame raw-GIF uploads. Every required acknowledgement was sequence-matched, checksum-valid and status zero.

docs.title: Hardware and identity
docs.text:
• Advertised names begin YS or TL and include a device serial. This is a platform match, not proof of an AUTOBABA controller revision. A LOY name belongs to the separate LOYPRO candidate.
  • Main display service: 0000fff0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb.
  • Display writes: 0000fff2-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, write-without-response only.
  • Display notifications: 0000fff1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, notify.
  • The tested information reply reported 64×64 geometry, fixed brightness 7 and remote support. Unit-specific identity and CID values are intentionally not published.

Rediscover by exact advertised name plus FFF0 rather than persisting an old address. A separate 5833ff01-9b8b-5191-6142-22a4536ef123 service was present but unused. It is an SBH OTA candidate only; do not send display, authentication or firmware commands there without a compatible capture and recovery path.

docs.title: Setup and pairing
docs.text:
Power the backpack and connect directly. No account, network provisioning or Bluetooth bond is established for the BLE display path. Do not infer Wi-Fi merely because the generic app supports it. The information reply's pwd token indicates password support, not whether a password is configured; use the owner's normal flow if one is set.

Subscribe to FFF1 before querying or sending a command. Use FFF2 with response=False. No factory reset is established; power-cycling only drops the connection and is not a factory wipe.

docs.title: Information query and geometry
docs.text:
This example asks for device information, panel parameters, power state and brightness. Sequence 1 is only a worked example; a client increments its sequence counter.

aa 55 ff ff 0e 00 01 00 c1 03 0a 00 1b 00 04 00 06 00 ff 03

The tested unit returned one complete 151-byte, checksum-valid reply. In panel TLV 0x1b, a leading panel-data-type byte is followed by little-endian width and height. 00 40 00 40 therefore means 64×64. This is deliberately different from SPOTLED's big-endian dimensions.

The reply's literal model field and version/capability strings are preserved in the research evidence but are not a retail-model identification. The initial 64×64 app state was not used as geometry evidence.

docs.title: Brightness
docs.text:
Fixed brightness uses TLV 06 02 00 <level>. The app offers 1–15 and maps zero to 15; only 6 and 7 were tested. Sequence 2 selected 6, sequence 3 restored 7, and a later information query confirmed the restored value:

aa 55 ff ff 0a 00 02 00 c1 02 06 02 00 06 da 03
aa 55 ff ff 0a 00 03 00 c1 02 06 02 00 07 dc 03

Both returned mode 0x82, matching sequence and status zero. This validates the command path and device-reported value; no visual brightness change was independently recorded.

docs.title: Frame and TLV format
docs.text:
The inner frame begins AA 55 FF FF, followed by little-endian length, sequence, flags/mode, TLV records and a little-endian additive checksum. Do not prepend the optional outer stream-record length to an individual GATT write.

Encoding Value length LL below 0x80 LL bytes 81 LL LL bytes, for 128–255 82 LL LH Little-endian 16-bit length, for 256 and above

Thus 13 81 c4 means TLV type 0x13 with 196 bytes of value. The official richer resource builder normally uses 960-byte logical chunks, a 997-byte TLV ceiling and a big-endian 16-bit chunk count. Those logical chunks are not GATT writes.

The simplified raw-GIF route is now confirmed on this unit:

  • 427-byte static GIF: READY, three 196-byte value chunks, FINALIZE.
  • 4558-byte, eight-frame GIF at 200 ms per frame: READY, 24 chunks, FINALIZE.
  • MTU 247 and 243-byte GATT writes; every required ACK had status zero.

READY example: aa 55 ff ff 0a 00 09 00 c1 02 08 02 00 00 dd 03. FINALIZE example: aa 55 ff ff 0b 00 0f 00 c1 02 36 03 01 00 00 14 04.

The simplified raw-GIF packet is aa55ffff | one-byte length | 00 <index> 00 | 27-byte sequence | total_chunks | 00 <index> 00 | c4000013 | 81c4 | 196-byte padded GIF data | little-endian u16 checksum. The first six payload bytes are GIF89a; pad every chunk, including the last, with zeros to exactly 196 bytes. Length is 0xed = 236 data bytes + 1, so a complete packet is 243 bytes (47 bytes of overhead). The spec's worked_chunk_hex is a complete index-0 example with checksum 0d09. Do not generalize these example sequence numbers or this chunk size to every firmware. A device-originated mode-06 message was also observed and remains undecoded.

docs.title: Remote and maintenance boundaries
docs.text:
A read-only telecontrol query (34 03 02 aa bc) returned remote model 43711 and 17 ordinary button mappings to programs 76–92. Four special records are not assigned invented meanings. The unit reported remote but not car_linkage, so this is remote- button configuration evidence, not proof of accelerometer or vehicle-triggered animations.

Power, rotation, playback, deletion, password, reset, official-app MTU behavior and the secondary maintenance protocol remain unverified.

docs.title: Bafang BBS02 Mid-Drive Motor
docs.text: Status: Research Protocol: UART (serial); BLE only via an aftermarket bridge display Manufacturer: Suzhou Bafang Electric Motor Science-Technology Manufacturer Status: Active (no official app or radio for this motor family)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The BBS02 is Bafang's 36–48 V mid-drive conversion kit (250–750 W), sharing a controller architecture and configuration protocol with the BBS01 and the BBSHD. The controller is integrated into the motor housing and speaks a simple 1200-baud UART protocol to the display over the kit's main harness.

The important thing for Liberated Bread: the BBS02 has no radio and no official app. There is no Bluetooth in the motor, and Bafang's own "Bafang Go"/BESST tooling targets the newer CAN-bus M-series (M500/M510/M600), not the BBS family. Everything that talks to a BBS02 does so over that UART bus. The app layer is therefore always something someone else bolted on:

Route Transport Notes Bafang Config Tool (Stefan Penov) USB programming cable → UART Windows; the de-facto standard for years OpenBafangTool USB cable → UART (also CAN) MIT-licensed, open source, supports BBS01/BBS02/BBSHD EggRider V2 display BLE → UART bridge Phone app (com.eggbikes.EggRider); read/write params with no cable bbs-fw replacement firmware Open-source firmware for the BBS02/BBSHD controller itself

This protocol is already open

Unlike most targets in this registry, the BBS02's configuration protocol is fully documented in public, MIT-licensed community work — there is no proprietary blob to liberate. The opcode tables below are transcribed from that work. The genuine gap is that reaching the bus still means a USB cable or a proprietary BLE display; a small open BLE↔UART bridge would close it. See the target sheet for that scope.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Family BBS01 / BBS01B, BBS02 / BBS02B, BBSHD (shared protocol) Nominal voltage 36 V or 48 V (BBSHD 48–52 V) Rated power 250 W / 350 W / 500 W / 750 W Controller Integrated in the motor housing Radio None — UART only Display bus 1200 baud serial, shared harness (display, throttle, brake cutoffs)

docs.title: Serial parameters
docs.text: Setting Value Baud rate 1200 Framing 8N1 (standard) Bus Shared display/controller line on the main harness

docs.title: Packet formats
docs.text:
Read request — most reads are bare code bytes (0x11 0x52, 0x11 0x53, 0x11 0x54) with no length or checksum. The device-info/connect read is the exception: it carries two payload bytes and a checksum, 0x11 0x51 0x04 0xB0 0x05, where 0x05 is (0x51 + 0x04 + 0xB0) mod 256. Do not assume every read is bare.

Read response:

Offset Length Description 0 1 Code — identifies which request this answers 1 1 Length — number of data bytes 2 n Data 2+n 1 Checksum — sum of all other bytes, mod 256

Write request:

Offset Length Description 0 2 Code — two-byte opcode 2 1 Length — number of data bytes 3 n Data 3+n 1 Checksum — sum of the second code byte, the length byte and all data bytes, mod 256

Write response:

Offset Length Description 0 1 Code 1 1 Error parameter index, or the length if no error 2 1 Checksum — sum of code and data, mod 256

The two checksum rules differ

Read responses sum every preceding byte. Write requests skip the first code byte. This asymmetry is the most common source of rejected writes.

docs.title: Read commands
docs.text: Code Returns Format 0x11 0x50 Firmware version ASCII (e.g. CRX10B4812E010026.3) 0x11 0x51 0x04 0xB0 0x05 Complete device info 16 bytes — manufacturer (4), model (4), hardware version (2), firmware version (4), voltage (1), max current (1) 0x11 0x52 Basic parameters 24 bytes — see below 0x11 0x53 Pedal assist parameters 11 bytes — see below 0x11 0x54 Throttle parameters 6 bytes — see below 0x14 0x12 Power specification code ASCII (e.g. MAX_DS48V250W) 0x14 0x13 System code ASCII (e.g. MAX01_V2.2_DS) 0x14 0x14 Serial number ASCII (e.g. 201608080001) 0x14 0x15 Error codes Byte array; empty when no faults 0x14 0x16 Model data ASCII (e.g. 20160808)

docs.title: Write commands
docs.text:
Each write takes the same payload layout as the matching read returns.

Code Writes Payload Advanced 0x16 0x52 Basic parameters 24 bytes Yes 0x16 0x53 Pedal assist parameters 11 bytes Yes 0x16 0x54 Throttle parameters 6 bytes Yes 0x17 0x01 Serial number ASCII Yes

Advanced — these retune a vehicle you ride

All four writes should carry advanced: true in any spec that declares them: available, behind a deliberate action, with the reason shown at that moment. Here is what each one actually costs you if it goes wrong:

  • Current limits are thermal limits. Raising max current beyond the motor's rating is the classic way to cook a BBS02's nylon primary gear or the controller MOSFETs. The motor will not stop you.
  • Low-voltage cutoff protects the battery. Setting it below the pack's real cutoff pushes cells into over-discharge.
  • Throttle and speed-limit settings change legal class. Enabling throttle-from-zero or lifting the speed limit can move the bike out of pedelec/EAPC classification — changing what licence, insurance and road access apply.
  • The serial number write is effectively irreversible and can break warranty and dealer-tool workflows. It has real uses — restoring identity after a controller swap is a normal repair-bench job — so it is documented like anything else; just know that there is no undo.

Read the block first and keep a copy. The write payload is the whole block, so a partial edit means writing back fields you did not intend to change — and an archived block is your restore path for every item above.

docs.title: Basic parameter block (0x52, 24 bytes)
docs.text:
Offsets are into the 24-byte data payload (i.e. the frame less its 0x52 code, length byte and trailing checksum — the full frame is 27 bytes).

Offset Length Field Encoding 0 1 Low battery protect volts 1 1 Current limit amps 2 10 Assist 0–9 current limit percent, one byte per level 12 10 Assist 0–9 speed limit percent, one byte per level 22 1 Wheel diameter code, 0x1F–0x3C for 16″–30″; 0x37 = 700C 23 1 Speedmeter model bits 1–2: 00 external, 01 internal, 10 motor phase

The assist limits are two arrays, not interleaved pairs

Current limits for levels 0–9 occupy ten consecutive bytes, then speed limits for levels 0–9 occupy the next ten. They are not ten (current, speed) pairs. Parsing them as pairs yields plausible-looking nonsense — every value lands on the wrong level and half of them are read as the wrong quantity. Corroborated across two independent implementations.

docs.title: Pedal assist parameter block (0x53, 11 bytes)
docs.text: Offset Field Encoding 0 Pedal sensor type 0x00 none, 0x01 DH-12, 0x02 BB-32, 0x03 double-signal-24 1 Designated assist 0x00–0x09, or 0xFF = follow display 2 Speed limit 0x0F–0x28 km/h, or 0xFF = follow display 3 Start current percent, 0x00–0x64 4 Slow-start mode 0x01–0x08 5 Startup degree pedal signal count before assist engages 6 Work mode 0x0A–0x50 (angular speed × 10) 7 Time of stop value × 10 ms 8 Current decay 0x01–0x08 9 Stop decay value × 10 ms 10 Keep current percent

docs.title: Throttle parameter block (0x54, 6 bytes)
docs.text:
Offset Field Encoding 0 Start voltage value × 100 mV 1 End voltage value × 100 mV 2 Mode 0x00 speed, 0x01 current 3 Designated assist 0x00–0x09, or 0xFF = follow display 4 Speed limit 0x0F–0x28 km/h, or 0xFF = follow display 5 Start current percent

Verification: reported, with one known ambiguity

Block sizes, field order and the encodings above are corroborated across three independent implementations (OpenBafangTool and two bafang-python forks), so they are reported — well attested, but not confirmed, because nothing here has been read back from a physical unit by us.

The write length byte is genuinely ambiguous. Sources give 0x16 0x52 0x24 for the basic-block write and 0x16 0x53 0x11 for the pedal block, yet the corresponding read responses carry lengths 0x18 (24) and 0x0B (11). 0x24 and 0x11 are exactly 24 and 11 written as if decimal were hex, which looks like a documentation slip propagated between forks — but it could equally be a real protocol quirk where writes use a different length convention. Capture a vendor-tool write before trusting either value. Nothing else in this doc depends on it.

docs.title: Device spec
docs.text:
device-specs/devices/bafang-bbs02.yaml carries this protocol as a machine-readable bus spec (protocol: uart, style: request_response), with every read and write above catalogued, the field tables encoded as fields entries, and the four writes flagged advanced.

The assist-limit trap is encoded rather than merely described: assist_current_limit and assist_speed_limit are two array_len: 10 fields at offsets 2 and 12, which is structurally unable to be read as ten interleaved pairs.

The write length byte is the one thing the spec deliberately does not assert — see the ambiguity note above. The write messages carry their 16 5x code and stop there.

docs.title: Related mid-drives
docs.text: The other common DIY mid-drive is the Tongsheng TSDZ2, and it is worth knowing it is a different bus, not a variant of this one: 9600 baud (not 1200), packets starting 0x43 motor→display and 0x59 display→motor, an 8-bit sum checksum, and a continuous telemetry stream (8 frames/second up, 15 down) rather than the request/response exchange used here. Its protocol is documented in full by the community, and open-source firmware already replaces the stock firmware outright. Tracked as tsdz2-tongsheng in targets.csv.
