docs.title: BanlanX / Sperll SP6xxE LED Controllers
docs.text: Status: In Progress Protocol: BLE (Wi-Fi provisioning on dual-mode models) Manufacturer: SPLED (BanlanX) / Shenzhen Sperll Optoelectronic Manufacturer Status: Active (closed protocol)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The SP6xxE family is a line of addressable-pixel (SPI) and analogue (PWM) LED strip controllers — SP601E through SP64xE — sold under the BanlanX/Sperll brand and driven by the SceneX app (com.spled.scenex). All of them are controllable locally over BLE with no account and no cloud; the vendor cloud (app.ledhue.com) only adds remote control, Alexa linking and firmware updates.

The family is already reverse engineered by the open-source UniLED Home Assistant integration, whose five BanlanX modules are the primary citation for everything on this page. What is new here: SceneX 3.3.2 adds an authenticated BLE channel ("ELS") on recent firmware that UniLED does not cover — see Open Questions.

One app, five frame formats

Every model uses the same GATT service (0xFFE0) and characteristic (0xFFE1), but the frame format depends on the model generation. Identify the model — from its manufacturer-data advertisement or a status query — before choosing a command set.

Models Role Frame format SP601E 2ch SPI RGB, music AA <op> <len> <payload…> SP602E / SP608E 4ch / 8ch SPI RGB, music 88 <op> <len> <payload…> SP611E / SP617E / SP620E / SP621E SPI/PWM ("v2") A0 <op> <len> <payload…> SP613E / SP614E / SP623E / SP624E SPI/PWM ("v3") <op> <len> <payload…> (no header) SP630E reconfigurable SPI/PWM combo 53 <cmd> <key> 01 00 <len> <payload…> SP631E–SP63AE / SP641E–SP64AE single-function SPI or PWM same 53 frame as SP630E

SP63xE models are BLE-only; SP64xE are the dual-mode (BLE + Wi-Fi) counterparts of the same eleven functions.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Models SP601E/602E/608E, SP611E/613E/614E/617E/620E/621E/623E/624E, SP630E–SP63AE, SP641E–SP64AE Chipset Custom firmware on a generic BLE SoC (no chip-vendor SDK in the app) Radio BLE; 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi on SP64xE dual-mode models LED support WS2812-family pixels (SPI models) and analog PWM strips (mono/CCT/RGB/RGBW/RGBCCT) Audio Built-in mic music-reactive modes; aux/player inputs on some models

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No for BLE control (all models) Method ble_direct; optional softap_http-style Wi-Fi provisioning on SP64xE Setup AP / advertised name Device SoftAP at 192.168.4.1 (2.4 GHz only) during Wi-Fi config Passphrase protection not_applicable (BLE); Wi-Fi handoff protection undocumented Confidence medium (BLE path per UniLED + app; SoftAP flow from app strings only)

BLE-only models advertise as soon as they are powered and accept a connection from any central — no account, no PIN, no bonding on legacy firmware. Dual-mode SP64xE units optionally receive Wi-Fi credentials through their own hotspot during the app's network-configuration flow; local BLE control never requires this.

Factory reset: not documented for this family. BLE models store no credentials, so there is nothing to clear — power-cycling drops the current connection, which is also the remedy for the common failure mode of the controller already being connected to another phone. On SP64xE units a reset would clear the stored Wi-Fi credentials; the physical procedure is unknown.

Rebinding to a new network: BLE models bind to nothing — just connect from the new controller (remove the OS-level Bluetooth entry on the old phone first, so it stops auto-reconnecting and holding the single link). For SP64xE Wi-Fi, re-run the SoftAP provisioning flow against the new network; no evidence the old network needs to be online.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 0000ffe0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb BanlanX LED Control Primary service on all models 0000ffe1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Control Write-without-response commands + status notifications 5833ff01..04-9b8b-5191-6142-22a4536ef123 ELS vendor characteristics New authenticated channel in SceneX 3.3.2 — unmapped, see Open Questions

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text: Signal Meaning Manufacturer data, company id 0x5053 ("SP" LE) BanlanX/SPLED family member …payload [model_id, 0x10] SP63xE/SP64xE; model_id 0x1F–0x35 identifies the exact model (0x1F SP630E … 0x35 SP64AE) …other first bytes (0x01, 0x02, 0x05, 0x17, 0x1B…) Older families (SP601E, SP602E, SP608E, SP617E, SP620E per UniLED) Service 0xFFE0 advertised Command service present

docs.title: SP6xxE commands (SP630E, SP63xE/SP64xE)
docs.text:
Frame: 53 <cmd> <key> 01 00 <len> <payload…>. key is 0x00 for plaintext; a nonzero key marks an encrypted payload (unsupported by UniLED — drop, don't parse). Written verbatim to 0xFFE1.

Command Bytes Description State query 53 02 00 01 00 01 01 Status returns as notification, cmd 0x02 Power on / off 53 50 00 01 00 01 0X X = 1 on, 0 off Brightness 53 51 00 01 00 02 W LL W: 0 color / 1 white level Static RGB + level 53 52 00 01 00 04 RR GG BB LL Static modes RGB color 53 57 00 01 00 03 RR GG BB Dynamic/sound modes Mode + effect 53 53 00 01 00 02 MM EE Mode 1–7 (static/dynamic/sound × color/white, custom) CCT 53 60 00 01 00 02 CC WW Cold/warm (0x61 in static modes) Effect speed / length 53 54 … VV / 53 55 … VV Direction / loop / play 53 56 … / 53 58 … / 53 5D … Audio input / gain 53 59 … / 53 5A … Gain 1–16 On/off animation 53 08 00 01 00 05 01 EE SS PH PL Effect 1–4, speed 1–3, pixels 1–600 BE Power-restore 53 0B … MM 0 off / 1 on / 2 last state Coexistence 53 0A … XX Drive SPI + PWM simultaneously Chip order 53 6B … OO RGB order index Light type (SP630E) 53 6A 00 01 00 02 01 TT Advanced — re-maps output hardware

The ~53-byte status payload carries the firmware version string, the light-type config byte (decode this first — it selects SPI/PWM and channel count), power, mode, effect, color/white levels, speed/length/direction, audio gain/input and more; the full offset table is in the machine-readable spec (device-specs/devices/banlanx-sp6xxe.yaml).

docs.title: SP601E commands
docs.text:
Frame: AA <opcode> <len> <payload…>. Channel byte addresses one output (master = channels−1 per UniLED).

Command Bytes Description State query AA 2F 00 Reply: 53 43-flagged multi-packet notification Power AA 22 02 CH 0X Per channel Brightness AA 25 02 CH LL Static RGB AA 29 05 CH RR GG BB FF Trailing FF fixed Effect AA 23 02 CH EE 0x19 solid, 0x01–0x18 dynamic, 0x65–0x74 sound Effect speed AA 26 02 CH SS 1–10 Scene AA 2E 01 NN Recall scene 1–9

The SP602E/608E (0x88 header), "v2" (0xA0 header) and "v3" (headerless) families follow the same shape with their own opcode maps — see the UniLED modules banlanx_60x.py, banlanx2.py, banlanx3.py.

docs.title: OTA and cloud
docs.text: Firmware updates are a custom BLE OTA (no Nordic DFU service). The app checks https://app.ledhue.com/spiot/device/check-update, which returns the firmware download. No firmware is mirrored here — query the endpoint on your own unit.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
• ELS authenticated channel (new in SceneX 3.3.2). Four vendor characteristics 5833ff01–04-… carry a connect-time auth handshake and an encrypted session backed by https://app.ledhue.com/spiot/els/v1. Cipher and message format unknown, and — critically — whether new firmware requires it or still accepts the legacy plaintext framing is untested. Needs an HCI snoop of a first-pairing session on a recent SP63xE/SP64xE.
  • All command bytes on this page are community-sourced (UniLED), not captured by this project — spot-verify on hardware.
  • Roles of 0000ff12/ff14/ff15 (likely an accessory/remote family) and of each 5833ff0x characteristic.
  • SoftAP provisioning exchange and the on-Wi-Fi control path of SP64xE models (local or cloud-relayed?).

docs.title: Beddit Sleep Tracker (Bluetooth Classic generation)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (static analysis of the last Android app; no capture, no hardware) Protocol: Bluetooth Classic (SPP over RFCOMM, insecure socket) Manufacturer: Beddit (Apple) Manufacturer Status: Shutdown: cloud off since 2018-11-15, hardware discontinued, apps pulled

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Beddit made thin sensor strips that lie under the bed sheet and record ballistocardiography (BCG): the tiny mechanical forces that the heartbeat, breathing and body movement put into a mattress. Apple bought Beddit in 2017, shut Beddit Cloud down on 2018-11-15, stopped selling the hardware in 2022 and pulled the apps in 2024.

The last Android app (2.3.12) drives three sensor generations. This page covers the one it reaches over Bluetooth Classic, which the app tags with the hardware type BT2. The two BLE generations (BTLE and BTLEv3) are documented separately in Beddit Sleep Monitor 3 / 3.5.

The protocol is small: an insecure SPP socket, a two-line ASCII handshake (OK, INFO), then START 5 and a stream of CRC-32-checked binary frames of raw 16-bit force samples. While streaming, the host sends CONT about every ten frames (first after frame 10, then before every 11th frame), and it sends STOP at the end.

The sensor sends only the raw waveform. The app computes sleep stages, heart rate, respiration and the sleep score on the phone, in a native signal-processing library it bundles. So a client built from this spec gets a live BCG signal, and deriving heart rate or sleep stages from it is a separate job. The app has no command that downloads a stored night.

Which product is this?

The research this page started from calls this sensor the "Beddit 2 (Smart)", and the spec file keeps that name (beddit-2-sleep-tracker). The evidence points elsewhere:

  • Beddit Smart, which retail listings titled "Beddit 2.0 Smart Sleep Tracker" (2015), connected over Bluetooth Smart, which is BLE (Sleep Review, 2015).
  • Beddit's November 2015 Android announcement names two supported products: Beddit Smart and Beddit Classic.
  • In October 2015 a commenter who said he worked for Beddit in the US described them as "Classic (the original) and Smart", with Bluetooth Smart and automatic tracking only on the Smart (9to5Mac, reader comment; a weak source).
  • The app has exactly two pre-Beddit-3 hardware types: BT2, reached over Classic SPP, and BTLE, the GATT service f82fd8a8-329d-4c44-a178-e82f91ec9fe6 in the BLE spec. Beddit 3 is BTLEv3. The three labels name radios, not products.
  • Wolfram's device catalogue lists the original Beddit Sleep Tracker as Bluetooth 2.0.
  • The app's server-side replacement check covers BT2 and BTLE and exempts only Beddit 3. In April 2017 Beddit told owners of every pre-Beddit-3 sensor that it would stop working with the app, and offered a free Beddit 3 in exchange (Wareable).

So BT2 is most likely the first-generation Beddit (2013, later sold as "Beddit Classic"), and "BT2" most likely stands for Bluetooth 2.x rather than "Beddit 2". Beddit Smart 2.0 is most likely the app's BTLE type. One fact strains this: the first generation launched with an iPhone app (Cult of Mac, 2013), the 2015 comment says the Classic still worked with the iOS app of the day, and an SPP-only sensor reaches an iPhone only through Apple's MFi accessory channel. This is a hypothesis. A Classic inquiry of a labelled unit would settle it.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Product Beddit sensor strip, Bluetooth Classic generation (most likely the 2013 first generation / "Beddit Classic"; see above) Sensor Thin-film force sensor under the sheet (ballistocardiography) Radio Bluetooth Classic (BR/EDR), SPP. Bluetooth 2.0 per Wolfram's catalogue (weak source). Classic-only: no BLE side Bluetooth module Bluegiga: the app treats the Bluegiga OUI 00:07:80 as the mark of this generation. The module model is unknown Power Mains power adapter, per the app's setup text Companion apps Beddit for Android (last version 2.3.12, delisted). An iPhone app from the 2013 launch on, which reached the sensor by a route nobody has analysed (see the Bluetooth Classic profile table) FCC ID None found. No Beddit filing covers this generation; the module's own grant is unidentified Manual None found

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method none (insecure RFCOMM socket, nothing to provision) Inquiry name Starts with beddit, compared case-insensitively. Real name unrecorded; probably includes the device number printed on the back Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence low (static analysis only)
  1. Lay the strip on the bed under the bottom sheet and plug its power adapter into the wall. The app's instructions say no more than this. Exact placement on the mattress is not recorded.
  2. Run a Bluetooth Classic inquiry and pick the device whose name starts with beddit. A household with several strips tells them apart by the device number on the back of each one.
  3. Open an insecure RFCOMM socket to SPP 00001101-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb. If that fails, wait about 2 s and connect straight to RFCOMM channel 1, as the app does.
  4. Send OK, then INFO. Save the address, the channel order, the sample rate and the version.

That is the whole of the vendor app's "setup". It closes the socket after INFO and reconnects by address for each night, and never scans again.

Factory reset: none known, and nothing known to clear. The app writes nothing to the sensor except the five session lines, and it never bonds. For a wedged sensor, unplug the adapter for a few seconds. That is a power cycle, not a reset.

Rebinding: nothing is bound. A new phone or client just connects.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No (reported) Security mode none: insecure RFCOMM socket Bonding none: the app never bonds PIN source n/a (no PIN known) One central at a time Unknown (probably: serial modules usually carry one SPP link) One bond at a time n/a Confidence low

The app opens the socket insecure and has no code that bonds, sets a PIN or reacts to a pairing request. It never tells the user to pair in the OS settings either. A module that demanded authentication would make Android show a PIN dialog the app never mentions, so the firmware almost certainly accepts an unauthenticated link. Bonding is recorded as none, the catalogue's rule for a device whose only profile is opened insecure. The one doubt is a module with Bluetooth 2.1 or later: the phone's stack might run Secure Simple Pairing Just Works on its own and keep a key. That would not change what a client does.

Entering pairing mode: no button and no window are known. The app asks only for power and a phone nearby.

Unpairing: nothing to unpair.

Recovery: close the vendor app, which holds the socket all night while recording, then power-cycle the strip.

docs.title: Bluetooth Classic profile
docs.text:
Property Value Control profile SPP 00001101-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, RFCOMM channel 1 (the app's fallback; SDP not browsed) Socket Insecure (no bond) Dual-mode No iOS reachable No, not through CoreBluetooth, which has no RFCOMM. The vendor's iPhone app (2013 onwards) implies an MFi (iAP) route that nobody has analysed, and that app is gone from the App Store Android Yes: the vendor app's own path, Android 4.0 and up Linux Should work: a plain BlueZ RFCOMM socket, no agent (hypothesis, untested) macOS IOBluetooth exposes RFCOMM; untested

The app decides at scan time whether a beddit… device is BLE or Classic:

Android reports App uses LE BLE path (the other spec) Classic or dual-mode This SPP path Unknown type, address starts 00:07:80 This SPP path Unknown type, any other address BLE path (Android older than 4.3) Always this SPP path

docs.title: Session
docs.text:
All text is US-ASCII, and each line ends in a single LF (0x0a), with no CR.

Step Host sends Bytes Sensor answers App's limits 1 OK 4f 4b 0a OK + LF, exactly 5 s, LF within the first 10 bytes 2 INFO 49 4e 46 4f 0a one line: INFO + KEY:VALUE;… 5 s, 999 bytes before the LF 3 nothing Idle until a recording starts. No keep-alive, no timeout 4 START 5 53 54 41 52 54 20 35 0a binary frames, no text ack each read 5 s 5 CONT 43 4f 4e 54 0a nothing once 10 frames have arrived, then before every 11th 6 STOP 53 54 4f 50 0a unknown (the app reads nothing) only on an orderly stop

The meaning of the 5 in START 5 is not visible in the app, which always sends that literal. What the sensor does without CONT is unknown, so copy the app's cadence.

docs.title: INFO reply
docs.text:
INFO, then pairs separated by ;. Each pair splits at its first :. Keys are trimmed and case-insensitive, and values are trimmed. A value containing , is a list.

Key Required Meaning CHANNELS yes Channel names, comma-separated, in the order their samples are interleaved. The app renames normal to force and keeps only that channel SAMPLERATE yes Samples per second per channel, in Hz. Decimal; the app parses it as a float VERSION no Firmware version string (the app records undefined when absent)

No real INFO line has been recorded. The shape is INFO CHANNELS:<name1>,<name2>;SAMPLERATE:<hz>;VERSION:<fw>, and every value in it is a placeholder.

docs.title: Stream frame
docs.text:
Offset Length Field Type Notes 0 4 counter uint32 LE 0 for the first frame after START, then +1 per frame 4 2 payload length L uint16 LE, bytes The app rejects anything over 65000 6 L payload bytes Interleaved samples ch0[0], ch1[0], …, ch0[1], …. Each sample is a uint16 LE. L / (2 × N) samples per channel for N channels 6 + L 4 CRC-32 uint32 LE Over bytes 0 … 6+L−1 (header and payload)
  • Samples are raw, uncalibrated force counts. The app declares the force channel to its analysis as unsigned 16-bit. Sample n was taken n / SAMPLERATE s after the first sample following START.
  • CRC is the standard zlib / IEEE 802.3 CRC-32 (CRC-32/ISO-HDLC): reflected polynomial 0xedb88320, init 0xffffffff, final XOR 0xffffffff, check value 0xcbf43926. The app verifies with the platform's standard CRC-32, so this is the variant it accepted.
  • Errors: a counter gap, an oversize length or a CRC mismatch ends the session. There is no resync. Close the socket, reconnect and handshake again.
  • Timing: each of a frame's three reads (header, payload, CRC) must complete within 5 s, or the app drops the link.

Test vectors (invented values):

Frame bytes Decodes to 00 00 00 00 08 00 02 01 04 03 06 05 08 07 a0 8f 12 8f counter 0, L 8, two channels: ch0 = 258, 1286; ch1 = 772, 1800; CRC 0x8f128fa0 01 00 00 00 04 00 00 80 ff 7f 01 cb 72 25 counter 1, L 4: ch0 = 32768, ch1 = 32767; CRC 0x2572cb01 
import socket, struct, zlib

s = socket.socket(socket.AF_BLUETOOTH, socket.SOCK_STREAM, socket.BTPROTO_RFCOMM)
s.connect(("aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff", 1))           # your strip's address, RFCOMM channel 1
f = s.makefile("rb")

def line():
    return f.readline().rstrip(b"\n").decode("ascii")

s.sendall(b"OK\n")
assert line() == "OK"
s.sendall(b"INFO\n")
info = line()
fields = {}
for part in info[len("INFO"):].split(";"):     # same rules as the app's parser
    if ":" in part:
        key, value = part.split(":", 1)
        fields[key.strip().upper()] = value.strip()
chans = [c.strip() for c in fields["CHANNELS"].split(",")]
rate_hz = float(fields["SAMPLERATE"])
force = chans.index("normal")                  # the app's "force" channel

s.sendall(b"START 5\n")
expected, since_cont = 0, 0
while True:
    since_cont += 1
    if since_cont > 10:                        # the app's CONT cadence
        s.sendall(b"CONT\n")
        since_cont = 0
    hdr = f.read(6)
    counter, length = struct.unpack("<IH", hdr)
    payload = f.read(length)
    (crc,) = struct.unpack("<I", f.read(4))
    assert counter == expected and zlib.crc32(hdr + payload) == crc
    expected += 1
    per_chan = length // (2 * len(chans))      # the app ignores any remainder
    samples = struct.unpack(f"<{per_chan * len(chans)}H", payload[:per_chan * len(chans) * 2])
    force_samples = samples[force::len(chans)]

The sketch is untested and has no timeouts. The app gives up on any read that takes more than 5 s.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
These are defects in the vendor app, found in the static read. They explain failures an owner still running the old app will see, and they are traps a new client should not copy.

Symptom Cause The old Android app fails setup, or cancels every recording, with an error saying the server could not be reached After each connection to a BT2 (or BTLE) sensor, the app asks Beddit's replacement service (replacements.beddit.com) whether the sensor is blocked, and it treats a network error as fatal. The host returns NXDOMAIN (checked 2026-09-28). The vendor app cannot be used with this sensor any more. A client built from this spec needs no server Session ends right after INFO The app's parser cannot take a CHANNELS value with no comma (one channel), or a VERSION that contains a comma Session ends on a large frame The app reads the payload length sign-extended, so 32768–65535 ends the session. Read it unsigned Recording dies on one bad frame No resync: any counter gap or CRC error is fatal Handshake fails on a reconnect The app sends STOP only on an orderly stop. After a crash the sensor may still be streaming (unconfirmed). Close, wait and retry An iPhone never sees the strip CoreBluetooth has no RFCOMM. No workaround is known; the only other iOS route is MFi, which needs the vendor's own app

docs.title: Cloud (dead)
docs.text:
Host Role cloudapi.beddit.com Account sign-in and history sync (Beddit Cloud, shut down 2018-11-15) replacements.beddit.com Sensor blocking and replacement check (GET /blocking_status/<address without colons>?hardware_type=BT2), which blocks the old app today

Neither is part of the sensor protocol.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Which product this is (see the warning above).
  • The inquiry name, the Class of Device and the SDP record.
  • What 5 in START 5 means, and what CONT does.
  • A real INFO line: channel names beyond normal, the sample rate and the version format.
  • Whether the module ever asks for a PIN, and whether it stores a bond.
  • How the 2013 iPhone app reached the sensor. An MFi (iAP) channel beside SPP would explain it. Finding none would cast doubt on the first-generation mapping.
  • Buttons, LEDs, and whether a reset exists.

An Android Bluetooth HCI snoop log of the old app would answer most of these. Its setup wizard runs OK and INFO before the dead-server check fails, so even a failed setup attempt captures the handshake and a real INFO line. See Common Bluetooth Classic Patterns.

docs.title: Beddit Sleep Monitor 3 / 3.5
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (read from the last Android app; not yet replayed against hardware) Protocol: BLE (vendor GATT service, two layouts) Manufacturer: Beddit Oy, acquired by Apple in 2017 Manufacturer Status: Shutdown (cloud off 2018-11-15, hardware discontinued 2022, apps removed 2024)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Beddit made thin under-mattress sensor strips that measure ballistocardiography (BCG): the tiny body movements caused by each heartbeat and breath. Apple bought the company in May 2017, shut down Beddit Cloud on 2018-11-15 and launched a model 3.5 a few weeks later, in December 2018. It stopped selling the hardware in January 2022 and removed the iOS apps for models 3.0 and 3.5 from the App Store in September 2024. Android support had been dropped earlier. Owners are left with working sensors and no app.

The main finding is what the strip actually sends: a raw force waveform, nothing else. Sleep stages, heart rate, respiration, efficiency and the sleep score were all computed on the phone, by a native analysis library bundled with the app, from that live stream. Snoring came from the phone's own microphone. The protocol itself is small and open: no pairing, no authentication, no stored history. A client can collect the waveform after a few reads and a one-byte write. Getting the numbers the app showed means reimplementing BCG analysis, which is outside this spec.

Every protocol fact here comes from a static read of com.beddit.beddit 2.3.12, the last Android build available to us, so it is verification: reported. There are no captures. The FCC listings for both models and the model 3.5's user guide and radio test report (Internet Archive copies) add hardware and setup facts, and none of them describes the protocol.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Model Number Beddit 3 (model 3.0, 2016) and Beddit 3.5 (model 3.5, December 2018). Apple part numbers MR9P2LL/A (3.0) and MUFM2LL/A (3.5), from the store links in MacRumors' coverage Form Flexible strip about 2 mm thick, laid on the mattress under the sheet Power USB cable to the supplied USB power adapter. No battery ("nothing to charge"). The 3.5 guide warns against powering it from a computer's USB port Chipset Unknown. The 3.5's schematic, block diagram and parts list were filed as confidential Radio Bluetooth Low Energy only. Both filings list one 2402–2480 MHz line, equipment class DTS, and no Classic (DSS) line FCC ID 2AI4U-B3: Beddit 3, filed by Beddit Oy (application dated 2016-08-12), about 1.5 mW. Only the listing summary was seen; its exhibits were not reachable. BCG-B35: model 3.5, filed by Apple, granted December 2018, 5.02 dBm peak conducted output, integrated antenna, test firmware v004ef1

Beddit 3 was also sold as measuring room temperature and humidity. The Android app's BLE session reads no characteristic for either (see Open questions).

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name Name starting with beddit, compared case-insensitively (the app's filter; the real name has never been seen in a scan) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence low (read from the app only)

The app's onboarding: lay the strip on the mattress under the sheet, plug its power adapter into the wall, then connect. The model 3.5 user guide adds the placement: across the mattress, dark rubber side down, at chest level and clear of the pillows, on top of any mattress protector and under the fitted sheet, on your own side of a shared bed. There is no button and no pairing-mode step.

With several sensors in range, the Android app tells the owner to find the device number on the back of the strip, and the 3.5 guide says the ID number is printed on the cable close to the sensor. Both suggest that each unit's advertised name carries that number. Nobody has confirmed it with a scan.

Factory reset: none is known, and none seems needed. As far as the app shows, the sensor holds no bond, credential or owner binding. The only candidate procedure is generic: unplug the adapter for about ten seconds. It is not from any Beddit document and has not been tried.

Rebinding: nothing ties the strip to a phone at the BLE layer. Connect from the new client once the old one has let go of the link.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No (inferred) Security mode none Bonding none PIN source not applicable One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time not applicable Confidence low

The app opens a plain GATT connection (no autoConnect) and never requests a bond. That fits open GATT but does not prove it. Android pairs automatically when a characteristic answers "insufficient authentication", so the app's code would look the same if the sensor asked for Just Works pairing somewhere.

Entering pairing mode: not needed. There is no button and the app has no pairing-mode step.

Unpairing: nothing is bonded, so there is nothing to clear.

Recovery: if the sensor cannot be found or connected to, close or uninstall the vendor app on any phone that used it, then power-cycle the strip.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
The app connects, discovers services and walks them in discovery order. It uses whichever of the two Beddit services it meets first and aborts if it finds neither.

Layout Service App's hardware-type label Channels BTLEv3 e6807d20-b90a-11e5-a837-0800200c9a66 BTLEv3/<hw rev> 2, self-describing BTLE f82fd8a8-329d-4c44-a178-e82f91ec9fe6 BTLE/<hw rev> 1, "force"

e6807d20-… is a time-based UUID minted on 2016-01-12, seven months before Beddit Oy filed the Beddit 3 radio with the FCC (2AI4U-B3) and nine months before Beddit 3 reached shops. So the BTLEv3 layout is very likely Beddit 3. Whether the Beddit 3.5 uses it too is assumed but not shown: this Android app may predate the 3.5.

Two things point to the BTLE layout being an earlier generation. Its label has no "v3". And the app sends BTLE sensors, like the classic-Bluetooth ones, through a server-side replacement check that BTLEv3 sensors skip. The Bluetooth Classic spec argues from 2015 press coverage that it is the Beddit Smart (2015). That has not been verified here, and which retail models used the BTLE layout is not established.

docs.title: BLE Services: BTLEv3 layout
docs.text:
UUID Name Properties Description e6807d20-b90a-11e5-a837-0800200c9a66 Sensor service Selects this layout e6807d21-b90a-11e5-a837-0800200c9a66 Control point read, write Write 01 to start streaming. Read once at connect (value unused) e6807d22-b90a-11e5-a837-0800200c9a66 Status read, notify Subscribed to but never acted on. Byte 0 is a bitfield; the app's code tests bit 0x02 e6807e21-b90a-11e5-a837-0800200c9a66 Channel 1 description read See below e6807e20-b90a-11e5-a837-0800200c9a66 Channel 1 data notify Sample packets e6807e25-b90a-11e5-a837-0800200c9a66 Channel 2 description read See below e6807e24-b90a-11e5-a837-0800200c9a66 Channel 2 data notify Sample packets

Earlier write-ups have these roles wrong

One gave the service as e6807e20-…. Another paired the descriptions with e6807e20/e6807e24 and the data with e6807e21/e6807e25. The app's session code reads e6807e21 and e6807e25 and parses them as descriptions. It subscribes to e6807e20 and e6807e24 and parses their notifications as samples. To check on a real unit without trusting either version: the description is the readable one with ASCII u2 at bytes 2–3.

docs.title: BLE Services: BTLE layout
docs.text: UUID Name Properties Description f82fd8a8-329d-4c44-a178-e82f91ec9fe6 Sensor service Selects this layout f82fd8aa-329d-4c44-a178-e82f91ec9fe6 Sample rate read uint16 LE, whole Hz f82fd8a9-329d-4c44-a178-e82f91ec9fe6 Control and force data write, notify Write 01 to start; force packets arrive as notifications

docs.title: Device Information (both layouts)
docs.text:
UUID Name App's use 00002a25-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Serial Number String Sensor serial 00002a27-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Hardware Revision String Appended to the hardware-type label 00002a26-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Firmware Revision String Labelled the bootloader version 00002a28-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Software Revision String Main firmware version

All four are read at connect under service 0000180a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb. The app aborts the session if any of them is missing.

docs.title: Session sequence
docs.text:
1. Connect. Do not bond.
  2. Discover services and pick the layout.

  3. Read the four Device Information strings, then:

    • BTLEv3: e6807d21, e6807d22, e6807e21, e6807e25
    • BTLE: f82fd8aa

    Do one read at a time. 4. Enable notifications (CCCD 01 00), one descriptor write at a time: - BTLEv3: e6807d22, e6807e20, e6807e24 - BTLE: f82fd8a9 5. To start recording, write 01 to e6807d21 (BTLEv3) or f82fd8a9 (BTLE). 6. Decode notifications until done, then disconnect. No stop command exists.

docs.title: Command: Start streaming
docs.text:
Request: write one byte to the control characteristic.

Offset Length Description 0 1 0x01

Response: no acknowledgement is documented. Sample notifications simply begin.

docs.title: Channel description (BTLEv3, read)
docs.text:
Offset Length Description 0 2 Sample rate × 100, uint16 little-endian (raw / 100.0 Hz) 2 2 ASCII type code. Must be u2 (75 32) = uint16 samples. Anything else aborts the app 4 to end Channel name, UTF-8, at least 1 byte

The value must be at least 5 bytes. The app's analysis needs one channel named exactly force, and processes samples in 0.2-second frames, so a real sample rate is a multiple of 5 Hz. The actual rates and the second channel's name are unknown.

Example (constructed, not a capture): 10 27 75 32 66 6f 72 63 65 → 100.00 Hz, uint16, force.

docs.title: Sample packet (BTLEv3, notify on e6807e20 / e6807e24)
docs.text:
Offset Length Description 0 1 Sequence counter, uint8, per channel, wraps 255 → 0 1 2 × n n ≥ 1 samples, uint16 little-endian, raw sensor counts

The length is odd and at least 3. Example (constructed): 00 10 27 11 27 12 27 → sequence 0, samples 10000, 10001, 10002.

docs.title: Force packet (BTLE, notify on f82fd8a9)
docs.text:
Offset Length Description 0 1 Packet type, 0x80 or 0x90. Anything else aborts the app. The difference between the two is unknown 1 1 Sequence counter, uint8, wraps 255 → 0 2 2 × n n ≥ 1 force samples, uint16 little-endian

The length is even and at least 4. Example (constructed): 80 00 e8 03 e9 03 ea 03 → type 0x80, sequence 0, samples 1000, 1001, 1002.

docs.title: Lost packets
docs.text: The app keeps one expected-sequence counter per channel. It starts at 0 when notifications open and becomes (sequence + 1) mod 256 after each packet. When a packet's sequence does not match, the app works out lost = (sequence − expected) mod 256 packets. It then inserts lost × (samples in this packet) copies of this packet's second sample before the packet's own samples. For example, with 5 expected and 07 10 27 20 27 30 27 received, the app emits six copies of 10016, then 10000, 10016, 10032. Packets carry no timestamp, so sample n of a channel falls at n / rate seconds.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
These are defects and quirks found in the app's code. A replacement client should know about them.

  • The vendor app cannot record a BTLE-layout sensor any more. After connecting to a sensor whose layout is not BTLEv3, the app asks replacements.beddit.com whether the sensor is blocked. It does this in the setup wizard and again before every recording. A network failure is fatal: the app shows an error and abandons setup or cancels the night. Neither that host nor cloudapi.beddit.com resolved on 2026-09-28. The sensor takes no part in this check, so a client built from this spec is unaffected. BTLEv3 sensors skip the check.
  • Status is ignored. The app subscribes to e6807d22 but does not route its notifications to the routine that would decode them. That routine does nothing anyway. The status bits have never been used, so nothing depends on them.
  • Start race on the BTLE layout. The app reports the session as open as soon as it sends the notification-enable write on f82fd8a9, without waiting for it to complete. A client should wait for the CCCD write to complete before writing 01.
  • Padding is crude. Lost packets are filled with repeats of the next packet's second sample, not interpolated. A one-sample packet pads with 0, and the app assumes the lost packets were the same size. It also assumes the counter starts at 0: if the sensor's first packet carries any other sequence number, the app pads at the very start of the recording. Record the gap instead if your analysis can cope with one.
  • No reconnect. Any GATT error or disconnect ends the recording. The app does not reconnect mid-night.
  • All four Device Information strings are required. The app aborts if one is missing. A client need not.
  • Dual-mode routing. Once a name has matched, the app uses BLE only when Android reports the device as LE. A device that Android reports as classic or dual-mode goes to the classic SPP path, which belongs to an older sensor generation. So does a device of unknown type whose address starts with the Bluegiga OUI 00:07:80. A client written for this spec should connect over LE regardless.
  • One Samsung handset. On the Galaxy S III (GT-I9300) the app runs a 2-second LE scan before connecting. This is a quirk of that phone, not of the sensor.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
• Sleep analysis. Stages, heart rate, respiration and score are computed by the app, not sent by the sensor.
  • The classic-Bluetooth sensor generation. The same app drives it over SPP; see Beddit Sleep Tracker (Bluetooth Classic).
  • Beddit Cloud (cloudapi.beddit.com), shut down on 2018-11-15, and the replacement service (replacements.beddit.com). The sensor never needed either to stream.
  • Firmware update. The Android app has no OTA or DFU code and carries no firmware images.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• The advertised name, address type, and any advertised service UUIDs.
  • Which retail models use each layout, and whether the 3.5 exposes e6807d20 at all.
  • Real sample rates and channel names.
  • What the e6807d22 status bits mean, and what distinguishes packet type 0x80 from 0x90.
  • Whether any characteristic indicates rather than notifies.
  • Whether the sequence counter restarts on each connection or on each start write.
  • Whether more than one central can connect, and whether the sensor accepts or asks for a bond.
  • Where Beddit 3's room temperature and humidity readings travel. They might be the second BTLEv3 channel, or they might exist only in the iOS app's protocol.
  • Whether the sensor stops streaming by itself, for example when the bed is empty.
  • The chipset, and what the Beddit 3 filing's exhibits (2AI4U-B3) say.

docs.title: Beurer PO60 Pulse Oximeter
docs.text: Status: Capture verified (existing Android HCI capture; not driven end to end by this project) Protocol: BLE (custom GATT service — not the standard PLX profile) Manufacturer: Beurer GmbH (Ulm, Germany) Manufacturer Status: Active (no cloud dependency at all — the device is phone-to-device over BLE only)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Beurer PO60 is a Bluetooth Smart (BLE 4.0) fingertip pulse oximeter. It measures SpO2 and pulse rate, keeps up to 100 measurement sessions on-device, and syncs them to a phone over a small custom GATT protocol. It is one of the easiest devices in this knowledge base to liberate: there is no cloud in the loop at all — the only radio is BLE, the companion apps work in guest mode, and the entire sync protocol is three commands.

Medical device

SpO2 and pulse values synced through this spec are a personal log, not a clinical measurement, and must never decide whether someone needs oxygen, a medication or urgent care. Chart them if you like; act on the device's own display and a professional's advice. The spec carries a safety_advisory saying so.

The protocol was recovered from two companion apps and cross-verified between them: the legacy beurer HealthManager (com.beurer.connect.healthmanager v2.17, unobfuscated) and the current beurer HealthManager Pro (com.beurer.healthmanager v1.17.1, obfuscated Kotlin). A third-party, hardware-tested Python (bleak) script — Shreyan1/Beurer-PO60-PulseOximeter-Bluetooth-Integration — independently uses the same UUIDs and command bytes, and is a working reference client.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Model Number Beurer PO60 Aliases PO60, PO 60 Category / hierarchy health + ["measurement", "health", "pulse_oximetry"] Manufacturer Beurer GmbH Companion app Current: beurer HealthManager Pro (com.beurer.healthmanager); older manuals name regional/historical apps Chipset Unknown — firmware uses the "ilink" BLE SDK family shared across the Beurer/Sanitas medical line Radio BLE 4.0 (Bluetooth Smart) only — no Wi-Fi, no other radio FCC ID Not found — the US manual carries only a generic Part 15 statement; needs a label photo / fccid.io visual search

Color OLED display; stores up to 100 measurement sessions. No firmware-update path exists in either app, and no firmware image is public.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No — nothing to provision (no network, no account) Method ble_direct (connect during SYNC, bond, download history) Setup AP / advertised name Advertises with the exact local name PO60 Passphrase protection not_applicable (no Wi-Fi); BLE bonding uses a random six-digit PIN shown on the PO60 display Confidence medium (vendor workflow and SMP bonding confirmed; complete client flow not replayed here)

Enable Bluetooth on both devices and open a compatible app, or have a third-party client ready to connect. After a measurement, remove your finger: the PO60 enters SYNC and tries to connect for approximately ten seconds. To transfer stored measurements later, hold the function button for five seconds while the PO60 is switched off until SYNC appears. The device's Bluetooth setting must be ON for either route.

  1. Scan for the exact name PO60 and connect during the SYNC window.
  2. On first pairing, enter the random six-digit PIN shown on the PO60 display, not a fixed PIN from the manual. Reuse a valid existing bond on later transfers.
  3. Enable notifications on the FF02 characteristic.
  4. Set the clock (command 0x83); the device acks with F3 00.
  5. Query the stored-record count (90 05 15), then page the history log (see below) through its end marker. The PO60 transfers all stored measurements and switches off automatically.

Do not hold an idle connection expecting live SpO2 notifications. How reliably a third-party central can reuse the bond, and whether an unbonded client can write the time-set command, remain open.

Factory reset / memory clearing: no owner-accessible procedure to clear the stored measurements is documented, and no reset procedure was found in either app or the examined manuals. The device holds measurement history plus BLE bonding state. Don't guess one — to move the device to a new phone, remove the old bond in the previous phone's OS Bluetooth settings and re-pair using the newly displayed PIN; measurement history survives.

Rebinding: in place, no reset needed — ordinary BLE re-bonding.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
All UUIDs are 16-bit aliases on the standard 0000xxxx-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb base.

UUID Name Description 0xFF12 Pulse Oximeter service The only application service 0xFF01 Command Client writes all commands here 0xFF02 Response / data Acks and measurement data, as notifications

Full GATT discovery in the reviewed capture found no standard BLE Pulse Oximeter profile (0x1822 PLX), agreeing with both apps. No application-layer encryption was found: BLE bonding is the only protection, and all numeric fields are 7-bit-masked integers.

docs.title: Command: Read storage info
docs.text:
Request (write to FF01): 90 05 15

Response (notify on FF02): carries the number of stored measurement records. Exact length/offset of the count byte is not yet pinned down (open question).

docs.title: Command: Set date/time
docs.text:
Request (write to FF01):

Offset Length Description 0 1 Command ID 0x83 1 1 Year − 2000 2 1 Month 3 1 Day 4 1 Hour 5 1 Minute 6 1 Second 7–8 2 00 00 pad 9 1 Checksum: (sum of bytes 0–8) & 0x7F

Response: ack F3 00 on FF02. (The legacy app wrote placeholder 05 05 05 in the seconds/pad positions; the Pro app sends real seconds — send real time.)

docs.title: Command: Get measurements page
docs.text:
Request (write to FF01): 99 pp CKS — pp = 0x00 START / 0x01 NEXT; for this command the checksum is (pp - 0x67) & 0x7F, giving the observed wire bytes 99 00 19 and 99 01 1A.

Response (notify on FF02): measurement records stream as 20-byte notification chunks; concatenate and slice into 24-byte records. The app issues 99 01 1A every 12 records (page size 12 inferred, not confirmed) until the end-of-transfer record arrives, then disconnects ~3 s later.

Record layout (24 bytes, after reassembly):

Offset Length Description 0 1 Header 0xE9 1 1 Low nibble = record index; high nibble 0x4 = end-of-transfer 2–7 6 Start time: year−2000, month, day, hour, minute, second 8–13 6 End time, same layout 14 1 Pulse-rate escape flags: bit 2 → +128 to PR max, bit 3 → PR min, bit 4 → PR avg 15–16 2 Unknown 17 1 SpO2 max (%) 18 1 SpO2 min (%) 19 1 SpO2 avg (%) 20 1 PR max (bpm) 21 1 PR min (bpm) 22 1 PR avg (bpm) 23 1 Unknown

All value fields are plain 7-bit integers; pulse-rate values ≥ 128 escape via the flag byte at offset 14.

docs.title: Cloud Dependency & Home Assistant Guidance
docs.text:
There is nothing to keep alive. The PO60 never touches the internet: no Wi-Fi, no cloud, no account. Beurer's HealthManager clouds (sync.connect-beurer.com, hmpro[-us].connect.beurer.com, SSO hosts) exist only as optional sync storage inside the phone apps, both of which also run in guest mode — and Beurer is a healthy, actively-maintained vendor anyway. Any cloud shutdown, today or in ten years, changes nothing for this device.

For Home Assistant: no HA/ESPHome integration exists yet. A small bleak script (or an ESPHome Bluetooth proxy driving one) can use the Shreyan1 repository as a starting point, but should connect during the device-initiated SYNC window rather than polling for continuous samples. The reviewed capture shows a clock write and a bounded history transfer, not live measurements; the record parser still needs validation against annotated real readings.

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
• [x] App static analysis (HealthManager 2.17 and HealthManager Pro 1.17.1)
  • [x] Vendor manuals and PLUX PO60 workflow guide
  • [x] Existing Android HCI capture, reviewed 2026-11-07: SMP/MITM bonding, full GATT discovery, 0x83 clock write, 99 00 19 history start and 20/20/8-byte notification chunks; no PLX service or live stream observed
  • [ ] Annotated hardware run for record parsing and the open questions below

The capture contains no physical finger-state signal, so the finger-removal trigger comes from the vendor/PLUX workflow, not from the capture.

docs.title: Open Questions (need hardware)
docs.text:
• Does the PO60 expose a battery service alongside FF12? Full GATT discovery in the reviewed capture found no PLX service, agreeing with the app analysis.
  • Exact format of the storage-info response to 90 05 15, and the real page size of the 99 command (12 records/page is inferred).
  • How reliably can a third-party central reuse the bond? Can an unbonded client write time-set?
  • Behavior of other firmware/app versions, including any live-streaming path.
  • FCC ID from the device label.
  • Record bytes 15, 16 and 23.

docs.title: Beurer Series 800 (Premium 800 / BM92) Blood Pressure Monitor
docs.text: Status: Research Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Beurer GmbH Manufacturer Status: Active (vendor in business; cloud strictly optional)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Beurer "Series 800" — sold as the "Premium 800", model BM92 — is an upper-arm Bluetooth blood-pressure monitor with voice output, a 2-user × 120-reading memory, WHO risk classification, and cuff-position and arrhythmia indicators. It belongs to Beurer's HealthManager family and pairs with the "beurer HealthManager Pro" app (com.beurer.healthmanager).

Medical device

Readings synced through this spec are a personal log, not a clinical measurement, and must never be the sole basis for a medication decision or for deciding whether to seek care. Chart them if you like; dose from the monitor's own display and your care team's instructions. The spec carries a safety_advisory saying so.

The good news up front: the BM92 implements the standard Bluetooth SIG Blood Pressure Profile, so there is no proprietary command protocol to liberate — any generic BLE BP-profile client can read it, and the vendor cloud is optional account sync, not a dependency. What this spec adds on top of the published profile is the set of Beurer quirks in the record format (big-endian SFLOATs, a kPa unit flag, appended user-slot and status bytes) recovered from the vendor apps and corroborated by community work on the sister BM85.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number BM92 (US "Series 800" / "Premium 800"); wrist sister BC54W advertises as PREMIUM800W Category / hierarchy health + ["measurement", "health", "blood_pressure"] Manufacturer Beurer GmbH Companion app beurer HealthManager Pro (com.beurer.healthmanager); no account required for local use Chipset Unknown (no teardown/FCC detail retrieved) Radio BLE only — no WiFi FCC ID Unknown — device.report lists a filing dated 2023-08-30 but is bot-blocked; the printed manual should carry it BLE name PREMIUM800

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Nothing to provision or register. Enable Bluetooth in the monitor settings, select the user memory before inflation, and connect when the monitor transfers the saved result.

Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Advertised name PREMIUM800 (BM92), PREMIUM800W (BC54W) Passphrase protection not_applicable (no WiFi, no PIN found in app code) Confidence medium (app analysis and vendor manual; not replayed against hardware)

The app requests OS bonding and carries no PIN of its own. Beurer's manuals for sibling HealthManager Pro monitors (BM 96, BM 54) have the monitor show a PIN on its display at first connection, entered on the phone — so expect an OS passkey prompt (six digits on the BM 54). Unconfirmed for the BM92 until someone pairs one.

The BM92-specific manual workflow is:

  1. With the monitor switched on, hold MEMORY to enter settings. The 2023 US manual says three seconds; the Pro 1.17.2 tutorial says five seconds. Follow the prompt for the actual device/app version rather than generalizing either hold time.
  2. Advance through the settings until the Bluetooth icon flashes, select On with the arrow buttons, and confirm with START/STOP. Set a valid date/time before taking offline measurements.
  3. Select user memory 1 or 2 with the User button, then inflate the cuff and take a measurement. The result saves automatically.
  4. With HealthManager Pro or another BLE client ready, connect and bond when the monitor advertises for its automatic transfer. Do not power it off during transfer.
  5. Write standard Current Time (0x2A2B on service 0x1805) so subsequent records carry correct timestamps.
  6. Enable indications on 0x2A35 (CCCD write of 0x0002) and collect saved records, parsing them per the format below.

This is post-measurement saved-record transfer, not app-controlled cuff inflation or continuous live-pressure streaming. The manual does not establish that merely powering on an already-paired monitor exports every missed record; use the Pro reconnect/transfer prompt or take a new measurement until a capture establishes other behavior. Measurements still work without the phone and remain in the two 120-entry user memories.

Factory reset: unknown. Neither app contains a BP-monitor reset procedure and no hardware was available. Check the printed manual; do not guess a button sequence. A reset would presumably clear the measurement memory and user configuration.

Rebinding to a new phone: just pair from the new phone. There is no network credential to move. If the device stops accepting new bonds, remove the OS-level bond on the old phone first (a common single-bond peripheral symptom, not yet confirmed on this device).

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 0x1810 Blood Pressure Standard SIG service; the entire measurement surface 0x1805 Current Time Clock sync via 0x2A2B write (standard 10-byte CTS format) 0x180A Device Information Model 0x2A24, firmware 0x2A26, hardware 0x2A27 0x180F Battery Standard level 0x2A19 (0–100 %)

Characteristics of interest:

UUID Name Properties Notes 0x2A35 Blood Pressure Measurement indicate Record stream; enable via CCCD 0x2A49 Blood Pressure Feature read Listed for the family; presence on BM92 unverified 0x2A2B Current Time write Standard CTS write

docs.title: Record format (0x2A35 indication payload)
docs.text:
IEEE-11073-style, with Beurer quirks (from the classic app's BM85-family parser, corroborated by smurfix/ble-stuff):

Offset Length Description 0 1 Flags: bit0 = values in kPa (multiply by 7.50061683 → mmHg); bit1 = timestamp present 1–2 2 Systolic, SFLOAT big-endian (quirk — swap bytes before decoding) 3–4 2 Diastolic, SFLOAT big-endian 5–6 2 Mean arterial pressure, SFLOAT big-endian 7–8 2 Year, little-endian uint16 (only if flag bit1) 9–13 5 Month, day, hour, minute, second 14–15 2 Pulse, SFLOAT big-endian (high byte observed zero) 16 1 User slot (which of the 2 memories) 17 1 Unused in the BM85 layout 18 1 Status: bit2 (0x04) = irregular heartbeat; bits 6–7 = resting (HSD) indicator (00 = insufficient rest, 01 = sufficient)

Unverified for BM92 specifically: the Pro app's measurement model also tracks afib and triple-measurement flags, so BM92-era firmware may use extra status bits or append bytes past 19. One btsnoop capture of a sync settles this — it is the top open question.

docs.title: Command: Set Current Time
docs.text:
Write to 0x2A2B (CTS), standard format:

Offset Length Description 0–1 2 Year, little-endian uint16 2 1 Month (1–12) 3 1 Day (1–31) 4 1 Hour (0–23) 5 1 Minute 6 1 Second 7 1 Day of week (1=Mon…7=Sun, 0=unknown) 8 1 Fractions (1/256 s; 0 is fine) 9 1 Adjust reason bitmask (0x01 = manual update)

There is no other command surface: no OTA path exists for the BM92 in either app (firmware update support exists only for the BF880/BF980/BF990 WiFi scales).

docs.title: Cloud Dependency & Keep-Alive (Home Assistant)
docs.text:
The device does not depend on the cloud at all. It has no WiFi and never phones home; all measurement transfer is local BLE. The Beurer cloud (hmpro.connect.beurer.com EU / hmpro-us.connect.beurer.com US, plus SSO and classic-sync hosts — all alive and responding as of 2026-08-18, with Beurer actively shipping product) only provides optional account sync/backup in the app, which itself works fully without registration.

Practical guidance:

  • Use a BLE Blood Pressure Profile client with the Beurer parser above. In Home Assistant, an ESPHome Bluetooth proxy plus a parser for the big-endian SFLOATs and kPa flag is the likely route, but this spec remains untested on a BM92 and has no dedicated HA integration yet.
  • Blocking or DNS-redirecting hmpro*.connect.beurer.com and sync.connect-beurer.com does not impair local BLE operation, if you want the vendor app but not its telemetry.
  • smurfix/ble-stuff demonstrates fully cloud-free sync of the sister BM85 over the identical 0x1810/0x2A35 path — supporting evidence for local access, not a substitute for a BM92 capture.

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
• [x] Static analysis of both vendor apps (Pro 1.17.2, classic 2.17)
  • [x] Live HTTPS probes of the cloud endpoints (2026-08-18)
  • [x] US BM92 manual and Pro workflow review (2026-11-07)
  • [ ] No BM92 packet capture yet — bonding type, 0x2A49 presence, exact record tail, and history-transfer behavior still need hardware

docs.title: Big Ass Fans i6 / es6 / Haiku (firmware 3.x)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available Protocol: WiFi (plain TCP 31415, SLIP-framed protobuf; BLE for setup) Manufacturer: Big Ass Fans (Delta T LLC) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This spec covers Big Ass Fans' residential ceiling fans, the Haiku H/I and L series, i6 and es6, plus Haiku lights and wall controls, running firmware 3.x. In April 2022 Big Ass Fans moved the Haiku line to the protocol the i6 already spoke, replaced the Haiku app with the Big Ass Fans app, and dropped the legacy SenseME ASCII protocol from those fans. Integrations built on the old protocol stopped working overnight. The legacy protocol has its own spec, big-ass-fans-senseme.

The protocol is local and needs no account:

  • The fan announces _api._tcp over mDNS.
  • It accepts a plain TCP connection on port 31415, with no TLS, no key and no login.
  • Every message in both directions is one protobuf message inside a SLIP frame.
  • A client queries a group of properties or commits one property.
  • The fan answers queries and pushes changes to connected clients. A commit is acknowledged only by the fan pushing the new value back.

Big Ass Fans documents none of this. The protocol was worked out by aiobafi6, which Home Assistant's baf integration has shipped since 2022.6, and by oogje's Homebridge plugin. The field numbers exist only in aiobafi6's hobbyist .proto. This page and the spec restate them in our own tables and do not reproduce that file. A static check of the vendor Android app (v3.3.4, cross-checked against v3.4.0) confirmed the transport, framing, mDNS browse, BLE setup channel, colour presets and firmware-upload port. Everything taken from it is marked reported. Nothing here has been run against a fan by this project.

Choose the protocol from the advertisement, not the product name. A usable _api._tcp.local. record and API version select this SLIP/protobuf profile. Legacy UDP replies select the SenseME profile. Do not send both formats to discover which one a fan accepts. Haiku firmware 3.0 was the migration boundary, but API versions vary independently: a public SmartThings implementation reports H/I firmware 3.3.7 with API version 8.

Out of scope:

  • the legacy SenseME firmware
  • the vendor cloud, beyond what it is for
  • firmware image bytes
  • the Bluetooth remote's own pairing, beyond how to do it
  • Matter, which current smart boards also support (they ship with a Matter QR sticker)

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Model Number i6: MK-i61-* (051806, 061806, 071806, 051800, 061800, 051906, 061906, 071906 …). es6: MK-ES62-052306/062306/072306. Haiku: MK-HK4-. Haiku i: K3127-, K3150-*. Haiku L: FR112C-U1H, FR127C-U1H/J, FR150C-U1H/J. Model strings on the wire: i6, es6, Haiku H/I Series, Haiku L Series, Haiku Light, Haiku Switch. The app also knows Turbo6, Mammoth, Bison, Speakeasy Chipset Not identified. One published example MAC carries OUI 20:F8:5E (Delta Electronics), which suggests a Delta Wi-Fi module (low confidence) Radio Wi-Fi (control) and BLE (setup, plus a fallback channel for the same messages). The smart board is a replaceable part: "SenseME board" on Haiku, "smart board" on i6/es6. Haiku L needs its optional Wi-Fi module for any app control FCC ID Not found. None is printed in the manuals held, and fccid.co lists no Big Ass Fans or Delta T grantee

Where the temperature comes from

On some models the temperature and humidity readings, and so Auto Comfort, come from the Bluetooth remote or wall control, not the fan. Home Assistant's documentation says so, and oogje says it for the i6. If the fan loses its remote, those values stop updating while the fan stays reachable.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes Method ble_provisioning (the Big Ass Fans app) Setup AP / advertised name No AP. The app scans for BLE service e0fc1000-1fb1-4168-96df-b3f057a86e01 Passphrase protection unknown (sent over an unbonded BLE channel; the message is not documented) Confidence low (vendor help page plus a static read of the app; not replayed)

The vendor's help page and the app agree on the flow:

  1. Install and power the fan. It beeps once on power-up unless beeps are turned off.
  2. In the app, choose Add Product. The app searches over Bluetooth.
  3. Press Identify. The chosen fan beeps and flashes its LEDs.
  4. Choose the home network and enter its passphrase. The app sends it over BLE.
  5. Name the fan.
  6. The fan then appears as _api._tcp on the LAN.

The BLE channel is known at the transport level: a vendor service with a write characteristic and a notify characteristic, carrying the same SLIP-framed protobuf as the LAN socket. The message that carries the Wi-Fi credentials is not, so onboarding still needs the vendor app. It is also not established whether the app lets you finish onboarding without signing in. There is a cloud claim step, and one reviewer describes backing out of sign-up to reach local devices. Haiku L fans bought before 2023 join over Wi-Fi rather than Bluetooth (the app offers a "Wi-Fi (before 2023)" route). That route is not documented here.

Factory reset: the i6 manual gives two routes. Neither has been tried here.

  • From the paired remote: hold fan power for 5 s until the remote's LEDs blink and the fan beeps, then press fan minus. The fan beeps and its LED blinks slowly. The reset is complete when the LED blinks green.
  • Without the remote: switch the fan off at the wall switch or breaker for about 5 s, then on for about 5 s. Do this four times in all. The reset is complete when the fan's LED turns green.

A reset erases all settings, including the fan's name and its Wi-Fi network. The Haiku board instructions only point at the support site, so whether the same steps apply to Haiku and es6 is not established.

Rebinding to a new network: physical reset only, as far as is known. The app's advice is to reset the product's network settings and then Add Product again. No way to change Wi-Fi over the LAN socket is known.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none Bonding none PIN source not applicable One central at a time Unknown (Home Assistant and the vendor app are routinely used side by side) One bond at a time not applicable Confidence medium (three independent clients connect with nothing but a socket)

Nothing pairs on the control path. Anything on the LAN can open 31415 and drive the fan. The app also uses the BLE setup channel without bonding (reported).

The Bluetooth remote and wall control pair with the fan itself. This is separate from anything a client does:

  • To pair: hold the remote close to the fan and press any button. The remote's LEDs cycle while it searches, and the fan plays a jingle when pairing completes.
  • To move a remote to another fan: hold fan power and fan minus until the LEDs flash, which clears all of the remote's pairings. Then press any button near the new fan.

Recovery: none needed for LAN clients. If a remote stops working, power cycle the fan and pair the remote again (i6 manual).

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Signal Value mDNS service _api._tcp.local., SRV port 31415 TXT keys name, model, uuid, api version (with a space) Match api version present and model starting with i6, es6, Haiku, Turbo6, Mammoth, Bison or Speakeasy (case-insensitive) Identity TXT uuid, which equals the fan's own property field 10 BLE (setup only) service e0fc1000-1fb1-4168-96df-b3f057a86e01

aiobafi6 ignores fans whose api version is below 4. Occupancy readings need API version 5, which is firmware 3.1. Home Assistant's zeroconf matcher only accepts haiku* and i6*, so it misses es6. The vendor app also browses _http._tcp, for a reason not established; do not use that as a fan signal.

docs.title: Transport and framing
docs.text:
• Socket: plain TCP to the SRV port (31415). The vendor app uses a 10 s connect timeout and TCP keepalive.
  • Frames: RFC 1055 SLIP. Each message is c0, then the message, then c0. Inside a message, c0 is sent as db dc and db as db dd. There is no length field and no checksum.
  • Empty frames: a c0 c0 pair can occur. Skip it, as the vendor app does. aiobafi6 drops the connection instead.
  • Messages: protobuf (proto2). Every number and boolean is a varint (base-128, least-significant group first). Strings and nested messages are length-delimited. Temperatures are int32, so a value below 0 °C is a 10-byte varint.
  • Size: aiobafi6 caps a message at 4096 bytes and says none is expected to be larger.

Every frame in either direction uses the same message tree. The names below are ours:

Message Field Carries outer 2 envelope envelope 2 commit (client → fan) envelope 3 query (client → fan) envelope 4 query result (fan → client, answers and pushes) commit 3 one property set query 1 group (varint) query result 2 (repeated) property sets: merge each one, later values win query result 3 (repeated) schedules (group 5); format unknown Query group Meaning 0 Everything. Send it on connect 1 / 2 Fan / light properties 3 Firmware, clock and API properties. The vendor app repeats this one on a timer (about every 15 s, per oogje) 4 Network 5 Schedules 6 Sensors (oogje sends it first and calls it capabilities) 7, 8 Present in the app's enum; meaning unknown

docs.title: Client rules
docs.text:
1. Connect, then send query group 0 at once. Merge every property set in the replies into one running copy.
  2. Keep the socket open. The fan pushes every change, and that push is the only confirmation a commit gets.
  3. Re-query now and then for values the fan does not push, such as RPM and the clock. aiobafi6 defaults to every 60 s and Home Assistant uses 300 s.
  4. Put one property per commit. Every known client does, and whether the fan accepts more is unknown.
  5. To run at a chosen speed, commit fan mode = 1 (on), then commit speed. This is what Home Assistant does.
  6. Skip unknown fields, and leave the volatile ones (clock, uptime, RPM) out of change detection.
  7. The fan occasionally drops the connection (oogje). Reconnect, and resend a command that was in flight.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
These are the fields a client needs. The spec's protocol_details.baf_i6_api.properties has the full table, including fields only oogje names, which are marked hypothesis.

Field Name (ours) Access Values / units 1 name r string 2 model r string, as TXT model 7 firmware_version r string 10 service_uuid r equals TXT uuid 13 api_version r decimal string 17 capabilities r sub-message of flags (below) 43 fan_mode rw 0 off, 1 on, 2 auto 44 reverse rw 0 forward, 1 reverse. The app offers it but advises against it 45 speed_percent r 0–100 % 46 speed rw 0–7. 1–7 are the app's seven speeds; 0 stops rotation 47 comfort_enabled rw Auto Comfort on/off 48 comfort_ideal_temperature rw int32, 0.01 °C (2350 = 23.50 °C) 50 / 51 comfort_min_speed / comfort_max_speed rw 0–7. Min 0 = no minimum, max 7 = no maximum 52 / 53 fan_motion_sense / timeout rw bool / seconds 54 / 55 fan_return_to_auto / timeout rw bool / seconds 58 whoosh rw bool 60 / 61 / 62 heat_assist / speed / reverse rw bool / 1–7 / bool 63 / 64 target_rpm / current_rpm r rpm. Current RPM is not pushed 65 eco rw bool (Haiku) 66 fan_occupancy r bool. API 5+; clears about 4.5–5 min after the last motion 68 light_mode rw 0 off, 1 on, 2 auto 69 light_brightness rw 0–100 % (0 = off) 70 light_brightness_level rw 0–16. Home Assistant uses this one 71 light_color_temperature rw kelvin, not mireds 73 / 74 / 75 light motion timeout / return to auto / timeout rw seconds / bool / seconds 77 light_dim_to_warm rw bool 78 / 79 warmest / coolest colour temperature r kelvin: the light's range 82 light_target rw 0 both, 1 downlight, 2 uplight (oogje, hypothesis) 85 light_occupancy r bool. API 5+; clears about 9.5 min after the last motion 86 temperature r int32, 0.01 °C 87 humidity r % (aiobafi6: whole percent; oogje divides by 100, unresolved) 120 ip_address r string 124 wifi r sub-field 1 SSID 134 / 135 / 136 LED indicators / beep / legacy IR remote rw bool

The capability flags (field 17) say which controls to draw. aiobafi6 and oogje disagree on one of them:

Flag oogje aiobafi6 1 temperature sensor comfort flag 1 3 occupancy sensor comfort flag 3 4 downlight has light 6 colour-temperature control has uplight (conflict) 11 uplight — 14 eco mode —

Home Assistant offers Auto Comfort only when flags 1 and 3 are both set.

Light colour. The app's picker offers the presets below, hiding any that fall outside the light's range in fields 78–79. Picking one commits field 71.

Kelvin App label 2200 Warm 2700 Warm White 3000 Soft White 3500 Natural White 4000 Bright White 5000 Cool White 6500 Daylight

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
A commit is c0 12 <len> 12 <len> 1a <len> <tag> <varint> c0. The tag is varint(field << 3). Each frame below was produced by an independent encoder and matches aiobafi6's serializer byte for byte.

Command Field Example Frame (hex) Query everything — group 0 c0 12 04 1a 02 08 00 c0 Query group — group 3 c0 12 04 1a 02 08 03 c0 Fan mode 43 auto (2) c0 12 07 12 05 1a 03 d8 02 02 c0 Speed 46 3 c0 12 07 12 05 1a 03 f0 02 03 c0 Reverse 44 on c0 12 07 12 05 1a 03 e0 02 01 c0 Whoosh 58 on c0 12 07 12 05 1a 03 d0 03 01 c0 Auto Comfort 47 on c0 12 07 12 05 1a 03 f8 02 01 c0 Ideal temperature 48 23.5 °C (2350) c0 12 08 12 06 1a 04 80 03 ae 12 c0 Comfort min speed 50 2 c0 12 07 12 05 1a 03 90 03 02 c0 Comfort max speed 51 7 c0 12 07 12 05 1a 03 98 03 07 c0 Heat Assist 60 on c0 12 07 12 05 1a 03 e0 03 01 c0 Heat Assist speed 61 1 c0 12 07 12 05 1a 03 e8 03 01 c0 Light mode 68 on c0 12 07 12 05 1a 03 a0 04 01 c0 Light brightness 69 50 % c0 12 07 12 05 1a 03 a8 04 32 c0 Light colour 71 4000 K c0 12 08 12 06 1a 04 b8 04 a0 1f c0

A push from the fan, with an escape. This frame reports speed 3 and a temperature of 22.40 °C:

c0 12 0d 22 0b 12 03 f0 02 03 12 04 b0 05 db dc 11 c0

The raw temperature 2240 encodes as the varint c0 11, so its c0 goes out as db dc. After un-escaping, the query result holds two property sets: field 46 = 3, then field 86 = 2240.

docs.title: BLE setup channel (reported)
docs.text:
UUID Role e0fc1000-1fb1-4168-96df-b3f057a86e01 Vendor service. The app's Add Product scan filters on it e0fc1003-1fb1-4168-96df-b3f057a86e01 Write with response. SLIP frames are split into 20-byte pieces e0fc1004-1fb1-4168-96df-b3f057a86e01 Notify. Carries SLIP frames from the fan

The app requests a 250-byte MTU, enables notifications through the standard 00002902-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb descriptor, and reads Model Number and Serial Number from the Device Information service. Earlier research notes listed three "vendor BLE UUIDs" as the wall remote's pairing channel. Those strings are not GATT UUIDs at all: in the app they identify thermostat integrations. They are deliberately left out of the spec.

docs.title: Firmware update
docs.text:
This is reported from the app and is only here so a reader knows what the port is. Do not drive it from anything but the vendor app.

  1. The app asks the cloud for a firmware token, which requires an account.
  2. It downloads the image.
  3. It uploads the image to the fan's HTTP server on TCP 31416.

The request path and body are left out on purpose, and whether the fan is prepared for the upload by a message on 31415 is not established. The app can also downgrade a Haiku to the legacy firmware, but only when support asks for it. A downgrade factory resets the fan, which must then be added again with the old Haiku app.

docs.title: Cloud
docs.text:
api.bigassfans.com uses OAuth and a versioned vendor media type. It handles:

  • claiming a device to an account
  • control from outside the home network
  • Alexa and Google Assistant
  • thermostat links
  • firmware tokens

The LAN protocol never touches it, and fans keep working locally without internet access.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Collected from store reviews, the app's own messages and the open-source projects:

  • The app cannot find the fan over Bluetooth on Android. One reviewer could only add the fan from an iPhone; Android control worked after that. A fan that is already on a network will not re-enter setup until its network settings are reset.
  • "Could not find the device on the network" after setup. The app detects VPNs and asks for them to be turned off. mDNS and the LAN socket do not cross a VPN, and they do not cross an AP with client isolation either. One reviewer had to switch phone Wi-Fi off while the fan joined.
  • The Wi-Fi password is rejected. The product does not support a double quote in the passphrase.
  • Firmware update fails with "preparation failed". One reviewer saw this on Android 15 on three of four fans; the same update succeeded from an Android 9 phone.
  • The integration stopped working after the April 2022 update. The fan is now on firmware 3.x and no longer speaks SenseME. Switch to an i6-protocol client such as aiobafi6 or Home Assistant's baf integration.
  • Temperature and Auto Comfort go unavailable while the fan stays online. On those models the readings come from the remote. Restore the remote's pairing.
  • A command is ignored now and then. The fan occasionally resets the connection (oogje). Reconnect and resend.
