docs.title: Big Ass Fans Haiku with SenseME (legacy firmware)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available Protocol: WiFi (ASCII "SenseME" protocol on UDP and TCP port 31415) Manufacturer: Big Ass Fans (Delta T LLC) Manufacturer Status: Active. The vendor has replaced this protocol, but the products are still supported.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page covers Big Ass Fans' residential Haiku ceiling fans with SenseME, the Haiku L with its Wi-Fi module, the standalone Haiku Light and the Haiku Wall Control, while they still run the legacy firmware below 3.0. Every published parameter dump comes from firmware 2.5.x or 2.6.0. That firmware speaks a small ASCII protocol on port 31415. Anyone on the LAN can use it, with no account, no cloud and no authentication. It covers:

  • fan power, speed 0–7, direction, Whoosh and sleep mode
  • Smart Mode (the vendor's "Auto Comfort"), with its temperature target and speed bounds
  • light level, and colour temperature on the Haiku Light
  • the motion (occupancy) sensor
  • the room grouping

The protocol is worth writing down because it is disappearing. Firmware 3.0, from April 2022, replaced it with a protobuf protocol (see the big-ass-fans-i6 spec and aiobafi6). Accepting the firmware update offered by the current Big Ass Fans app moves a legacy device to 3.x. aiosenseme, the library Home Assistant used, was archived in 2023 for that reason. The protocol now lives only in half a dozen archived hobby clients. The spec gathers it in one place, per key, with units.

Out of scope:

  • firmware 3.x, i6 and es6 (the protobuf protocol)
  • the vendor cloud (account claim, Alexa, remote access)
  • firmware upload framing
  • the Bluetooth wall-remote pairing, a 3.x-era accessory

The current app will take the device off this protocol

Opening a legacy fan in the current Big Ass Fans app leads to a firmware update. After that update the fan speaks only the 3.x protocol, and every SenseME integration stops working. Owners' reviews and the openHAB and aiosenseme projects all record this. The app does have a support-only "downgrade" path, which factory-resets the device back onto legacy firmware. To stay on SenseME, decline the update.

Nothing here has been run against hardware by this project, and no capture of real traffic is held. The protocol facts come from open-source clients that were written against real fans. The rest comes from a static reading of the current vendor Android app (3.3.4, cross-checked against 3.4.0), which still has a legacy-device handler. Everything is marked reported.

Select this profile only after observing a legacy UDP discovery reply such as FAN,HAIKU,SENSEME, or an established owner firmware history. A usable _api._tcp.local. record selects the i6 / firmware 3.x profile. Do not broadcast both protocol formats as a capability test: Haiku is a family name, not a reliable protocol selector.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number Identified on the wire by model string, not part number: FAN,HAIKU,SENSEME (Haiku with SenseME), FAN,HAIKU,HSERIES (Haiku H), FAN,LSERIES (Haiku L with Wi-Fi module; the current guide lists FR112C-U1H, FR127C-U1H/J, FR150C-U1H/J), LIGHT,HAIKU (Haiku Light, discontinued), SWITCH,SENSEME (Haiku Wall Control) Firmware Legacy SenseME 2.x. Families FW000003 (Haiku fan), FW000004 (wall control), FW000005 (Haiku L), FW000006 (Haiku Light) in the published dumps Chipset Not identified. Published device MACs sit in 20:F8:5E, a block registered to Delta Electronics, most likely the Wi-Fi module's maker Radio Wi-Fi (band not established). Legacy fans shipped with an infrared remote Sensors Occupancy (motion) on the Haiku fan and the wall control; optional on the Haiku L (DEVICE;OPTION;SENSORS). The fan uses a temperature reading internally for Smart Mode, but no legacy client reads it FCC ID Not found. No Big Ass Fans or Delta T grantee turned up, and none is printed in the held manuals

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes Method softap_udp: the device's own setup access point, then a join request over the SenseME protocol Setup AP / advertised name Not established Passphrase protection plaintext Confidence low (inferred from the protocol keys and the vendor app; not replayed)

A legacy device joins Wi-Fi from its own access point. GETALL reports NW;AP;STATUS and NW;DHCP, and both read OFF once the device is provisioned. The current vendor app's legacy handler can ask the device to scan and can send it a join request. Onboarding runs over the same protocol and port as normal control:

  1. Power a device with no network stored and join its setup access point. Its name and security are not established.
  2. Broadcast <ALL;DEVICE;ID;GET> to UDP 31415. The device answers (name;DEVICE;ID;mac;model).
  3. Optionally send <mac;NW;SCAN>. The reply format is not established.
  4. Send <mac;NW;JOIN;ssid;passphrase>, backslash-escaping < > ; ( ) + , and \ in both fields. The passphrase travels in plain text.
  5. Move the client back to the home network and broadcast the probe again.

The alternative is the vendor's older Haiku by BAF app (earlier Haiku Home). The current app names it as the app legacy products are designed for. Whether it can still be installed is not established.

Factory reset: no reset procedure specific to legacy firmware is held. The candidate is the current app's remote-control reset:

  1. Hold Fan Power for about 5 s, until the LEDs blink and the fan beeps.
  2. Tap Speed Minus or Speed Plus. The app shows one or the other, depending on the product.
  3. The reset is done when the LEDs stop blinking. A fitted light comes on.

That sequence was written for current-firmware fans and the Bluetooth remote, so it may not apply to a legacy fan with an IR remote (verified: false). A reset loses the network connection. The i6 manual says a reset erases names and Wi-Fi settings, but that is for the i6. Whether room membership, schedules and Smart Mode settings survive is not established. Do not confuse the reset with the Haiku L guide's reboot (hold fan On/Off until the LEDs blink, then press it again within 30 s), which clears nothing. No protocol message that resets the device is known.

Rebinding to a new network: in place, while the old network is still up. Send NW;JOIN with the new credentials and the device moves; the current app does exactly this. Once the old router is gone, the only route is a factory reset and the setup-access-point flow.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none Bonding none PIN source not applicable One central at a time No. Several TCP clients can be connected at once One bond at a time No Confidence medium (several independent clients; not replayed)

Nothing pairs. There is no key, token or client registration, and every command works for anything on the LAN. aiosenseme keeps a TCP connection open while the vendor app and the remote are in use and receives their changes as pushes, so clients coexist.

Entering pairing mode: not applicable.

Unpairing: there is nothing to unpair. To stop a client, take it (or the device) off the network.

Recovery: nothing holds the device exclusively. If a client sees no state, it has probably missed the initial GETALL. Reconnect and read again.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text:
Property Value Discovery UDP broadcast to port 31415; one reply datagram per device Control TCP port 31415, one long-lived connection; also accepted as UDP datagrams (Indigo plugin) Framing Request <target;TOKEN;…>; reply and push (name;KEY…;VALUE…). No length, checksum or terminator Encoding ASCII. Free text escapes < > ; ( ) + , and \ with a backslash Target The device's MAC as it reports it (upper-case, colon-separated). Some clients use the name; the probe uses ALL Authentication None Push Yes, on an open TCP connection: every change, from any source

The legacy protocol and firmware 3.x share port numbers. Per the current vendor app, 3.x devices also accept TCP on 31415 (protobuf) and advertise mDNS _api._tcp. An open TCP port therefore proves nothing. A reply to the UDP probe is the legacy signal.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Send the 19 ASCII bytes <ALL;DEVICE;ID;GET> (3c414c4c3b4445564943453b49443b4745543e) to UDP 31415. The published clients and the vendor app all send from local port 31415 with SO_REUSEADDR. aiosenseme sends to 255.255.255.255 once a second for 5 s. The vendor app sends to the subnet-directed broadcast every 5 s.

Field Example Meaning 0 Living Room Fan Device name (user-assigned, escaped) 1–2 DEVICE, ID Fixed 3 20:F8:5E:AA:BB:CC MAC: the stable identity and the target for every request 4 FAN,HAIKU,SENSEME Model family, comma-separated

aiosenseme drops a reply unless it has exactly five fields and is 31–200 characters long.

docs.title: Request forms
docs.text: Form Example Meaning <T;CAT;ATTR;ON> / …;OFF> <mac;FAN;PWR;ON> Switch a boolean <T;CAT;ATTR;SET;V[;V]> <mac;FAN;SPD;SET;3> Write a value <T;CAT;ATTR;GET[;QUAL]> <mac;FAN;SPD;GET;ACTUAL> Read one value. The qualifier goes after GET in the request and before the value in the reply <T;GETALL> <mac;GETALL> Dump every setting (40–55 replies). Leaves out the occupancy status

docs.title: Replies
docs.text: A reply ends at the first ) that is not preceded by a backslash. A TCP read can hold several replies or part of one, so buffer and split. Token 0 is the device name, followed by the key and then the value or values. Most keys carry one value, but DEVICE;ID carries two (mac;model), FAN;BOOKENDS/LIGHT;BOOKENDS two (min;max) and NW;PARAMS;ACTUAL three (address;netmask;gateway). A parser therefore has to know the key to split it. aiosenseme's own accessors swap the netmask and gateway fields; the published dumps show the order above.

docs.title: Main keys
docs.text:
Key Values Command FAN;PWR ON/OFF fan_turn_on / fan_turn_off FAN;SPD;ACTUAL 0–7 (0 = stopped; bounded by FAN;SPD;MIN/MAX, 1 and 7) fan_set_speed FAN;DIR FWD/REV (REV = winter / Heat Assist) fan_set_direction FAN;WHOOSH;STATUS ON/OFF (write FAN;WHOOSH;ON) fan_whoosh_on / _off FAN;AUTO, LIGHT;AUTO ON/OFF, switch on with motion fan_motion_auto_*, light_motion_auto_* FAN;BOOKENDS room speed limits min;max fan_set_room_speed_limits LIGHT;PWR ON/OFF light_turn_on / _off LIGHT;LEVEL;ACTUAL 0–16 (bounded by LIGHT;LEVEL;MIN/MAX, 1 and 16) light_set_level LIGHT;COLOR;TEMP;VALUE 2200–5000 K, Haiku Light only light_set_color_temp SMARTMODE;STATE OFF/COOLING/HEATING/FOLLOWTSTAT (SMARTMODE;ACTUAL = in effect) smartmode_set LEARN;ZEROTEMP Smart cooling target, hundredths of °C (2111 = 21.11 °C) cooling_set_ideal_temp LEARN;MINSPEED / MAXSPEED 0–6 (0 = no min) / 1–7 (7 = no max) cooling_set_min_speed / _max_speed SLEEP;STATE ON/OFF sleep_on / sleep_off SMARTSLEEP;IDEALTEMP sleep target, hundredths of °C sleep_set_ideal_temp SMARTSLEEP;MINSPEED / MAXSPEED 0–7 sleep_set_min_speed / _max_speed SNSROCC;STATUS OCCUPIED/UNOCCUPIED, not in GETALL read with get_occupancy SNSROCC;TIMEOUT;CURR ms, 60000–86400000 occupancy_set_timeout WINTERMODE;HEIGHT fan height, cm (274 ≈ 9 ft) not declared GROUP;LIST, GROUP;ROOM;TYPE room name (EMPTY = none), room category 0–28 read only DEVICE;BEEPER, DEVICE;INDICATORS ON/OFF beeper_*, indicators_* DEVICE;LIGHT PRESENT / NOT PRESENT / PRESENT;COLOR draw light controls only when present NW;SSID, NW;TOKEN, FW;NAME, TIME;VALUE network, per-device UUID, firmware family, ISO-8601 UTC clock read only

The full table, with the less-understood keys (FAN;TIMER, SLEEP;EVENT, SCHEDULE;*, LIGHT;COLOR;LEVEL, ERRORLOG;*), is in the spec's protocol_details.senseme.state_keys.

docs.title: Messages only the vendor app sends
docs.text: Message Role <mac;DEVICE;SIGNAL;SET;10000> Identify. The unit of 10000 is not established <mac;NW;SCAN> Wi-Fi scan (reply not established) <mac;NW;JOIN;ssid;passphrase> Join a network (the spec marks it advanced) <mac;NAME;VALUE;SET;name> Rename

docs.title: Connection lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Open TCP 31415.
  2. Send <mac;DEVICE;ID;GET>, <mac;SNSROCC;STATUS;GET> and <mac;GETALL>.
  3. Keep the connection open. Changes arrive as pushes.
  4. Re-send those three reads about once a minute (aiosenseme adds jitter). Treat about 90 s of silence as a dead connection and reconnect.

docs.title: Firmware update
docs.text: The vendor app downloads a token-gated image from its cloud. For a legacy device it requests a "-GEN3" image, meaning firmware 3.x. It then uploads the image to the device over plain HTTP on port 31416. The spec records the direction and consequence only, never the upload format. For this protocol the update is effectively one-way.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Integration stopped working after using the new app. The fan was updated to firmware 3.x. A Play Store review describes exactly this for a Hubitat driver, and openHAB and aiosenseme record the same break. Either move the integration to the 3.x protocol (aiobafi6, Home Assistant's baf integration) or ask vendor support about the downgrade path, which factory-resets the device.
  • Occupancy never shows. GETALL does not include it. Send SNSROCC;STATUS;GET after connecting.
  • Gateway and netmask look swapped. aiosenseme's accessors read NW;PARAMS;ACTUAL in the wrong order. The order is address;netmask;gateway.
  • Whoosh turned itself off. Setting a speed switches Whoosh off (observed by aiosenseme).
  • TCP 31415 is open but nothing answers the ASCII. It is probably a 3.x device, which uses the same port for protobuf. Check for a UDP probe reply.
  • Setup fails at the join step. Owners of the vendor app report having to take the phone off Wi-Fi by hand while the fan joins the network. A phone OS that holds on to the setup network, or prefers mobile data, can hide the device on either side of the move. No join result is established on the wire.
  • Two clients fight over state. Any client can change anything. Always render from pushes, not from what you last sent.

docs.title: BIO-key TouchLock BT
docs.text: Status: Research Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: BIO-key International, Inc. (app/OEM: com.champion.lock, Play Store developer Keyssmart) Manufacturer Status: Abandoned (company alive; TouchLock consumer hardware line discontinued, product pages gone)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The TouchLock BT family is a line of Bluetooth Low Energy keyless locks — padlocks (XS/XL), a TSA luggage lock, a bike lock and a U-lock — sold by BIO-key from about 2017 and now discontinued. The protocol was recovered by decompiling the official Android app (TouchLock BT v2.2.1, com.champion.lock, jadx output; sha256 in the spec's sources), and the key parts are now confirmed by an over-the-air capture of that app driving a real lock (2026-08-30 — see the spec's evidence).

Two facts make this family unusually rescue-friendly:

  • There is no cloud at all. No HTTP client, endpoint, account, sync or OTA mechanism exists anywhere in the app. The lock cannot die from a server shutdown; the only vendor risk is the app vanishing from Google Play, and the protocol below replaces it entirely.
  • There is no real cryptography. The rolling credential is literally the current timestamp split into bytes. A local client can generate valid commands with no secrets beyond a one-time enrollment.

No Home Assistant/ESPHome integration or public reverse-engineering repo for this family was found — this spec is the starting point.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Model Numbers BL0509 (TouchLock BT XS), BL1209 (TouchLock BT XL), BS1609 (TouchLock TSA BT); bike lock and U-lock variants; OEM rebadges (e.g. Joi_Lock) Chipset Unknown (not identifiable from the app) Radio BLE 4.x (single-mode, 2402–2480 MHz) FCC ID 2AIKJ-BL (grantee BIO-KEY; padlock models)

Non-BLE TouchLock variants (fingerprint sensor on the lock, no Bluetooth) exist and are not covered here.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
There is no network to join — "setup" is BLE enrollment, required before the lock will open. The enrollment exchange below was observed end-to-end in the 2026-08-30 capture; it has not yet been replayed by a third-party client.

Property Value Setup required Yes (admin enrollment, BLE only) Method ble_provisioning Advertised names TSA_BT, TSA_PLUS, XL_BT, XL_PLUS, Ble_Lock, Bike_BT, Bike_Pr, Joi_Lock, U_Lock, ULockPr (fallback: any name containing LOCK) Passphrase protection not_applicable (no WiFi; BLE bonding is Just Works) Confidence high (enrollment observed on hardware in the capture)

Enrollment flow:

  1. Scan unfiltered; match the name patterns above plus the presence of a manufacturer-data status byte.
  2. Connect, bond (no PIN — the lock initiates security immediately and no GATT discovery completes before the bond exists), discover services, enable notifications on 67ac8801-…, wait ~1.2 s.
  3. Send RegisterAdmin (0x80) with a fresh client-generated 8-byte admin ID and the current time-based password. An already-enrolled lock answers error 05 — that, not any status-byte bit, is the reliable "already registered" signal.
  4. Store the admin ID and password locally — they are the only credentials.

Factory reset: a BLE command, not a button. FactoryInit (0x8f) carries the admin ID plus the 8-character factory password (one hex-digit character per byte; the app's own dialog hints the default is 00000000). It clears the admin, all enrolled users, and returns the lock to the unregistered state. No physical reset procedure is documented in the app. This has not been executed against hardware — on a lock, treat reset flows with care.

Rebinding to a new phone/controller: in place, no reset needed. The new client gets the admin's current password out-of-band (the official app sends it by SMS — there is no server), sends UserRegistrationRequest (0x90) with that password and its bytewise complement, then UserRegistration (0x91) to install its own credentials. A reset is only needed when every credential is lost.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 67ac8800-a0eb-11e6-80f5-76304dec7eb7 TouchLock lock service The only application service 67ac8801-a0eb-11e6-80f5-76304dec7eb7 Response/status (notify) Responses + unsolicited status (opcode ff) 67ac8802-a0eb-11e6-80f5-76304dec7eb7 Command write (write-no-response) All commands, 20-byte frames

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Every command is exactly 20 bytes, written to 67ac8802-…:

Offset Length Description 0 1 Opcode 1 1 0x00 2–9 8 Payload A 10–17 8 Payload B 18 1 0x00 19 1 Checksum = (0x5A − sum(bytes[0..18])) & 0xFF

Response (notify): every observed frame is 5 bytes:

Byte Description 0 Echoed opcode 1 Error code: 00 ok, 01 invalid command, 02 checksum, 03 wrong password, 04 invalid user ID, 05 already registered, 06 user record full, 07 unbonded device 2 Status byte 3 Frame flag (00/01 in the capture; excluded from the checksum) 4 Checksum — observed responses fit (0x5A − sum(bytes[0..2])) & 0xFF

Status byte (working model, partially disputed): bit 7 = lock state (polarity unconfirmed), bits 2–0 = battery 0–7. The decompile said bit 4 = registered flag, but the capture contradicts it: the observed sequence was 0x13 → 0x03 (bit 4 cleared by a successful RegisterAdmin) → 0x01, and the low bits dropping 3 → 1 within minutes is suspiciously fast for a battery gauge. One controlled lock/unlock with a battery reading will settle the layout. The same byte is broadcast in manufacturer advertisement data while disconnected — state and battery can be tracked passively.

Opcode table: 00 OpenLock · 01 TimeStamp (RTC sync, must precede unlock) · 80 RegisterAdmin ✓ · 81 RemoveUser · 82 GetUserInfo (unused) · 8c/8d change factory password ✓ · 8f FactoryInit · 90/91 user registration · ad GetMac ✓ (reply carries the client's own BT address, byte-reversed) · cc FindLock (fixed payload 22 44 66 88 88 66 44 22 / 11 33 55 77 77 55 33 11) · ff UpdateStatus (unsolicited, device→client, ~1 Hz for the whole connection). ✓ = observed on the wire in the capture. OpenLock/TimeStamp were never observed — the vendor app crashed before sending them.

The "rolling password" is the current timestamp yy-MM-dd-HH-mm-ss-SSSS split into eight two-digit decimal groups, each written as one hex-parsed byte — capture-confirmed (a RegisterAdmin frame's password bytes equal the session's wall-clock time). Unlock = send TimeStamp, then OpenLock with the stored password in payload A and the new time-based password in payload B; on success the new password becomes the stored one.

docs.title: Cloud Dependency & Home Assistant Guidance
docs.text:
None. No cloud exists, nothing needs a keep-alive, and nothing breaks when the vendor disappears. The app itself is archived (see the spec's sources) in case the Play Store listing goes away.

For Home Assistant:

  • There is no ready-made integration. Everything needed to write one is in the spec: static 128-bit UUIDs, the 20-byte frame format, the additive 0x5A-seeded checksum, and the time-derived password generator.
  • The lock is BLE-only, so use an ESPHome bluetooth_proxy (or any BLE adapter) within radio range; "remote access" just means a bridged local connection.
  • Track state and battery passively from the advertisement status byte — no connection needed. The manufacturer-data company ID is still unknown (the capture contains no advertising reports), so identify adverts by name pattern until then.
  • Bonding is mandatory and confirmed: the lock sends an SMP security request as its first packet, pairing is legacy Just Works (no PIN), and no GATT service discovery completes before the bond exists — a client that never pairs discovers zero services and gets dropped. The lock refuses unbonded writers with error 07. The official app deliberately unpairs on disconnect — an integration that keeps a persistent bond is in uncharted-but-plausible territory.
  • Honor the app's pacing: ~1.2 s pause after enabling notifications, and always sync the RTC (TimeStamp) before OpenLock. Once notifications are on, expect an unsolicited ff status frame about once per second.

docs.title: Blueair Cabin P2i Car Air Purifier
docs.text: Status: Spec Available Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Blueair AB (BLE stack and SDK by Airboxlab, the company behind Foobot) Manufacturer Status: Active (the product is controlled locally over BLE, but the vendor app wants an account and uploads readings)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Cabin P2i is a 12 V purifier for a car. The purifier unit is strapped behind a front-seat headrest. It holds a Particle+Carbon filter and a laser particle sensor from the Plantower family. A 4.5 m cable runs from the unit to a control knob that sits in the car's 12 V socket. The knob powers the system, shows air quality and fan speed on a ring of LEDs, and has its own USB charging port. The unit has a second USB port. The manual lists a twin-unit Cabin P2iD beside it.

Inside the Blueair app the product is called ICP. Its Bluetooth side is not Blueair's own work. The BLE SDK in the app was written by Airboxlab (Foobot), and so was the firmware update service it uses. That lineage explains the update-mode name "AirBoxLab" and why the firmware is hosted in a Foobot storage bucket.

Everything a user can do from the app works locally over BLE with no cloud:

  • fan speed (low, medium, high)
  • fan mode (manual, auto)
  • live PM1 / PM2.5 / PM10 and six particle-count bins
  • filter life
  • a fault bitfield
  • a history of stored readings

The cloud account is only where the app sends those readings.

Out of scope. Blueair's Wi-Fi purifiers (Classic i-series, Sense+, Aware, Blue Signature, HealthProtect 74xx/77xx, Blue Pure / Blue Max 211i–511i) and its humidifiers and fans come through the same app, but none of them uses this protocol. The app onboards them with Espressif protocomm over BLE (advertised service 4772911e-d07c-4617-8241-f4d10948d6ae) or through a SoftAP, and then controls them through Blueair's cloud.

None of this has been driven against hardware by this project, and no capture exists. Every byte below comes from static analysis of the Android app and of two of the vendor's BLE-module firmware packages, plus the vendor manual. The service layout, the security levels and the advertising data were read out of the module's own firmware, which is as close to a GATT dump as you get without the hardware, but still not one. In the spec it is all reported, and the spec is untested.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number Cabin P2i (single unit). Cabin P2iD (two units) appears in the manual's performance table; its BLE identity is not known Chipset Three processors. BLE module: Nordic nRF52. The DFU packages target hw_version 52 and SoftDevice S132 v5.0.0, and a 220 KB application beside S132 only fits an nRF52832, so that part number is an inference. Main MCU in the purifier unit: the firmware the update package carries for it is an Arm Cortex-M image linked at 0x08000000, the STM32 convention, so probably an STM32 or a clone (also an inference). Knob MCU, which the app and firmware call the "plug" Sensor Laser particle sensor, Plantower family (the BLE module's log strings name Plantower sensor errors). Exact model not established Radio BLE only (2.4 GHz). No Wi-Fi Power 12 V from the car's socket through the knob. The manual recommends an ignition-switched outlet FCC ID 2ARIK-P2I, grantee Blueair Tech (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd. Filed 2018-11-06, equipment class DTS, 2402–2480 MHz Bluetooth LE. Details are from the fccid.io listing as a search engine indexed it; the site refuses scripted requests, so the exhibits were not retrieved

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No. The only one-time step is the Bluetooth bond Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name Local name starting Blueair P2i (firmware 1.2.3 and 1.2.11) or Blueair ICP, matched case-insensitively as a prefix Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (decompiled app and vendor manual; not replayed here)

To bring a unit up from a client:

  1. Fit the filter and the top cover. The unit refuses to start without the cover. Plug the knob into the 12 V socket and switch the ignition on.
  2. Flick the knob left or right once to turn the unit on. A blue LED on the top cover lights, and the fan resumes its last setting.
  3. Turn the knob clockwise and hold it for about 5 seconds. The knob's LEDs run a cycling animation, which is pairing mode. Any phone already connected is dropped.
  4. Scan for Blueair P2i / Blueair ICP and connect. The app scans for 30 s and takes the first match, not the strongest.
  5. Bond, and wait for the bond to complete.
  6. Request a larger ATT MTU. The app asks for 517. At least 41 is needed, because the stored-record notifications are 38 bytes.
  7. Discover services and run the connect sequence under Protocol Summary.

Factory reset: not established. The BLE module erases every bond when the main MCU tells it to, and the main-MCU image inside the update package has a factory-reset routine of its own. No gesture in the manual or the app is known to reach either. Two things are easily mistaken for a reset:

  • The FILTER RESET button on the purifier base only restarts the filter counter. The module's logs say it resets it to 360 h.
  • Turning the knob anticlockwise and holding for 3 s only puts the unit into idle, with the lights off.

Nobody has worked out what clears the bond list. For anyone adopting a second-hand unit, that is the open question.

Rebinding to a new network: not applicable, since there is no network. To add a phone, repeat the knob pairing gesture. The unit keeps a bounded list of bonded phones, and its logs show it replacing an entry when the list is full.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required Yes. The app always bonds before it touches a characteristic Security mode just_works (LE legacy pairing). From the module's firmware, not observed on air Bonding required PIN source None known One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time No. There is a bonded-peer list with a maximum size, which is not established Confidence medium (app flow, firmware log strings and the firmware's pairing parameters; the exchange itself was never observed)

The firmware makes pairing mode matter more than usual. Once the unit holds any bond, the BLE module advertises only to whitelisted (bonded) phones. With an empty bond list and no pairing mode, it does not advertise at all. An unbonded client can therefore get in only while pairing mode is active.

The firmware also settles how the pairing goes:

  • Pairing parameters. Bonding is on, I/O capabilities are none, and LE Secure Connections is off. Keys are 7 to 16 bytes, and encryption and identity keys are distributed both ways. The module also sets the MITM and OOB flags, but a phone has no OOB data for it, so LE legacy pairing falls back to Just Works with unauthenticated keys.
  • Encryption is required. Every custom characteristic value, and every CCCD, is registered with security mode 1 level 2: an encrypted link, with unauthenticated keys accepted. Without a bond, a read, write or subscribe is refused with an insufficient-encryption error, and most host stacks then pair on their own.
  • One exception. The factory AT-command service 0x1337 drops the requirement while the unit is in its factory test-rig mode.

Entering pairing mode: with the unit on, turn the knob clockwise and hold it for about 5 seconds, until the knob's lights cycle. The main MCU tells the BLE module to enter pairing mode, and the module disconnects any current phone and advertises to everyone. Pairing mode ends when a bond completes or when a timeout runs out. The timeout's length was not recovered.

Unpairing: no user-facing route is known. The firmware can erase all bonds when the main MCU asks, but nothing found here makes it ask. Forgetting the unit on a phone clears only the phone's half.

Recovery:

  • If another phone holds the link, close the vendor app or switch Bluetooth off on that phone. Entering pairing mode from the knob also drops it.
  • If bonding fails after the unit lost its half of a bond, forget the unit in the phone's Bluetooth settings and repeat the knob gesture.

docs.title: UUIDs: 16-bit shorts on the SIG base
docs.text:
Every custom UUID here is a 16-bit short on the Bluetooth SIG base, 0000xxxx-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, services and characteristics alike. The shorts are not SIG-assigned. The app builds its characteristic UUIDs that way and the module registers them that way, so write them exactly as expanded.

The app never names a service. It runs discovery and then addresses each characteristic by its full UUID, and a client should do the same. The service layout below comes from the module's own firmware, where each service is registered as a primary service with a 16-bit UUID. It has not been seen in a GATT dump.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 00000001-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Identity, clock and status Firmware versions, clock, fault flags, unit type, unit state (0x0001–0x0005). Always advertised 00000002-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Fan and air quality Fan speed and mode, run-time counters, stored records, live sensor frames (0x0011–0x0017). Advertised in normal operation 00000003-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Update progress 0x0060 only. Not advertised 00001337-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Factory AT-command channel 0x0040 / 0x0041, for the factory test rig. Leave it alone (see below) 0000180a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Device Information (SIG) Serial, firmware and hardware revision, manufacturer 0000fe59-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Nordic Secure DFU Buttonless DFU entry

Every characteristic in the four custom services carries a Characteristic User Description with a short English label, so a GATT explorer shows names. Every value is fixed-length in the module's table (the stack's variable-length flag is off), so write exactly the length shown below.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
UUID Service Properties Length Role 00002a25-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x180a read text Serial number and BLE address, UTF-8 <serial>;<address> 00002a26-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x180a read text Firmware revision, UTF-8. The app replaces it with field 0 of 0x0001 00002a27-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x180a read text Hardware revision, UTF-8 00002a29-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x180a read text Manufacturer name, UTF-8 00000001-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x0001 read 84 Firmware versions, UTF-8 ble;main;knob;, padded to 84 bytes 00000002-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x0001 read, write 4 Clock: Unix time in seconds, uint32 LE. The app writes it on every connection and never reads it 00000003-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x0001 read, notify 4 Fault flags (see below) 00000004-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x0001 read, notify 1 Single/duo unit type, probably. In the app's table but never accessed; code values unknown 00000005-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x0001 read, notify 1 Unit state (see below). Firmware 1.2.11 and later only; the app does not know it 00000011-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x0002 read, notify 1 Fan speed reported (what the unit is running) 00000012-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x0002 write 1 Fan speed requested 00000013-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x0002 read, notify 1 Fan mode reported 00000014-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x0002 write 1 Fan mode requested 00000015-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x0002 read, notify 28 Fan and filter run-time counters 00000016-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x0002 notify 38 Stored air-quality records. Notify only: it cannot be read, and the app subscribes and receives a burst 00000017-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x0002 notify 26 Live particle-sensor frames 00000060-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x0003 read, notify 9 Firmware-update progress 00000040-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x1337 write 128 Factory AT command. Do not write 00000041-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0x1337 notify 128 Factory AT command response 8ec90003-f315-4f60-9fb8-838830daea50 0xfe59 write, indicate – Nordic buttonless DFU entry (without bond sharing)

The properties and lengths of the custom characteristics come from the module's GATT table. They agree with how the app uses each one, and add three things the app never touches: 0x0002 is readable, 0x0004 is read/notify, and there are the 0x0005 and 0x1337 characteristics. The Device Information and DFU properties are the stack's defaults.

docs.title: Advertising
docs.text:
The firmware builds its advertising data from these parts:

  • Flags 0x06: LE General Discoverable, BR/EDR not supported.
  • Name: Blueair P2i.
  • Appearance: included. The value was not traced.
  • Complete list of 16-bit service UUIDs: 0x0002, 0x0001 in normal operation. In the factory test-rig mode it is 0x0001, 0x1337 instead.

It advertises fast, then slow. Whenever it holds bonds and is not in pairing mode, it filters by the whitelist. The spec leaves the service UUIDs out of its scan matcher on purpose. They come from static analysis, and 16-bit values this generic would pull in other hardware. Match on the name, as the app does.

docs.title: Factory AT-command service (0x1337)
docs.text:
The module carries a text channel into an AT-style command interpreter, for the factory test rig. The same vocabulary runs its serial link to the main MCU, and it reaches fan control, the filter counters, the clock, bond deletion and the main-MCU and knob update steps.

At boot the module enters a test-rig mode when its stored settings are uninitialised or its stored device ID is all zeros. In that mode the service is advertised and open. On a unit that has left the factory it is present but needs an encrypted link, like everything else.

Several of those commands can wipe state or leave a board without firmware. None has been tried, and which of them this characteristic accepts was not traced, so the spec declares no commands for it. A client should not use it.

docs.title: Connect sequence
docs.text:
This is the order the app uses after the bond, MTU request and service discovery:

  1. Read 0x0060 (update progress), then subscribe to it. While byte 0 is 2–5 the unit is still updating its main MCU or knob. The SDK can hold everything else until byte 0 reads 1 (not needed) or 6 (finished). The shipped app does not use that option, but a careful client should wait.
  2. Read 0x2a25, 0x2a26, 0x2a27, 0x2a29 and 0x0001, then 0x0003, 0x0011, 0x0013 and 0x0015.
  3. Write the phone's Unix time, as a uint32 LE, to 0x0002.
  4. Subscribe to 0x0003, 0x0011, 0x0013, 0x0015 and 0x0017.
  5. Optionally subscribe to 0x0016. The app does this only when a user is signed in, because it forwards the stored records to the cloud. It batches them in groups of up to 10 records or 10 s.

docs.title: Fan speed and mode
docs.text:
A write goes to the requested characteristic. The BLE module passes it to the main MCU and then fetches the current value back, and the result arrives as a notification on the reported characteristic. The knob and auto mode change the same values, so render only the reported characteristic.

Code Fan speed (0x0011 / 0x0012) Fan mode (0x0013 / 0x0014) 0 Defined, meaning unknown. The app never writes it and displays a reported 0 as low Unknown 1 Low Manual (the speed on 0x0012 applies) 2 Medium Auto (the unit picks the speed from its sensor) 3 High Max. Defined, but the app never writes it and the knob has no such position

The app writes only speeds 1–3 and modes 1–2, and drops any reported value that is not exactly one byte in the range 0–3. The spec offers speed 0 and mode 3 only as advanced commands, because nobody has seen what the unit does with them.

docs.title: Fault flags (0x0003, and bytes 8–11 of every stored record)
docs.text:
Four bytes, one per board. All zero means no fault.

Byte Bit Meaning 0 (purifier) 0x01 Top cover open or filter not seated. The unit will not run 0 0x02 Button fault 0 0x04 Battery fault 0 0x08 Particle sensor not responding 0 0x10 Particle sensor out of range 0 0x20 Malfunction 1 (knob) 0x01 Knob not responding. Probably the manual's "disconnected from the control plug" 1 0x02 LED driver fault 1 0x04 Buttons fault 1 0x08 Malfunction 1 0x10 USB overload. The manual says the system shuts down until the load is removed 2 (BLE module) 0x01 Lost contact with the main MCU 3 (second unit, Duo) 0x01 Top cover open 3 0x02 Malfunction

docs.title: Unit state (0x0005, 1 byte, firmware 1.2.11 and later)
docs.text:
The main MCU's operating state, which the BLE module keeps and notifies when it changes. Firmware 1.2.3 does not have this characteristic, and the app never uses it. The names are paraphrases of the firmware's own state-name table.

Value State 0 Unknown 1 Powered off 2 Starting up 3 Filter due 4 Normal 5 Going to standby 6 Standby 7 Pairing mode 8 Error 9 Firmware update

docs.title: Run-time counters (0x0015, 28 bytes)
docs.text:
Seven 32-bit little-endian counters, all in minutes. The app decodes each one as signed.

Offset Field 0 Minutes at speed 0 (meaning of "speed 0" not established) 4 Minutes at low 8 Minutes at medium 12 Minutes at high 16 Total fan-on minutes 20 Live minutes (probably total powered time) 24 Filter time remaining. 21600 (360 h) after a filter reset

The manual rates a filter at about 360 hours of running, which it describes as about 6 months at 2.5 h a day. The app shows filter life as remaining × 100 / 21600, truncated to a whole percent and shown as 0 when remaining is 0 or less.

docs.title: Stored record (0x0016, 38 bytes, all little-endian)
docs.text:
Offset Length Field 0 4 Timestamp, Unix seconds, from the clock set through 0x0002 4 4 Record number in the unit's data store 8 4 Fault flags (the 0x0003 layout) 12 2 PM1, µg/m³ 14 2 PM2.5, µg/m³ 16 2 PM10, µg/m³ 18 2 PM1, second figure 20 2 PM2.5, second figure 22 2 PM10, second figure 24 2 Count > 0.3 µm 26 2 Count > 0.5 µm 28 2 Count > 1 µm 30 2 Count > 2.5 µm 32 2 Count > 5 µm 34 2 Count > 10 µm 36 1 Fan speed (signed byte, the 0x0011 codes) 37 1 Fan mode (signed byte, the 0x0013 codes)

The app drops any record that is not exactly 38 bytes.

docs.title: Live sensor frame (0x0017, 26 bytes)
docs.text:
Offset Length Field 0 1 Sensor status, signed. 0 = ok, −100 = CRC error, −102 = timeout; anything else is unknown 1 1 Not read by the app 2–25 12 × 2 The same twelve uint16 LE values as bytes 12–35 of the stored record

The twelve values follow the order of the data words in a Plantower PMS frame. If Plantower's convention holds, the first PM set is the "CF=1" figure, the second is the "atmospheric environment" figure, and the counts are per 0.1 L of air. That is a hypothesis. The frame carries no timestamp, and the app shows the first PM set stamped with the phone's own clock.

docs.title: Update progress (0x0060, 9 bytes)
docs.text:
Byte Meaning 0 Step: 0 not started, 1 not needed, 2 BLE module updating, 3 main MCU updating, 4 copying the knob image to the main MCU, 5 knob updating, 6 finished, 7 enum bound 1 / 2 BLE module: status, percent 3 / 4 Main MCU: status, percent 5 / 6 Knob image copy: status, percent 7 / 8 Knob: status, percent

The status codes are 0 unknown, 1 not needed, 2 in progress, 3 finished and 4 enum bound. The app treats the unit as settled when the step is 1 or 6, or when the knob stage reads finished.

docs.title: Firmware update
docs.text:
The update uses Nordic Secure DFU. The app hands the unit's address and a package to the Nordic Android DFU library, with keep-bond set. The library enters the bootloader through the buttonless characteristic 8ec90003-f315-4f60-9fb8-838830daea50, and the bootloader comes up at the unit's address + 1. In update mode the unit advertises a name starting AirBoxLab. The app also accepts a name starting Dfu, which is generic, so tie it to this product only while an update you started is in progress.

The cloud tells the app where the package is. The app fetches it over plain HTTP from firmware.foobot.io, a publicly listable Foobot/Airboxlab bucket that also holds Blueair's other firmware. The two packages read for this spec (application 1.2.3 and 1.2.11) are application-only and need S132 v5.0.0. They carry an ECDSA P-256 signed init packet, so a replacement client can deliver the vendor's packages but cannot build its own. Both packages declare application version 0, so the bootloader's version check will not tell releases apart.

The BLE module's application image carries the main MCU's firmware inside it: there are embedded Arm Cortex-M images with vector tables linked at 0x08000000. Where the knob's image sits was not traced. After the BLE module reboots, the unit carries on by itself. It pushes new firmware to the main MCU and then to the knob, reporting each stage on 0x0060, and the knob glows green meanwhile. The manual says not to power the unit off until it restarts. The spec marks the bootloader entry as advanced and reproduces no image or init-packet bytes.

The app has a separate path for resuming an update on a unit it finds already in update mode. By flash arithmetic, a 220 KB application beside S132 on an nRF52832 leaves no room for a second bank. An interrupted transfer therefore probably leaves the unit in its bootloader. Getting it out needs a Nordic DFU client and the vendor package.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Scan finds nothing. The unit advertises only to phones it has bonded with, and not at all when it has no bonds. Put it into pairing mode with the knob (clockwise, about 5 s). Also check that the 12 V socket is live with the ignition on and that the top cover is seated.
  • Bonding fails or the link drops right after connecting. Pairing mode was not active or had timed out. Repeat the gesture. If the phone remembers an old bond, forget the unit first.
  • Reads or subscriptions fail with an insufficient-encryption (or authentication) error. Every custom characteristic needs an encrypted link. Bond first; most stacks start pairing on this error by themselves, but some need it asked for explicitly.
  • Stored-record or counter notifications are cut short. The MTU was not raised. At the default MTU a notification carries 20 bytes, and the app drops anything that is not exactly 38 or 28 bytes.
  • Filter life never updates after a filter change. The counter resets only from the FILTER RESET button on the purifier base. No BLE command for it is known.

Defects found in the vendor app, which a replacement client should not copy:

  • The fault-flag parser accepts a 3-byte value and then reads a fourth byte, which throws.
  • The live-frame parser has no length check. A short frame throws and ends the stream until the next connection.
  • The live-frame status table includes −200 (sensor not initialised), which the signed byte it reads cannot represent.
  • Onboarding takes the first matching advertiser within its 30 s scan. With two units in pairing mode it can bond the wrong one.
  • Stored records are collected only while a user is signed in, because they go to the cloud. A phone used only locally never drains them.
  • Resuming an interrupted update looks the unit up in the cloud account's device list. Without the cloud, a stuck unit needs a generic Nordic DFU tool and the package.

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
• [x] Static analysis of the Blueair Android app (v4.x, 2026-09), covering its embedded Cabin BLE SDK and the app layer that drives it
  • [x] Static reading of two Cabin P2i BLE-module DFU packages from the vendor's public bucket: manifests, init-packet structure and log strings. No bytes are reproduced
  • [x] A disassembly of the 1.2.11 BLE-module application's BLE setup code: the GATT table (services, properties, lengths, security levels), the advertising data and the pairing parameters
  • [x] The vendor's Cabin P2i user manual (English/Japanese, 2018)
  • [ ] nRF Connect against a real unit, to confirm the service layout, properties, advertising data and pairing method read from the firmware: still needed

docs.title: BlueDriver Bluetooth Pro OBD-II Scan Tool (Bluetooth LE)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (third-party capture-derived; not replayed against hardware here) Protocol: BLE (Silicon Labs BGX13P Xpress Streaming profile, XOR-encoded ELM327-style stream) Manufacturer: Lemur Vehicle Monitors (BlueDriver) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
BlueDriver is a plug-in OBD-II scanner that ships with a vendor phone app. This page covers the Bluetooth LE units, which advertise a local name starting BlueDriv or LSB2-. The vendor marks these with an engraved LE on the side, and the BlueDriver Pro Next-Gen is always LE. The original Bluetooth Classic BlueDriver (no "LE" marking, paired from the phone's Bluetooth settings) is a different radio path and has not been researched.

The radio side is a stock Silicon Labs BGX13P "Bluetooth Xpress" module. Behind it sits an ELM327-style OBD core. Four vendor-specific rules sit on top of the module's standard streaming profile, and a client that misses any one of them gets nothing back:

  1. Every stream byte is XORed with 0x26, except CR (0x0d) and > (0x3e), which pass through unchanged.
  2. The client announces a receive window on DATA (00 ff 7f) and then must acknowledge every DATA notification with 01 <len> 00. Without the acknowledgements the scanner stops after the first fragment.
  3. A fixed nine-command LM init must run before any PID query works.
  4. After the init, standard AT commands are forbidden. ATZ, ATE0 and the rest corrupt the firmware state, and every later query answers NO DATA.

Everything here comes from the open project sjalkote/bluedriver-reverse-engineering. Its author decoded iOS PacketLogger HCI logs of the vendor app pairing and streaming live data, then replayed the session in a Python Bleak client. Two further sources fill in around it. Silicon Labs' public BGX documentation supplies the service UUID and the meaning of the flow-control bytes (both inferred, and marked so). Vendor support articles supply the pairing window, the LED meanings and the existence of firmware updates. This project holds no capture of its own and has driven no hardware. Every fact is reported, and the spec's device.testing is untested.

Generic ELM327 behaviour lives in OBD-II Bluetooth Adapters. PID formulas live in the obd2-pid-reference spec (device-specs/devices/obd2-pid-reference.yaml). Also see Common OBD-II Patterns.

Out of scope: the vendor app's enhanced and manufacturer diagnostics (ABS/SRS/TPMS and similar), repair reports, cloud features, firmware update (only its existence is recorded) and DTC clearing (mode 04). The source never exercised mode 04. It erases stored codes and resets readiness monitors, so any client that adds it should treat it as an advanced, confirm-first action.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Model code LSB2 (the CERT note and the owner's guide both use it; the LSB2- name prefix matches). Neither source says whether it names the LE unit, the Classic one or both Models covered BlueDriver Pro with "LE" engraved; BlueDriver Pro Next-Gen (always LE, per vendor). Which unit the upstream author had is not stated Not covered Bluetooth Classic BlueDriver (no "LE" marking) Radio module Silicon Labs BGX13P (upstream); its GATT profile matches the stock BGX Xpress Streaming service OBD core ELM327-style; reached only through the vendor's LM commands and raw mode-01 requests Advertised name Prefix BlueDriv or LSB2- Firmware string LMI replies carry an "OSAPI" version, e.g. OSAPI v2.60 Power OBD connector pin 16 (usually unswitched, so unplug the scanner when you are done) FCC ID Not harvested

LED meanings, per the vendor:

LED Meaning Solid blue at plug-in Starting up Flashing red (Pro) / green (Next-Gen) Powered and talking to the vehicle; no app connected Flashing blue Talking to a phone; stops flashing after a while Solid red at plug-in Firmware recovery mode after an interrupted update; only the vendor app's update flow recovers it

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No provisioning. A one-time LE bond is made on first connect (see Pairing) Method ble_direct (pairing required) Advertised name BlueDriv*, LSB2-* Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (working open client plus vendor articles; not replayed here)
  1. Turn the ignition on (engine running, or key-on/engine-off), then plug the scanner in.
  2. Within 60 seconds, scan for the name prefix and connect.
  3. Run the connection handshake below. Its read of the encrypted characteristic makes the host pair on first contact.
  4. Poll mode-01 PIDs one request at a time.

The documented path needs no account. Per the vendor, codes, freeze frame and live data all work offline in its own app. Only repair reports, VIN decoding and firmware downloads need the vendor's servers.

Factory reset: none documented. Unplugging the scanner is a power cycle, not a reset. It restarts the 60 s pairing window, but no source says it drops bonds. A stock BGX13P keeps up to 14 bonds and evicts the least recently used one when a new host bonds. Whether this product keeps that default is not confirmed.

Rebinding: pair the new phone or client inside the 60 s window. A phone that bonded earlier may reconnect first and take the only connection. Turn Bluetooth off on it, or forget the scanner there, before pairing the new one.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
See Pairing, Bonding and Unpairing.

Property Value Pairing required Yes Security mode just_works: the scanner answers SMP with IO capability NoInputNoOutput, forcing LE Secure Connections Just Works, with no PIN and no dialog Bonding required: the bond persists (macOS lists the scanner afterwards), and an unbonded host can only pair inside the window PIN source none One central at a time Yes (BGX13P limit; vendor troubleshooting assumes another phone can take the connection) One bond at a time No. Several phones stay paired (vendor); the stock module keeps 14 bonds Confidence medium

How pairing is triggered: CoreBluetooth has no pairing call, so the vendor app reads the encrypted characteristic 12e868e7-c926-4906-96c8-a7ee81d4b1b3 and the stack pairs on the resulting security requirement. Upstream does the same. On later connections the read runs over the encrypted link, or fails harmlessly when the bond is cached. That characteristic's service is not recorded, so look it up by UUID.

Entering pairing mode: there is no button. The scanner is pairable for about 60 seconds after it powers up from the connector (vendor). To reopen the window, unplug it and plug it back in. No source says whether an already-bonded host can reconnect outside the window.

Why the window exists: CERT/CC VU#615456 (CVE-2016-2354, April 2016) found that the "BlueDriver LSB2" accepted Bluetooth connections with no PIN, so anyone in range could reach the vehicle's diagnostic bus. The vendor's fix was firmware that limits discoverability to one minute after plug-in (not at every ignition-on). The LE units covered here ship with that window, so the spec records the note as history rather than as an active security_advisory. Just Works still means that anyone who can plug the scanner in can pair with it. The note's word "discoverability" leaves open whether the scanner stops advertising after the minute or only stops accepting new pairings. A stock BGX13P can do the latter: with pairing turned off, bonded hosts still connect.

Unpairing: no scanner-side route is documented. On the host, forget the scanner in the OS Bluetooth settings. The vendor gives exactly this remedy when a bonded iPhone will not reconnect.

Recovery: fully close the vendor app, including in the background. Turn Bluetooth off on every other phone or tablet that has paired with the scanner. Then unplug, replug and connect within 60 s.

docs.title: BLE services
docs.text:
The three streaming characteristics are the stock Silicon Labs BGX Xpress Streaming characteristics. Upstream lists them by UUID without naming their service. The service UUID below is inferred from the BGX documentation and has not been seen in a BlueDriver GATT dump. Look the characteristics up by UUID.

UUID Name (upstream / BGX) Properties Use 331a36f5-2459-45ea-9d95-6142f0c4b307 BGX Xpress Streaming service (service) Inferred a9da6040-0823-4995-94ec-9ce41ca28833 CMD / Peripheral Receive (Rx) write, write-without-response, notify XOR-encoded ASCII commands in; stream control messages out a73e9a10-628f-4494-a099-12efaf72258f DATA / Peripheral Transmit (Tx) write-without-response, notify, indicate XOR-encoded reply fragments out; window and acknowledgement messages in 75a9f022-af03-4e41-b4bc-9de90a47d50b STATUS / Stream Mode (Mode) read, write, notify, indicate Status bursts, not decoded. Never write it: on a BGX module a Mode write takes the module out of streaming 12e868e7-c926-4906-96c8-a7ee81d4b1b3 ENCRYPTED read (encryption required) Pairing trigger; service not recorded 0000180a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Device Information (service) Standard 00002a24-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Model Number String read Display only 00002a26-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Firmware Revision String read Display only

docs.title: Wire encoding
docs.text:
wire = plain ^ 0x26 for every stream byte, except 0x0d (CR) and 0x3e (>), which are sent as-is. Decoding applies the same rule. The three-byte stream control messages are not encoded.

A consequence of the rule, worked out here rather than observed: plaintext + (0x2b) and 0x18 would encode to 0x0d and 0x3e and so cannot be represented. Neither appears in ELM327 command or reply text.

Plain Wire LMI CR 6a 6b 6f 0d LMX0 CR 6a 6b 7e 16 0d 010C CR 16 17 16 65 0d 0F 80 CR > (upstream's reply to 010C: 0x0f80 / 4 = 992 rpm) 16 60 06 1e 16 06 0d 3e OK CR > 69 6d 0d 3e NO DATA CR > 68 69 06 62 67 72 67 0d 3e

docs.title: Flow control
docs.text:
The bytes are upstream's. The field names come from the BGX "Fast-Ack" streaming control message, a 3-byte message of the form opcode, count (u16 little-endian). Opcode 0x00 is Initial Buffer Size and 0x01 is Buffer Bytes Freed.

Bytes Direction Upstream says BGX reading 00 ff 07 scanner → client, CMD notify, on connect status message Initial Buffer Size = 2047 bytes 00 ff 7f client → scanner, DATA write, before the first command opens a 255-byte credit window Initial Buffer Size = 32767 bytes 01 01 00 scanner → client, CMD notify, after each command ACK Buffer Bytes Freed = 1 01 <len> 00 client → scanner, DATA write, for every DATA notification per-fragment ACK Buffer Bytes Freed = <len>

Open question: under the BGX reading the scanner has 32767 bytes of credit and should not need a per-fragment acknowledgement, yet upstream saw it stall after one fragment without them. Acknowledge every fragment, as the vendor app does.

docs.title: Connection sequence
docs.text:
# Characteristic Action 1 CMD Subscribe (the scanner sends 00 ff 07) 2 DATA Subscribe 3 STATUS Subscribe 4 ENCRYPTED Read. This pairs on first contact (inside the 60 s window); upstream allows 20 s 5 Device Information Optionally read the firmware and model strings 6 DATA Write 00 ff 7f, then wait about 100 ms 7 DATA From now on, write 01 <len> 00 for every notification, then XOR-decode it and append it to the reply buffer until > 8 CMD LM init (below), waiting for > after each command

Upstream subscribed before pairing and ran only on macOS, which pairs on its own when a subscription needs encryption. On a stack that instead refuses the subscriptions, doing step 4 first is the untested fallback.

docs.title: LM init
docs.text:
Each command is sent XOR-encoded with a trailing CR over CMD. Wait for > before sending the next one (upstream allows 3 s, then pauses 50 ms).

# Command Expected reply Role 1 LMI ?, or OSAPI v2.60 CR OK Firmware identity probe 2 LMD OK Unknown 3 LML0 ? Unknown; the ? is expected 4 LMI OSAPI v2.60 CR OK Firmware identity probe 5 LMD OK Unknown 6 LMDP protocol number CR OK Auto-detected OBD protocol 7 LMI OSAPI v2.60 CR OK Firmware identity probe 8 LMX1 OK Exhaustive timing, ~200 ms per query 9 LMX0 OK Fast timing, ~45 ms per query; ready for live polling

After the init the ELM core runs with echo off, headers off, linefeeds off, spaces on and automatic protocol selection. The vendor app switches to LMX1 only for its one-time monitor and freeze-frame scans, and uses LMX0 for live data.

LMDP returns the ELM327 protocol numbers: 1 J1850 PWM, 2 J1850 VPW, 3 ISO 9141-2, 4/5 ISO 14230-4 KWP (5-baud / fast init), 6–9 ISO 15765-4 CAN (11/29-bit at 500/250 kbit/s), A SAE J1939.

docs.title: Reading PIDs
docs.text:
Mode-01 PIDs are sent raw (e.g. 010C CR). A single-PID reply carries only the data bytes, with no 41 and no PID echo (0F 80 CR >). Strip a leading 41 <pid> defensively anyway. NO DATA, UNABLE, ERROR, STOPPED, SEARCHING or ? mean no value.

The PIDs upstream tested, with J1979 formulas (A, B are data bytes in reply order; multi-byte values are big-endian):

PID Parameter Formula 010C Engine RPM (A·256 + B) / 4 rpm 010D Vehicle speed A km/h 0105 Coolant temperature A − 40 °C 010F Intake air temperature A − 40 °C 0104 Engine load A·100/255 % 0111 Throttle position A·100/255 % 012F Fuel level A·100/255 % 010B Intake manifold pressure A kPa 0142 Control module voltage (A·256 + B) / 1000 V

Multi-PID: on CAN vehicles only, one mode-01 request may carry up to six PIDs (e.g. 010C0D0504110B). Each PID number comes back ahead of its data, with no leading 41. Drop any 0:/1: frame markers. If fewer PIDs come back, the vehicle does not support combined requests, so fall back to one PID per request.

No pipelining: any write while a query is in flight aborts that query.

Timing (upstream): serial polling takes about 40–50 ms per PID, so a six-PID refresh takes about 0.25–0.3 s, matching the vendor app. The connection interval is about 15 ms.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Cause First fragment arrives, then nothing A DATA notification was not acknowledged (01 <len> 00), or 00 ff 7f was never written Every query answers NO DATA An AT command was sent after the LM init, which breaks the firmware state. No recovery is documented; unplugging and re-initialising is the obvious (untested) remedy. The init may also have been skipped ATRV / ATDP answer NO DATA By design. Use PID 0142 and LMDP Random timeouts, truncated replies A command was written before the previous > arrived Live data updates about once a second The scanner is in LMX1; send LMX0 Scanner not found, or the pairing read times out More than 60 s since plug-in on an unbonded host; another bonded phone or the vendor app holds the connection; ignition off; stale bond on the host (forget it and re-pair) Solid red LED at plug-in Firmware recovery mode. Only the vendor app's update flow recovers it

The vendor also notes that many aftermarket Android head units run a ROM that blocks the scanner from pairing, and knows of no workaround.

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
• Upstream: Apple Bluetooth logging profile + sysdiagnose + PacketLogger (iOS HCI capture), and a Python Bleak client on macOS.
  • This project: documentation review only (the upstream repository, Silicon Labs BGX documentation and data sheet, vendor support articles, the LSB2 owner's guide, the CERT/CC note). No capture, no hardware.

docs.title: References
docs.text:

  • BlueDriver LSB2 Bluetooth Pro OBDII Scan Tool instruction guide (manuals.plus, which refuses non-browser clients with a 403): the owner's guide for model LSB2. It covers the app's features, including the sensor firmware update, but has no pairing steps and does not say which radio it describes.

docs.title: Blueriiot Blue Connect (Go / Plus) Pool Analyser
docs.text: Status: Spec Available. The measure-now path is corroborated by an open integration and by community frames posted beside the vendor app's values, but has not been replayed by this project. Protocol: BLE (plus Sigfox and an optional Wi-Fi bridge, both out of scope) Manufacturer: Blueriiot (Riiot Labs SA, now part of Fluidra) Manufacturer Status: Active. The vendor cloud is required for history, advice and Sigfox, but not for a BLE reading.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Blue Connect is a floating (or pipe-mounted, with the Blue Fit50 clamp) pool and spa analyser. The Plus measures water temperature, pH, ORP and conductivity, from which salinity is estimated. The Go drops the conductivity probe. It has three uplinks:

  • Sigfox: automatic readings a few times a day, straight to the vendor cloud. This needs the Plus pack or a Premium subscription.
  • BLE: an on-demand "measure now" from a phone within about 10 m.
  • Blue Extender: an optional mains-powered bridge that collects readings over BLE and forwards them over Wi-Fi.

Only the BLE path is local, and it is short. Connect without pairing, subscribe to one characteristic, write 0x01 to another, and about 8 s later one notification arrives carrying temperature, pH electrode voltage, ORP, a conductivity value and battery voltage. That makes the analyser fully usable from Home Assistant or any BLE client with no account and no subscription.

The spec is device-specs/devices/blueriiot-blue-connect.yaml. Where the two disagree, the spec wins.

Not the Zodiac Blue Connect

Zodiac-branded "Blue Connect" Gold/Silver analysers advertise as BC3…, use different vendor services and require a 9-character access code for on-demand measurements. That is a different protocol and is not covered here.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Models Blue Connect Plus (EU ref. 71663; AU ref. 73661), Blue Connect Go (ref. 73014), earlier plain "Blue Connect", first-generation "blue by Riiot" (2017) Chipset Cypress (Infineon) PSoC 4 BLE: inferred from the Cypress bootloader service, the Cypress address block 00:A0:50 and company ID 0x0131 Radio BLE, 10 dBm, plus Sigfox (EU 868 MHz; US and AU 902/920 MHz editions) Battery 3.6 V lithium thionyl chloride primary cell, about two years' life, reported on the wire in mV Advertised name B + generation digit + 8 hex digits (vendor app's filter ^B[12][0-9A-Fa-f]{8}$; not yet seen on air) FCC ID None found. The manual carries an FCC Part 15 statement for serial numbers beginning with 4, but prints no FCC ID, and fccid.co has no Blueriiot, Riiot Labs or Fluidra grantee. Rated ranges pH 0–14, temperature 5–50 °C, ORP 0–999 mV, conductivity 250–15 000 µS/cm (Plus)

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No (for a local BLE reading) Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name ^B[12][0-9A-Fa-f]{8}$ (update mode: blue v2 - OTA) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (open integration and community scripts, not replayed here)

Cloud activation happens in the vendor app, which scans the QR code on the storage cap or takes the printed key and the last three serial digits. It links the unit to an account and to Sigfox, and a local BLE reading does not need it. The one physical step is waking a new unit (or one coming out of winter standby): shake it with one sharp movement, and two beeps confirm activation. Keep the top of the analyser out of the water, since the antenna lives there.

Factory reset: none is documented for the analyser. The account link lives in the cloud and BLE stores no bond, so nothing local needs clearing. The vendor's fix for an unresponsive unit is a forced restart: take it out of the water, unscrew the top (left-hand thread, so turn it clockwise), unplug the white battery connector for about 10 seconds, reconnect it, reseat the seal and screw it back anticlockwise.

Rebinding: nothing binds the BLE surface. Any client in range can measure. Moving the unit to a different vendor account is a cloud operation.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none Bonding none PIN source n/a One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time No (nothing bonds) Confidence medium (vendor help centre plus the open integration)

The vendor's own help centre explains that the analyser uses Bluetooth without pairing, which is why it never shows up in the phone's Bluetooth list.

Entering pairing mode: not applicable. The analyser advertises whenever it is awake.

Unpairing: nothing to unpair.

Recovery: if a connection or measurement fails, close the vendor app and unplug any Blue Extender, since the Extender is itself a BLE central that connects to the analyser. Then retry. If the analyser still does not answer, do the forced restart above.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: All UUIDs share the vendor base -f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00. iopool's probes use the same base, so never identify on it alone.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description f3300001-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 Analyser service Main vendor service f3300002-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 Measure request Write 0x01 (with response) to start a measurement f3300003-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 Measurement notification One frame per request, about 8 s later f3300020-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 Command One-byte opcodes (below) f3300008-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 Flash settings (older firmware) Configuration record. Layout not decoded, so treat it as read-only f3300012-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 Flash settings (2.3.0+) Same record on current firmware f3320001-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 Production info service f3320011-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 BLE firmware version Read. Layout below 00060000-f8ce-11e4-abf4-0002a5d5c51b Cypress bootloader service Update mode only 00060001-f8ce-11e4-abf4-0002a5d5c51b Bootloader command Write plus notify, Cypress bootloader packets f3380001-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 Blue Extender service On the Extender, not the analyser. Command write f3380002, notify f3380003; command set not documented

docs.title: Command: Measure now
docs.text:
Request: enable notifications on f3300003, then write to f3300002:

Offset Length Description 0 1 0x01

Response: one notification on f3300003. All multi-byte fields are little-endian u16.

Offset Length Field Decode 0 1 Header low nibble = message type (3), high nibble = format version: 0x23 on firmware ≤ 2.2.x (11 bytes), 0x33 on 2.3.0 (12 bytes) 1 2 Water temperature raw × 0.01 °C 3 2 pH electrode mV = raw × 0.25 − 512; uncalibrated pH = (2048 − raw) / 232 + 7 = 7 − mV / 58 5 2 ORP raw × 0.25 mV 7 2 Conductivity (raw) µS/cm ≈ 1 061 500 / raw (community fit). Reads 0 or 1 on a Go (no probe) 9 2 Battery mV (about 3620 on a healthy cell) 11 1 (version-3 frames only) Meaning unknown

The vendor app applies the temperature, pH-electrode and ORP scalings above itself. The pH figure is the ideal-electrode formula the community fitted, and the app shows a calibrated value that can differ by a few hundredths.

Test vectors (raw frames posted in the Home Assistant community thread, beside what the vendor app or cloud showed):

Frame Decoded here Vendor showed 23 ab 09 32 07 ab 0a 78 00 24 0e 24.75 °C, pH 7.888, ORP 682.75 mV, 8846 µS/cm, 3.620 V 24.8 °C, pH 7.93, 685 mV, 8742 µS/cm, salinity 4.9 g/L 23 a9 0b ff 07 aa 08 01 00 25 0e 29.85 °C, pH 7.004, 554.5 mV, no probe, 3.621 V 29.8 °C, pH 7.0, 554 mV 23 18 0b 7f 07 0d 0a 00 00 2b 0e 28.40 °C, pH 7.556, 643.25 mV, no probe, 3.627 V 28.4 °C, pH 7.6, 645 mV 33 a5 0a b0 07 bc 0a 01 00 2c 0e 22 27.25 °C, pH 7.345, 687.0 mV, no probe, 3.628 V, trailing byte 34 (firmware 2.3.0 frame)

docs.title: Command characteristic opcodes
docs.text:
Each is one byte written with response to f3300020.

Opcode Role Advanced 0x31 Software reset (the app's "restart my analyser") No 0x20 Select the US Sigfox radio zone Yes: radio-regulatory 0x21 Select the AU Sigfox radio zone Yes: radio-regulatory 0x50 Reboot into the Cypress bootloader (firmware update) Yes: the unit cannot measure until an image is delivered

docs.title: Firmware version (f3320011)
docs.text:
Offset Length Field 0 1 Major 1 1 Minor 2 2 Build year (LE) 4 1 Build day 5 1 Build month 6 1 Build minute 7 1 Build hour (UTC) 8 8 Source-revision hash (shown as hex)

This is the BLE part's own version. One user's app showed v0.2 2019-11-12 beside product firmware 2.2.1.

docs.title: Advertisement
docs.text: The vendor app also reads measurements from the advertisement. The manufacturer data is company ID 0x0131 (Cypress's), then one message with the same header byte as above, then two trailing bytes. The message types that arrive there (compressed status records) are not decoded in this spec.

docs.title: Firmware update
docs.text: The analyser is a Cypress PSoC 4 BLE part. After opcode 0x50 it reboots into Cypress's stock BLE bootloader, advertises as blue v2 - OTA and serves the bootloader service. There the app writes the .cyacd image row by row using the standard Cypress bootloader host protocol. The app bundles firmware 2.3.0. An interrupted update leaves the unit in the bootloader, and the app offers to finish it. The spec documents the transport by role only and contains no flashing sequence. See Firmware Update.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The write succeeds but nothing arrives. Subscribe to f3300003 before writing 0x01. Otherwise another central (the vendor app, an Extender) may hold the link, the top of the analyser may be under water, or you may be out of the short BLE range. The vendor's last resort is the battery-disconnect restart. A forum user needed it after a firmware update left the unit unreachable.
  • Conductivity of about a million µS/cm. You have a Go. It reports 1 (sometimes 0) where the Plus reports its conductivity reading. The open integration only guards against 0.
  • Battery always 100 %. The open integration multiplies its battery percentage by 100 twice before clamping. Use the voltage instead. With this cell chemistry a percentage derived from voltage says little until the very end.
  • Battery drains fast. Every BLE measurement powers the probe. Poll every 30 minutes or less often, as the integration does by default and as the vendor's help centre advises.
  • The vendor app will not take a Bluetooth measurement on Android. Older builds required location services to be on before a BLE scan. That is an Android permission requirement, not a device one.
  • pH or ORP is slightly off from the app. This spec's values are uncalibrated. The app applies a per-unit calibration from its pH 7/pH 4/ORP reference-solution routine. Check a test strip before dosing chemicals.

docs.title: Bluetooth LED Name Badge
docs.text: Status: Complete Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Generic (multiple OEMs) Manufacturer Status: Abandoned

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Cheap programmable 11x44 monochrome LED dot-matrix badges sold under many brands on AliExpress and distributed at events like 35c3. Extensively reverse engineered by the FOSSASIA community.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Display 11x44 LED matrix (charlieplexing, 24 control pins) Chipset CH582M (RISC-V) or MM32L062PF (ARM M0) Radio BLE 4.x FCC ID Not applicable (generic)

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 0xFEE0 Badge Service Primary service 0xFEE1 Badge Data Write-only characteristic for all data

docs.title: Packet Format
docs.text: All data is written as 16-byte BLE GATT writes to 0xFEE1 with 100ms delay between writes.

docs.title: Header (64 bytes)
docs.text: Offset Length Field Description 0-3 4 Magic 0x77616E67 ("wang") 4 1 Reserved 0x00 5 1 Brightness 0x00=100%, 0x10=75%, 0x20=50%, 0x40=25% 6 1 Flash flags Bitfield: bit N = message N blinks 7 1 Marquee flags Bitfield: bit N = message N has animated border 8-15 8 Speed+Mode (speed << 4) | mode per message 16-31 16 Message sizes 2 bytes big-endian per message (up to 8) 38-43 6 Timestamp YY, MM, DD, HH, MM, SS

docs.title: Animation Modes (low nibble of speed+mode byte)
docs.text: Value Mode 0x00 Scroll left 0x01 Scroll right 0x02 Scroll up 0x03 Scroll down 0x04 Fixed/static 0x05 Snowflake 0x06 Picture/drop-down 0x07 Curtain/animation 0x08 Laser

docs.title: Bitmap Data (bytes 64+)
docs.text: Each character is 11 bytes (8 pixels wide x 11 rows). MSB = leftmost pixel, 1 = LED on.

docs.title: Key Properties
docs.text:
• No pairing required
  • Write-only (no reads, no acknowledgments)
  • Stateless -- each write replaces all stored messages
  • Persistent -- messages stored in flash, survive power cycles
  • Max 8 messages, max 8192 bytes total payload

docs.title: Bluetti Power Station (EP500 family)
docs.text: Status: Complete (V1 read path hardware-verified; writes and V2/encrypted documented from prior art) Protocol: BLE (MODBUS-RTU over GATT) Manufacturer: Bluetti (Shenzhen Poweroak Newener Co., Ltd.) Manufacturer Status: Active — cloud-independence spec, not an abandonment rescue

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Bluetti portable power stations (EP500, EP500P, AC200M, AC300, AC500, AC60, EP600, EB3A and kin) expose full telemetry and output control over plain local BLE — no pairing, no authentication, no cloud. The vendor app routes telemetry through Bluetti's IoT cloud, but every reading and switch below is local GATT. Three mature open implementations (bluetti_mqtt, bluetti-bt-lib / hassio-bluetti-bt, Bluetti_ESP32_Bridge) drive these units offline.

The read path of this spec was verified against real EP500 hardware (2026-08-14): the model string read from register 10 and the serial from register 17 matched the unit's advertised name EP500<serial> exactly, and the status block returned live telemetry (SOC 50 %, AC output on under a 1 kW load) with valid CRCs.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model verified EP500 (2 kW inverter / 5.1 kWh LiFePO4) BT module OUI 00:15:83 (IVT Corporation stack vendor); advertises 16-bit service 0xFF00 Radio BLE 4.x GATT, public address Advertised name <MODEL><serial>, e.g. EP5002142000061564

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct — connect, subscribe 0xFF01, write MODBUS frames to 0xFF02 Passphrase protection not_applicable (no pairing, no authentication on the plain protocol) Confidence high (verified live + three working open implementations)

Factory reset: nothing BLE-relevant to clear — no bonds, no credentials.

Rebinding: single-connection peripheral; any client may connect once the previous central (including the vendor app) disconnects.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: MODBUS-RTU frames over GATT: address byte 0x01, function 0x03 (read holding registers) / 0x06 (write single register), registers big-endian, CRC-16/MODBUS appended little-endian. Requests fit one ATT write; responses fragment across 0xFF01 notifications — reassemble to 2*qty+5 bytes, then CRC-check. One command in flight at a time.

docs.title: Protocol generations
docs.text: Generation Detection Identity registers Plain V1 (EP500 class) silence on 0xFF01 after subscribe type @ 10 (ASCII), serial @ 17, SOC @ 43 Plain V2 (AC70/AC180/EL30 class) same silence, V1 identity reads fail type @ 110 (byte-swapped), serial @ 116, SOC @ 102 Encrypted (newer firmware) unsolicited 2A 2A push right after subscribe AES/ECDH handshake, not covered

docs.title: Key registers (EP500 / V1)
docs.text:
Register Field Notes 10 (×6) model string hardware-verified 17 (×4) serial (u64, low word first) hardware-verified 36–39 DC-in / AC-in / AC-out / DC-out power (W) hardware-verified 43 battery SOC % hardware-verified 48 / 49 AC / DC output state hardware-verified 3007 / 3008 AC / DC output control (write 1/0) prior art; switches real loads 91–121 pack voltages, per-cell voltages prior art

See device-specs/devices/bluetti-power-station.yaml for the full map, polling ranges and safety notes.
