docs.title: Eurotronic Comet Blue Bluetooth Radiator Thermostat
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (static analysis of the vendor apps, cross-checked against two open implementations; no capture, not run against hardware) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Eurotronic Technology GmbH (rebadged as Sygonix HT100 BT, Xavax (Hama) and Lidl Silvercrest RT2000BT) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Comet Blue is a battery-powered radiator thermostat (TRV) head sold in Europe since 2014. It runs the valve from a weekly schedule stored on the device. The phone only reads and writes settings. The only radio is BLE, and the phone talks to the valve directly. There is no bonding, no hub and no cloud. EUROprog 2 goes online only to download firmware, and ET Blue's only links are to the vendor's help pages. If the vendor disappeared tomorrow, a client would lose nothing it needs.

Access control is an application-layer PIN, not Bluetooth pairing. After connecting, a client writes the PIN to one characteristic. The valve refuses every other write until that one succeeds. Each setting is a fixed-length value on its own characteristic, with no framing, checksum or encryption.

The machine-readable spec is device-specs/devices/eurotronic-comet-blue.yaml. Everything in it is verification: reported. The byte layouts come from static analysis of the two vendor Android apps (2026-09-27), and they agree with im-0/cometblue and rikroe/eurotronic-cometblue. The authors of those two projects ran them against real units. This project has not.

In scope: the Comet Blue and its rebadges.

Out of scope:

  • Progmatic Blue (a programming stick) and Progtime Blue (a socket timer). The same EUROprog 2 app drives both, and they use the same UUID base, but the protocol is not the same. See Telling the siblings apart.
  • Comet Zero Blue. It is in neither vendor app's device list. Do not assume it speaks this protocol.
  • Genius BLE100. ET Blue drives it with the same Comet Blue UUIDs, so it probably shares this table. That is unverified.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number Eurotronic Comet Blue. Rebadges: Sygonix HT100 BT, Xavax (Hama), Silvercrest RT2000BT (Home Assistant and rikroe's list) Chipset Not recorded. The app's name for the radio image points to Dialog's SUOTA lineage, so a Dialog DA1458x radio is possible (inferred only) Radio Bluetooth 4.0 LE (vendor flyer) Power Replaceable batteries. The manual forbids rechargeable cells. Schedules survive a battery change Valve fit M30 × 1.5 directly. Danfoss RA, RAV and RAVL through the bundled adapters (manual) FCC ID None. The product is sold only in the EU and carries a CE Declaration of Conformity

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No (nothing to provision over the air) Method ble_direct Advertised name Comet Blue (exact, per EUROprog 2). The rebadges' names are not recorded Advertised service 47e9ee00-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 (the Home Assistant / rikroe filter; needs active scanning) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence high (two working open implementations; not replayed here)

The valve has to be commissioned on its own buttons first. After the first battery insertion it asks for the date and time on its display. It then drives the motor to the install position. Mount it only while the display shows the install prompt. After mounting it runs an adaptation, opening and closing the valve to learn its stroke. A unit that has not finished adapting still answers over BLE but does not regulate.

After that, a client does the following on every connection:

  1. Scan for the advertised service 47e9ee00-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67, or for the exact local name Comet Blue.
  2. Connect. No bonding is requested.
  3. Optionally read the revision strings (00002a26-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, 00002a28-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb). They are readable before the PIN.
  4. Write the PIN to 47e9ee30-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 as a uint32 little-endian, with a write request. The factory PIN is 00 00 00 00. Write status 0 means it was accepted; any other status means a wrong PIN.
  5. Write the clock (47e9ee01-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67), then read and write settings.
  6. Disconnect. rikroe's library documents that the valve applies writes when the link closes.

EUROprog 2 waits 1 s before the PIN write on units whose firmware revision sorts below a reference revision. Waiting 1 s every time is harmless.

Factory reset: use All reset in the valve's own menu. Press MENU, turn the wheel to the reset item, press OK, and press OK again when it flashes. Per the manual, the valve returns to factory settings: comfort 21 °C, eco 16 °C, and one heating period from 07:00 to 22:00. It then restarts the initial-operation flow. Whether it also restores PIN 0 is not established. That question decides whether a second-hand unit with an unknown PIN can be recovered at all. Pulling the batteries for a few seconds is a different operation. It is the manual's fix for an error code, and it keeps the schedule. (Source: manual; not performed here.)

Rebinding: the valve has no network membership and no bond. A new phone or controller needs only the current PIN.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required Yes, but at the application layer (the PIN write). Nothing pairs at the link layer Security mode app_layer Bonding none PIN source fixed_default = 0. The manual prints it as "000 000"; on the wire it is 00 00 00 00 One central at a time Unknown (the vendor apps hold one connection per valve) One bond at a time No (nothing is bonded) Confidence medium

Entering pairing mode: not needed. The valve accepts a connection and a PIN write whenever it is powered.

The PIN:

  • It is 0–999999, at most six digits.
  • Owners change it in EUROprog 2. Writing a new value to the PIN characteristic, in a connection already authenticated with the old one, sets the new PIN. im-0's set pin works the same way.
  • ET Blue makes the owner choose a per-room PIN and refuses 0. A valve set up with ET Blue no longer answers to 0.
  • The PIN crosses the air in cleartext on an unencrypted link. Anyone who sniffs one session learns it.

Unpairing: there is no bond to drop. The only way to revoke a client is to change the PIN, and every other client then has to be given the new one.

Recovery: close EUROprog 2, ET Blue, Home Assistant or any other controller that holds a connection, then connect.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: All vendor UUIDs share the base 47e9xxxx-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67, and only the four hex digits after 47e9 change. The tables below give the full UUID for each. Temperatures are one byte of °C × 2 everywhere. The only multi-byte field is the PIN, a uint32 little-endian.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 47e9ee00-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 Comet Blue service Every setting, the PIN gate and the firmware-update channel 0000180a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Device Information (assumed) Model, firmware, software and manufacturer strings, readable without the PIN. Both clients find these characteristics by UUID alone, so the parent service is assumed rather than dumped

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
The properties are inferred from how the apps use each value. Nobody has published a GATT dump. Match characteristics by UUID, not by handle.

UUID Len Access Meaning 47e9ee01-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 5 R/W Clock: minute, hour, day, month, year − 2000 (local time; the valve handles summer time itself) 47e9ee10-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 … 47e9ee16-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 8 R/W Monday … Sunday: four (start, end) comfort periods, minutes since midnight ÷ 10, 0xff = unused 47e9ee20-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 … 47e9ee27-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 9 R/W Holiday slots 1–8: start hour/day/month/year, end hour/day/month/year, temperature 47e9ee2a-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 3 R/W Flags. Byte 0 bit 7 = child lock (vendor app); byte 0 bit 0 = manual mode (rikroe). The other bits are unknown 47e9ee2b-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 7 R/W Temperature block (below) 47e9ee2c-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 1 R Battery %, 0xff = not yet measured 47e9ee2d-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 ? R A string im-0 calls "firmware revision #2". The apps never read it 47e9ee2e-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 2 R/W Read and ignored by the vendor app. im-0 calls it an LCD timer (preload, current) 47e9ee30-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 4 W PIN, uint32 LE: authenticates, and once authenticated, sets a new PIN 47e9ee40-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 20 W/N Firmware-update channel. Leave it alone (see below) 00002a24-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb str R Model number ("comet blue" when lower-cased) 00002a26-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb str R Controller firmware revision 00002a28-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb str R Radio software revision. im-0's example unit shows a Sygonix suffix here 00002a29-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb str R Manufacturer ("eurotronic gmbh" when lower-cased)

docs.title: The PIN gate
docs.text:
• The vendor app sends nothing to the valve except the PIN write and reads of the two revision strings until the PIN write returns status 0. im-0 also treats every vendor read as needing the PIN.
  • A non-zero write status is a wrong PIN.
  • Whether a wrong PIN produces an ATT error, a disconnect or both is not established. Nor is whether repeated wrong PINs lock the valve out.

docs.title: Temperature block (47e9ee2b-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67)
docs.text:
Offset Field Encoding 0 Measured temperature °C × 2, read-only. Always write 0x80 1 Active setpoint °C × 2. Writing it overrides the schedule until the next switch point, like turning the wheel 2 Eco setpoint °C × 2, factory 16 °C (0x20) 3 Comfort setpoint °C × 2, factory 21 °C (0x2a) 4 Offset int8 °C × 2, −10…+10 (−5.0…+5.0 °C) 5 Open-window sensitivity 4 high, 8 medium, 12 low 6 Open-window close time minutes: 10, 20, … 60
  • Setpoint codes: 15 (7.5 °C) = OFF, which closes the valve (frost protection stays active). 57 (28.5 °C) = ON, which opens it fully. 16–56 = 8.0–28.0 °C in 0.5 °C steps. That is exactly the range of the vendor app's pickers and the valve's wheel. The spec documents nothing wider.
  • 0x80 means "leave this field unchanged" (im-0, rikroe). Send it in every byte you are not changing. For example, comfort 21.0 °C is 80 80 80 2a 80 80 80.
  • The vendor app does something different. It reads the block, edits its own fields and writes all seven bytes back.

docs.title: Flags (47e9ee2a-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67)
docs.text:
This is a read-modify-write. Read the three bytes, change only the bit you mean, and write them all back.

  • Byte 0 bit 7 (0x80) is the child lock. It is the only bit the vendor app touches. It is the same lock the OK + timer key chord sets on the valve.
  • rikroe reads byte 0 bit 0 as manual mode.
  • 0x80 is not an "unchanged" filler here, because it is the child-lock bit. The spec marks the flags write advanced for this reason.

docs.title: Schedules and holidays
docs.text:
Schedules:

  • Each day carries up to four comfort periods. Outside them the valve holds the eco setpoint.
  • A time byte is minutes since midnight ÷ 10. So 07:30 is 45, and 144 is 24:00.
  • The factory schedule is 2a 84 ff ff ff ff ff ff, one period from 07:00 to 22:00.
  • Unused pairs are handled three ways:
  • The vendor app writes 0xff in its "2 periods a day" mode and 0x00 in its "4 periods" mode.
  • rikroe writes 0x00.
  • im-0 writes 0xff.

All of them treat start == end as empty.

Holidays:

  • The holiday temperature uses the same codes as the setpoints.
  • The vendor app's empty slot is 80 01 01 ff 80 01 01 ff 0f. im-0 clears a slot with nine 0x80 bytes.
  • rikroe reports that a holiday in progress reads back hour 128 in its start. The manual mentions six vacation profiles, but the valve exposes eight slots and every client addresses all eight.

docs.title: Firmware update (role level only)
docs.text:
Characteristic 47e9ee40-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 carries EUROprog 2's update. The app opens notifications and writes a 20-byte header naming the image and its length. It then streams 20-byte blocks, each with a block number, 16 image bytes and a CRC-16. The valve paces the transfer with notifications carrying a block number and a status code:

Status Meaning 0xaa Header accepted, send the first block 0x01 Block received, send the next 0xbb Busy. The app waits 3 s and resends 0x02 Restart. The app begins again with the header

The image is unsigned and checked only by the per-block CRC. The vendor's image downloads now return 404, and nothing is known about recovering from an interrupted or malformed transfer. The spec therefore flags this path advanced and does not document the header bytes, the image names or an upload recipe. The status table is here so an owner who sees these notifications knows what they are, and so a client knows to leave ee40 alone.

docs.title: Telling the siblings apart
docs.text:
EUROprog 2 sorts a characteristic into a product by the four hex digits after 47e9 in its UUID:

Range Product Notes below ee50 Comet Blue (this page) Advertised name Comet Blue ee50–ef4f Progmatic Blue Characteristics 47e9ef01-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 to 47e9ef41-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 ef50 and up Progtime Blue Characteristics 47e9ef51-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 to 47e9ef62-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67; its PIN is 47e9ef62-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67

If a connected device shows ef.. characteristics and no ee.. ones, it is not a Comet Blue.

docs.title: Test vectors
docs.text:
These were built from the layouts above, not captured. The temperature read reproduces the values im-0's README prints for its unit.

What Bytes PIN 0 00 00 00 00 PIN 123456 (rikroe's test) 40 e2 01 00 Clock 2026-09-28 14:05 05 0e 1c 09 1a Factory schedule, 07:00–22:00 2a 84 ff ff ff ff ff ff Set comfort 21.0 °C 80 80 80 2a 80 80 80 Set active setpoint OFF 80 0f 80 80 80 80 80 Set offset −1.5 °C 80 80 80 80 fd 80 80 Temperature read: 23.0 / 16.0 / 16.0 / 21.0 / 0.0 / high / 10 min 2e 20 20 2a 00 04 0a Holiday 2026-12-24 18:00 → 2027-01-02 12:00 at 16.5 °C 12 18 0c 1a 0c 02 01 1b 21

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
These are defects and quirks found in the vendor apps and the open implementations.

  • Every write fails straight after connecting.
  • No PIN has been written in this connection yet.
  • The PIN is wrong. A unit set up with ET Blue has a room PIN and refuses
    1. A second-hand unit carries its previous owner's PIN.
  • On older firmware the PIN write went out too soon after connecting. Wait 1 s and retry.
  • A name-filtered scanner does not find the valve. EUROprog 2 matches only the exact name Comet Blue and applies no UUID filter, and a rebadge may advertise another name. Filter on service 47e9ee00-47e9-11e4-8939-164230d1df67 instead, with active scanning on.
  • The valve turns OFF after a third-party client changed only comfort or eco. This is a defect in rikroe's library. When the setpoint is not supplied, it leaves 0x00 instead of 0x80 in byte 1 of the temperature block. rikroe's Home Assistant component says in a code comment that the valve turns OFF otherwise, and its climate entity works around the defect by always resending the setpoint. Send 0x80 in every field you are not changing.
  • Switching to manual or auto mode also clears the child lock. rikroe's mode switch writes flags byte 0 as 0x01 or 0x00 without reading it first, which drops bit 7. Do a read-modify-write instead.
  • A value reads back unchanged in the same connection. The valve applies writes when the link closes (rikroe). Disconnect, reconnect and read again.
  • The setpoint does not stick. In AUTO the valve returns to its schedule at the next switch point, by design. If a holiday slot is running, the valve holds the holiday temperature. Home Assistant's documentation says holiday mode can only be ended from the valve's MENU button.
  • The battery shows 255, or stops updating at 100 %. 0xff means the valve has not measured the battery yet, so re-read after a second. The vendor app's parser accepts only −1…99. It silently drops a reading of exactly 100 and keeps showing the previous value. Home Assistant's documentation also warns the reading may not be very accurate.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• The real GATT table: handles, properties, and whether the Device Information strings sit in a standard 0000180a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb service.
  • What a wrong PIN looks like on the air, and whether the menu reset restores PIN 0.
  • The flag bits beyond child lock and manual mode.
  • What the valve does with a temperature byte outside 15–57 that is not 0x80.
  • The advertised names of the Sygonix, Xavax and Silvercrest rebadges, and whether every unit advertises the 47e9ee00 service.
  • Whether Genius BLE100 shares this table.
  • The meaning of ee2d and ee2e.
  • Why im-0's example unit reports open-window sensitivity 4 when the manual says medium is the default.

docs.title: Even Realities G1 Smart Glasses
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (from the vendor's open-source demo and community research; no capture, not run against hardware by this project) Protocol: BLE, two peripherals (one per temple), each a Nordic UART service Manufacturer: Even Realities Manufacturer Status: Active. Direct sales ended on 2026-09-15; security support is promised until at least 2029-06-25

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Even Realities G1 is a pair of prescription-capable smart glasses. Each lens has a monochrome green waveguide display, and each temple tip has a TouchBar. There are microphones, and an ambient light sensor on the right temple. The phone app shows notifications, a head-up dashboard, text, navigation, a teleprompter, and captures voice notes ("QuickNote") and voice questions ("Even AI").

Three facts shape any client:

  1. The glasses are two BLE devices. Each temple advertises, connects, bonds and takes commands on its own. The right temple is the master. A client pairs the two advertisements by the channel number in their names and drives both.
  2. Display content is not relayed between the temples. Text, images, navigation cards and dashboard content must be written to both, and some flows want the left done before the right.
  3. The link must be kept busy. If nothing is sent for about 30 seconds, the glasses drop the connection and show a disconnected icon, so every client runs a heartbeat on both temples.

Even Realities publishes part of the protocol in its own open-source demo app (EvenDemoApp, BSD-2-Clause): TouchBar events, the microphone, text and BMP images. The rest comes from community work. The largest source is Cheddies1/even-g1-companion, built from that author's captures of the official app on firmware 1.6.6 and from notes on a third-party firmware decompilation. Gadgetbridge and emingenc/even_glasses fill in further commands. Upstream labels some findings "Confirmed"; those are the upstream author's observations, not ours. This page and the spec mark everything as reported.

Out of scope: firmware and OTA update (the opcode exists and is deliberately not documented), the vendor's cloud AI features, and the Even G2 and later models.

The machine-readable version is device-specs/devices/even-g1-glasses.yaml.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number Even G1 (glasses) with the G1 charging case. The device-info reply carries a frame-style letter, A or B Chipset Probably a Nordic nRF53-class dual-core part (upstream firmware notes describe an application core plus a network core running Nordic sample code). Not confirmed by a teardown Radio BLE. Each temple exposes a Nordic UART service; the two temples also share a private radio link Display 488 px wide text area, 5 lines per screen in text mode; BMP images 576 × 136, 1 bit per pixel Inputs TouchBar on each temple tip (tap, double, triple, long press), head-tilt detection, wear sensor, microphones (the right temple streams audio) Power Built-in batteries in each temple (about 1.5 days, 2–3 h to charge per the vendor FAQ); the charging case has its own battery and a USB-C port FCC ID 2BFKR-G1 (glasses), 2BFKR-G1CASE (charging case). User-manual exhibit

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No provisioning: no Wi-Fi, account or key exchange on the wire. A new unit must be activated once in the case, and each temple must be bonded Method ble_direct Advertised name G1_<channel>_L_<id> and G1_<channel>_R_<id>, possibly with an Even prefix (Gadgetbridge matches Even G1_…). <id> is per unit Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (vendor documentation plus three public implementations, none replayed here)
  1. Activate (first use only). Fold the left temple first, put the glasses in the charging case and connect the case to power for 5–10 seconds. A flashing orange case light means the glasses are not seated properly.
  2. Free the temples. Close the Even Realities app on any phone that was driving them, since it holds both links.
  3. Scan and pair up. Match names against ^(Even )?G1_[0-9]+_[LR]_[0-9A-Za-z]+$. Split on _: the field after the model is the channel, the next is the side. Offer a pair once a left and a right with the same channel are both seen.
  4. Per temple: connect, discover services, enable notifications on 6e400003-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e, request ATT MTU 251, then bond (Just Works) if no bond exists yet.
  5. Heartbeat. Start 25 06 00 <seq> 04 <seq> on each temple straight away and keep it at no more than 8 seconds apart.

Whether glasses that were never set up with the official app will accept a third-party client is not established: every public client ran on glasses the vendor app had already onboarded.

Factory reset: not documented anywhere we looked. The vendor documents a soft restart: tap the left TouchBar five times quickly, then the right TouchBar five times, and the glasses restart in about 10 seconds. The app also has Settings → Reset Options → Quick Restart. Neither is stated to clear pairing, notes or settings.

Rebinding to a new phone: in place. In the vendor app use My G1 → Device Info → Unpair G1, forget both temples in the old phone's Bluetooth settings, then pair from the new client.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required Yes (medium confidence; see below) Security mode just_works (no PIN or passkey appears in any source) Bonding required, one bond per temple PIN source none One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time Unknown Confidence medium

Every public client bonds each temple after the MTU exchange: the vendor demo on Android, the Cheddies1 companion and Gadgetbridge. The companion's own code notes that writes fail silently when bonding fails, which suggests the UART characteristics need an encrypted link. The vendor's troubleshooting also treats the phone's stored bond as part of the connection. No source shows the glasses actually refusing an unbonded write, so "required" rests on that consistent practice.

Entering pairing mode: nothing to do. Once activated and out of the case, each temple advertises whenever no central holds it.

Unpairing: unpair in the vendor app (My G1 → Device Info → Unpair G1), then forget both temples in the phone's Bluetooth settings. Gadgetbridge names a dedicated unpair opcode (0x47) that no other source describes.

Recovery: force-stop the vendor app or turn Bluetooth off on the phone that runs it, then reconnect. If that fails, use the soft restart. Remember it is two links: a client can end up bonded to one temple and not the other.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
The same service is present on both temples.

UUID Name Description 6e400001-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e Nordic UART service Carries every command and event 6e400002-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e UART write Host → glasses. Public clients write with response, one write in flight per temple 6e400003-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e UART notify Glasses → host: replies, events, audio. Enable its CCCD (00002902-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb)

docs.title: Frame rules
docs.text:
• Byte 0 is the opcode, in both directions. There is no checksum and no trailer.
  • Some families carry a length. In 0x06, 0x08, 0x0A, 0x1E, 0x21, 0x22, 0x25, 0x26, 0x39, 0x50 and 0x52, bytes 1–2 are the total frame length, uint16 little-endian. The firmware drops a frame with a wrong length and says nothing. Byte 3 is then a host-chosen sequence number and byte 4 a sub-command. The other opcodes (0x01, 0x0E, 0x15, 0x16, 0x18, 0x4B, 0x4E and so on) have no length field.
  • Replies echo the opcode and usually put a status at byte 1: 0xC9 success, 0xCA failure, 0xCB "chunk accepted, send the next".
  • Size: stay at or under about 180–194 payload bytes per frame. MTU 251 is what every client negotiates.

docs.title: Which temple gets what
docs.text:
Send to Opcodes Both, left first, right after the left answers 0x4E text, 0x18 exit, 0x25 heartbeat Both, independently or in parallel 0x15/0x20/0x16 BMP, 0x52/0x53 streaming text, 0x06 dashboard, 0x1E note slots, 0x01 brightness, 0x03 silent mode, 0x08 head-up action, 0x26 double-tap, 0x27 wear detection Both, interleaved frame by frame 0x0A navigation (right, 10 ms, left, 20 ms, pause 50 ms every 10 pairs) Right only 0x0E microphone, 0x1E QuickNote audio request/ack, 0x0B/0x32 head-up angle, 0x50 dashboard lock (the left rejects it) Left only 0x4B notifications, 0x04 notification app whitelist

Events come from both temples. Microphone audio, QuickNote frames and head-up events have been seen from the right.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
All from public sources, not replayed here. <seq> is a host counter unless noted.

Command Bytes Reply / notes Heartbeat 25 06 00 <seq> 04 <seq> 25 … with 04 at byte 4 Exit to dashboard 18 18 C9 Brightness 01 <level 0–42> <auto 0/1> Then F5 12 <level applied> Brightness read 29 29 65 <level> <auto> Silent mode on / off 03 0C / 03 0A Triple tap toggles the same state Wear detection 27 <0/1> Head-up angle 0B <0–60°> 01 Right temple; read with 32 Head-up behaviour 08 06 00 <seq> 03 <00 dashboard / 02 no overlay> Persisted on the glasses Double-tap action 26 06 00 <seq> 05 <action> 00 none, 02 translate, 03 teleprompter, 04 dashboard, 05 transcribe Device info 2C <01 Android / 02 iOS> Byte 1 frame style A/B, byte 2 battery % Glasses serial 34 Bytes 2–17 are ASCII (per unit, do not publish) Per-lens status 39 04 00 00 6 bytes; byte 5: 00 idle, screen id, or FF bad length Microphone 0E <0/1> Right temple; 0E C9 <state> or 0E CA <state> Text chunk 4E <seq> <total> <index> <status> <pos_hi> <pos_lo> <page> <pages> <utf8…> See below BMP first chunk 15 00 00 1C 00 00 <194 bytes> No reply per chunk BMP chunk 15 <index> <≤194 bytes> BMP end 20 0D 0E 20 C9 BMP CRC / show 16 <crc32, big-endian> 16 <crc> C9 Dashboard lock 50 06 00 00 01 01 Right temple only Streaming text init 52 06 00 00 01 01 After the dashboard lock Streaming text line 52 <len LE> <seq> 02 02 00 <line> 00 <flags> 00 00 <utf8> 0A Line 1 = lone LF marker, line 2 = visible text Streaming keep-alive 53 Every 5 s Navigation control 0A 06 00 <seq> <00 init / 04 sync / 05 exit / 06 arrived> 01 No positive ack Navigation card 0A <len LE> <seq> 01 <dir> <x LE> <y LE> <5 NUL-terminated strings> Remaining time, remaining distance, road, turn distance, speed Dashboard layout 06 07 00 <seq> 06 <mode> <pane> Clock + weather 06 15 00 <seq> 01 <secs u32 LE> <ms i64 LE> <icon> <temp °C> <unit> <12/24h> Local time encoded as if UTC Quick-note slot 1E <len LE> <seq> 03 01 00 01 00 <slot 1–4> 01 <tlen> <title> <blen LE> <body> An empty body deletes the slot QuickNote audio request 1E 06 00 <seq> 02 <slot> Right temple QuickNote audio ack 1E 06 00 <seq> 04 01 Glasses answer 1E 06 00 <seq> 04 00 Notification 4B <msg_id> <total> <index> <≤176 bytes JSON> Left temple; {"ncs_notification": {…}}

docs.title: Text (0x4E)
docs.text: Byte 4 is a status: low nibble 1 = new content, high nibble = mode. 0x71 is plain text; 0x31–0x61 are the vendor's Even AI states. Split the UTF-8 into chunks of at most 176 bytes, all with the same seq, and send them to the left temple, then to the right. Every chunk but the last gets CB, the last gets C9. The right temple later sends 4E C9 <seq> <total> <last index> when it has finished. The vendor wraps to 488 px, font 21, 5 lines per screen. The byte order of the character position (bytes 5–6) is disputed: the vendor puts the high byte first. Everyone sends 0.

docs.title: BMP images
docs.text: Send the whole .bmp file, header included: 1 bit per pixel, 576 wide. Split it into 194-byte chunks, put the storage address 00 1C 00 00 in the first chunk only, then send 20 0D 0E and wait for 20 C9. Last, send CRC-32/XZ (the zlib CRC) computed over 00 1C 00 00 + the file, big-endian. Both temples can be sent to at the same time. 18 removes the image.

docs.title: Navigation (0x0A)
docs.text: The official app sends the dashboard lock, then INIT, SYNC, the card, 13 direction-icon bands, 90 route-map slices and SYNC, then SYNC every second for the whole session. The glasses will not draw a card that arrives without the images. The icon is 136 × 136, two 1-bit layers, run-length coded as <count><byte> pairs. The map area is 488 × 136. String limits including the NUL: 24, 24, 64, 24 and 24 bytes. A string over its limit makes the glasses reject the whole card.

docs.title: Voice: Even AI and QuickNote
docs.text:
• Left long-press: F5 17 → host sends 0E 01 to the right → audio arrives as F1 <seq> <200 bytes LC3>, exactly 202 bytes per frame → F5 18 on release → 0E 00. Maximum 30 s.
  • Right long-press (works even while disconnected): the glasses record and store the note, then send 0x21 on release (15-byte "this note" or 42-byte "all notes" form). The host must ask for the audio with 1E 06 00 <seq> 02 <slot>; it is never sent unprompted. Chunks arrive as 1E C8 00 … (10-byte header, 190 bytes of audio), and the stream ends with a short 0x1E control frame.
  • Decoding: LC3, 16 kHz mono, 200-byte frames. For QuickNote, join the audio bytes of all chunks first, then cut the result into 200-byte frames. Cutting at the 190-byte chunk edges produces clicks.

docs.title: Events (0xF5)
docs.text:
F5 <code> [value], from either temple. Labels are upstream's; none is confirmed by this project.

Code Meaning Upstream status 00 Double tap closed a feature / went home confirmed upstream 01 Single tap (vendor README) not forwarded on 1.6.6: single taps stay on the glasses 02 / 03 Head up / head back down confirmed upstream 04 / 05 Silent mode on / off (triple tap) confirmed upstream 06 / 07 Worn / not worn confirmed upstream 08 / 0B In case, lid open / lid closed confirmed upstream 09 Charging state flag suspected 0A <pct> Glasses battery (every 1–2 s while worn) confirmed upstream; 94–100 % is synthesised by the firmware 0E <flag> Case cable state suspected 0F <pct> Case battery confirmed upstream 12 <level> Brightness actually applied confirmed upstream (Gadgetbridge calls 12 a long press) 17 / 18 Left long-press start / release vendor README; 18 confirmed upstream 1E / 1F Dashboard opened / closed follow-ons suspected 20 Double tap with a host-handled action configured (arrives 1–6 s late) confirmed upstream

docs.title: Readbacks
docs.text: 0x29–0x3F are readbacks. The useful ones: 29 brightness, 2C device info and battery, 32 head-up angle, 33/34 serials, 35 the channel the temples share, 36 notification counts, 39 per-lens screen state (the only way to check that a lens really shows what you sent). Several others are named in the spec's protocol_details.readbacks.

docs.title: Firmware update
docs.text: Out of scope. The glasses update through the vendor app, and the case has a desktop updater. The opcode that starts an update is deliberately left out of the spec. See Firmware Update for why this catalogue treats update paths with care.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Only one temple shows up in a scan. The other is still held by the vendor app on some phone, or the glasses are asleep in a closed case or were never activated.
  • The write succeeds but nothing appears. For the length-bearing families, check bytes 1–2: a wrong total length is dropped without a word. Check you wrote to both temples, since display content is not relayed. For navigation, send the icon and map images as well as the card.
  • The two lenses disagree (for example, different notification counts). One temple reconnected first and got content alone; the vendor lists this as known issue 014. After any reconnect, resend the current content to both temples.
  • The link drops about every 30 seconds. No heartbeat. Send one to each temple at least every 8 seconds; Android can add sleep time on top of your timer.
  • QuickNote audio clicks. The LC3 frames were cut at chunk boundaries; join the payloads first, then cut every 200 bytes.
  • Single taps do nothing in a third-party app. Expected: firmware 1.6.6 handles single taps on the glasses and does not report them. Use double tap (F5 20 with a host-handled double-tap action) or head-up events.
  • Things to leave alone. The firmware-update opcode, and the firmware's test mode (which unlocks a raw-PCM microphone). Neither is documented here.

docs.title: Exway Electric Skateboards (X1 / Flex / Wave / Atlas)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Exway Manufacturer Status: Active (this generation's app, "Exway", is superseded by ExSkate for newer hardware)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Exway's second-generation electric skateboards are the X1 Pro, X1 Max, X1 Skate, Flex, Flex SE, Flex (2022), Wave and Atlas. They talk to a phone over BLE. The phone connects straight to the board's receiver, the radio module that also links the handheld R1/R2 remote and passes messages on to the board's one or two ESCs. The vendor app for this generation is Exway (com.exway.app).

Exway's third generation (R3 remote, ESC 3.0) works differently. Its ExSkate app pairs the phone with the R3 remote rather than the board, and Exway's own ExSkate guide tells R1/R2 owners to keep using the older Exway app. This page covers the second generation only.

Everything here was read out of the vendor's Android app (version 1.8.1) and checked against Exway's manuals. Nobody on this project has connected to a board. There is no capture, no FCC filing and no screenshot of the app in the research store, so every byte fact is reported, not confirmed.

In scope: identifying the board and its model, live telemetry, battery pages, reading the settings memory, saving, and a small set of settings the vendor app itself offers.

Out of scope, on purpose:

  • the handheld remote's own radio link to the board
  • firmware and bootloader updates for the receiver, the remote and the ESCs
  • writes to the per-gear speed limits, acceleration and brake curves and currents, turbo, wheel size, gearing, the power-system type and the mileage counters

This is a vehicle, and the link has no authentication

Settings written over this link change how a moving skateboard shifts, cruises and brakes. Change them only with the board stopped and nobody on it. The vendor app will not open its board-settings page unless the board reports less than 2 km/h. Anything within radio range of a powered board can do what the app does. Wheel size and gearing feed the speed the board calculates, and the mileage counters gate the new-rider gear limit, which is why this spec does not document writing them.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number X1 Pro, X1 Max, X1 Skate, Flex, Flex SE, Flex (2022), Wave, Atlas (told apart by a model string the board reports; see Identification) Chipset Not identified. The receiver sits behind a BLE module with its own AT-command configuration port (OK+... answers) Radio BLE to the phone. A separate radio link to the handheld remote, not covered here Drive Hub motors or Exway's "Riot" belt drive, one or two ESCs (Atlas 4WD has two, each with its own power button) FCC ID Not found. fccid.co has no Exway grants under "Exway", "Exway Technology" or "electric skateboard"

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name Not established. The app lists every named BLE device and lets the user pick; the name can be changed through the module's AT port Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence low (app-derived, not replayed)

To connect:

  1. Hold the board's power button for about three seconds. The status light turns solid green (Atlas Carbon manual).
  2. Close the vendor app on any other phone.
  3. Scan and connect. The board's primary service is 0000f1f0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb. Whether it is advertised is not known, so be ready to fall back to picking the board from a list of named devices.
  4. Subscribe to notifications on 0000f1f2-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb.
  5. Write the heartbeat b0 00 00 70 to 0000f1f1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb. A 4-byte reply starting b1 means the receiver is running normally.
  6. Read the five information pages and check the model string.

Factory reset: not established. The manuals describe no reset of the board's settings, and for a phone there is nothing to reset: the board keeps no bond and no credential. The vendor app's "Restore default" item is not a factory reset. It rewrites the stored mileage counter, which puts the board back under the new-rider gear limit, so this spec leaves it out. Holding the power button for eight seconds with the board off pairs the handheld remote, not the phone.

Rebinding to a new network: not applicable. A new phone connects the same way once the old one has disconnected.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none Bonding none PIN source not applicable One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time not applicable Confidence medium (the vendor app never bonds or encrypts; not replayed)

Entering pairing mode: not needed. The board accepts a connection whenever it is on.

Unpairing: nothing to unpair.

Recovery: close the vendor app on every other phone, then power-cycle the board if it still does not answer.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 0000f1f0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Receiver data service Request/reply channel to the board 0000f1f1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Request Write requests here 0000f1f2-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Reply Every reply arrives here as a notification 0000f2f0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb BLE module AT service The module's configuration port (send 0000f2f1, receive 0000f2f2). Not a second ESC

An earlier research note had the request and reply characteristics swapped. The app's own set-up call writes to f1f1 and listens on f1f2, and that is what the spec follows.

The app also contains 0000fee9 with d44bc439-abfd-45a2-b575-925416129600 / d44bc439-abfd-45a2-b575-925416129601, and 0000fee8 with 003784cf-f7e3-55b4-6c4c-9fd140100a16 / 013784cf-f7e3-55b4-6c4c-9fd140100a16. Those are defaults of the open-source BLE library the app is built on (aicareles/Android-BLE). The app overrides them at start-up and never uses the library's OTA helper, so they say nothing about Exway hardware.

docs.title: Framing
docs.text:
Every request is [head][arguments][check]. The check byte is the low byte of CRC-16/MODBUS over everything before it (reflected polynomial 0xA001, init 0xFFFF, no final xor). Only the low byte is sent. All multi-byte values are big-endian. Replies end the same way.

Shape Bytes Used for Short request [head][arg high][arg low][check] heartbeat, monitor, battery, information pages, save, mode change Parameter read [74][addr high][addr low][len high][len low][00][00][check] reading settings memory, 16 bytes at a time Parameter write [75][addr high][addr low][value][check] (1 byte) or [75][addr high][addr low][value high][value low][check] (2 bytes) changing a setting

Send one request at a time and wait for its reply. The app waits up to 500 ms (1.5 s for a save). Replies can arrive split over notifications or run together, so reassemble by head: 91, 92 and b4 replies are 20 bytes; 74/75 replies are 4 bytes plus the data; b1, b3 and 76 replies are 4 bytes.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Request (hex) Reply Purpose b0 00 00 70 b1 ... (4 bytes) Heartbeat. 11 ... instead means the receiver is in its bootloader 90 f0 0f 75 91 ... (20 bytes) Live telemetry (below) 92 00 00 d0 / 92 00 01 11 92 ... (20 bytes) Battery page 0 (charge, voltage, temperature, cycles) / page 1 (battery firmware, capacities) b4 00 0n <check> (n = 0-4) b4 00 0n + 16 bytes + check Receiver information, five pages 74 00 90 00 10 00 00 ee ... 74 00 d0 00 10 00 00 ef 74 00 addr + 16 bytes + check Settings memory 0x90-0xdf 74 00 cc 00 04 00 00 7e 74 00 cc + 4 bytes + check Total mileage, 0.1 km units 76 00 00 90 76 ... (4 bytes) Save settings to flash b2 70 00 f4 b3 70 status .. Return the receiver to its normal mode

The information pages' check bytes are 31, f0, b0, 71, 30 for pages 0-4. The spec lists every request as a complete byte string, because the schema has no way yet to fill in a truncated CRC.

Information pages. Concatenated, the five pages are 80 bytes holding five 16-byte UTF-8 strings: firmware version (e.g. SE-01.01.10), hardware version, model string, bootloader version and a per-unit code. Don't publish the per-unit code.

docs.title: Identification
docs.text:
The app tells the models apart by the model string on information page 2 and compares it as a whole string:

Model string Notes exway X1 Pro Firmware at or below SE-01.01.10 stores wheel size as a list index (80/83/85 mm) exway X1 Max exway X1 Skate Wheel size as a list index; the app hides the gearing item exway Flex Also a prefix of the next two, so compare exactly exway Flex SE exway Flex(2022) No space before the parenthesis exway Wave The only model the app shows its lighting page for; cruise control hidden exway Atlas

docs.title: Live telemetry (reply 91)
docs.text:
Offset Length Field Decoding 0 1 head 0x91 1 2 speed uint16 BE × 0.001 km/h 3 2 output int16 BE; the app divides by 32 and shows it as "power output". Unit not established 5 2 ESC temperature 12-bit ADC count; see below 7 2 motor temperature 12-bit ADC count; see below 9 2 trip uint16 BE × 0.1 km 11 2 (unlabelled) uint16 BE; the app scales it by 0.1 and never shows it 13 2 battery voltage uint16 BE × 0.001 V 15 1 battery bits 0-6: percent; bit 7: charging 16 2 battery temperature int16 BE × 0.1 °C (shown only when byte 18 is 1 or more) 18 1 pack code 0, 1 or 2; the app assumes a 26, 22 or 32 km full-charge range 19 1 check CRC-16/MODBUS low byte of bytes 0-18

Worked example (synthetic): 91 48 44 01 40 08 00 08 00 00 7b 00 00 9b 78 4b 00 f5 01 42 is 18.5 km/h, output 10, ESC 63 °C, motor 23 °C, trip 12.3 km, 39.8 V, 75 % and not charging, battery 24.5 °C, pack code 1.

Temperatures. The ESC and motor readings are ADC counts. The app works out a thermistor resistance, R = raw × 10000 / (4095 − raw) ohms, and looks it up in a per-degree table from −11 °C to 199 °C, reporting the lower degree of the step. A beta-model curve with B ≈ 3877 K, referenced to 24 °C at 47.0 kΩ (ESC) or 10.0 kΩ (motor), reproduces the app within about 1 °C. For example, ESC raw 2048 reads 63 °C and motor raw 1000 reads 52 °C. When nothing matches, the app reports −11 and shows "−".

docs.title: Settings memory
docs.text:
The settings memory is 256 bytes. The spec's protocol_details.parameter_memory maps all of it. The addresses the declared commands touch:

Address Setting Values In this spec 0x94 (148) Safe mode 1 = on Advanced 0x95 (149) Safe mode's highest gear 1-4 Advanced 0x96 (150) Gear change while moving 1 = allowed Advanced 0x97 (151) Free mode (wheels spin backwards on reverse throttle) 1 = on Advanced 0x98 (152) Cruise control 1 = available Advanced 0xc2 (194) Standby timer 1 = on Yes 0xc3 (195) Standby time hours: 2, 24, 48, 168 Yes 0xd0 (208) Light animation 0 throttle, 1 comet, 2 breath, 3 colour breath, 4 steady, 5 none Yes 0xd5 (213) Brake light 1 = on Yes 0xd7 (215) Tail light 1 = on Yes

Ride settings go through a write and then the save request (76 00 00 90), as the app does. The app writes light settings without a save so they preview live. Reading addresses 0x9a-0xc1 shows the per-gear speed limits, curves and currents, which the spec documents for reading only.

New-rider limit. The app's quick guide says a new board allows only gears 1 and 2 until it has covered 10 km. The app treats a mileage counter below 10 km as that state and warns that settings changes are void until then.

docs.title: Firmware updates
docs.text: The app updates the receiver, the remote and the ESCs over this same link, using images it looks up from Exway's API (api.exwayboard.com). The routine that enters the update path did not decompile to source, and the flashing bytes are left out on purpose. A receiver left in its bootloader answers the heartbeat with 11 instead of b1, and the vendor app then goes straight to its firmware page.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Nothing answers the heartbeat. The vendor app on another phone is probably still connected. Also check that you write to f1f1 and listen on f1f2; an earlier write-up had them the other way round.
  • The heartbeat reply starts 11. The receiver is in its bootloader, usually after an interrupted firmware update. Only the vendor app's firmware page recovers it; this spec does not document that path.
  • A saved setting reads back unchanged. The board has covered less than 10 km, or it was moving. The app only offers settings below 2 km/h.
  • The app's settings screen shows a value you did not set. As decompiled, after a write retry the app can file the echoed data at the wrong offset in its cached copy of the settings. Re-read the page after writing.
  • A session starts with the mode unknown. The app's mode lookup returns before its own query finishes. Wait for the heartbeat reply before sending anything else.

docs.title: Eye-Fi X2 / Mobi / Mobi Pro Wi-Fi SD Cards
docs.text: Status: Spec available; source/offline validated only Protocol: Card-initiated cleartext HTTP/SOAP on TCP 59278 Manufacturer: Eye-Fi (services discontinued)

docs.title: What can be rescued
docs.text:
An already-configured Eye-Fi card can push photographs to a local receiver without the retired Eye-Fi/Keenai services. The card connects to the receiver: a phone, computer, router or NAS listens on TCP 59278. This is not an outbound camera API and exposes no shutter, delete, format or firmware command.

A card must already know its Wi-Fi/receiver configuration or have working direct mode. Historical first-party X2 activation called the retired vendor registration service, so this guide does not promise to activate a reset card. The mobile app currently has no secure Eye-Fi server transport; the spec is a host-implementation contract.

docs.title: Receiver contract
docs.text:
Step Path / action What the receiver does StartSession POST /api/soap/eyefilm/v1, SOAPAction: "urn:StartSession" Read card MAC, client nonce and transfer fields; return credential, fresh server nonce and upsyncallowed=false GetPhotoStatus Same path, SOAPAction: "urn:GetPhotoStatus" Verify second credential and item metadata; return fileid and offset UploadPhoto POST /api/soap/eyefilm/v1/upload, SOAPAction: "urn:UploadPhoto" Require multipart parts in order: SOAPENVELOPE, FILENAME, INTEGRITYDIGEST; FILENAME is a TAR archive and the digest is 32 lowercase hex characters MarkLastPhotoInRoll Base path, matching SOAP action Close/expire the roll using a capture-selected compatibility response

Match XML elements by local name, not namespace prefix. Bound metadata and request sizes; reject DTDs, external entities, duplicate fields, wrong-path actions, malformed multipart bodies and replay after roll completion.

Roll completion differs by implementation: the community X2 server returns an empty success, the reviewed Mobi server does not implement it, and historical Windows receivers return SOAP fault 2 (Last Photo) before closing. Do not choose one as universally correct without a card capture.

docs.title: Credentials and nonces
docs.text:
Concatenate the specified hexadecimal strings, decode them to bytes, MD5 those bytes and emit lowercase hex. Do not hash ASCII hex text. The card MAC is 12 hex characters without colons.

Profile StartSession response GetPhotoStatus credential X2 with owner upload key MD5_bytes(mac + cnonce + upload_key) MD5_bytes(mac + upload_key + snonce) Reviewed Mobi receiver Same, with 32 ASCII zeroes as the key Same, with the same placeholder

The Mobi placeholder decodes to 16 zero bytes; it is legacy behavior, not a recommended secret. Mobi Pro infrastructure mode can use its real upload key, exported from an already-configured mounted card through token 0xfd.

StartSession alone does not authenticate the card. Verify the second credential in constant time, bind state to card/session/server nonce/item, use single-use expiring nonces and define one outstanding transfer policy per card. Never log owner keys, credential inputs, direct-mode passphrases or real MAC addresses.

The YAML and scripts/test_eye_fi_cards.py carry synthetic X2/Mobi vectors using a documentation-range MAC and invented keys.

docs.title: Uploads, resume and safe TAR handling
docs.text:
filesize is TAR bytes. Media is the first entry and an optional event log is second. Community stubs returning fileid=1, offset=0 do not prove the real protocol lacks resume. Vendor receiver analysis establishes state keyed by filesignature, reuse of its file ID, new-destination offsets rounded down to 4 KiB and offset=filesize for complete items. The filesignature algorithm is unknown. Start with offset zero until an interruption capture exists.

INTEGRITYDIGEST is exactly 32 lowercase hexadecimal characters. The reported algorithm covers each complete 512-byte TAR block: compute the 16-bit Internet checksum over big-endian 16-bit words with end-around carry, invert it, and serialize the result as two big-endian bytes. Concatenate those checksum bytes in block order, append the authorized item's 16-byte upload key, then MD5 the result. A trailing partial block is not covered.

The YAML and scripts/test_eye_fi_cards.py carry a reproducible synthetic vector: bytes 00 through ff repeated twice produce block checksum 7f80 and, with the invented X2 key, digest 9190630d60a776ce999f3e1563172826. This checks the transcription only; the wire algorithm remains capture-unverified.

Before returning success, match the upload metadata and TAR size to the item authorized by GetPhotoStatus for this card/session, then recompute and compare INTEGRITYDIGEST using that authorized item's upload key. Reject a mismatch; do not reuse a key selected only from unverified upload metadata.

Do not deploy the old extraction code on an untrusted network. A first receiver should be single-card and JPEG-only:

  • Spool to a bounded temporary file and validate the entire archive before extracting anything.
  • Accept only regular files/harmless directories. Reject absolute, traversal and backslash paths, links, devices, FIFOs, unknown types and normalized or case-folded collisions.
  • Bound compressed request, expanded total, member count and member size. Require consistent JPEG size/start/end markers.
  • Use exclusive creation in a controlled destination, never overwrite different content, and remove partial output on failure.
  • Skip historical geolocation/log sidecars and do not invoke external services.

Return success only after complete safe storage.

docs.title: Setup and direct mode
docs.text:
For an already-configured card, back it up and read its existing receiver and network configuration. X2 and Mobi Pro infrastructure profiles need the owner upload key. A historical O 0x06 mounted-card record may allow listener provisioning, but it is not first-party or hardware-verified; the spec does not automate it.

Mobi direct mode uses SSID Eye-Fi Card (trailing space included) plus the last six card-MAC hex digits, WPA2 with the card activation code and DHCP from the card. Join that existing network and run the restricted receiver. Listener hints followed by bounded subnet candidates are reported, but the selected receiver IP after DHCP is not established; do not scan indefinitely.

Changing routers/receivers may require mounted-card reconfiguration, not a factory reset. No reset procedure or offline reactivation path is established; do not erase a working card to test the retired cloud flow.

docs.title: Mounted-card configuration
docs.text:
The public configuration utility uses four 16384-byte zero-padded files under EyeFi/, not one XML file:

Record Role reqm Host request buffer reqc Request sequence rspm Card response buffer rspc Response sequence/status

An information request is ASCII o plus a one-byte subcommand. A one-byte write is ASCII O, subcommand, length 01, value. Increment the previous response sequence (seed 0x1234 if zero), write reqc, poll rspc up to 50 times at 300 ms intervals and accept only a fresh matching response. The reference Linux utility treats sequence values as native u32/little-endian; do not generalize that without checking the card representation.

Read tokens include MAC 01, firmware 02, upload API 04, transfer mode 11, direct-mode SSID/passphrase 22/23, timers 24/25, and owner-only upload key fd. Network changes, AP start and reboot are unverified writes; back up and obtain owner consent. The utility also has a compiler-reported mount-path lifetime warning.

docs.title: Security and firmware boundaries
docs.text:
Use an isolated direct-mode network or trusted segmented LAN. Never expose TCP 59278 publicly. Photographs are private: avoid content logs, onward sync and unbounded retention. Set upsyncallowed=false for a local-only receiver.

A receiver can reportedly offer fwversion, after which the card requests GET /api/firmware/<MAC>. Signed-image enforcement is reported but untested; no image, compatibility or recovery claim is made. This is an advanced card-pull mechanism, not a generic update command.

Remaining evidence needed: real X2/Mobi/Mobi Pro sessions, roll completion, receiver-IP selection, filesignature, nonzero resume, concurrent cards, RAW/video variants and reset-card activation.

docs.title: Fardriver ND-series Motor Controller
docs.text: Status: Research Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Nanjing Fardriver Controller Co. Manufacturer Status: Active (app-tethered; no documented local API)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Fardriver ND-series controllers are sine-wave (FOC) brushless motor controllers used throughout the Chinese light-EV supply chain — QS Motor hub-motor kits, e-motorcycle builds, and classic-scooter EV conversions. The controller carries a BLE bridge and is driven by the vendor "FarDriver" Android app, which shows live speed, pack voltage, current, RPM, temperatures and state of charge, and writes tunable parameters (gear-mode curves, speed limiting, regen, throttle response).

We document it because it is the app layer behind app-connected classic-scooter EV conversions. Kits such as Retrospective Classic's "Project:E" Vespa/Lambretta conversion (72 V, 4 kW hub motor, keyless ignition) are advertised as "connected by app", where the app reports speed, battery status, range and the selected riding mode, and where the speed limit can be restricted or derestricted. That is a rider-facing dashboard bound to a proprietary app — exactly the dependency OpenGreenIoT exists to remove.

Vendor attribution is inferred, not confirmed

Retrospective publishes no app name and no controller brand — their product pages, the kit listings, their FAQ, and every press piece covering the kits say only "sinusoidal motor controller", "keyless ignition/remote" and "connected by app". The Fardriver identification here is inferred from the published bill of materials (sine-wave controller, QS-style 4 kW 72 V hub motor, app-adjustable speed restriction) matching the ND-series feature set, and from QS Motor shipping its 4 kW hub kits paired with Fardriver ND72xxx controllers. Confidence: MEDIUM. Confirm on your own scooter before relying on it — see Confirming what your scooter actually runs. The main alternative is the Votol EM-series; see If it's not Fardriver.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Family ND-series (e.g. ND72200, ND72260, ND72680, ND84530) Typical pack voltage 60–84 V nominal (72 V common; ND72xxx tolerate ~88 V) Commutation Sine wave / FOC, with regenerative braking MCU (ND84530_24_ABH64) GigaDevice GD32F303 Radio BLE via a bolt-on bridge module (varies per unit) Companion app "FarDriver" (Android; distributed as a direct APK, not via Play)

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUIDs are per-unit — verify before use

Fardriver controllers ship with different BLE bridge modules, so transport UUIDs vary between units even when the framing below is identical. The pair below is the commonly observed HM-10-style set and is a starting point only. Scan your own controller with nRF Connect and record what you find.

UUID Name Description 0000ffe0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb BLE Bridge Service HM-10-style serial bridge service

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text: UUID Name Properties Description 0000ffec-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Telemetry Notify Notify Free-running 16-byte status frames 0000ffe1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Serial Data Read, Write, Write Without Response, Notify Bidirectional serial channel on HM-10-style modules

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
• Autodetection: not provided, deliberately. The spec declares no identification or discovery block — see the warning below.
  • Selection: manual. Pick the controller by address after confirming it with a scan.
  • CCCD: standard 0x2902 to enable notifications
  • Pairing: no bonding on HM-10-style bridges ("Just Works" or none)
  • Keep-alive: none required — the controller pushes telemetry unprompted once notifications are enabled

0xFFE0 is not a Fardriver signature — do not match on it

0xFFE0 is the generic HM-10/HM-19 BLE-UART service. The MoTool Slacker spec already uses it as its sole identification signal, and SP107E LED controllers advertise it as well. A registry matcher keyed on that UUID would classify a single advertisement as several different devices — and could then point Fardriver telemetry, or an advanced write, at unrelated hardware. Combined with this device's own per-unit UUID variation, it is not a safe auto-match signal.

Automatic identification can be restored once a discriminating signal exists: a unique local-name prefix, manufacturer-specific advertisement data, or a read-only framing probe (subscribe, confirm 16-byte 0xAA frames).

docs.title: Status frame format
docs.text:
The controller free-runs status frames as BLE notifications. Each is 16 bytes:

Offset Length Description 0 1 Magic — always 0xAA 1 1 6-bit block ID + 2-bit flags 2 12 Payload (mirror of a controller memory block) 14 2 CRC16

When the ID field is < 0x37, it indexes a 55-entry table of flash addresses spanning 0x00–0xFA, and the payload is the mirror of that region. Frames rotate through nearly all addresses, with hot blocks repeated roughly every 3–4 frames.

Reassembly: collect frames until the addressed blocks cover the range, and you have a 512-byte (0x200) image of controller memory. The field table below is decoded from offsets into that reassembled image — these are not offsets into any single frame.

docs.title: CRC16
docs.text:
Parameter Value Polynomial 0x8005 Init 0x7F3C RefIn true RefOut true XorOut false

Implemented vendor-side as a dual hi/lo lookup table seeded a = 0x3C, b = 0x7F.

docs.title: Decoded telemetry fields
docs.text:
Offsets are into the reassembled 512-byte image.

Field Offset Type Scaling Pack voltage 0x1D0 int16 ÷ 10 → volts Line current 0x1D4 int16 ÷ 4 → amps Measured speed 0x1C8 uint16 via configured wheel parameters Throttle depth 0x1DE int16 relative to low-speed threshold Motor torque 0x1CC, 0x1CE int16 ((unkE6² + unkE7²) << 9) / TorqueCoeff Phase A current 0x1E0 24-bit 1.953125 × √value Phase C current 0x1E6 24-bit 1.953125 × √value MOSFET (controller) temperature 0x1AC int16 °C Motor temperature 0x1E8 int16 °C Battery SOC 0x1EA int8 percent

docs.title: Configuration registers
docs.text:
These are the register addresses the write path below targets. Reading them is ordinary; writing them is advanced — see the write path.

Setting Offset Bits Brake config 0x0C 0–3 Temp sensor type 0x0C 4–6 Throttle response (Line / Sport / ECO) 0x32 2–3 Gear config (ride mode) 0x33 5–7 CAN baud (250K / 500K / 1M) 0x178 0–1 Speed limit mode 0x196 0–3

docs.title: Write path
docs.text:
Parameter writes use a shorter variable-length frame (typically 8 bytes) with flags = 1:

Offset Length Description 0 1 Magic — 0xAA 1 1 Computed length (flags = 1) 2 2 Register address (hi, lo) 4 n Payload, little-endian 4+n 2 CRC16 (same parameters as above, computed over the frame)

System commands write 0x88 XX to address 0xA0 — self-balance/calibration, data gather, and controller reset.

Both write commands are declared in the spec with advanced: true:

Command Effect write_parameter Generic register write — current limits, regen, speed limiting system_command Controller-level operations: calibration, data gather, reset

Advanced — read this before writing anything

These opcodes are documented and meant to be usable. They also retune a road-going vehicle, so here is what you are taking on:

  • Confirm before trusting. The frame shape is MEDIUM confidence (derived from community RE). Exact per-parameter payload encodings and CRC byte order are unverified — capture the vendor app writing a known value on your own unit first.
  • Validate on a stand, wheel off the ground, never while moving.
  • Wrong values can overheat the motor or controller; a mistimed self-balance or reset can leave the controller unable to drive until reconfigured.
  • Derestricting a speed limit may change the vehicle's legal classification and invalidate insurance. Documented because it is your vehicle and your call — but make it knowingly.

Writes are excluded from autodetection: discovery stays scan-and-read only. Consumers should keep these available behind a deliberate action — a signpost, not a gate.

docs.title: Confirming what your scooter actually runs
docs.text:
Five minutes with a phone, before writing any code:

  1. Scan. Power the scooter on, open nRF Connect (Android/iOS), and scan next to the controller. Note every advertised device name, its address, and its service UUIDs. Fardriver bridges often advertise a short generic name and a 0xFFE0-family service.
  2. Record the real UUIDs. Connect and enumerate. Write down the service plus the characteristic that carries notify. This is the per-unit value that matters — the UUIDs in this doc are a starting point, not a guarantee.
  3. Check the framing. Subscribe to the notify characteristic and watch raw bytes with the ignition on. If you see a steady stream of 16-byte frames each starting AA, that is the Fardriver framing above and this spec applies.
  4. Check the phone. Whatever app the installer put on your phone at handover is the ground truth. Grab its package ID (Android: Settings → Apps → App info) and add it to targets/targets.csv.
  5. Capture, don't guess. Enable Developer options → Enable Bluetooth HCI snoop log, drive one connect + one mode change in the vendor app, and pull btsnoop_hci.log. That single capture resolves the write path far more reliably than inference.

If step 3 shows 16-byte 0xAA frames, the vendor attribution above is confirmed for your unit and this page's status can move from Research to In Progress.

docs.title: Where else this spec applies
docs.text: Scooter conversions are not the only place these controllers turn up. The ND/NS-series is a common upgrade on light electric off-road bikes — Sur-Ron Light Bee, Talaria (MX3/MX4/Sting R) and Segway X260 — typically as the ND96680/NS96680 at 48–96 V, sold alongside Sabvoton, Kelly and Nucular as the competing options. The framing, CRC and write path documented here are the same family; only the voltage class and per-unit BLE bridge differ. If you are working on one of those bikes, start here rather than from scratch, but re-confirm the UUIDs and register values on your own unit exactly as below.

docs.title: If it's not Fardriver
docs.text:
The main alternative in this class is the Votol EM-series (EM50/EM100/EM150/EM200), also sine-wave, also common in 72 V conversions, and also supporting keyless "one-key start". Distinguishing signs:

  • Votol's official tooling is a Windows configurator plus a WeChat mini-program, with per-unit Bluetooth-ID binding performed by the seller — noticeably clunkier onboarding than a plain APK.
  • Votol needs battery voltage wired to the lock signal to power up for programming.
  • Community BLE access typically goes through a CAN-to-BT bridge, not a serial bridge, so you would see CAN-shaped traffic rather than 16-byte 0xAA frames.

If your scan shows a CAN bridge or the framing does not match, open a separate target sheet rather than stretching this spec.

docs.title: Battery telemetry is probably a separate device
docs.text: Kits of this type usually pair the controller with a smart BMS in the removable pack (JBD/Xiaoxiang and ANT are the common ones), each with its own BLE service and its own app. If "battery status" in your app is richer than the controller's single SOC byte — per-cell voltages, cycle count, balance state — it is coming from the BMS, not the controller, and needs its own spec. Scan with the pack in and the pack out to tell the two radios apart.

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:

  • [ ] Android HCI snoop log (btsnoop_hci.log) — connect + mode change capture
  • [ ] Wireshark — frame reassembly and CRC verification
  • [ ] scripts/detect_devices.sh — BLE discovery sweep
