docs.title: Fisher-Price Lumalou (GLD09)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Fisher-Price (Mattel) Manufacturer Status: Shutdown (the Smart Connect app was delisted in March 2025 and its backend went dark in August 2025; the device itself is controlled locally)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Lumalou "Better Bedtime Routine System" is a cloud-shaped night light for a child's room. It mounts on the wall. It has:

  • a colour night light with ten presets, including rainbow
  • a speaker with twelve lullabies and six sound loops (pink noise, ocean, rain, brown noise, nature, highway)
  • a clock
  • a sleep-trainer star: red means "stay in bed", green means "OK to wake"
  • a strip of routine task icons: eight fixed tasks and three custom ones
  • an infrared button remote that toggles soothing and checks off tasks

Most features were set up from the Fisher-Price Smart Connect app. The app is gone, but it never used the cloud for control. Everything goes over a local, encrypted BLE session, and any client in range can open one. No per-device secret, no account and no bond are needed. The upstream write-ups call the vendor's BLE stack "MPID", and this page does too.

Two independent open-source clients drive the unit today: stramanu/lumalou (Python, TypeScript and a web app) and kvdb/gld09-control (Python). Both authors report running them against real hardware. This spec is built from their write-ups and source, the vendor manual and the vendor FAQ. This project has not run anything against a unit and holds no capture. Every protocol fact in the spec is reported, and the spec is untested.

Out of scope. The Nordic DFU service on the same device: never write to it. Other Smart Connect products are also out of scope. The upstream author says the Bunny (gmn58) and Whisper (ghp38) share this generation's handshake but not its commands, and nobody has tested them. The older swings, mobiles, sleepers and soothers use a different protocol.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number GLD09 (vendor app product code gld09, API level 1) Chipset Not confirmed. The Nordic legacy DFU service implies a Nordic nRF5 BLE module. The upstream write-up calls the part behind it the "toy IC" Radio BLE only. No Wi-Fi Power 5 V 1 A AC adapter (the unit draws 0.3 A max). The remote takes two AAA cells Clock Volatile: lost on any power cut Firmware seen 0.3.7 in the advertisement, on both open clients' units FCC ID None printed in the manual (Part 15 Class B and ISED text only). No GLD09 grant was found under Mattel's grantee code PIY

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No. Nothing is provisioned. The client should set the clock Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name The unit's ten-digit AP number (not "Lumalou"). Match manufacturer data instead: company 0x03B6 (Mattel) with payload starting 4d 42 ("MB") Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (two open clients, unreplayed here)

To bring a unit up from a client:

  1. Plug the unit in. The clock lights at once.
  2. Close the Smart Connect app on any phone that still has it. The unit takes one central at a time.
  3. Scan for manufacturer data company 950 (0x03B6) with a payload starting 4d 42. Byte 3 of the payload should be 0x00 (idle). Bit 7 set means a central is already connected.
  4. Connect, subscribe to rx, read the factory token, do the ECDH, write the session characteristic, and send ENABLE_RX. See the handshake below.
  5. Send SET_CURRENT_DATE with local time. The manual says routines and the sleep trainer stay off until the clock is set after a power cut.

The vendor app's flow used the pairing button on the unit: open the app, stand within about 6 ft (1.8 m), press the button, and wait for the clock to update. The open clients do not press it, so it is not part of the protocol a replacement client needs. It is kept in the spec as a historical method.

Factory reset: none is documented. The manual's only reset is a power cycle: unplug the AC adapter for about 10 seconds and plug it back in. That loses the time. Whether schedules, routines and the custom playlist survive is not known. The spec lists the power cycle as verified: false with the manual as its basis.

Rebinding: nothing binds the unit to a phone. A new controller just connects once the old one lets go.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none. The MPID session is key agreement, not authorisation Bonding none PIN source None. The vendor FAQ warns that pairing from phone settings shows a PIN prompt; the app never needed one One central at a time Yes (vendor FAQ: "Someone else is already connected") One bond at a time Not applicable: no bond is made Confidence medium (vendor FAQ and two open clients)

Entering pairing mode: not needed. The pairing button puts the unit in operation mode 4 and sets bit 6 of the advertised state byte. That only served the vendor app's own flow, which ended with a command whose arguments are not documented (SEND_PAIRING_COMPLETE, 0x34). Do not send it.

Unpairing: nothing to unpair.

Recovery: if the unit will not accept a connection, close the Smart Connect app or the other client. The FAQ says to wait about 30 seconds after that. If it still refuses, unplug the adapter for 10 seconds.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 4cea0001-c678-4202-b5d3-712dbb5e5b14 MPID control The whole control surface. Not advertised 00001530-1212-efde-1523-785feabcd123 Nordic legacy DFU Firmware update. Never write to it: the upstream author reports a wrong write bricks the unit UUID Name Properties Role 4cea0002-c678-4202-b5d3-712dbb5e5b14 tx write, write without response Encrypted command frames, app to device 4cea0003-c678-4202-b5d3-712dbb5e5b14 rx notify Encrypted responses and events, device to app 4cea0004-c678-4202-b5d3-712dbb5e5b14 factory read 192-byte manufacturing token, cleartext 4cea0005-c678-4202-b5d3-712dbb5e5b14 session write App public key and nonce, once per connection

docs.title: Advertising
docs.text:
Company 0x03B6 is "Mattel" in the Bluetooth SIG company list. The payload after the company ID:

Offset Length Field 0 2 ASCII MB (4d 42) 2 1 Format byte, opaque 3 1 Connection state: bit 7 connected, bit 6 pairing, 0x00 idle 4 rest Firmware version, ASCII (e.g. 0.3.7)

The local name is the unit's AP number, a ten-digit decimal string that also sits inside the factory token's serial. The service UUID is not advertised.

docs.title: Factory token (4cea0004)
docs.text:
192 bytes, readable by anyone. Field map from kvdb/gld09-control:

Offset Length Field 0 1 Token version (10 on reported units) 1 24 ASCII serial. Bytes 7–16 are the AP number, bytes 19–24 the item number 25 33 Device P-256 public key, compressed 58 5 Not described 63 2 Machine ID 65 3 Manufacturing key ID, big-endian (12 on reported units) 68 2 Config table ID 70 54 Config table 124 64 ECDSA P-256 / SHA-256 signature over bytes 0–123, raw r ‖ s 188 4 Device salt (outside the signed part)

A client may check the signature against the manufacturing public key the vendor app carries for key ID 12. That key is not reproduced here. The open clients carry it, and skipping the check still gives a working session. It only drops the assurance that the peer is a genuine unit.

docs.title: Handshake (every connection)
docs.text:
1. Subscribe to rx.
  2. Read the factory token. Take the device key from bytes 25–57 and the salt from the last four bytes.
  3. Make an ephemeral P-256 key pair and 4 random bytes (the app nonce). shared = ECDH X coordinate, 32 bytes.
  4. Stretch it. Start with state = shared. For each round r from 0 to 99, encrypt all 32 bytes of state in place with AES-128-CTR. The key is state[0:16]. The IV is 00 00 00 00 ‖ r (uint32 BE) ‖ 00 "mattel" 00. The session key is state[0:16] after the last round. "mattel" is a fixed protocol constant, not a secret.
  5. Write the 33-byte compressed app key and then the nonce (37 bytes) to session, with response. Wait about 400 ms.
  6. Send ENABLE_RX (plaintext 01 50 01) as the first encrypted frame. Until this is sent the unit only acknowledges requests. After it, the unit streams CURRENT_DATE about once a second. It also pushes GLOBAL_STATE and routine progress whenever something changes on the unit.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
A command is built in layers, then encrypted:

application command   opcode, args...
FE frame              fe | n | opcode, args... | x        n = 1 + len(args), x = n XOR every opcode/arg byte
route                 01 10 | FE frame                   (to the toy controller)
MPID frame            7e | seq u32 BE | len u16 BE | crc8(7 header bytes) | AES-128-CTR(plaintext | crc8(plaintext))
Item Value len Plaintext length + 1 (the CRC byte) IV, app to device seq ‖ app nonce ‖ device salt ‖ 00 00 00 00 IV, device to app seq ‖ device salt ‖ app nonce ‖ 00 00 00 00. Nonce and salt swap places CRC-8 Poly 0x07, init 0xFF, no reflection, no final XOR (check value 0xFB over 123456789) Sequence Starts at 1 for ENABLE_RX; +1 per frame Spacing About 150 ms between writes; the upstream author says the unit dislikes bursts MTU Frames reach 29 bytes, so an ATT MTU above 23 is needed. Common stacks negotiate one on their own

On rx, application responses are 01 50 | FE frame holding the response opcode and data. Acknowledgements 00 7f 01 XX 00 00 00 00 00 and 01 10 XX 00 carry no data. Match replies by opcode: the unit also pushes state on its own. The spec's protocol_details.mpid.test_vectors has our own vectors (invented keys) for every step. Both open clients reproduce them.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
The spec declares each of these on tx as a template of the plaintext body.

Opcode Command Arguments 0x03 Soothing on/off 1 byte: 1 start, 0 stop 0x3C Light colour (turns the light on) 1 byte: 0 warm, 1 red, 2 yellow, 3 orange, 4 green, 5 blue, 6 purple, 7 night light, 8 cool, 9 rainbow 0x3A Light brightness 1 byte, 0–9 0x3E Light off none 0x6C Light timer 1 byte: 0 15 min, 1 30, 2 60, 3 90, 4 continuous, 5 1 min 0x3F Play sound 1 byte: 0 sleep playlist, 1 custom playlist, 2 pink noise, 3 ocean, 4 rain, 5 brown noise, 6 nature, 7 highway 0x38 Sound off none 0x37 Volume 1 byte, 0–9 0x42 Sound timer 1 byte: 0 15 min, 1 30, 2 60, 3 90, 4 120, 5 continuous, 6 1 min 0x40 Custom playlist 12 bytes: song IDs 1–12, 0 = empty slot 0x30 Set clock 4 BCD bytes: hour, minute, second, weekday (0 = Sunday) 0x79 Clock settings 2 bytes: display on/off; brightness << 4 \| format (0 = 12 h, 1 = 24 h) 0x44 Sleep trainer on/off 1 byte 0x48 / 0x46 Bedtimes / wake times 14 bytes: seven [BCD hour, BCD minute] pairs, Sunday first; ff ff = none 0x4A Wake alarms 4 bytes: seven nibbles Sunday first, then one trailing nibble. 0 at wake time, 1–8 = 15–120 min after, 9 none, 10 = 1 min after 0x4D Start nap 1 byte: 0 stop, 1–10 = 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 105, 120, 150, 180 min, 11 = 1 min 0x58 Routines on/off 1 byte 0x5A–0x66 (even) Day routine, Sunday to Saturday 14 bytes: start time (BCD, or ff ff) then 12 slots of step << 4 \| task icon 0x69 Routine music and reward sounds 2 bytes: music on/off; task reward << 4 \| routine reward 0x77 Routine volume 1 byte (range assumed 0–9) 0x7B Start routine now none 0x6B Routine control 1 byte: 0 complete task, 1 previous, 2 restart, 3 complete routine, 4 cancel 0x53 Request state none. Reply 0x02 0x52 Clock speed (test) Advanced. 0 real time, 1 10×, 2 60×, 3 3600×. Always set it back to 0

Task icons: 1 change clothes, 2 wash up, 3 brush teeth, 4 go potty, 5 pack bag, 6 eat, 7 read, 8 clean up, 9–11 the three custom tasks.

Requests with known reply layouts: current date (0x31 → 0x13), playlist (0x41 → 0x19), clock settings (0x7A → 0x99), bedtimes (0x49 → 0x23), wake times (0x47 → 0x22), alarms (0x4C → 0x27), day routines (odd opcodes 0x5B–0x67 → 0x2B–0x2F, 0x90, 0x91) and routine progress (0x68 → 0x94). The spec lists every other known request and response opcode in protocol_details.opcodes.

Left undeclared on purpose:

  • 0x01 aggregate state setter: kvdb/gld09-control reports the unit applies only part of it.
  • 0x4F nap alarm: reported inert.
  • 0x34 pairing complete: arguments unknown, listed unsafe upstream.

docs.title: GLOBAL_STATE (response 0x02)
docs.text:
Thirteen bytes, read as 26 nibbles, high nibble first. The nibble number is also the position in the reply's data.

Nibble Field Values 0 Operation mode 0 soother, 2 daytime awake, 3 sleepy time, 4 pairing, 5 firmware update, 6 nap time, 7 routine 1 Activity state Not established 2 Music status Not established (likely playing / not) 3–4 Current song 0 none, 1–12 lullabies, 13–18 sound loops 5 Volume 0–9 6 Sound timer As command 0x42 7 Light status 0 off, 1 on 8 Light brightness 0–9 9 Light colour As command 0x3C 10 Nap status Not established 11 Nap length As command 0x4D 12 Sleep trainer 0 off, 1 on 13 Wake alarm status Not established 14 Clock speed As command 0x52 15 Stage 0 none, 1 ready, 2 settle, 3 sleep 16 Clock display 0 off, 1 on 17 Clock brightness 0–9 18 Clock format 0 12 h, 1 24 h 19 Routine music Raw 20 Task reward sound Raw 21 Routine reward sound Raw 22 Light timer As command 0x6C 23 Routine volume Raw 24 Routines 0 off, 1 on 25 Alarm sounding Not established

GLOBAL_STATE is a runtime summary. It leaves out the playlist, schedules, alarms and routines; read those with their own requests.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• No replies at all. ENABLE_RX was not sent. The unit then only sends acknowledgement events.
  • Every notification fails its CRC. The receive IV has the device salt first and the app nonce second, the mirror of the transmit IV. The other common mistake is using the raw ECDH secret instead of the 100-round stretch.
  • Routines and the star do nothing. The clock was lost in a power cut. Send SET_CURRENT_DATE. kvdb/gld09-control also reports that the red-to-green cycle needs both a bedtime and a wake time. The green star only changes when an audible alarm is armed for that day. For a silent wake cue, that project uses a one-icon routine instead.
  • Routine icons disappear later in the day. The unit clears a morning routine on its own, some hours after the start time. There is no command to clear or extend it (kvdb/gld09-control, observed).
  • Nap will not start. kvdb/gld09-control reports a nap only starts with the sleep trainer on.
  • Upstream naming trap. spec/protocol.json in stramanu/lumalou at 9fa5ecf calls 0x68 SET_ROUTINE_TASK_STATUS. It is a request: send it without arguments and read reply 0x94. PR #2 there corrects it.
  • Playlist rejected. Song IDs above 12 are refused. The sound loops are played with 0x3F, not queued in the playlist.

docs.title: Flowtoys Connect Props (capsule 2 / vision) via Connect Bridge
docs.text: Status: Research Protocol: BLE (to bridge) + WiFi/OSC (to bridge) + proprietary nRF24 RF (bridge to props) Manufacturer: Flowtoys Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Flowtoys LED flow-arts props — capsule 2.0/2.C light engines (podpoi, capsule poi, staffs, batons) and vision props (vision poi/staff/club/wand) — do not speak BLE directly. They use a proprietary 2.4 GHz "flowtoys connect" radio protocol that runs on nRF24L01+-compatible radios. A hardware "connect bridge" (ESP32 + nRF24, sold as USB or pocket bridge) translates between the official "flowtoys connect" mobile app and the props. The app talks to groups, not individual props: every prop in a group shares one 16-bit radio group ID.

Flowtoys commissioned and published the bridge firmware (benkuper/FlowtoysConnectBridge) and a companion app (benkuper/FlowtoysConnect), so most of the protocol is documented by open source; the production app's newer BLE service UUIDs were recovered from the official APK (com.flowtoys.app).

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number capsule 2.0 / 2.C, vision core props, connect bridge (USB / pocket) Chipset Bridge: ESP32 + nRF24L01+ (props: nRF24-compatible 2.4 GHz radio) Radio BLE 4.x (bridge↔phone), WiFi 802.11n (bridge), proprietary 2.4 GHz nRF24 (bridge↔props) FCC ID —

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No (BLE to bridge); grouping required before props are addressable Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name BLE: FlowConnect <name>; WiFi fallback AP: FlowConnect <name> (WPA2, password findyourflow) Passphrase protection plaintext (WiFi credentials sent cleartext over unencrypted BLE) Confidence medium (published source; not exercised against hardware here)

Grouping props: from off, hold the prop button ~10 seconds until the LEDs flash or turn white. Every prop needs a group, even a single one. There are 5 fixed "public" groups (IDs 1–5) plus private groups with other 16-bit IDs. To have the bridge learn a private group, put the props on their sync page/mode (page 2 mode 1 on older firmware; the current app says page 5 mode 1) and start sync from the app/bridge.

Factory reset: the bridge stores WiFi credentials, its name and learned group IDs in ESP32 NVS — clearing NVS (reflash) resets it. A prop's group membership is overwritten by re-grouping (the ~10 s button hold).

Rebinding to a new network: in place — send the n<ssid>,<password> command over BLE or the /wifiSettings OSC message; no reset needed.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
Three hops, any of the first two can drive the third:

  1. BLE → bridge. Open firmware: Nordic UART Service 6e400001-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e; write ASCII commands to 6E400002-…, notifications on 6E400003-…; the app requests MTU 48. Production app: service 49550001-aad5-59bd-934c-023d807e01d5 with characteristics 49550002-…, 49550003-…, 49550005-… (roles unverified — recovered from the APK's compiled Dart library).
  2. WiFi/OSC → bridge. Bridge mDNS-advertises _osc._udp (instance flowtoysconnect) and listens for OSC over UDP (firmware port 9000; the early app sent to 8888).
  3. nRF24 RF → props. 250 kbps, channel 2, 3-byte address {0x01, 0x07, 0xF1}, CRC-16, no auto-ack; a 20-byte packed sync packet per group broadcast at ~30 ms cadence. Any nRF24 node can drive props directly with these parameters.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 6e400001-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e Nordic UART (open bridge firmware) ASCII command channel 6e400002-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e NUS RX Write commands (write / write-no-response) 6e400003-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e NUS TX Notifications 49550001-aad5-59bd-934c-023d807e01d5 Flowtoys Connect service (production) Vendor service used by com.flowtoys.app; characteristic roles unverified

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Commands are ASCII strings, decimal comma-separated fields, terminated by \n or 0xFF. Capital letters target public groups 1–5; lowercase target private (learned) groups; group 0 = all groups.

docs.title: Command: set pattern
docs.text:
p<group>,<page>,<mode>,<actives>,<hue>,<sat>,<brightness>,<speed>,<density>,<lfo1>,<lfo2>,<lfo3>,<lfo4> (P for public groups).

Field Description group Group ID (0 = all) page, mode Effect selector (modes are numbered within pages; mode metadata ships in the app as base_modes.json) actives Bitmask: bit0 LFO, bit1 hue, bit2 sat, bit3 brightness, bit4 speed, bit5 density hue, sat, brightness, speed, density, lfo1–4 uint8 0–255

Solid color: page 2, mode 7, actives 255, with HSV hue/sat/brightness.

docs.title: Command: wake / power off
docs.text: w<group> / W<group> wake; z<group> / Z<group> power off.

docs.title: Command: sync
docs.text: s<timeout_seconds> starts RF sync (learn private groups); S stops; a forgets all private groups.

docs.title: Command: configuration
docs.text: n<ssid>,<password> sets WiFi credentials; g<name>,<mode> sets bridge name and radio mode (0 = WiFi, 1 = BLE, 2 = both; bridge reboots); r restarts the bridge.

docs.title: OSC equivalents (UDP)
docs.text: /wakeUp (int group, int isPublic), /powerOff, /sync (float timeout), /stopSync, /resetSync, /pattern (14 ints: group, isPublic, page, mode, actives, hue, sat, brightness, speed, density, lfo1–4), /wifiSettings (2 strings), /globalConfig (string name, int mode), /play, /stop, /pause, /resume, /seek (float), /rgb/brightness (float).

docs.text: Offset Length Description 0 2 group ID (uint16, byte-swapped on the wire) 2 4 padding/sequence counter (incremented per change) 6 4 LFO values 1–4 10 5 global hue, saturation, value, speed, density 15 1 active flags (bit per parameter: lfo/hue/sat/val/speed/density) 16 2 reserved 18 1 page 19 1 mode + command bit flags packed in the final byte region (adjust, wakeup, poweroff, force_reload, save, delete, alternate)

docs.title: FOREO Peach 2 (IPL hair removal)
docs.text: Status: Capture verified (stock app; no replacement-client replay) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: FOREO AB (active; cloud not required for local control)

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
IPL can permanently damage skin and eyes

This handset emits intense pulsed light, up to 7.3 J/cm². Misuse can cause burns, blistering, discoloration, scarring or serious eye injury. Patch-test first, match intensity to skin tone, never treat broken, tanned, tattooed or moled skin, and keep it away from eyes. This project is experimental and unaffiliated; FOREO's manual and safety guidance govern. Do not bypass the skin-contact or eye-safety interlocks.

  • Manufacturer safety guidance
  • Archived safety guidance

docs.title: Overview and evidence
docs.text:
The Peach 2 family — Peach 2, go, Pro MAX and Duo — uses BLE and the FOREO For You app. Static analysis of app 4.4.1 (559) recovered the offline activation algorithm, command dialects and app-side subscription enforcement.

A 2026-11-07 Android HCI capture then recorded two stock-app connections to an already-activated PEACH2 running PEACH2 F.REV.K. It confirms the FFF0 GATT layout, security-access write, no-pairing session, 0A20 read, new-dialect intensity/mode writes, and seven-byte cooling profile. It does not show a locked-unit activation, Pro-mode write or replacement client implementing this spec.

Two findings remain important but have different evidence levels:

  1. Offline unlock is app-derived. Static analysis shows that the activation bytes are a keyless permutation of the device BLE MAC, so the cloud registration call is not needed by the firmware. The captured unit already returned activation state 01, so the actual locked-unit write was not verified.
  2. Pro mode is gated by the app, but direct firmware acceptance is unknown. Normal Pro selection requires an active eligible subscription; a separate testing flag bypasses that UI branch. Once permitted, the app writes 0ad0 06. The capture has seven Basic writes (0ad0 01) and no Pro write, so it proves neither a downgrade nor firmware behavior outside the entitlement path. Security access on 0A10 is not a Pro unlock token.

docs.title: Initial setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No network provisioning; locked units need BLE activation Exact configured names PEACH2, PEACH2GO, PEACH2Duo, PEACH2ProMAX Reported aliases PEACH 2, PEACH™ 2, PEACH2 Pro MAX Pairing / bond None Offline setup confidence Security/read path capture-confirmed; activation write reported
  1. Select the model and scan for its exact configured name. The app disables fuzzy matching and uses a 30-second timeout. It also interprets an activation-state marker from the raw advertisement; the specific flag in this capture is undecoded.
  2. Connect without bonding and discover services. FFF0 contains FFF1, 0A10 and 0A20 on the captured firmware.
  3. Write security access 01 a1 <MAC[3]> <MAC[4]> <MAC[5]> to 0A10. The live write matched this derivation exactly; the app retries up to three times. After the ATT Write Response, it waits 500 ms and validates no challenge response. This is connection setup, not Pro activation.
  4. Read SW revision 2A28. The captured suffix K selects the new dialect.
  5. Read 0A20. If it starts with 00, static analysis says to write 01 02 <8-byte chipId>. If it already starts with 01, do not rewrite it.
  6. Only if 0A30 exists, read it and write 01 when wake-up is not already enabled. The captured new-dialect unit did not expose 0A30; do not make this step mandatory.

PEACH2/GO/Pro Max skip the stock app's pre-connect device-information API lookup. That is only a local scan exception: account registration is a separate later step and its complete server behavior is not established by this research.

docs.title: chipId derivation (app-derived)
docs.text:
With MAC bytes m0…m5 in printed order and b = [m5, m4, m3, 0, 0, m2, m1, m0], all arithmetic mod 256:

out[0] = (b[2] & 0x0f) | (b[7] & 0xf0)
out[1] = (b[5] & 0x0f) | (b[1] & 0xf0)
out[2] = (b[7] & 0x0f) + (0xf0 - (b[6] & 0xf0))
out[3] = 0xff - b[6]
out[4] = b[5] + 1
out[5] = (b[1] & 0x0f) + (0xf0 - (b[2] & 0xf0))
out[6] = (b[0] & 0x0f) | (b[5] & 0xf0)
out[7] = (b[6] & 0x0f) | (b[0] & 0xf0)

Documentation-only MAC aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff gives security access 01 a1 dd ee ff, chipId ad ec 4a 44 cd 2e cf fb, and activation write 01 02 ad ec 4a 44 cd 2e cf fb. The unit's real MAC, serial and activation value are not published in this repository.

Factory reset is unknown. Rebinding needs no reset: scan, connect and run the security handshake from the new client. There is no bond to forget.

docs.title: Protocol summary
docs.text: FFF1 commands are raw opcode || payload, with 0a for set and 0b for query. Write the query, then read FFF1 back. ff ff ff ff means busy; the app retries up to five times. Observed settings writes returned an 18-byte value beginning 01.

docs.title: Captured GATT structure
docs.text:
UUID Role 0000fff0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Command and security service, confirmed 0000fff1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Command channel, read + write 00000a10-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Security access, read + write 00000a20-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Activation, read + write 00000a02-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Serial number; 14 ASCII bytes read, no write attempted 00000a0c-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Accelerometer input; 180 one-byte reads, axes/units unknown 00000a18-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Body NTC; 165 one-byte notifications, units unknown 00000a19-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Head NTC; 110 one-byte notifications, units unknown 00000a0d-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Vibrator setting; 15 one-byte notifications, vocabulary unknown 0000181c-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Separate service containing 0A05 0000180a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Standard device information

FFF0 also contains direct 0A01/0A02/0A03/0A04/0A06/0A08/0A09/0A40/0A44/0A50/0AF0 characteristics. The spec records their live properties. The roles of 0A44 and 0A09 are undecoded. Notably, 0A08 is read + notify, not an OTA-trigger write on this unit.

The captured normal-mode table had no 0A30, 0A07, Battery Service 0x180f, TI OAD or D0FF service. Their behavior on other firmware or in a separate update mode remains unknown.

Client integration: protocol_handler: ipl_foreo selects the mobile setup surface for security access, conditional activation and wake-up. Activation requires the actual BLE MAC address; platforms that expose only a CoreBluetooth UUID must not substitute it.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Meaning Evidence 0a 01 <level> Set intensity 0–5 Levels 3 and 5 captured 0b 01 Read intensity, first byte Returned 5 0a d0 01 Basic removal mode Seven captured writes 0a d0 06 Pro removal mode App constant; not captured, direct acceptance unknown 0b d0 Read mode; 01 Basic, ≥6 Pro Basic captured 0a c0 0a Automatic fan Accepted on new-dialect unit 0a c4 <7 bytes> New cooling profile Several captured; mapping incomplete 0b c4 00 07 Read seven-byte cooling profile Captured; 18-byte response 0a c0 <value> Old single-byte cooling write Static analysis 0b c0 Old cooling read Static analysis 0a a2 <mode ×5> Old flash mode and separate Duo path App constants; Duo Basic/Pro not captured 0b a2 Old flash-mode read Static analysis

The cooling profile is not a one-byte level. One wire example is 0a c4 14 0d 21 02 1c 14 14; it is evidence of the seven-byte layout, not a universal recommended setting. Read the current profile first and do not send arbitrary values on an IPL device. A separate 0a b1 a5 write was accepted after calibration polling, but its semantics are unknown.

Duo Basic is 0a a2 02 02 02 02 02; Duo Pro is 0a a2 03 03 03 03 03. These are model-specific app constants, not observed traffic. Duo's Pro switch is hidden in the app.

docs.title: Cloud dependency
docs.text: No cloud is needed for the captured local control path. FOREO's servers handle account registration and subscription entitlement. Offline locked-unit activation is implementable from static analysis but unverified. Pro's confirmed entitlement gate is in the app; direct firmware acceptance outside that path is unknown.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Locked-unit activation and persistence, plus the exact advertisement activation flag.
  • Registration-server behavior after the PEACH2/GO/Pro Max pre-connect API exception.
  • Direct Pro-mode acceptance, Duo command behavior and old-dialect suffix edge cases.
  • Cooling-profile fields, NTC/accelerometer/vibrator conversion, other notification streams and the 0AB1 write.
  • Temperature/NTC/voltage payload layouts and read-back formats.
  • OTA entry, image transfer, update-mode identity and recovery; 0A08 is not a verified trigger.
  • Single-central exclusivity and whether any model exposes a remote-fire command.

docs.title: Frigidaire Connected Air Conditioners
docs.text: Status: Research Protocol: WiFi (cloud-connected; local setup only) Manufacturer: Frigidaire (Electrolux) Manufacturer Status: Unsupported (cloud-dependent — if Electrolux shuts down servers, app control is lost)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Frigidaire sells WiFi-connected air conditioners across three product families: window units, portable units, and wall-mounted/PTAC units. All are controlled through the Frigidaire app (Electrolux platform) and communicate via the Electrolux cloud. This makes them vulnerable to bricking if Electrolux discontinues the cloud service.

This is the first HVAC/climate device category in the OpenGreenIoT project. APK static analysis has now been completed for the active Frigidaire Android app package. The control protocol still needs authenticated traffic captures for exact payload schemas, but local discovery is no longer open: no post-pairing LAN control path was found.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
Static Analysis Finding

Frigidaire com.electrolux.oneapp.android.frigidaire v1.24 / versionCode 5851, v2.0 / versionCode 6895, and v3.6 / versionCode 504110958 were pulled from APKPure via apkeep and decompiled with jadx. The older v1.24/v2.0 builds contain more legacy local setup machinery than v3.6, including a Delta NIU TCP/TLS provisioning stack on 192.168.6.1:3002, DELTA_NIU_HTTP_REQUEST, LOCAL_ROBOT_PASSWORD, and in v2.0 a cleartext network-security exception for 192.168.0.1. These are still provisioning/enrollment paths. No mDNS, SSDP/UPnP, .local, AWS Greengrass, MQTT local proxy, static-IP REST API, or post-pairing LAN control path was found for AC control.

docs.title: Discovery and Authentication
docs.text:
• Device class: WiFi cloud appliance.
  • Local discovery: Closed as cloud-only for post-pairing control. No SSDP, mDNS, NSD, .local, UPnP, static-IP HTTP API, MQTT LAN broker, or AWS Greengrass/local proxy path was found in APK static analysis.
  • Local provisioning: Present. The app references appliance SoftAP names beginning with AJ, @E, IOT, Air_Conditioner, or Dehumidifier, AllJoyn onboarding/enrollment, UDP broadcast on port 3000, and 192.168.6.1:3002.
  • User discovery path: Pair the AC in the Frigidaire/Electrolux app, then enumerate appliances from the authenticated Electrolux cloud/OCP account.
  • Replacement implication: A local-first replacement likely needs confirmed cloud API behaviour, DNS redirection plus protocol capture, or firmware work. A LAN scan alone is not expected to produce a usable post-pairing control endpoint.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text:
• Primary: WiFi to Electrolux OCP cloud over HTTPS REST plus websocket paths observed in APK strings.
  • Local API: No steady-state LAN control API found.
  • Provisioning: App-based pairing over SoftAP/AllJoyn/OCP provisioning.

docs.title: Frigidaire APK and Local API Evidence Report
docs.text:
Date: 2026-07-15

Package: com.electrolux.oneapp.android.frigidaire

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Older Frigidaire APKs were found and downloaded: 1.24, 2.0, and 3.6. The older 1.24 and 2.0 builds contain more legacy local provisioning code than the current 3.6 build, including a Delta NIU TCP/TLS setup channel, DELTA_NIU_HTTP_REQUEST, LOCAL_ROBOT_PASSWORD, and a cleartext exception for 192.168.0.1 in 2.0.

No evidence was found for a steady-state post-pairing LAN control API for Frigidaire AC/dehumidifier devices in 1.24, 2.0, or 3.6. The local code found is setup/enrollment only. App control paths remain Electrolux OCP cloud REST/websocket paths.

docs.title: APK Hunt Results
docs.text:
Play metadata for the current release was read with google-play-scraper (version 4.26, release date Mar 27 2023, 18 declared permissions); it exposes no historical APK list. Three older builds were located and archived through public APK mirrors — 1.24, 2.0 and 3.6. Nothing below 3.0 exists on the mirrors that still list the package, in the Internet Archive's Wayback CDX for the APKPure landing page, or in GitHub code search.

Archived builds (XAPK bundles):

Version versionCode SHA-256 1.24 5851 67e79350b1e39d1b084b6578d5a46925db3fc06ba7b9dbb35a46775c0862f3cf 2.0 6895 032e869b706275e94dd1fa2b3222e6d4e8a5d2591d7344f95bd7147869170f66 3.6 504110958 0fa212791d3f488eaffbbb1dbc628b7c988d786e1546be32fcc297795a6c99aa

The binaries and the raw search transcripts are kept in the local, gitignored research workspace — see the clean-room rules.

docs.title: Decompilation
docs.text:
The old XAPKs were extracted and their base APKs decompiled for static analysis; the decompiler output is kept out of the repo per the clean-room rules.

Each XAPK contained a base com.electrolux.oneapp.android.frigidaire.apk plus resource/config split APKs. Static analysis used the base APK.

docs.title: v3.6
docs.text:
Requested pattern results:

192.168.x patterns             1
localhost patterns             2
local HTTP server patterns     0
mDNS / NSD patterns            1
SSDP / UPnP patterns           0
local REST / WebSocket         0
local feature flags            0
AWS IoT patterns               0
provisioning patterns       1739
cloud endpoint patterns      466

Key evidence:

  • A socket class connects to 192.168.6.1 port 3002.
  • A URL builder constructs http:// or https:// URLs from a discovered setup server IP during provisioning.
  • No http://192..., ws://192..., mDNS, SSDP, UPnP, Greengrass, local MQTT broker, or local_control/lan_control feature flag was found.

docs.title: v1.24
docs.text:
Key counts:

local HTTP/IP patterns          2
discovery/mDNS/SSDP patterns    6
local/AWS flag patterns         0
provisioning patterns        2470
cloud endpoint patterns       249

Key evidence:

  • A caller of the TCP socket service passes 192.168.6.1.
  • The socket class opens a TCP/TLS channel to port 3002.
  • A command-constant class declares DELTA_NIU_HTTP_REQUEST, DELTA_NIU_COOKIE_SIGN, DELTA_NIU_SET_CLOUD_PASSWORD, DELTA_CLOUD_POST_APPLIANCE, and DELTA_NIU_UAR.
  • Another declares SET_LOCAL_ROBOT_PASSWORD_REQUEST and LOCAL_ROBOT_PASSWORD.
  • The cloud command path appliance/api/v2/appliances/{applianceId}/command is present.
  • LOCAL_NETWORK appears, but its usage is tied to the provisioning flow and permissions, not AC command dispatch.

docs.title: v2.0
docs.text:
Key counts:

local HTTP/IP patterns          2
discovery/mDNS/SSDP patterns    9
local/AWS flag patterns         0
provisioning patterns        2705
cloud endpoint patterns       272

Key evidence:

  • A caller of the TCP socket service passes 192.168.6.1.
  • The socket class opens a TCP/TLS channel to port 3002.
  • The app's network security configuration permits cleartext traffic for 192.168.0.1.
  • A command-constant class declares DELTA_NIU_HTTP_REQUEST, OCP_NIU_UAR, OCP_CLOUD_POST_APPLIANCE, and the AllJoyn setup commands AJ_NIU_CONNECT_AND_DISCOVER, AJ_NIU_WIFI_SCAN, AJ_NIU_ONBOARD.
  • Another declares SET_LOCAL_ROBOT_PASSWORD_REQUEST and LOCAL_ROBOT_PASSWORD.
  • The cloud command path appliance/api/v2/appliances/{applianceId}/command is present.
  • LOCAL_NETWORK appears, but its usage is tied to the provisioning flow and permissions, not AC command dispatch.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The older versions support the hypothesis that early Frigidaire/Electrolux apps had more local-first setup machinery. However, the local code found is not a post-pairing LAN API:

  • The hard-coded local endpoints are setup SoftAP IPs (192.168.6.1, and a v2.0 security exception for 192.168.0.1).
  • The local transport is a provisioning socket on port 3002, not a REST appliance-control API.
  • Local commands are NIU setup/enrollment operations: WiFi scan/connect, cookie signing, cloud password, cloud post appliance, UAR, AllJoyn onboard.
  • AC control commands in all inspected versions route through OCP cloud API paths such as /appliance/api/v2/appliances/{applianceId}/command.
  • No mDNS/Bonjour, SSDP/UPnP, static LAN REST endpoint, local websocket, AWS Greengrass proxy, or LAN MQTT broker pattern was found.

docs.title: Home Assistant / PyPI Check
docs.text:
Findings:

  • Home Assistant core homeassistant/components/electrolux path returned 404 from GitHub at the requested dev URL.
  • bm1549/home-assistant-frigidaire describes itself as using the "Frigidaire 2.0 (Electrolux) cloud API".
  • TTLucian/ha-electrolux uses the official Electrolux Group Developer API and SSE.
  • sanchosk/electrolux_status describes the Electrolux Connectivity Platform and previously used pyelectroluxconnect.
  • pyelectroluxconnect summary: "Interface for Electrolux Connectivity Platform API".
  • pyelectroluxgroup summary: "Python client for the Electrolux Group API" and depends on aiohttp-sse-client.
  • pyelectrolux is not present on PyPI.
  • pyhOn is for hOn/Haier-family devices and depends on awsiotsdk; it is not evidence of a Frigidaire local API.

No Home Assistant or PyPI project found in this pass documented a Frigidaire local LAN control endpoint.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Older APKs below 3.0 were found and decompiled. They contain local provisioning transports and stronger setup hints than v3.6, but no usable post-pairing local HTTP/LAN control API was found. The replacement path remains cloud API reverse engineering, setup-flow capture on 192.168.6.1:3002 or 192.168.0.1, or firmware/device-side work.

docs.title: Furbo Dog Camera
docs.text: Status: Spec Available Protocol: WiFi (ThroughTek TUTK/Kalay P2P over UDP); BLE for Wi-Fi onboarding Manufacturer: Tomofun Co., Ltd. Manufacturer Status: Active (cloud-dependent; alerts and clips need a Furbo Nanny subscription)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Furbo is a Wi-Fi pet camera with two-way audio and a treat launcher. The 360 models also pan. Tomofun sells a Furbo Nanny subscription for cloud alerts, clips, captions and daily summaries.

Current models use ThroughTek TUTK/Kalay P2P for video, microphone, talkback, settings, pan and treat toss; the app exposes no RTSP or ONVIF client. Independently published hardware research did establish RTSP on the older Furbo 2, so there is no family-wide "no RTSP" rule. A client on the camera's subnet finds it by UDP broadcast and gets a LAN-mode session. Otherwise the session goes direct P2P through NAT, or through a Kalay relay. The catch is the credential: a client must log in to the Furbo cloud to get one. The cloud issues a new key on every fetch, and each new key stops the previous one working.

Setup is a BLE flow in the vendor app. It is not just a Wi-Fi handover: once the camera is on the network it asks for registration data and registers itself with the Furbo cloud.

The spec, device-specs/devices/furbo-dog-camera.yaml, records three things:

  • the P2P session, both IOCTRL opcode sets and the audio/video formats, from the MIT-licensed ha-furbo project, which verified them on a Furbo 360 (FB0030, firmware 108)
  • how the cloud issues the P2P credential, from the same project
  • the BLE onboarding protocol, from our own static analysis of the vendor app (7.83.1)

Nobody on this project has driven a Furbo from the spec. The research store holds no capture and no firmware. The spec is identify_only: the schema has no transport for TUTK IOCTRL yet, so the opcode tables live in protocol_details rather than as executable commands. The TUTK transport itself needs the vendor SDK or a clean reimplementation such as go2rtc's pure-Go TUTK package. The Wyze Cam page covers the same transport family.

Out of scope: the cloud REST API beyond the credential flow, the cloud treat-toss endpoint, AI, alert and Nanny features, and OTA updates.

The treat launcher dispenses real food

One toss fires one treat across the room. The vendor app sends one toss per button press, and that is all the spec documents. If you script tossing, rate-limit it and keep a person watching the live view. Repeated tossing can overfeed a pet, and a jam or an empty hopper is not reported reliably enough to trust an unattended loop.

Privacy

This is an always-on camera and microphone. Barking, crying, person, smoke alarm and activity alerts, clips, captions and summaries all come from the vendor's cloud, so the audio and video they are built from leave the house. The app also asks the owner to label its detections, which trains the vendor's models. At setup it writes the phone's latitude and longitude to the camera.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number Sticker models (vendor table): Furbo2, Furbo2.5 (Furbo Dog Camera), Furbo3 (Dog Camera 360), FurboCat (Cat Camera 360), FurboMini. Cloud ProductIds: FB001, FB002, FB0025, FB0030, FB0035, FBC0030, FBC0035, MC0010, MC0020, MC0030. Only FB0030 = Furbo 360 is established; every other mapping is a hypothesis Chipset Furbo 2: Ambarella S2Lm. Furbo Mini: Augentix. Both from Somerset Recon's teardowns, not checked here. Furbo 360: not identified Radio 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi (802.11b/g/n, US channels 1–11) and BLE. The Mini shares one dipole antenna between them (FCC leaflet) Power 5 V 2 A (Furbo2.5T label) FCC ID 2AIBVTFFBV3 (Furbo Dog Camera, model Furbo2.5T, granted 2020-07-30); 2AIBV-MINICAM (Furbo Mini, granted 2020-09-15). No grant is indexed for the original 2016 Furbo or the 360 models

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes Method ble_provisioning (vendor app), which also registers the camera with the cloud Advertised name Current generation: the name contains -S3. Families: Furbo3…, Furbo3C…, Furbo4…, M2-…, M3-…, M4-…, …MINICAM…, F2… Passphrase protection device_encrypted: AES-256-CBC under a key that is the same in every copy of the app Network 2.4 GHz only, WPA2 (the vendor says WPA3 does not work). A hidden SSID can be typed in by hand Confidence low (static analysis of the app; nothing replayed)

The camera shows setup mode on its status light: blinking yellow on the 360 and Mini models, green on the original Furbo. The app scans for it, connects without bonding, and follows the camera's status code. The code is an ASCII number on a read/indicate characteristic.

  1. Read the status. 2 or 4 means ready.
  2. Trigger a Wi-Fi scan and read the AP list back in up to four chunks.
  3. Write the SSID and passphrase, then set the "details ready" flag.
  4. The camera joins Wi-Fi (status 8, 9, 10, 12).
  5. On status 20, write the account, a cloud endpoint and a short-lived registration token. The camera registers itself (13, 14).
  6. On status 21, write the phone's longitude and latitude, the country code, speaker volume 60 and the time zone.
  7. The camera starts P2P (22, 15) and reports 0 when a session is possible.

The per-status timeouts, the status table and every characteristic are in the spec's setup.methods and protocol_details.ble_onboarding_v4.

Factory reset (vendor help centre; not run by this project):

Model Button Hold Confirms Furbo 360 / 360 Cat Under the camera about 5–10 s (one vendor article says 30 s) Light blinks yellow Original Furbo (2 / 2.5T) Pinhole on the back, pin or paper clip, plugged in about 20 s Light changes, then turns green Furbo Mini Pinhole, plugged in 5–10 s Light blinks yellow Furbo Mini 360 Under the device until it changes Light blinks yellow

A hard reset clears Wi-Fi but not the cloud binding. Remove the camera from the old account in the app ("Remove Device"), or the next setup fails. The P2P opcode set also has a remote reset request. The spec marks it advanced and does not document it further.

Rebinding to a new network: done in place. The app's "Reset Wi-Fi" menu item re-runs the BLE flow on a bound camera, whose light blinks blue when it has lost its network. The vendor says not to press the reset button for this. Over BLE the app writes 2 to the reset-setup characteristic and adds an encrypted ownership proof. If the proof is missing the camera reports -101; if it is wrong, -102. The P2P UID belongs to the camera, not the network, so sessions need no change afterwards.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none Bonding none PIN source not applicable One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time No (nothing bonds) Confidence low (from the app)

Entering pairing mode: nothing to pair. Setup mode (above) is what makes the camera advertise.

Unpairing: nothing bonds. Ownership lives in the cloud account; "Remove Device" in the app clears it.

Recovery: the conflict that bites is on the P2P side. Each cloud fetch of the P2P credential makes the key every other client holds stop working. If the vendor app and a bridge fetch on their own, they knock each other off, and the AV channel fails with -20011. Use one shared session per camera.

docs.title: P2P session (TUTK/Kalay)
docs.text:
Per ha-furbo:

Step What happens SDK init Set the SDK licence string, which the vendor app embeds and which is not reproduced here. Initialise IOTC on a random local UDP port, then initialise AV Credential Cloud login, then one P2P credential fetch per camera, just before connecting Connect Connect by the camera's 20-character UID with its 8-character AuthKey (auth type 0). Session mode: 0 P2P, 1 relay, 2 LAN AV channel AV client on channel 0: identity P2PAccountId, password P2PAccountKey, security mode 1 (DTLS, PSK-AES128-CBC-SHA256) Legacy (FB002) The cloud returns no AuthKey. Use the plain connect by UID, then the AV client with the account id and the device record's P2PAccessToken, security mode 0 Register V2 cameras only: send the account's DeviceToken

LAN mode needs one broadcast domain. The SDK only offers broadcast search, with no connect-by-IP. Across VLANs, allow UDP both ways between the hosts (the session then comes up as direct P2P) or relay the broadcast.

docs.title: Getting the credential (cloud)
docs.text:
All calls are JSON POSTs to product.furbo.co.

  1. /v5/account/read/login with the email, the RSA-encrypted password and a client-chosen MobileId.
  2. If the reply is 12101, an emailed code is needed: /v4/account/mfa/login/send-code, then /v4/account/mfa/verify, then /v2/account/login.
  3. /v2/account/{AccountId}/device lists the cameras, with their UIDs.
  4. /v5/device/p2p_connection/get returns AuthKey, P2PAccountId and a fresh P2PAccountKey.

Keep the MobileId and the MFA proof to avoid a new code on every login. The login token lasts about a day and cannot be refreshed. All of these values are per-owner secrets.

Offline recovery is a candidate, not a promise. Owner-exported account fields and the on-camera p2p_auth.json state are two plausible ways to preserve an existing credential across reboots. Reset or regeneration invalidates it. Nobody has yet shown a session with both the Furbo cloud and TUTK relays blocked, so this is not cloud-free first-time adoption. Furbo 2 RTSP uses different credentials again: do not substitute the TUTK key for its Digest password.

docs.title: IOCTRL messages (V3: Furbo 360, 360 Cat, Mini 2/3)
docs.text:
A reply's opcode is the request's plus one, and its payload starts with a status byte (0 = OK). A refused request comes back as 0x40001 with [status, opcode low byte, opcode high byte, 0, 0]. Only the low 16 bits of the opcode are echoed, so 0x10009 and 0x20009 look alike in a refusal.

Opcode Our name Request Reply 0x10001 get device info 4 × 00 status, camera on at [1], volume at [5], four NUL-padded version fields from [9] 0x10009 / 0x1000b get / set camera on [on,0,0,0] [status, on] 0x10013 / 0x10015 get / set night vision [mode,0,0,0]: 0 auto, 1 on, 2 off [status, mode] 0x10017 / 0x10019 get / set sound sensitivity [level,0,0,0]: 0 off, 1 low, 2 medium, 3 high [status, level] 0x1001b / 0x1001d get / set speaker volume [0–100 %,0,0,0] [status, volume, muted] 0x10023 / 0x10025 get / set treat size [0 large / 1 small,0,0,0] [status, size] 0x10027 / 0x10029 get / set auto tracking [cruise, live, live zoom, 0] [status, cruise, live] 0x10011 get upgrade info 4 × 00 four ASCII version fields from [2] 0x20007 toss treat 4 × 00 status, then notification 0x30005 0x20009 pan [1 left / 2 right, degrees, 0, 0, 0, 0] status, then notification 0x30007 0x2000d play treat sound 4 × 00 status

The spec lists all 45 V3 entries (requests, notifications and the refusal), the older V2 set in the 0x900 range (Furbo 2 / 2.5T, first Mini; no pan), and the advanced ones (upgrade, reboot, upload logs, remote reset). The app turns 60° per pan press, or 50° on a Mini 3. ha-furbo verified these on hardware: the state read, setting the volume, a pan, and one treat toss.

docs.title: Audio and video
docs.text: Stream Format Video Start with standard opcode 0x1ff and an int32 LE quality number. V3 numbers: 0 = 1080p, 1 = 720p, 2 = 360p, 3 = 1440p. The FB0030 gives H.264 1920×1080 at 25 fps for quality 0, after one 640×360 preview frame, and 640×360 for qualities 1–3 Microphone Start with 0x300. The FB0030 labels its frames codec id 135; the format is not established Talkback G.711 µ-law, 16 kHz, mono, 320-byte frames (20 ms). Send speaker-start 0x350 with the channel number, then open an AV server on that channel with DTLS (security mode 3). Each frame has a 16-byte header: codec id 137, flags 14

docs.title: BLE onboarding (current generation)
docs.text:
The service UUID is not established; the app matches characteristics by UUID alone. Values are ASCII text, written with response.

docs.title: BLE onboarding (older generations)
docs.text: Service 77f9a069-2ff9-4ff9-93b7-4db9689f4b53, write 026048ab-fafc-48e5-9db0-a9bc46368055, notify 30c95538-58f8-4db4-a62e-08af4bae4cb0. Requests are JSON: {"c":"0001", …} for the AP list, and "0002" for the Wi-Fi and registration details. Each request ends with an ENM marker write. The app runs the JSON through a transform in its native library, which we have not analysed, so no byte-exact example exists.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Video or controls die, with -20011 on the AV channel. Another client fetched a P2P credential, often the phone app. Hold one session per camera and share it.
  • The session reports relay. Client and camera are on different subnets, or UDP between them is blocked. See the LAN mode note above.
  • Setup fails for a camera that was set up before. A hard reset does not unbind it. Remove it from the old account first.
  • The network is missing from the scan. It is 5 GHz-only, hidden or weak. Furbo joins 2.4 GHz WPA2 networks only.
  • Two vendor articles disagree on the Furbo 360 reset hold (5–10 s against 30 s). Hold until the light blinks yellow.
  • The cloud treat toss is no proof. It answers success for any action string (ha-furbo's negative finding), so do not treat its reply as a toss.
  • App defects seen in the decompile (not tested on hardware). The older setup controllers set the notification descriptor value but never write it, so whether those cameras notify without a CCCD write is open. The phone's latitude and longitude are formatted in the phone's locale, so a comma-decimal locale may send 51,5074000.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Somerset Recon published root exploits against older models, 2021–2022. None has been checked here, and the Furbo 360 is not named in any of them.

  • Furbo 2: RTSP on TCP 554 with an authentication-parser overflow (CVE-2020-24918).
  • Furbo 2.5T: a root command injection behind its web server.
  • Furbo Mini: unsigned firmware fetched without certificate checks.

The spec carries these as a reported security advisory. Somerset's Furbo 2 research establishes RTSP at /stream on TCP 554, with Digest authentication after an update/reset; an early unmodified unit allowed unauthenticated viewing. This does not establish RTSP on Furbo 3/4 or Mini, so the spec does not expose a generic camera stream. No exploit or owner credential was used for this research.

docs.title: Gocycle G4 / G4i / G4i+ E-Bike (GocycleConnect BLE)
docs.text:
Status: Spec Available (app-derived; not replayed against hardware) Protocol: BLE (Silicon Labs BGX13 Xpress Streaming Service carrying a framed 16-bit opcode protocol) Manufacturer: Karbon Kinetics Ltd (Gocycle) Manufacturer Status: Active

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/gocycle-ebike.yaml. Where this page and the spec disagree, the spec wins.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Gocycle makes folding e-bikes. On the G4 family (G4, G4i, G4i+) the GocycleConnect phone app is the only way to change riding modes, lights and settings, and to see battery, speed and trip data. It also enforces account sign-in and cloud registration before it will connect. This page documents the bike's own Bluetooth LE protocol, so that a bike can be read and adjusted without the vendor app.

The radio is a stock Silicon Labs BGX13 "Bluetooth Xpress" module used as a serial bridge. Behind it, the bike's junction box and motor controller speak a framed binary protocol with 16-bit opcodes. The same opcode set is older than the BLE link: the G2, G3, G3+, G3C, GS, GX and GXi bikes carry it over Bluetooth Classic SPP. That path is only summarised here.

What a client can do from the spec:

  • poll the live dash block: battery %, voltage and current, speed, cadence, gear, odometer, trip distance, calories, moving time, pedal and motor energy
  • read versions, the identity reply and the hardware-type byte
  • switch the front and rear lights; set DRL flashing, the DRL default mode and the "DRL switch controls lights" selector
  • toggle predictive shifting (G4i / G4i+)
  • reset the trip
  • read the riding-mode definitions and the diagnostic counters

Riding-mode selection (Eco / City / Turbo / Demand) is fully documented, but the spec deliberately gives no ready-to-send frame for it. The record the app writes to select a mode also carries that mode's speed ceiling and the pedalling-required flag, which together set the bike's legal class. See Riding modes.

Safety and scope

This spec controls a road vehicle's motor assistance and lights. Change settings only when the bike is stopped: the vendor manual warns against changing mode in motion. The following are deliberately left out, and named by role only: the writes for maximum speed and throttle (on-demand) permission, the miles and time limits, the frame number, factory state, the controller locks and the anti-theft flag, and every firmware-flashing step.

docs.title: Which Gocycles use BLE
docs.text:
The app picks the transport from the model code on the bike's cloud build record. A code starting G4 goes to the BLE scan, and anything else goes to the Classic serial flow. Gocycle's own help centre splits the families the same way. G4-family firmware is 2.x, while GXi/GX/G3/GS/G2 firmware is V8x. Diagnostics have separate flows, and the Bluetooth-reset article covers only G4, G4i and G4i+.

Model Link Covered here G4, G4i, G4i+ (and the "Mk2" builds the app names) BLE (BGX13) Yes GX, GXi, G3, G3+, G3C, GS, G2 Bluetooth Classic SPP Summary only CX / CXi / CXi+ (cargo) Not referenced by the app Unknown

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: Everything comes from static analysis of GocycleConnect 9.6.2. It is a Capacitor app whose bike logic ships as plain JavaScript, so the frame builder, the receive parser and every screen that sends a command were read directly. Gocycle's manuals and help-centre articles supply the behaviour: riding modes, Factory and Delivery State, the Bluetooth reset and the forced firmware update. Silicon Labs' public BGX documentation identifies the GATT service and the module's pairing defaults. There is no capture, and no FCC grant (none is indexed for Gocycle or Karbon Kinetics, and no manual prints an FCC ID). No open-source Gocycle client exists: an earlier note claimed a Home Assistant integration, and it could not be found. Every fact is reported, and the spec's device.testing is untested.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Models covered G4, G4i, G4i+ Radio module Silicon Labs BGX13 "Bluetooth Xpress" (identified by its stock Xpress Streaming Service) Controllers Junction box and motor controller behind the module; separate firmware versions Advertised name Gocycle + six-digit frame number (for example Gocycle123456); some units upper-case GOCYCLE Radio power Only while the battery is switched on; the battery turns itself off after about 30 minutes without motor activity Firmware G4 family 2.x. The app treats anything below 2.8 as needing an update FCC ID Not found (no grant indexed; not printed in the manuals)

The frame number doubles as the bike's identity in the vendor's cloud: service history, ownership and registration are all keyed on it.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No provisioning. A BLE bond is made on first connect (see Pairing) Method ble_direct, plus the vendor's cloud_account activation for a never-activated bike Advertised name Gocycle… / GOCYCLE… Passphrase protection not_applicable (no Wi-Fi) Confidence low (read from the app; not replayed)

For an activated bike, the whole setup is: switch the battery on, close the vendor app (and turn Bluetooth off on any other phone that uses the bike), scan for the Gocycle name, connect, subscribe to Peripheral TX, and start writing framed commands.

A new bike is not usable until the vendor app activates it. A bike shipped directly is in Factory State, with the motor disabled. A dealer-prepared bike is in Delivery State, with 60 miles (100 km) of assist. The owner's Setup in the vendor app registers the bike and lifts the restriction. Those state changes are writes this spec omits, so this spec cannot activate a bike. On a used bike still registered to someone else, the vendor app refuses to connect until the previous owner transfers ownership.

Factory reset: there is no owner-accessible factory reset. Factory and Delivery State are activation states set by the vendor's dealer and factory tooling. The only owner-side reset is the Bluetooth reset, which clears the bike's stored bonds (see Pairing).

Rebinding to a new phone or client: in place. Disconnect the old phone and pair from the new one. The BGX module keeps up to 14 bonds by default.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required Yes (inferred) Security mode just_works (inferred) Bonding required: the bike stores bonds (inferred) PIN source None; no PIN appears anywhere in the app or documentation One central at a time Yes, per the vendor's multiple-devices article One bond at a time No. The module's bond table holds 14, and the vendor documents one bike on several phones Confidence low

Silicon Labs documents the BGX streaming service as requiring an encrypted link, with bonding requested by default. The app never calls a bond API and never shows a PIN, so the phone's OS pairs implicitly on the first access to the streaming characteristics, and Just Works is the expected model. The vendor's instruction to "forget the Gocycle" in the phone after a bike-side Bluetooth reset fits a bike that stores bonds. Gocycle could have reconfigured the module, and one GATT session against a bike would settle it.

Entering pairing mode: not needed. The bike is connectable whenever its battery is on.

Unpairing (Bluetooth reset), per the vendor, needs firmware 2.3 or later:

  1. Close the vendor app.
  2. With the bike on, hold the boost button (G4) or the left twist switch down (G4i, G4i+) for 30 seconds, until the bike beeps.
  3. Forget the bike in every phone's Bluetooth settings, then pair again.

Recovery: if the bike is not visible or will not connect, close the vendor app, turn Bluetooth off on any other phone that has used it, forget it in the OS Bluetooth settings, and as a last resort do the Bluetooth reset.

docs.title: BLE services
docs.text:
UUID Name Role 00001800-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Generic Access 00002a00 Device Name gives the full Gocycle<frame number> name when the advertisement is truncated 331a36f5-2459-45ea-9d95-6142f0c4b307 BGX13 Xpress Streaming Service Carries the bike protocol. Shared by every BGX13 product, so it is not an identification signal on its own ↳ a9da6040-0823-4995-94ec-9ce41ca28833 Peripheral RX Client → bike. Write every command here, with response. Leave its notifications off ↳ a73e9a10-628f-4494-a099-12efaf72258f Peripheral TX Bike → client. Subscribe; every reply arrives here ↳ 75a9f022-af03-4e41-b4bc-9de90a47d50b BGX Mode The module's own mode switch (1 stream, 2 local command, 3 remote command). Never write it

Enabling notifications on Peripheral RX switches the BGX into Fast-Ack flow control, which sends 3-byte window messages on RX. The vendor app enables them and then immediately disables them again, and ends up in legacy flow control (RX notifications off, writes with response). A client should simply not enable them.

The app's UUID table also lists two groups of Silicon Labs OTA UUIDs. The app never uses them, and whether the bike exposes them is unknown.

docs.title: Frame format
docs.text:
Both directions on BLE use a long frame:

Offset Length Field 0 1 0x40 start byte 1 2 Payload length N, uint16 little-endian (payload only) 3 2 Opcode, uint16 little-endian; bit 15 set on the flagged opcodes below 5 N Payload 5+N 2 Checksum: uint16 LE sum of bytes 1 … 4+N (the start byte is not summed)
  • Bit 15. On send, the app sets bit 15 on the motor-controller opcodes (0x2021, 0x2022, 0x2031, 0x2035, 0x2036, 0x203f, 0x2047, 0x2049, and some omitted writes). On receive it masks the bit off every opcode. A plausible reading is that the bit routes the frame to the motor controller, but that is a hypothesis.
  • Short frame. The parser also accepts 0x21 <len C> <type> <C bytes> <sum8>, where the checksum is the 8-bit sum of bytes 1 … 2+C. Only type 0x01 (ACK) is used, and it carries the acknowledged opcode.
  • ACK and NACK. An ACK is opcode 0x0001 and a NACK is 0x0000. Either carries the answered opcode as a uint16 LE payload.
  • Byte stream. The BGX is a byte-stream bridge. Reassemble frames by the length field and verify the checksum before decoding. A frame can span notifications.

Test vectors:

Frame Decodes to 40 00 00 31 a0 d1 00 opcode 0x2031 (dash data, bit 15 set), no payload, sum 0x00d1 40 01 00 35 a0 04 da 00 opcode 0x2035, payload 04, sum 0x00da 40 04 00 3c 10 ff 01 ff ff 4e 03 opcode 0x103c (set DRL), payload ff 01 ff ff, sum 0x034e 21 02 01 3c 10 4f short ACK of 0x103c

docs.title: Connection sequence
docs.text:
1. Connect. On a phone without a bond, the first access to the streaming service triggers pairing.
  2. Subscribe to Peripheral TX (a73e9a10-…). Do not enable notifications on Peripheral RX.
  3. Send read_mc_version. The app sends G4 bikes below 2.8 to its update page.
  4. Send read_max_speed, then poll read_dash_data every 1000 ms. The app stops polling after three unanswered polls.
  5. On the first poll the app also reads the lights state and the active and custom mode definitions.

There is no login, key exchange or clock sync. The app's set-time command is mis-wired and never reaches the bike.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
All frames are complete, including the checksum. Write them to Peripheral RX as they stand.

Command Opcode Frame Reply read_dash_data 0x2031 40 00 00 31 a0 d1 00 Dash block (below) read_mc_version 0x2021 40 00 00 21 a0 c1 00 minor u16, major u16 read_jb_version 0x2026 40 00 00 26 20 46 00 as above (unconfirmed on G4) read_id 0x1002 40 00 00 02 10 12 00 0x1003: unit type, app/bootloader, version read_gocycle_type 0x204b 40 00 00 4b 20 6b 00 byte 0: hardware type 1-5 read_mode_definition_active 0x2035 40 01 00 35 a0 04 da 00 Mode definition 4 read_mode_definition_custom_1 / _2 0x2035 …35 a0 02 d8 00 / …35 a0 03 d9 00 Custom modes (definitions 2, 3) activate_mode_slot 0x1009 40 01 00 09 10 03 1d 00 ACK read_lights_enable 0x3023 40 00 00 23 30 53 00 byte 0: 0 off, else on lights_on / lights_off 0x3022 40 01 00 22 30 01 54 00 / …22 30 00 53 00 ACK read_lights_selector 0x3020 40 00 00 20 30 50 00 byte 0: 0 disabled, else enabled lights_selector_on / _off 0x3021 40 01 00 21 30 01 53 00 / …21 30 00 52 00 read_drl 0x103a 40 00 00 3a 10 4a 00 0x103b: on, flash allowed, current mode, default mode drl_flash_on / _off 0x103c 40 04 00 3c 10 ff 01 ff ff 4e 03 / …ff 00 ff ff 4d 03 drl_default_* 0x103c 40 04 00 3c 10 ff ff ff <m> … m: 0 Low, 1 Low flashing, 2 High, 3 High flashing, 5 Off predictive_shifting_on / _off 0x3013 40 01 00 13 30 01 45 00 / …13 30 00 44 00 reset_trip 0x203f 40 05 00 3f a0 01 01 01 01 01 e9 00 read_max_speed 0x2047 40 00 00 47 a0 e7 00 mph × 100 (read only) read_allow_on_demand 0x2049 40 00 00 49 a0 e9 00 non-zero = throttle-only assist permitted (read only) read_diagnostic_data 0x204a 40 00 00 4a 20 6a 00 Sensor and switch counters read_stress_counts 0x3027 40 00 00 27 30 57 00 6 × float32 LE

In set DRL (0x103c), a byte of 0xff means "leave unchanged". The spec has the full frames for every DRL default mode.

docs.title: Dash data (reply to 0x2031)
docs.text:
Offsets are into the payload, which starts at frame offset 5. All multi-byte fields are little-endian.

Payload offset Type Field Scale / unit 0 u16 Battery voltage × 0.001 V 2 u16 Battery current × 0.001 A 10 u32 Odometer × 0.01 mi 16 u8 Battery level 0-10 → × 10 % 20 u16 Trip calories kcal (inferred) 22 u32 Trip distance × 0.01 mi 28 i16 Miles limit (demo / Delivery State) mi; −1 = none 36 u16 Speed ÷ 32 mph 38 u16 Gear 40 u16 Cadence × 0.1 rpm 42 u32 Pedal energy since trip reset J 46 u32 Motor energy since trip reset mJ 50 u32 Moving time since trip reset ms 54 u16 Predictive shifting enabled non-zero = on 56 u8 Dealer review pending 58 u16 Service reminder pending

The app reads speed onward only when the payload is longer than 40 bytes, energy onward only when it is longer than 46, and the last two flags only when it is longer than 57. Current firmware sends at least 60 bytes (a 67-byte frame). Distances are always miles on the wire.

docs.title: Riding modes
docs.text:
The four mode buttons do not select a numbered mode. Each writes a pedal-power curve into mode definition 4 with opcode 0x2036 (sent as 0xa036), then sends activate_mode_slot (0x1009, payload 03). The definition record is the same 10 bytes the bike returns for 0x2035:

Payload byte Field 0 Definition number (app writes 4; G4 keeps Custom 1 and 2 in 2 and 3) 1 Torque-sensing flag (app writes 1) 2 Boost / power level (0 in every preset) 3 0 = pedalling required, 1 = assist without pedalling allowed. Region-dependent 4-5 Speed ceiling, mph × 100, u16 LE. Region-dependent 6-7 Pedal effort at which assist starts, W, u16 LE 8-9 Pedal effort for full assist, W, u16 LE Preset Start (W) Full (W) City 50 400 Eco 200 600 Turbo 50 200 Demand 600 600

The app identifies the active preset from definition 4's wattage pair, and equal values mean Demand. It fills bytes 3-5 from the region on the cloud record: the EU 25 km/h EPAC ceiling with pedalling required, or the 20 mph US ceiling. A replacement client should instead read definition 4, change only bytes 6-9, and write it back, with the bike stopped. Done that way, a mode change can never raise the speed ceiling or enable throttle-only assist. The spec declares the write as an advanced command with a byte layout but no frame. The checksum is a 16-bit sum that the schema's template vocabulary cannot yet compute, and the two copied fields need a read-back the vocabulary cannot express.

docs.title: Firmware update
docs.text: G4 images ship inside the app as Intel HEX (2.80, 2.86 and 2.87, chosen by hardware type). The app streams them over the same framed channel. Nothing in the app signs them, and whether the bootloader checks more than a CRC is unknown. The vendor's forced update holds the boost button (G4) or the left twist switch (G4i) while powering on, and is the documented recovery after a failed update. The spec records only this role. The flashing opcodes and bytes are intentionally absent.

docs.title: Bluetooth Classic bikes (G2 / G3 / GS / GX / GXi)
docs.text: This is a summary only. The app lists bikes the phone has already paired in its OS settings, then connects over SPP (00001101-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb) through the open-source cordova BluetoothSerial plugin. It writes bare [opcode high, opcode low, payload…]: a big-endian opcode with no start byte, length or checksum. It parses replies with the same 0x40 / 0x21 parser. No source says whether that un-enveloped form is exactly what the bike accepts. Firmware for these bikes is downloaded from the vendor's servers and flashed over SPP. Whether the iOS app can reach them at all is unknown, because iOS exposes no RFCOMM.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Likely cause Bike not found in a scan The battery is off (it auto-offs after 30 min idle), or another phone or the vendor app is connected. On Android, location or Bluetooth scanning is off Pairing fails or drops at once The phone holds a bond the bike has discarded (after a Bluetooth reset). Forget the bike and pair again. Firmware below 2.3 has no bike-side reset Connected, but nothing answers Wrong checksum or opcode byte order (the opcode is little-endian; check the bit-15 set). RX notifications left on (Fast-Ack). A reply split across notifications and not reassembled Commands work, motor does not assist Factory State (5 beeps) or unregistered/Delivery State used up (3 or 4 beeps). Only the vendor app's Setup clears it Seven beeps at power-up A dealer service rating is pending in the vendor app (dash review_pending)

Known vendor app defects, which explain much of the store-review frustration:

  • The app requires sign-in, cloud ownership of the frame number and, on a new bike, registration before it will connect. Reviews report re-registration on reinstall and accounts that stop working.
  • Its receive parser does not resynchronise cleanly after stray bytes. One bad notification can wedge it until reconnect.
  • Its RX-subscribe, RX-unsubscribe, TX-subscribe sequence races. It works only because RX notifications end up off.
  • The set-time and frame-number calls are mis-wired and never reach the bike.
  • It splits frames over 150 bytes into 256-byte writes, above the BGX's 250-byte limit.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• No GATT dump yet. The characteristic properties and pairing model are the BGX defaults, not observed.
  • Does a 67-byte dash frame arrive in one notification at a phone's negotiated MTU?
  • The meaning of bit 15, of the boost byte, of dash miles-limit −2, and of the dash bytes the app ignores.
  • Which marketing model each hardware-type value 1-5 is, and whether the CX cargo bikes are G4-family BLE bikes.
  • Whether the "Lights: Auto" state seen in an older app screenshot still exists. The analysed build offers only on/off.

docs.title: Govee H5075 Thermometer/Hygrometer
docs.text: Status: Complete (hardware-verified 2026-08) Protocol: BLE (passive advertisements + optional GATT connection) Manufacturer: Govee (Shenzhen Intellirocks Tech Co., Ltd.) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Battery BLE thermometer/hygrometer that broadcasts temperature, humidity and battery in its manufacturer advertisement — live readings need no connection, no pairing and no account. Connecting adds three things scanning cannot give: the reading at two decimals instead of one, the stored record count, and the history buffer (about 20 days at the measured record rate).

Verified end to end against one unit (GVH5075_BBCC, firmware 1.04.07, hardware 1.03.02) from a Raspberry Pi 5 on BlueZ 5.82 with bleak 3.0.2, on 2026-08-12/13 (sub-zero sign-bit check 2026-08-16). Seventeen sibling models (H5051/H5052, H5071/H5072/H5074, H5100–H5112 family, H5129, H5174/H5177–H5179) are covered by the spec but were not tested — their advertisement layouts differ and are carried from community parsers.

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/govee-h5075-thermo.yaml.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Model Number H5075 (+ 17 untested sibling models, see spec device.variants) Chipset Telink TLSR8253F512 BLE SoC Radio BLE (legacy advertising, ~2.04 s interval) FCC ID 2AQA6-H5075 (grantee Shenzhen Intellirocks Tech, granted 2019-12-13) Advertised name GVH5075_XXXX (H5074 and H5179 use Govee_<model>_XXXX) Advertised service 16-bit UUID 0xEC88 (0000ec88-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb) Manufacturer company ID 0xEC88 (60552)

The scan response carries an iBeacon frame whose proximity UUID spells INTELLI_ROCKS_HW in ASCII (494e5445-…-4857). A passive scanner never sees it, and it is not advertised as a service UUID — though a GATT service with that UUID does exist once connected. Note that btmon prints iBeacon fields byte-swapped.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct (passive scan) Setup AP / advertised name GVH5075_XXXX Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence high (verified on hardware, correlated to the device LCD)

Passive scan for company ID 0xEC88 and decode the 6-byte manufacturer payload. Connect only when you want the two-decimal reading, the record count, or history.

Factory reset: pull the batteries for 10+ seconds. There are no stored credentials and no pairing state to clear (not executed on the test unit — expected behaviour of a broadcast-only device).

Rebinding: trivial — no persistent connection state; just scan from the new controller.

docs.title: Advertisement (6-byte manufacturer payload under company ID 0xEC88)
docs.text:
Offset Length Description 0 1 Reserved (0x00 in every packet observed) 1–3 3 24-bit big-endian packed value. Bit 23 = temperature sign flag; bits 22–0 hold (temp × 10000) + (humidity × 10) 4 1 Battery percent, 0–100 5 1 Reserved (0x00; not the battery)

Decode by splitting the decimal digits, not by dividing the whole value:

v = bits 22–0            # mask 0x7FFFFF, NOT 0x7FFFF
temperature °C = (v // 1000) / 10.0, negated if bit 23 set
humidity %     = (v % 1000) / 10.0

Two traps, both confirmed on hardware:

  • Masking with 19 bits (0x7FFFF, as some community loggers do) agrees below 52.4 °C and wraps above it — at a true 52.6 °C it reads 0.1 °C and 87.7 % humidity.
  • Computing v / 10000.0 for temperature leaves the humidity digits inside the temperature, so the reading drifts with humidity.

Worked example: 00 04 18 87 61 00 → raw 0x041887 = 268423 → 26.8 °C, 42.3 %, battery 97. The payload is Celsius whatever the display is set to. The encoding has no room for exactly 100.0 % humidity (would carry into the temperature digits); clamp vs overflow is untested.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 494e5445-…-4857 Govee INTELLI_ROCKS_HW Service Main service; present without pairing 494e5445-…-2011 Device Data / Command (read/write/notify) 20-byte command channel; byte 0 = 0xAA read / 0x33 set, byte 1 = opcode, byte 19 = XOR of bytes 0–18 494e5445-…-2012 History Download Request (read/write/notify) Write 33 01 here to start a history transfer 494e5445-…-2013 History Download Response (read/notify) Subscribe before writing …2012; subscribing afterwards yields nothing and is not recoverable 00010203-…-1912 Govee Auth Service Carries only …2b12 on this unit; no handshake was required — every command answered in the clear 00010203-…-2b12 Auth Config (read/write-without-response/notify) Reads back a single 0x00 00001800-…-34fb Generic Access Device name, appearance (unset), connection params 0000180a-…-34fb Device Information PnP ID only — no version strings; use aa 0d/aa 0e instead

There is no standard Battery Service (0x180F) on this unit: battery comes from advertisement byte 4 or aa 08.

docs.title: Commands (on …2011, 20-byte packets, XOR checksum at byte 19)
docs.text:
Command Purpose aa 0a Current reading at two decimals: temp as signed int16 LE hundredths at bytes 2–3, humidity uint16 LE hundredths at bytes 4–5 (unsigned decode of the temp reads 649.77 °C at −5.61 °C) aa ef Stored record count, uint32 BE at bytes 2–5 — exact, where a dump can be truncated; ask before requesting history aa 08 Battery percent in byte 2 aa 0d / aa 0e Hardware / firmware revision, ASCII (the only route to version strings) aa 0c / aa 0f MAC (reversed byte order); aa 0c adds a further pair other sources call a serial aa 03 / aa 04 Humidity / temperature alarm thresholds (int16 LE hundredths, low then high) aa 06 / aa 07 Temperature / humidity calibration offsets aa fe A 16-character per-device string (serial or key material; not recorded) 33 03/04/06/07 Setters mirroring the alarm/calibration reads — untested (flagged advanced in the spec: they write persistent state; read and save current values first)

Caveats confirmed on the bench: the first command after connecting is dropped roughly two rounds in three — send a throwaway write or retry. aa 01, listed elsewhere as the current measurement, never answered on this unit. The device hangs up after ~11.9 s idle (writes stretch it to ~20 s; reconnecting costs ~8.4 s), and it keeps advertising while connected.

docs.title: History download
docs.text: Subscribe to …2013, then write 33 01 <first u32 LE> <last u32 LE> 00…<xor> to …2012. Records stream back as 20-byte notifications on …2013: a 2-byte big-endian offset followed by six 3-byte records in the same 24-bit packed encoding as the advertisement. Byte 19 is record data, not a checksum. Offset 0 is the newest record; the stream ends when the offset reaches 0 — do not stop early at offset ≤ 6 (the final packet carries real records) and do not wait for an end marker (ee 01 was never sent across five dumps). Padding past the buffer end is ffffff. The two u32 arguments do not select a range: ask for the lot (first=100 returned a full buffer in every trial) and read the offsets you actually get. Records are written every ~61.3 s (measured, one unit's crystal — take two counts a few hours apart on the unit in front of you), not 60; at 60 s assumed, the oldest record of a full buffer ends up ~10 hours adrift.
