docs.title: Govee H5080 Smart Plug
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (wire-verified by third parties, untested by us) Protocol: BLE (local control); Wi-Fi + cloud binding also present Manufacturer: Govee (Shenzhen Intellirocks Tech / iHoment) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
WiFi + BLE smart plug family. Local BLE control uses the classic Govee 20-byte binary packet — [2-byte command][17-byte payload][1-byte XOR checksum] — wire-verified by two independent implementations (egold555's H5080 notes and virtuald/govee-ble-plugs), and works with no WiFi and no cloud. BLE switching is gated by an application-layer token auth: the plug's static 16-byte key can only be read while the physical button is held.

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/govee-h5080-plug.yaml.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Model Number H5080 (single); family: H5081, H5082/H5083 (dual), H5085 (Pro, Matter), H5086 (Pro Energy Monitoring), H5089/H5160/H5161 (triple) Radio BLE + 2.4 GHz WiFi (802.11 b/g/n, 2412–2462 MHz per FCC 2AQA6-H5080) Rating 15 A / 1800 W max, ETL + FCC certified Advertised name ihoment_H5080_… (duals ihoment_H5082_…, Pro GVH5086…) Advertised service 00010203-0405-0607-0809-0a0b0c0d1910 (whether the 128-bit UUID is in the ADV packet is unverified — needs one capture) Manufacturer company ID 0xEC88 (60552) when the 88 EC bytes lead the payload; newer firmware prepends a version byte so hosts report 0x88XX (e.g. 0x8803) — match 88 EC at payload offset 0 or 1. goodsType 2 bytes BE after the company bytes (43=single, 50 & 307=dual, 90=triple); last manufacturer-data byte carries on/off state

Firmware seen: 1.00.21 and 1.02.00 (RE captures), 1.00.22 in the wild; the app treats firmware ≤ 1.00.08 as a reduced-feature "old H5080". OTA is in-app only — no public firmware downloads.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No (but BLE control needs a one-time, button-gated key retrieval) Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name ihoment_H5080_… Passphrase protection unknown (no WiFi passphrase crosses the BLE control link) Confidence high (auth flow wire-verified by two independent implementations)

No BLE bonding/pairing, but there is an application-layer token auth:

  1. Power the plug and scan for the ihoment_H5080_ name prefix.
  2. Connect; subscribe to notifications on …2b10.
  3. Press and hold the physical button on the plug.
  4. Send AAB1 while the button is held to read the 16-byte auth key; store it. Without the button held, the plug returns a random decoy.
  5. Authenticate the connection with 33B2 <key>, then write control commands (e.g. 3301). Unauthenticated switch commands are silently ignored.

The key is static and never rotatable, so after first retrieval it can be reused without further physical access. Note the residual risks: the key travels in cleartext during a legitimate session and cannot be rotated.

Factory reset: not established — no source covers a reset procedure. The plug is not stateless (it holds WiFi credentials, a cloud binding and the static BLE auth key), so a real reset would have something to clear; cutting mains power is not known to clear anything.

Rebinding: in place. The plug accepts one BLE client at a time; any client holding the auth key can reconnect and re-authenticate once the previous client disconnects. WiFi/cloud state is unaffected.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: All commands are 20-byte packets written to …2b11; responses echo the command id and arrive on …2b10. The plug also sends unsolicited 3301 state notifications on physical-button presses.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 00010203-…-1910 Govee H5080 Plug Service Shared 00010203 GATT family with the legacy bulbs 00010203-…-2b11 Control Write (read, write-without-response) Primary control channel; requires 33B2 auth before 3301 is honored 00010203-…-2b10 State Notify (read, notify) Command responses (id echoed) and unsolicited state notifications

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command (bytes 0–1) Purpose 33 01 <byte> Set on/off. Single-plug H5080: 0xFF on / 0xF0 off (all-ports selector) AA 01 Query on/off state AA 06 / AA 20 / AA 21 Firmware version (ASCII in payload) AA 07 Hardware version AA 00 Power metrics (H5086 only → EE19 response: seconds-on, Wh ×0.1, voltage/current/power ×0.01, power factor %) AA B1 Read the static 16-byte auth key (valid only while the physical button is pressed) 33 B2 <key> Authenticate this connection (sent immediately before every switch command)

Full frames (verified): on = 33 01 ff 00×16 cd; off = 33 01 f0 00×16 c2; state query = aa 01 00×17 ab; auth-key read = aa b1 00×17 1b.

On/off byte encoding (multi-plug units): bits 0–3 carry the on-state per port (1=port0, 2=port1, 4=port2, 15=all), bits 4–7 the port selector (0x10=port0, 0x20=port1, 0x40=port2, 0xF0=all). E.g. 0x11 = port 0 on, 0x22 = port 1 on, 0x10 = port 0 off. On the H5082 dual, port0 is the right outlet and port1 the left. The single-plug H5080 is driven with the all-ports 0xFF/0xF0 form.

docs.title: Govee H6001 Smart Bulb
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (untested by us) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Govee (Shenzhen Intellirocks Tech / iHoment) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
BLE-only smart bulb from Govee's legacy bulb family (H6001, H6005; Minger rebadges exist). Documented from static analysis of the Govee Home Android app, cross-referenced with an on-device HCI-snoop capture of a real H6001 (chvolkmann/govee_btled) and two independent community protocol write-ups. The protocol is the classic Govee 20-byte fixed packet with an XOR checksum in the final byte, on the shared 00010203-…-1910 GATT profile.

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/govee-h6001-bulb.yaml.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Model Number H6001 (sibling H6005; Minger-branded H6001s exist) Radio BLE only Advertised name ihoment_H6001_…, Minger_H6001_… or Govee_H6001_… (unconfirmed — no source records this bulb's name; the three forms are what the app's name grammar produces for a legacy sku) Advertised service 00010203-0405-0607-0809-0a0b0c0d1910 Manufacturer company ID 0xEC88 (60552) when the 88 EC bytes lead the payload; firmware with a leading version byte reports 0x88XX instead — match 88 EC at payload offset 0 or 1. Bulb family goodsType = 20

The H6001 supports Govee's local Wi-Fi API alongside BLE per the Home Assistant govee_light_local integration, though the BLE protocol here is the documented local path.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name ihoment_H6001_… Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence high (on-device GATT profile confirmed; setup flow unverified)

No pairing or bonding: the bulb advertises on power-up and accepts open BLE writes from any connected central. Power on, scan, connect, write.

Factory reset: unverified. Rapid power cycling is the near-universal reset for mains-powered smart bulbs and is what Govee's published help text points users at, but the exact toggle count was not recovered — some generations want five cycles, others three. Toggle power ~5 times (about a second in each state) and watch for a self-initiated blink followed by re-advertising as unprovisioned; if the bulb just comes back on unchanged, try three cycles.

Rebinding: nothing to rejoin. The bulb is BLE-only and holds no bond — any central may connect once the previous one disconnects.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: Every command is a 20-byte fixed-length packet: byte 0 = 0x33 (control) or 0xAA (ACK/keep-alive), byte 19 = XOR of bytes 0–18. A short write is a rejected write. While connected, a keep-alive AA 01 00..00 AB is sent roughly every 2 s.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 00010203-…-1910 Govee Legacy Bulb Service HCI-snoop-confirmed on-device profile 00010203-…-2b11 Control Write (write, write-without-response) All control commands go here 00010203-…-2b10 Control Notify (read, notify) ACKs and responses 0000fd00-…-34fb Govee OTA Service Firmware update; unverified — present in the app but no public H6001 GATT dump confirms it on-device 0000fd01-…-34fb OTA Write (write) — 0000fd02-…-34fb OTA Notify (notify) —

The 0xFFE0/0xFFE1 profile sometimes attributed to this bulb belongs to the H6101/H6104 sibling classes (see Govee H6101/H6104 TV Backlight), not to the H6001.

docs.title: Command: Power on / off
docs.text:
Offset Length Description 0 1 0x33 control prefix 1 1 0x01 power command 2 1 0x01 on / 0x00 off 3–18 16 Zero padding 19 1 XOR of bytes 0–18

Full frames: on = 33 01 01 00×16 33; off = 33 01 00 00×16 32.

docs.title: Command: Set brightness
docs.text: Offset Length Description 0 1 0x33 1 1 0x04 2 1 Brightness, raw 0–255 (the vendor app maps its 1–100 % slider onto roughly 0x14–0xFE) 3–18 16 Zero padding 19 1 XOR checksum

docs.title: Command: Set color
docs.text:
Offset Length Description 0 1 0x33 1 1 0x05 color/mode command 2 1 0x02 manual color mode 3–5 3 R, G, B 6–18 13 Zero padding 19 1 XOR checksum

White / colour temperature uses fixed warm/cold shades rather than arbitrary Kelvin: 33 05 02 FF FF FF 01 <shade R> <shade G> <shade B> 00×9 <xor> — the 0x01 flag selects the warm/cold-white LED set and the shade triple comes from the vendor's fixed table. Additional color-mode sub-commands exist in the wider family (music 0x01, scene 0x04, DIY 0x0A per the community H6127 notes).

docs.title: Command: Keep-alive
docs.text: AA 01 00×17 AB, sent every ~2 s while connected.

docs.title: Govee H6101/H6104 TV Backlight
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (app-derived, untested on hardware) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Govee (Shenzhen Intellirocks Tech / iHoment) Manufacturer Status: Active (these two models discontinued)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Early BLE-only TV backlight strips, both discontinued (the app still carries their modules). They are the odd family out: the only Govee lights on the legacy 0xFFE0/0xFFE1 GATT profile — every other family, from the H6001 bulb to current RGBIC strips, uses service 00010203-…-1910. The wire protocol itself is the shared Govee 20-byte fixed packet. Documented from static analysis of the Govee Home Android app (v7.5.30); no independent on-device capture of this pair is known, so confidence is medium overall.

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/govee-h6101-backlight.yaml.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number H6101, H6104 Radio BLE only Advertised name ihoment_H6101_… / ihoment_H6104_… (unconfirmed; Minger rebadges of contemporary gear exist) Advertised service 0000ffe0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Manufacturer company ID 0xEC88 (60552), or 0x88XX when a version byte leads the payload — match the 88 EC bytes at offset 0 or 1. App-confirmed as the parser requirement, but unverified on the air for this discontinued pair

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name ihoment_H610… Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (app-derived; no on-device capture)

No pairing or bonding: the strips advertise on power-up and accept open writes from any connected central. Power on, scan, connect, write to 0xFFE1.

Factory reset: unverified. Rapid power cycling is the near-universal reset for mains-powered smart lights and what Govee's published help text points users at, but the toggle count varies across the family. Toggle power ~5 times (about a second in each state) and watch for a self-initiated blink followed by re-advertising as unprovisioned; if the strip just comes back on unchanged, try three cycles.

Rebinding: nothing to rejoin — BLE-only, no bond held; any central may connect once the previous one disconnects.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: Same framing as the rest of the Govee family: 20-byte fixed packets, byte 0 = 0x33 (control) / 0xAA (query), byte 19 = XOR of bytes 0–18. Write ACKs echo the command id with payload byte 0 = 0 on success. A keep-alive AA 01 00..00 AB goes out every ~2 s while connected.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 0000ffe0-…-34fb Govee Legacy Backlight Service Used only by the H6101/H6104 pair (app-confirmed) 0000ffe1-…-34fb Control Write/Notify (write, write-without-response, notify) Single characteristic for commands, ACKs and group-control writes

Group control in the app writes to 0xFFE1 under 0xFFE0 for these two models specifically; other families get group writes on the standard …2b11 characteristic, with FFE0/FFE1 as fallback only when the 1910 service is absent.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Packet Purpose 33 01 01 00×16 33 Power on 33 01 00 00×16 32 Power off 33 04 <0–100> 00×16 <xor> Set brightness (percent) 33 05 02 <R> <G> <B> 00×13 <xor> Set RGB color (manual mode) 33 05 04 <id_lo> <id_hi> 00×14 <xor> Apply built-in scene (16-bit little-endian id) AA 01 00×17 AB Keep-alive / power-state query (response payload byte 0 = power) AA 04 … / AA 05 … Query brightness / current mode (payload byte 0 = sub-mode, rest = sub-mode state)

Legacy color-mode sub-modes of 33 05: 0x02 manual RGB, 0x04 scene, 0x0A DIY, 0x11 music.

docs.title: Govee RGB Lights (classic, non-segmented)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (core protocol high-confidence; per-model list app-derived) Protocol: BLE (+ Wi-Fi variants) Manufacturer: Govee (Shenzhen Intellirocks Tech / iHoment) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Govee's plain-RGB light family: bulbs (H6071/H6075, H6085/H6086/H6089, H60A0), non-segmented strips (H6110, H614B/H614E, H6159, H6160, H6178), car lights (H6114, H6118, H6194) and assorted older strips. All speak the shared Govee 20-byte BLE protocol on service 00010203-…-1910, characteristic …2b11 (write and notify on the same characteristic). "Classic" means colour is whole-device only — there are no per-segment commands; units that report segment support instead answer the extended commands in Govee RGBIC / DreamColor Lights, which is the superset spec.

Documented from static analysis of the Govee Home Android app (v7.5.30), cross-referenced with chvolkmann/govee_btled and egold555/Govee-Reverse-Engineering.

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/govee-rgb-light.yaml.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number ~30 SKUs; see device.variants in the spec for the per-model list Radio BLE; many members (H6085/H6086/H6089 bulbs, H61xx strips) are WiFi+BLE Advertised name GVH6…/GVH7… (modern), ihoment_H6…/ihoment_H7… (legacy), Govee_H…, Minger_H… — both sku ranges this spec covers, in each of the four name forms (low confidence per form) Advertised service 00010203-0405-0607-0809-0a0b0c0d1910 (presence in the ADV packet varies by model, unverified for most) Manufacturer company ID 0xEC88 (60552), or 0x88XX when a version byte leads the payload — match 88 EC at offset 0 or 1. goodsType (2 bytes BE after the company bytes) distinguishes BLE-first models (57=H6071, 67=H6075, 188=H60A0, …); WiFi-first models carry generic values there and are named by the local name

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No (a minority of units need a button-gated key exchange, below) Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name GVH6… Passphrase protection plaintext (WiFi models: SSID/passphrase travel inside the BLE provisioning frame, unbonded) Confidence high for BLE control (no pairing); provisioning flow app-derived

No BLE pairing/bonding for local control: power on, scan, connect, write to …2b11. A minority of units demand an application-layer key exchange: AA B1 reads an 8-byte per-device key (some models only return the real key while the physical button is held, as on the H5080 plug), and the connection then authenticates once with 33 B2 <key>. Most lights in this family skip auth entirely. Newer firmware may instead require the AES session handshake documented in the RGBIC spec — the device announces this through the BGC-info characteristic, so a client discovers it rather than guessing.

WiFi onboarding is optional and only needed for cloud / LAN-API use: it is a BLE provisioning write (shared frame documented in the RGBIC spec); the bulbs additionally fall back to a softAP (Govee_bulb_<sku>) hosting a TCP provisioning socket on 192.168.1.1:7200.

Factory reset: low confidence, not recovered per model. Rapid power cycling (~5 toggles, a second in each state) is the generic pattern for mains-powered Govee lights; WiFi models additionally have an in-app restore path. The confirming signal is a self-initiated blink and re-advertising as unprovisioned — if the light just comes back on unchanged, try three cycles. Clears WiFi credentials and cloud binding on WiFi models.

Rebinding: BLE control needs no rejoin. WiFi models rejoin the WLAN via the BLE provisioning write; BLE remains usable throughout.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: 20-byte fixed frames: [0]=0x33 control / 0xAA query, [1]=command, [2..18]=payload zero-padded, [19]=XOR(0..18). Write ACKs echo the command id with payload byte 0 = 0 on success. Keep-alive AA 01 every ~2 s while connected; after connecting, state is synced with AA 01 (power), AA 04 (brightness), AA 05 (mode). Unsolicited 0xEE notify frames report async events (WiFi connect status, device status report); 0x30 detail notifies cover light status, battery and music.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 00010203-…-1910 Govee Light Command Service Shared command profile across Govee lights 00010203-…-2b11 Control Write/Notify (write, write-without-response, notify; CCCD 0x2902) All control and query traffic

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Packet Purpose 33 01 01 00×16 33 / 33 01 00 00×16 32 Power on / off 33 04 <0–100> 00×16 <xor> Set brightness (percent; the H6001 legacy bulb is the exception with a raw 0–255 wire value) 33 05 02 <R> <G> <B> 00×13 <xor> Whole-device RGB (manual mode) 33 05 02 FF FF FF 01 <Wr> <Wg> <Wb> 00×9 <xor> White / color temperature via the vendor's fixed Kelvin→RGB shade table (app range 1000–10000 K; no Kelvin value crosses the link). A color+white mix form …R1 G1 B1 01 R2 G2 B2… also exists 33 05 04 <id_lo> <id_hi> 00×14 <xor> Built-in scene (16-bit LE id; seen in the app: 1=sunset, 4=movie, 5=date, 7=romantic, 8=blinking, 9=candlelight, 10=breath, 15=snow, 16=dynamic, 21=chase, 22=stream) 33 05 11 <effect> <sensitivity> … Legacy music mode: effects 16=energy, 17=rhythm, 18=spectrum, 19=scroll; the latter three add [dynamic, colorFlag, R, G, B] (colorFlag 0 = use the fixed RGB) 33 05 0A <code_lo> <code_hi> 00×14 <xor> Apply a stored DIY effect (code 0x00FE = most recently uploaded) AA 01 00×17 AB Keep-alive / power query; response byte 0 = power, byte 1 = battery/charge bits on battery models AA 04 00×17 AE Query brightness (0–100) AA 05 00×17 AF Query mode: payload byte 0 = sub-mode (0x02 color, 0x04 scene, 0x0A DIY, 0x11 music), remainder = sub-mode state

docs.title: Wi-Fi variants
docs.text: Some firmware exposes Govee's local Wi-Fi (LAN) API once enabled in the app — the toggle is a BLE-protocol frame (write type 0xE3, sub 0x01, payload 0x01) and the LAN protocol itself (UDP 4001/4002/4003, JSON) is firmware-side. See the Home Assistant govee_light_local integration.

docs.title: Govee RGBIC / DreamColor Lights (segmented)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (framing high-confidence; multi-frame layouts app-derived) Protocol: BLE (+ Wi-Fi variants) Manufacturer: Govee (Shenzhen Intellirocks Tech / iHoment) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Govee's segment-capable light family — RGBIC/DreamColor strips, neon rope, bulb string lights, TV sync lights, table/floor lamps, car lights and permanent outdoor lights (well over 80 SKUs; see device.variants in the spec). Every modern SKU uses exactly the same transport: service 00010203-…-1910, single characteristic …2b11 (write + notify, CCCD 0x2902) — there is no per-SKU UUID configuration. This spec is the superset of the classic RGB family: it adds per-segment colour, Kelvin colour temperature, timers, multi-packet transfers and the optional encrypted session layer.

Documented from static analysis of the Govee Home Android app (v7.5.30), cross-referenced with public RE (egold555/Govee-Reverse-Engineering, blog.coding.kiwi).

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/govee-rgbic-light.yaml.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number 80+ SKUs (H6102, H6125–H6127, H6143–H6147, H6171–H6176, H618A–H618F, H619A–H619E, H61xx neon, H70xx/H80xx outdoor, H605x lamps, …) Radio BLE; most current models are WiFi+BLE Advertised name GVH<sku>…, GVR…, ihoment_H…, Govee_…, Minger_…, GBK_… Advertised service 00010203-0405-0607-0809-0a0b0c0d1910 Manufacturer company ID 0xEC88 (60552), or 0x88XX when a version byte leads the payload (0x8802/0x8803/0x8843 observed 2026-08-22) — match 88 EC at offset 0 or 1. goodsType (2 bytes BE after the company bytes) identifies BLE-first models (234=H612A–F, 13=H6145–H6147/H6171, …); WiFi-first lights (H6076/H607C/H6099 seen on-air) carry generic 00 01/00 02 there — take the model from the Govee_H<sku>_<mac> local name

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No (some units need the key exchange or AES session layer, below) Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name GVH<sku>… (WiFi fallback softAP: Govee_bulb_<sku> / Govee_gateway) Passphrase protection plaintext (WiFi models: credentials travel inside the BLE provisioning frame unless the AES session layer was negotiated first) Confidence high for BLE control; provisioning frame app-derived

No BLE pairing/bonding for local control: power on, scan, connect, enable notifications on …2b11, write commands. If writes are ignored, the unit wants the application-layer auth: read AA B1 for the 8-byte per-device key (hold the physical button if the returned key looks random — some models only return the real key while it is held) and authenticate with 33 B2 <key> per connection. Many light SKUs never require it.

Newer firmware can instead demand an AES session layer, announced via the BGC-info characteristic (see below) — a client discovers it rather than guessing.

Factory reset: low confidence, not recovered per model. Mains-powered models use the generic rapid power-cycle pattern (~5 toggles); many current models also have a physical button hold (typically 5+ s until a blink). The confirming signal is a self-initiated blink and re-advertising as unprovisioned. Clears WiFi credentials and cloud binding on WiFi models.

Rebinding: BLE control needs no rejoin. WiFi models rejoin the WLAN via the BLE provisioning frame (command 0x11 multi-packet write); BLE remains usable throughout.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: Single frame (20 bytes): [0]=0x33 write / 0xAA read / 0x3A write-with-read, [1]=command, [2..18]=payload zero-padded, [19]=XOR(0..18). Write ACKs echo the command with payload byte 0 = 0 on success. Keep-alive AA 01 every ~2 s (paused during multi-packet transfers). After connecting, state sync is: write 33 09 (time sync), then read AA 23 FF (timers), AA 01 (power), AA 04 (brightness), AA 05 (mode).

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 00010203-…-1910 Govee Light Command Service The shared command profile for every modern light 00010203-…-2b11 Control Write/Notify (write, write-without-response, notify) All command, query, multi-packet and notify traffic 00010203-…-2b12 BGC Info (read), on service …1910 Encryption probe: response byte 0 = 1 → version at byte 1; byte 0 = 2 → extended form. Absent = plaintext protocol 00010203-…-1912 Govee Telink OTA Service Firmware update channel on Telink-based units (hw version 1.xx.xx). Not needed for control 00010203-…-2b12 OTA Data (write, write-without-response), on service …1912 Same UUID as BGC Info, different role — the Telink OTA channel

Beken (F000FFC0-…, hw 2.01.xx) and Freqchip (02f00000-…-fe00, hw 3.xx.xx) OTA profiles exist on other hardware generations.

docs.title: Core command map (33/AA <op>)
docs.text: Opcode Purpose 0x01 Power: payload [0]=0/1. AA 01 = keep-alive; response byte 1 carries battery band (bits 4–6), charging (bit 3), low-battery (bit 7) on battery models 0x04 Brightness 0–100 percent 0x05 Mode — see sub-modes below 0x06 Firmware version (read; ASCII) 0x07 Device info: sub 0x02=UUID, 0x03=hw, 0x04=sw, 0x07=DSP, 0x0A=MCU sw, 0x0B=MCU hw 0x09 Time sync: [year, month, day, hour, 1, tzHourOffset, tzMinOffset] — written right after connecting 0x0A (command) Legacy single timer [enable, onH, onM, offH, offM, group, repeat] 0x0B Delay-off [enable, hours, minutes]; read returns remaining time too 0x0F Segment-count setting 0x11 / 0x12 Sleep schedule / wake-up schedule 0x14 Gradual (fade) on/off, BLE-only models; WiFi+BLE models use 33 A3 01/00 0x23 Four-slot timer; read with payload 0xFF returns all four slots 0x40 IC count / device splicing 0xB1/0xB2 Auth: AA B1 reads the 8-byte key (possibly button-gated); 33 B2 <key> authenticates the connection

docs.title: 33 05 sub-modes (payload byte 0 at frame offset 2)
docs.text:
Sub-mode Purpose 0x02 Manual color [R,G,B] whole-device; white/CCT on RGB-only hardware: [FF FF FF 01 Wr Wg Wb] 0x04 Scene [id_lo, id_hi] (built-ins: 1=sunset, 4=movie, 5=date, 7=romantic, 8=blinking, 9=candlelight, 10=breath, 15=snow, 16=dynamic, 21=chase, 22=stream) 0x0A DIY apply [code_lo, code_hi]; 0x00FE = most recent upload 0x0B Legacy segment color (15 segments): [R,G,B, 0x00, maskLo, maskHi]; kelvin variant inserts [K_hi, K_lo] before the mask 0x0D Color temperature [R,G,B, K_hi, K_lo, Wr,Wg,Wb] — Kelvin big-endian uint16 0x11 Legacy music [effect, sensitivity, …] (16=energy … 19=scroll) 0x13 Music v1 [effect, sensitivity, dynamic, fixedColorFlag, R,G,B]; effects 0=rhythmPower, 1=rhythmSoft, 3=rhythm, 4=spectrum, 5=energy, 6=scroll 0x15 Main segment color (RGBIC): [0x01, R,G,B, 0×5, segMask…] (2-byte mask ≤16 segments, bit-packed beyond); kelvin form [0x01, FF,FF,FF, K_hi,K_lo, tR,tG,tB, mask…]; 3-color form [0x05, …]; per-segment brightness [0x03, b0..b14]; brightness+mask [0x02, …]; kelvin-only [0x04, K_hi, K_lo] 0x16 Music (library effects): [effectCode_lo, effectCode_hi, sensitivity] 0x2C color_multi: [0x03, K_hi, K_lo] or [0x04, R,G,B, (K_hi, K_lo)]

Ready-made command frames in the spec: power on/off, brightness 0–100, set_color as 33 05 15 01 R G B 00×4 FF FF 00×5 <xor> (all-segments mask), kelvin-only 33 05 15 04 K_hi K_lo …, scene, music v1, keep-alive and state queries.

docs.title: Multi-packet (0xA3) — per-segment writes, DIY upload, scene blobs
docs.text:
Framing V0: start frame [0xA3, 0x00, 0x00, <totalPacks+2>, <cmd>, 0x00…], data frames [0xA3, <seq 1..N>, <17 payload bytes>], end frame [0xA3, 0xFF, <last chunk>] — every frame still 20 bytes with the XOR checksum at byte 19. Newer stacks use 0xA4/0xA6 with the same layout; 0xA1/0xA2 are the older write/read pair.

  • cmd 0x40 per-segment strip write: [count] then count records — type 0x00 color [0x00, numSegs, R,G,B, segIdx…], type 0x01 brightness [0x01, numSegs, brightness, segIdx…], type 0x02 CCT on gradient strips [0x02, numSegs, K_hi, K_lo, tR,tG,tB, segIdx…]. Segment indices are 0-based, one byte each.
  • cmd 0x02/0x04 DIY upload: [modeCode, param0, param1, rgbLen=3n, R,G,B × n, effLen=2m, (param, value) × m]; param0=0xFF marks the effect block present. Activate afterwards with 33 05 0A FE 00.
  • cmd 0x01/0x02/0x07/0x0A "new scenes": the payload is a server-generated effect blob (base64 in the cloud scene record) sent verbatim — the app does not build these locally, so a clean-room client can only replay captured blobs.

docs.title: Async notify (0xEE)
docs.text: frame[0]=0xEE, frame[1]=sub-type, 17-byte payload. Sub-types: 0x11 WiFi connect status (payload 0 = connected), 0x22 IC count, 0x40 10-byte device status report, 0x54 movie-feast on/off; detail family 0x30: 1=light status, 2=energy saving, 3=battery, 4=music, 5=volume, 6=without-interrupt, 7=sleep.

docs.title: Encrypted firmware (app-derived, unverified on hardware)
docs.text: Newer firmware can demand an AES session layer. Read the BGC-info characteristic (…2b12 on service …1910); no characteristic = no encryption. Version 1: 20-byte frames [0xE7, sub, payload…, xor] on …2b11 — sub 0x01 requests a 16-byte session key, sub 0x02 confirms; steady-state traffic is AES-128-ECB per 16-byte block with an RC4 tail. Version 2: AES-128-GCM with an 8-byte IV-key per direction and a 4-byte big-endian message counter (counter‖ciphertext‖tag). Handshake keys are embedded in the app binary and, per clean-room policy, are not reproduced here — the spec documents the mechanism only. Most units in the field still accept plaintext commands.

docs.title: WiFi provisioning and LAN API
docs.text:
WiFi onboarding is a BLE write: command 0x11 as a multi-packet transfer, payload [ssidLen][ssid][pwdLen (0 if open)][pwd][runMode][tzOffsetHours] [iotVersion][tzOffsetMinutes] plus optional Matter/security extensions. Some bulbs/strings fall back to a softAP (Govee_bulb_<sku>, Govee_gateway) hosting a TCP provisioning socket on 192.168.1.1:7200 / 192.168.4.1:8200 (10-byte AA 33 header + JSON).

WiFi models can expose Govee's local Wi-Fi (LAN) API (UDP 4001/4002/4003, JSON scan/devStatus/onOff/brightness/colorwc/pt). That protocol is device-firmware-side — the app only toggles it with a BLE-protocol frame (write type 0xE3, sub 0x01, payload 0x00/0x01; read type 0xEA), gated on a per-device WiFi function-list bit and minimum firmware versions. See the Home Assistant govee_light_local integration.

docs.title: Hasbro Furby Connect (2016)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (unverified) Protocol: BLE (vendor GATT service, phone-direct) Manufacturer: Hasbro Manufacturer Status: Abandoned. The companion app is deprecated and the toy is unsupported

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Furby Connect is the 2016 Furby. It has LCD eyes, an antenna that lights up in RGB and also works as a joystick, tickle and pet sensors, an accelerometer, a speaker and motors. The Furby Connect World app controlled it directly over Bluetooth LE. The app also downloaded "DLC" packs of new songs, eye animations and reactions from Hasbro's servers and flashed them into the toy. That app is now deprecated. PyFluff's README calls the toy "now unsupported", and neither source gives a date.

Everything the app did locally can be done without it. You can play any built-in action sequence, set the antenna colour, set the mood meters, switch the eye backlight, set the Furby's name, receive sensor reports and upload DLC files. This page and the spec consolidate bluefluff, the original reverse engineering, with PyFluff, a modern Python port of it.

Hasbro content is out of scope

The spec describes how a DLC file is uploaded and what is known about the container's structure. It does not describe the content of Hasbro's own DLC files, audio or images, and it does not reproduce bluefluff's catalogue of what the Furby says for each action.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Furby Connect (2016) Chipset Nordic nRF51-series BLE SoC (inferred from its stock DFU service) in front of a GeneralPlus MCU that runs movement, speech and the eyes Radio Bluetooth LE FCC ID Not recorded Category / hierarchy other Aliases Furby Connect, Furby 2016 Companion apps Furby Connect World (Android/iOS, deprecated) Firmware seen GeneralPlus 04, Nordic 19 00 00 00 (bluefluff's unit)

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct: connect, subscribe, then write a keep-quiet byte every 3 s Advertised name Furby (exact) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (two published clients; not replayed here)

Neither source records any advertised data besides the name, and other devices may use the same name. Confirm the device after connecting by finding the Fluff service. PyFluff reports that a Furby busy playing with another Furby (F2F) can stop advertising. Touching or shaking it brings advertising back.

While a client is connected it must keep the Furby busy, or the toy chats and moves on its own. Both open clients write 00 every 3 seconds. The vendor app wrote 20 06 instead.

Factory reset: unknown. Neither source describes one, and no instruction sheet was fetched for this spec. delete_dlc_slot clears downloaded content but is not a reset.

Rebinding to a new phone: nothing to rebind. There is no bond. A client that crashes without disconnecting can leave the Furby refusing connections (bluefluff). The sources give no recovery. Removing the batteries is the obvious thing to try, but it is not documented.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none Bonding none One central at a time Unknown Confidence medium

The Furby keeps advertising while it looks asleep, including with the sleep mask on.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 00001800-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Generic Access Device Name is listed read/write. No source writes it 0000180a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Device Information Six standard strings 00001530-1212-efde-1523-785feabcd123 Nordic legacy DFU Stock buttonless DFU. Never written by either source dab91435-b5a1-e29c-b041-bcd562613bde Fluff service Everything Furby-specific

Fluff service characteristics. All share the tail -b5a1-e29c-b041-bcd562613bde:

UUID Name Use dab91383-… GeneralPlus write Commands to the main MCU (write without response) dab91382-… GeneralPlus listen Replies, events, sensor reports (notify) dab90757-… Nordic write Commands to the BLE SoC dab90756-… Nordic listen Nordic replies and upload acks (notify) dab90758-… File write Raw DLC bytes during an upload dab90755-… RSSI listen Subscribed by both clients. No data was seen dab91440-… / dab91441-… Unknown Suspected Furby-to-Furby channel. Unused

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Each command is one write of 1–20 bytes with the opcode first. There is no length byte, no checksum and no encryption. Replies come back with the same opcode-first shape.

Command Bytes Notes Keep quiet 00 Every 3 s while connected Play action 13 00 input index subindex specific 10/11/12 fix only the first 1/2/3 numbers and the Furby picks the rest Antenna colour 14 R G B 14 00 00 00 is off Set name 21 n n = 0–128. Follow it with 13 00 21 00 00 n so the Furby says the name Mood meter 23 mode type value mode 1 sets, 0 adds. Type 0 excited, 1 displeased, 2 tired, 3 fullness, 4 wellness Eye backlight cd 01 / cd 00 Replies 20 17 / 20 18 Debug screen db Cycles through seven LCD debug screens Sensor stream 20 0d / 20 0e Starts or stops continuous 21 reports Packet acks (Nordic) 09 01 00 / 09 00 00 Enable before a DLC upload Announce DLC upload 50 00 size(3, BE) slot name(12, NUL-padded) 00 00 Advanced. Exactly 20 bytes Load / activate / deactivate DLC 60 slot / 61 / 62 slot Delete DLC slot 74 slot Advanced. Official DLC cannot be downloaded again

bluefluff's opcode table lists the mood meter command as 0x24. Its own client and PyFluff both send 0x23, so the spec uses 0x23 and records the conflict.

The names are 13 first syllables combined with 10 second syllables, in a fixed order, without "Tay-Tah": 129 in total. Index 0 is Ah-Bay and index 128 is Way-Toh. The spec carries the syllables and the rule.

docs.title: Notifications (GeneralPlus listen)
docs.text: Byte 0 Meaning 20 xx Event: sequence playing/ended, out of range, sleep mask on/off, LCD on/off, … 21 + 7 bytes Sensor report covering the antenna joystick, tickle/pet sensors and accelerometer. The 7 bytes are not decoded by any source 22 + 18 bytes "I'm here" reply to 20 06. Not decoded 24 xx DLC transfer status: 02 ready, 05 OK, 06 error, 03 timeout, 01 exists fe xx GeneralPlus firmware version

docs.title: DLC upload (structure only)
docs.text:
1. Enable Nordic packet acks (09 01 00).
  2. Send the announce frame with the file size, the slot and the name.
  3. Wait for 24 02.
  4. Write the file raw to File write in 20-byte pieces, about 5 ms apart. There is no header and no sequence number. Watch for 09 xx acks. A 0a reply means the writes are too fast.
  5. Wait for 24 05. This takes 3–5 minutes.
  6. Send Load (60 slot), then Activate (61). The content plays as action input 75.

The sixth debug screen shows each slot's state: 0 empty, 1 partial, 2 downloaded, 3 active. The container format itself has not been reversed. Only two facts about it are published: the audio uses the GeneralPlus A1800 codec in 40-byte, 20 ms blocks, and the Furby does not checksum a file it receives.

docs.title: Firmware update
docs.text: The Nordic SoC carries the stock nRF5 SDK legacy DFU service. The spec declares the stack's default entry command (01 04 to the control point) as advanced and as a hypothesis. No source has sent it to a Furby, no Furby firmware image is public, and nothing says the GeneralPlus MCU can be updated over BLE.

docs.title: Hello Fairy Fairy / Curtain / Tree Lights
docs.text: Status: Research Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Avatar Controls (Hello Fairy brand) Manufacturer Status: Active (protocol closed/proprietary)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Hello Fairy is Avatar Controls' brand of app-controlled addressable light strings — fairy/string lights, curtain lights, Christmas-tree lights (some with a controllable tree-top star), wall "painting" lamps, plus solar and battery variants. Everything is driven over Bluetooth LE from the Hello Fairy phone app (com.lenzetech.hellofairy); there is no Wi-Fi, no cloud pairing, and no account. That makes these devices excellent candidates for local-only control: the BLE protocol documented here is the entire control surface, and the vendor cloud is only used for firmware images, scene artwork and telemetry.

The protocol has been fully mapped statically from the vendor app (v3.3.3) — services, framing, checksums and the core opcode set — but has not yet been verified against live hardware. The machine-readable spec is hello-fairy.yaml.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model numbers Reported by the device via GetDeviceInfo (e.g. BMSL64); dozens of SKUs Chipset Lenze ST17H66 BLE SoC (most common); ESP32 and Bluetrum variants exist Radio BLE Firmware Public Intel HEX / .bin / .fot images via the vendor OTA manifest

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
No provisioning is needed — the device advertises as soon as it is powered.

Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Advertised name contains Hello Fairy Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (static app analysis; not yet run against hardware)

Factory reset: there is no credential or network state to clear — nothing binds the device to a phone or account. If the app can't connect, the usual cause is that the device is already connected to another phone (only one BLE central at a time): remove power for a few seconds and reconnect.

Rebinding to a new controller: just connect from the new one. If the old phone keeps grabbing the link, remove the device from the vendor app (and from the OS Bluetooth list if a bond was cached) first.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
All control happens on one ISSC-style transparent-UART GATT service:

UUID Name Description 49535343-fe7d-4ae5-8fa9-9fafd205e455 Control service Primary service 49535343-8841-43f4-a8d4-ecbe34729bb3 Command write All commands written here 49535343-1e4d-4bd9-ba61-23c647249616 Response notify Enable notifications first

Command frame: [0xAA][cmd][length][payload...][sum8] where sum8 is the sum of all preceding bytes (head included) mod 256. Responses arrive on the notify characteristic in the same framing. Multi-byte payload fields are big-endian. A second framing — [0xBB][cmd][length u32 BE][payload][0xBB] — is used only for bulk DIY/GIF file transfer.

docs.title: Commands (core set)
docs.text:
Cmd Name Payload 0x00 Get device info empty — returns fw version, model string, LED count, capabilities 0x01 Get device status empty — countdown, power, active mode, mode state 0x02 Power 1 byte: 0x01 on / 0x00 off 0x03 Set light mode sub-mode byte 0x00 warm-white / 0x01 HSV / 0x02 scene / 0x03 music, then mode fields 0x04 Countdown seconds u32 BE + enable byte 0x05 Set time epoch u32 BE + tz sign + tz offset minutes u16 BE 0x06/0x07 Schedule timers read/write 4-byte records (slots 1-4 / 5-8) 0x09 Battery level empty — returns version + level (battery SKUs) 0x0A Series / segments empty 0x0B Power mode [0x00] — returns SAVING/POWER 0x0C Scene speed empty (get) / 1 byte 0-100 (set) 0x14 Current limit empty (get) / u16 BE (set, advanced) 0x30-0x33 File / DIY transfer GIF & DIY-mode upload (see spec)

The HSV sub-mode of 0x03 takes hue (0-360), saturation and value (both per-mille, 0-1000) as big-endian u16s — that is the colour control.

docs.title: Firmware updates (OTA)
docs.text:
Firmware images for every model are public, listed in plain JSON at https://hellofairyota.s3.amazonaws.com/hello_fairy_ota_pro.json and keyed by the model string the device reports. On the common ST17H66-based units the update runs over a dedicated OTA service (5833ff01-…): writing [01 02] reboots the device into an OTA identity that re-advertises at MAC+1, then partitions (CRC16/MODBUS-checked) are streamed and a final [04] reboots into the new firmware. ESP32 SKUs use the Silicon Labs Gecko OTA service UUIDs (1d14d6ee-…, GATT only, never advertised); Bluetrum (.fot) SKUs are not yet mapped. Flashing firmware is an advanced operation — only use the image matching your model string.

Privacy

The vendor app (not the device) sends telemetry — device MAC, model, firmware version, GATT UUID list — to a vendor backend at 121.40.220.76:20003, and fetches cloud-storage credentials at runtime. A local-control client needs neither.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
• Nothing is wire-verified yet: the whole map comes from static analysis of the vendor app. First live capture should cover connect → info → status → power → colour.

  • The vendor app's device-lock ("password") feature: wire mechanism unknown — if a unit stops responding after a password was set, this is the suspect.

docs.title: Hestan Cue Smart Cooking System
docs.text: Status: Spec Available Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Hestan Smart Cooking Manufacturer Status: Abandoned (app retired 2025-07-21)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Hestan Cue is a guided-cooking system with four kinds of part: a portable induction burner, pans and pots with a Bluetooth "capsule" in the handle, a later clip-on Smart Probe, and a phone app. Each piece of hardware is its own BLE peripheral, and the phone talks to each one directly. There is no hub. The vendor cloud held accounts, recipes and firmware. The control paths themselves are local.

The vendor retired the app on 2025-07-21. Its support site says the burner still works as an ordinary induction hob from its own touch controls, and that every "smart" function ended with the app. The smart functions are temperature-controlled cooking and guided recipes. This spec is the local BLE protocol the app spoke, so that the cookware can be read again and the burner driven again.

Two findings from the app shape everything below:

  • The burner closes the temperature loop, not the phone. The app routes one piece of cookware to the burner, then writes a target in °C and six controller gains. The burner takes readings from that cookware and holds the target itself. It relays each reading back to the app as an event.
  • The burner does not let an app heat until a person confirms at the burner. After the app asks for control, someone has to press the burner's power button and then its next button. This spec declares nothing that skips that step.

In scope: the Cue induction burner, and the pans, pots and Smart Probe that carry the handle service 0000fa81-8a11-4222-9610-53f79479ca03.

Out of scope: the built-in and Wi-Fi cooktops of other brands that the same app drove, the smart-oven stub, every cloud API, and firmware image transfer.

Everything here was read out of the vendor's Android app. None of it has been run against hardware, so every protocol fact is reported.

This drives a 1600 W induction burner

Cue's own guidance is that its pans are safe empty to about 400 °F (204 °C) and should never exceed 450 °F (232 °C) with food in them. The app's Control Mode allowed up to 260 °C (500 °F). The vendor also says that an unattended stainless pan at full power can pass 750 °F before the burner's cut-out trips. Stay at the burner, keep to the vendor's limits, and finish with disable_heating.

Start read-only. The cookware broadcasts its temperature in its advertisements. A thermometer client needs no connection, no write and no burner.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number Burner: 41000 (US, 110–120 V 60 Hz, up to 1600 W) and 41004–41009 (240 V 50 Hz regions), per the vendor. The app also knows a 220 V partner build and a 100 V build. Cookware: 11-inch fry pan, 5.5 qt chef's pot, 3.5 qt pot and 11-inch non-stick fry pan, in first and second generations. Smart Probe: model 417 Chipset Not identified. The Nordic legacy and Secure DFU stacks the app uses suggest Nordic nRF5-series SoCs (hypothesis) Radio BLE 4.x (the vendor asks for a Bluetooth 4.0 LE phone). The FCC test report for the probe lists 2402–2480 MHz GFSK Power Burner: mains, ungrounded plug. Pan and pot: one AAA cell in the handle end cap (a quarter-turn back switches the capsule off). Probe: one CR2450 FCC ID Smart Probe: 2AYY4-41701 (Hestan Smart Cooking Inc., granted 2021-04-14). No grant was found for the burner or the pan and pot capsules under Hestan's grantee code Bluetooth company ID 0x03F1 (1009), registered to Hestan Smart Cooking Inc.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No provisioning. There is no account, no Wi-Fi and no bond on the BLE path Method ble_direct (primary). The vendor's cloud_account flow is historical Setup AP / advertised name Local name: 8 characters of base64 encoding the device's address and type (see below). Manufacturer data is under company ID 0x03F1 Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence low (from the app alone; never replayed)

One caveat can no longer be fixed. The vendor says a factory-fresh burner and cookware needed a firmware update from the app before they would cook, or even turn on. The firmware came from the retired cloud, and the app ships no images. A unit that was never updated may be stuck. Nobody has checked what factory firmware answers over BLE.

To drive the burner:

  1. Fit a fresh AAA cell in the pan handle and screw the end cap fully home. For the probe, fit a CR2450. Plug the burner in, and centre the pan on it.
  2. Connect to the burner. Read the firmware version from 00001537-1212-efde-1523-785feabcd123 (or take it from a type-3 advertisement). The app sends no command until it has a version.
  3. Enable indications on 00001546-6209-4984-454e-f27d42fb55e3 and notifications on 00001545-6209-4984-454e-f27d42fb55e3. Read 00001545, 00001542 and 00001543.
  4. If 00001543 reports any mode but 4, turn the next-button light off and write mode 4 (disable_heating). The app always does this first.
  5. If 00001542 does not hold the pan's address (least-significant byte first), write it with route_cookware and read it back.
  6. Send ask_for_app_control (opcode 0x08 on 00001547-6209-4984-454e-f27d42fb55e3).
  7. At the burner: press the power button when event 0x6013 arrives, then the next button when 0x6014 arrives. Event 0x6015 means control is granted, and byte 1 of 00001545 then reads 3.
  8. Write set_target_temperature (or set_power_position), then read 00001543 back.
  9. To stop, turn the next-button light off, then send disable_heating.

Factory reset: none is documented. The only client-visible state is the cookware ID the burner last had routed to it, and the next client overwrites that. Unplugging the burner clears an overheat lock-out, according to the vendor. Turning the handle's end cap a quarter-turn back and then tightening it again power-cycles a pan capsule.

Rebinding: nothing binds the burner or the cookware to a phone or an account. A new client connects, routes its cookware and asks for control. If a phone bonded during an old firmware update, forget the device in that phone's Bluetooth settings.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none Bonding optional (only the app's legacy firmware-update path bonds) PIN source not applicable One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time Unknown Confidence medium (the app's product table and the vendor's support articles agree)

The app treats the Cue burner and all Cue cookware as unpaired devices. It connects, discovers services and talks with no bond. The vendor told owners not to pair Cue devices from the phone's own Bluetooth settings.

There is one exception. Before a firmware update of a burner build or a first-generation pan (both use Nordic's legacy DFU), the app asks the phone to bond. The vendor's firmware article says to accept that prompt.

Entering pairing mode: nothing to enter. The burner advertises whenever it is plugged in. The cookware advertises while its end cap is tight and its battery is live.

Unpairing: only relevant after a legacy firmware update. Forget the device in the phone's settings.

Recovery: close the vendor app if it is still installed. Turn Bluetooth off on other phones and tablets, because the vendor says they can hold an old connection. On Android, turn location services on. The vendor also documents an OS pair-then-unpair workaround for phones that never see the devices.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: All multi-byte values are little-endian. Temperatures, gains and power positions are IEEE 754 binary32 floats. The schema has no float type yet, so the spec carries a float that a command writes as a uint32 bit pattern (for example, 200.0 °C is 0x43480000, sent as 00 00 48 43).

docs.title: Advertisements (read-only path)
docs.text:
The local name is 8 base64 characters. They decode to 6 bytes: the device address, least-significant byte first. The top two bits of the last byte are replaced by the device type: 00 pan, 01 pot, 10 burner. OR 0xC0 back in to get the address. For example, q4lnRSOB is a burner at C1:23:45:67:89:AB (an invented address).

Manufacturer data sits under company ID 0x03F1. Offsets below count from the first byte after the company ID:

Offset Length Description 0 4 Unknown u32 (the app discards it) 4 1 Frame counter 5 1 Frame type: 1 first-generation cookware, 2 second-generation cookware or probe, 3 burner

Frame type 2 (second-generation cookware and Smart Probe):

Offset Length Description 6 1 Firmware major 7 1 Firmware minor 8 2 Product ID (8 fry pan, 9 chef's pot, 10 3.5 qt pot, 13 Smart Probe, 18 non-stick pan) 10 1 Battery, raw (scale unknown) 11 4 Temperature, float32, °C 15 1 Cold junction, raw 16 1 Thermocouple status: 0 ok, 1 open, 2 too high, 3 too low, 4 not initialised, 5 computation error

Frame type 1 (first-generation cookware) carries battery at 6, cold junction at 7, two floats at 8 and 12 (the app uses the one at 12), and a fault byte at 19. Frame type 3 (burner) carries firmware major and minor at 6–7 and the product ID at 8–9. The product IDs are 32 (US), 47 (220 V), 48 (220 V partner build) and 96 (100 V).

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 00001541-6209-4984-454e-f27d42fb55e3 Burner control Burner only. Every write goes here 00001542-6209-4984-454e-f27d42fb55e3 Cookware route read/write, 20 bytes: request ID, the cookware's 6-byte ID, 12 zero bytes 00001543-6209-4984-454e-f27d42fb55e3 Burner mode read/write, 36 bytes (below) 00001545-6209-4984-454e-f27d42fb55e3 Burner status read/notify, 20 bytes. The first 8 bytes are one code each 00001546-6209-4984-454e-f27d42fb55e3 Burner events indicate, 20 bytes: request ID, event code, body. Must be enabled 00001547-6209-4984-454e-f27d42fb55e3 Burner command write, 3 bytes: request ID and an opcode 0000fa81-8a11-4222-9610-53f79479ca03 Cookware handle / probe Pan, pot and (per the app) probe 0000fa83-8a11-4222-9610-53f79479ca03 Thermometer frame 20 bytes (below) 0000fa84-8a11-4222-9610-53f79479ca03 Handle info read, 6 bytes, meaning unknown. The app only length-checks it 0000fa85-8a11-4222-9610-53f79479ca03 Handle events The app enables indications and parses nothing from it 00001530-1212-efde-1523-785feabcd123 Nordic legacy DFU The stock DFU characteristics, not declared. Two vendor additions follow 00001535-1212-efde-1523-785feabcd123 Device identity read, 4 bytes: u16 device type, u16 revision 00001537-1212-efde-1523-785feabcd123 Firmware version read, u16. Needed before any 00001547 command

Every write starts with a 16-bit request ID. The app draws them from one counter for all devices, 1 to 32767, then wraps to 0.

docs.title: Burner mode (00001543)
docs.text:
Offset Length Description 0 2 Request ID 2 1 Mode: 0 manual (the user is at the burner), 1 hold temperature, 2 fixed power position, 3 off, 4 disabled 3 4 Target, float32: °C in mode 1, fraction of full power in mode 2, otherwise 0 7 24 Six float32 controller gains (mode 1), otherwise zeros 31 1 Flag, always 01 from the app 32 4 Timeout, u32 seconds

What the app sent:

Command Mode Target Gains Timeout set_target_temperature 1 37–260 °C, 1 °C steps the app's fallback set 0.008, 0.006, 0.06 (twice) 86400 Control Mode, 3600 recipe hold set_power_position 2 5 % idle, or level 1–10 = 10–100 % zeros 86400 Power tab, 9000 idle disable_heating 4 0 zeros 0

For example, 200 °C for one hour with request ID 8:

08 00 01 00 00 48 43 6f 12 03 3c a6 9b c4 3b 8f c2 75 3d
6f 12 03 3c a6 9b c4 3b 8f c2 75 3d 01 10 0e 00 00

A variant that takes caller-supplied gains is declared advanced. Wrong gains can drive a pan far past its target.

docs.title: Burner commands (00001547)
docs.text: Opcode Meaning Status in the spec 0x02 / 0x03 / 0x04 Next-button light on / off / blinking ordinary (set_next_button_light) 0x08 Ask for app control. Starts the two-touch confirmation ordinary: it only asks 0x05 Declares the app in control. Never sent by the app advanced: it may bypass the confirmation 0x06 App lockout. Never sent by the app advanced 0x07 Clear status. Never sent by the app advanced: it may clear a latched fault

docs.title: Status (00001545, bytes 0–7)
docs.text: Byte Meaning 0 App control permitted: 0 yes, 1 no 1 App control: 0 none, 1 waiting for power button, 2 waiting for next button, 3 app has control 2 Line voltage: 0 ok, 1 low, 2 high 3 Power transistor temperature: 0 normal, 1 power limited, 2 over temperature, 3 thermistor fault 4 Glass temperature: 0 normal, 1–2 reducing power, 3 over temperature, 4–5 thermistor fault 5 Power limit: 0 none, 1 one step down, 2 fixed cap, 3 intermittent, 4 no power 6 Cookware: 0 present, 1 not detected, 2 timed out 7 Cookware sensor: 0 missing, 1 ok, 2 corrupt, 3 open, 4 high, 5 low, 6 uninitialised, 7 computation error, 8–9 usable but high or low

docs.title: Events (00001546)
docs.text:
Code Meaning Body (offsets from byte 0) 0x7001 Heartbeat 4: float32 counter 0x7002 Power-stage telemetry 4: current, 8: line voltage, 12: energy (float32 each); 16: pan-detect pulses; 17: glass temperature; 18: s16 power-transistor temperature 0x7003 Burner telemetry 4: float32 position (fraction); 8: controller temperature 0x7004 Routed cookware identity 4: device type, 6: revision, 8: software version (u16 each) 0x7005 Routed cookware reading 4–7: counter, version, battery, cold junction; 8 and 12: float32 °C (12 is the one used); 16–17: sensor slots; 18–19: faults 0x6008 Status change 4: counter; 6, 8, 10: status codes (u16); 12: u32 action (bit 0 burner off, bit 1 history overflow) 0x6013–0x6016 App control: press power, press next, granted, revoked none 0x600a The user took control at the burner none. The app stops driving 0x600e / 0x600f / 0x6010 No cookware / cookware back / cookware timed out none 0x5009, 0x500f–0x5012 Over temperature, handshake needed or rejected, decrypt failures none. The app stops the cook

The full event and status-code tables are in the spec.

docs.title: Thermometer frame (0000fa83, 20 bytes)
docs.text: Offset Length Description 0 1 Frame version 1 1 Battery, raw 2 1 Frame counter 3 1 Cold junction, raw 4 4 u32 timestamp (unit unknown) 8 4 float32 °C (logged only) 12 4 float32 °C, cookware base temperature (-999.0 means no reading) 16 2 Sensor slots 18 1 Fault for the base reading 19 1 Other fault

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The burner ignores every command. The vendor app never sends a command before it has the firmware version, and whether the burner itself requires that is not established. Read 00001537 first. If the burner never took the app's first firmware update, it may not run at all, and the image source is gone.
  • A setpoint is written but nothing heats. Nobody finished the two-touch confirmation, the burner was not in mode 4 when control was requested, or the cookware is missing or not induction-compatible. It may also be in an overheat state. Let it cool, then unplug it and plug it back in.
  • The burner switches itself off mid-cook. The controls are capacitive, and the vendor says a pan slid over them, or clothing near them, can press them. Turn the burner so the controls sit to the side.
  • Direct 0000fa83 frames never arrive. The app enables indications only on 0000fa85. It takes most readings from advertisements, or relayed by the burner as event 0x7005. Use those.
  • The first three bytes of a reading look scrambled. The app's two parsers disagree on their order. The direct frame reads version, battery, counter, and the burner relay reads counter, version, battery. The temperature offsets agree.
  • Status bytes 5 and 6 look swapped. The app's built-in mock burner writes them in the opposite order to its real parser. The spec follows the parser.

docs.title: Hisense VIDAA TV (remoteapp MQTT)
docs.text: Status: Documented from community sources; not replayed against hardware by this project Protocol: WiFi (SSDP/DLNA + MQTT v3.1.1 on TCP 36669, plain/TLS/mTLS by firmware generation) Manufacturer: Hisense Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Hisense smart TVs (VIDAA OS, and the earlier Android-based sets) run an on-device MQTT broker on port 36669 that exists to serve the official RemoteNow and VIDAA mobile apps. Everything — remote keys, volume, input switching, app launching, pairing — is publish/subscribe on topics under /remoteapp/. Hisense publishes nothing about the interface; it was reverse-engineered by the community (Krazy998 2019, newAM, sehaas, and most completely warrenrees/pyvidaa, which verified the current credential algorithm byte-for-byte on a live set in August 2026).

A premise correction worth stating: no source documents a listener on port 36668. The "older remoteapp protocol" is the same broker on 36669 without TLS and with a static login, not a different port.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
• SSDP M-SEARCH for urn:schemas-upnp-org:device:MediaRenderer:1 (DLNA renderer; also try ssdp:all). This target is not Hisense-specific — keep only responses whose descriptor has manufacturer "Hisense" or a modelDescription containing vidaa_support=1 / transport_protocol=.
  • Identity: fetch http://<ip>:38400/MediaServer/rendererdevicedesc.xml (18400 on some VIDAA versions; try both). friendlyName is the display name; modelName is often literally "Renderer"; the useful identity is in modelDescription, a newline-separated key=value map: mac, macEthernet, macWifi, brand, vidaa_support, transport_protocol (the auth-generation selector).
  • UDP broadcast on port 36671 with {"request":"discover"} is a Hisense-specific alternative used by pyvidaa.
  • Keep the MAC(s): Wake-on-LAN is the only power-on path, and it must target the interface the TV actually uses (Ethernet far more reliably than WiFi).

docs.title: Authentication — three generations
docs.text:
Which one a TV speaks follows its transport_protocol value (pyvidaa's thresholds):

Generation transport_protocol Login TLS static < 3000 hisenseservice / multimqttservice, client id {MAC}$normal or any name none, self-signed, or mTLS by model legacy dynamic 3000–3289 derived per connect from unix time (suffix h*i&s%e!r^v0i1c9, plain timestamp) usually mTLS modern dynamic ≥ 3290 same with suffix h!i@s#$v%i^d&a*a and timestamp XOR 0x569814772b03a968 mTLS mandatory

The dynamic algorithm (MD5 hex, uppercase; PATTERN = 38D65DC30F45109A369A86FCE866A85B; uuid = client-chosen MAC-shaped id):

  • client_id = {uuid}$his${md5(PATTERN$uuid)[:6]}_vidaacommon_001
  • legacy: username = his${ts}, modern: username = his${ts ^ 0x569814772b03a968}
  • password = md5({ts}${md5("his" + crosssum(ts)%10 + suffix)[:6]})

Worked example (algorithm verified on hardware by pyvidaa), using an RFC 7042 documentation MAC as the client-minted uuid: uuid 00:00:5E:00:53:01, ts 1766974704 → client_id 00:00:5E:00:53:01$his$E49CB3_vidaacommon_001, username his$6239759786168176024, password C3BA44782E18ABF4892AC44D79A622D2. Only client_id depends on the uuid; username and password derive from ts alone.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Commands from an unpaired client id are ignored. Pairing puts a 4-digit PIN on the TV screen (~60 s timeout):

  1. Static generation: publish (empty) to /remoteapp/tv/ui_service/{client_id}/actions/gettvstate → PIN appears → publish {"authNum": "XXXX"} to .../actions/authenticationcode → {"result": 1} on /remoteapp/mobile/{client_id}/ui_service/data/authenticationcode.
  2. Modern generation: publish {"app_version":2,"connect_result":0,"device_type":"Mobile App"} to .../actions/vidaa_app_connect → PIN appears (or {"connect_result":1} means already paired) → authenticationcode as above → publish {"refreshtoken": ""} to /remoteapp/tv/platform_service/{client_id}/data/gettoken → read accesstoken/refreshtoken (+ durations) from /remoteapp/mobile/{client_id}/platform_service/data/tokenissuance. The accesstoken becomes the MQTT password until it expires; refresh by re-publishing gettoken with the saved refreshtoken.

docs.title: The cert-provisioning gap
docs.text: Modern firmware demands mutual TLS, and the TV has no protocol for enrolling a new client certificate. Every working client presents the cert baked into the official app (CN=VidaaAppAndroidV01, issuer CN=RemoteCA), held in a password-protected PKCS#12 keystore bundled inside the VIDAA Android app. Its location and store password are vendor key material and are not reproduced here; pyvidaa's VIDAA_PROTOCOL_ANALYSIS.md documents how a user extracts the certificate and key from their own copy of the app, and a client should ask the user for that PEM pair rather than ship it. RemoteNow-era sets that demand certs accept an older certificate-chain / private-key pair from the RemoteNow app (circulated in d3nd3/Hisense-mqtt-keyfiles). A clean-room client cannot complete pairing without redistributing Hisense's key material or having the user extract it — this, not the topic vocabulary, is the barrier to a fully open implementation.

docs.title: Command channel
docs.text:
Commands publish to /remoteapp/tv/{service}/{client_id}/actions/{action}; replies arrive on /remoteapp/mobile/{client_id}/{service}/data/{datatype} or broadcast topics. Payloads are plain JSON, or a bare string where noted.

Service Action Payload Notes remote_service sendkey bare KEY_* name the whole remote — see below ui_service gettvstate empty also the static-era pairing trigger; unanswered on some firmware ui_service sourcelist empty reply: array of {sourceid, sourcename, displayname, ...} ui_service changesource {"sourceid":"3"} ids 0 TV, 1 AV, 2 Component, 3–6 HDMI 1–4 ui_service applist empty reply: name/appId/url per app ui_service launchapp {"name":..,"urlType":37,"storeType":0,"url":"netflix"} Android-based sets: package name in url, urlType 0 ui_service changechannel {"channel_param":"<opaque>"} string learned from livetv state; no way to construct from a channel number platform_service getvolume / changevolume empty / bare 0–100 reply {"volume_type":0,"volume_value":N} ui_service vidaa_app_connect, authenticationcode JSON pairing, above platform_service data/gettoken {"refreshtoken": ..} token mint/refresh

State is broadcast on /remoteapp/mobile/broadcast/ui_service/state (retained — a fresh subscriber gets the current state immediately), keyed by statetype: fake_sleep_0 (standby), fake_sleep_1 (waking, not asleep), remote_launcher (home), remote_setting, sourceswitch (external input, carries sourceid/sourcename/displayname), livetv (channel + channel_param, EPG on older firmware). Volume broadcasts on /remoteapp/mobile/broadcast/platform_service/actions/volumechange.

The key vocabulary (sendkey payload): KEY_POWER (toggle — no power-on key; wake is WoL only), KEY_UP/DOWN/LEFT/RIGHT/OK, KEY_RETURNS (back), KEY_MENU, KEY_HOME, KEY_EXIT, KEY_VOLUMEUP/VOLUMEDOWN/MUTE, KEY_CHANNELUP/CHANNELDOWN, KEY_PLAY/PAUSE/STOP/FORWARDS, KEY_BACK (rewind, not back), KEY_0..KEY_9, KEY_RED/GREEN/YELLOW/BLUE, KEY_SUBTITLE, KEY_INFO, plus long-press and pointer-mode variants in the APK. Power-off is KEY_POWER; power-on is Wake-on-LAN only — the broker is down in standby.

KEY_POWER has no discrete pair, so the spec's stateful Power switch entity binds it as toggle, gated on the ui_service state broadcast (statetype: fake_sleep_0 = standby, do not send) (Spec Evolution P13).

docs.title: Transport gap
docs.text:
The reference app implements HTTP (GET/POST, empty body) and SOAP only. This device needs an MQTT client with TLS and client-certificate support, per-connection dynamic credential generation, the PIN pairing flow, token storage/refresh, and JSON payloads — none of which maps onto either supported transport. The spec's commands therefore declare transport: "mqtt" (schema-legal) and are not executable by the reference app today; they are written so an MQTT transport can run them unchanged once one exists.

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/hisense-vidaa.yaml

docs.title: Hörmann BiSecur Gateway
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (unverified) Protocol: LAN (UDP 4001 discovery with replies on UDP 4002, TCP 4000 hex-ASCII frames) Manufacturer: Hörmann Manufacturer Status: Unsupported — replaced by the homee hub; no sales since December 2020

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The BiSecur Gateway connects Hörmann's BiSecur radio garage and gate operators to the home network. Hörmann now sells homee in its place, and the BiSecur app and remote relay are reported gone, but the gateway still answers on the LAN. A client can find it by broadcast, log in as a gateway user, list the doors, read each door's position and status, and send the same impulse a hand transmitter sends.

Safety: an impulse moves a heavy door or gate. Send one only as a deliberate action with the door in view. A PORT_ERROR reply does not mean the door stayed put: halacs reports that on ports added by copying a hand transmitter's code, SET_STATE answers PORT_ERROR (10) although the door moves. Never resend an impulse automatically. Security: the protocol is not encrypted and sessions can be taken over from the LAN (SEC Consult, 2020), so keep the gateway on a trusted segment and never expose TCP 4000.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text: Property Value Setup required No (a gateway set up in the app keeps its users and doors) Method Discover, connect to TCP 4000 and log in Discovery UDP broadcast <Discover target="Gateway" /> to port 4001; the reply goes to UDP 4002 on the sender, so bind 4002 first. bisdk and pysecur3 send target="LogicBox" instead Credentials A gateway user name and password, sent in clear Confidence medium

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
Every frame is sent as upper-case hex ASCII:

Bytes Field 6 Source address (gateway MAC, or the client's own small id) 6 Destination address 2 Packet length, big-endian (9 + payload) 1 Tag, echoed by the reply 4 Session token (0 before login) 1 Command id (reply sets bit 7) n Payload 1 Packet checksum: length value + byte sum of tag through payload, mod 256 1 Transport checksum: sum of the ASCII codes of the hex text before it

The commands a client needs: LOGIN (0x10), JMCP (0x06) with {"CMD":"GET_GROUPS"} to list doors and ports, HM_GET_TRANSITION (0x70) to read a port's position (0–200, halve it for percent) and status bits, SET_STATE (0x33) to send a port's impulse, and LOGOUT (0x11). Errors come back as command 0x01 with a one-byte code. User, port and Wi-Fi management commands exist but are left out of the spec.

Session behaviour reported by halacs from one gateway: a token lasts about 30 minutes, then commands get PERMISSION_DENIED (12). If a connection closed without LOGOUT, the next LOGIN is preceded by one LOGOUT frame (tag 0xFF) per stale session, which a client skips. LOGOUT gets no reply. Leave about 100 ms between commands and poll HM_GET_TRANSITION no faster than every 2 s, or the gateway resets the connection. Ports added by copying a hand transmitter's code return PORT_ERROR instead of a position, and about 20 % of polls on other ports return a transient PORT_ERROR.

scripts/test_hormann_bisecur_gateway_spec.py rebuilds every example frame from the rule. The rule also reproduces all 30 frames in halacs/BiSecur's tests.

See device-specs/devices/hormann-bisecur-gateway.yaml for the full spec.

docs.title: Hot Wheels id Race Portal (FXB53)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (unverified; read-only) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Mattel Manufacturer Status: Abandoned — Hot Wheels id system discontinued 31 December 2023 (Mattel FAQ); apps delisted, cloud data deleted. Community dates the shutdown 2024-01-01.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A rechargeable piece of Hot Wheels track with an NFC reader in the floor and a BLE radio. Every Hot Wheels id car carries an NFC tag; the portal reads it when a car is placed on or rolls through, and pushes the car's identity (NFC UID, serial number, the tag's NDEF record) and a per-pass speed figure to a connected phone as GATT indications. The vendor app turned those into speeds, laps and a collection and synced them to Mattel's cloud, which is gone.

The portal still boots, advertises and reports cars with no cloud at all. This spec is read-only on purpose. A community client supplies a working unauthenticated event stream. Analysis of the recovered official 3.9.0 app adds a separate MPID session layer and signed-image OTA service, but not a safe complete command sequence to offer here. Lap counting was never a portal feature — the vendor app and the open client both derive it from successive speed indications.

The community path comes from mtxmiller/hotwheels-portal (MIT), captured against one portal on firmware 1.2.5. MPID, OTA and the richer application model were independently recovered from the official app on 2026-10-31. Keep those evidence classes separate: the official app does not contain the community client's 000c service map.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct — connect, enable indications, wait for a car Advertised Local name HWiD (service UUIDs in the advertisement not recorded) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (one open implementation)

Factory reset: unknown. No instruction sheet for FXB53 could be found on Mattel's service site or anywhere else, so buttons and LED behaviour are not documented here. The recovered application model names reset and clear-bond commands, but their outer envelope and safety sequence are unresolved. Do not send them on the community control channel or invent a button sequence.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No for the read-only event stream Security mode No link-layer pairing on the community path; the official path uses an application-layer MPID session Bonding Unknown One central at a time Unknown Confidence medium

Recovery: close any phone still connected to the portal before connecting.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
All UUIDs are af0a6ec7-XXXX-YYYY-84a0-91559fc6f0de: YYYY is the service (000a MPID session, 000b OTA, 000c community control) and XXXX is 0001 for the service, 0002 upward for its characteristics.

UUID Name Properties Description af0a6ec7-0001-000a-84a0-91559fc6f0de MPID session service Official encrypted-session path af0a6ec7-0002-000a-84a0-91559fc6f0de MPID packets write, indicate Encrypted packets in both directions af0a6ec7-0003-000a-84a0-91559fc6f0de Manufacturing token read Reading starts session setup; variable-length, per unit af0a6ec7-0004-000a-84a0-91559fc6f0de Session public key and salt write, indicate Written after parsing the token af0a6ec7-0001-000b-84a0-91559fc6f0de OTA service Vendor-confirmed signed-image path af0a6ec7-0002-000b-84a0-91559fc6f0de OTA commands write, indicate Start, block, complete and error messages af0a6ec7-0003-000b-84a0-91559fc6f0de OTA payload write_without_response Signed-image chunks af0a6ec7-0001-000c-84a0-91559fc6f0de Portal control service Community read-only path af0a6ec7-0002-000c-84a0-91559fc6f0de Firmware version read ASCII, e.g. 1.2.5 af0a6ec7-0003-000c-84a0-91559fc6f0de Car serial read, indicate ASCII digits of the car on the reader; empty when none af0a6ec7-0004-000c-84a0-91559fc6f0de Car NDEF record indicate URI record https://www.pid.mattel/<token>; empty on removal af0a6ec7-0005-000c-84a0-91559fc6f0de Car detection indicate 04 + 6-byte NFC UID; empty on removal af0a6ec7-0006-000c-84a0-91559fc6f0de Speed / timing indicate float32, little-endian, one per pass af0a6ec7-0007-000c-84a0-91559fc6f0de Control register write, read, indicate 5 bytes; byte 4 = 02 with a car present af0a6ec7-0008-000c-84a0-91559fc6f0de Command channel write, indicate No safe write sequence established

MPID setup reads the manufacturing token, parses its version, serial, compressed public key, manufacturing key id, signature and salt, then writes the phone's public key and salt on 0004. Per the app analysis, generation-one tokens are 136 bytes and other formats vary, at least 182 bytes. The community client's protocol notes separately record a 148-byte read on its unit. That observation matches neither format and is unexplained (a third format, a truncated read or a firmware difference), so a parser goes by the token's own version and lengths, never a fixed size. Later packets on 0002 are encrypted. The complete session state machine and outer official command envelope remain out of scope.

OTA requests MTU 247 in the recovered app and verifies an image signature before sending it. Commands cover new image, request/response, block, chunk, complete, error and stop. No firmware or update is offered without a hardware compatibility check.

Connect: enable indications on 0003, 0004, 0005, 0006 and 0007 of the control service, read 0002 for the firmware. Car placed: control register 00 fe 00 fe 02, then serial, then 04+UID, then the NDEF record. Car passes: one speed indication. Car removed: NDEF, UID and serial indicate empty values; control register 00 72 9b fe 00.

Speed is an IEEE 754 binary32, little-endian (b0 1c 14 3e → 0.1446), decoded by the schema's float32 field type. Its unit is unconfirmed: the community source hedges between metres per second and a passage time, while the official descriptor proves only a float named speed. The dashboard's "scale mph" is raw value × 64 with a label, not a settled conversion.

Car ID: the NDEF URI's token is 28 URL-safe base64 characters decoding to 21 bytes — 2-byte version (01 00), 4-byte model id, 4 bytes of flags, 5 bytes of extra data and the 6-byte NFC UID last. Mattel's model-id-to-name table is not reproduced. The record header is 0x91 (Message-End clear), so a further record the source calls a signature follows; its layout is unpublished.

scripts/test_hot_wheels_id_race_portal_spec.py holds the spec's float examples to struct '<f', rebuilds the example NDEF URI record from the invented car-ID token with the standard library, and checks the UUID scheme.

See device-specs/devices/hot-wheels-id-race-portal.yaml for the full machine-readable spec.
