  • Mattel: Hot Wheels id System Discontinuation FAQs
  • Mattel consumer service: FXB53 product page — no instruction sheet is hosted

docs.title: HT36 Smartwatch
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (from an open client whose author ran it against one watch; no capture here, not run against hardware by this project) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Unbranded (YC nadal SDK platform) Manufacturer Status: Active (the GloryFitPro companion app is still listed on Google Play; the vendor cloud publishes no firmware for this watch)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The HT36 is a budget colour-screen smartwatch sold without a brand for use with the GloryFitPro phone app. The app bundles a vendor SDK from YC (the SDK calls itself "nadal"), and the watch speaks that SDK's command set over an ordinary BLE GATT link. Nothing in this page needs the vendor app or its cloud: the watch answers any central that connects and subscribes. There is no pairing, no bond and no application-layer login.

Everything here comes from tcsenpai/ht36, an MIT-licensed TypeScript client written from a decompile of the vendor app. Its author ran it against an HT36: pushed notifications rendered on the wrist, the watch buzzed on command, battery and device info decoded, and a day of fitness history and a night of sleep came back. Every byte in the machine-readable spec is therefore verification: reported. This project holds no capture, FCC grant or manual for the watch and has not connected to one.

The machine-readable spec is device-specs/devices/ht36-smartwatch.yaml.

In scope: discovery by name; the command envelope; battery, device info, find/vibrate and the find-state query; set-time (documented as not working on this firmware); GPS position push; the chunked XOR-8 transfers for the notification switches, notification push and weather push; and fitness, sleep and workout history sync.

Out of scope:

  • Firmware update. The update characteristic e49a3002-f69a-11e8-8eb2-f2801f1b9fd1 is documented as do-not-write, with no bytes. Upstream warns that a stray byte there can brick the watch.
  • Watch-face upload. The .bin format is described; the transfer is not, and it does not work upstream anyway once the watch's face slots are full.
  • AGPS almanac and route uploads, the health-measurement setters and every SDK feature upstream has not mapped (call alerts, camera remote, alarms, reminders, music).
  • Other YC-SDK watches sold under other names. They may share the whole GATT table (see Identification) and still differ.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number HT36 (advertised name). The firmware calls itself AT364D followed by V and a six-digit build, and reports device type NAL-WB00 Chipset Not established. Upstream's early notes say Telink TLSR8232/8258, inferred only from the e49a…-f69a-11e8-8eb2-f2801f1b9fd1 UUID base; that base is not Telink's published OTA service (00010203-0405-0607-0809-0a0b0c0d1912). Upstream's later watch-face notes name an Actions ATS3085-class part, which fits the screen and face-slot sizes better Radio BLE Screen Colour, 240 × 296 as the watch reports it; watch faces target 240 × 240 GNSS The watch answers an ephemeris query with a GPS/BeiDou/Galileo list, which upstream reads as an on-board multi-GNSS receiver; not otherwise established Companion app GloryFitPro (Android com.yc.gloryfitpro) Bluetooth address The one unit on record sits in OUI 78:02:B7 (ShenZhen Ultra Easy Technology Co., Ltd.). One unit is not enough for a prefix matcher FCC ID None found. No FCC grant, label photo or manual naming one has turned up for the HT36

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name HT36 (exact) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (one public implementation ran it; not run here)

There is nothing to provision: no account, no Wi-Fi, no bond. Every connection runs the same steps:

  1. Wake the watch and make sure the GloryFitPro app is not connected to it.
  2. Scan for the exact local name HT36 and connect.
  3. Enable notifications on 000034f2-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb (service 000056ff-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb). The watch shows a spinner and vibrates once: it has entered its connected-to-app state.
  4. Wait about 500 ms, then write commands without response to 000034f1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb. The battery query 01 a4 aa 16 is a good first write: the reply starts 01 a4 aa 16 and carries the percentage at byte 7.

Nothing else arrives on 34f2 for about 19 seconds after subscribing; after that the watch sends a pair of frames roughly every 10 s. A client that listens for a few seconds and sees nothing has not failed.

Factory reset: not established. The vendor SDK has a factory-reset call, but its bytes were not mapped and no manual for the HT36 has been found. Upstream's advice to hold the button for 10–15 s (or let the battery run down) is for recovering a frozen watch, a forced restart, not a reset, and it is generic advice for this class of watch rather than something confirmed on the HT36.

Rebinding: nothing a client does binds the watch. The vendor app registers the watch to its cloud account, but the watch answered the open client without being unbound. To move to a new client, stop the vendor app (or turn off Bluetooth on its phone) so it cannot hold the link.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none Bonding none PIN source Not applicable One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time No (nothing is bonded) Confidence medium

Entering pairing mode: not needed. The watch is connectable whenever it is awake and no other central holds it.

The open client connects from macOS with a plain GATT connection and never pairs or bonds, and every command on this page worked that way. The vendor SDK also has application-layer pairing-request and authorization-code calls; upstream never needed them, and what they do on this watch is not known.

Unpairing: there is no bond to drop.

Recovery: close the GloryFitPro app, or turn Bluetooth off on the phone that normally talks to the watch, then scan again.

Host stacks: upstream built and ran its client on macOS (CoreBluetooth, Apple Silicon). Its README names Linux as a target but reports no Linux run. See the MTU note under Troubleshooting before sending chunked transfers from BlueZ or Android.

docs.title: Identification
docs.text:
Scan by the exact name HT36. Whether the advertisement carries a service UUID or manufacturer data is not recorded, so the spec filters on neither. After connecting, the protocol is confirmed by the 34f1/34f2 pair under 000056ff-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb and a battery reply.

The GATT table alone is not an identification. A GloryFitPro watch sold as "Stratos 2 Ultra" shows exactly the same table (Gadgetbridge issue #5541), and another GloryFit device writes a different command dialect, frames starting eb 02, to the same 34f1 characteristic (Gadgetbridge issue #5505).

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 000056ff-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Command service Write 000034f1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb (write without response); notify 000034f2-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb. Everything on this page. The service UUID is from the upstream README and its archived nRF Connect table, and matches the sibling watch 000055ff-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Secondary config channel 000035f1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb (read, write), 000035f2-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb (notify). The single byte a1 returns the system-version string. Set frames written here take effect, queries get no reply. Upstream's reading of the SDK puts this pair under 0000ffe0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb instead, so find it by characteristic UUID 0000180a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Device Information Model number 2a24, manufacturer 2a29, PnP ID 2a50. Values not recorded 0000ffd0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Unused ffd1 (write), ffd2 (notify), ffd3 (write, notify). Writes to ffd1 get no reply; upstream calls it a decoy e49a3001-f69a-11e8-8eb2-f2801f1b9fd1 Firmware update Never write e49a3002-f69a-11e8-8eb2-f2801f1b9fd1. Notify e49a3003-f69a-11e8-8eb2-f2801f1b9fd1. No bytes documented e49a25f8-f69a-11e8-8eb2-f2801f1b9fd1 Secondary data Write e49a25e0-f69a-11e8-8eb2-f2801f1b9fd1, notify e49a28e1-f69a-11e8-8eb2-f2801f1b9fd1. Purpose unknown; never written upstream

A research note in circulation spells the update characteristic as 0000e49a3002-… on the 16-bit base. That form is malformed; the characteristic is e49a3002-f69a-11e8-8eb2-f2801f1b9fd1.

docs.title: Frame envelope
docs.text:
Offset Length Field Notes 0 1 Prefix Always 01 1 1 Group Command domain (table below) 2 1 Marker aa query, ab set, ac device push or acknowledgement 3 1 Opcode 4 1 Length Payload length. Absent on bare queries (01 a4 aa 16). In a chunked transfer this byte is the section index, and fd marks the trailer 5 n Payload
  • Replies to queries echo the request's four bytes, aa marker included, then add length and payload.
  • Set commands are acknowledged in several forms: vibrate with 01 a5 ac 05 01 01, the health settings with an echo of 01 e1 ab <op>, GPS with an echo of the whole frame.
  • Frames the watch sends on its own use marker ac.
  • Single frames carry no checksum.
  • Set-time (group a3) breaks the pattern: after the group come tag-length-value entries, 01 04 <time> and 10 02 <zone>.
Group Domain a2 / a3 Time (older / current SDK form) a4 Battery and device information a5 Find/vibrate, find state, default configuration b0 Notification push (chunked) b2 Notification switches (chunked) c5 History index c6 History data (opcode 01 fitness, 04 sleep) and the spontaneous stream e0 Weather push (chunked) e1 Health-measurement settings (reference only) e3 Watch faces (out of scope) e8 Workout history e9 GNSS: position push, ephemeris query (file transfers out of scope)

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
All written to 000034f1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb; replies on 34f2. Multi-byte numbers are big-endian.

Command Bytes Reply / effect Battery 01 a4 aa 16 01 a4 aa 16 06 01 01 <level> 02 01 <x>; level in % at byte 7 (58 = 88 %). Byte 10 unknown, always 00 so far Device info 01 a4 aa aa Chunked reply; see Device info Find watch 01 a5 ab 04 01 01 Physical buzz; acknowledged 01 a5 ac 05 01 01 Find state 01 a5 aa 07 01 a5 aa 07 01 01. Upstream calls it the wear state after the SDK's name for it; whether it means "on the wrist" or "find function on" is not established Default config 01 a5 aa 01 Seven entries <index> 01 <state>; meaning unknown GPS position 01 e9 ab 02 0c <time u32> <lat i32> <lon i32> Echoed back. Latitude and longitude are degrees × 10⁷, two's complement. Nothing visible on the watch Ephemeris parameters 01 e9 aa 01 Status bytes, then ASCII f1e1G3;f1e1C3;f1e1E3 Fitness index 01 c5 aa 01 08 <start u32> <end u32> 01 c5 aa 01 01 <count> Fitness data 01 c6 aa 01 0a <start u32> <end u32> <frame u16> Chunked 01 c6 aa 01 <section> …, trailer 01 c6 aa 01 fd <xor8> Sleep history 01 c6 aa 04 08 <start u32> <end u32> Chunked, trailer ends fd fd <xor8> Workout history 01 e8 aa 01 08 <start u32> <end u32> Upstream's watch had none: 01 e8 aa 01 00 00 00 00, then fd fd Set time (SDK form) 01 a3 01 04 <time u32> 10 02 <zone> <fraction> Acknowledged, clock unchanged (upstream, twice) Set time (older form) 01 a2 ab 01 06 <time u32> <zone> <fraction> Never tried Version string a1 (raw, to 000035f1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb) On 35f2: a1 then ASCII AT364D, V and a six-digit build

Times are seconds since 1970-01-01 as the open client sends them (UTC); whether the watch stores UTC or local seconds is not established. The set-time zone byte is sign-magnitude hours: 0x80 plus the hours for UTC+0 and east, the bare hours for west. The fraction byte is minutes past the hour as hundredths of an hour (UTC+5:30 sends 85 32).

docs.title: Chunked transfers
docs.text:
Upstream calls these "subpackaged". Anything longer than one write travels as numbered chunks and a trailer, in both directions:

  1. Cut the payload into slices of at most 16 bytes.
  2. Chunk n is <head hi> <head lo> <flag hi> <flag lo> <n> <slice>. Head is 01 plus the group; flag is the marker/opcode pair.
  3. The trailer is <head> <flag> fd <xor8>, where xor8 is the XOR of every byte of every chunk frame, headers and section bytes included.
  4. Write the frames in order. The open client leaves 150 ms between them and does not wait for acknowledgements.
Head / flag Carries 01b2 / abab Notification switches 01b0 / abab Notification push 01e0 / abab Weather push 01a4 / aaaa Device-info reply 01c6 / aa01 Fitness-history reply 01c6 / aa04 Sleep-history reply 01c6 / ac01 Spontaneous stream

The watch acknowledges each chunk and answers the trailer with an fd frame, but upstream published neither layout. One section byte plus the fd marker caps a transfer at 253 chunks (about 4 KB). A 16-byte slice makes a 21-byte write; see Troubleshooting for the MTU consequence.

docs.title: Notification push
docs.text:
First write the notification switches in the same connection:

01 b2 ab ab 00 ab 01 01 01 ab 02 01 01     chunk: incoming calls on, messages on
01 b2 ab ab fd b0                          trailer

Then send the notification body (group b0) as chunks. The body is a list of <tag 2 bytes> <length 1 byte> <value> entries, text in UTF-16BE:

Tag Field Value ab01 App name UTF-16BE (the open client sends HT36) ab02 Contact UTF-16BE ab03 Content UTF-16BE; the watch truncates long text ab04 Id 1 byte, id modulo 255 ab05 Phone number UTF-16BE ab06 Source package UTF-16BE ab07 Title UTF-16BE ab08 Type 1 byte. Required: without it the watch acknowledges and shows nothing. Upstream sends 1 ab09 Vibrate 1 byte, 1 or 0. Always present ab0a Message id 4 bytes; the SDK sends it only for types 7 and 52

Worked example (app X, content Hi, type 1, vibrate):

01 b0 ab ab 00 ab 01 02 00 58 ab 03 04 00 48 00 69 ab 08 01 01
01 b0 ab ab 01 ab 09 01 01
01 b0 ab ab fd 7d

docs.title: Weather push
docs.text:
Group e0, same chunking. Body entries in this order, numbers big-endian:

Tag Field Value ab02 Unit 1 byte: 0 Celsius, 1 Fahrenheit ab04 AQI 2 bytes ab05 City UTF-16BE ab06 Current temperature 2 bytes, signed, whole degrees in the ab02 unit ab07 High 2 bytes, signed ab08 Low 2 bytes, signed ab09 Condition icon 1 byte; table not mapped (the open client sends 1) ab0a PM2.5 1 byte, µg/m³ ab0b Published time 4 bytes, Unix seconds ab0c Wind Byte 0 direction code, byte 1 force level ab0f Humidity, UV Byte 0 relative humidity %, byte 1 UV index

The spec's protocol_details.test_vectors has a full five-frame example.

docs.title: Device info
docs.text:
The reply to 01 a4 aa aa reassembles into repeated aa <tag> <len> <value> entries:

Tag Length Field 01 6 Bluetooth address 02 8 Device type, ASCII (NAL-WB00) 03 6 Hardware revision, ASCII digits 08 4 Firmware version, ASCII (V1.0) 09 4 UI version, ASCII 0d 8 Model code, ASCII 15 13 System version string, ASCII (same as the a1 answer) 16 6 Battery block 01 01 <level> 02 01 <x> 04, 05, 0f, 12 1 Unknown flags 13 4 Unknown version string 14 0 Empty

docs.title: History
docs.text:
Fitness. Ask c5/01 for the frame count, then c6/01 for a frame. Strip 01 c6 aa 01 <section> from each chunk and concatenate. The result is <frame index u16> <start time u32> followed by per-minute slots: <minute offset u16>, a function mask, then one value per present function. The mask is one to four little-endian bytes; a byte with its top bit set is followed by another, and bit n−1 set means function n is present (functions 8, 16 and 24 are the continuation bits, not functions).

Function Field Bytes 1 Steps 1 2 Calories (unit not established) 1 3 Distance, m 2 4, 5, 6, 7 Heart rate: resting, max, min, dynamic (bpm) 1 each 9 SpO2, % 1 12 Heart rate average, bpm 1 17 Blood pressure: systolic, diastolic (mmHg) 2 27 Blood sugar, raw / 10 2 others See the spec (mood, PAI, HRV, …) 2 unless listed

Upstream only requests frame 0. A 24-hour window returned 60 per-minute records, so a full sync probably walks frame indexes up to the count; that is not verified. Upstream also drops an unexplained leading 00 from some buffers.

Sleep. 7-byte records: <start u32> <minutes u16> <stage>, stage 1 deep, 2 light, 3 REM, 4 awake, 7 and 8 session markers with 0 minutes. A single night decodes cleanly upstream. Multi-night pulls come out misaligned. This project's guess, unverified: sleep and workout replies use a two-byte section index (they end fd fd, and the empty workout reply is 01 e8 aa 01 00 00 00 00), so stripping five bytes per frame leaves one stray byte per continuation frame.

docs.title: The spontaneous stream
docs.text:
About every 10 s the watch sends a 16-byte frame 01 c6 ac 01 00 0a <time u32> b8 08 <4 bytes> and a 6-byte 01 c6 ac 01 fd <xor8>. The second is the chunk trailer of the first: upstream confirmed its last byte is the XOR of the 16-byte frame in four of four complete pairs. Upstream ignores both.

This project's reading, unverified: the time field is a Unix timestamp (the capture decodes to the minute it was taken), and b8 08 is a function mask in the fitness-history encoding meaning resting, maximum, minimum and average heart rate, followed by four one-byte values (73–86 in the capture). If that holds, the watch does push live heart rate, contrary to upstream's conclusion that it does not.

docs.title: Watch faces
docs.text: Described so a file can be recognised; no upload bytes. The 24-byte little-endian header holds a dial id of 0x0005a871 (bytes 71 a8 05 00, upstream's "magic"), the data size, a CRC-32 of everything after the header, width and height (240 × 240), and two compression words. 24-byte element records follow, ending in a u16 of 0, then the pixel data: RGB565 stored byte-swapped, with a per-row run-length codec for element types 4–42, 47, 48 and 71. Upstream's codec is a port of the open editor janaboy74/wfeditormk66. The watch reported a 409,600-byte face slot and held nine faces, its maximum; the upload is refused at that point, and no delete command is known.

docs.title: Firmware update
docs.text: The watch has an update service, e49a3001-f69a-11e8-8eb2-f2801f1b9fd1. Its write characteristic e49a3002-f69a-11e8-8eb2-f2801f1b9fd1 is the one thing upstream says can brick the watch, and no client should write it. The vendor app checks the vendor's web service for a newer build; upstream replicated that check and got "no new version" for every build number it tried, so no firmware image for this watch is publicly obtainable. The update stack is not identified. See Firmware Update.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
These come from upstream's notes and code.

  • A notification push is acknowledged but nothing appears.
  • The notification switches (01 b2 …) were not written earlier in this connection.
  • The ab08 type tag is missing.
  • Set-time is acknowledged but the clock does not change. Reported upstream after two tries; the format this firmware wants is not matched. The older a2 form has not been tried. Until then the vendor app sets the clock.
  • Nothing arrives on 34f2 after subscribing. Normal for about 19 s; write a battery query for an immediate answer. If that gets nothing, the vendor app is probably holding the watch.
  • Writes to ffd1 get no reply; queries written to 35f1 get no reply. Wrong channel. Use 000034f1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb.
  • Chunk writes fail or are truncated on Linux or Android but work on macOS. A 16-byte slice makes a 21-byte write, one more than a default 23-byte ATT MTU allows. CoreBluetooth negotiates a larger MTU on its own; elsewhere, request one. Smaller slices (the SDK's file transfers use 15 bytes) may work, but that is not established for these pushes.
  • Decoded device info has no model string or battery. The open client's decoder keys its labels by the decimal numbers 15 and 16 (0x0f, 0x10). The watch sends the model string as tag 0x15 and the battery block as 0x16, as upstream's own decode log shows.
  • A multi-night sleep pull decodes to nonsense. A known upstream limit; see History for a likely cause.
  • Heart-rate or SpO2 measurement commands are acknowledged but no reading arrives. Upstream tried every trigger for 90 s worn: results are not pushed. Read the values from fitness history (and see the spontaneous stream).
  • The watch freezes after an experiment. Upstream suggests holding the button for 10–15 s or letting the battery drain; unconfirmed on this model.
  • A watch-face upload is refused as "too many faces". The slots are full, and the reorder command reorders without deleting. Out of scope here.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• The set-time frame this firmware accepts.
  • Whether notification and weather chunks sliced smaller than 16 bytes reassemble.
  • The layout of the chunk acknowledgements and of the fd answer, and whether a wrong XOR is rejected.
  • Whether the spontaneous 01 c6 ac 01 frames are live heart rate.
  • Whether sleep and workout replies use a two-byte section index.
  • How many fitness frames a window holds, and whether frame indexes past 0 return the rest.
  • Whether history timestamps are UTC or local.
  • The notification type values other than 1, and the weather icon and wind code tables.
  • What the find-state query and the seven default-config entries mean; how long the find buzz lasts and whether value 0 stops it.
  • Whether the advertisement carries a service UUID, and whether the address is public.
  • Whether the watch accepts more than one central at a time.
  • The SoC, and so the update stack.
  • What the e49a25f8 and ffd0 services are for.
  • Any factory-reset route, and what it clears.

docs.title: Philips Hue Bridge
docs.text: Status: Discovery, link-button pairing and basic per-light control verified on a BSB002 Protocol: WiFi (mDNS/SSDP + CLIP v1 REST over HTTPS/HTTP) Manufacturer: Signify / Philips Hue Manufacturer Status: Active (protocol closed; local API needs no account)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Hue Bridge is a Zigbee-to-LAN gateway: one network presence fronting a population of lights and sensors that are the owner's, not the spec's, to enumerate. Its local REST API (CLIP v1) survives entirely without the vendor cloud — pairing is a physical button press, the issued credential never expires, and every control call stays on the LAN. That makes the bridge a model citizen for cloud-free rescue even while Signify remains in business: the v1 round bridge (BSB001) is genuinely abandoned hardware, and every generation — BSB001, BSB002 square, and the 2025 Bridge Pro (BSB003) — answers the same v1 API.

Three things a client does, all executable from device-specs/devices/hue-bridge.yaml alone (scripts/test_hue_spec.py proves it with nothing but the standard library):

  1. Find the bridge — mDNS _hue._tcp, SSDP as a fallback.
  2. Pair — poll POST /api while the user presses the link button.
  3. Drive — one GET …/lights enumerates every light with its state; PUT …/lights/<id>/state writes; read back after writing.

A maintainer manually completed link-button pairing and basic per-light on/off control on 2026-11-08. This verifies the normal v1 path on the BSB002; it does not promote brightness, authenticated CLIP v2, eventstream, sensors, groups, scenes or the other bridge generations to hardware-confirmed status.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Primary discovery is mDNS _hue._tcp.local.. The TXT record carries bridgeid and modelid only — no mac, no apiversion; anything else a client wants comes from GET /api/config, which answers without authentication. Current firmware advertises SRV port 443 (HTTPS primary); 2019-era firmware advertised 80. Use the advertised port.

bridgeid is the stable identity everything keys off — credentials, TLS pins, scan dedupe — because the IP is just a DHCP lease. It is the Ethernet MAC in EUI-64 clothing: 00:17:88:aa:bb:cc becomes 001788FFFEAABBCC (splice FFFE into the middle, uppercase). The spec's Bridge Config example satisfies that rule and the test suite checks it.

SSDP is the fallback for the BSB001/BSB002: the bridge answers the generic upnp:rootdevice / urn:schemas-upnp-org:device:Basic:1 targets, which every router and printer also answers — so SSDP can find a bridge but only the description XML (or a follow-up GET /api/config) can say that is what you found. The Bridge Pro has no SSDP at all; mDNS is its only local discovery. A third path, N-UPnP (https://discovery.meethue.com/), returns registered bridges' LAN addresses from the cloud — documented in the spec's notes, deliberately not something a local-first client should lean on.

python scripts/hue_discover.py --timeout 5

docs.title: Pairing (link button)
docs.text:
No account, no cloud, no expiry — the link button is a proximity proof:

  1. POST /api with {"devicetype":"opengreeniot#hub","generateclientkey":true}.
  2. The bridge answers HTTP 200 with the v1 array envelope either way: error type 101 ("link button not pressed") means keep polling, not failure.
  3. The user presses the round button; within the ~30 s window the same POST answers [{"success":{"username":…,"clientkey":…}}].
  4. Store both keyed by bridgeid, never by IP. The username goes into every later path; the clientkey is the Entertainment DTLS PSK and is only obtainable at creation time, which is why the spec sends generateclientkey unconditionally.

commands.create_user is this flow as an executable command; payload_formats.V1Envelope is the envelope's parse contract, including the error types a client must know: 101 (keep waiting), 1 (unauthorized — the stored username is gone, re-pair), 201 (attribute not modifiable while off).

docs.title: Driving lights
docs.text:
The spec's Hue Light entity is a template stamped out per light (instances: {keyed_by: id, label_path: name}): GET /api/<username>/lights answers a JSON object keyed by light id, so enumeration and every child's full state ride one request. Poll that — never the lights one at a time; community rate-limit guidance is roughly ten light writes a second and far fewer whole-bridge reads.

Writes go to PUT /api/<username>/lights/<id>/state:

Command Body Note light_turn_on {"on":true} light_turn_off {"on":false} light_set_brightness {"on":true,"bri":200} bri is 1–254, and rides with "on":true because a bare bri to an off light answers error 201

The reply acknowledges each changed attribute ([{"success":{"/lights/1/state/on":true}}]) rather than reporting state — read the Lights endpoint back after any write. Honour state.reachable: a bulb powered off at the wall keeps its last state with reachable: false, and a live toggle drawn for it is a lie.

Colour and colour temperature are documented on the Set Light State endpoint (hue/sat, xy, ct in mireds) but deliberately not bound to entity roles yet — a set_color role needs multi-value parameters no consumer resolves today.

docs.title: HTTPS and the bridge's certificate
docs.text:
Every current bridge serves HTTPS on 443; the Bridge Pro serves only HTTPS, and Signify has announced plain-HTTP retirement on the BSB002. The certificate is a per-device leaf whose subject CN is the bridgeid in lowercase hex, issued by Signify's private bridge root CA (issuer CN root-bridge) — not a public chain, so stock TLS verification fails on every bridge by design. Verify the Hue way:

  1. Check the leaf CN equals the bridgeid you expect (from mDNS TXT or /api/config).
  2. Pin that leaf on first use, keyed by bridgeid.
  3. Treat a later pin mismatch as a different device or an interception — never re-pin silently, and never fall back to plain HTTP on a pin failure.

Plain HTTP on port 80 remains the compatibility path for the BSB001 and older BSB002 firmware; on it the username travels in the URL, which is the spec's stated reason to prefer HTTPS wherever 443 answers.

docs.title: CLIP v2, sensors, groups
docs.text: The spec documents where the modern API lives — /clip/v2/resource over HTTPS with the hue-application-key header (same credential), plus the server-sent event stream at /eventstream/clip/v2 — and stops there: v1 covers on/off/brightness on every bridge generation, v2 needs a headers: vocabulary the schema does not have yet (flagged in P12). Sensors, groups and scenes are enumerated as endpoints; the sensor entity stays declarative because the population is heterogeneous — each sensor type carries a different state shape, and a guessed mapping would be worse than none.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text: Two Zigbee-side RCEs are documented in the spec's notes — CVE-2020-6007 (patched in fw 1935144040) and the Pwn2Own Cork 2025 family CVE-2026-3555…3562 — both fixed in current firmware; keep bridges updated. The firmware check API is public and unauthenticated (firmware.meethue.com/v1/checkupdate). The API username is a long-lived LAN secret: treat it like one, and delete unused whitelist entries.

docs.title: Machine-readable spec
docs.text:
device-specs/devices/hue-bridge.yaml — discovery, identification, pairing, the executable commands: block, the instanced light entity, and a live BSB002 probe (2026-07-16) under evidence. scripts/test_hue_spec.py transcribes pairing, rendering, and child enumeration from the YAML alone and diffs them against the spec's own examples.

Home Assistant: the core Philips Hue integration consumes this local bridge API in production.

docs.title: HumsiENK Smart BMS (HS-prefixed LiFePO4 batteries)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (from one community protocol document and its working ESP32 client; no capture, not run against hardware by this project) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: HumsiENK (Shenzhen HumsiENK New Energy Technology Co., Ltd.) Manufacturer Status: Active (the "HumsiENK Smart BMS" app was updated in September 2026)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
HumsiENK sells 12 V, 24 V, 36 V and 48 V LiFePO4 batteries. The models with "Smart" or "Mini Smart" in the name have Bluetooth. Their built-in battery management system (BMS) advertises a BLE name starting HS and answers a small binary request/response protocol over GATT. A client can read voltage, current, state of charge and health, capacities, cycle count, six temperatures, 24 cell-voltage slots and a 32-bit protection and warning word. It can also switch the charge and discharge MOSFETs and the heater, clear status, and recalibrate the current sensor. There is no pairing, no password, no account and no cloud.

The machine-readable spec is device-specs/devices/humsienk-bms.yaml. Everything in it is verification: reported. The only description of the protocol is the community project humsienk-esp32, an ESP32 bridge to Home Assistant. Its protocol document says it was reverse-engineered from the vendor's Android app (1.2.0) and checked against a real 4-cell pack. Its firmware is a working client. This page restates the layouts in our own words. This project has not connected to a pack.

In scope: packs whose BMS advertises HS… and serves service 00000001-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, the protocol the upstream write-up calls "BMC".

Out of scope:

  • The "WATT" protocol. The same vendor app has a second protocol for differently-branded packs, derived from the PACE/Pylontech BMS protocol, on service 0000fff0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb. It was not researched. A pack showing 0000fff0 and no 00000001 service is not covered here.
  • Writing protection thresholds. The threshold block (command 0x58) is read-only here because no write command is documented. Guessing one on a battery's protection settings is not something to publish.
  • Firmware update. None is documented.

This interface switches a battery's power path

Command 0x51 with data 00 cuts power to everything the battery feeds, such as an inverter, UPS, trolling motor or bilge pump. 0x50 with 00 stops charging, so a pack on solar can run flat. The current-calibration commands rescale how the BMS counts current. A wrong value corrupts the state of charge and the over-current accounting the protections rely on. The vendor app shows the FET controls as ordinary buttons, and owners running a UPS have asked for a way to lock them. The spec marks FET-off, forced heating, clear status and all three calibrations advanced.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Model Number Bluetooth models: 12V 100Ah Smart, 12V 100Ah Max Smart, 12V 100Ah Max Plus Smart, 12V 314Ah Mini Smart, 12V 320Ah Smart, 12V 640Ah Smart; 24V 100 / 150 / 320 Smart; 36V 100Ah GC Smart, 48V 100Ah GC Smart / Ironguard Smart, 48V 150Ah GC Smart (from the vendor manuals). Which of them advertise HS and speak this protocol has not been checked model by model. Upstream tested one 4-cell (12 V) pack. Chipset Not established Radio BLE (always on while the pack is on; no Bluetooth button) Advertised name HS<serial>. The one published name is HS plus 16 upper-case hex digits, apparently a per-unit serial. FCC ID None printed in the manuals, and none found. The manuals list FCC among the pack certifications without an ID. Vendor app "HumsiENK Smart BMS": Android uni.UNI3890CA7, iOS App Store id6741700213 (1.2.5, 2026-09)

The 12 V manual gives the BMS behaviour a client will see in the status word. Charge is refused below 0 °C, discharge continues to −20 °C, and discharge is cut at 70 °C. An over-current or short-circuit trip stays latched until the battery cables are removed. The golf-cart packs list discharge low-temperature protection down to −25 °C, so temperatures below zero are normal readings on these packs.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name HS<serial> (matched as ^HS[0-9A-F]{16}$) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence high (working open implementation; not replayed here)

There is nothing to provision. The pack has no Bluetooth button and advertises whenever it is on. A client:

  1. Scans for a local name matching ^HS[0-9A-F]{16}$.
  2. Connects without pairing and discovers services. It requires service 00000001-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb with write characteristic 00000002-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb and notify characteristic 00000003-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, and disconnects otherwise.
  3. Optionally requests an ATT MTU of 247, as the vendor app does.
  4. Enables notifications on 00000003.
  5. Writes the handshake AA 00 00 00 00 and waits for a checksum-valid frame echoing command 0x00.
  6. Polls battery info (0x21), cell voltages (0x22) and running status (0x20), one request at a time.

HS is a weak prefix. Two letters match plenty of unrelated devices, so the spec matches the one published name shape, HS plus 16 upper-case hex digits, rather than the bare prefix the open bridge uses; a pack named any other way is missed until a second example widens it. The service UUID 00000001-… is a 16-bit custom UUID that at least one unrelated product also uses. Treat even a matching name as a candidate and confirm with the GATT table plus a valid handshake echo. The spec does not use the service UUID as a scan matcher. Whether it is advertised at all is not established, and a scan filter on it would match any device advertising 16-bit service 0x0001.

Factory reset: none is documented anywhere: not in the manuals, the protocol document or the app listing. The BMS holds no pairing or network state a client would need cleared. Command 0x53 "clear status" exists, but what it clears is not documented, and nothing suggests it restores defaults.

Rebinding to a new network: not applicable. There is no network membership and no bond. A new phone or bridge connects as soon as no other client holds the link.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none Bonding none PIN source none One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time Not applicable (nothing bonds) Confidence medium (working open implementation, unreplayed)

Entering pairing mode: not needed. The pack is always connectable while on. Owners confirm there is no Bluetooth button.

Unpairing: nothing to unpair.

Recovery: if a client cannot connect, close the vendor app on every nearby phone and stop any bridge polling the pack. Whether the BMS accepts a second central is not established. The open bridge disconnects after every poll sweep, which leaves the pack free either way.

The handshake has a fixed request and is not authentication. Anyone in range can read the pack and switch its FETs.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 00000001-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb BMC service 16-bit custom service 0x0001 on the SIG base 00000002-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Command write Request frames. The open client writes with response. 00000003-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Response notify Every response, possibly split across notifications

docs.title: Frame
docs.text:
Requests and responses share one shape:

Offset Length Field Notes 0 1 start always 0xAA 1 1 command the request's opcode. A response echoes it. 2 1 data length N 0–255. A read request has N = 0. 3 N data parameters or response payload 3+N 2 checksum (sum of bytes 1 … 2+N) & 0xFFFF, little-endian. The 0xAA is not summed.

Reassembly. A response is N + 5 bytes, and N is in the third byte of the first notification. At the default MTU a battery-info response (31 bytes) arrives in two notifications and a cell-voltage response (53 bytes) in three. Append notifications until N + 5 bytes are held, then check the checksum and the echoed command byte.

Byte order. Every multi-byte response field is little-endian. Upstream notes that assuming big-endian produced garbage. The one exception is the int16 reference current in commands 0x67 and 0x68, which is big-endian.

One request in flight. The vendor app queues its requests. Send the next command only after the previous response arrived or timed out. The open client allows 2.5 s.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Code Name Request data Response Notes 0x00 handshake none echo, data undocumented once per connection, first 0x10 manufacturer name none ASCII 0x11 pack name none ASCII 0x20 running status none running status poll 0x21 battery info none battery info poll 0x22 cell voltages none cell voltages poll 0x58 protection parameters none int16 block, partial read once 0xF5 firmware version none ASCII read once 0x50 charge FET 01 on / 00 off echo on success off is advanced 0x51 discharge FET 01 on / 00 off echo on success off is advanced 0x52 heating 01 on / 00 off echo on success on is advanced; only packs with a heater 0x53 clear status none echo on success advanced: may release a latched protection 0x66 calibrate static current none echo on success advanced 0x67 calibrate charge current int16 BE mA echo on success advanced 0x68 calibrate discharge current int16 BE mA echo on success advanced

Ready-made frames (checksums computed):

Command Bytes handshake AA 00 00 00 00 battery info AA 21 00 21 00 cell voltages AA 22 00 22 00 running status AA 20 00 20 00 firmware version AA F5 00 F5 00 charge FET on / off AA 50 01 01 52 00 / AA 50 01 00 51 00 discharge FET on / off AA 51 01 01 53 00 / AA 51 01 00 52 00 heating on / off AA 52 01 01 54 00 / AA 52 01 00 53 00 charge calibration, 10.000 A AA 67 02 27 10 A0 00

The calibration checksum is a true 16-bit sum, so its high byte is not always zero: 32.767 A is AA 67 02 7F FF E7 01, because 0x67 + 0x02 + 0x7F + 0xFF = 0x01E7. The spec's schema has no automatic 16-bit-sum field, so the two calibration commands declare their checksum as a parameter the client must compute. The 16-bit field caps the calibration current at 32.767 A. Which sign the app sends for a discharge reference is not documented.

docs.title: Battery info (0x21)
docs.text:
Offsets are into the data (add 3 for the frame offset). The data is 26 bytes on the tested pack.

Offset Length Field Type Scaling 0 4 pack voltage int32 LE mV → ÷1000 = V 4 4 current int32 LE, signed mA → ÷1000 = A; positive = charging 8 1 state of charge uint8 % 9 1 state of health uint8 % 10 4 remaining capacity int32 LE mAh 14 4 full capacity int32 LE mAh 18 2 cycle count uint16 LE count 20–23 1 each temperatures 1–4 int8 °C, no offset 24 1 ambient temperature int8 °C, no offset 25 1 MOS temperature int8 °C, no offset

The temperatures are whole degrees with no offset: no +40 and no Kelvin, unlike several other BMS families. The upstream table calls them unsigned. Its firmware reads them signed, and these packs operate well below 0 °C, so the spec declares int8. A sub-zero reading has not been observed on hardware. Which cell each probe sits on, and what an unfitted probe reads, are not documented. The pack does not report power. Compute voltage × current.

docs.title: Running status (0x20)
docs.text:
Offset Length Field Type 0 2 uptime, days uint16 LE 2 1 uptime, hours uint8 3 1 uptime, minutes uint8 4 4 status word 32 bits, LE (read unsigned) 8 4 cell-balance flags one bit per cell, order not documented 12 3 cell-disconnect flags 24 bits for 24 slots, order not documented

The status word names all 32 bits. A set bit means the condition is active or the FET is on. This is the only place a client learns why a pack has stopped charging or discharging.

Bit Mask Meaning Bit Mask Meaning 0 0x00000001 charge over-current protection 16 0x00010000 discharge over-current protection 1 0x00000002 charge over-temperature protection 17 0x00020000 discharge over-temperature protection 2 0x00000004 charge under-temperature protection 18 0x00040000 discharge under-temperature protection 3 0x00000008 cell over-voltage protection 19 0x00080000 cell under-voltage protection 4 0x00000010 pack over-voltage protection 20 0x00100000 short-circuit protection 5 0x00000020 AFE (measurement chip) error 21 0x00200000 pack under-voltage protection 6 0x00000040 charging stopped 22 0x00400000 discharging stopped 7 0x00000080 charge FET on 23 0x00800000 discharge FET on 8 0x00000100 charge over-current warning 24 0x01000000 discharge over-current warning 9 0x00000200 charge over-temperature warning 25 0x02000000 discharge over-temperature warning 10 0x00000400 charge under-temperature warning 26 0x04000000 discharge low-temperature warning 11 0x00000800 cell over-voltage warning 27 0x08000000 cell under-voltage warning 12 0x00001000 pack over-voltage warning 28 0x10000000 pack under-voltage warning 13 0x00002000 cell voltage-difference warning 29 0x20000000 MOS over-temperature warning 14 0x00004000 cell voltage difference too large 30 0x40000000 MOS over-temperature protection 15 0x00008000 heating 31 0x80000000 pre-discharge FET on

The layout is symmetric: charge-side conditions sit in the low half-word and discharge-side ones 16 bits higher. The upstream author fixed the bit order by matching the app's bit tests against the field order of the app's status model.

docs.title: Cell voltages (0x22)
docs.text: Exactly 24 slots of uint16 LE millivolts (48 data bytes), with no count byte. Slots for cells the pack does not have read 0. The number of non-zero slots is the cell count, and min, max and spread are taken over those only.

docs.title: Protection parameters (0x58)
docs.text: A run of int16 values holding the protection thresholds, not mapped upstream. Some temperature thresholds appear to be encoded as °C × 10 + 2731 (tenths of a kelvin). Field order, count and even byte order are not documented. No write command is known, and the spec declares none.

docs.title: Test vectors
docs.text:
Request frames above are the upstream worked examples, recomputed. These response frames are synthetic, built from the layout with invented values to test a decoder. None was captured.

Frame Decodes to aa 21 1a f0 33 00 00 7e eb ff ff 57 64 d8 53 01 00 a0 86 01 00 0c 00 15 15 16 15 14 17 5f 08 13.296 V, −5.250 A, SOC 87 %, SOH 100 %, 87.0 / 100.0 Ah, 12 cycles, 21/21/22/21 °C, ambient 20 °C, MOS 23 °C aa 21 1a 30 33 00 00 00 00 00 00 28 64 40 9c 00 00 a0 86 01 00 03 00 fb fb fc fb fa fd 14 09 13.104 V, 0 A, SOC 40 %, probes −5/−5/−4/−5 °C, ambient −6 °C, MOS −3 °C aa 22 30 fd 0c fc 0c fe 0c f9 0c + 40 × 00 + 72 04 3.325 / 3.324 / 3.326 / 3.321 V, 4 cells, 5 mV spread aa 20 0f 03 00 04 05 80 00 80 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 3b 01 uptime 3 d 4 h 5 min, status 0x00800080 (both FETs on, no faults)

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
These come from Play Store reviews of the vendor app and from the 12 V manual. The app-side ones do not affect a third-party client, but they explain what owners run into.

  • The vendor app cannot find the battery (Android). The app insists on the precise location permission and will not scan when location is set to "ask every time" (reported against 1.1.5–1.2.4). The pack needs no location. Also stay close: owners connect from about 1 m (1–3 ft).
  • The scan button opens a QR-code camera, or nothing happens. Early app versions (1.0.17–1.1.1) opened a QR scanner from the scan button, and some failed on camera permission. One later version drew the Bluetooth connect control invisibly in a top corner. These are app defects. The BLE protocol has no QR or pairing step.
  • The app does not show cycle count or per-cell voltages. Some app versions left them out. Both are in the protocol (0x21 offset 18 and 0x22), so a third-party client can show them.
  • A client connects and is dropped after a few seconds. One report, app 1.1.9, new pack on charge. The cause is not established. Send the handshake promptly after subscribing, as the open client does, and make sure no other phone or bridge holds the pack.
  • The pack reads 0 V and does not answer. A protection has cut the output. Per the 12 V manual, an over-current or short-circuit trip stays latched until the cables are removed. Disconnect the load, measure, and reconnect only above 10.8 V (12 V packs). When the BMS still answers, the status word (0x20) names the protection.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• The handshake response's data, and whether the BMS drops a client that skips the handshake.
  • Whether the advertisement carries the service UUID or any manufacturer data.
  • Whether more than one central can connect at once.
  • The 0x58 block's layout and byte order, and how the app writes parameters (its store listing mentions parameter setting).
  • The sign convention of the 0x67 / 0x68 reference current, and the preconditions the app enforces before calibrating.
  • What 0x53 clear-status clears.
  • The bit order of the balance and disconnect flags.
  • Sub-zero temperature encoding on real hardware, and what an unfitted probe reads.
  • Which models have a heater.
  • Behaviour on 8S, 12S and 16S packs (only 4S tested upstream), and whether any "Smart" model uses the WATT protocol instead.
  • A Play reviewer says a third-party app called KIJO reads and locks their HumsiENK pack. Which protocol that app speaks was not examined.

docs.title: Hyperice Hypervolt Plus
docs.text: Status: Research Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Hyperice, Inc. Manufacturer Status: Active (healthy; no cloud-shutdown risk — and the device needs no cloud anyway)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Hypervolt Plus (Bluetooth) is a 90 W percussion massage gun — 3 speeds, 5 heads — and the BLE-connected variant of the original Hypervolt. It was reverse engineered by decompiling the current vendor Android app (com.hyperice.app 2.7.0) in August 2026. All control is local BLE; the cloud only serves the app's account, guided-routine library and firmware metadata. One protocol covers the whole legacy family: Hypervolt, Hypervolt Plus, Hypervolt 2 / 2 Pro, and the Vyper 3 / Vyper Go rollers. (The newer Hypervolt 3, Normatec, Venom 2 and Hyperice X families in the same app use different UUIDs and are out of scope here.)

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number 54020 001-00 (per device.report listing) Chipset Unknown (Nordic-based, per sibling products' FCC filings) Radio BLE FCC ID Not confirmed; Hyperice's grantee code is 2AY3Y (sibling filings)

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Nothing to provision — no network, no account, no cloud. The gun works standalone from its physical speed button; BLE adds app control.

Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name HV+; (legacy family: HV;, HV2;, HV2P;, VY3;, VYGO;) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence low (derived from decompiled app, not replayed on hardware)

The one wrinkle is a per-connection handshake: after connecting, read the "secure" characteristic, take its last 3 bytes as a seed, and — unless the seed reads back 00 00 00 — derive a 4-byte password from the seed and the device MAC (algorithm in the YAML spec) and write it back with response. Whether fresh units answer with an all-zero seed, making the password write unnecessary, is the top open question.

Factory reset: no reset procedure was found in the app, and the pairing model (a per-connection derived password rather than a stored bond) suggests there may be nothing persistent to clear. Whether a hardware button-combo reset exists is unknown.

Rebinding to a new controller: trivial — BLE-only, no network binding. A new phone or Home Assistant instance just scans, connects and handshakes. If a unit refuses to connect, the usual cause is another client (often the vendor app) still holding the single BLE connection.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
Two custom characteristics under a 31CB45xx-3C31-4E56-8C2B-E8F479D2B056 base (containing service UUID not pinned in the app — clients should match the characteristics), plus the standard Device Information Service.

UUID Name Properties Description 31CB4570-… Secure R / W-with-response Read: session seed (last 3 bytes). Write: derived 4-byte password {01, b1, b2, b3} 31CB456C-… Level Control Notify / W-without-response Single-byte percussion level, both directions 00002A26 Firmware Revision R Standard DIS 00002A25 Serial Number R Standard DIS 00002A27 Hardware Revision R Standard DIS 00002A28 Software Revision R Standard DIS

There is no battery characteristic (the LED ring shows charge) and no OTA/DFU path on this family.

docs.title: Command: Stop / reset level
docs.text:
Request (write without response to 31CB456C-…):

Offset Length Description 0 1 0x00

docs.title: Command: Set level
docs.text:
Request (write without response to 31CB456C-…):

Offset Length Description 0 1 Level, expected 0–3 (0 = off + 3 hardware speeds; range unverified)

docs.title: Command: Session password
docs.text:
Request (write with response to 31CB4570-…):

Offset Length Description 0 1 Constant 0x01 1 3 Derived from the device MAC and the 3-byte seed via a fixed 256-entry lookup table (full algorithm in the YAML spec)

Response / state: notifications on 31CB456C-… carry the current level as one byte. Whether they echo the commanded speed or a force-sensor pressure band is unverified.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
• Advertised local name starts with HV+; (case-insensitive, note the trailing semicolon)
  • Bluetooth SIG company ID 0x08BA (2234, Hyperice) as a secondary signal
  • The vendor app connects with a 15 s timeout and 7 retries

docs.title: Cloud Dependency
docs.text:
None for control. The cloud (app.hyperice.com/v1, Okta-issued JWT, alive as of 2026-08-18) serves the account, the guided "HyperSmart" routine library, routine-completion sync, and firmware-update metadata — all phone-side features. If it disappeared tomorrow the gun would lose nothing: it runs standalone from its button and remains fully controllable over BLE.

For Home Assistant users there is therefore nothing to keep alive — no DNS redirect, no blocking rules needed. An esphome_ble_client integration is straightforward: read the seed, run the documented derivation, write the password, subscribe and write single-byte levels. The only hardware check still needed is whether the seed read returns 00 00 00 on a fresh unit, which would let the handshake be skipped entirely.

docs.title: iDeal LED Pixel Strings & Trees
docs.text: Status: In Progress Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Heaton OEM (app com.tech.idealled) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
iDeal LED is the companion app for a family of Heaton-OEM addressable RGB products — pixel strings, curtain/waterfall lights and pixel trees (firmware product codes TR21xx/TR22xx/TR23xx). Everything the app does to the lights is local BLE; the vendor cloud only feeds the app's firmware check and pattern library, so the hardware is fully usable without it.

The protocol belongs to the same OEM family as Magic Display and Shining Glasses: 16-byte [length][ASCII opcode] command blocks, AES-128-ECB encrypted with a static, publicly documented key, written to the d44bc439-…-1296xx characteristics. This branch of the family runs on a JieLi control chip and speaks string/tree opcodes (SGLS/MULT/DOOD) rather than panel opcodes. iDotMatrix is a sibling by vendor ecosystem only — its wire protocol differs.

Two open-source projects independently implement this protocol: 8none1/idealLED (which published the AES key and ships HCI captures) and koying/ha_ideal_led_ble.

Brick hazard

The 8none1/idealLED author bricked one set of lights by sending out-of-family bytes during development. Stick to the documented opcode set; do not fuzz these devices.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number TR2107R (pixel tree), TR2110R (curtain), TR2202R (25-lamp string), others Chipset JieLi (JL; OTA via jl_bt_ota SDK, .ufw firmware container) Radio BLE Pairing None — no bonding, no auth App iDeal LED (com.tech.idealled, analyzed v3.0.4)

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name BLE name prefix IDL Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (vendor-app analysis + open-source corroboration; not run in-repo)

There is no provisioning: power the device, scan, connect, write. Commands are encrypted with a fixed public key, so no key exchange is needed either.

Factory reset: there is no credential state to clear. Power-cycling drops the current connection — the actual remedy for the common failure mode, which is the device already being connected to another central (one link at a time).

Rebinding to a new network: not applicable — no network. Switching controllers is just connecting from the new one. If the old controller was a phone, also remove the device from the OS Bluetooth list so a cached bond doesn't keep reclaiming the link. After a firmware OTA the device may reappear with its BLE address minus 1 LSB — rescan rather than reusing the old address.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: Reverse engineered from the vendor app and corroborated by 8none1/idealLED (HCI captures + working client).

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Properties Description 0000fff0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Control service — Primary service; the scanner gate d44bc439-abfd-45a2-b575-925416129600 Command write Encrypted 16-byte command blocks d44bc439-abfd-45a2-b575-925416129601 Notification notify Encrypted acks (decrypt → ASCII) d44bc439-abfd-45a2-b575-925416129602 Firmware version read Version bytes at [6],[7] after decrypt d44bc439-abfd-45a2-b575-92541612960a Bulk data write Fragmented multicolor/doodle/image payloads d44bc439-abfd-45a2-b575-92541612960b Auxiliary write Bound by the app; role not pinned down 0000ae00-… / …ae01 / …ae02 JieLi OTA write/notify Standard JieLi RCSP OTA, .ufw images

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
• Advertised name prefix IDL; the dependable signal is the 0xFFF0 service UUID.
  • Manufacturer advertisement (AD type 0xFF) starts with 54 52 00 61 ("TR" + 0x0061). Byte 6 = device group id, byte 7 = vendor/device id, bytes 11–12 = lamp count (uint16 LE).
  • Some lights advertise as IDL or ISP but speak a different protocol (8none1) — confirm the service and characteristics before driving.

docs.title: Command Framing
docs.text:
Every command is a 16-byte block, AES-128-ECB encrypted (single block, no IV) with the static family key published by 8none1/idealLED:

Offset Length Description 0 1 Payload length (count of meaningful bytes that follow) 1 4–9 ASCII opcode + parameter bytes rest — Zero padding

docs.title: Commands (plaintext, before encryption)
docs.text:
Opcode Parameters Description TURN 1B (01/00) Power on/off LIGHT 1B Brightness COLO 3B G,R,B (note order) Solid color MODE / DIRECT 1B Mode / effect-mode select SPEED 1B Effect speed SGLS 1B index Built-in effect; ack SGLSOK MULT model−10, !reverse, 100, speed, colorCount, saturation Multicolor header; RGB triplets follow fragmented on the bulk channel; acks MULTCPOK/MULTOK/MULTREOK DOOD 2B index, mode, speed, R, G, B Doodle/freehand pixel; completion DOOTCP SMVE SMVEW 01 Enter DIY mode ANIM / IMAG 1B index Built-in animation/image select BEGU / PLAY / PLACP / MANCP 1B / — Upload begin / play / transfer-complete markers CONNECT 7B Post-connect handshake (payload undecoded) CHECKLINE 00/01 Link check CONFIRM 2B ASCII (G=0x47, B=0x42, R=0x52) RGB channel-order confirm LAMPQ — Lamp-count query; reply LAMPNMAX+val or LAMPNCANNOT LEDS / LEDFIRST / LEDSECOND 1B / — LED-count and daisy-chain config

Bulk payloads fragment as [chunk_len+1][frame_index][data…] — 96-byte chunks with a negotiated MTU, else 18.

Device replies arrive encrypted on the notify characteristic; after decryption they are plaintext ASCII: MULTOK, MULTCPOK, MULTREOK, SGLSOK, PLACPOK, PLAREOK, LAMPNMAX+value, LAMPNCANNOT, ERROR.

docs.title: OTA
docs.text: Standard JieLi BLE OTA (service 0xAE00, write 0xAE01, notify 0xAE02), firmware in the JieLi .ufw container. The app bundles 14 product-keyed images and checks for updates via POST https://api.e-toys.cn/api/getFirmwareInfo.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
• Exact post-connect handshake order (CONNECT / CHECKLINE / CONFIRM / LAMPQ) — needs one live capture.
  • Whether bulk-channel (…960a) fragments are raw or ECB-encrypted (the sibling Magic Display encrypts its bulk channel; the 96-byte fragment format here suggests raw).
  • SCHD schedule layout, MIC music mode, CAMERA capture, and the DEN/LEWPT opcodes.
  • Whether notify replies longer than 16 bytes are multi-block ECB.

docs.title: iDotMatrix Pixel Display
docs.text: Status: Complete Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: iDotMatrix Manufacturer Status: Unsupported

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Small RGB pixel displays in 16x16 or 32x32 sizes. Supports static images, GIF animations, text, clock, countdown, and graffiti (pixel-by-pixel drawing). Cloud content library is optional.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Display 16x16 or 32x32 RGB LED matrix Chipset Unknown Radio BLE FCC ID Not documented

docs.title: BLE Characteristics
docs.text:
UUID Name Properties 0000fa02-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Write Data Write 0000fa03-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Read Data Read

Device advertised name prefix: "IDM-"

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Variable-length bytearrays written to 0xFA02.

Command Bytes Description Screen On 05 00 07 01 01 Turn display on Screen Off 05 00 07 01 00 Turn display off Freeze 04 00 03 00 Freeze/unfreeze display Set Brightness 05 00 04 80 VV Brightness 5-100% Flip Screen 05 00 06 80 VV 0=normal, 1=rotated 180 Set Speed 05 00 03 01 VV Animation speed DIY Mode 05 00 04 01 VV 0=disable, 1=enable image mode Set Time 0B 00 01 80 YY MM DD WW HH mm SS Set clock Set Password 08 00 04 02 01 HH MM LL 6-digit password

docs.title: Framed Upload Protocol (recovered — com.tech.idotmatrix)
docs.text:
The recovered app (service 0xFEE9, characteristic d44bc439-…-925416129600) sends GIF / image / text as framed 4096-byte payload chunks, each prefixed by a 16-byte header. This is the authoritative layout, derived from the app's GIF-agreement class (see the evidence report and the device-spec YAML, which use the same layout):

Offset Length Field 0-1 2 Total packet length (uint16, big-endian) 2 1 Command type: 1=GIF, 2=Image, 3=Text/MultiColor, 6=Phrase 3 1 Sub-type: 0x00=data, 0x02=MultiColor/Phrase 4 1 Chunk flag: 0x00=first, 0x02=continuation 5-8 4 Total data length (uint32, little-endian) 9-12 4 CRC32 of the entire data payload (java.util.zip.CRC32, little-endian) 13-14 2 Time/delay (uint16, big-endian) 15 1 Speed/type byte 16+ var Payload (image / GIF / text data)

For a GIF chunk, bytes [2..3] are therefore 0x01 0x00; for an image, 0x02 0x00. Each chunk is written with acknowledgment (response=True). BLE chunking: 509 bytes when MTU is negotiated, else 18; 20 ms/chunk for GIF/image, 50 ms/chunk for text. The exact image pixel encoding (RGB565, laid out per device type) is MEDIUM confidence and needs live-capture confirmation.

The 0xFA02 byte commands in the Commands table above belong to the legacy / community python-idotmatrix protocol (service 0xFA02). A given unit speaks either the framed 0xFEE9 protocol documented here or the legacy 0xFA02 one; the device spec YAML documents both.

docs.title: Ignis Pixel LED Flow-Arts Props
docs.text: Status: In Progress Protocol: BLE (Nordic UART Service) Manufacturer: Ignis Pixel Manufacturer Status: Active (protocol unpublished; firmware distributed publicly)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Ignis Pixel makes programmable LED flow-arts props — pixel poi, staffs, fans, buugeng, hoops, clubs, juggling props, jumpropes and lamps. You upload images or timelines from the companion app (com.ignispixel, Android/iOS) or the desktop Ignis Pixel Utility, and the prop renders them as persistence-of-vision pictures while spun. The vendor's public firmware catalogue lists ~137 device types.

The vendor is in business and updates the app and firmware regularly — the catch for longevity is that the BLE protocol is unpublished and the app's content library is cloud-fed. The good news: the entire firmware catalogue and the desktop updater are public, unauthenticated HTTPS downloads, and the BLE transport, framing and message format are mapped. What is still missing is the numeric command-opcode table, so a third-party client cannot quite be built from today's notes alone — see Open Questions.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Models ~137 device types: poi, staffs, fans, hoops, clubs, jumpropes, lamps ("iPixel" line) Main MCU STM32F103 / STM32F411 BLE nRF52832 running a Nordic UART Service bridge Pixels WS2812 Sync radio nRF24L01+ 2.4 GHz (Wireless Sync "I" models only; prop-to-prop, not BLE) Companion app com.ignispixel (Android, Qt6/QML), iOS equivalent, desktop Ignis Pixel Utility

Device families (the FW_DevType the prop reports, matching the Type= attribute in the firmware catalogue): 0x04xx classic poi · 0x05xx/0x06xx gen2 props (NG poi, hoops, fans, buugeng, staff) · 0x07xx gen3 "toys" (BubblePoi/JellyPoi, sticks, clubs, cubes) · 0x0Axx jumpropes · 0x25xx–0x2Axx "I" models with the internal sync radio.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name Advertised name not yet captured; scan for the Nordic UART Service UUID Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (app analysis; no live capture yet)

Power the prop on and it advertises over BLE immediately — no account, no pairing, no app-mediated onboarding. The vendor app's own scanner looks for the Nordic UART Service UUID (6e400001-…) and nothing else.

The NUS UUID is not unique to Ignis Pixel

The Nordic UART Service is a stock platform UUID used by countless UART-bridge gadgets. After connecting, confirm you are really talking to an Ignis Pixel prop by issuing the get-id / hardware-info request and checking the reported device type — do not trust the advertisement alone.

Factory reset: there is no pairing or credential state to clear. Power-cycling drops the current connection — which is also the fix for the most common failure mode, the prop still being connected to another phone. Radio-sync settings (channel/group) live on the prop and are changed from its own system menu, not wiped over BLE. If the prop no longer boots (e.g. an interrupted firmware update), recovery is a reflash with the vendor's public desktop utility and the release .fw file for your exact model — both linked under References.

Rebinding to a new controller: just connect from the new phone — nothing binds a prop to an owner. Remove the prop from the old phone's OS Bluetooth list if it keeps grabbing the link. One caveat: a prop switched into RF slave mode (Wireless Sync) stops accepting BLE control until it is power-cycled, unless its radio mode was saved.

docs.title: Wireless Sync (prop-to-prop)
docs.text: Models with the Wireless Sync option carry an nRF24 radio that syncs whole groups of props — one prop acts as controller and the rest follow. Per the vendor FAQ there are 13 radio channels × 32 groups; props that share a channel and group stay in sync, and different channels/groups run independently. Configuration happens on the prop itself: hold the UP+DOWN buttons for 5 seconds to enter the system menu, where menu point 2 selects the channel and point 3 the group (the app exposes the same settings through its RF-configuration commands). This link is not BLE and its on-air protocol is unmapped.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 6e400001-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e Nordic UART Service Sole transport service 6e400002-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e NUS RX Phone → device, written with response 6e400003-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e NUS TX Device → phone notifications (enable via CCC 0x2902)

docs.title: Framing and message format
docs.text:
Every packet on either characteristic:

0xFF                                  start marker
payload (each 0xFF byte sent as FF FE) escaped body
0xFF 0xFF                             end marker

There is no length field — a received packet is complete when the stream ends in FF FF. The unescaped payload begins with an 8-byte header:

Offset Length Description 0 1 Message type ID 1 4 Time (uint32 LE) 5 2 CRC-16/CCITT (poly 0x1021, init 0, no final XOR; computed with this field zeroed) 7 1 Reserved (1 in phone→device requests — unconfirmed)

Phone→device requests are 13 bytes: command ID at offset 8, one uint32 LE argument at offsets 9–12, CRC filled in, then framed. Bulk data (images, firmware) rides in blocks protected by a separate CRC32. The device answers with one of ~21 typed message structs (ACK, device/hardware info, journal data, …); the hardware-info reply reports MCU/radio/IMU types, battery level, firmware version (packed uint32, e.g. 0x03002100 = v3.0.33) and the device-type ID used in the family table above.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: About 70 command names are recovered — brightness, display modes (ball, creeping line, swing, volchok, player), alarms and off-timer, system settings (run-on-start, stillness dimming, sensor), training journal, image upload/erase, RF sync configuration and group actions, and the firmware-update sequence (go-to-bootloader → erase → CRC32-protected blocks → return-to-main). The numeric opcode bytes are not yet extracted — the command entries in the machine-readable spec are symbolic placeholders. See device-specs/devices/ignis-pixel.yaml for the full vocabulary.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
• Numeric opcode map — the one blocker for a working third-party client. The constants sit next to the command-name strings in the app's native code; a scripted extraction pass is planned.
  • NUS write chunking / MTU behaviour for large image and firmware transfers.
  • Exact image-block and extended-command field layouts; whether .fw files are obfuscated.
  • On-air protocol of the nRF24 sync link.
  • Advertised BLE local name (never captured — record it on first hardware contact).

docs.text:

  • [x] Live firmware-server catalogue harvest (Update.xml, hash.md5)
  • [ ] HCI snoop of a live prop (pending)

docs.title: IKEA TRÅDFRI Gateway (E1526)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (unverified) Protocol: LAN (CoAP over DTLS-PSK, UDP 5684) Manufacturer: IKEA of Sweden Manufacturer Status: Unsupported — no new products or features since April 2024; support promised until at least June 2026

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The TRÅDFRI gateway is IKEA's first Zigbee hub. It is a small box with only an Ethernet connection, and it runs TRÅDFRI bulbs, control outlets, blinds, STARKVIND air purifiers and remotes. Its local API needs no cloud: CoAP secured with DTLS in pre-shared-key mode on UDP 5684. A client enrols once using the security code printed on the label. After that it reads, writes and observes JSON resources whose keys are numbers.

IKEA says it will release no new products or features for the gateway after April 2024, because the gateway has run out of memory. It promises the system will keep working at least until June 2026. Gateway firmware has still come out since then: 1.21.44 in July 2025, 1.21.51 in February 2026 and 1.21.57 in May 2026. The successor is the DIRIGERA hub. The new IKEA Home smart app cannot control this gateway.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes — enrol a client with the label security code Method wired, then a security-code enrolment stage Discovery mDNS _coap._udp, instance gw-<12 hex mac>, TXT version; also HomeKit _hap._tcp (model TRADFRI) Passphrase protection not_applicable — Ethernet only Confidence medium

Enrolment:

  1. Open a DTLS-PSK session to UDP 5684. Use the identity Client_identity and the 16-character security code as the key.
  2. POST {"9090":"<identity>"} to /15011/9063. Pick an identity that is unique to your install.
  3. The gateway replies 2.01 with {"9091":"<psk>","9029":"<firmware>"}.
  4. Reconnect using <identity> and <psk>. Store both, and do not store the security code.

One community write-up reports that a PSK expires after six weeks without use.

Factory reset: lift off the lid and push a pin into the pinhole on top for at least 5 seconds. This erases every paired device, group, scene and issued PSK. A lost PSK never needs a reset: enrol again instead.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
Path Method Meaning /15001 GET Device ids (array) /15001/<id> GET / PUT / observe One device /15004, /15004/<id> GET / PUT / observe Groups /15005/<group>/<scene> GET Scenes (moods) /15011/15012 GET / PUT Gateway info; 9061 opens accessory pairing /15011/9063 POST PSK enrolment /15011/9030, /15011/9031 POST Reboot, factory reset

A device write puts the state inside a one-element array keyed by the kind of device. A group write uses a flat object.

Write Payload Light on / off {"3311":[{"5850":1}]} Light brightness (0–254) {"3311":[{"5851":127}]} Colour temperature (250–454 mired) {"3311":[{"5711":370}]} Colour xy (0–65535 each) {"3311":[{"5709":30138,"5710":26909}]} Outlet on {"3312":[{"5850":1}]} Blind position (% closed) {"15015":[{"5536":50}]} Group on / scene {"5850":1} / {"5850":1,"9039":196608}

To subscribe to a resource, GET it with the CoAP Observe option set to 0. Each notification carries the whole object. Remotes and motion sensors report their battery level and nothing else useful.

Still unknown: the DTLS cipher suite the gateway picks, the rules for identities, whether a PSK really expires, and which value stops a blind.

See device-specs/devices/ikea-tradfri-gateway.yaml for the full spec.

docs.title: iLEDColor LED Matrix Panels
docs.text: Status: Minimally verified (Connect, TestPass, static and animated upload) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Shenzhen I-ledshow Technology Co., Ltd. (active)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
iLEDColor drives programmable RGB LED matrix panels, including recent LEDs 2 RAVE 4 DreamPanel v3 boards. It is a different protocol from SPOTLED, not a newer version of it. A tested iLEDColor panel exposed no SPOTLED 0xFF20 service.

The vendor account is only needed for the online material library. Local discovery, handshake and content upload work without an account. The protocol is recovered from the vendor's published led_bt_jl_ota Flutter plugin, an independent Rust implementation, and live owner-device validation on 2026-11-07.

docs.title: Hardware and identification
docs.text:
Property Value Display RGB LED matrix; geometry varies by panel Geometry source Big-endian width and height in manufacturer data Tested geometry 32×64, reported in the vendor field order; not a mounting-orientation claim Radio BLE Companion app iLEDColor (com.led.iledcolor) Reset Unknown

Discovery signals are an iledcolor- name prefix, advertised 0000af30-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, or the documented manufacturer-data patterns. AF30 is only an advertisement signal: fresh GATT discovery on the tested unit exposed A950 and AE00, not AF30. Do not send commands to AF30.

For DreamPanel v3, a horizontal serial-number display selects iLEDColor; vertical selects SPOTLED. Always confirm the GATT services rather than assuming from the retail name.

docs.title: Initial setup and pairing
docs.text:
No provisioning, vendor account or Bluetooth bond is required.

  1. Power the panel, scan and connect.
  2. Discover service 0000a950-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb and subscribe to A953.
  3. Write Connect (54 0d 00 03 00 00 64) to A951 without response. Expect 54 0d 00 04 00 00 00 65 on A953.
  4. Test the six-byte password. The factory-default request is 54 0f 00 08 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 6b. Response status 1 means accepted, 2 wrong password and 3 no password configured. The tested unit returned 3.
  5. Read panel width and height from the advertisement before rendering.

Panels can have a user-set six-byte application password. That is separate from Bluetooth pairing. If one is configured, use the owner's normal app flow rather than guessing it.

Factory reset is unknown. Uploaded-program persistence across power cycles and a clear/reset procedure were not tested. Rebinding needs no reset: disconnect the old client, rediscover and connect from the new one.

docs.title: Protocol summary
docs.text:
UUID Role Live properties 0000a950-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Display service Confirmed 0000a951-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Commands Write without response 0000a952-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Bulk program data Write without response 0000a953-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Responses and transfer progress Notify 0000ae00-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb JieLi OTA service Enumerated, not used 0000ae01-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb OTA writes Write without response 0000ae02-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb OTA responses Notify

A951 command packets are:

[54] [handle:u8] [length:u16 BE = payload + 2] [payload…] [checksum:u16 BE]

The checksum is the simple sum of every preceding packet byte. Known handles include Continue 0x00, EndStream 0x01, program item 0x03, StartStream 0x06, brightness 0x09, LedEnable 0x0a, Connect 0x0d, SetPass 0x0e and TestPass 0x0f. EndStream's fixed frame is 54 01 00 03 01 00 59; payload status 1 is success.

StartStream's 11-byte payload is [item CRC32C:4][logical transfer length:u32 BE][00 00 00], framed with handle 0x06, the normal u16 packet length and checksum. The complete worked request is 54 06 00 0d b8 a8 bd 77 00 00 48 4c 00 00 00 03 8f (17 bytes): CRC32C b8a8bd77, transfer length 0x484c = 18,508, then three reserved zero bytes and checksum 0x038f.

Bulk chunks on A952 are complete 0x54 packets with a sequence, chunk length, data and checksum. The validated static and animated uploads used 492-byte data chunks at MTU 517. Continue responses are 11 bytes with status at response byte 8. StartStream status is not a chunk count; EndStream status is at response byte 4.

docs.title: Geometry and upload evidence
docs.text:
The tested manufacturer value reported width 32 and height 64. The spec's resolution_advertisement offsets index the manufacturer value after its two-byte company ID. Width and height are big-endian u16 fields at value bytes 5-6 and 3-4; the schema reads one byte per dimension, so the spec points at the low bytes (offsets 6 and 4), which caps an advertised side at 255.

  • A 6164-byte RGB static program completed StartStream, 13 acknowledged chunks and EndStream. Its stream had a CRC32C prefix and 6188 bytes total.
  • An eight-frame, 200 ms-per-frame GIF-container upload completed four acknowledged chunks and EndStream, but restored the old program. It is transport evidence only, not proof of active animation.
  • A corrected vendor-native three-frame animation used item type 2, a 22-byte item header (geometry, type, frame count, effect, speed, dwell, border and brightness), three 6144-byte raw row-major RGB frame buffers, then three two-byte big-endian frame-rate values (00 01 = one frame per second). That is 22 + 18,432 + 6 = 18,460 item bytes. A four-byte item CRC, four-byte programme header and 16-byte partition address table wrap it into an 18,484-byte stream body. StartStream is 17 bytes and EndStream is 7, giving 18,508 logical transfer bytes before per-chunk overhead. It completed 38 chunks and stayed active; a static RGB fallback also visibly replaced the old text. This is the path clients should implement for animation.
  • These are protocol and visual confirmations for one panel, not universal geometry or maximum resource-size claims.

Brightness, playlist management, password changes, maximum resource size, old-protocol framing, factory reset and OTA remain untested. The OTA service is enumerated only; no image format, entry command or recovery path is asserted.
