docs.title: Inkbird IBS-TH1 / IBS-TH2 Thermometer-Hygrometer
docs.text: Status: Complete (parser-library-derived) Protocol: BLE (passive advertisements + optional GATT poll) Manufacturer: Inkbird Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Cheap battery BLE temperature/humidity sensors (IBS-TH1, IBS-TH2, and the IBS-P01B pool thermometer) that broadcast every reading in BLE advertisements — no connection, pairing or account needed. Documented from the Bluetooth-Devices/inkbird-ble parser library (which backs the Home Assistant core inkbird integration) and its capture-pinned test suite, plus a jadx decompile of the official Engbird app v2.3.9 (com.inkbird.engbird) which confirmed the layouts and documented the connected-mode characteristics. The older com.inkbird.inkbird package is delisted from Google Play and all public mirrors as of 2026-08.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number IBS-TH1, IBS-TH2, IBS-P01B Radio BLE 4.x (legacy advertising) Advertised name sps (IBS-TH1), tps (IBS-TH2/P01B) Advertised service 0000fff0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct (passive scan) Setup AP / advertised name sps / tps Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence high (production parser library + captured advertisements)

Factory reset: none documented, and none needed — the device holds no credentials or bindings. Removing the battery for 10+ seconds is the only meaningful reset.

Rebinding: in place, trivially. The sensor is broadcast-only; any client can listen, and switching controllers is just scanning from the new one.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: Advertisement quirk: there is no company ID — the temperature occupies the company-ID position of the manufacturer-data AD structure, so BLE stacks report the temperature itself as the "manufacturer id" and every new reading looks like a new manufacturer-data entry. Match on name + service UUID + 9-byte length, never on a company id.

docs.title: Manufacturer data (9 bytes, on-air AD content)
docs.text:
Offset Length Description 0 2 Temperature, s16 LE, /100 °C (fc 07 → 0x07FC → 20.44 °C) 2 2 Humidity, u16 LE, /100 % (c7 12 → 48.07 %) 4 1 Channel-layout selector (0-3) — picks which bytes carry internal vs external-probe values 5 2 Secondary channel value, s16 LE, /100 (external temp or humidity per the selector byte) 7 1 Battery percent (0x56 → 86) 8 1 Flags (0x06/0x08 observed), unknown

Example frame fc 07 c7 12 00 c8 3d 56 06 → 20.44 °C, 48.07 %, 86 %. Decoded humidity above 100 % marks a corrupt packet — drop it whole.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 0000fff0-...-00805f9b34fb Inkbird Sensor Service Shared with the iBBQ family — not sufficient for identification 0000fff2-...-00805f9b34fb Sensor data (read) Optional poll: temp s16 LE /100 @ bytes 0-1, humidity @ bytes 2-3, probe indicator @ byte 4; no battery byte 0000fff1-...-00805f9b34fb Config (read/write) 16-byte block: calibration offsets (x0.01) @ 1-2/3-4/5-6, logging interval u32 LE seconds @ 7-10, firmware version chars @ 11/13, CRC16-Modbus of bytes 0-13 @ 14-15 on writes 0000fff6-...-00805f9b34fb History data (notify) Streams the on-device log; 10 samples compressed to two s16 LE endpoints + linear interpolation, CRC16 trailer 0000fff8-...-00805f9b34fb History command (write) 2/1/7 = temp header/content/CRC; 4/3/8 = humidity header/content/CRC 0000fff9-...-00805f9b34fb Control (write) 0x01 clear logged history, 0x06 graceful disconnect

The app also does PhyPlus BLE OTA updates: the device reboots to an OTA-mode name PPlusOTA (SLB service 0000feb3, write 0000fed5/0000fed7, notify 0000fed8); firmware URLs come from POST https://api-inkbird.com/api/bleDevice/firmware.

Note the fff0 service is shared with the iBBQ BBQ thermometers (spec device-specs/devices/ibbq-meat-thermo.yaml), and the IBT/IBBQ-4BW line uses a completely different 0000ff00 ASCII-hex protocol (spec device-specs/devices/inkbird-bbq-thermometer.yaml). Discriminate by name + manufacturer-data length + service UUID.

docs.title: InMotion Electric Unicycles
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (untested) Protocol: BLE (two incompatible generations) Manufacturer: INMOTION Technologies (active)

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: A command that changes ride behaviour while someone is on the wheel can throw the rider. Read telemetry with the wheel stationary and nobody riding it. Do not experiment with speed limits, ride modes, calibration, lock state, lights or motor commands on a moving wheel. The spec marks consequential commands advanced and records recovery information where it is known.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The spec covers V5/V8/Glide 3/V10-era wheels and V2 models from V9 through V14. It includes discovery fingerprints, setup order, telemetry layouts, model-specific command differences and worked vectors: device-specs/devices/inmotion-euc.yaml. Nothing has been driven from this document by the project; public WheelLog code and captured frames are the principal evidence.

docs.title: Setup and pairing
docs.text: No link-layer pairing or bonding is required on either control protocol. Disconnect the previous phone before connecting another client. The vendor cloud's owner binding and any separate Bluetooth-audio pairing are unrelated to this BLE control path.

docs.title: Legacy wheels
docs.text:
Use this route when the GATT table has services 0000ffe0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb and 0000ffe5-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, but no Nordic UART service:

  1. Power the wheel, scan for its advertised name and connect.
  2. Subscribe to 0000ffe4-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb.
  3. Send the application-layer password message described in the spec. It carries six ASCII digits and two zero bytes; do not confuse this with a Bluetooth PIN or publish an owner's changed password.
  4. Poll slow information until serial, model and firmware are known, then poll fast information for telemetry. Writes to 0000ffe9-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb are split into at most 20-byte chunks.

docs.title: V2 wheels
docs.text:
Use this route when Nordic UART service 6e400001-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e is present:

  1. Connect and subscribe to 6e400003-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e.
  2. Request car type, serial and versions before issuing controls.
  3. Read settings once, then alternate real-time and total-statistics requests.
  4. Select the reply layout from the model and firmware, not merely from the product name. Early V11 firmware differs from later V2 layouts.

docs.title: Factory reset and rebinding
docs.text:
No factory reset is established for either generation. Ride settings, the legacy application password, any touch-screen access code, lock state and the vendor-cloud owner binding are separate pieces of state; no known operation clears them all.

A new phone uses the same direct BLE connection after the old one disconnects. No Wi-Fi rejoin or cloud transfer is needed for the protocol in this spec.

docs.title: Protocol summary
docs.text: Both generations use request/response messages around 250 ms apart, but their GATT endpoints, message IDs and payload layouts differ. Decode serial and model information before choosing a telemetry parser. The YAML carries the field offsets, signedness, units, scaling and per-model command tables needed to implement a client without copying WheelLog code.

docs.title: Insta360 360° and Action Cameras
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (untested) Protocol: BLE GATT, camera Wi-Fi AP with TCP 6666, or station-mode LAN Manufacturer: Insta360 / Arashi Vision Inc. (active)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The spec covers X3/X4/X5, ONE X/X2/RS/R, Ace/Ace Pro and GO 2/GO 3 families, with later model identifiers recorded where evidence is weaker. These models do not share one settled control implementation: direct BLE framing, GPS remote emulation and Wi-Fi TCP differ by generation. Read the model matrix in device-specs/devices/insta360-camera.yaml before sending anything.

The spec contains authorization and sync order, message framing, command and notification codes, station-mode provisioning, preview-stream structure and worked examples. This project has not replayed them on a camera.

docs.title: Direct BLE setup
docs.text:
1. Power the camera, scan for the model-specific advertised name and connect.
  2. Request a larger MTU and subscribe to the notify characteristics listed in the spec.
  3. Send CHECK_AUTHORIZATION with a stable client identifier. If refused, send REQUEST_AUTHORIZATION and approve the client on the camera.
  4. GO-line models also require the sync exchange before normal commands.
  5. Select the model's framing and command dialect. Do not send both candidate framings as an identification probe.

No ordinary Bluetooth bond is required; authorization is an application-layer prompt. Status-number interpretations differ between public sources, so the spec records the discrepancy instead of hiding it.

docs.title: Camera Wi-Fi and station mode
docs.text:
For the camera-hosted network, enable Wi-Fi and join its SSID. The established gateway is 192.168.42.1; connect to TCP port 6666 and send the documented sync packet, then keep the session alive. Older firmware used the fixed passphrase 88888888; other firmware can generate a per-device passphrase. Treat those as product facts, never as an owner's current credential.

Station mode is an alternative: over an authorized BLE session or the AP's TCP session, send SET_WIFI_CONNECTION_INFO with the home SSID and passphrase. The passphrase is a plain protobuf string. Wait for the result notification and the camera's new address rather than guessing it.

docs.title: Factory reset and rebinding
docs.text:
Reset effects are not established. A RESTORE_FACTORY_SETTINGS message (code 57, empty body) exists, but it is untested and may clear AP credentials, saved networks, authorized clients and settings. Use it only with owner consent and a recovery path, not as a discovery probe.

A new phone needs a fresh BLE authorization. A new router can be supplied by repeating station-mode provisioning without a factory reset.

docs.title: Privacy and security
docs.text: The camera's AP and TCP protocol are not a secure boundary by themselves. Public research on an older ONE RS also reported a root shell reachable from its AP. Keep the camera on a trusted network, do not expose its AP or TCP services to untrusted users, and keep firmware current. Photos, videos, location and Wi-Fi credentials are private; examples in the spec use invented or documentation-range identifiers.

docs.title: Instant Pot Smart Bluetooth (Smart-60)
docs.text:
Status: Spec Available (unverified; source disagreements noted) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Instant Brands (now Instant Pot Brands) Manufacturer Status: Abandoned — app reported withdrawn from both stores; vendor through Chapter 11 in June 2023

Remote start heats a sealed pot

These commands start pressure-cooking programs. Only start one with someone at the cooker, and always offer Cancel.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Instant Pot Smart (Smart-60, 6 qt) was Instant Pot's first Bluetooth cooker. Its companion app is reported withdrawn and no longer runs on current phones, but the cooker still talks BLE straight to a phone with no account: 20-byte frames start and cancel programs, and the cooker notifies its state, remaining time, pressure and temperature.

The one public reverse-engineering is OpenPot, whose README and code disagree in several places. The spec follows the code (which drove a cooker) and lists every disagreement in remaining_unknowns.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No network setup; a one-time BLE bond Method ble_direct after bonding Advertised name Instant Pot Smart Confidence medium (manual + OpenPot)

Erase pairings: hold Pressure 10 s (long beep). Bluetooth off/on: hold Adjust 10 s. No full factory reset is documented.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required Yes Security mode just_works (inferred) Bonding required One central at a time Yes Confidence medium

Entering pairing mode: while the phone pairs, hold Adjust about 3 s until a short beep, then accept the phone's prompt.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 0000dab1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Command 20-byte frames starting aa 55 5a 01 0000dab2-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Status Notify; frames start aa 55 40 02 0000daa1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Clock uint32 LE seconds since 2001-01-01 local 0000daa2/daa3 Delay timers 1/2 [hours, minutes] 0000dac1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Recipe step Undocumented beyond the README

Every frame's last byte makes all 20 bytes sum to 0 mod 256. Cancel is aa555a010e000000000000000000000000000098; Manual high pressure for 30 minutes is aa555a010c20300000001e00000000000000002c. scripts/test_instant_pot_spec.py checks these against the rule.

See device-specs/devices/instant-pot-smart-bluetooth.yaml for the full spec.

docs.title: Insteon Hub (2245-222 Hub v2 / 2242-222 Hub v1)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (unverified) Protocol: LAN (Hub v2: HTTP 25105 with Basic auth; Hub v1: raw modem bytes on TCP 9761) Manufacturer: Insteon Technologies (formerly SmartLabs) Manufacturer Status: Active. SmartLabs turned the servers off in April 2022; a buyer led by Insteon users revived the company in June 2022, and it still sells the Hub 2 in 2026.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Insteon Hub is the Ethernet gateway into an Insteon network: switches, dimmers, plug-in modules, sensors and keypads that talk over the house wiring and 915 MHz RF. Each hub contains an Insteon Modem (PLM), and both hub generations expose that modem's published command set on the LAN. A client on the LAN can drive every linked device with no cloud, no account and no app. That local path kept working through the April 2022 shutdown. The revived company's app now needs a paid subscription, but the LAN API does not.

Hub v2 wraps the modem in HTTP. You send a frame as hex in a URL and poll a 200-character hex ring buffer for the replies. Hub v1 is the same modem as a plain binary TCP stream on port 9761.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes. Wire it to Ethernet and read the label credentials (v2) Method wired; devices are then linked with Set buttons (button_pairing) Discovery None documented. Find the hub in the router's DHCP list and reserve its address Credentials Hub v2: username and password printed on the bottom label, sent as HTTP Basic auth in clear text. Hub v1: none Passphrase protection not_applicable (wired) Confidence medium

Linking a device: send start all-linking (02 64 01 00), or press the hub's Set button. Then hold the device's Set button for about 3 seconds until it beeps. An 02 53 frame in the buffer gives the new device's address.

Factory reset: unplug the hub, hold Set while plugging it back in, and release when the long beep ends. Hub v2 double-beeps, then beeps again about 30 s later; unplug and replug it once more. Hub v1 double-beeps and its light turns blue. The reset erases links, scenes and schedules.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
Hub v2 HTTP wrapper (port 25105, Basic auth):

Request Meaning GET /3?<hex frame>=I=3 Send one modem frame, e.g. /3?02621A2B3C0F11FF=I=3. A successful send zeroes the buffer GET /buffstatus.xml Read the buffer. Its BS element holds 200 hex characters of ring, then 2 hex digits for the write position GET /1?XB=M=1 Clear the buffer GET /index.htm Hub type, firmware and modem address (HTML)

Poll the buffer about twice a second. To read it, keep a cursor, take ring[cursor:position], and handle the wrap at 200. Every reply to a command arrives in the buffer, not in the HTTP response.

Modem frames (the same on both hubs):

Frame Layout Send standard 02 62 <addr:3> 0F <cmd1> <cmd2> → echo + 06 (ACK) / 15 (NAK) Send extended 02 62 <addr:3> 1F <cmd1> <cmd2> <D1..D13> <D14>, D14 = (-(cmd1+cmd2+D1+…+D13)) & 0xFF Receive standard 02 50 <from:3> <to:3> <flags> <cmd1> <cmd2> Receive extended 02 51 … plus 14 data bytes Get IM info 02 60 → 02 60 <addr:3> <cat> <subcat> <fw> 06 All-Link DB 02 69 (first) / 02 6A (next) → 06 then an 02 57 record, or 15 at the end cmd1 Meaning 11 On at level cmd2 (00–FF) 12 / 14 Fast on / fast off 13 Off 19 Status request. The device's ACK carries the level in cmd2 2E Extended get/set (settings)

Flags byte: bits 7–5 are the message type (000 direct, 001 ACK, 101 NAK, 110 all-link broadcast), bit 4 means extended, bits 3–2 are hops left and bits 1–0 are max hops.

The modem's 06 only means the hub accepted the frame. Whether the device heard it shows up in its own 02 50 ACK. Firmware 1012 on the 2245-222 has published Talos advisories (2018), and the local API is plain HTTP, so keep the hub off the internet.

See device-specs/devices/insteon-hub.yaml for the full spec. The checksum rule and the frame layouts are tested in scripts/test_insteon_hub_spec.py.

docs.title: iopool EcO / EcO Salt Pool Water Monitor
docs.text: Status: Spec Available. Everything was recovered from the vendor app and nothing has been run against a probe yet. The pH and temperature scalings are inferences. Protocol: BLE (readings are broadcast in advertisements; a small GATT service switches modes, sets the clock and beeps) Manufacturer: iopool SA (Belgium) Manufacturer Status: Active. The vendor cloud holds history, advice and calibration, but a local client needs none of it to read the probe.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The EcO is a sealed probe that floats in a pool or spa and measures pH, ORP (the app calls it "disinfection potential"), water temperature and conductivity. It also reports its battery level. It is sold in iopool's EcO Start pack, and there is a salt-water version, the EcO Salt. The only radio is Bluetooth LE. An optional iopool Connect box relays readings to Wi-Fi when no phone is near the pool.

Reading the probe needs no connection. It broadcasts its latest measurement in its advertisements (manufacturer data under company ID 0x074C), so any BLE listener in range can decode pH, ORP, temperature, conductivity and battery with no account, no pairing and no cloud. Connecting is only needed to switch the probe between monitoring and winter standby, to set its clock, to start a burst of live measurements, or to make it beep so you can find it.

The spec is device-specs/devices/iopool-eco.yaml. Where the two disagree, the spec wins.

Uncalibrated values

The probe broadcasts raw values. iopool keeps each probe's pH and ORP calibration in its cloud, so a local client gets uncalibrated readings. The pH scale (1/100) and the temperature scale (0.01 °C) in this spec are inferences that nobody has checked against a probe. Compare with a test strip and a thermometer before you dose chemicals.

Out of scope: the iopool Connect gateway (the app's IGW and I10–I40 generations), the Ecotab chlorine-tablet dispenser, the iopool cloud API, and pHin monitors. The iopool app also reads pHin advertisements, but that format belongs to the separate pHin candidate (research-notes/phin-pool-monitor.md).

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Models EcO (FCC model "EcO v01"), EcO Salt. The app runs one parser and one command set for both, and no on-air difference between them is known. Chipset Texas Instruments CC2640R2F (legible in the FCC internal photos), plus an 8-pin part whose marking is not legible (possibly serial flash), a buzzer, and a two-lead switch Radio Bluetooth 4.0 LE only, 2402–2480 MHz, integral antenna Battery 3.7 V internal cell (FCC test report). The welcome guide gives two years' life with no recharging. The vendor's current product page describes a newer generation with a replaceable battery and sensors. Advertised name Exactly 8 characters: the probe's code, which the cloud registers against a pool. The exact format has not been seen on air. Manufacturer data Company ID 0x074C (on air ff 4c 07 …). This ID is not in the Bluetooth SIG registry. FCC ID 2AVNQECO-V1 (iopool SA, Belgium, granted 2020-04-15)

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes: a new or wintered probe has to be switched to monitoring mode. Nothing is provisioned. Method ble_direct (primary, no account); cloud_account (the vendor app) Setup AP / advertised name 8-character name with manufacturer data 0x074C, record mode byte = 3 Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (read from the vendor app, not replayed)

A new probe, or one in winter standby, advertises maintenance-mode records (mode byte 3). The vendor app activates one like this:

  1. The owner turns the probe upside down and back upright. The app asks for this gesture, and the switch in the FCC photos may be a tilt switch.
  2. The app waits up to 5 s for a mode-3 advertisement and keeps its name.
  3. It connects with no pairing and a 12 s timeout, then discovers services.
  4. It writes the current Unix time to the clock characteristic f3a00008, which it does first on every connection.
  5. It reads the software version from f3a00011 as ASCII text.
  6. It writes 0x04 (monitoring mode) to f3a00002, then disconnects.

None of these steps uses an account or a token. The vendor app then links the probe's code and version to a pool in its cloud, after the owner has scanned the EcO Start pack's QR code. Winter standby is the reverse: connect, set the clock, write 0x05, disconnect.

Factory reset: none is documented, and the probe holds no bond or credential to clear. The app's pool settings have a "reset EcO" action that sends 0x01 to f3a00002. What that clears is not established, so the spec marks it advanced.

Rebinding: nothing binds the probe to a phone. Anyone in range can read it and switch its mode. Moving it to another pool or account is a cloud operation.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none Bonding none PIN source n/a One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time No (nothing bonds) Confidence medium (the vendor app's own flow, not replayed)

Entering pairing mode: not applicable. Turning the probe over wakes it into maintenance mode. That is a setup step, not a pairing window.

Unpairing: there is nothing to unpair.

Recovery: if a connection fails, close the vendor app and unplug any iopool Connect gateway near the pool, since the gateway is itself a BLE client of the probe. Then retry.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: All vendor UUIDs share the base -f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00. Blueriiot's Blue Connect analyser uses the same base (its f330… services), so never identify a device on the base alone.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description f3a00001-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 EcO probe service The only vendor service the app uses f3a00002-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 Command One-byte opcodes, written with response f3a00008-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 Clock Unix time in seconds, 8 bytes little-endian. Written on every connection f3a00009-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 Beep c8 00 (uint16 LE 200) sounds the buzzer once f3a0000a-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 Live-mode counter [count, 0x00] starts a run of live measurements. Write only: nothing in the app reads or subscribes to it f3a00011-f0a2-9b06-0c59-1bc4763b5c00 Software version Read, decoded as ASCII

Not the EcO's. Earlier notes attributed three more services to the probe. In the app, each belongs to a different product:

UUID Belongs to f4000001-… (write f4000002, read f4000003) iopool Connect BLE-to-Wi-Fi gateway f4100001-… (write f4100010, read f4100011) Ecotab chlorine-tablet dispenser, including its firmware update 0000fe63-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, 3206152c-76fd-4996-952b-2a1be2cb9450 Adopted pHin monitors

The app has no firmware-update path for the EcO. Its firmware-URL configuration belongs to the gateway and the Ecotab, and no TI OAD service UUID appears anywhere in it.

docs.title: Advertisement record
docs.text:
The app keeps an advertisement when its local name is exactly 8 characters long and it carries manufacturer data under 0x074C. Offsets below count from the first byte after the company ID. Multi-byte fields are big-endian.

Offset Length Field Decode 0 1 Format version uint8. The values in use are not known 1 1 Mode 1 standard, 2 live, 3 maintenance, 4 backup (meaning unknown) 2 1 Sequence uint8 measurement counter. Counts from 1 in a live run 3 2 pH int16 BE. × 0.01 is a hypothesis 5 2 ORP int16 BE. mV is a hypothesis 7 2 Temperature uint16 BE. × 0.01 °C is a hypothesis; 0.1 °C is the alternative 9 2 Conductivity uint16 BE. Unit unknown, and the app does not upload it 11 1 Activity / battery bits 7–6 activity (meaning unknown); battery % = (byte & 0x3f) × 2 12 2 Time of day minutes after 00:00 UTC = byte12 × 8 + (byte13 >> 5)

Dating a reading. The record carries only the time of day, taken from the probe's own clock. The app dates it today (UTC), or yesterday if that would be more than 15 minutes in the future. If the result is more than 30 minutes old or more than 5 minutes ahead, the app decides the clock has drifted: it uses the current minute instead and reconnects to reset the clock. It also resets the clock with the first reading it sees each day.

Deduplicating. A record repeats in every advertisement until the next measurement. Treat it as new only when the name, sequence or time changes. Skip mode-3 records, and treat mode-2 records as a live or calibration run, as the app does.

Test vectors. These are built from the app's parser and are not captures. The format-version byte and every value are invented.

Record Decodes to 01 01 07 02 e4 02 b2 0a 1e 04 d2 b2 5a a0 standard, seq 7, pH 7.40, ORP 690 mV, temp raw 2590 (25.90 °C if centi-degrees), conductivity 1234, activity 2, battery 100 %, 12:05 UTC 01 02 01 02 d5 ff 38 07 d0 00 00 5e 7d 1f live, seq 1, pH 7.25, ORP −200 mV, temp raw 2000, activity 1, battery 60 %, 16:40 UTC 01 03 00 03 0c 01 f4 09 c4 00 00 32 00 00 maintenance: what the app waits for when adding a probe, not a measurement

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
All commands are written with response, after the clock write that opens every connection.

Command Characteristic Bytes Notes Monitoring mode f3a00002 04 Activates a new probe or wakes a wintered one Maintenance mode f3a00002 05 The app's winter standby Reset f3a00002 01 Effect unknown. Advanced Set clock f3a00008 Unix seconds, 8 bytes LE 1790000000 → 80 3b b1 6a 00 00 00 00 Beep f3a00009 c8 00 The app's buzzer test beeps three times, 500 ms apart Live mode f3a0000a [count, 00] Default count 5. The calibration wizard uses 21 (15 00)

Calibration. The app's calibration wizard has the owner hold the probe in a reference solution, starts a 21-measurement live run, and accepts the run once the collected values of the channel being calibrated spread by less than 5 raw units. The raw samples go to the vendor cloud. Nothing about calibration is written to the probe.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
These are defects and traps found in the vendor app.

  • Negative ORP shows as about 65 000 mV on Android. The app's iOS build reads ORP as signed, but its Android build reads the same two bytes unsigned. Decode it as int16.
  • Readings carry the wrong time. The probe dates readings from its own clock. A client that never connects never corrects it. Connect and write the clock at least once a day, as the app does.
  • A new probe cannot be found. It has to be woken by turning it upside down and back, and until it is activated it only advertises mode-3 records. A scanner that filters by service UUID or drops duplicates will miss it, because the app does neither.
  • The same reading appears again and again. That is normal: the record repeats until the next measurement. Deduplicate on the sequence and time.
  • pH or ORP differs from the vendor app. The app shows values the cloud has calibrated, and this spec's values are raw. Check with a test strip.
  • Battery reads above 100 %. The field can hold up to 126. Clamp it.

docs.title: iPixel Color LED Matrix Panel (TIRO/Heaton)
docs.text: Status: Research Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Shenzhen Heaton Technology Co., Ltd. / TIRO (OEM; many storefront brands) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The ubiquitous flexible silicone RGB LED matrix panel / scrolling sign sold on AliExpress, Amazon and regional marketplaces for car rear windows, shop fronts and advertising tickers — 5 V USB powered, often IP65, adhesive backing, in sizes from 32×16 up to 448×32 pixels. Known re-seller SKUs include JTPD-03-011 (many sizes, "QYJSD" and other labels) and the HCZ-001 / HCZ-002 "Smart Car Screen" panels. There is no single model number; all of them are driven by the iPixel Color app (com.wifiled.ipixels).

The panel is built on a JieLi BLE SoC and is controlled entirely over local BLE with no pairing, bonding, or encryption. Several working FOSS clients already exist — the device is usable cloud-free today. The vendor cloud (Heaton) is only a clip-art store and firmware-update service.

Same OEM family as led-helmet-display ("TIRO FA02" family): same FA02 command characteristic, framing convention, JieLi OTA machinery and Heaton cloud backend — but a different opcode map and panel geometries, so the command tables are not interchangeable.

Family boundary — read this first. These are not this device despite similar marketplace appearance: CoolLED1248 / Juntong (coolledx-led-sign), the LOY family (service FFF0), and the Quintic AES-128-ECB Shining Mask family. This family is identified by the FA02 write characteristic under service 0x00FA and LED_BLE… advertising names.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number No single model number — OEM platform; marketplace SKUs include JTPD-03-011, HCZ-001, HCZ-002 Display RGB LED matrix, 32×16 … 448×32 pixels (query the device — listings are unreliable; one HCZ-001 listing claims an impossible "32×23") Chipset JieLi BLE SoC (firmware in JieLi OTA format, chip-key scrambled) Radio BLE; some variants add Wi-Fi (undocumented path) and an IR remote FCC ID Unknown (marketplace listings carry no FCC ID) Firmware obtained 8 OTA images captured from the vendor cloud 2026-08-19 (sha256s in the spec's sources)

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name BLE name prefix LED_BLE Passphrase protection not_applicable (a password mechanism exists in the protocol; flag 255 = no password is the norm) Confidence high (multiple FOSS clients do this on real hardware)

Power the panel on, scan for the LED_BLE prefix, connect, locate FA02 (write) and the notify characteristic (FA03, or vendor UUID d44bc439-… on some firmware), enable notifications, then send the time-sync command — the panel replies with a device-info record whose byte 4 maps to the panel geometry.

Factory reset: no physical procedure is documented. The clear command (04 00 03 80 to FA02) is documented by community clients as wiping all stored content and settings — a software factory reset (confidence: low; inferred, not observed).

Rebinding: there is no network to rebind. If a client cannot connect, the usual cause is the vendor app still holding the single BLE connection.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 000000fa-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb iPixel Command Service All display commands 0000ae00-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb JieLi OTA Service Firmware update (presence inferred from the bundled JieLi OTA SDK — hypothesis) UUID Name Properties Purpose 0000fa02-… Display Command Write, Write Without Response All commands (frame format below) 0000fa03-… Display Notify Notify Command ACKs, device-info response. Some firmware uses vendor UUID d44bc439-abfd-45a2-b575-925416129601 instead — enumerate, don't hardcode 0000ae01-… / 0000ae02-… JieLi OTA Write / Notify Write / Notify Firmware update data/result

docs.title: Command frame format
docs.text:
All commands are raw byte arrays written to FA02:

Offset Length Description 0–1 2 Total frame length, little-endian u16 (covers the whole frame) 2–3 2 Opcode, little-endian u16; the high byte sub-selects within a command group 4.. N−4 Payload

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Opcode Frame Meaning 0x0107 05 00 07 01 v Power on/off 0x8004 05 00 04 80 v Brightness 0–100 0x0104 05 00 04 01 v DIY ("fun") mode on/off 0x0105 0A 00 05 01 00 r g b x y Set one pixel (DIY mode) 0x8006 05 00 06 80 v Orientation, index 0–3 0x0106 0B 00 06 01 style fmt24 showdate yr mo day dow Clock mode (style 0–8) 0x8001 08 00 01 80 h m s lang Sync time; panel replies with device info (byte 4 = device-type → geometry map, byte 10 = password flag) 0x0201 10 00 01 02 style l1..l11 Music-rhythm mode, 11 level bands (0–15) 0x0200 06 00 00 02 t style Alternate rhythm mode 0x8008 07 00 08 80 01 00 slot Show stored slot 1–9 (community docs also record a 5-byte 0x8007 variant — likely firmware-revision dependent) 0x0102 07 00 02 01 01 00 slot Delete a stored slot 0x8003 04 00 03 80 Clear all stored content + settings 0x0002 / 0x0003 windowed PNG / GIF upload — see below

Image/animation upload (0x0002 PNG, 0x0003 GIF): the image is resized client-side to the panel geometry and sent in ~12 KB windows. Every window is a complete frame: u16-LE length, opcode bytes, option byte (0x00 first window, 0x02 continuation), u32-LE total payload size, u32-LE CRC32 of the payload, tail byte (0x00 PNG / 0x02 GIF), save slot (0 = show only, 1–9 = store), then the chunk. Each window is ACKed on the notify characteristic before the next is sent. Text is rendered client-side to an image — there is no separate text wire format.

docs.title: Cloud Dependency
docs.text:
The device is fully usable without the cloud — BLE models have no internet path at all; only the companion app talks to the Heaton backend (all hosts alive 2026-08-19):

  • POST manage.heaton.com.cn/api/rm/getFirmwareInfo — firmware checks (form body appid=137&project_no=<TR…>&version=<n>; answered unauthenticated with a browser-like User-Agent; images download from images.heaton.com.cn only with a matching Referer)
  • api.e-toys.cn — clip-art/material library
  • app.heaton.cn — app config JSON, manuals, logos

If the Heaton cloud dies: everything local keeps working — power, brightness, modes, clock, DIY drawing, PNG/GIF upload, slot management. What breaks is the clip-art library and OTA checks, and a captured firmware image can still be flashed via the local JieLi OTA service.

Home Assistant guidance: use cagcoach/ha-ipixel-color (HACS) or the ESPHome component; for scripting, pypixelcolor is the cleanest reference.

docs.title: Generic IPP Network Printer (status)
docs.text: Status: Status only (discovery signature and IPP status from public standards; untested — no hardware) Protocol: mDNS / DNS-SD (Bonjour printing) + IPP (RFC 8010/8011) Manufacturer: Various (IPP Everywhere / AirPrint printers) Manufacturer Status: Active — status read over IPP; printing left to the OS print system

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Office and home network printers advertise themselves over mDNS/DNS-SD using standard, vendor-neutral service types. This app identifies them and reads their status over IPP — state, what is wrong, ink or toner levels, the paper loaded — with one standard Get-Printer-Attributes request, and deep-links to the printer's embedded web interface. It does not send print jobs itself: printing is the job of the OS print system (AirPrint, IPP Everywhere / driverless printing), which already reaches these printers with no vendor software.

docs.title: Status over IPP
docs.text:
POST http://<ip>:<port>/<rp> with Content-Type: application/ipp, where <port> is the one the service advertises (631 by default) and <rp> the TXT rp key (the Bonjour default is empty, so a missing or empty rp is /; IPP Everywhere printers advertise one, conventionally ipp/print, which is the second guess when the advertised path answers not-found). TLS on the same port for _ipps._tcp, self-signed — pin on first use. The body is an RFC 8010 Get-Printer-Attributes request (operation 0x000B) asking for printer-state, printer-state-reasons, printer-state-message, printer-make-and-model, the marker-* supply attributes, media-ready and document-format-supported. The full byte layout is in the spec's protocol_details.ipp_status.

Only _ipp._tcp / _ipps._tcp carry this surface; a printer seen only as _pdl-datastream or _printer is linked to its admin page, nothing more. The spec states that by key (protocol_details.ipp_status.requires_service_types) because the schema cannot yet tie a handler or an entity to one discovery method; that field is proposed as Spec Evolution P16.

docs.title: Discovery Summary
docs.text:
• DNS-SD service types (Bonjour Printing Specification):
    • _ipp._tcp — IPP, modern print protocol (TCP 631)
    • _ipps._tcp — IPP over TLS
    • _printer._tcp — legacy LPD (515)
    • _pdl-datastream._tcp — raw socket / JetDirect (9100)
  • TXT keys: rp, ty (make/model, for display), pdl, UUID (stable per-printer id, advertised by IPP Everywhere printers), adminurl, note, product.
  • Stable key: TXT UUID, falling back to hostname. Display: mDNS instance name (or ty).

Admin: http://<ip>/ (most printers serve an embedded web server at the root; prefer TXT adminurl when present). Scheme/port may be reconfigured.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• https://developer.apple.com/bonjour/printing-specification/
  • https://www.pwg.org/ipp/everywhere.html
  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8010

docs.title: iRobot Roomba (Wi-Fi models)
docs.text: Status: Local protocol documented from public reverse engineering; not replayed against hardware here Protocol: WiFi (MQTT over TLS, TCP 8883, on the robot itself) Manufacturer: iRobot — Chapter 11 filed 2025-12-14, acquired by Picea Robotics 2026-01-23 Manufacturer Status: Active (company alive; the local protocol is what's endangered)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Wi-Fi Roombas run an MQTT broker on the robot itself — TLS on TCP 8883, username = the robot's BLID, password = a per-device secret you can pull off the robot without an iRobot account. It is the same channel the vendor app uses when the phone is on the LAN, so local control is not a scraped-together fallback: it is the primary interface, and it keeps working with the robot firewalled off the internet entirely.

This is dorita980's work

Every byte on this page was recovered by koalazak/dorita980 (Node.js, MIT) — the UDP-5678 discovery probe, the password-disclosure magic packet and its reply offsets, the MQTT-over-TLS session, the cmd/delta vocabulary and the account route to the credentials. Its README is the authoritative text; this page transcribes it into our format. pschmitt/roombapy carries the same protocol into Python and backs Home Assistant's roomba integration. If you want a supported, hardware-tested client, use one of those — this document exists to describe the protocol, not to compete with the people who worked it out.

Covered generations: 690, 890, 960, 980, e5/e6, i3–i8, j7/j9, s9, plus the Braava jet m6.

The 2025 line has no local broker

Roomba 105 / 205 / Combo 405 — the "V4 protocol" reboot — refuse connections on 8883. Connection refused, not a timeout: there is nothing listening. Cloud credentials are still retrievable, but there is no local broker to use them against. Reported against firmware p25-105 (Home Assistant community, 2026-04). If you are buying a robot to control locally, buy a 2024-or-earlier model.

One local client at a time

The robot accepts a single local MQTT connection, and a new one evicts the old. A client that holds the socket open locks the owner out of their own app. Connect, read, act, disconnect — that is why Home Assistant's integration is iot_class: local_polling and why dorita980 tells callers to .end() after a command.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Broadcast the nine ASCII bytes irobotmcs to 255.255.255.255:5678. An awake iRobot robot on the segment answers with a JSON datagram sent back to whatever UDP source port the probe came from — dorita980 binds and sends from 5678, so its replies land on 5678; roombapy sends from an ephemeral port and reads the reply there. Either works. Send the probe more than once: UDP is lossy, and a dropped probe is a robot never found.

A docked, idle robot answers nothing

A robot that has been docked and idle powers its radio down and goes silent on the LAN — it will not answer this probe, an mDNS query, or a TCP connection to 8883. Wake it first (press a button, or hold CLEAN for ~20 seconds to reboot it) and probe within the wake window. This is the single most common reason a scan of a segment that provably has robots on it comes back empty.

The reply:

{
  "ver": "3",
  "hostname": "Roomba-3192000000000000",
  "robotname": "Robot",
  "ip": "192.168.1.50",
  "mac": "12:12:12:12:12:12",
  "sw": "v2.4.16-126",
  "sku": "R980020",
  "nc": 0,
  "proto": "mqtt"
}

hostname is the identity carrier: it is Roomba-<blid> (or iRobot-<blid> on Braava), so the BLID is the substring after the first hyphen — and the BLID is the MQTT username. A datagram whose hostname starts with neither prefix is not a robot; the probe reaches every host on the segment, so filter on it.

Send the probe more than once. UDP is lossy, and a dropped datagram is a robot never found. Robots answer the probe but do not beacon on their own, so a consumer that only listens finds nothing — the spec's discovery method records that as passive_ok: false.

Port 5678 is shared with MikroTik MNDP

MikroTik's neighbour-discovery protocol (mikrotik-routeros) uses the same UDP port, so one broadcast draws replies from both and a consumer scanning for either will see the other's datagrams. They are told apart by the shape of the reply, not by the port: MNDP answers with big-endian TLV records, a Roomba with a JSON object whose hostname carries one of the two prefixes above. A parser that assumes everything arriving on 5678 is its own protocol will report somebody's router as a robot.

There is no mDNS entry here on purpose

Robots are reported to be visible on 5353, but nothing this page draws on names the service type they advertise — so the spec declares no mdns discovery method. An earlier revision guessed _amzn-wplay._tcp, which is Amazon's Whisperplay (Fire TV) and not iRobot at all. A wrong service type is worse than a missing one: it sends a client hunting on somebody else's protocol and reports their hardware as robots. The UDP broadcast is the documented path; if someone captures the real mDNS type, it can be added.

Discovery needs broadcast to reach the robot, so a client-isolated guest SSID or a VLAN that does not forward broadcast will find nothing even though the robot is up and its broker is answering — falling back to a known IP is always valid.

docs.title: Getting the password
docs.text:
There are two routes to the same pair of values. Do this before you firewall the robot: the button route is local and unaffected, but the account route needs both the phone and iRobot's API reachable.

The password is stable — community reports have it changing only on a factory reset. Write it down. It is the same BLID/password pair Home Assistant, dorita980 and every other local client will ask you for.

docs.title: Route 1: the HOME button (no account)
docs.text:
dorita980's get-roomba-password <ip>.

  1. Put the robot on its dock, powered on, and close the iRobot app on every phone — the robot serves one client at a time.
  2. Hold HOME for about two seconds, until the robot plays a series of tones, then release. The robot is now in password-disclosure mode for a short window.
  3. Open TLS to <robot-ip>:8883. The certificate is self-signed — pin it on first sight rather than trying to validate it against a CA.
  4. Write the seven-byte probe and read one reply.
Probe f0 05 ef cc 3b 29 00 0xf0 — an MQTT reserved packet type0x05 — payload lengthef cc 3b 29 00 — the payload Reply [0xf0][length][payload]. Read until you have 2 + length bytes. Extraction Drop the 2-byte header, drop any remaining leading non-printable bytes, decode the rest as UTF-8, strip trailing NULs. That whole remaining string is the password. Not in disclosure mode A reply shorter than 8 bytes. Release, re-hold HOME, retry. Model can't disclose A reply equal to f0 05 ef cc 3b 29 03. Use the account route.

Why a rule and not an offset

Published clients each hardcode a different fixed offset for the same reply: roombapy slices at 7 of the whole reply, dorita980 at 13 when the socket delivers everything in one read and at 9 when the 2-byte header arrives separately. Scanning for the printable run is correct under all three, which is why that is what the spec states as the contract and the offsets are recorded only as evidence.

That rule is our hypothesis, not anyone's transcription

Everything else on this page came out of a working client. The extraction rule did not — it was derived by asking what single rule satisfies all three offsets, and it assumes every byte between the header and the credential is non-printable. Nobody has confirmed that against a robot, here or upstream. If a firmware puts a printable byte in that gap, the rule returns it glued to the front of the password and the only symptom is the broker refusing your login.

A cautious client implements the rule and a fixed slice at each observed offset, and warns when they disagree. If you hit a robot where they disagree, report it to dorita980 and roombapy — they own this protocol, not us.

Keep the whole string. A Roomba password looks like :1:1486937829:gktkDoYpWaDxCfGh — it starts with a colon and contains colons, and clients that "helpfully" split on the first one break.

The reply also carries the BLID, but the UDP-5678 announcement's hostname is the easier read.

j-series TLS resets

j7-era firmware is reported to reset the TLS connection on the first attempt or two before answering. Retry inside the window rather than treating one reset as a refusal — the homebridge-roomba issue tracker is the best public record of the timings that get past it.

Legacy TLS ciphers

Older firmware negotiates only AES128-SHA256 (TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA256) and expects legacy renegotiation. Runtimes whose TLS stack has retired that suite — anything on BoringSSL, which includes Dart and Chromium — cannot complete the handshake at all, and fail before the probe is written. dorita980 works around it with the ROBOT_CIPHERS and ROBOT_TLS_LEGACY environment variables. A client that cannot select ciphers should say so plainly rather than reporting the robot as unreachable.

docs.title: Route 2: the iRobot account (credential extraction only)
docs.text:
dorita980's get-roomba-password-cloud <email> <password>. Use this when the button handshake will not complete. It returns the same BLID and password the local route would have — nothing about steady-state control needs an account.

  1. GET https://disc-prod.iot.irobotapi.com/v1/discover/endpoints?country_code=<CC> for the regional Gigya API key and the two base URLs.
  2. POST {gigyaBase}/accounts.login with the account email and password → UID, UIDSignature, signatureTimestamp.
  3. POST {httpBase}/v2/login with that assertion and the client's app_id → a robots map keyed by BLID, each entry carrying password, name, sku and softwareVer.

Treat the account password as write-never: use it for the one login call and keep nothing. Store password against blid, discard the Gigya assertion.

docs.title: The local MQTT session
docs.text:
Transport MQTT 3.1.1 over TLS, TCP 8883, on the robot Certificate Self-signed. Pin it; do not expect a CA chain. Client ID The BLID Username The BLID Password The extracted per-robot secret Ciphers AES128-SHA256 on older firmware; newer firmware negotiates TLS 1.3 suites

Subscribe to # after connecting: it picks up delta and the shadow topics in one go, which saves guessing which topic shape a given firmware publishes locally.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Publish to the cmd topic. The payload is a JSON envelope:

{"command":"clean","time":1755129600,"initiator":"localApp"}

time is Unix epoch seconds from the sender's clock at the moment of sending — that is how every published client fills it. What the robot does with the value is undocumented and untested here, so send a real timestamp rather than a constant. initiator is localApp for a LAN client.

command Meaning clean Start or resume a full cleaning mission. start is accepted as a synonym. pause Pause the mission; the robot stays where it is. stop End the mission. The robot stops and stays put — it does not go home. resume Resume a paused mission. dock Return to the dock. Only accepted from a paused or stopped state, which is why a single "send home" button sends stop then dock. find Beep so you can find the robot under the sofa. Silent while docked.

docs.title: State
docs.text:
The robot pushes changes to delta as {"state":{"reported":{...}}}, and publishes the full shadow to an $aws/things/<blid>/shadow/update-shaped topic. The fields worth binding:

Path under state.reported Type Meaning batPct integer % Battery charge cleanMissionStatus.phase string charge, run, stop, hmUsrDock (going home on request), hmMidMsn (going home to recharge), hmPostMsn (going home, mission done), evac, stuck cleanMissionStatus.cycle string none, clean, spot, evac, dock bin.full boolean Bin needs emptying bin.present boolean False when the bin has been removed name / sku / softwareVer string Identity, model, firmware

Newer firmware in this generation stops reporting the robot's x/y pose. Bind mission phase, not position.

docs.title: Keep it off the internet
docs.text:
The single biggest risk to everything on this page is an over-the-air firmware update that removes the local broker — which is exactly what happened to the 2025 models. dorita980's README has said so for years: block the robot's internet access.

What you lose by blocking it: remote (off-LAN) control from the vendor app, cloud-side scheduling, map sync on the mapping models, and OTA updates. What keeps working: everything in this document.

The hosts to block are in the spec's cloud.hosts, marked reported rather than confirmed — this project has not captured a robot's DNS traffic, so log the robot's own lookups at your router for a day before trusting any blocklist. A step-by-step guide for UniFi, MikroTik and the other common home platforms is at liberatedbread.com/firewall/.

Order matters: extract the credentials first. The account route stops working the moment the robot or the phone is cut off.

docs.title: Setup and reset
docs.text:
Initial provisioning (getting a factory-fresh robot onto Wi-Fi) is a vendor app job and is not documented outside iRobot. What a third-party client needs is the credential extraction above, which applies to an already-provisioned robot.

Factory reset clears the Wi-Fi credentials and the cloud registration, and — importantly — mints a new local password. A robot reset since you wrote its password down will refuse the old one. Maps and mission history are lost on the models that keep them.

  • 600/800/900 series: hold DOCK + SPOT Clean + CLEAN together until the robot signals the reset, then release.
  • i/j/s series: hold HOME + SPOT Clean + CLEAN together until the ring swirls clockwise, then release.

Holding CLEAN alone is a reboot, not a reset

It restarts the robot and changes nothing else. That distinction matters more here than it usually would: this page tells you a reset mints a new password, so someone who reboots believing they reset will either wait for a credential change that never comes, or decide their saved password is dead and redo the whole handshake for nothing. Both procedures above are multi-button holds for exactly that reason.

Rebinding to a new router does not need a factory reset. A provisioned robot can be put back into Wi-Fi setup mode and pointed at the new network — vendor-documented and widely reported, though not replayed here, so treat it as low confidence and be ready to fall back to a reset.

The useful consequence: if the move doesn't reset the robot, the password survives it. A credential you saved before changing routers keeps working — which is why anything storing one should key it on the BLID rather than on the address the robot happened to have.

docs.title: Johnson JLX LDM330 / LDM130 Laser Distance Meter
docs.text: Status: Verified and manually confirmed on LDM330; LDM130 remains untested Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Johnson Level & Tool (Precaster Enterprises OEM platform) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Johnson JLX LDM330 (model 40-6013) is a 330 ft Bluetooth laser distance meter with an integrated angle sensor; the LDM130 is its 130 ft sibling. Both pair with Johnson's "Measure-Up" app (Android package com.winho.measure_up). The OEM behind the "winho" package root is Precaster Enterprises Co., Ltd. (Taichung, Taiwan): the same app codebase also builds Precaster's own iM2 app plus sibling-branded apps (Starrett STR3, Ronix, MeasureMate, MeasureCam/TargetCam variants), so the protocol below covers a family of rebadged meters. Four sibling APKs (iM2, Measure Mate, RonixMeasureBox, RonixTargetCam) were acquired and confirmed at the binary level to carry the same f151/f154 UUIDs and frame literals.

The protocol was recovered from Measure-Up, then verified against a live LDM330 and a vendor-app capture: advertised identity, f150/f151/f154, init, keep-alives and measurement frames were all observed. A maintainer manually confirmed the normal LDM330 measurement flow again on 2026-11-08. It is minimally verified rather than complete: LDM130 has not been tested, the remote m command works only while the display is awake, and stock BlueZ cannot finish enumeration because of the separate 0x2b3a stall described below.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number LDM330 (40-6013); sibling LDM130 BLE module Precaster BT A8105; hardware A810501, firmware 0001, software 1000 Radio BLE (GATT server), public address and advertised f150 service FCC ID Not found

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Advertised name Laser Distance Meter with service 0000f150-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb; the vendor app itself scans unfiltered Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence high for LDM330 (live + capture); low for LDM130

Factory reset: none exists or is needed. The meter holds no bonds, credentials, or client state — the app connects without pairing. Removing the batteries (2×AAA) is the only reset relevant to a BLE client.

Rebinding to a new network: not applicable (no Wi-Fi). Any client can connect at any time; when the meter powers its radio down it sends a Zbleoff notification first, and the vendor app simply reconnects.

To enable Bluetooth on the meter, press and hold its Bluetooth button (per the vendor quick-start guide), then select the meter from the app's scan list.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Role 0000f150-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Confirmed primary LDM service; advertised and enumerated 0000f151-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb command_rx (write/write-without-response): init, keep-alive, measure 0000f154-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb data_tx (notify): handshake and measurement frames 0000fff3-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Secondary vendor service with fff4 notify and fff5 write/write-without-response; role and payload unknown, do not use 00001802-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Immediate Alert (2a06) 00001803-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Link Loss (2a06) 00001804-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Tx Power (2a07) 0000180d-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Stock Heart Rate service (2a37/2a38); no measurements observed, not a distance channel 0000180f-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Battery Level (2a19), read/notify 0000180a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Device Information identifying the Precaster module

A 2026-11-07 independent GATT report confirms the fff3 pair and standard services, with responses: []: those are property observations, not command or response evidence. Do not send the f150 init/measure frames or another product's protocol to fff3.

docs.title: Command: init
docs.text:
Request (write to f151, 6 bytes, fixed):

Offset Length Description 0 6 03 0D 0A 03 0D 0A — sent after subscribing, and in reply to Ztest01

docs.title: Command: measure
docs.text:
Request (write to f151, 13 bytes):

Offset Length Description 0 1 0x23 (#) header 1 1 0x0A (LF) header 2 1 ASCII command 'm' 3 9 NUL padding 12 1 Checksum 0x9A = 8-bit sum of bytes 0–11

Full bytes: 23 0A 6D 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 9A

docs.title: Command: link keep-alive
docs.text:
Answer to the device's Ztest02 notification (write to f151, 13 bytes): 23 0A 4C 69 6E 6B 00 00 00 00 00 00 BB — '#' LF "Link", NUL-padded, checksum 0xBB.

Note: the Ronix build carries a dead, unreferenced second copy of the BLE service class that writes the identical Link payload with checksum 0xDB instead of 0xBB. The live path uses 0xBB, but the duplicate hints a firmware variant with a different checksum may exist — worth testing if a meter rejects the link frame.

docs.title: Notifications (device → app, f154, 10-byte ASCII, NUL-padded)
docs.text:
Frame Meaning Ztest01 Handshake request → client writes the init frame Ztest02 Keep-alive request → client writes the link frame Zbleoff Meter is powering its BLE radio down; treat as clean disconnect error1…error6 (Hypothesis) measurement failure codes; the app compares against these strings but never produces them — and a literal errorN frame actually crashes the app's Float.parseFloat (uncaught NumberFormatException), so this build silently drops error frames before the comparison runs other Measurement frame, see below

Measurement frame:

Offset Length Description 0 1 Type/prefix character; the vendor app discards it (meaning unknown) 1 6 Fixed-width ASCII decimal value, always meters (e.g. 12.345) 7 1 Unit code = device display setting: a=m, b=ft, c=in, d=ft'in" 1/32, e=in 1/32, f=in 1/16, g=in 1/8, h=in 1/4, i=in 1/2, j=Taiwanese/Chinese foot 8 2 NUL padding

The value is meters regardless of the unit code; the app converts for display. A unit code outside a–j hits the app's default: branch and is surfaced to the UI as Zbleoff — treat unknown unit codes as unknown, not as a power-down. The LDM330's angle sensor does not appear in the recovered BLE code of any acquired build (Measure-Up, iM2, MeasureMate, Ronix) — every frame carries a single scalar distance, so angle is likely on-device only (unverified).

docs.title: Linux desktop sees zero services
docs.text:
A BlueZ-based client — bleak, flutter_blue_plus on Linux, anything layered on bluetoothd — connects to this meter, negotiates an MTU, and then discovers no services at all. That is this device, not your code.

On a first connection, right after the MTU exchange, bluetoothd sends a Read By Type for Server Supported Features (0x2b3a) and queues primary discovery behind it (src/shared/gatt-client.c, unchanged from BlueZ 5.66 through master; reproduced on 5.72 and 5.85). The meter answers that read with silence rather than an error, so bluetoothd waits out the 30 s ATT transaction timeout, abandons init, and reports the device "resolved" with an empty database — about 32.5 s in, with the ATT channel left dead. A client that gives up sooner (the app retries discovery for ~6 s) just sees the empty result earlier; waiting longer does not help, because the database is still empty when bluetoothd finally answers. (An earlier version of this page blamed the Database Hash, 0x2b2a; bluetoothd reads that before discovery only when a cached database already contains one, never on a first contact.)

What still works: plain Read Requests by handle (every Device Information string and the battery level read fine), Exchange MTU, and — over a raw ATT channel — discovery, writes and notifications. Android and iOS are unaffected.

Narrower than it first looked. In the vendor-app HCI capture the meter answered every Read By Type it received (29 by-type and 9 by-group-type requests, 38 responses, no silences), including correct Attribute Not Found (0x0a) errors for by-type reads of UUIDs it does not carry. The handler is not broken in general; what that capture never contains is a read of 0x2b3a. Android skips it for a peer like this one, which reports LL version 0x01 and no LE features.

No bluetoothd setting fixes it. Cache = no under [GATT] in /etc/bluetooth/main.conf suppresses only the cached hash read, and no key skips the 0x2b3a read. What works on Linux is a client that owns the ATT fixed channel (L2CAP CID 4) itself and never sends 0x2b3a: gatttool, or an app that opens the channel directly. The spec records this as device.host_compatibility (stack: bluez, status: incompatible, workaround: raw_att), so such a client can go direct from the first connection. Otherwise, drive the meter from Android or iOS.

docs.title: Family survey (Bluetooth laser distance meters)
docs.text:
Family Transport Notes Precaster Enterprises platform (this spec) BLE Johnson LDM130/LDM330 (Measure-Up app), Precaster iM2, Starrett STR3, Ronix, MeasureMate, MeasureCam/TargetCam builds share one codebase (per the APK's internal list of brand builds; Ronix builds use the older com.wiho package root). ASCII frames over f151/f154. Mileseey (P7/T7/R2B/M120/DT20-old, Suaoki rebadges) BLE Open protocol, transmits unit; supported by ImageMeter. Newer models (DT20-new, D5/D5T/D9 Pro, S50) moved to an encrypted protocol and are listed as unsupported by ImageMeter; D9 Pro rides the Tuya Smart Life app. Bosch GLM 50 C / 100 C / PLR 30-50 C Bluetooth Classic SPP Reverse engineered; see philipptrenz/BOSCH-GLM-rangefinder (pymtprotocol). Remote trigger supported. Bosch GLM xx-27 C generation BLE Newer closed BLE protocol (MeasureOn app); ImageMeter supports with manual protocol selection; partial RE in pklaus/bsch. Leica DISTO (D1/D2/X3/X4/D810…) BLE Leica publishes its DISTO BLE interface documentation; ImageMeter supports broadly (some models need "Unencrypted App Mode"). CEM iLDM series BLE (new) / Classic (old) Open protocol, transmits unit + remote trigger; ImageMeter-supported.

See the ImageMeter supported-devices table for the broadest cross-brand catalogue (70+ models, noting which transmit units and which are encrypted/unsupported).

docs.title: ChefSteps Joule Sous Vide
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (untested) Protocol: BLE GATT; optional vendor-cloud Wi-Fi Manufacturer: Breville, formerly ChefSteps (active)

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: Joule is an 1100 W immersion heater and the protocol can start a cook at up to 98 °C at sea level. Use it only with the vessel, water level and food prepared as the manual requires, with someone able to stop it. Keep stop-cooking one command away in any client. Read the device's limits instead of assuming the 98 °C ceiling applies to every unit. On UL-listed hardware, a cook above 85 °C additionally requires a physical top-button press.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This spec covers the original CS10001 stainless and CS20001 white Joule, not the later Joule Turbo. It includes the app-layer key exchange, request and response envelopes, live-feed messages, temperature and timer commands, Wi-Fi provisioning, firmware references and safety limits: device-specs/devices/joule-sous-vide.yaml.

The BLE path can run locally without the vendor cloud. Wi-Fi is for the vendor app's remote/cloud functions, not a prerequisite for local BLE control. Nothing here has been run against hardware by this project.

docs.title: Pairing and local setup
docs.text:
Do not pair from the phone's ordinary Bluetooth settings. Joule uses an application-layer credential instead:

  1. Plug in Joule and connect to the advertiser with service 700b4321-9836-4383-a2b2-31a9098d1473 (or company ID 0x0159).
  2. Subscribe to 700b4325-9836-4383-a2b2-31a9098d1473 and wait about 500 ms.
  3. Send start_key_exchange to 700b4322-9836-4383-a2b2-31a9098d1473.
  4. While the LED blinks white, press the button on top of Joule. The vendor flow allows about 35 seconds for this.
  5. On the doorbell notification, read the reply from 700b4323-9836-4383-a2b2-31a9098d1473 and store the returned secret key as a credential, never in public notes or logs.
  6. Present that key with submit_key on this and later connections. Only then send identification, limits and live-feed requests.

The key is per device and is not a Bluetooth PIN. A factory reset invalidates it.

docs.title: Factory reset and rebinding
docs.text:
The vendor documents this procedure; it has not been tried here:

  1. Unplug Joule and reconnect power.
  2. Immediately hold the top button for at least 15 seconds (older vendor text says 10) until the LED blinks yellow.
  3. Wait for the reset to finish and the LED to return to steady white.

Reset removes the name, Wi-Fi settings and authentication/ownership data. Pair again to obtain a new key.

To change routers without resetting, authorize over BLE, send disconnect_wifi, then provision the replacement network with connect-Wi-Fi. Newer firmware can retain multiple Wi-Fi profiles. Only the owning vendor account can configure Wi-Fi through the vendor app.

docs.title: Protocol summary
docs.text: BLE requests use a small envelope followed by a length-delimited protobuf body; replies are correlated by handle through the read/doorbell pair. The YAML declares the envelope, oneof choices, fixed-width and varint fields, floating-point temperature representation, scaling, limits and worked vectors. Do not send a numeric Celsius value as an integer: temperature setpoints use their IEEE 754 binary32 bit pattern in little-endian order.
