docs.title: Platform clusters
docs.text: Apps cluster into a small number of OEM platforms. Recognising the cluster short-circuits most of the reverse-engineering work.

docs.title: popled.cn / LOY SPACE cluster
docs.text: LOY SPACE (com.yskd.loywf), NYAN GEAR (com.nyan.gear) and very likely LED space (com.yj.led) are all built on the popled.cn backend. Signals: BLE name prefix YS or TL, Wi-Fi SSID containing YS with default password 12345678, UDP discovery on port 9090 to the subnet broadcast 192.168.4.255, and an aa 55 framed TLV packet carrying JSON commands. The LED space product literature names the panel YSP-001, which is the same naming family. Confirming the LED space link would fold an entire second app into an already-documented protocol.

docs.title: SPOTLED / iLEDColor cluster
docs.text: Both are matrix-panel design apps in the same product niche, and both have shipped on Lunchbox DreamPanel hardware. SPOTLED is fully mapped and spans products from dozens of unrelated resellers — hats, badges, chest panels, banner signs — so the 0xFF20 service is worth probing on any unknown wearable matrix panel. Whether iLEDColor shares that wire protocol is unknown and worth a direct test: a DreamPanel v3 that pairs with iLEDColor should be probed for 0xFF20 before assuming a new protocol.

docs.title: Quintic QPP cluster
docs.text: Magic Display, Shining Mask and Shining Glasses all sit on Quintic (NXP QN-series) silicon using the Quintic Private Profile: service 0xFEE9, OTA on 0xFEE8, AES-128 payload encryption via a bundled libAES.so. Same UUIDs, different command sets. A new LED wearable advertising 0xFEE9 with an libAES.so in its APK belongs here.

docs.title: CoolLED generations
docs.text: CoolLED* is one advertising name across at least seven hardware generations with two protocol families. The advertisement itself carries panel width, height and colour mode, so a client can adapt without user configuration — but the generation determines the command table. See the CoolLEDX doc.

docs.title: Triage checklist for an unknown LED sign
docs.text:
1. Identify the app. Product page screenshot, printed insert, or what's on the owner's phone. Record the exact package ID — display names are reused freely across unrelated apps.
  2. Scan before connecting. ./scripts/detect_devices.sh — capture the advertised local name, service UUIDs and the raw manufacturer data. Several of these families encode panel geometry and colour depth in the advertisement.
  3. Match against the clusters above before doing any new work.
  4. Prefer asking the device over guessing. SPOTLED has GetDisplayInfo; CoolLEDX puts geometry in the advertisement; the popled.cn platform has {get:"dev_info"}. Hardcoding a resolution from a marketing spec is how a replacement app breaks on the next batch.
  5. Static-analyse the APK (./scripts/run_static_target.sh <target>) for UUIDs, chunk sizes and CRC routines. A build with no UUIDs in the decompiled output usually means dynamic setup or a cloud-mediated path — escalate straight to a live capture.
  6. Capture connect + upload one small GIF. That single flow exercises handshake, geometry negotiation, chunking and flow control, which is most of what a replacement app needs.

docs.title: Common patterns across the category
docs.text:
• Design happens on the phone. The panel receives bitmaps or frame sequences, not vector or text primitives. A replacement app is a renderer plus a chunked uploader.
  • Flow control is device-driven. Every mapped protocol in this category has a continue/ack response that gates the next chunk. Ignoring it produces truncated uploads that look like corruption.
  • MTU is a common failure mode. SPOTLED explicitly reports a pause-sending error for chunks that are too large or too small.
  • No pairing, no auth. Most of these connect without bonding and accept commands from anyone in range. Treat as a privacy consideration for the wearer, not as a protocol obstacle.
  • Accounts are bolted on. Cloud login typically gates only the content library, not device control — which is why local-first replacements are viable for nearly all of them.

docs.title: LED space Wi-Fi LED Screen (YSP-001 family)
docs.text: Status: Complete (app-analysis based; no hardware capture in this project) Protocol: Wi-Fi (device AP, UDP 9090) + BLE variant Manufacturer: LOY SPACE / popled.cn Manufacturer Status: Active (LED space app itself stale since 2023)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Wi-Fi-controlled programmable LED screens marketed as YSP-001 — backpack screens, advertising vests, LED clothing and dynamic bags. Driven by the LED space app (com.yj.led, iOS id 1431362600). Static analysis of the app confirms this is a third app binding on the LOY SPACE / popled.cn platform already documented for the AUTOBABA LED Backpack and NYAN BT Image Controller: identical GATT UUIDs, identical JSON command vocabulary serialized to binary TLV by the same native library, popled.cn backend hosts throughout.

The same board family ships in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth variants; the app drives both. The Wi-Fi path is the interesting one here — it is fully local (device-hosted AP, no account) and needs no new reverse engineering beyond what the app itself reveals.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number YSP-001 (product listings; dev_model default "gy" in app) Display Full-color LED matrix; default geometry 64x64, 160x32 also seen; round panels carry "CXB5" in the model string Chipset Unknown (ESP-style AP behaviour on Wi-Fi units) Radio Wi-Fi (device AP) or BLE, per board variant FCC ID Unknown

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
No provisioning is required for AP-mode control — the panel permanently hosts its own hotspot. See Initial Device Setup; the machine-readable spec mirrors this in device.setup.

Property Value Setup required No Method softap_udp (device-hosted AP, UDP control) Setup AP / advertised name SSID starts with YS Passphrase protection plaintext (AP password; default 12345678 per the app's own help text) Confidence medium (from decompiled app; not replayed against hardware)

Factory reset: no account or owner binding exists to clear. Content can be wiped with the platform command {"cmd":{"delete":{"del_all":1}}}; a power cycle restores the AP. If the AP password was changed from the default and lost, no software recovery path is documented — check the unit for a hardware reset button. Confidence: low.

Rebinding to a new controller: trivial — join the device AP from the new client and re-run UDP discovery. Nothing ties the panel to a network or owner. The app does contain a station-mode provisioning command (param_wifi set with user/pwd/ip_svr/port_svr/sec_hb) that can move the panel onto a home network pointed at a server; that path is not needed for local control and its post-provisioning behaviour has not been captured.

docs.title: Wi-Fi Control Path
docs.text:
1. Join the device hotspot (SSID starts with YS, default password 12345678).
  2. Broadcast the TLV serialization of {"cmd":{"get":"dev_info"}} to 255.255.255.255:9090. The same probe documented for the AUTOBABA backpack (aa 55 ff ff 08 00 01 00 c1 03 0a 00 d4 03) applies.
  3. The device replies with {"ack":{"dev_info":{id_dev, model, version, ...}},"sno":N}; the app adopts the reply sender's address (expected to be the AP gateway 192.168.4.1, though the app does not hardcode it).
  4. All further commands go unicast to the learned address on UDP port 9090.

Transport details (from the com.yj.led app's UDP packet builder, its packet date/sequence utilities and its constants class): each datagram chunk carries an outer u16-LE length prefix; large sends split into 180-byte chunks (120 on the app's other send path) at ~5 ms intervals; sequence numbers start at 4294901761; the app resends up to 10 times at 8 s intervals until an ACK with the expected sno arrives; error replies are {"cmd":"err"} / {"cmd":"failed"}.

docs.title: Packet Format
docs.text: Same 0xAA55-framed binary TLV as the BLE path — see the AUTOBABA doc. JSON is the app-internal command form; the app's bundled native TLV library serializes it to the wire and decodes replies.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
The shared LOY SPACE vocabulary (power, light 0–15, get dev_info, delete del_all, rotate, pgm_play with the 60-slot ids_pro array) applies; see the AUTOBABA doc. Commands first seen in the LED space app:

Command JSON Description Get screen params {get:"param_dev"} Screen geometry / model Get Wi-Fi params {get:"param_wifi"} Wi-Fi configuration Set Wi-Fi params {param_wifi:{type:0,user:...,pwd:...,ip_svr:...,port_svr:"9090",sec_hb:30}} Station-mode provisioning Dispatch program {dispatch:{type:1,id_pro:N,play_fixed_time:32767}} Play one program for a fixed time Show flag {get:"show_dev"} / {show_dev:N} Device show flag Program flicker {pgm_flicker:{type:0,count_pgm:N,time:T}} Cycle through programs Bluetooth control {bluetooth:{type:0,val:N}} / {get:"bluetooth"} Radio control Set time {timing:"<timestamp>"} Device RTC Delete by id {delete:{del_ids:[...]}} Delete specific programs

Program upload uses the pkts_program JSON structure: property_pro (width/height/gray/type_color), list_region geometry, and list_item entries of type text_pic (text/color/font) or graphic carrying a zip_bmp payload — a zlib-compressed 24-bit BMP rendered app-side. App templates use id_pro 11–19; the platform supports 60 sparse program slots.

docs.title: BLE Variant
docs.text: Identical GATT surface to the AUTOBABA backpack: service 0000fff0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, write …fff2…, notify …fff1…, advertised name prefix YS / TL. See the AUTOBABA doc for the full BLE protocol.

docs.title: Backend API
docs.text: popled.cn hosts seen in the app: a.popled.cn (main), auth.popled.cn, wxbtapp.popled.cn:8443 (material), app.popled.cn (help/privacy pages). None are needed for local control. Vendor backend credentials recovered from the app are excluded per the project clean-room rules.

docs.title: LEDs2RAVE4 / Lunchbox Dream LED
docs.text: Status: Minimally verified SPOTLED generation, plus official multi-frame capture Protocol: BLE (three incompatible controller generations) Manufacturer: SPLED / Host No.4 Technology / Shenzhen I-ledshow

docs.title: Choose the controller first
docs.text:
These panels are not one protocol. Identify the design app and GATT service before choosing a client.

Generation Design app Controller / protocol Dream LED Skin v1 LED CHORD (com.spled.pzse) SP107E, 0xFFE0 Dream LED Skin 2.0 SPOTLED (com.led.spotled) Matrix panel, 0xFF20 Dream Skin 3.0 early SPOTLED Matrix panel, 0xFF20 Dream Skin 3.0 recent and future iLEDColor (com.led.iledcolor) Separate A950 protocol

For DreamPanel v3, a horizontal serial-number display selects iLEDColor; vertical selects SPOTLED. The tested iLEDColor unit had no FF20 service and is documented in iLEDColor LED Matrix Panels. The v1 skin is an SPI pixel-strip product; later products are matrix panels whose geometry must be queried, not inferred from marketing counts.

docs.title: Hardware validation
docs.text:
Property Value v1 controllers SP107E / SP110E, source-derived tables SPOTLED test unit 96×16 RGB888, advertised frames 20, receive window 7280 bytes iLEDColor test unit 32×64, separate spec Radio BLE Power External USB power bank

This project completed all three SPOTLED information queries and static / single-frame native-scroll uploads on 2026-11-07/08. A supplied 2026-11-10 official-app capture then confirmed one- and three-frame RGB888 uploads, visible RGB order and receive-window resume. Those captures were analysed, not generated by our client. Arbitrary frame counts, other geometry, SP107E and SP110E remain unverified.

docs.title: SPOTLED protocol
docs.text:
The canonical reference is SPOTLED LED Panels. The Lunchbox legacy service map is:

UUID Role Live properties 0000ff20-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb SPOTLED service Confirmed 0000ff21-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Commands and responses Write without response, notify 0000ff22-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Bulk data Write without response 0000ff10-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb OTA service Reported; see canonical spec
  1. Connect and enable FF21 notifications through the GATT client.
  2. Send Version 04 10 00 00, DisplayInfo 04 12 00 00 and BufferSize 04 14 00 00, awaiting response types 17, 19 and 21.
  3. Use DisplayInfo geometry and the receive-capacity notification; do not issue an ATT read or write descriptor bytes to FF21 itself.

Uploads use a 15-byte data header and typed records on FF22. Writes may not exceed MTU − 3, but the official app chose 182-byte chunks at MTU 512. Start succeeds with type 2 and finish with type 4, both status zero. Resume from the device-driven ContinueSending offset: the official three-frame transfers paused at exactly 7280 bytes and completed at 13902 bytes. PauseSending type 254 alone does not diagnose MTU.

Earlier custom-client three/eight-frame attempts failed, but the official path proves three-frame RGB works. Their byte-level difference and the advertised 20-frame guarantee remain open. Static and animated decoded images from the official capture match the physical panel.

docs.title: SP107E / SP110E commands
docs.text: All commands are four bytes [d0] [d1] [d2] [cmd] on 0xFFE1. These tables remain source-derived rather than live-verified.

docs.title: SP107E
docs.text: Command Bytes Description Power on 00 00 00 aa Turn on Power off 00 00 00 bb Turn off Set colour rr gg bb 0c Static RGB; 0x04 is colour order, not static colour Set brightness vv 00 00 0a 0–255 Set effect vv 00 00 08 1–180 dynamic, 181 static Set speed vv 00 00 09 1–186 Set sensitivity vv 00 00 13 Audio gain Query status 00 00 00 02 26 bytes in two packets

docs.title: SP110E
docs.text:
Command Bytes Description Power on 00 00 00 aa Turn on Power off 00 00 00 ab Turn off Set colour rr gg bb 1e Static RGB Set brightness vv 00 00 2a 0–255 Set effect vv 00 00 2c 1–120 dynamic, 121 static Set speed vv 00 00 03 0–255, not the SP107E range Query status 00 00 00 10 12-byte reply

Real SP110E hardware uses FFE0/FFE1. The older assignment of its opcodes to the FF20 SPOTLED transport was a misattribution.

docs.title: Discovery, pairing and reset
docs.text:
Known name prefixes are SP1, LBXDRMSKIN_LED_ and SpotLED_. FF20 identifies SPOTLED when advertised; some short samples contain only 0x1812, which is a shared HID service and must not be matched alone. Confirm GATT after connecting.

No account or network provisioning is needed. Bondless SPOTLED clients work. The official app can optionally initiate legacy Just Works pairing; the panel responds No Bonding/no LTK and the phone enables encryption for that connection. There is no persistent bond or PIN, but it is inaccurate to say pairing never occurs. Other controller generations remain source-derived.

No factory-reset procedure is established. Power-cycling drops a connection but is not a factory wipe. Rebinding is a fresh scan after closing the old central.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:

  • SPOTLED OTA wire compatibility/recovery, AE30, other geometries, text/font records, settings writes and reset behavior.
  • iLEDColor settings beyond its separately documented Connect/TestPass and upload flows.

docs.title: LEGO Smart Play Smart Brick
docs.text: Status: Spec Available Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: LEGO Manufacturer Status: Active (LEGO sells the sets and runs the LEGO SMART Assist app; the protocol is undocumented)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The SMART Brick is the 2x4 electronic brick at the centre of LEGO's SMART Play system, launched in 2026. It has:

  • a speaker and a sound synthesiser
  • an LED array
  • an accelerometer, colour and light sensing, and a microphone for sound pressure
  • coils that charge it wirelessly, read SMART Tags and SMART Minifigures, and sense how far away other bricks are and which way they face

It plays on its own, with no phone. The LEGO SMART Assist app is for grown-ups. It shows the battery level, registers the brick to a LEGO account and installs firmware updates.

This page covers one mode only: the brick talking to a phone while it sits on its SMART Charger. In that mode any BLE client can read the model, firmware version, battery level and MAC, and can read and set the name and the volume. None of that needs an account, a signature or pairing. Registration, telemetry consent, factory reset and firmware updates are different. Each one needs a signature that only LEGO's servers can make.

The spec is built from the node-smartplay research notes and library. Its authors took the facts from Android HCI captures of the vendor app, a decompile of that app and a disassembly of the brick's firmware. The WDX part is checked against Arm's open-source Cordio BLE stack, which the brick runs. This project has not run anything against a brick and holds no capture. Every protocol fact in the spec is reported or hypothesis, and the spec is untested. Upstream calls its own notes incomplete and says some payloads are encrypted.

Out of scope:

  • Brick-to-brick play. It uses Bluetooth 5.4 PAwR on a separate address, with its own internal registers.
  • The WDX file-transfer channels (firmware images, fault log, telemetry).
  • LEGO Powered Up, BOOST and SPIKE hubs. They speak LWP3, a different protocol.
  • MINDSTORMS NXT and EV3, which are Bluetooth Classic.

SMART Tag events are not on the BLE surface at all. Upstream's firmware analysis found no register or notification that reports a tag.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number SMART Brick. Device Information reports manufacturer LEGO, model Smart Brick. It ships with a SMART Charger in the All-in-One sets (Star Wars 75421, 75423, 75427; Pokémon 72164, 72167) Chipset EM Microelectronic EM9305 BLE 5.4 SoC running the Arm Cordio stack, plus a custom LEGO mixed-signal ASIC for the coils, sensors, LEDs and sound (upstream, from teardown photos) Radio BLE only. It uses an LE random address that rotates often. The real MAC (OUI 9c:9a:c0, LEGO System A/S) is in register 0x84 Power Rechargeable battery. It charges wirelessly on the SMART Charger, which takes up to two bricks. The charger's LED shows red, yellow or green for the battery level Buttons None. The brick wakes when shaken (LEGO's getting-started page) Firmware seen 2.29.2 in upstream's capture FCC ID NPI106929 ("Smart brick", LEGO System A/S, granted 2025-12-10). Our manuals pass found this grant on fccid.co. We could not re-fetch the page while writing this, so treat the ID as unconfirmed

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No. Nothing is provisioned. The brick must have started up on its charger Method ble_direct (primary). The vendor app route is cloud_account Setup AP / advertised name Smart Brick (exact), company 0x0397 (LEGO), service 0xFEF6 Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (upstream captures and a published open client, not replayed here)

The one rule: the brick accepts connections only if it started up on the SMART Charger. Upstream's firmware analysis says the brick checks for the dock once, at boot. Two dock types qualify. Nothing after that turns on connectable advertising: not motion, not play, not a timer, and not setting a running brick on the charger.

How the brick started What a scanner sees On the charger Connectable Smart Brick advertising with 0xFEF6 Off the charger, single-brick content Nothing Off the charger, multi-brick content Smart Brick advertising that cannot be connected, plus PAwR on another address On the charger, then lifted off Probably still connectable. Upstream infers this: the stack restarts advertising after each disconnect without checking the dock again Firmware update Its own update-mode advertising only

To bring a brick up from a client:

  1. Let the brick go to sleep, set it on a SMART Charger, and wake it there. LEGO's guide says a SMART Brick wakes when shaken. Nobody has documented whether setting a sleeping brick on the charger starts it by itself.
  2. Close the SMART Assist app on any phone near by.
  3. Scan for a connectable advertisement named exactly Smart Brick with manufacturer data under company 0x0397. Service 0xFEF6 is advertised too, but every Cordio WDX product uses it. The address rotates, so do not store it.
  4. Connect, open notifications in the vendor app's order, and run the handshake (see Connection sequence).
  5. Keep polling about every 500 ms. Each poll reads 0x93, sends the keepalive, and reads 0x20.

Factory reset: there is one, but only through the app. Register 0x95 resets the brick, and it acts only after a server-signed command of type 3 in the same connection. So the reset needs the SMART Assist app, signed in, with the brick docked. No button or charger gesture is known. What the reset clears (registration, name, volume, consent, bonds) is not documented. The spec records the procedure as verified: false, with upstream's register map as its basis.

Rebinding: there is no network to rejoin. The local surface belongs to no phone, so any client can connect to a brick that started on the charger. Moving a brick to a different LEGO account is a registration matter for the app and LEGO's backend (ownership proof is signature-gated), not a BLE one.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode app_layer. Link-layer pairing is not needed; privileged operations need an ECDSA signature Bonding optional. Reading register 0x86 makes the brick request pairing PIN source None One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time Unknown Confidence medium

Entering pairing mode: here this means connectable mode, which is the one rule above: start the brick on the charger. The brick shows no sign that it is connectable. The charger's LED shows the battery level.

Unpairing: unknown. The stock WDX register set has a delete-bonds register (0x07), but nobody has shown that LEGO implements it. Forgetting the brick in the phone's Bluetooth settings drops the phone's half of any bond.

Recovery: close the SMART Assist app. If a phone asks to pair out of nowhere, something read register 0x86. Nothing on the local surface needs that register.

docs.title: Advertising
docs.text: Field Value Local name Smart Brick Address LE random, rotates often AD flags 0x06 (LE General Discoverable, BR/EDR not supported) Service UUIDs 0000fef6-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb (WDX; SIG member UUID of Wicentric, shared by every Cordio WDX product) Manufacturer data 97 03 (company 0x0397, LEGO System A/S) then 00 60 00 00 00 00 in the one published capture. The meaning is unknown, so do not match on it

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 00001800-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Generic Access Device Name Smart Brick, Appearance 0x0000 00001801-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Generic Attribute Service Changed 00002a05-… (the app subscribes to it) 0000180a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Device Information Manufacturer LEGO, model Smart Brick, firmware and software revision (e.g. 2.29.2) 0000fef6-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb WDX Cordio's Wireless Data Exchange service; characteristics below 005f0002-2ff2-4ed5-b045-4c7463617865 Control Point write + notify. Every register read and write goes here. This is Cordio's Device Configuration characteristic 005f0003-2ff2-4ed5-b045-4c7463617865 File transfer control write without response + notify. Cordio's File Transfer Control. Not documented here 005f0004-2ff2-4ed5-b045-4c7463617865 File transfer data write without response + notify. Cordio's File Transfer Data. Not documented here 005f0005-2ff2-4ed5-b045-4c7463617865 WDX authentication write + notify. Idle in normal use. LEGO's signed commands use register 0x87 instead 005f0001-3ff2-4ed5-b045-4c7463617865 LEGO custom service Purpose unknown 005f0009-3ff2-4ed5-b045-4c7463617865 Unknown input write. Takes writes and shows no effect 005f000a-3ff2-4ed5-b045-4c7463617865 Unknown channel read, write, notify. Sends empty notifications now and then

The last seven bytes of the WDX base, 45 4c7463617865, spell "exactLE" backwards. That was the stack's name before it became Arm Cordio. The UUIDs and properties of 0002–0005 match the open-source Cordio definitions exactly.

docs.title: Register framing
docs.text:
Everything goes through the Control Point, written as an ATT Write Request.

Frame Bytes Direction Read 01 RR client → brick Write 02 RR VV… client → brick Reply / update 03 RR VV… brick → client, by notification
  • A reply echoes the register it answers. Match replies to requests by register, and keep one request per register in flight.
  • A reply has no status byte. If you need to know that a write took, read the register back.
  • Do not count on a reply to a write. The keepalive gets none. node-smartplay waits for 03 81 after a volume write, but upstream shows no reply there, and the library does not wait after a name write.

These are Cordio's WDX get, set and update operations. Registers 0x01–0x25 are the stock Cordio set; 0x80–0x96 are LEGO's.

docs.title: Register map
docs.text:
Sizes count value bytes only, without the 03 RR header.

Local surface (no signature):

Reg Access Value Notes 0x08 read uint16 LE ATT MTU (f4 00 = 244 in upstream's capture) 0x20 read uint8 Battery, 0–100 % 0x21 read string, 18-byte field, null-terminated Model identifier 0x22 read 16 bytes ASCII, null-padded Firmware version, e.g. 2.29.2 0x80 read/write up to 12 bytes UTF-8, null-padded Brick name. The limit is 12 bytes, not characters 0x81 read/write uint8 code Volume: 0x0a low (10), 0x28 medium (40), 0x64 high (100) 0x84 read 6 bytes, most-significant first Brick MAC, e.g. 9c 9a c0 dd ee ff. The stable identity 0x85 read uint8 code Upgrade state: 0 ready, 1 in progress, 2 battery too low 0x88 read 20 bytes Firmware build fingerprint. Upstream found it the same on every brick it checked 0x89 read uint8 code Build pipeline stage (development, QA, staging or release). The number-to-stage mapping is unknown 0x90 write ea 00 Keepalive. No reply 0x93 read uint8 Charging/connection state. Only 0xa1 has been reported; the bits are unknown

Needs a signature first:

Reg Access Role 0x23 / 0x24 write / read Enter diagnostic mode / diagnostic mode complete 0x25 write Disconnect and reset 0x26 write Disconnect, arm the firmware update, reset (the last step of an update) 0x91 write Ownership proof 0x95 write Factory reset

Signed-command registers: 0x86 (read, 8-byte nonce; reading it triggers pairing) and 0x87 (write, 75 bytes). See Signed commands.

Stock WDX link registers:

  • 0x01: ask for a connection-parameter update
  • 0x02: current connection parameters
  • 0x03: ask the brick to disconnect
  • 0x04: security level
  • 0x05: ask for link security
  • 0x06: service changed
  • 0x07: delete bonds
  • 0x09: ask for a PHY update
  • 0x0a: current PHY

Not understood:

  • 0x82: file-transfer write offset
  • 0x83: internal state
  • 0x92: one byte; upstream guesses it is tag-reader status
  • 0x94: upstream reads it as a hardware timer
  • 0x96: travel (shipping) mode. The payload and the effect are not documented, and the spec declares no command for it

docs.title: Connection sequence
docs.text:
This is the vendor app's sequence as upstream captured it. node-smartplay follows it.

  1. Open notifications in this order:
  2. 005f000a-3ff2-…
  3. 005f0002-2ff2-… (the Control Point)
  4. 005f0003-2ff2-…
  5. 005f0004-2ff2-…
  6. 005f0005-2ff2-…
  7. 00002a05-…

The first CCCD write to the Control Point may fail. Retry it after about 5 s. 2. The brick may send 03 02 00 0c 00 00 00 f4 01 before any request. Upstream calls this frame an idle beacon. 3. Handshake reads (the app runs these four reads three times over): 

→ 01 22    ← 03 22 "2.29.2" + nulls   firmware, 16 bytes
→ 01 81    ← 03 81 64                 volume high (100)
→ 01 84    ← 03 84 9c 9a c0 dd ee ff  MAC (placeholder after the OUI)
→ 01 80    ← 03 80 "Smart Brick"      name
4. Setup: send 02 90 ea 00 (the keepalive, no reply), then 01 08. The reply 03 08 f4 00 is the MTU. 5. Poll every ~500 ms: 01 93 → 03 93 a1, then 02 90 ea 00, then 01 20 → 03 20 xx.

Nobody has established whether the brick drops the link when the keepalive stops.

The idle beacon, a hypothesis. The beacon has exactly the shape of the connection-parameter update in the open-source Cordio WDX profile. Cordio sends that update each time the link's parameters change (wdxs_main.c, wdxs_dc.c). Read that way it decodes as:

  • register 0x02
  • status 0
  • connection interval 0x000c × 1.25 ms = 15 ms
  • latency 0
  • supervision timeout 0x01f4 × 10 ms = 5 s

If this is right, the frame is the brick reporting the parameters the central just negotiated, and it will come again whenever they change. Nobody has confirmed it on a brick.

docs.title: Volume and name
docs.text:
→ 01 85        ← 03 85 00      upgrade state must be 0 (ready)
→ 02 81 0a                     volume low (0x28 medium, 0x64 high)
→ 01 81        ← 03 81 0a      confirm

→ 02 80 <1-12 bytes UTF-8, no terminator>
→ 01 80        ← 03 80 <name, null-padded>   confirm

docs.title: Signed commands
docs.text:
The privileged operations need an ECDSA P-256 challenge-response. The brick checks the signature against a public key built into its firmware. The matching private key exists only on LEGO's servers, and the app asks LEGO's backend to sign for the signed-in owner. A replacement client cannot make these signatures. This spec gives no way round that. It documents the layout so an implementer recognises the exchange.

  1. Read 0x86 → 03 86 + 8-byte nonce. The nonce is fresh on every connection. This read makes the brick request link-layer pairing.
  2. message = nonce ‖ 02 02 01; digest = SHA-256(message).
  3. The signature is r ‖ s, 32 bytes each, big-endian, made with LEGO's key.
  4. Write 02 87 + the 75-byte payload below.
  5. The brick replies 03 87 01 (accepted) or 03 87 00 (rejected). The app then writes the operation's register.
Offset Length Field 0 8 Nonce echo, exactly as read from 0x86 8 3 02 02 01 (the only value in published captures) 11 32 ECDSA r, big-endian 43 32 ECDSA s, big-endian

Upstream lists four signed command types: 1 unlock, 2 telemetry consent, 3 factory reset and 4 start firmware upgrade. Nobody has shown whether the last suffix byte carries the type.

Test vector for building the message (invented nonce):

  • nonce 0123456789abcdef
  • message 0123456789abcdef020201
  • SHA-256 5c8468499fbcba5e62727e9301ff46ec15ad99f4ba916376a81f1705b6592bf6

The 77-byte write needs an ATT MTU of at least 80. Everything on the local surface fits the default 23-byte MTU.

docs.title: Firmware updates
docs.text:
Updates come only through SMART Assist, with images from LEGO's backend. Upstream gives an outline and says it inferred it from the decompiled app:

  1. Check that 0x85 is 0.
  2. Upload the image over the WDX file-transfer characteristics in chunks of at most 100 bytes.
  3. Verify the image.
  4. Write 0x26, which disconnects, arms the update and resets the brick.

Starting an upgrade needs a signed command (type 4). The image header has a signature field. No update bytes appear in the spec, and a client should never interrupt an update in progress. The spec records this as a firmware_update feature, vendor_ble, in_place.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• A "Smart Brick" is in the scan but will not connect. The brick started off the charger, or it is in multi-brick play. It checks for the dock only at boot. Let it sleep and restart it on the charger.
  • No "Smart Brick" at all. The brick is asleep, or it started off the charger with single-brick content, which does not advertise. It could also be mid-update, which uses a different advertisement.
  • Enabling notifications on the Control Point fails. Upstream saw the first CCCD write fail. Wait about 5 s and try again.
  • The phone suddenly asks to pair. Something read 0x86. The local surface never needs it.
  • Volume will not change. 0x85 was not 0: an update is running (1) or the battery is low (2). The only levels known are 10, 40 and 100.
  • A reply "never arrives" after a write. Many writes get no reply. Read the register back instead of waiting.
  • Replies arrive in the wrong order. The unprompted 03 02 … frame can come first. Match replies by register byte.

docs.title: LG webOS TV Second Screen Protocol (SSAP)
docs.text: Status: Documented from open-source clients — not replayed against hardware here Protocol: WiFi (SSDP + WebSocket JSON on ports 3000/3001) Manufacturer: LG Electronics Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every LG smart TV since webOS 1.0 (2014) exposes the same local control protocol: a WebSocket on port 3000 (wss on 3001), a JSON register/pairing handshake that the user must accept on the TV screen, and SSAP URIs (ssap://audio/volumeUp, ssap://system/turnOff, …) for every command afterwards. LG never published a wire-format document; the protocol is known through LG's own open-source Connect SDK and the community clients (aiowebostv, bscpylgtv, openHAB's lgwebos binding).

Transport gap: control needs a WebSocket transport with client-key pairing — not yet supported by the reference app, whose command transports are HTTP and SOAP. The spec therefore records each command's wire spelling (action) and the frame format (webos_common) without declaring an executable transport:; nothing in it should be turned into an HTTP request.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
SSDP M-SEARCH with:

ST: urn:lge-com:service:webos-second-screen:1

The response LOCATION is a standard UPnP device-description XML (on the TV's own UPnP port, not 3000) carrying UDN, serialNumber, friendlyName and modelName. Use UDN then serialNumber for identity, friendlyName for display. The TV sends ssdp:byebye for this search target when it powers off, which doubles as an availability signal. There is no mDNS advertisement for the second-screen service.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Prerequisite on the TV: Settings > Network > LG Connect Apps = On (older firmware: Settings > General > Mobile App). Then, per connection:

  1. Open ws://<ip>:3000; on refusal or a rejected upgrade, fall back to wss://<ip>:3001 (self-signed certificate — clients disable verification; late firmware enforces wss).
  2. Send {"id":"hello","type":"hello","payload":{}}, then a pre-registration ssap://system/getSystemInfo request (newer firmware expects it first).
  3. Send the register frame (pairingType: "PROMPT", pairing manifest with the permissions list and the boilerplate signed block every client copies from Connect SDK — the exact bytes are in aiowebostv's handshake.py).
  4. First time, the TV shows an accept prompt on screen; on acceptance a second message of type registered delivers the client-key (32 hex chars). Store it: it is included in the register payload on every later connection and is bearer credentials until revoked on the TV.

docs.title: Command channel
docs.text:
Commands are JSON text frames on the paired socket:

{"id": 12, "type": "request", "uri": "ssap://audio/volumeUp", "payload": {}}

type: "subscribe" turns any query into a push stream on the same id. Success answers type: "response" with payload.returnValue: true; failure answers type: "error" — 404 no such service or method means the URI is absent on that firmware, 401 insufficient permissions means it is outside the pairing manifest.

docs.title: SSAP URIs (reported, from bscpylgtv / aiowebostv)
docs.text:
Group URI Notes Power ssap://system/turnOff Standby; socket drops with the TV Screen ssap://com.webos.service.tvpower/power/turnOffScreen / turnOnScreen webOS 4+; older sets used the removed com.webos.service.tv.power/* pair Volume ssap://audio/volumeUp / volumeDown / setVolume / setMute / getVolume / getStatus Absolute set works on internal speakers only Channel ssap://tv/channelUp / channelDown / openChannel / getChannelList / getCurrentChannel Tuner input Input ssap://tv/getExternalInputList / switchInput Inputs are apps too (com.webos.app.hdmi1…) Apps ssap://com.webos.applicationManager/listLaunchPoints / listApps / getForegroundAppInfo; ssap://system.launcher/launch / close launch takes {id}, optional params, contentId deep link Media ssap://media.controls/play / pause / stop / rewind / fastForward Acts on the foreground app Notify ssap://system.notifications/createToast Icon payload ignored on newer firmware Text ssap://com.webos.service.ime/insertText / sendEnterKey / deleteCharacters On-screen keyboard fields System ssap://system/getSystemInfo, ssap://api/getServiceList, ssap://com.webos.service.update/getCurrentSWInformation Identity/version reads

Removed by firmware (kept for the record): ssap://system/turnOn, the 3D pair, the webOS <4 screen-power pair.

docs.title: Remote buttons (pointer input socket)
docs.text:
Button presses are not SSAP requests. Request ssap://com.webos.service.networkinput/getPointerInputSocket, open the second WebSocket its socketPath returns, and send plain-text frames:

type:button
name:HOME

(key:value lines, blank-line terminated; also type:move/click/scroll for the Magic Remote pointer). Known names: LEFT, RIGHT, UP, DOWN, ENTER (the OK button), BACK, EXIT, HOME, INFO, digits 0-9, RED/GREEN/YELLOW/BLUE, PLAY, PAUSE, STOP. On the earliest webOS 1.x sets (2014–2015) the socket is accepted but inert — a firmware limitation; only SSAP commands work there.

docs.title: Power on
docs.text:
There is no network power-on (ssap://system/turnOn was removed). Wake is Wake-on-LAN, gated on the TV: Settings > General > Mobile TV On > Turn On Via WiFi (2017+ models), or Settings > Support > IP control settings > Wake on LAN (2025+ models); it works most reliably over Ethernet and requires the TV's MAC, captured while it is on.

Power in the spec is therefore one-way: a stateful Power switch entity binds only turn_off: power_off (Spec Evolution P13) — no turn_on to bind, no power state to read; an unreachable socket is the closest thing to "off" webOS offers.

docs.title: Blocking updates without losing the clock
docs.text: Firmware updates come from snu.lge.com (the check) and su.lge.com / su-ssl.lge.com (the image) — the names the webOS Homebrew Channel's "Block system updates" option points at localhost. Blocking them, and LG's ad and telemetry names, is safe. Blocking the Service Delivery Platform (<country>.lgtvsdp.com, and nextlgsdp.com on newer sets) is not: the TV takes its clock from it (it is not known to use NTP), and apps fail certificate checks once the clock resets. The spec's cloud.egress records each name and its cost; the generated lists leave the clock out. See Blocking Vendor Updates and the Cloud.

docs.title: LIFX Z
docs.text: Status: Local discovery and UDP LAN protocol summary documented Protocol: WiFi (mDNS + binary UDP on port 56700) Manufacturer: LIFX Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: LIFX Z strips use the LIFX binary LAN protocol over UDP port 56700 with no authentication. The observed devices advertise HomeKit HAP records with md=LIFX Z; after mDNS resolution, clients should send LIFX GetService message type 2 to port 56700.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Use:

python scripts/lifx_discover.py --timeout 5

The script browses _hap._tcp.local., filters TXT md=LIFX Z, resolves the host address, and sends a UDP GetService probe.

docs.title: LAN Protocol
docs.text: Message Type Description GetService 2 Discover LIFX service type and port StateService 3 Service discovery response Get 101 Request light state SetColor 102 Set HSBK color State 107 Light state response SetPower 117 Set power

docs.title: Setup (adopting a reset strip)
docs.text:
An unprovisioned or factory-reset strip hosts an open AP named with the LIFX prefix and sits at 172.16.0.1 on it. The credential exchange is the deprecated access-point message family the original published LAN protocol documented — GetAccessPoints (0x130), SetAccessPoint (0x131, plaintext passphrase, interface = STATION), StateAccessPoint (0x132) — over the same UDP port 56700. Transcribed from legacy public reverse-engineering documentation (magicmonkey/lifxjs), unverified against hardware here, and LCM3/Matter-era firmware onboards over BLE instead. Full layouts, timing and troubleshooting: device.setup in the machine-readable spec.

Home Assistant: the core LIFX integration speaks the LAN protocol documented here.

docs.title: LimitlessLED / Mi-Light WiFi Bridge (legacy)
docs.text: Status: Complete (discovery + transport hardware-verified; command tables from public docs) Protocol: WiFi (UDP/TCP 8899 legacy byte protocol; UDP 48899 discovery) Manufacturer: LimitlessLED / Mi-Light (Futlight) Manufacturer Status: Abandoned

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The LimitlessLED/Mi-Light WiFi bridge relays LAN commands to 2.4 GHz RF bulbs (RGB, dual-white, RGBW, RGBW/WW-CW). It was sold 2012–2017 under many brands (LimitlessLED, Mi-Light, Easybulb, applight, …) and its protocol was published by the vendor and is now community-maintained prior art. This spec covers the legacy v1–v5 generation — the one verified live on our LAN — and includes the v6 ("iBox") layout for recognition only.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Model Number WiFi Bridge v1–v5 (observed unit reports module HF-LPB130) Chipset Shanghai High-Flying WiFi module (HF-LPB1xx) + MCU + PL1176/LT8900-class 2.4 GHz transceiver Radio WiFi 802.11n (2.4 GHz) + proprietary 2.4 GHz RF to bulbs FCC ID —

Observed unit: 192.0.2.194, MAC 34:EA:E7:AA:BB:CC (OUI Shanghai High-Flying), TCP 8899 open, HTTP admin on :80 behind Basic auth.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes (bridge must join home WiFi) Method softap_http Setup AP / advertised name open AP named milight* / HF-*; bridge at 10.10.100.254 Passphrase protection plaintext (web UI form posts; Basic auth with default admin/admin) Confidence medium (public vendor docs; not re-run against our unit)

Join the setup AP, browse to http://10.10.100.254, set Work Mode to STA, choose the home SSID, enter its passphrase (WPA2PSK/AES), restart. Then rediscover on the home LAN by broadcasting HF-A11ASSISTHREAD (or Link_Wi-Fi on older firmware) to UDP 48899 — the reply is a CSV line ip,mac,module.

Bulb pairing: power the bulb, then send the target zone's ON command within ~3 s; the bulb flashes to confirm. Unlink by sending zone ON five times in the same window. (Public docs; not hardware-verified here.)

Factory reset: restore from the module web UI's management page (or the hardware reset button where exposed); the module falls back to AP mode. Bulb pairings generally survive. Confidence: low.

Rebinding to a new network: possible in place from the web UI, but the module only hosts its setup AP while it cannot see its configured network — power-cycle the bridge with the old SSID gone and it falls back to AP mode.

docs.title: Discovery (hardware-verified 2026-08-19)
docs.text: Broadcast ASCII HF-A11ASSISTHREAD to UDP 48899 → reply 192.0.2.194,34EAE7AABBCC,HF-LPB130 from source port 48899. The older probe Link_Wi-Fi got no reply from this unit (its firmware answers only the HF-A11 string). The v6 session handshake on UDP 5987/8899 is not answered by this unit — it is a legacy-generation bridge.

docs.title: Legacy commands (v1–v5, port 8899)
docs.text: Every command is 3 bytes: <cmd> <arg> 0x55 (arg = 0x00 except brightness and colour). No acknowledgements — repeat ~3× with ≥100 ms spacing.

docs.title: RGBW bulbs
docs.text: Command Bytes Notes All on / off 42 00 55 / 41 00 55 Zone 1–4 on 45/47/49/4B 00 55 Zone 1–4 off 46/48/4A/4C 00 55 All white C2 00 55 zone: C5/C7/C9/CB Set color 40 <hue> 55 wheel starts at violet: 0x00 violet … 0xB0 red … 0xF0 lavender Set brightness 4E <lvl> 55 0x02–0x1B, applies to last-addressed zone Disco cycle / faster / slower 4D / 44 / 43 00 55 Night mode OFF, then OFF|0x80 ~100 ms later e.g. 46 00 55 then C6 00 55

docs.title: Dual-white bulbs
docs.text: Command Bytes All on / off 35 00 55 / 39 00 55 Zone 1–4 on / off 38/3D/37/32 / 3B/33/3A/36 (+00 55) Warmer / cooler 3E 00 55 / 3F 00 55 Brightness up / down 3C 00 55 / 34 00 55

docs.title: Lippert OneControl BLE Gateway
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (untested) Protocol: BLE GATT with application-layer unlock Manufacturer: Lippert Components / LCI (active)

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: This gateway can move RV awnings, slide-outs and levelling jacks, and can control a generator. A command sent without a person watching the mechanism can crush someone, damage the vehicle or create a carbon-monoxide hazard. Start with read-only discovery and status. Keep people, pets and obstructions clear, use the manufacturer's interlocks, and never experiment while the RV is occupied by someone unaware of the test.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The spec covers the Unity X270D, X270L, X1.5 and X180T gateways (the X4 is named but not scoped): device-specs/devices/lippert-onecontrol-ble.yaml. It records the advertisement, the pairing variants, the GATT initialization order, and the decoded MyRvLink command templates for lights, relays, HVAC zones and the generator. This project has not driven a gateway from the document.

The spec is incomplete. It was first published truncated, and the blocks it relied on (the TEA unlock and step-2 key layouts, the COBS/CRC-8 framing, the event and device-table layouts, the advertisement TLVs and the X180T IDS-CAN tunnel) were never in the repository. Its remaining_unknowns lists each gap; the facts live in the community integration phurth/ha-onecontrol and have to be re-derived from there. Awning commands are not declared at all.

docs.title: Setup and pairing
docs.text: Two pairing routes exist. Do not assume that one gateway supports both.

docs.title: Push-to-Pair gateways
docs.text:
1. Scan for a name beginning LCIRemote and check the pairing-available bit in the manufacturer data.
  2. Begin pairing, then press Connect on the OneControl panel. Depending on the panel this is a physical or on-screen control.
  3. Connect immediately, request MTU 185 and complete a Just Works bond. On BlueZ, register a NoInputNoOutput agent first.
  4. Run the spec's initialization: unlock on 0x0012/0x0013, then subscribe to 0x0034 and 0x0011.
  5. If a four-byte seed arrives on 0x0011, ask for the six-digit owner-tag PIN and answer with the step-2 key described in the spec. Some X270L units use this application-layer check even though their BLE bond was Just Works.

docs.title: PIN gateways
docs.text:
1. Read the six-digit PIN from the gateway's owner tag.
  2. Connect directly from a local Bluetooth adapter with an agent that returns that PIN as the SMP passkey.
  3. Run initialization and answer any application-layer seed as above.

An ESPHome Bluetooth proxy cannot relay the passkey exchange and cannot share a BlueZ host's bond. Pair from the radio that will run the client.

Do not publish the sticker PIN, derived keys, a unit's MAC address or its RV configuration. Those belong to the owner, not to the protocol document.

docs.title: Factory reset and rebinding
docs.text:
No reset that clears phone bonds is established. The gateway also stores the RV manufacturer's output mapping, switch inputs and interlocks; losing that configuration is not an acceptable experiment. Do not send a reset or configuration write speculatively.

To add a phone or host, repeat the appropriate pairing route with a fresh Connect press or the sticker PIN. Whether a new bond evicts an older one is unknown. There is no Wi-Fi network to rejoin.

docs.title: Protocol summary
docs.text: Authentication has three separate layers: SMP bonding, an application-layer TEA unlock on every connection, and on some gateways a second PIN-derived answer. A generic BLE client cannot skip the latter two. The YAML declares the initialization order, the relevant UUIDs, the seed sizes and byte order, the advertisement variants and its remaining unknowns, but not the TEA details or the step-2 key layout. Every MyRvLink frame is COBS-encoded with a CRC-8, so its custom protocol handler is required for the command surface; no generic entity support is claimed.

docs.title: References
docs.text: The spec links the public phurth/ha-onecontrol integration (MIT), which every byte here comes from, and cites the issue reports that distinguish Push-to-Pair, application-PIN and SMP-PIN variants. Those community findings are reported here, not hardware verification by this project.

docs.title: LIVISI SmartHome Controller (SHC 1 / SHC 2)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (from public sources; not replayed against hardware) Protocol: LAN: HTTP on port 8080 (OAuth2 bearer token) plus a WebSocket event stream Manufacturer: LIVISI GmbH (formerly innogy SmartHome / RWE SmartHome) Manufacturer Status: Shutdown. Cloud services retired 2024-03-01

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The LIVISI SmartHome Controller (SHC) is the hub of the German smart-home system first sold as RWE SmartHome and then as innogy SmartHome. It drives LIVISI's own 868 MHz radio devices: plugs, in-wall switches, dimmers and shutter actuators, radiator and wall thermostats, contacts, motion and smoke detectors, remotes and sirens.

heise reported on 2022-03-01 that LIVISI would end its services on 2024-03-01, and the servers went off that day. Before then LIVISI shipped Local SmartHome, available for every controller from 2022-09-26. It is a local web app plus a local copy of the cloud API that runs on the controller. It is now the only way in.

Unlike the devolo estate, the child devices are proprietary radio, not Z-Wave or Zigbee, so they cannot move to another controller. The rescue is keeping the SHC itself usable, and its local API already makes that possible.

docs.title: What died, what still works
docs.text: Function State after 2024-03-01 LIVISI account, app login, cloud backup Gone; LIVISI said the data was deleted Remote access, push notifications, Alexa / Google / IFTTT Gone Local web app on the controller (http://<controller>/) Works. Device teaching, rules and settings Rules and schedules on the controller Run locally Local SmartHome API (port 8080 + WebSocket) Works. openHAB, Home Assistant and ioBroker use it

docs.title: Generations
docs.text: SHC 1 ("Classic") SHC 2 Device type in GET /device SHC SHCA controllerType in GET /status Classic Avatar Local SmartHome minimum firmware 1.914-3.1.1043.0 (via 1.913-3.0.1008.0) 8.17-1.2.39.443 (via 8.17-1.1.36.426) Default local-web-app password Digits after "SN" on the underside label Characters after "PIN:" on the label Host name (vendor how-to) SMARTHOME01 SHCONTROLLER01 Event WebSocket ws://<host>:8080/events?token=… ws://<host>:9090/events?token=… GET /status shape flat gateway facts under gateway GET /device/{id}/state wrapped in {"state": …} bare map Room setpoint property pointTemperature setpointTemperature Button confirmation at first setup From software 3.1.1056.0 Not stated

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes Method wired: Ethernet, then the controller's local web app Passphrase protection not_applicable (Ethernet) Confidence medium (vendor community posts + two open-source clients)
  1. Wire the controller to the router and reserve its DHCP address.
  2. Open http://<address>/, log in with the label default (see the table), set a new local password and accept the terms. Password rules: at least 10 characters, with upper case, lower case, a digit and a special character, and no ?. An SHC 1 on software 3.1.1056.0 or later asks for a button press on the controller.
  3. A client logs in as the fixed user admin:
POST /auth/token HTTP/1.1
Host: 192.168.1.50:8080
Authorization: Basic Y2xpZW50SWQ6Y2xpZW50UGFzcw==
Content-Type: application/json

{"username":"admin","password":"<local password>","grant_type":"password"}

The Basic header is the fixed OAuth client clientId:clientPass. It appears in both openHAB's binding and the planbnet library and is not a secret. The reply's access_token (a JWT) goes into Authorization: Bearer … on every later request. It expires: on errorcode 2007, log in again and retry once.

Everything is plain HTTP. The password and the token cross the LAN in clear. Keep the controller on a trusted network, and use a VPN rather than a port forward for remote access.

Factory reset: not established from any source read. Treat a lost local password as an open question rather than resetting blind (see Remaining unknowns).

docs.title: Control
docs.text:
Every write is POST /action with an action object. The target is a capability id, found by listing GET /capability and joining on device: "/device/<id>":

{"type":"SetState","namespace":"core.RWE",
 "target":"/capability/0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef",
 "params":{"onState":{"type":"Constant","value":true}}}
Capability type Property / action Values SwitchActuator onState true / false DimmerActuator dimLevel 0–100 % RollerShutterActuator shutterLevel; StartRamp (rampDirection RampUp/RampDown), StopRamp, namespace CosipDevices.RWE 0–100 % ThermostatActuator pointTemperature; operationMode 6–30 °C; Auto / Manu RoomSetpoint (VRCC) setpointTemperature (SHC 2) / pointTemperature (SHC 1) 6–30 °C BooleanStateActuator value true / false SirenActuator activeChannel None / Alarm / Notification / Feedback

A successful write answers {"resultCode":"Success"}. The new state arrives on the WebSocket as a StateChanged event whose properties carry the same names, flat. Reading one capability (GET /capability/{id}/state) returns {"<property>": {"value": …, "lastChanged": …}}.

The device and capability lists are JSON arrays, so the spec's instances mechanism cannot enumerate them yet. The spec declares the full command set but binds entities only for controller-level readings.

docs.title: Remaining unknowns
docs.text:
• The token lifetime and the reply fields beyond access_token.
  • controllerType at the top level of /status on SHC 2. openHAB's fixture shows only gateway, but the planbnet library picks the SHC 2 event port from a top-level Avatar, so it is almost certainly there. The SHC/SHCA device type remains the fallback.
  • The namespace for a shutter SetState: CosipDevices.RWE (planbnet) or core.RWE (openHAB).
  • Factory reset, local-password recovery, and which button confirms setup on SHC 1.
  • Discovery. No mDNS/SSDP announcement is documented, and clients take the host by hand.
  • LIVISI GmbH's status. It was registered 2018-12-11 at Amtsgericht Essen (HRB 29622). A register aggregator shows that entry deleted with a later Munich record, which looks like a seat move but is unconfirmed. No source was found for an insolvency or liquidation.

docs.title: LotusLamp X LED Controllers
docs.text: Status: Complete (GATT control path); mesh/encrypted variants in progress Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Shenzhen ELK Manufacturer Status: Unsupported

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
LotusLamp X (com.szelk.ledlamppro) is the design app for a family of cheap, widely-rebadged BLE LED strip and lamp controllers from Shenzhen ELK, sold under advertised names starting with ELK-, MELK-, ELBU- and a long list of OEM variants (HX6-, HCW-, BYC-, SHY-, MHRS-, THUNDEROBOT, "LED LIGHT STRIP", "LED Constellation Lights", …). They are addressable-RGB controllers: colour, brightness, speed and 213 built-in animations, plus timers, microphone rhythm and (on some models) mesh groups.

The good news: the devices are fully local. The app speaks BLE only — no Wi-Fi, no account — and the core protocol is independently reverse engineered and live-tested by the lotus-lamp Python library, so these lamps will keep working long after the app is gone.

Privacy

The vendor app uploads device stats/telemetry to lotus.elkled.com:8082 (and self-updates from elkble.com). The lamp itself never uses the network — a local BLE client gives you everything the hardware can do without the telemetry.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model numbers ELK-/MELK-/ELBU- prefixed (reference unit: MELK-OA10) Chipset Unknown (generic low-cost BLE SoC; chip-agnostic from the app side) Radio BLE FCC ID

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name ELK-*, MELK-*, ELBU-* or OEM variant Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (static analysis + public, live-tested RE library)

Power the lamp and it advertises immediately. Scan for one of the name prefixes above (the 0xFFF0 service is shared with unrelated products and is not an identity signal), connect, and write command frames to characteristic 0xFFF3. There is no pairing, PIN or account. Subscribe to 0xFFF4 if you want state notifications.

Factory reset: no credential state exists, so there is nothing to clear. The app exposes a restore-factory opcode (0x87) but its frame and effect are unverified. The practical remedy for "can't connect" is a power cycle — the lamp accepts only one BLE connection at a time, and if the previous phone is still hanging onto it, remove the device from that phone's OS Bluetooth list so it stops auto-reconnecting.

Rebinding to a new controller: in place. Nothing ties the lamp to an owner; connect from the new client after disconnecting the old one.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 0000fff0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Control Service Primary (and only custom) service 0000fff3-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Command Write All commands, write-without-response 0000fff4-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb State Notify Status echoes (payload layout not fully mapped)

The app also reads the standard Device Information characteristics and Battery Level on connect.

docs.title: Commands — E1 frame family
docs.text:
All commands are 9-byte frames: 7E <len> <cmd> <p0..p4> EF. Unused parameters pad with 0xFF. The <len> byte is not strictly validated by the firmware — emit the values below, but a mismatch is not fatal.

Command Frame Description Power on 7E 07 04 01 01 FF FF 00 EF Turn on Power off 7E 07 04 01 00 FF FF 00 EF Turn off Set color 7E 07 05 03 RR GG BB 10 EF Static RGB color Set brightness 7E 07 01 VV FF FF FF 00 EF Brightness 0-100 (app emits len 04) Set speed 7E 04 02 VV FF FF FF 00 EF Animation speed 0-100 Set animation 7E 07 03 VV FF FF FF 00 EF Mode 0-212 (213 named modes) Sync time 7E 06 83 HH MM SS DW 00 EF Clock; weekday 1=Mon..7=Sun Set timer 7E 07 82 HH MM 00 TT DD EF TT 0=on-timer/1=off-timer; DD = days bitmask, bit7 enables, bits 0-6 = Mon..Sun

The full ~70-opcode map (scenes, DIY image upload, rhythm, mesh groups, OTA) is documented in device-specs/devices/lotuslamp-x.yaml.

docs.title: Variants worth knowing about
docs.text:
• E2/E3 frame families (8E … and 2E … 2F): other device types sharing this app (pixel strips, curtain/TV backlights). See the spec for framing.
  • Connectionless control: the phone can advertise commands itself — company ID 0xE190/0xE290 for broadcast, 0xBE99 for mesh groups (22-byte packet, CRC16 derived from the BLE CRC-24 core).
  • Encrypted firmware (ELK* names, * as 4th character): wraps the power/mode/brightness frames in XOR obfuscation with an app-embedded preset key. Obfuscation, not security.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
• Exact 0xFFF4 notification payload semantics (state readback) — needs a live HCI capture.
  • Which opcodes beyond power/mode/brightness take the obfuscated frame on ELK* firmware.
  • Mesh group provisioning flow (familyId/roomId/groupId assignment).
  • Only the MELK-OA10 is live-tested (by the lotus-lamp library); other models may shuffle mode numbers.

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
• [x] APK static analysis (jadx)
  • [x] Community open-source implementation (lotus-lamp, live-tested)
  • [ ] HCI snoop (pending — notify-channel semantics, mesh provisioning)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• lotus-lamp on PyPI — independent reverse engineering, tested on MELK-OA10

docs.title: LOY / LOYPRO Helmet and B3 Tail-Light LED Displays
docs.text: Status: Minimally verified query, plus decoded official-app upload/DFU capture Protocol: BLE, AA55 binary TLVs Manufacturer: LOY / YSKJ OEM family

docs.title: Identity and family boundary
docs.text:
The LOYPRO app (com.yskj.loypro) accepts advertised names beginning LOY. Reviewed LOY PLAY and AUTOBABA/LOY SPACE versions accept only YS and TL. Keep the separate LOYPRO candidate rather than expanding another spec's filter.

The captured product is a B3 motorcycle tail light supplied with bicycle and helmet mounts; its firmware family contains MTYB3BGR. This does not make every LOY-named product the same retail shell. The older Shining Display/TR platform uses FA02 and is covered by TIRO LED Helmet Display, not by this protocol.

FFF0 is not a device type. Keep 0000fff0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb in the GATT declaration, never as an independent scan matcher.

docs.title: Setup and read-only identification
docs.text:
No account, provisioning or pairing was required in the live query or official capture. The device reports optional password support; if an owner enabled one, use the normal app flow rather than guessing or bypassing it.

  1. Rediscover the LOY name; do not rely on a stale address.
  2. Confirm 0000fff2-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb write-without-response and 0000fff1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb notify.
  3. Subscribe to FFF1 and issue this 20-byte dev_info_all query on FFF2 with response=False:
aa 55 ff ff 0e 00 01 00 c1 03 0a 00 1b 00 04 00 06 00 ff 03

Increment sequence numbers in a real client and reassemble replies by declared AA55 length. The checksum-valid 159-byte reply established 48×16 geometry, fixed brightness 15, power type 1, firmware V2.9.1#V18 and capabilities pwd, remote, car_linkage, brake, HS:2, MTU:512 and power. The MTU token is a capability, not the negotiated value. Stop if the dialect differs.

No factory reset is established. Rebinding is a fresh scan and connection; do not use delete-program or firmware messages as reset/identification probes.

docs.title: AA55 transport
docs.text:
Offset / field Encoding Header aa 55 ff ff Length u16 LE; sequence + flags + command type + payload + checksum; packet bytes = length + 6 Sequence u16 LE; can be reused by later operations Flags c1 host command, 81 ordinary response Command types 02 program/control, 03 query, 04 resource upgrade; responses 82, 83, 84, notification 06 Checksum u16 LE sum of every preceding byte, including the AA55 header, modulo 65536

The capture negotiated MTU 512/517 and host ATT values were at most 509 bytes. Join ATT fragments before checking AA55 length/checksum or matching an ACK. A logical 960-byte media chunk is a TLV inside an AA55 packet, not one ATT write.

TLV lengths are one byte below 0x80, 81 LL for 128–255, and 82 LL LH (little-endian u16) for larger observed values.

Ordinary 82 ACKs are the exception to TLV payloads: byte 10 is one raw status byte. A captured successful ACK for sequence 0x0016 is aa 55 ff ff 07 00 16 00 81 82 00 1d 04. Match flags 81, type 82, the request sequence and status zero before continuing. Nonzero is a rejection; no nonzero device error values or error-code taxonomy were captured. The YAML includes a synthetic nonzero vector solely to test that rejection path.

docs.title: Stored program upload
docs.text:
08 02 00 00 deletes/replaces program zero. It is not an upload-ready probe. The earlier delete-only READY attempt therefore asked the wrong operation and its timeout did not disprove GIF support. Choose the stored slot deliberately.

  1. Send a program header with replacement (08), save (09), program (0c), play configuration (1c), region (0d) and geometry (1d) TLVs.
  2. Send a graphic item with item (0e), effect (14) and media declaration (11) TLVs.
  3. Send media in ascending zero-based chunks. Every chunk repeats 09 01 01 and the graphic item's program (0c), region (0d) and item (0e) values before tags 12 and 13. Tag 12 carries total count, index and maximum chunk size (960 in the capture) as LE16 values plus 00; tag 13 carries the media bytes.
  4. After every type-2 packet, wait for response 82 with the matching sequence and status 00. All 84 such packets in the capture were ACKed.
  5. Finalize with tag 35: zero-based program byte, 20-byte resource key and u32 LE timestamp. Require its ACK too. Deduplicate retransmitted chunks by program/item/index.

Raw GIF bytes stay GIF. Other graphics use the separate YSTP01 image encoder; text uploads are rendered image pages, often ending in a blank page, not a simple string command. Locally generated resource IDs use eight characters from the one-based app/UI program number (wire_program_index + 1) plus zero padding, followed by MD5 of the input description. Wire program zero thus uses prefix 10000000, not 00000000. Decode the resulting 40 hex characters to 20 bytes. Hash original input bytes, not converted YSTP01. Captured cloud keys may use another scheme; they are identifiers, not credentials.

docs.title: YSTP01 media encoding
docs.text:
YSTP01 starts with this 15-byte header; all integer fields are little-endian:

Offset Size Meaning 0 6 ASCII YSTP01 6 2 Width in pixels 8 2 Height in pixels 10 2 Page count 12 2 Raw delay value; its time scaling is unknown 14 1 Bits per pixel: 8 or 24 are capture-confirmed

An 8-bit stream has 256 three-byte RGB palette entries immediately after the header. A 24-bit stream has no palette and stores each pixel as R, G, B. Pages follow consecutively without per-page headers, with rows ordered top to bottom and pixels left to right. Palettized indices are packed least-significant bit first; each row occupies (width * depth + 7) // 8 bytes and starts on a byte boundary. Emit zero in unused high padding bits. Total media length is 15 + palette_bytes + pages * height * row_stride.

The spec's ystp01.synthetic_vectors block provides reproducible 24-bit and 8-bit media. scripts/test_loypro_led_display.py independently encodes, decodes and hashes both vectors using only the standard library. Text rasterization, delay units and other YSTP depths or variants remain unverified.

docs.title: Geometry and media evidence
docs.text:
• Device-information and TLV canvas: 48×16.
  • Captured animated GIF: 48×15, 65 frames, 4551 bytes in five logical chunks.
  • Two custom 24-bit single-page images, three coloured text sequences and four static 48×16 GIF resources were also reconstructed.
  • The offline builder reproduces all eight packets of the captured GIF upload byte-for-byte. This proves the official protocol path, not a new third-party hardware write or visible rendering by our client.

Tag 36 controls playback model/index/program-ID lists. Its value has one-byte model at offset 0, one-byte index at offset 1, then zero-based program IDs as one byte each. Preserve the exact list order; the app displays each ID plus one. For example, sequence 17 selects model 0, raw index 2 and programs 0–9: aa 55 ff ff 14 00 11 00 c1 02 36 0c 00 02 00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 56 04. Model 1 loops and other models select single-play behavior. The raw index's numbering semantics are not established. Short type-6 tag-36 notifications are playback data, not accelerometer axes.

docs.title: Firmware update — advanced only
docs.text:
A distinct type-4 resource-upgrade stream transferred 360448 bytes in 377 chunks, with 377 matching type-84 ACKs. Like ordinary ACKs, each upgrade ACK has flags 81 and one raw status byte at offset 10; require the request sequence and status zero before continuing. Captured sequence-zero success is aa 55 ff ff 07 00 00 00 81 84 00 09 04. The first chunk carries text metadata with model, sum16 and a resource ID; the reconstructed image matches both that sum16 and its MD5. Device information changed from V2.9.1#V18 before the transfer to V2.9.1#V24 after disconnect/reconnect.

MD5/sum16 are integrity checks, not proof of a vendor signature or safe image for another unit. Do not replay the captured stream, use the normal image uploader as DFU, or guess recovery. Wrong-image and interrupted-update behavior are unknown.

docs.title: Vehicle inputs and remaining questions
docs.text:
The unit reports remote, car_linkage, brake and power; the updated image also contains an MSA311 driver string. App-assignable programs are 67 left, 68 right, 69 brake, 70 hazard and 71 reverse. None of this establishes an integrated accelerometer, wired input, remote mechanism or motion map. A capture actuating one input at a time is still needed.

Other open items are visible third-party rendering, arbitrary geometry/media, password setup, reset, maintenance services in other firmware states and safe firmware recovery.

docs.title: Lutron Caseta Smart Bridge 2
docs.text: Status: Local discovery and service map documented Protocol: WiFi (mDNS + LEAP newline-delimited JSON over TLS) Manufacturer: Lutron Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Lutron Caseta Smart Bridge 2 exposes multiple local services. LEAP on port 8081 is the modern local control protocol. LAP on port 8083 is deprecated. _lutron._tcp.local. exposes stable bridge metadata such as MACADDR, CODEVER, SYSTYPE, and DEVCLASS.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Use:

python scripts/lutron_discover.py --timeout 5

Stable identity should prefer TXT MACADDR from _lutron._tcp.local., with hostname as a fallback.

docs.title: Local Services
docs.text:
Service Port Description _leap._tcp.local. 8081 Modern control: newline-delimited JSON over TLS _lap._tcp.local. 8083 Deprecated local protocol (also hosts cert pairing) _lutron._tcp.local. 22 Status/identity TXT records _hap._tcp.local. 4548 HomeKit accessory service

LEAP frames are one JSON object: {"CommuniqueType": ..., "Header": {"Url": ...}, "Body": ...}. Pairing runs on port 8083 while the rear button is held: Execute /pair with CommandType=CSR and the client's PEM CSR returns the signed client certificate plus the bridge CA in Body.SigningResult. Zone control is a CreateRequest to /zone/{id}/commandprocessor — dimmers GoToDimmedLevel (Level 0–100), switches GoToSwitchedLevel (On/Off), shades GoToShadeLevel/GoToTilt. (Verified against vendor app com.lutron.mmw 26.7.0.5, 2026-08-20.)

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/lutron-caseta-smart-bridge.yaml

Home Assistant: the core Lutron Caséta integration uses the Smart Bridge LEAP protocol documented here.

docs.title: Magic Display
docs.text: Status: Complete Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: tirohk / AiTURE Manufacturer Status: Abandoned

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Bluetooth-controlled LED displays for shoes, bags, hats, and crafts. Uses a Quintic (NXP QN-series) BLE chipset with QPP (Quintic Private Profile). All traffic is AES-128 encrypted via the vendor's bundled native AES library. Shares the same BLE UUIDs as Shining Mask/Glasses (both use the Quintic QPP platform) but has a distinct command set and device identification.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Display Monochrome LED matrix (5x36, 12x48, 14x56, or 16x64) Chipset Quintic (NXP QN-series) Radio BLE FCC ID Unknown Max connections 6 simultaneous devices (app-side limit in the app's configuration)

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 0000fee9-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb QPP Service Primary BLE service (Quintic Private Profile) 0000fee8-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb OTA Service Firmware update (Quintic OTA protocol)

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text: UUID Name Properties Purpose d44bc439-abfd-45a2-b575-925416129600 Command (WRITE1) Write AES-encrypted 16-byte commands d44bc439-abfd-45a2-b575-925416129601 Notification Notify Device responses (STYPE, DATSOK, etc.) d44bc439-abfd-45a2-b575-92541612960a Bulk Data (WRITE2) Write Image/text bitmap frames (AES-encrypted 16-byte blocks) d44bc439-abfd-45a2-b575-92541612960b Auxiliary (WRITE3) Write Live DIY pixel writes and music/rhythm level frames (AES-encrypted 16-byte packets) 013784cf-f7e3-55b4-6c4c-9fd140100a16 OTA Write (on 0xFEE8) Write Quintic OTA meta/data/verify/exec, 256-byte packets, unencrypted 003784cf-f7e3-55b4-6c4c-9fd140100a16 OTA Notify (on 0xFEE8) Notify Quintic OTA result codes

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
• Algorithm: AES-128 via the vendor's bundled native AES library (its default key-expansion routine)
  • Mode: ECB with fixed default key compiled into the native binary
  • Key (recovered): 34522a5b7a6e492c08090a9d8d2a23f8 — 16 bytes at a fixed offset in the APK split's arm64 build of the bundled AES library; identical to the public iDeal LED family key. App-derived, not yet verified against hardware.
  • All command/notify traffic and WRITE2/WRITE3 data is encrypted before write; responses decrypted on receive. OTA traffic on 0xFEE8 is not encrypted.

docs.title: Device Discovery
docs.text:
Identified by manufacturer-specific advertising data (not by name):

  • AD type 0xFF, payload starts with {0x54, 0x52, 0x00, 0x27} ("TR" + 0x0027)
  • 0xFEE9 is the generic Quintic QPP service used by unrelated products; do not select this spec from that service alone. Discover it after connecting for control.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
All commands are 16-byte fixed-length packets (plaintext, before AES encryption). Format: [length, ASCII_CMD..., params..., zero_pad_to_16].

Command Bytes (plaintext) Description STYPE [5, 'S','T','Y','P','E'] Query display dimensions (builder exists in the app but is never called — the device pushes STYPE unsolicited after connect) LEDON [5, 'L','E','D','O','N'] Turn display ON LEDOFF [6, 'L','E','D','O','F','F'] Turn display OFF LEDFIRST [8, 'L','E','D','F','I','R','S','T'] Address unit as first of a daisy chain LEDSECOND [9, 'L','E','D','S','E','C','O','N','D'] Address unit as second of a daisy chain LIGHT n [6, 'L','I','G','H','T', n] Set brightness LIGHTON [7, 'L','I','G','H','T','O','N'] Torch/flashlight ON LIGHTOFF [8, 'L','I','G','H','T','O','F','F'] Torch/flashlight OFF SPEED n [6, 'S','P','E','E','D', n] Set animation speed MODE 1 [5, 'M','O','D','E', 1] Static display MODE 2 hi lo [7, 'M','O','D','E', 2, hi, lo] Flash (ms, big-endian) MODE 3 n [6, 'M','O','D','E', 3, n] Scroll left MODE 4 n [6, 'M','O','D','E', 4, n] Scroll right MODE 7 [5, 'M','O','D','E', 7] Rhythm/music mode (level frames go to WRITE3) MODE 8 n [6, 'M','O','D','E', 8, n] Daisy-chained scroll right, with speed byte MODE 9 n [6, 'M','O','D','E', 9, n] Daisy-chained scroll left, with speed byte EVERT [5, 'E','V','E','R','T'] Invert/flip display ANIM n [5, 'A','N','I','M', n] Select animation frame TIME h m s [7, 'T','I','M','E', h, m, s] Set device clock SCHD on h m [7, 'S','C','H','D', on, h, m] Timer auto-off schedule STSC [4, 'S','T','S','C'] Read timer schedule (response prefix SBHD) CALL s t [6, 'C','A','L','L', status, time] Phone call notification SMVEW n [6, 'S','M','V','E','W', n] DIY sync draw: 1 = enter, 0 = exit, 2 = save-and-exit STOPR [5, 'S','T','O','P','R'] Stop music/rhythm mode

The sibling Shining Glasses multi-frame MANY <count> <profile> … MANCPOK transaction does not exist in this app (no such command or dispatch code in the decompiled APK); animation upload here is a plain DATS/data/DATCP transfer. All command bytes above are verified directly against com.tirohk.magicdisplay 1.5.6 by static analysis of its protocol-agreement class.

docs.title: Data Transfer Protocol
docs.text:
1. DATS on WRITE1: [8, 'D','A','T','S', len_hi, len_lo, 0, link_flag]
  2. Device responds DATSOK on notify
  3. Send data chunks on WRITE2: [payload_len, ...data] — 16-byte blocks carrying up to 15 payload bytes each, each block AES-128-ECB encrypted with the same static key; 60 ms pacing for images, 50 ms for animations. No per-chunk acknowledgement; flow control is timing-only.
  4. DATCP on WRITE1: [5, 'D','A','T','C','P']
  5. Device responds DATCPOK on notify

docs.title: Display Types
docs.text:
Reported via STYPE response after connection:

Type Grid (WxH) Bitmap bytes Notes STYPE5X36 5 x 36 36 1 byte/col, 5 bits used STYPE5X36N 5 x 72 72 Two linked 5x36 STYPE12X48 12 x 48 72 Column-pair encoding STYPE12X48N 12 x 96 144 Two linked 12x48 STYPE16X64 16 x 64 128 2 bytes/col (rows 0-7, 8-15)

docs.title: Bitmap Encoding
docs.text:
Monochrome, 1-bit-per-pixel (any RGB channel >= 128 = ON):

  • 5x36: 1 byte per column, bits 4-0 = rows 0-4
  • 12x48: Column pairs produce 3 bytes per pair (packed 12-bit rows)
  • 16x64: 2 bytes per column, byte 0 = rows 0-7 (bits 7-0), byte 1 = rows 8-15

docs.title: Connection Sequence
docs.text:
1. Connect, requestConnectionPriority(HIGH)
  2. Discover services, find 0xFEE9
  3. Enable notifications on ...9601
  4. Send LEDFIRST or LEDSECOND (multi-device position)
  5. Wait 200ms, send TIME with current time
  6. Wait 200ms, send STSC (read timer schedule)
  7. Device pushes STYPE unsolicited, identifying display resolution

docs.title: Vendor Cloud (not required)
docs.text: The app — never the device — contacts http://api.e-toys.cn/api/ for an OTA-version check (app/lastOtaUpdate), ads (ad/getAdInfo) and telemetry (app/uploadLog, app/runningLog). As of 2026-07-31 the server is alive but returns empty data for this app id; no OTA firmware is served. All control is local BLE, and four OTA images (TR1805R03-9/-10, TR1806R06-2/-3, ~39 KB each) are bundled in the APK assets, so the device remains fully usable — including firmware update — if the backend disappears.

docs.text:

  • [x] Native AES library key extraction (arm64 build, fixed offset)
