docs.title: Marshall Bluetooth Headphones, Earbuds and Speakers
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (untested) Protocol: BLE GATT for control; optional Bluetooth Classic audio pairing Manufacturer: Zound Industries / Marshall (active)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The spec covers Motif II A.N.C., Major IV, Monitor III A.N.C., Willen, Stanmore and Woburn families: device-specs/devices/marshall-bluetooth.yaml. It separates ordinary Classic audio pairing from the encrypted LE control link, maps modern and legacy characteristic UUIDs, and records model-specific reset and firmware-update boundaries. Nothing has been replayed by this project.

docs.title: Setup and pairing
docs.text:
The simplest route does not require a prior Classic audio pairing:

  1. Power the product on. For earbuds, place them in the case with the lid open.
  2. Scan for the LE advertisement named after the model with a [LE] suffix, such as MOTIF II A.N.C. [LE] (or carrying company ID 0x065A), and connect to that LE address. The suffix on its own is not Marshall-specific.
  3. Bond with Just Works / NoInputNoOutput. No PIN is needed. On BlueZ, register an agent before calling Pair().
  4. Discover service fa302d24-d775-4343-b9ed-8cc68ace3284. Resolve each function by UUID across all services: modern 0000{code}-1337-1dea-feed-c0ffee70c0de first, then its documented legacy 0000aaXX-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb alias. Hide a function the product does not expose.

The vendor app can instead pair Classic audio first and then start the LE bond. Some firmware derives the LE keys from the Classic bond; other models, including Motif II A.N.C., still require the separate LE bond. Proprietary characteristics refuse unbonded access.

docs.title: Factory reset and rebinding
docs.text:
Reset clears user settings and remembered pairings, not installed firmware. Afterwards, remove both the ordinary entry and the [LE] entry from each host before pairing again.

Model Vendor-documented procedure Indicator Motif II A.N.C. Both earbuds in the open case; hold the case button for 10 seconds Case LED turns purple Monitor III A.N.C. With headphones on, hold M-button and ANC together for 5 seconds LED turns purple Willen With speaker on, hold the Bluetooth button for 7 seconds Indicators turn off and the speaker restarts

These procedures come from the manuals and were not run by this project. Do not apply them to a different model merely because it shares the control protocol.

A new client can pair using the normal LE route. The manuals document up to eight remembered Classic hosts on some products; LE bond capacity and eviction behaviour are unknown.

docs.title: Protocol summary
docs.text: The LE control link carries battery, EQ, noise-control, playback and model-specific functions. UUID schemes and payload support vary, so model detection and a modern-to-legacy fallback are mandatory. Firmware update uses different mechanisms across the family; the spec identifies Qualcomm GAIA and other update paths only to the depth established by evidence and does not offer a generic flashing recipe.

docs.title: Meizu MYVU / Star Air AR Glasses
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (untested) Protocol: BLE session plus Bluetooth Classic RFCOMM relay Manufacturer: Meizu / Hubei Xingji Meizu Group (active)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The spec covers MYVU / Star Air XGA010C and records evidence for later V2 GATT layouts separately: device-specs/devices/meizu-myvu-glasses.yaml. It documents the two-link setup, application-layer ECDH exchange, session initialization, heartbeat, per-session Classic relay, message framing and worked vectors. The public unofficial SDK is the main evidence; nothing has been replayed by this project.

docs.title: Setup and pairing
docs.text:
Both links are required, in order:

  1. BLE session. Connect over LE and run the application-layer bond on characteristic 0x2020: version negotiation, an ECDH P-256 exchange and encrypted DeviceInfo in both directions. Complete the RunAsOne initialization and maintain the heartbeat. The LE link itself is not bonded through the operating system.
  2. Classic relay. Read the per-session RFCOMM service UUID announced over BLE, then open the Classic relay to that UUID. This phase needs a BR/EDR bond. Do not reuse a channel number captured in another session; the UUID and SDP record select the current relay.

There is no certificate or shared installation secret in the app-layer ECDH step, and no vendor account is required. Treat session keys, device identity and captured traffic as owner-private even though the cryptographic exchange itself is described in the spec.

docs.title: Factory reset and rebinding
docs.text:
The public SDK names a factory-reset action over the relay, but its wire form and cleared state are not documented. Use the vendor app's own reset option; the menu path was not recorded. The 8-second power-button hold is only a hard reboot, not a known factory reset.

To move to a new phone or client, disconnect in the vendor app and remove or disable the glasses in the old phone's Bluetooth settings. Then repeat both link phases. ECDH keys are per session; whether the glasses retain multiple BR/EDR bonds is unknown. There are no Wi-Fi credentials to rejoin.

docs.title: Protocol summary
docs.text: The BLE side establishes session state and carries link control. The Classic side carries the main application relay. Message IDs, ordering, heartbeat and acknowledgement rules matter: a duplicated or skipped sequence can leave messages buffered indefinitely. The YAML declares the initialization order, packet types, encryption envelopes, field encodings, relay discovery and negative findings. Do not reduce the device to a single GATT command characteristic.

docs.title: MikroTik RouterOS Device (identify-only)
docs.text: Status: Complete (MNDP discovery hardware-verified 2026-08-14; identify-only) Protocol: MNDP (UDP 5678) / LLDP Manufacturer: MikroTik Manufacturer Status: Active — recognised and linked to WebFig, not controlled here

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
MikroTik routers, switches and APs announce themselves with MNDP (MikroTik Neighbor Discovery Protocol). This app identifies them — shows a router pictogram and deep-links to WebFig — rather than implementing RouterOS control (the API/WebFig/Winbox all exist and are out of scope as home infrastructure).

Verified live 2026-08-14 against three RouterOS devices: a CCR2004-1G-12S+2XS gateway ("core-router", RouterOS 7.13), a CRS354-48P-4S+2Q+ ("core-switch") and a CRS326-24S+2Q+ ("edge-switch"), each decoded from its MNDP TLVs.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
• MNDP, UDP 5678. Devices broadcast unsolicited ~every 60 s (listen with no probe), or solicit with a 4-byte zero datagram to 255.255.255.255:5678.
  • Payload: 4-byte header (0x0000 + u16 seq) then TLVs, type and length u16 big-endian. Key TLVs: 0x0005 Identity (name), 0x0007 Version, 0x0008 Platform ("MikroTik"), 0x000c Board (model), 0x0001 MAC. The device's IPv4 is the source IP of the datagram.
  • Also emits LLDP (passive L2 listen).

Admin: http://<ip>/webfig/ (or https://<ip>/ with www-ssl); Winbox on TCP 8291.

docs.title: MoTool Slacker
docs.text: Status: In Progress Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Slacker LLC (formerly MoTool) Manufacturer Status: Active (subscription gates app cloud features only; device control is local)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Digital motorcycle suspension sag measurement tool (V4/V5). Attaches to fork or shock and communicates over BLE to the companion Flutter app. Basic device control is NOT paywalled: the standalone "Slacker Virtual Remote" app is 100% free with full Reset/Auto Zero/display control, and the Service Assistant subscription (via RevenueCat) only gates cloud/notes/multi-bike features. The goal is to reverse engineer the BLE serial protocol so the device can be driven by any local client without the vendor app or cloud.

The device uses a standard HM-10/HM-19-style BLE UART module (CC2541/CC2640 based), so the protocol is serial pass-through over a single BLE characteristic. All command construction is in Dart AOT-compiled code (libapp.so), so exact command bytes need HCI snoop capture confirmation.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Models MoTool Slacker V4, V5 Chipset HM-10/HM-19 BLE UART module (CC2541/CC2640) Radio BLE 4.0+ FCC ID Unknown

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 0000ffe0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb UART Service Standard HM-10 serial pass-through service

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text: UUID Name Properties Description 0000ffe1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Serial Data Read, Write, Write Without Response, Notify Single bidirectional serial channel

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
• Scan filter: Service UUID 0xFFE0 (app filters by service UUID, not device name)
  • CCCD: Standard 0x2902 for enabling notifications
  • Pairing: No bonding required (HM-10 modules use "Just Works" or no pairing)

docs.title: Known Commands (from Dart string analysis)
docs.text:
The app sends commands to the device via writes to FFE1 and receives responses via notifications. From AOT binary string extraction (Service Assistant v7.1.0, libapp.so):

Command Description Direction Reset Reset the device/measurement Phone -> Device Auto Zero Zero/tare the sensor reading Phone -> Device Display Mode Change Switch between mm and percentage display Phone -> Device Travel Selection Set fork/shock travel for percentage calculation Phone -> Device

Write path (derived from the snapshot string table): commands are assembled as hex strings (buildTravelHex / hexBuilder / masterHexValue; debug logs "Hex Builder Travel Hex String Data", "Wrote Travel Hex String Data"), decoded to bytes with the package:convert HexDecoder, and written to FFE1 via flutter_blue. Device->app traffic arrives as FFE1 notifications parsed into deviceState / mtbMode / currentReadingInt. The exact command byte sequences are NOT statically recoverable (see Next Steps) and are deliberately not listed here — do not invent opcodes.

docs.title: Data Model (from Dart strings)
docs.text:
The app tracks these measurement values:

Field Type Description currentReadingInt Integer Current raw sag reading sagFS Float Front static sag sagFR Float Front rider sag sagRS Float Rear static sag sagRR Float Rear rider sag frontSagRiderPercent Float Front sag as % of travel rearSagRiderPercent Float Rear sag as % of travel travelFork Float Fork travel setting (mm) travelShock Float Shock travel setting (mm)

docs.title: V4 vs V5 Differences
docs.text:
• V4: Displays raw measurement in mm
  • V5: Adds percentage-of-travel display mode. Requires fork/shock travel settings to be configured in the app (buildTravelHex function constructs hex data for travel configuration)

docs.title: App Architecture
docs.text: Component Technology App analyzed Service Assistant v7.1.0 (versionCode 710, targetSdk 35; XAPK, armeabi-v7a only) Framework Flutter (Dart AOT-compiled) BLE Plugin flutter_blue (pauldemarco) — confirmed via plugins.pauldemarco.com/flutter_blue/methods channel string Subscription RevenueCat (Google Play + Amazon IAP; paywall/customer-center activities in AndroidManifest.xml) Backend Firebase (Firestore, Auth, Messaging) Firebase Project motool-service-assistant

docs.title: Subscription/Paywall
docs.text:
The Service Assistant subscription is gated by RevenueCat entitlements, but it only covers cloud/notes/multi-bike features — the standalone Slacker Virtual Remote app provides full basic device control for free. Subscription plans include: Weekly, Monthly, Bimonthly (2-month), Quarterly (3-month), Semiannual (6-month), Annual, and Lifetime.

The BLE protocol itself has no authentication or subscription check — the paywall is entirely app-side.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. HCI snoop capture: Record a BLE session during sag measurement to capture exact command bytes (practical route)
  2. Dart AOT snapshot analysis: attempted 2026-08-18 — the snapshot is fully position-independent (no ELF relocations); heap objects in .rodata are serialized clusters and constants are referenced through the string table by index, so recovering the command-building logic needs a full Dart cluster deserializer. Existing tools (blutter, Doldrums) target ARM64 only, and this app ships armeabi-v7a only.
  3. BLE proxy: Use nRF Connect or a BLE proxy to intercept and replay commands
  4. Protocol documentation: Once command bytes are known, document the full serial protocol

docs.title: Nissan Leaf (ZE0 / AZE0 / ZE1) — battery data over OBD-II
docs.text:
Status: In Progress (read-only decode transcribed from open-source clients; not yet run against a car) Protocol: OBD-II connector: ISO 15765-4 CAN (11-bit, 500 kbit/s) with ISO-TP, KWP-style 21 group reads and UDS 22/19 reads Manufacturer: Nissan Manufacturer Status: Active. The NissanConnect EV cloud service for Leafs built up to May 2019 ended on 30 March 2026.

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/nissan-leaf-obd2.yaml.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
On 30 March 2026 Nissan switched off the NissanConnect EV app for Leafs built up to May 2019 and for e-NV200 vans, in the UK and in at least Ireland and Cyprus. Owners lost remote charge status, remote charging and pre-conditioning. Nissan still exists and so does the car. Only the cloud path is gone.

The battery data the app showed is still available locally. A phone or a home server connects to a plug-in ELM327-class OBD-II adapter (usually a BLE one, such as the LeLink2). Through it, the client polls the Li-ion Battery Controller (LBC): requests go to CAN ID 0x79B and replies come back on 0x7BB. Nothing here requires a session or security access, and this page documents reads only.

Read-only, on purpose

The open sources this is drawn from also implement LBC writes: clearing DTCs, and a seed/key-gated routine that resets the pack's degradation history. They are left out deliberately and listed in the spec under protocol_details.excluded_services. A tool that can rewrite a battery's reported health has no place in a spec that people use to judge a used car.

Polling etiquette

The open clients poll gently. The Home Assistant integration polls every 10 s with the car on and every 5 minutes with it off, because on some cars each poll of a sleeping car clicks a relay. OVMS does not poll the LBC at all while the car is off. Battery-Emulator stops polling while another tester is using 0x79B, because the LBC drops a request that arrives mid-reply. Run one poller at a time.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Model Number ZE0 (2010–2012, 24 kWh), AZE0 (2013–2017, 24/30 kWh), ZE1 (2018+, 40/62 kWh) Chipset n/a (vehicle); the adapter is ELM327-class, see OBD-II Bluetooth adapter Radio None on the car side; BLE or Classic on the adapter FCC ID n/a Category / hierarchy vehicle Aliases Nissan LEAF; Leaf 24/30 kWh; Leaf 40 kWh / 62 kWh e+ Companion apps NissanConnect EV (discontinued 2026-03-30 for pre-May-2019 cars)

ZE1 port isolation. On 2018+ cars a CAN gateway sits between the OBD-II port and the vehicle buses, and it powers down when the ignition is off. With the car off, polls go unanswered, so the car has to be switched on. ZE0/AZE0 ports stay reachable with the car off.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No (on the car) Method wired Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (public open-source clients)

Plug in the adapter, wake the car (switch it on for ZE1), connect to the adapter and run the ELM327 initialisation below.

Factory reset: not applicable. The car stores no client pairing or credentials.

Rebinding: physical swap of adapter or host. The car keeps no record of the last tool.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text: Nothing pairs with the car. Any pairing belongs to the adapter. See OBD-II Bluetooth adapter.

docs.title: ECU addressing
docs.text:
From the community CAN database README:

ECU Request Response Used here for LBC (battery controller / BMS) 0x79B 0x7BB SOC, SOH/Hx, Ah, pack V/A, cells, temperatures VCM 0x797 0x79A 12 V battery, charge counts, gear, plug state, VIN M&A (meter) 0x743 0x763 odometer, tyre pressures CHARGER 0x792 0x793 — INVERTER/MC 0x784 0x78C — BCM / HVAC / ABS 0x745 / 0x744 / 0x740 0x765 / 0x764 / 0x760 — SHIFT (ZE0 only) 0x79D 0x7BD —

docs.title: ELM327 session (py-nissan-leaf-obd-ble)
docs.text:
ATZ            reset; wait 1 s, ignore the reply
ATE0           echo off
ATSP6          ISO 15765-4 CAN, 11-bit, 500 kbit/s
ATH1           print CAN IDs
ATL0 / ATS0    no linefeeds, no spaces
ATCAF0         auto-formatting off: client writes the PCI byte and reassembles
AT RV          optional: < 6 V means no live socket

# whenever the target ECU changes (<hdr> = 79B, 797 or 743)
ATSH <hdr>
ATFCSH <hdr>
ATFCSD 30 00 00     flow control: ContinueToSend, block size 0, STmin 0
ATFCSM 1            use that user-defined flow-control frame

022101         LBC group 0x01 (PCI 02 + 21 01)
03221156       VCM DID 0x1156 (PCI 03 + 22 11 56)

Over BLE the library defaults to the LeLink GATT layout: service 0000ffe0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, with 0000ffe1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb used for both notify and write.

A client on a native CAN interface (Battery-Emulator) answers each LBC frame itself with 30 01 00 FF FF FF FF FF on 0x79B, a block size of 1. The community spreadsheet says that frame must follow within 15 ms.

docs.title: ISO-TP reassembly
docs.text:
• 0x single frame: low nibble = length.
  • 1L LL first frame: 12-bit length, then 6 data bytes. Group 0x61 is 331 bytes, so its first frame is 11 4B.
  • 2n consecutive frame: sequence 1..F, wrapping to 0, then 7 data bytes. Group 0x02 wraps the counter more than once, so count frames.
  • Truncate to the announced length. A single frame 03 7F <svc> <NRC> is a negative response, not group data.

All offsets below index the reassembled payload, where payload[0] = 0x61 and payload[1] is the group number. OVMS offsets are 2 lower.

docs.title: LBC groups (service 0x21)
docs.text:
Group Contents Reply length 01 current, pack V, 12 V, insulation, Hx/health, SOC, Ah 41 (ZE0) / 43 (AZE0) / 53 (ZE1) 02 96 cell voltages + pack and bus voltage 198 04 pack temperatures 16 (ZE0/AZE0) / 31 (ZE1) 06 balancing shunts (layout disputed) 26 61 health block: Hx, SOH, bars, capacity (ZE1) 331 62 L1/L2 and quick-charge counts, usage histograms 118 / 120 (ZE1) 83 / 84 battery part number / pack serial (ASCII) —

The group 0x01 reply length identifies the generation. A ZE1 that has just woken sometimes answers with 0x2C (44 bytes), a layout no source maps; poll again.

docs.title: Group 0x01 — ZE0 (41 bytes)
docs.text: Field Offset Len Decode Unit Confidence HV current 1 2 4 signed / 1024 A hypothesis HV current 2 8 4 signed / 1024 A hypothesis HV pack voltage 20 2 / 100 V hypothesis 12 V supply 22 2 / 1000 V reported Insulation resistance 24 2 ×1 kΩ reported Hx 28 2 / 100 % reported State of charge 31 3 / 10000 % reported Capacity 34 4 / 10000 Ah reported

docs.title: Group 0x01 — AZE0 (43 bytes)
docs.text: Field Offset Len Decode Unit Confidence HV current 1 / 2 2 / 8 4 signed / 1024 A hypothesis HV pack voltage 20 2 / 100 V hypothesis 12 V supply 22 2 / 1000 V reported Insulation resistance 24 2 ×1 kΩ reported Hx 28 2 / 100 % reported State of charge 31 3 / 10000 % hypothesis (ZE0 offset assumed) Capacity 34 4 / 10000 Ah reported

docs.title: Group 0x01 — ZE1 (53 bytes)
docs.text:
Field Offset Len Decode Unit Confidence HV current 1 / 2 2 / 8 4 signed / 1024 A reported HV pack voltage 20 2 / 100 V reported 12 V supply 22 2 / 1000 V reported Insulation resistance 24 2 ×1 kΩ reported Health ("Hx") 30 2 / 102.4 % reported, disputed State of charge 33 3 / 10000 % reported Capacity 37 3 / 10000 Ah reported

On ZE1, OVMS and py-nissan-leaf-obd-ble read payload[30..31] / 102.4 as health. Battery-Emulator reads no Hx from this layout and takes ZE1 Hx and SOH from group 0x61 instead.

docs.title: Group 0x02 — cells (all generations)
docs.text: 96 × u16 big-endian millivolts at payload[2 + 2i]. 0xFFFF (or ≥ 5000 mV) means no reading. Pack voltage is at payload[194..195] / 100 V and bus voltage at payload[196..197] / 100 V.

docs.title: Group 0x04 — temperatures
docs.text: There are four sensor slots, each a u16 thermistor raw value at payload[2 + 3i] followed by one byte at payload[4 + 3i] holding whole °C. The third slot (i = 2) reads FF FF FF on 2013+ packs, which have only three sensors. payload[14] is a fifth temperature in °C. OVMS converts raw to °C as -0.102 × (raw − 710). Only the first 16 bytes of the ZE1 reply are mapped.

docs.title: Group 0x61 — health block (ZE1)
docs.text: Field Offset Len Decode Unit Hx 2 2 / 100 % SOH 4 2 / 100 % Dash capacity bars 6 1 raw — SOH, unfiltered 7 2 / 100 % SOH, filtered 9 2 / 100 % Capacity 14 4 / 10000 Ah

docs.title: VCM and meter (UDS 0x22)
docs.text:
Request 03 22 <DID> to 0x797 (VCM) or 0x743 (meter). The reply is 0L 62 <DID> <data>, and the single-frame length gives the data width.

ECU DID Meaning Decode VCM 1103 12 V battery voltage × 0.08 V VCM 1183 12 V battery current signed16 / 256 A VCM 1203 / 1205 quick / L1-L2 charge count u16, FFFF = none VCM 1156 gear 1 P, 2 R, 3 N, 4 D (Eco: 5 or 7, sources differ) VCM 1304 power switch bit 7 set = on VCM 1234 / 114E plug state / charge mode enums VCM 115D ambient temperature x / 2 − 40 °C (disputed) VCM 121A speed signed16 / 10 km/h Meter 0E01 odometer 24-bit km Meter 0E25–0E28 tyre pressures FR, FL, RR, RL × 1.7236894 kPa (0.25 psi)

The VIN comes from 21 81 on the VCM: a 19-byte reply holding 17 ASCII characters and 2 zero bytes. Never publish a real one.

docs.title: Worked example (invented values)
docs.text:
A ZE1 group 0x01 reply:

7BB 10 35 61 01 FF FF F8 00     current_1 = 0xFFFFF800 / 1024 = -2.0 A
7BB 21 00 00 FF FF F8 00 FF
7BB 22 FF FF FF FF FF FF FF
7BB 23 94 70 32 00 03 E8 FF     pack 0x9470/100 = 380.00 V, 12 V 0x3200 = 12.8 V, 1000 kΩ
7BB 24 FF FF FF 25 80 00 0B     health 0x2580/102.4 = 93.75 %
7BB 25 71 B0 00 0F 42 40 FF     SOC 0x0B71B0/10000 = 75.0 %, 0x0F4240/10000 = 100.0 Ah
7BB 26 FF FF FF FF FF FF FF
7BB 27 FF FF FF FF FF FF FF

scripts/test_nissan_leaf_obd2_spec.py decodes this and the other vectors in the spec (ZE0, AZE0, group 0x02, 0x04, 0x61, VCM and meter frames) from the spec's own tables.

docs.title: What is still unknown
docs.text:
1. The AZE0 SOC offset, which is assumed from ZE0.
  2. Which ZE1 health figure is the "real" SOH: group 0x01 health / 102.4, or group 0x61.
  3. The group 0x06 balancing-bit layout, where OVMS and Battery-Emulator disagree.
  4. Whether ZE0/AZE0 answer group 0x61.
  5. Whether the ELM327 needs ATCRA 7BB with these headers, and how its flow control behaves under ATCAF0.
  6. Which J1962 pins reach the LBC on each generation.

The full list is in the spec's remaining_unknowns.

docs.title: NIU Electric Scooter
docs.text: Status: Research Protocol: Cloud HTTP API (documented) + BLE (undocumented) Manufacturer: Niu Technologies Manufacturer Status: Active, cloud-dependent

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
NIU scooters report telemetry — battery state, position, odometer, ride history — through NIU's cloud. The companion app (com.niu.manager) authenticates against NIU's account service, receives an OAuth2 token, and reads everything back from NIU's servers. The scooter also has a BLE link the app uses when it is next to the bike.

This one is on the registry for the reason the project exists: if NIU turns the service off, the app stops working, and every documented data path goes with it. Per the project's scope rules, cloud-only devices are documented and deprioritised — so this page records the cloud dependency accurately, and names the local path as the gap worth closing.

The documented API is the dependency, not the escape from it

Everything below runs through NIU's servers. It is genuinely useful today — it is what the Home Assistant integrations use — but it is not local control, and it does not survive the service being retired. The BLE link is the local-first target and it is not publicly documented. Closing that gap is the actual work here.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Models N/M/U/G series (varies by market) App com.niu.manager (Android) Radios Cellular (scooter → NIU cloud), BLE (scooter ↔ phone) Battery Removable; single- and dual-battery variants differ in API shape

docs.text:
Constant Value Account service https://account-fk.niu.com API service https://app-api-fk.niu.com

The -fk hosts are the ones current integrations use; older captures show app-api.niu.com. Hosts appear to be region-dependent — confirm against your own account rather than assuming.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Item Value Path POST /v3/api/oauth2/token (on the account host) Scheme OAuth2 → bearer token Credentials The owner's own NIU app account Scope Most data calls also need the scooter's serial number (sn)

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Path Returns /v5/scooter/list Scooters on the account, with serial numbers /v5/scooter/motor_data/index_info Main telemetry — state of charge, position, odometer /v3/motor_data/battery_info Battery detail (dual-battery models report per-pack) /motoinfo/overallTally Lifetime totals /v5/track/list/v2 Ride/track history

Note the mixed versioning: telemetry and listing moved to v5 while battery detail is still v3. Both are live — this is the API's actual shape, not a transcription slip.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
reported. Hosts and paths are taken from a maintained Home Assistant integration and corroborated by independent captures, but none have been exercised by us. The original API capture work explicitly covers dual-battery scooters only; single-battery models may differ in response shape.

Credentials and tokens

A token is tied to the owner's account and grants access to their scooter — including its live location. Capture tokens only from your own account, never commit one, and treat a captured token like a password. Nothing in this repo should carry a real token or serial number.

docs.title: BLE — the gap
docs.text:
The app talks to the scooter directly over BLE when in range. NIU publishes nothing about it, but the spec now records the service and characteristic UUIDs, the frame layout and the pairing story from static analysis of the vendor app (not hardware-tested): before the link answers, the client runs a two-frame challenge handshake under a per-vehicle AES key, and that key is fetched from NIU's cloud (/v5/smart_key/ble_info). So BLE is a real control channel, but not yet a cloud-free one.

Prior work exists on adjacent scooters — Ninebot/Segway's BLE protocol has been reverse engineered independently — but nothing transfers without a capture. This is the highest value experiment on this page:

  1. Scan a powered scooter with nRF Connect; record advertised name, address, service and characteristic UUIDs.
  2. Enable Android HCI snoop logging and capture the app performing one connect plus one simple action.
  3. Establish whether the BLE link is a full control channel or only a proximity/unlock handshake with everything else deferred to the cloud. That answer decides whether local control is achievable at all.

docs.title: Device spec
docs.text:
device-specs/devices/niu-escooter.yaml records this device as what it is: cloud-only, via a cloud block carrying required: true, the hosts, the OAuth2 shape, the endpoint list, an explicit failure_mode, and data_leaves_device naming location and ride history as personal data.

A spec may satisfy the schema on cloud alone. That is deliberate — it makes "no local path exists" a machine-readable state rather than prose buried in a notes field, so a consumer can present the device as vendor-tethered instead of quietly offering endpoints that will one day 404.

docs.title: Freeing it takes a different controller
docs.text:
The spec's local_access block is status: replacement_hardware, and its covers / not_covered split is the honest part:

Covered by fitting an aftermarket Bluetooth controller motor drive parameters — max speed, acceleration, per-mode speed limits, current, battery config, over the replacement part's own BLE app Not covered telemetry, position and ride history (still NIU's cloud); GPS and alarm (the vendor advertises these as continuing to work unchanged — i.e. still tethered); the stock BLE link, still undocumented either way

One such part is the escootparts NIU Bluetooth controller — sold as a performance upgrade for N1S/N1/NQi/UQi/MQi variants, replacing the stock motor controller, reversible if you keep the original.

Replacing the controller does not free the scooter — it frees the throttle map

It is worth being precise about what this buys, because the shape is common across the aftermarket: a replacement part liberates one subsystem while the rest stays tethered. Here the drivetrain becomes locally programmable and every connected feature remains cloud-dependent. The vendor's own selling point — that the NIU app, dashboard, GPS and alarm keep working — is precisely the evidence that the cloud stack is untouched.

Recorded as documentation of what exists, not as an endorsement: untested by us, a third-party commercial listing, and raising current limits on a road vehicle carries the usual thermal and legal consequences.

If the stock BLE link turns out to be a full control channel, this device drops to bridge_hardware or native and this section shrinks to a footnote. Establishing that is the highest-value experiment on this page.

docs.title: OBD-II Bluetooth Adapters (ELM327 / STN)
docs.text: Status: Complete (adapter link layer) / In Progress (per-model GATT coverage) Protocol: Bluetooth Classic SPP or BLE GATT, carrying an ASCII ELM327 command set Manufacturer: Generic (ELM327 clones), ScanTool.net (OBDLink), Vgate, LELink and others Manufacturer Status: Active (clones are unsupported and undocumented; firmware is cloned from a discontinued Elm Electronics part)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every vehicle target in this repo is reached through one of these dongles, so the adapter deserves its own spec: it is the transport under the transport. The vehicle-side protocol is OBD-II / UDS; the phone-side protocol is a Bluetooth serial link carrying ASCII text.

That ASCII property is what makes these adapters so useful for reverse engineering. Capture the Bluetooth link between a vendor app and the dongle and you can read the vendor's diagnostic requests directly — no decryption, no protobuf, no obfuscation. A btsnoop HCI log of a paid tool doing a paid function is a plain-text transcript of the protocol it is charging for.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Property Value Original part Elm Electronics ELM327 (discontinued; the market is clones) Quality chipsets OBD Solutions STN11xx / STN21xx / STN22xx (OBDLink LX / MX / MX+ / CX), ARM Cortex-M0 (UniCarScan) Link Bluetooth Classic SPP (RFCOMM), BLE GATT, or dual-mode Vehicle side ISO 15765-4 CAN, ISO 9141-2, ISO 14230-4, SAE J1850 Power Parasitic from OBD pin 16 (unswitched +12 V on most vehicles)

Leave nothing plugged in

Pin 16 is usually unswitched. Cheap dongles do not sleep reliably and will flatten a battery over a week — especially on a motorcycle. Unplug after each session.

docs.title: Link layer 1: Bluetooth Classic (SPP)
docs.text:
Property Value Profile Serial Port Profile over RFCOMM, usually channel 1 Advertised names OBDII, OBDII-BT, V-LINK, Vgate, OBDLink LX, OBDLink MX, OBDLink MX+, UniCarScan Pairing PIN 1234, 0000 or 6789 depending on firmware Linux bind sudo rfcomm bind 0 <mac> 1 → /dev/rfcomm0

Generic Bluetooth Classic dongles cannot be used from an iPhone — iOS requires BLE or an MFi-certified Classic device (OBDLink MX+ and vLinker FS are MFi). Android apps such as Torque Pro require Classic SPP and will not see a BLE-only adapter. This split is why most vendor tools are Android-first.

docs.title: Link layer 2: BLE GATT
docs.text:
BLE adapters expose a two-characteristic serial pipe: write your ASCII command to one, receive the reply as notifications on the other. Three families cover almost the whole market:

Family Service Notify (adapter → phone) Write (phone → adapter) Seen on A 0000fff0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0000fff1-… 0000fff2-… OBDLink CX and a large share of generic adapters B 000018f0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 00002af0-… 00002af1-… Vgate iCar Pro 2S BLE, LELink2 C 0000ffe0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb 0000ffe1-… 0000ffe1-… (same characteristic) HM-10-module clones (community-reported)

Family C is the same HM-10 serial pass-through pattern documented for the MoTool Slacker — a single bidirectional characteristic rather than a pair. A client that wants to work with arbitrary hardware should probe for all three rather than hardcoding one. FFE0 is shared with unrelated serial modules, so it selects family C only after an OBD name or family-B advertisement has identified the adapter; it is not scan-time identity on its own.

Notes that matter in practice:

  • Enable notifications via the standard CCCD (0x2902) before writing anything.
  • Replies arrive split across notifications and are only complete when the > prompt byte appears. Buffer until >, do not parse per-notification.
  • MTU is often 20 bytes; long replies (a ATI banner, a multi-line CAN response) always span several notifications.
  • No authentication, no encryption, no pairing on most BLE adapters. Anyone in range of a plugged-in dongle has the same access the owner does. The exception is the OBDLink CX, which bonds with a fixed passkey of 123456 during the first five minutes after power-on and always encrypts the link.

docs.title: Application layer: the ELM327 command set
docs.text:
Two request kinds share one channel, distinguished by prefix:

Prefix Meaning Example AT… Adapter configuration ATSP6 — select ISO 15765-4, 11-bit, 500 kbit/s ST… STN-only extensions STP33 — STN protocol select hex digits Payload sent to the vehicle 22F190 — UDS ReadDataByIdentifier

Commands are \r-terminated. Replies end with >.

Command Effect ATZ Reset; returns the firmware banner (ELM327 v1.5, STN2120 …) ATI Identify without resetting ATE0 / ATL0 / ATS0 Echo, linefeeds, spaces off — do this first when scripting ATRV Adapter's estimate of battery voltage (approximate; not from the ECU) ATSP<n> / ATDP Set / display protocol ATSH <hhh> Set request header (physical ECU addressing, e.g. ATSH 7E0) ATCRA <hhh> Filter received frames to one response ID ATFCSH / ATFCSD / ATFCSM Flow-control header, data and mode for multi-frame ISO-TP ATCAF0 CAN auto-formatting off — raw frames, ISO-TP is yours to do ATST <hh> Response timeout

docs.title: Known adapters
docs.text:
The models named by vendor tools, and what each actually provides. Chipset attributions marked (reported) come from vendor/community documentation rather than our own teardown.

Adapter Chipset Link iOS Tier Notable UniCarScan UCSI-2100 ARM Cortex-M0 (WGSoft in-house) Bluetooth 4.0 (BLE) Yes advanced-stn-equivalent Accepts messages up to 255 bytes where a stock ELM327 stops at 8. Field-updatable firmware. Certified for MotoScan, BimmerCode, TuneECU OBDLink MX Bluetooth STN1170 (reported) Bluetooth Classic v3.0, SPP No advanced-stn First Bluetooth tool to reach SW-CAN and MS-CAN. ~100 PIDs/s OBDLink MX+ STN2255 (reported) Bluetooth Classic v3.0, MFi Yes advanced-stn MS-CAN + SW-CAN and iOS — the only wireless iOS adapter that reaches those buses OBDLink LX STN110-class Bluetooth Classic No advanced-stn The adapter TuneECU names most often for Triumph OBDLink CX STN-class BLE (GATT family A) Yes advanced-stn BLE-native Vgate vLinker MC+ ELM327 v4.3.2-class BLE + Classic Yes standards-elm327 Works for some vendor functions, not all Generic "ELM327 v2.1" Cloned firmware varies varies basic-clone Legislated reads only

Three things worth pulling out of that table:

  • The UCSI-2100's 255-byte message support is the single most useful property for the work in this repo. Long diagnostic writes stop being a flow-control negotiation and become one command, which is why it appears in TuneECU's supported list alongside the STN adapters despite not being an OBD Solutions part.
  • MX has no iOS support at all; MX+ adds MFi. If a tool is documented as "MX or MX+", an iPhone narrows that to MX+.
  • MS-CAN and SW-CAN are a capability, not a protocol version. They are manufacturer buses on non-standard pins, and no amount of ELM327 command compatibility substitutes for hardware that can reach them. The spec models this as the alt_can_bus capability.

docs.title: What vendor tools require
docs.text:
Matching tools to the capability tokens makes "which adapter do I need" answerable without trial and error:

Tool Vehicles Needs Practical adapters FORScan Ford / Mazda / Lincoln / Mercury alt_can_bus (MS-CAN) for body and chassis modules, plus custom_headers OBDLink MX+ / MX / EX; or a switched HS/MS ELM327 clone, which is why that oddity exists at all TuneECU Triumph, KTM, Aprilia, Benelli, Ducati, Moto Guzzi multiframe_tx, flow_control, custom_headers, raw_frames OBDLink LX / MX / MX+, UniCarScan UCSI-2100, Vgate vLinker MC+ TigerTool Triumph Tiger 800/900/Sport/Explorer/Trophy raw_frames, custom_headers, mid-session protocol switching, custom ISO init address Any adapter that honours ATCAF0/ATCRA/ATIIA MotoScan BMW motorcycles BMW KWP2000/D-CAN/UDS, long messages UniCarScan UCSI-2100 (the vendor's own reference adapter) BimmerCode BMW cars custom_headers, multiframe_tx UniCarScan UCSI-2100, OBDLink MX+ OBD Fusion Generic + enhanced PIDs single_frame; enhanced/manufacturer PIDs benefit from custom_headers Any; STN adapters for enhanced data Torque Pro Generic single_frame, Classic SPP only Any Classic adapter; will not see a BLE-only one

The pattern is the same one this repo keeps hitting: the legislated layer works everywhere, and everything an owner actually wants sits behind a capability the cheap hardware lacks.

docs.title: Capability tier
docs.text:
Which tier a dongle belongs to decides which functions it can run. See classifying OBD-II devices for the full capability matrix.

Class Typical hardware Runs basic commands Runs advanced commands basic-clone "ELM327 v2.1" clones Yes No — multi-frame transmit and flow control are unreliable standards-elm327 Genuine ELM327 v1.4/1.5 Yes Partly — firmware-dependent advanced-stn OBDLink LX / MX+ / CX Yes Yes native-can SocketCAN, PCAN, Kvaser Yes Yes, plus bus sniffing

alt_can_bus (Ford MS-CAN, GM SW-CAN) cuts across the tiers: only the MX, MX+ and EX provide it, so a advanced-stn adapter without it still cannot run FORScan's body-module functions.

The spec's baseline profile is standards-elm327, because that is what the whole family can be relied on to do; anything needing multiframe_tx or flow_control should be matched against an advanced-stn adapter specifically.

docs.title: Telling a good adapter from a clone
docs.text:
Clone firmware reports a version banner it did not earn (ELM327 v2.1 on a v1.4 core is common) and typically fails on:

  • multi-frame ISO-TP transmit — the direction needed for a UDS write
  • honouring an ECU's requested separation time in flow control
  • custom headers via ATSH on some protocols

Single-frame reads (03 for DTCs, 01xx for live data) work almost everywhere, which is exactly why vendor tools accept any adapter for reading and name specific ones for maintenance functions. If a documented function works on an OBDLink and fails on a clone, the function is multi-frame — that is a protocol fact you get for free.

A quick capability probe:

ATZ            → banner (claimed, not proven)
ATSP6          → OK
ATCAF0         → OK          clone firmware sometimes refuses
ATFCSM1        → OK          if this fails, multi-frame TX will fail

docs.title: Using one for capture
docs.text:
The reason this page exists. To recover a vendor tool's protocol:

  1. Android: Developer options → Enable Bluetooth HCI snoop log.
  2. Run the vendor app through the function of interest, once, cleanly.
  3. Pull btsnoop_hci.log (adb pull /sdcard/btsnoop_hci.log, path varies by OEM).
  4. Open in Wireshark, filter btrfcomm (Classic) or btatt (BLE), Follow Stream.
  5. Read the AT setup and the hex payloads directly out of the ASCII.

scripts/obd_discover.py speaks this same command set over /dev/rfcomm0 or a BLE serial bridge, read-only, for mapping which ECUs and DIDs a vehicle answers.

docs.title: OBDLink MX+
docs.text: Status: In Progress (static analysis complete; hardware capture pending) Protocol: Dual-mode Bluetooth — Classic v3.0 SPP/iAP2 (primary) + BLE GATT serial pipe Manufacturer: OBD Solutions LLC (ScanTool.net) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The OBDLink MX+ is the top of the OBDLink wireless line: an STN-chipset adapter (STN2255 originally, STN2256 on current production per FRPM rev F) that speaks the extended ST command set and is one of only three wireless adapters (MX, MX+, EX) that reach Ford MS-CAN and GM SW-CAN in addition to every legislated OBD-II protocol. MFi certification (iAP2) makes it the only wireless adapter in the family that works with iOS against those manufacturer buses.

Unlike the BLE-only OBDLink CX, the MX+ leads with Bluetooth Classic v3.0 (SPP + iAP2) and also exposes a BLE GATT pipe — the vendor app treats it as dual-mode and can demand Classic for some operations. See OBD-II Bluetooth Adapters for the generic ELM327/STN link layer this page builds on.

Everything below comes from static analysis of the official OBDLink Android app (7.4.0, recovered .NET assemblies) plus vendor/community documentation — nothing has been confirmed against hardware yet. The hardware-session checklist is in research-notes/obdlink-mx-plus-capture-plan.md.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model MX201 Chipset STN2255 (original, out of production) / STN2256 (current, reported) Radio Bluetooth Classic v3.0 (SPP, iAP2) + BLE; "secure 128-bit data encryption" (vendor claim) Vehicle side All legislated OBD-II protocols + Ford MS-CAN (J1962 pins 3/11) + GM SW-CAN (pin 1) Power 8–18 V from OBD pin 16; BatterySaver sleep < 2 mA (vendor claim) Button "Connect" button — physical-access gate for pairing; 15 s hold = factory reset

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes (pairing) Method button_pairing Advertised name OBDLink MX+ Passphrase protection not_applicable (button press is the proof of possession) Confidence medium (vendor docs + app strings; not replayed)

Pairing: press the Connect button — the blue LED blinks rapidly for a ~2 minute window — then pair from the host OS Bluetooth settings. On Android the OS-level bond is mandatory before the vendor app will connect (confirmed by an app error string). The adapter's pairing mode is configurable between Auto and Manual (a pairing-mode setting in the app). The app's setup wizard has a dedicated press-the-pair-button page with an instructional animation.

Factory reset: hold the button ~15 s until the green POWER LED flashes rapidly (vendor support article 43000714324). Clears adapter config and bonds; touches nothing on the vehicle.

docs.title: BLE GATT
docs.text:
UUID Role Evidence 0000fff0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Serial service string literal in the app: its default serial service 0000fff1-… Notify (adapter → host) the app's default receive characteristic 0000fff2-… Write (host → adapter) the app's default transmit characteristic

Same family-A pipe as the OBDLink CX. The app enables notifications via the standard CCCD (0x2902) with a Notify/Indicate fallback. Not yet observed on-air — the capture plan includes a GATT discovery dump to confirm the MX+ BLE side matches.

docs.title: Bluetooth Classic
docs.text:
SPP (UUID 00001101-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, string in the app) advertised as OBDLink MX+. Primary link per the vendor spec sheet; iOS uses it via MFi iAP2. The app raises a dedicated needs-Classic error when an operation needs Classic, so a BLE-only client should expect some functions (possibly including firmware update) to be Classic-only until proven otherwise.

The spec records this side in its bluetooth_classic block (dual_mode: true, ble_role: secondary_control; SPP as the secure control profile, iAP2 listed but not documented) and finds it with a bt_classic_inquiry discovery method (name prefix OBDLink MX+, SPP service class, discoverable only inside the Connect-button window). The stream is the same ASCII AT/ST command set as the BLE pipe, lines ending in CR (0d), a reply ending at the > prompt. The Classic bond lives in bluetooth_classic.pairing (required, inside a ~120 s window opened by the Connect button); device.pairing describes only the BLE pipe, whose pairing needs are still unknown. host_compatibility gives CoreBluetooth two verdicts: the Classic link is incompatible on iOS (no RFCOMM; workaround vendor_mfi, since iAP2 is reachable only through the vendor's own MFi app), and the BLE link is degraded, the path a third-party iOS client takes, minus whatever the app reserves for Classic.

docs.title: STN command surface visible in the app
docs.text: Beyond the ELM327 baseline, the app uses STI (STN ID/firmware — the clone discriminator), STIM, STMFR, STPBR, STSLCS, the STSL* sleep/wake trigger family (STSLVL*, STSLVG*, STSLU*, STSLX*), and STNFWv in the firmware path. Full reference: OBDLink FRPM rev F.

docs.title: Firmware update
docs.text:
In-app, over the existing serial link — no separate BLE OTA/DFU service. Flow recovered from the app's firmware-update code:

  1. App downloads a manifest and "v5" firmware file (parsed by a header reader and a file validator) from api.obdlink.com/devices — per-device-code manifests, Stable/Beta branches, optional private code.
  2. The app's firmware loader connects to the adapter bootloader, checks bootloader version bounds and the device ID (the app's list covers two MX hardware revisions, the LX, the CX and others).
  3. Upload is a start-upload command followed by chunked send-chunk commands; a dedicated validation image type verifies the flash afterwards.
  4. Recovery path exists: a firmware-recovery utility that asks the user to power-cycle the device, pick it from a list and retry.

Latest MX+ firmware reported in the wild: 5.12.x. Whether image validation is cryptographic (signature) or structural (header/checksum) is still open — the app's invalid-image check is client-side and needs either IL-level decompilation or an observed update to characterize.

docs.title: Omron BLE Blood Pressure Monitors (OMRON connect family)
docs.text: Status: Complete (hardware-verified by upstream RE projects, not by us) Protocol: BLE GATT (custom split-channel sync protocol) Manufacturer: Omron Healthcare Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Omron's Bluetooth blood pressure monitors (HEM-7xxx upper-arm, HEM-6xxx wrist; retail names M2/M3/M4/M7 Intelli IT, RS2/RS7 Intelli IT, EVOLV, Complete, Platinum, BP5xxx/BP7xxx) store measurements in on-device EEPROM and sync them to the OMRON connect app over BLE. The sync protocol is fully local — no cloud account on the wire — and has been reverse engineered independently three times: userx14/omblepy (Python CLI + per-model drivers), ichernev/omron-rs7-intelli-it (HCI-snoop protocol notes), and eigger/hass-omron (Home Assistant integration, 12 models verified). A 2026-08 teardown of the vendor app (Japanese OMRON connect jp.co.omron.healthcare.omron_connect; the US/Canada app is com.omronhealthcare.omronconnect) confirms the UUID set, the split-channel reassembly rule and the pairing exchange below, and ships per-model EEPROM memory-map configs for 86 model variants.

Medical device

Readings synced through this spec are a personal log, not a clinical measurement, and must never be the sole basis for a medication decision or for deciding whether to seek care. Chart them if you like; dose from the monitor's own display and your care team's instructions. The spec carries a safety_advisory saying so.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number HEM-6161T/6232T/7142T2/7155T/7322T/7361T/7600T/… Radio BLE 4.2+ Advertised name HEM-*; also service 0xFE4A and manufacturer id 0x020E

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes (one-time pairing before record download) Method button_pairing (hold BT button → blinking -P-) Passphrase protection not_applicable (no Wi-Fi); 16-byte client-chosen BLE key Confidence high (working open implementations against hardware)

Pairing: hold the monitor's Bluetooth button 3-5 s until -P- blinks; connect and enable notify on RX channel 0 (triggers OS-level BLE bonding); write 02 ‖ 16×00 to the unlock characteristic (response 8200 = key programming mode); write 00 ‖ <16-byte key> (response 8000). The key is chosen by the client. Later sessions just write 01 ‖ key → 8100.

Factory reset: not documented in the RE sources, and not needed — the single stored key is simply overwritten by pairing again.

Rebinding to a new client: in place — re-enter pairing mode and program a new key. The hardware holds exactly ONE key: rebinding evicts the previous client, including the official app (unpair/forget it at OS level on the old host). Using the vendor app and a local client simultaneously is impossible.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description ecbe3980-c9a2-11e1-b1bd-0002a5d5c51b Omron Sync Service Parent service (legacy 4-channel set) 49123040/4d0bf320/5128ce60/560f1420-aee8-… RX channels 0-3 Client→device writes, 16-byte chunks in channel order db5b55e0/e0b8a060/0ae12b00/10e1ba60-aee7/8-… TX channels 0-3 Device→client notifies, reassembled via length byte b305b680-aee7-11e1-a730-0002a5d5c51b Unlock Key programming (02/00) and session unlock (01)

Newer models may use a different/single-channel UUID set (per-model drivers in omblepy and hass-omron).

docs.title: Message framing
docs.text:
Offset Length Description 0 1 Total message length (incl. CRC) 1 2 Command type: 0000 start, 0100 EEPROM read, 01c0 write, 0f00 end (responses set the high bit: 8000/8100/81c0/8f00) 3 2 EEPROM address (big-endian) 5 1 Payload size 6 n Payload last 1 XOR checksum (all bytes XOR to 0)

Session: start (08 0000 0000 10 00 18) → EEPROM reads → optional writes (unread-counter reset, time sync — only these; stray EEPROM writes can destroy pressure calibration) → end (08 0f00 0000 00 00 07, status byte 0 = OK).

docs.title: Record layout (HEM-7322T, 14-byte record, bit-packed big-endian)
docs.text:
Bits Description 0-7 Diastolic mmHg 8-15 Systolic − 25 mmHg 16-23 Year − 2000 24-31 Pulse bpm 32 / 33 Body-movement / irregular-heartbeat flags 34-37, 38-42, 43-47, 52-57, 58-63 Month, day, hour, minute, second

Per-user ring buffers (HEM-7322T: users at 0x02AC / 0x0824, 100 records each); settings region at 0x0260 (write-back at 0x0286) holds the unread-record counters and the clock. Other models have their own layouts (omblepy deviceSpecific/*.py).

Known limits: HEM-7196T encrypts its traffic (unsupported); HEM-7380T1 / HEM-7377T1 read out without pairing; HEM-7530T EKG records undecoded; battery changes can reset the clock (re-run time sync).

docs.title: Onewheel (BLE)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (unverified) — active but hostile; firmware unlock handshake Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Future Motion Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Onewheel self-balancing board (V1/+/XR/Pint/GT) is controlled over BLE with a per-attribute GATT. Future Motion is hostile — firmware ≥ 4034 won't stream telemetry until the client answers a keyed challenge — so the community pOneWheel app implements the published unlock handshake.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
Service e659f300-…; per-attribute chars (f303 battery %, f30b speed RPM, f316 voltage, f311 firmware). Unlock (FW ≥ 4034): read challenge from f3fe, write CRX + MD5(challenge + published static key) to f3ff.

See device-specs/devices/onewheel-ble.yaml for the full machine-readable spec.

docs.title: Oral-B iO Smart Brush and iO Sense Charger
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (app/capture-derived; untested on hardware here) Protocol: BLE GATT and manufacturer advertisements Manufacturer: Procter & Gamble Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The iO brush and iO Sense charger expose local BLE state and control surfaces without requiring the Oral-B cloud for basic reads. Brush UUIDs use a0f0xxxx-5047-4d53-8208-4f72616c2d42. Protocol versions V001–V009 change layouts, so read the version before decoding version-dependent fields.

The November 2026 follow-up adds an independently captured iO Series 10 / iO Sense implementation. It establishes the charger service a0f03e00-…, its read-only native and brush-passthrough grammar, charger status bits, extended battery records and retained-session summaries. Its 488 tests passed upstream; this project did not connect to a brush or charger.

docs.title: Setup and Pairing
docs.text:
The brush needs no account or provisioning. Discovery uses manufacturer data under P&G company ID 0x00DC (wire bytes dc 00), not a service-UUID scan. The brush filter needs only five bytes but the complete brush advertisement is 15 bytes. The charger filter accepts a shorter packet, but decode its complete layout only with all 18 full-packet bytes.

The brush accepts one BLE client. The charger forwards brush reads only while it owns that connection. The charger is an outbound network client, not an inbound HTTP/HTTPS/SSH/MQTT management API. Wi-Fi provisioning credential sequencing and the durable upload queue remain undocumented.

No application-level bond is required by the documented paths. Reconnect after the previous client releases the brush.

docs.title: Reset and rebinding
docs.text:
The YAML distinguishes three operations:

  • Handle reset: hold the power button until the LED flashes. Published hold times vary, so follow the indicator rather than assuming an exact duration.
  • Display-model reset: use the handle's Settings/factory-reset menu; the same menu can simply disable Bluetooth.
  • iO Sense charger reset: touch and hold its button until an orange light appears, release, then tap once more while the light is showing.

These are not the same operation and do not clear identical state. Moving a client normally needs only a disconnect/reconnect, not a factory reset.

docs.title: Core GATT services
docs.text:
Service Role a0f0ff00-5047-4d53-8208-4f72616c2d42 Brush characteristics and OTA path a0f03e00-5047-4d53-8208-4f72616c2d42 iO Sense charger commands, payload, returned data and status

The charger characteristics were previously grouped under the brush service; that was incorrect. Their actual roles are:

Characteristic Role a0f03c00-… Command header and final delimiter, write a0f03c01-… Returned data, read/notify a0f03c02-… Command payload, write a0f03c03-… Command status, read/notify

Protocol-2 headers are [operation, command]: GET c0, POST c1, EXECUTE c2. Finish every transaction with e0 on C00 and validate C03 status [command, operation, result], where 01 was observed for success.

A passthrough brush read is:

C00: c1 37
C02: uuid_lsb uuid_msb 01 00
C00: e0

For example, 08 ff 01 00 reads FF08. Successful status is 37 c1 01; returned data is 37 c1 uuid_lsb uuid_msb operation success length data…. Serialize one complete transaction at a time—the tested charger rejects batched records. Native read-only command IDs include device info, Wi-Fi/IoT state, firmware, uptime, clock, brush/passthrough state, ring and night-light state. The YAML lists all 24 IDs without granting POST/EXECUTE permission.

docs.title: Battery record FF05
docs.text:
The older one-byte percentage remains valid. Later records are little-endian and length-gated:

Offset Field Rule 0 Battery percentage uint8 1–2 Estimated brushing seconds remaining uint16; 0xffff unavailable; zero unavailable only on protocol 6 3–4 Millivolts uint16, protocol 8+ 5–6 Signed milliamps int16, protocol 8+; -1 unavailable 7 Temperature int8 °C, protocol 8+

Do not decode absent fields from shorter packets. The spec binds percentage, runtime, voltage, current and temperature entities only with those version and sentinel rules.

docs.title: Retained session FF29
docs.text:
Protocol 7/8 uses a 21-byte little-endian retained-session record. Protocol 9 is registered for compatibility in the public implementation; protocol 6 has a different 20-byte layout and must not use this table.

Offset Meaning 0–3 Brush-clock start; not automatically a Unix timestamp 4–5 Packed session ID (& 0x1fff) and user ID (>> 13) 6–7 Packed target seconds (& 0x1fff) and sector count (>> 13) 8–9 Duration in seconds 10–13 High/low-pressure durations, each uint16 × 0.1 seconds 14 Average pressure, uint8 × 100 mN 15 Maximum pressure, uint8 × 100 mN 16–17 High/low-pressure event counts 18 Power-on count 19 Mode, decoded by packet protocol version 20 Ending battery percent when ≤ 100

The captured direct client reads the latest record after session settlement without an FF21 command. Charger reads have a separate availability window.

docs.title: Advertisements and diagnostics
docs.text:
The complete brush advertisement has 15 bytes: protocol/model/software, state, button/pressure flags, timer, mode, progress and quadrant data. It has no battery byte; battery comes from FF05.

The iO Sense manufacturer value is 14 bytes starting at full-packet offset 4. It carries protocol, charger type 0xa2, software version, server mode, an advertised MAC, body color and a final status byte. Redact the MAC in fixtures. Status bits are:

0 Wi-Fi, 1 internet, 2 cloud, 3 brush connected, 4 brush charging, 5 touchpad active, 6 brush paired, 7 demo mode. Advertisements do not carry timer, pressure, zone, score or completed-session data.

docs.title: ServiceDataA/B
docs.text:
These are 16-byte GATT diagnostics, not advertisements. All fields are little-endian.

  • ServiceDataA: uint16 ideal full capacity and average motor current, then uint32 total motor-runtime, pressure-time and charge-time seconds. Capacity and current units are unresolved.
  • ServiceDataB: eight uint16 fields: charge events, full-charge events, over/low-temperature events, brushing cycles, short-term motor current, recharge events and recharge hours. Current units are unresolved.

docs.title: SonosMetadata
docs.text: SonosMetadata is 14 bytes through V007 and 30 bytes from V008. It starts with 0xff, then model (M4=6, M5=5, M6=4, M7=3, M8=2, M9=1, M10=16), color, language, eight mode values, position-resolution byte and GumGuard (0 off, 1 on, 2 HD, 255 unavailable). V008 adds a 16-byte statistics block with 0xfe separating default/available screens and 0xff as end marker. The YAML declares all ten screen IDs.

docs.title: Remaining gaps and validation
docs.text:
Wi-Fi provisioning writes, charger upload-queue enumeration, firmware-container decryption, protocol-6 FF29, current/capacity units and the second drive-target word remain unresolved. No provisioning or speculative POST/EXECUTE operation is declared.

docs.title: Orbit B-hyve Bluetooth Hose and XD Timers
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (unverified) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Orbit Irrigation Products Manufacturer Status: Active. The per-mesh key comes from the Orbit cloud, once.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
These are battery valve timers that screw onto an outdoor tap: the HT25 and HT31 have one outlet, and the "XD" HT32A and HT34/HT34A have two and four. The B-hyve app drives them directly over BLE. Every timer on an account mesh shares one AES-128 network key, which the Orbit cloud generated when the mesh was created. With that key, a local client can start and stop watering and read status and battery entirely over BLE, and the cloud is never contacted again.

The models fall into two wire families. Both use the same GATT service and the same cipher:

Family Models Frame magic Inner message Mesh HT25-0000 (fw 0041, 0085) 0x10 Binary: [mesh id LE16][type][msg id LE16][body], no CRC Protobuf HT25G2-0001, HT25A-0001, HT25-0001, HT31-0001, HT32A-0001, HT34A-0001, HT34-0001 0x11 aa 77 5a 0f [len LE16][protobuf][CRC-16/XMODEM LE]

The hardware string in the owner's account record selects the family: HT25… ending in -0000 is the mesh family, and everything else is protobuf. The advertisement does not reveal the family.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes. The owner exports the mesh key once. Method cloud_account (one-time export), then local BLE only Advertised Service 0000fe32-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb (the BH1 hub uses it too) MAC prefix 44:67:55 (Orbit Irrigation OUI; medium confidence) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (two independent open-source clients)

Cloud dependence. The owner signs in to their own Orbit account once and copies these values into the local client:

  • the mesh network_key: base64 from the cloud, stored as 32 hex characters;
  • each timer's BLE address and hardware string;
  • for HT25-0000 only, the timer's own mesh_device_id and the hub's.

The upstream integration reads them from https://api.orbitbhyve.com/v1: POST /session, GET /devices, then GET /meshes/{mesh_id} (newer accounts use /network_topologies/{mesh_id}). On a rooted Android phone, the key can also be read from the B-hyve app's cache. If the cloud disappears before the key has been exported, no public method recovers it.

The key is a per-user secret. It opens every valve on the account. Every key and id in this repository is invented.

Factory reset: not documented by either source.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text: Property Value Pairing required No Security mode app_layer (mesh key + per-session AES handshake) Bonding none One central at a time Yes. Close the B-hyve app so it releases the timer. Confidence medium

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 0000fe32-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Service 00006c71-fe32-4f58-8b78-98e42b2c047f Handshake Write 20 bytes, read 20 bytes, once per connection 00006c72-fe32-4f58-8b78-98e42b2c047f Command Encrypted frames, host to device 00006c73-fe32-4f58-8b78-98e42b2c047f Reply Encrypted frames, notify 00006c76-fe32-4f58-8b78-98e42b2c047f (unused) Refuses writes; leave it alone

Session. Subscribe to 6c73. Then write 20 random bytes C (with C[11] = 0) to 6c71 and read 20 bytes D back. Set S = D[0:4] || C[4:20]. The nonce is S[0:12]. The host-to-device counter is S[12:16] and the device-to-host counter is S[16:20], both uint32 LE.

Keystream. Each block is AES-128-ECB(key, nonce || ctr LE32), and the counter increments once per 16-byte block. A frame consumes ceil(len/16) counter values, and the next frame continues from there. The two directions use independent counters.

Frame. [magic][len][ciphertext][trailer LE16], where the trailer is (magic + len + sum(plaintext)) mod 65536. The trailer is computed over the plaintext.

Commands (application plaintext before wrapping):

Command Family Plaintext Start zone n for s seconds protobuf 72 0b 08 02 12 07 1a 05 08 <n-1> 10 <s varint> (s 128–16383) Stop protobuf 72 04 08 02 12 00. On HT25A-0001 this frame starts a run, so use the next row. Controller off / auto protobuf 72 04 08 00 12 00 / 72 04 08 01 12 00 Status / battery request protobuf 7a 00 / ea 02 00 Start / stop HT25-0000 <mesh LE16> b6 0d 40 04 <s LE16> 00 00 00 00 / <mesh LE16> b7 0d 40 02 00 00 00 Health (battery) HT25-0000 <mesh LE16> 03 03 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 00. The reply has battery mV at offset 9, LE16.

Each HT25-0000 watering command needs a seven-frame init earlier in the same connection: set the clock, read status, health and info, write its own mesh id, write the hub's mesh id, then set the clock again.

docs.title: Run time and safety
docs.text:
Every start is timed on the timer itself. The valve closes when the run ends, whether or not a phone or client is still connected, so a dropped link cannot leave it open past the requested time. ljmerza's reliability notes say to rely on this on-device auto-close as the safety net, and the HT25-0000 also sends its own run-end frame.

The exception is the HT25A-0001 on fw0098. It ignores the requested time and always runs its default 1800 s, so the client has to send controller off when the time is up (and controller auto afterwards if programs should keep running). If the link drops before that, the valve stays open for up to 30 minutes. Never send the shared stop frame to this model, because it starts a new 30-minute run.

The device's own maximum run time is not known. The HT25-0000 start accepts up to 65535 s (about 18 h) and the protobuf start templates up to 16383 s (about 4.6 h), so a client should cap runs to what the owner intends.

scripts/test_orbit_bhyve_ble_spec.py transcribes the handshake, keystream, trailer and inner CRC. It reproduces every frame vector in the spec, which uses an invented key, and checks the CRC rule against four plaintext requests published upstream.

See device-specs/devices/orbit-bhyve-ble.yaml for the full machine-readable spec.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
• The schema has no framing scheme for this envelope. Every command needs a handler that implements it.
  • Protobuf-family status and battery come back as protobuf, so no sensor is bound for those models.
  • The sources disagree on whether the device enforces the outer trailer.
  • The upstream authors warn against firmware updates, because the protocol may change.

docs.title: Panasonic Viera Network Remote Control
docs.text: Status: Complete local discovery and control documented from community sources (nothing replayed against hardware here) Protocol: WiFi (SSDP + SOAP over HTTP on port 55000) Manufacturer: Panasonic Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Panasonic Viera smart TVs (Viera Cast 2011-2014, Firefox OS 2015-2018, My Home Screen 2019+) expose an undocumented local SOAP/UPnP remote-control API on TCP port 55000. On pre-2019 sets it is completely unauthenticated; from circa 2019 (FZ/GZ/HZ/JZ and later) every command rides inside an AES-128-CBC + HMAC-SHA-256 envelope after a one-time PIN-on-screen pairing. The reference implementation of both generations is the panasonic-viera Python library, which Home Assistant's Panasonic Viera integration drives daily.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
SSDP M-SEARCH with search target urn:panasonic-com:device:p00RemoteController:1; the LOCATION header points at http://<ip>:55000/nrc/ddd.xml, the UPnP device description. Identity comes from that document: UDN (unique id — observed Viera UDNs start uuid:4D454930-), friendlyName for display, and modelNumber. The sets also answer ssdp:all, but the p00RemoteController:1 target is the identifying signal.

Generation detection: fetch http://<ip>:55000/nrc/sdd_0.xml (the NRC service description). If its action list contains X_GetEncryptSessionId, the set requires PIN pairing and encrypted commands; otherwise plain SOAP works. Do not guess from the model string.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes (on the TV's own screen) Method device_ui Passphrase protection not_applicable (WiFi is configured on the TV) Client pairing Only on 2019+ sets: PIN shown on TV, one SOAP exchange Confidence medium (public sources; not run here)

On the TV: complete first-run setup, join the network, then check Settings > Network > TV Remote App Settings — enable network remote control, and "Powered On By Apps" / "Networked Standby" if power-on over the network is wanted (naming varies by model year). Without network standby the set answers nothing while off; Wake-on-LAN is the fallback, and several older plasma models on Home Assistant's supported list cannot power on over the network at all.

Client pairing (2019+ sets only) — one-time, yields an X_ApplicationId/X_Keyword credential pair to store:

  1. Client sends X_DisplayPinCode with <X_DeviceName>; the TV overlays a 4-digit PIN and the response carries X_ChallengeKey (16 bytes, base64).
  2. Client encrypts <X_PinCode>{pin}</X_PinCode> with AES-128-CBC keys derived from the challenge (key = reversed, bitwise-NOTed 4-byte groups of the challenge; HMAC key = a fixed 32-byte mask, published in the panasonic-viera library, XORed against the rotated challenge) and sends it to X_RequestAuth inside <X_AuthInfo>. Error code 600 = wrong PIN.
  3. The X_AuthResult reply decrypts to <X_ApplicationId> and <X_Keyword> — store both.

Each session then opens with X_GetEncryptSessionId and every command rides in X_EncryptedCommand with a per-session sequence counter. The byte-level detail (payload framing, both key derivations, the session-key swap) is in nrc_common.encrypted_session in the machine-readable spec.

Factory reset: Menu > Setup > System Menu > Factory Defaults (some model years: "Shipping Condition") — clears network credentials, paired clients, account link and settings. Confidence low; the menu path varies by generation and region. Rejoining a new WiFi network only requires re-running the network setup from the TV menu, never a factory reset.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
All control is SOAP POSTs on port 55000:

Service Control URL Purpose urn:panasonic-com:service:p00NetworkControl:1 /nrc/control_0 Remote keys, queries, app launch, pairing urn:schemas-upnp-org:service:RenderingControl:1 /dmr/control_0 Absolute volume 0-100 and mute (plain SOAP on both generations)

docs.title: NRC actions
Key vocabulary
docs.text: The full NRC_*-ONOFF vocabulary is in keys.py: navigation (NRC_UP/DOWN/LEFT/RIGHT/ENTER/RETURN/CANCEL/HOME/MENU/SUBMENU/INFO/EPG), playback (NRC_PLAY/PAUSE/STOP/REW/FF/SKIP_PREV/SKIP_NEXT/REC/30S_SKIP), volume (NRC_VOLUP/VOLDOWN/MUTE), tuner (NRC_CH_UP/CH_DOWN/R_TUNE/D0-D9), inputs (NRC_CHG_INPUT, NRC_TV, and the undocumented NRC_HDMI1-4), colour buttons, NRC_TEXT/STTL/ASPECT, and app keys (NRC_APPS, NRC_NETFLIX, NRC_MYAPP — the latter two undocumented but working per Home Assistant's docs). The spec's commands block carries one SOAP invocation per key; its entities block lays the remote out as button entities.

docs.title: Transport gap
docs.text:
2019+ sets are NOT controllable by the reference app today. Its soap transport renders plain SOAP envelopes, which is all pre-2019 sets need. The encrypted generation additionally requires: AES-128-CBC and HMAC-SHA-256 wrapping of every NRC command, base64, a persistent per-session sequence counter, stored pairing credentials, and the PIN pairing flow itself — all documented byte for byte in nrc_common.encrypted_session of the spec. A consumer must implement that wrapper around the same SOAP POST; until it does, the buttons in entities work only against pre-2019 sets. The DMR volume/mute service is plain SOAP on both generations and works today.

X_GetAppList's reply is a flat quote-delimited string, not XML elements, so the schema's options_source select contract cannot consume it — the App select carries the widely-deployed product_ids from apps.py as static options instead.

docs.text: Status: Complete Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: PAX Labs Manufacturer Status: Server-dependent (BLE control works locally)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Temperature-controlled vaporizer (PAX 3, Era, Era Pro). Uses AES-128 OFB encryption with a per-device key derived from the serial number. PAX is explicitly allowed by project policy.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Models PAX 3, PAX Era, PAX Era Pro Chipset Nordic Semiconductor (likely nRF5x) Radio BLE 4.x FCC ID 2AJWD-PAX3

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 8e320200-64d2-11e6-bdf4-0800200c9a66 PAX Service Primary service

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text: UUID (short) Properties Purpose ...0201 Read Read encrypted data packets ...0202 Write Send encrypted command packets ...0203 Read, Notify Notification trigger (data ready to read) ...0210 -- Internal service (pairing/enrollment) ...0212 Write Internal write (AES-CTR encrypted)

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
• Algorithm: AES-128 OFB (NoPadding)
  • Master key (hex): f7c866c38f78753086293bd57dd32540
  • Master key (bytes): {0xF7, 0xC8, 0x66, 0xC3, 0x8F, 0x78, 0x75, 0x30, 0x86, 0x29, 0x3B, 0xD5, 0x7D, 0xD3, 0x25, 0x40}
  • Key derivation: Read 8-char serial -> duplicate to 16 bytes -> AES-128-ECB encrypt with master key -> per-device key
  • Write flow: Generate random 16-byte IV from UUID -> AES-OFB encrypt payload -> prepend IV -> write [IV (16)] + [ciphertext]
  • Read flow: First 16 bytes = IV, remaining = ciphertext -> AES-OFB decrypt with per-device key and extracted IV
  • Default IV: deadbeefdeadbeefdeadbeefdeadbeef (fallback, not normally used)
  • Secondary mode: AES-128 CTR (NoPadding) for initial pairing via internal service ...0210

docs.title: Message Types
docs.text: Byte Name Direction Payload 0x01 ActualTemp Device->Host uint16 LE, value/10 = degrees C 0x02 HeaterSetPoint Bidirectional uint16 LE, value/10 = degrees C 0x03 Battery Device->Host uint8, 0-100% 0x06 LockStatus Bidirectional uint8, 0=unlocked, 1=locked 0x08 PodInserted Device->Host uint8 (Era/Era Pro only) 0x0A DisplayName Bidirectional Length-prefixed UTF-8 0x13 DynamicMode Bidirectional uint8 heating profile 0x18 SupportedAttributes Device->Host uint64 LE bitfield 0xFE StatusUpdate Host->Device Request full status

docs.title: Petronics Mousr
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (static-analysis-derived; untested on hardware) Protocol: BLE, Nordic UART Manufacturer: Petronics Inc. Manufacturer Status: Abandoned — consumer production and support ended

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Mousr is a phone-direct robotic cat toy. Ordinary operation does not require an account or cloud service. The recovered official 1.0.7 app supplies the command builders, command vocabulary, firmware recovery packages and user guide. No community protocol implementation was found.

The command envelope and drive-vector encoding are now recovered, but no toy or HCI capture has verified them. Notification payloads, auto-mode settings, physical scaling of drive values and firmware compatibility remain open.

docs.title: Initial Setup and Pairing
docs.text:
Charge and wake the toy, then connect to the Nordic UART service and enable notifications. Static analysis found no account or application-layer activation requirement. The user guide's "pairing" is the app's device list — press the chin pushbutton, open the app, tap the toy — with no PIN and no OS Bluetooth step, so the spec records no pairing (low confidence: not replayed).

Property Value Setup required No account found Service 6e400001-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e Command input 6e400002-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e Notifications 6e400003-b5a3-f393-e0a9-e50e24dcca9e Firmware update Nordic Secure DFU service 0000fe59-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb (bootloader control point 8ec90001-f315-4f60-9fb8-838830daea50, packet 8ec90002-f315-4f60-9fb8-838830daea50) Factory reset Unknown; DFU and tail calibration are not resets

An earlier note called 8ec90001/8ec90002 a Laird virtual serial port. They are the Nordic Secure DFU bootloader characteristics; no Laird VSP UUID (569a1101-…) was recorded for this toy.

The factory name is reported as exactly Mousr, and the spec matches it as an exact name together with the Nordic UART service. The service alone is not a match: many unrelated products carry it, and this spec has movement commands. The exact match also keeps out MousrDfu, the bootloader name, which the spec declares as update mode. The app lets an owner rename the toy; a renamed unit is not auto-matched and has to be added by hand.

docs.title: Command packet
docs.text:
Every ordinary command is exactly 15 bytes:

offset 0:  ASCII 30
offset 1:  12-byte payload, zero-filled when unused
offset 13: two-byte command code

A two-digit code is its two ASCII digits: code 18 ends 31 38. The second byte of a one-digit code is unresolved. The analysis behind this spec gave two readings that contradict each other, and no capture settles which is right:

  • form A, ASCII 0 then the digit: code 2 ends 30 32, code 0 ends 30 30;
  • form B, the digit then NUL: code 2 ends 32 00, code 0 ends 30 00.

The declared commands keep the bytes recorded for each, which mix the two (stop is form B; spin, move, reset heading and turn off are form A). Each one-digit command is therefore marked verification: hypothesis and its description gives the other form. Try stop in both forms first and keep whichever the toy obeys.

Code Command Code Command 0 stop 18 chirp 1 spin 19 set sound volume 2 move (drive vector) 23 tail flick 3 reset heading 24 reverse 4 request debug log 25 tail calibration 5 planned spin 26 set tail 8 enter bootloader (DFU) mode 28 initialize device 9 turn off 31 flip the robot over 10 sleep 41 configure driver assist 15 configure autonomous play mode 45 tutorial step 46 set time 100 invalid command

Only commands with an established payload are declared in the YAML. Auto-mode offsets, debug-log transfer, calibration, driver assist, set time and bootloader entry are listed so they can be captured, but their payloads cannot be inferred from a code number alone. Move and spin are flagged advanced because they drive a robot with no established physical scaling; sleep, turn off and reset heading are ordinary app controls and are not.

docs.title: Drive vector
docs.text:
The move command places three little-endian IEEE-754 binary32 values in the payload:

offset 1: speed, float32 LE
offset 5: hold, float32 LE
offset 9: angle, float32 LE
offset 13: code 2 (ASCII 02 as declared; see above)

These are app control values, not established m/s, degrees or percent. Valid ranges need a capture. The app therefore presents them as raw, unbounded float32 inputs with an attended-motion warning rather than inventing a physical scale. Stop is an independent fixed command and should be tested first.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: Recovered IDs include 15 auto acknowledgement, 28/29 firmware/hardware version, 30 initialization complete, 48 pose, 64 stuck distance sensor, 98 battery voltage, 99 stopped, 100 stuck and 255 negative acknowledgement. Their full payload layouts are not established, so the spec does not invent battery or pose decoders.

docs.title: Safety and recovery
docs.text:
This is a moving robot and tail assembly. Test stop and small movement in a clear area away from pets, people, cables and edges. Tail calibration needs a flat, unobstructed surface. Do not attempt DFU until ordinary control and charging state are established. The app's bundled recovery firmware is valuable, but is not shipped here and has no verified update sequence. The spec's features block records the Nordic Secure DFU path and the MousrDfu update-mode name.

scripts/test_petronics_mousr_spec.py checks packet lengths, that the declared stop and chirp bytes equal the spec's own vectors, and the integer and fractional float32 drive vectors. It does not establish the one-digit code byte: it checks that every one-digit command is marked hypothesis and that both forms are written down.

See device-specs/devices/petronics-mousr.yaml for the full spec.

docs.text:
