  • Official Mousr 1.0.7 app and bundled User Guide v1.2, analysed 2026-11-01 — command and safety evidence

docs.title: Philips Wi-Fi Air Purifiers and Humidifiers (encrypted CoAP)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (unverified) Protocol: WiFi (CoAP over UDP 5683, AES-128-CBC payload envelope) Manufacturer: Philips (Versuni, formerly Philips Domestic Appliances) Manufacturer Status: Active. Local access is unofficial, and some firmware updates are reported to remove it.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Philips connected purifiers, 2-in-1 purifier/humidifiers, humidifiers, fan heaters and fans have model numbers starting AC, AMF, CX and HU. Many of them run a small CoAP server on UDP port 5683. Any host on the home network can use it, with no Philips account and no pairing. Three resources carry the whole API:

Path Method Purpose /sys/dev/sync POST Swap a random 8-hex-digit value for the device's counter /sys/dev/status GET + Observe 0 Full status, pushed again on every change /sys/dev/control POST Write desired state; replies {"status":"success"}

Status and control bodies are wrapped in an envelope. The AES key comes from the counter and a fixed string, JiangPan, which is published as a constant in every open-source client. The key is the same on every unit, so the encryption hides traffic from a casual look but protects nothing.

The protocol was reverse engineered by Radoslav Gerganov (py-air-control). aioairctrl re-implemented it, and the kongo09 Home Assistant integration keeps the per-model key tables.

docs.title: Which units this covers
docs.text:
Philips has shipped three local protocols. This spec covers only the third:

  1. HTTP generation: older Wi-Fi units. They use HTTP on port 80 under /di/v1/products/..., with a Diffie-Hellman key exchange, AES and SSDP discovery. They are out of scope here.
  2. Plain CoAP: unencrypted JSON on 5683, sent after an ICMP "hello". This is also out of scope.
  3. Encrypted CoAP: every model the Home Assistant integration supports.

Inside generation 3 the JSON keys come in three dialects. The spec treats them as device.variants:

Key set How to tell Example models classic-keys status has modelid AC2729, AC2889, AC3829, AC3033, AC4236, AC5659 dashed-keys status has D01-05 AC1715, AC0850 (Wi-Fi string AWS_Philips_AIR) compact-keys status has D01S05 AC0850 Combo, AC0950, AC22xx, AC3420, AMF765, CX3120, HU4209, HU5710

The compact set needs JSON integers for every D03… value.

docs.title: Local access is fragile
docs.text: The integration's README warns about two problems. Some models have newer firmware that no longer allows local connections. Units that do work can also drop the CoAP session until they are power-cycled. No source names the firmware version that removed access. The AC0651 has never been made to answer, and some AC1715/11 units refuse the connection. Owners keep working firmware by blocking the purifier's internet access. Do this before an update arrives, not after.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes. Wi-Fi is provisioned by the Philips app with a Philips account Method cloud_account (pairing-mode hold on the unit, then the app) Setup AP PHILIPS Setup (open), while the Wi-Fi light blinks orange Passphrase protection unknown Confidence low

To enter pairing mode, power the unit on and hold its pairing button (or button pair) for about 3 seconds until it beeps. The button differs by model: the AC2729 uses power plus child lock together, and the AC0850/20 manual describes a single 3-second hold. Philips requires a 2.4 GHz network. No open-source client provisions this generation's Wi-Fi without the app.

After the unit is on the LAN, a local client only needs its address. The unit advertises no mDNS or SSDP service. Home Assistant finds it from DHCP: MAC prefixes 68:79:C4, B0:F8:93, 04:78:63, 84:9D:C2 and 80:A0:36, or a hostname starting with mxchip. Reserve the address in DHCP, and key a stored unit by the DeviceId in its status.

Factory reset: Philips support gives a general procedure. Hold power and mode together for 10 seconds until the unit beeps. It is meant for a unit that was registered to a different Philips account. This has not been verified per model. It is a different action from the 3-second Wi-Fi re-pair hold and from the 5-second mode hold that resets the filter counter (AC0850/20 manual).

Rebinding to a new network: enter pairing mode and provision the unit again from the app. No local command changes Wi-Fi on this generation.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text: Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none (the shared-key envelope is public) Bonding none One client at a time Unknown. The clients open independent sessions Confidence medium (three clients agree)

docs.title: Session
docs.text:
1. POST /sys/dev/sync with 8 random uppercase hex digits, for example 1A2B3C4D. The unit replies with its counter, for example 6D2C0F41.
  2. Before each envelope it sends, the client adds one to the counter. The first control write after that sync is sealed under 6D2C0F42. The counter is 32-bit, written as exactly 8 uppercase hex digits. aioairctrl wraps FFFFFFFF to 00000000.
  3. GET /sys/dev/status with Observe 0. Every notification is a full status. Home Assistant reconnects after three missed Max-Age periods; Max-Age defaults to 60 s.
  4. Write with POST /sys/dev/control. If the reply is anything other than {"status":"success"}, sync again and retry.

docs.title: Envelope
docs.text:
H       = upper(hex(MD5("JiangPan" + counter)))      # 32 ASCII chars
key, iv = ascii(H[0:16]), ascii(H[16:32])            # AES-128-CBC, PKCS#7
C       = upper(hex(AES_CBC(key, iv, json_plaintext)))
D       = upper(hex(SHA256(counter + C)))            # plain hash, not HMAC
wire    = counter + C + D

The key and IV are the hex characters themselves. Do not hex-decode them. protocol_details.envelope.test_vectors in the spec carries three worked envelopes built from invented counters, and scripts/test_philips_air_coap_spec.py rebuilds each of them.

docs.title: Control document
docs.text:
{"state": {"desired": {"CommandType": "app", "DeviceId": "", "EnduserId": "", "pwr": "1"}}}

The three fixed members are always sent empty. You can set several keys in one write.

docs.title: Main keys
docs.text:
Function classic dashed compact Power pwr "1"/"0" D03-02 "ON"/"OFF" D03102 1/0 Mode mode P/A/S/M/B/N/T/GT D03-12 "Auto General", "Sleep", "Turbo", … D0310C 0 auto, 1-5, 17 sleep, 18 turbo, 19 medium, 65 high Fan speed om 1/2/3/t with mode M; silent is om s with mode S n/a inside D0310C; AC0950 and AC3420 also need D0310D in the same write Child lock cl true/false n/a D03103 1/0 Display light aqil 0-100, uil "1"/"0" D03-05 100/0 D0312D / D03105 Timer dt hours 0-12 n/a D03110 code 0-13 Target humidity rhset 40/50/60/70 n/a D03128 Function func P/PH n/a D0310A PM2.5 pm25 D03-33 D03221 Allergen index iaql D03-32 D03120 Humidity / temp rh / temp n/a D03125 / D03224 (tenths of °C) Filters (hours left) fltsts0/1/2, wicksts D05-13, D05-14 D0520D, D0540E Water / errors wl, err n/a D03240

"n/a" means no source documents that key for the set. The full tables, value meanings and per-model notes are in protocol_details.key_sets.

docs.title: Philips jointSPACE TV API
docs.text: Status: Complete protocol reconstruction from published clients and docs; nothing probed against live hardware (this project owns no Philips TV) Protocol: WiFi (mDNS + HTTP/HTTPS JSON on ports 1925/1926) Manufacturer: Philips / TP Vision Manufacturer Status: Active (current TP Vision Android/Saphi TVs still ship the API; 2k9-2k13 jointSPACE models are long out of support)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Philips smart TVs expose a local REST-style JSON API whose URL prefix is the API major version: /1 on the original 2009-2013 jointSPACE models, /5 on 2014-2015 non-Android sets, /6 on Android (2014+) and Saphi/Linux TVs. Philips published the v1 documentation (and shipped it on the TV itself at http://<ip>:1925/1/doc/); v5/v6, the pairing flow and the secured transport were never officially documented and were recovered by suborb (2016 pairing), pylips (MITM of the official remote app) and haphilipsjs (the library behind Home Assistant's Philips TV integration).

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
The TVs announce themselves over mDNS with two service types — the same two Home Assistant's philips_js manifest listens for:

Service type Port Meaning _philipstv_rpc._tcp.local. 1925 Plain HTTP API, no auth _philipstv_s_rpc._tcp.local. 1926 Secured API: HTTPS + digest auth

mDNS yields an address and a display name only. Identification is completed with the unversioned probe — try http://<ip>:1925/system, then https://<ip>:1926/system — whose answer carries api_version.Major (pick your URL prefix from it), the TV name, and featuring.systemfeatures with secured_transport and pairing_type (pick your auth regime from those). Stable identity is serialnumber_encrypted / deviceid_encrypted in the same document: AES-128-CBC, key = first 16 bytes of the base64-decoded shared key (below), IV = first 16 bytes of the decoded payload, PKCS7 padding.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes — on-TV first-time installation wizard Method device_ui Passphrase protection not_applicable (typed on the TV itself) Confidence medium (public sources; not run by this project)

On 2k9-2k11 models only, the JSON API needs a one-time activation: while watching TV, type 5646877223 on the remote ("jointspace" in multitap digit entry), per the jointSPACE project page. 2014+ models have the API always on.

Factory reset: Settings > General settings > Factory settings (or "Reinstall TV" on Android models) — clears channel lists, network settings and paired-client credentials, returns to the installation wizard. Rejoining a new network: in place from the network settings menu; a factory reset is never needed for a router change, and pairing credentials survive it.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Two regimes, and the TV itself says which applies:

  • Open (pre-2016, v1/v5 and early Android): plain HTTP on 1925, no credentials at all. Anything on the LAN can drive the TV.
  • digest_auth_pairing (2016+ Android, v6): HTTPS on 1926 with a self-signed certificate, and every request — GETs included — answers 401 without HTTP digest auth.

Pairing (once per client; wire paths are /6/pair/request and /6/pair/grant — often miswritten "pairing/..." in secondary docs):

  1. POST /6/pair/request (no auth) with a device descriptor ({"device": {"id": <client-chosen id>, "device_name": ..., "device_os": ..., "type": "native", "app_id": ..., "app_name": ...}} plus requested scope). The TV answers {"timestamp", "auth_key", "timeout"} and shows a 4-digit PIN on screen.
  2. The user reads the PIN off the TV; the client POSTs /6/pair/grant with digest auth (username = device id, password = auth_key) and body {"auth": {"auth_AppId": "1", "pin": <PIN>, "auth_timestamp": <timestamp>, "auth_signature": base64(HMAC-SHA1(shared_key, str(timestamp) + pin))}, "device": {...}}. {"error_id": "SUCCESS"} ends the exchange.
  3. All subsequent requests use digest auth with device id / auth_key. Credentials survive until the TV is reset or unpaired.

The HMAC shared key is a constant published in open-source clients — suborb/philips_android_tv (philips.py) and haphilipsjs carry it (ZmVay1EQVFOaZhwQ4Kv81ypLAZNczV9sG4KkseXWn1NEk6cXmPKO/MCa9sryslvLCFMnNe4Z4CPXzToowvhHvA==, base64). One divergence in the sources: suborb's 2016 original base64-encoded the HMAC's hex digest; haphilipsjs base64-encodes the raw digest and is the maintained form Home Assistant pairs with today.

docs.title: Local API
docs.text:
All paths are prefixed /<api_version>/ (1, 5 or 6). POSTs carry a JSON object as the entire body.

Method Path Description GET /system (unversioned) Probe: API version, name, encrypted identity, secured_transport/pairing_type GET /{v}/system Same document, versioned; fields also GETtable individually (v1) POST /{v}/input/key Send one remote key: {"key": "Home"}; also {"unicode": "x"} for text entry GET/POST /{v}/audio/volume Volume/mute state; set with {"current": n, "muted": b} (device scale, not percent) GET/POST /{v}/powerstate Power state; set {"powerstate": "Standby"} (v6, not all firmwares) GET /{v}/screenstate Panel on/off (v5+) GET /{v}/channeldb/tv Channel-list index: list all plus favourite lists (v5+) GET /{v}/channeldb/tv/channelLists/{id} Channels of one list; ccid is the tunable value GET/POST /{v}/activities/tv Current channel; tune with {"channelList": {"id": "all"}, "channel": {"ccid": n}} (v5+; v1 spells it /1/channels/current) GET /{v}/applications Launchable apps with Android intents (v6 Android) GET /{v}/activities/current Foreground activity intent (v6 Android) POST /{v}/activities/launch Launch an app by replaying its intent; a SELECTURI intent also switches HDMI inputs where honoured GET/POST /{v}/sources + /sources/current Input list and switching — v1 only, removed in v5/v6 (use the Source key or a SELECTURI intent) POST /{v}/pair/request, /{v}/pair/grant Pairing (v6 secured models) POST /{v}/notifychange Long-poll state push: POST last-known state, TV answers with what changed (v6, models advertising notifyChange) GET/POST /{v}/ambilight/mode, /{v}/ambilight/power Ambilight control mode and on/off

docs.title: Remote key vocabulary
docs.text: POST /{v}/input/key takes one of (union of the official v1 reference, pylips' v6-tested list and Home Assistant's remote entity): Standby, PowerOn, PowerOff, CursorUp/Down/Left/Right, Confirm, Back, Exit, Home, Options, Adjust, Find, WatchTV, Source, List, Viewmode, TvGuide, Info, Subtitle, Teletext, ClosedCaption, Red/Green/Yellow/Blue/WhiteColour, Digit0-Digit9, Dot, Next, Previous, ChannelStepUp/Down, VolumeUp/Down, Mute, HeadphonesVolume, Play, Pause, PlayPause, Stop, FastForward, Rewind, Record, Online, SmartTV, PhilipsMenu, Setup, AmbilightOnOff, PictureStyle, SoundStyle, SurroundMode, 3dFormat, 3dDepth, 2PlayerGaming, Multiview. Availability varies by model; PlayPause maps to Play and PowerOff to Standby on Android. One POST is one complete press — there is no keydown/keyup split. In standby many models kill the API entirely; power-on is Wake-on-LAN or, on some Android sets, POST /6/powerstate {"powerstate": "On"}.

docs.title: Response quirks worth knowing
docs.text: Command POSTs answer 200 with an empty or junk body ("", "OkOk", "}", "Context Service not started"). Booleans arrive as "On"/"Off" strings. Some firmwares emit malformed JSON (doubled commas, a dangling "channelList": { "id": "version", "" } fragment) that haphilipsjs repairs with string surgery before parsing — a strict parser will choke where a real TV is merely sloppy. 401 = digest credentials missing/wrong; 403/404 = the endpoint does not exist on this firmware.

docs.title: Remote control surface
docs.text:
The spec's commands block names one invocation per remote key (a command's arguments map is the JSON body, with an api_version parameter feeding the /{api_version}/ path prefix), and its entities block declares the remote as button entities in remote-layout order: power, navigation and D-pad, transport, volume, channel stepping, digits, colour keys, then TV functions.

A stateful Power switch entity binds turn_on/turn_off to the discrete keys, toggle to Standby, and the powerstate resource as its state (Spec Evolution P13). Key availability varies by model and year; Standby is the one key every model takes, so the toggle — sent only after reading the state — is the off that works even where the PowerOff key is ignored.

The set_power_standby command writes the same resource the state reads. It is a second discrete off, but a narrower one, not a fallback for sets that ignore the PowerOff key: the powerstate resource is v6-only and "support varies by firmware" even there, so the older sets most likely to ignore the key have no such endpoint at all. Its value is on a v6 set that answers powerstate but does not honour the key, and in being an explicit state request rather than a keypress. The state read carries the same v6 limit, and a 403/404 there is endpoint-not-present, not standby.

docs.title: Transport gap — read before building on this spec
docs.text: JSON request bodies on every POST, plus HTTPS with a self-signed certificate and HTTP digest auth on 2016+ models — not yet supported by the reference app. The app's HTTP transport sends GET/POST with empty bodies and no auth headers, so no command in this spec is executable by it today, and its XML-shaped options_source/state_source select contract cannot parse this API's JSON channel/app lists either. A client that wants to drive a Philips TV from this spec must implement: JSON request-body rendering from a command's arguments, TLS with verification skipped (or TOFU pinning), digest auth, and the two-step PIN pairing flow. The commands are written the way the TV expects them anyway — an accurate spec with the gap recorded, per the registry's rule against fake empty-body commands.

docs.title: Piaggio Fast Forward gitamini / gita pro
docs.text: Status: Spec available (untested; static app analysis) Protocol: BLE with application-layer ECDH and AES-CBC Manufacturer: Piaggio Fast Forward, Inc. (active)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
gitamini is a self-propelled cargo robot that visually follows its owner using stereo depth/RGB cameras and radar. Following starts with the robot's physical Pair/Park button, not with a phone/GPS/Bluetooth-tracking API.

The mygita app exposes registration, Wi-Fi, settings, latch, logs and OTA. No ordinary remote-drive, velocity, steering or start-following command was found. activate robot is not evidence of such a command and is deliberately not offered as one.

Pro boundary: advertisement model 3 is named gita pro in the app, but no retail-Pro manual, packet capture or distinct protocol profile was found. Pro is a reported variant of this BLE family, not a separately verified product. Model 2 is gitamini. Unknown model IDs need a new profile rather than the app's original-gita fallback.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
Self-propelled robot

Start with passive advertisements and read-only GATT operations. Do not send activate robot, latch, network, SSH or firmware commands as discovery probes. Keep people, pets and obstacles clear during any owner-approved test, and never test motor behavior with an unregistered write.

docs.title: Discovery and advertisements
docs.text:
The app normally scans for service 00009999-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb and manufacturer company 0x083B (wire bytes 3b 08). There is no useful name prefix.

The manufacturer payload contains TLV records: serial, cloud object ID, color, three status bytes, battery, model, message code, connected user, checksum and odometry. Minimum length is 25 bytes. Model 2 is Mini; model 3 is the reported Pro. Battery is a percentage, with 255 meaning unknown. Primary states include ready, following, parked, charging and OTA states; secondary state reports latch; flags report mute, stealth, open access and smarts.

The checksum selector and negative byte-sum rule are recovered, but the exact suffix layout still needs a valid capture before generating or validating advertisements. Serials, cloud/user IDs and odometry are visible to nearby receivers and must be redacted from research captures.

docs.title: Initial setup and registration
docs.text: Property Value First enrollment Vendor account, serial barcode and single-use QR secret Existing registration Offline session-credential reuse is a candidate, not verified BLE pairing OS-level bond plus application-layer ECDH/session authentication Wi-Fi provisioning Encrypted BLE command; Mini supports 2.4/5 GHz Reset Unknown

docs.title: Existing registration (offline candidate)
docs.text:
1. Scan for service 0x9999 and company 0x083B, then select the correct model.
  2. Create the OS-level BLE bond. The physical Pair/Park button is for visual following, not BLE pairing.
  3. Read the robot ECDH public key on ...def6, generate a secp256k1 phone key pair and write its public key on ...def5.
  4. Subscribe to Wi-Fi (...def3), general (...def7) and registration/session (...def9) notifications before any authentication or session-key write.
  5. Request verification of the stored session credential with command 63 on ...defb; decrypt its type-109 response to recover n2 as detailed below.
  6. Authenticate with command 9 on ...def1 using n2, encrypted with the stored credential. The app selects existing-key verification when offline or within seven days; with connectivity and an older key it requests a fresh one. Start with read-only version, IP or OTA-status requests.

This path does not prove unlimited offline use. Revocation, reset, logout/reinstall and long-term policy need hardware tests.

docs.title: First enrollment (cloud required)
docs.text:
1. Create or sign in to a mygita account and scan the 10-character Code 128 serial and 20-character QR secret beginning pff.
  2. Match the serial to the robot and perform ECDH.
  3. Subscribe to registration/session feedback on ...def9 before command 60 or any session-key write, so replies are captured during the eight-second feedback wait.
  4. Request robot creation data with command 60 and exchange it with authenticated /gitas, then verify the response with command 61.
  5. Post the QR payload and robot verification message to authenticated /registrations.
  6. Set the returned identity, send command 68 and configure Wi-Fi/notifications.

Possession of the serial or advertisement alone is not enrollment. The printed QR is single-use. Never publish the QR secret, bearer token, verification payloads, session keys, ECDH secrets or owner identifiers.

docs.title: GATT service
docs.text:
All characteristics share 87654321-1234-5678-1234-56789abcdef0. The app requests MTU 185 and uses write-without-response. Properties are app-derived; no live GATT dump exists.

Suffix Role ...def1 Authenticated session command write ...def2 Operational encrypted command write ...def3 Plaintext Wi-Fi notifications ...def4 Per-phone identity write ...def5 Phone ECDH public-key write ...def6 Robot ECDH public-key read ...def7 General plaintext notifications ...def8 Version/build string read ...def9 Registration/session feedback notifications ...defa Registration command write ...defb Session-key exchange write

General operation timeout is 30 seconds; session feedback has an 8-second wait. Registration/session feedback uses a different encrypted and fragmented parser from normal plaintext notifications, with $$$$$ and ##### delimiters and a random 10-character phone identity prefix where applicable.

docs.title: Encryption and command framing
docs.text:
Two different credential layers must not be confused:

  1. Per-connection ECDH: derive a SHA-256 digest as specified below, render its 64 hexadecimal characters and split them in half. Hex-decoding each 32-character half gives a 16-byte AES key and 16-byte IV. Ordinary operational commands use this pair.
  2. Cloud-issued session credential: a 64-hex credential is also split into an AES key and IV and used to authenticate the robot session. It is stored by robot UUID. Fresh issuance needs the cloud; existing verification can work offline.

Write the phone public key to ...def5 as a raw 65-byte uncompressed SEC 1 point: 0x04 || X || Y, with both coordinates unsigned, big-endian and 32 bytes wide. The app's internal 130-character hex representation is hex-decoded before the write; do not send ASCII hex. On ...def6, accept either that form or a raw 33-byte compressed SEC 1 point (0x02/0x03 || X) and validate the point. The parser supports both, but no capture establishes which form every firmware emits.

The ECDH secret is the shared point's X coordinate converted to lowercase hexadecimal without leading-zero padding. SHA-256 the ASCII bytes of that hex text—not the raw or hex-decoded coordinate. Its length is normally 64 characters but can be shorter. The synthetic vector in protocol_details.ecdh.test_vector exercises a 63-character input, including both public keys and the resulting AES key/IV.

No-data plaintext is ten bytes: [opcode][0x7f][00 × 8]. Data-bearing plaintext is [opcode][0x7f][data…]. Encrypt the whole buffer with AES-128-CBC/PKCS#7 and send raw ciphertext, not Base64 text. Split ciphertext into 181-byte pieces and append 0 for more chunks or 1 for the final chunk.

docs.title: Saved-session authentication
docs.text:
Each nonce is 16 random bytes rendered as 32 lowercase hexadecimal ASCII characters. n1 is generated by the phone; n2 comes from the robot/cloud. The account user_id is not the robot UUID.

  1. With ...def9 already subscribed, write command 63 to ...defb with plaintext [0x3f][0x7f][user_id_utf8][n1_ascii], encrypted using the per-connection ECDH key/IV.
  2. Within eight seconds, accept a type-109 response. Reassemble the registration feedback, strip its identity prefix and ##### terminator, and decrypt the outer command using ECDH. The first plaintext byte is 0x6d (109). Decode the inner Base64 ciphertext and decrypt it using the saved session credential. Its plaintext is n1_ascii.n2_ascii; require n1 to match exactly. Type 110 means expired and type 111 means invalid; stop on either or on timeout.
  3. Write command 9 to ...def1 with plaintext [0x09][0x7f][n2_ascii], encrypted using the saved session credential. Send only n2, not the credential or n1. A newly issued credential uses command 8 with the same layout.
  4. The reviewed app parses no dedicated success response to command 9. Require a subsequent version read on ...def8 or another read-only response before calling the offline session established. Type 109 answers command 63, not command 9.

For fresh issuance, command 62 uses the same outer request as 63 with opcode 0x3e. Its successful type-62 payload is key_part.n2_ascii.payload; post key_part, payload and n1 to authenticated /session-keys, then use the returned credential and n2 with command 8. No authenticated request was made during research.

Normal notifications are a type byte followed by UTF-8/ASCII with trailing newlines trimmed. The separate notification fragment markers 251–255 must not be merged with the operational 0/1 continuation convention without a capture.

The reviewed Android package requests one native AES module name and registers another. This may be a compatibility defect or an unresolved bridge detail. The algorithm is recovered, but a normal app connection must confirm it before a third-party client is expected to work.

docs.title: Known command surface
docs.text:
Only commands with a documented no-data or payload shape are executable entries in the YAML. Other opcodes remain documentation, not instructions to send ten zero-padded bytes.

Operation Opcode / payload AP list 50 Join Wi-Fi 51 + ASCII <SSID> password <password> Disconnect / forget Wi-Fi 52 / 54 Get IP / current connection / profiles 53 / 55 / 56 Connect remembered network 57 Mute / stealth / open access 72 / 73 / 74 Latch lock / unlock 78 / 79 Install / download OTA 80 / 85 Get version / uptime 81 / 86 Toggle Wi-Fi / remove device 88 / 89 OTA status / start / stop notifications 90 / 91 / 92 Toggle smarts 93 Disconnect client 99 Enable SSH, support-gated 102

Authentication uses 7–9 and 62/63. Registration uses 60–68. Wi-Fi, latch, open-access, SSH and update commands are advanced operations, not scan probes. No motor-control entity is declared.

docs.title: OTA V2
docs.text:
Mini, reported Pro and every other non-original model select OTA V2:

  1. Read version/build capabilities on ...def8.
  2. With the owner's bearer token, request /ota-v2-check?gitaId=<id>&buildId=<build>.
  3. If an update ID is returned, request /ota-v2-infos/{id} for notes, build, minimum app version, upload date and total bytes.
  4. Send 85 to download or 80 to install. Notification 122 reports status/percent.

The robot retrieves the image over its own Wi-Fi; the reviewed phone path does not download it. No public firmware image or update URL was obtained. Staged and rollback states do not prove A/B partitioning on every component. OTA and SSH commands require deliberate authorization and a recovery path.

docs.title: Remaining unknowns
docs.text:
• Valid advertisement/GATT captures, checksum suffix, state values and odometry units.
  • Native crypto-module runtime behavior and per-op payload/response layouts.
  • Offline reuse across phone restart and the seven-day boundary, plus revocation/reset.
  • OTA image URL, format, signature and rollback behavior.
  • Any retail-Pro-specific profile or capability differences.
  • Exact compute/camera/radar modules; RealSense and radar filing 2AY6H-101187 are leads, not confirmed Mini mappings. Jetson TX2 is documented for original gita.
  • Robot-side bond/registration removal, SSH credentials and the meaning of activate robot (100).

docs.title: Pix Backpack / Pix Mini
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (untested) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Pix Inc. Manufacturer Status: Shutdown (vendor defunct, app delisted from Google Play)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Pix Backpack (Kickstarter 2018) is a backpack with a 16×20 RGB LED matrix sewn into the back panel; the Pix Mini (2019) is a smaller kids' variant. Both were driven by the vendor's Pix app (style.pix.app), a React Native app that has since vanished from the Play Store along with the vendor. The good news: the hardware never needed the cloud. Every control function — image and animation upload, brightness, scrolling text, widgets, games — is plain local BLE with no pairing, no account and no encryption. The full machine-readable protocol is in device-specs/devices/pix-backpack.yaml.

The vendor cloud only ever hosted the content marketplace, a news feed, and firmware files — all replaceable or unnecessary.

Everything here comes from static analysis of the vendor app. No hardware has been driven from this document yet, so byte layouts are reported, not confirmed.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number Pix Backpack (16×20 matrix), Pix Mini (geometry unconfirmed) Chipset Unknown — ESP32-class suspected (BLE + Wi-Fi combo, Wi-Fi OTA); unconfirmed Radio BLE (control); Wi-Fi used only by the device itself during firmware OTA Power External USB power bank (no internal battery) FCC ID Unknown (no grant found under Pix Inc.)

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name pix <12-hex-MAC> (e.g. pix aabbccddeeff) Passphrase protection plaintext (only during OTA — see below) Confidence medium (from app analysis; not yet exercised against hardware here)

Plug the backpack's internal USB cable into a power bank — the display powers on and advertises immediately. Scan for the pix … name (or the 0100 service UUID), connect from inside your app, and read the matrix width, height and max frame count from the device. There is no pairing, PIN, or account.

Factory reset: none exists — and there is little to reset, since the device holds no accounts or keys. The only persistent state is the saved animation, which you can erase over BLE (frame count 0, then save-to-flash). A hardware reset procedure is unknown.

Rebinding to a new controller: just connect from the new phone — nothing binds the backpack to a controller, and there is no network to rejoin (Wi-Fi is used only during a firmware update).

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none Bonding none PIN source — (no PIN) One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time No (nothing bonds) Confidence medium (app analysis; unreplayed)

Entering pairing mode: not needed — the backpack accepts a connection whenever it is powered.

Unpairing: nothing is stored on either side, so there is nothing to unpair, and a second-hand unit can be adopted without a reset.

Recovery: if a connect times out, close the vendor app (or whatever other phone last drove the backpack) and retry; unplugging the power bank for a few seconds drops any stale link.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 00000100-e984-11e7-b78e-ffd6fcc3450f Pix RPC (legacy base) Main service, legacy firmware 00000100-e984-11e7-b78e-ffd6fcc34510 Pix RPC (V1 base) Main service, current firmware 00000100-9552-4325-8021-a85f8136a5c4 Pix RPC (Mini) Mini variant — unconfirmed 0000180a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Device Information Firmware revision 00002a26-…, hardware revision 00002a27-…

Both original bases expose the same characteristics; pick the legacy base only if the device actually advertises it, otherwise V1. Characteristics (the xxxx part of 0000xxxx-e984-11e7-b78e-ffd6fcc3450f / …34510, same under each base): 0101 RPC write, 0103/0104/0105 width/height/max frames (read), 0106 brightness (write, one byte 0–255), 0107/0108/0109 OTA, 0110 demo.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Every command is a write to 0101: [callId, opcode, payload…] — callId is a rolling counter, and there is no checksum, no encryption and no ACK.

Opcode Name Payload 0 SET_FRAME frame index (u16LE), offset (u16LE, =0), frame bytes 1 SET_PALETTE start color index, RGB888 bytes (≤160 colors per call) 2 SET_FRAME_COUNT count (0 = erase) 3 SET_FRAMES_DURATIONS offset (u16LE), per-frame milliseconds (u16LE each; default 80) 4 SET_ANIMATION_DIRECTION 0 normal / 1 alternate / 2 normal-stop / 3 alternate-stop 5 SAVE_TO_PERSISTENT_MEMORY — (saved content autostarts on boot) 6 PRINT_MEMORY — (debug; never sent by the app's normal flows) 7 SET_CONFIG offset (u16LE), config bytes (≤512 per call); first byte = render mode 8 SET_INPUT input id (rolling), command (widget/game input) 9 RESTART —

Render modes (first SET_CONFIG byte): 0 blank, 1 animation, 2 scrolling text, 3 OTA progress, 6 clock, 7 bike, 8 countdown, 9 stopwatch, 16–18 games. Since each game and widget is a device render mode that takes input through SET_INPUT, they appear to run on the device rather than being streamed frame by frame from the phone (unconfirmed on hardware).

docs.title: Image / animation upload
docs.text:
Frames are one byte per pixel — an index into an RGB888 palette — row-major, 320 bytes per frame at 16×20. Upload sequence (all fire-and-forget writes):

  1. Blank the screen (SET_CONFIG mode 0) and erase (SET_FRAME_COUNT 0).
  2. Upload the palette (SET_PALETTE; a second call at index 160 if >160 colors).
  3. Upload each frame (SET_FRAME).
  4. Set durations, direction, then the real frame count.
  5. Optionally SAVE_TO_PERSISTENT_MEMORY so it plays on boot.

Scrolling text works by uploading 8×20 font sprites as ordinary frames and then a text config naming the sprite sequence.

docs.title: Firmware OTA (rescue notes)
docs.text:
Unusually, the device downloads its own firmware over Wi-Fi: the phone writes a config blob (Wi-Fi SSID/password, host, port 80, path, image size, MD5) to 0108, arms 0107, and the backpack joins that network and plain-HTTP GETs the image while still running its normal firmware — there is no bootloader to reboot into first. The vendor app only offers this on hardware revision 3.1 or later, and only on a 2.4 GHz network.

That makes OTA rescuable — any HTTP server on port 80 serving an image with the matching size/MD5 will do — but no firmware image is publicly archived, the image format is unknown, whether the device checks a vendor signature is unknown, and a bad flash can brick the backpack. The spec marks every OTA command advanced. Note the passphrase crosses the BLE link in cleartext; use a throwaway hotspot.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
• Does the RPC characteristic stream responses if you subscribe to notifications? (The vendor app never does.)
  • Real max-frame count and palette cap; partial-frame writes via SET_FRAME offset.
  • Config layouts for the clock/bike/timer widgets and the three games.
  • Pix Mini matrix geometry and whether its characteristic layout matches.
  • Chip family and firmware image format (needs an FCC ID or an archived image).
  • What the backpack advertises, if anything, while it downloads and flashes an update, and what an interrupted flash leaves behind.

docs.title: PurpleAir Air Quality Sensor
docs.text: Status: Complete (local JSON API hardware-verified 2026-08-14) Protocol: WiFi (unauthenticated HTTP JSON on port 80) Manufacturer: PurpleAir, Inc. Manufacturer Status: Active — fully local by design; cloud upload is optional

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
PurpleAir particulate sensors run an ESP (Espressif) SoC that serves a small unauthenticated JSON API on port 80 — every measurement is readable locally with no PurpleAir account, no ThingSpeak key, and no internet. The device pushes to the cloud, but the local /json read path is wholly independent of it, making PurpleAir one of the cleanest local-first sensors.

Verified live 2026-08-14 (firmware 7.02, hardware 2.0, BME280 + one PMSX003 laser): GET /json and /json?live=false returned the 120-second average, /json?live=true returned the instantaneous reading, unauthenticated.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Compute Espressif ESP SoC Sensors 1–2 × PMSX003 laser particle counter, BME280 temp/humidity/pressure Channels single-laser (channel A only) or dual-laser PA-II (adds _b fields) Identity SensorId (= MAC)

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text: Property Value Setup required No (to read a networked sensor) Method GET http://<ip>/json Passphrase protection device_encrypted (Wi-Fi via the PurpleAir-XXXX SoftAP + /config) Confidence high (verified live)

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
Endpoint Meaning GET /json / ?live=false 120-second average (what the web UI shows) GET /json?live=true instantaneous single sample

Key fields: pm2_5_atm (outdoor calibration, µg/m³ — use for outdoor; pm2_5_cf_1 for indoor), p_0_3_um…p_10_0_um (particle counts per deciliter), pm2.5_aqi + p25aqic (on-device US-EPA AQI + colour), current_temp_f (reads ~8 °F high — subtract for ambient), current_humidity (~4 %RH low), pressure (hPa). Dual-laser units repeat PM/count fields with a _b suffix for a data-quality cross-check.

Cloud dependency: none for local reads. The status_* flags report cloud/NTP reachability but a fully offline device still serves /json.

docs.title: QardioArm (A100) Blood Pressure Monitor
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (unverified) Protocol: BLE (standard Blood Pressure Service + one vendor command) Manufacturer: Qardio, Inc. (OEM Ya Horng Electronic, Taiwan) Manufacturer Status: Shutdown — cloud down 2025-04-29, apps delisted, company bankrupt

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The QardioArm is an upper-arm blood-pressure cuff that folds around its own pump unit. It has no screen and no button: unwrapping the cuff switches it on, wrapping it back switches it off, and every measurement is started from a phone over BLE. That made it entirely dependent on the vendor app, which would not show its START button without a signed-in Qardio account — so when the Qardio servers went down for good on 29 April 2025 the cuff stopped working, although nothing on the device had changed.

The protocol is almost entirely standard. The cuff implements the Bluetooth SIG Blood Pressure Service (0x1810) and delivers results as Blood Pressure Measurement (0x2a35) records; the one vendor addition is a control characteristic in the same service that takes a two-byte command to inflate or cancel. Two open-source clients, LibreArm (iOS) and its Android port, drive it daily with no cloud or account, and this spec is read from them.

Medical device

Starting a measurement inflates the cuff on whoever is wearing it; only do so for a consenting adult who is ready, and stay with them. Readings from a third-party client are a personal log, not a clinical measurement, and must never be the sole basis for a medication decision. The spec carries a safety_advisory saying so.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number A100 (FDA 510(k) K140067); the manual also lists an A101 Radio Bluetooth 4.0 LE; chipset not established (the vendor app bundles a Nordic DFU library) FCC ID 2ABF2-888ARM (IC 11885A-888ARM00) Power 4 × AAA alkaline; the manual excludes rechargeables Measurement range 40–250 mmHg, 40–200 bpm, 1 mmHg / 1 bpm resolution; cuff 22–37 cm

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No — no account, no network, no cloud Method ble_direct: unwrap, connect, bond, enable measurement updates, write start Advertised Service 00001810-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb; name believed to begin Qardio Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (two working open clients; not replayed here)

The cuff advertises only while unwrapped; wrapped, or after a few idle minutes, it is off. A client that cannot find it should tell the user to unwrap it, not to press anything.

Factory reset: the only reset the cuff has is the pairing reset. With the cuff unwrapped (on), press the button behind the pinhole on the battery compartment hatch with a straightened paper clip; a green light shines through the hatch. Then forget the QardioArm in the old phone's Bluetooth settings. From the vendor manual (v2.4, page 15) and LibreArm's recovery advice; not replayed.

Rebinding to a new phone: the pairing reset above. There is no network, and the cuff stores nothing but the bond.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required Yes Security mode just_works (inferred: code-free prompt, ATT auth/encryption errors when unbonded) Bonding required One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time Yes — a second phone cannot bond until the pinhole clears the first Confidence medium

Entering pairing mode: nothing to do; the cuff is pairable whenever it is on. The first secured operation (enabling measurement updates on 0x2a35) raises the OS pairing prompt.

Unpairing: the pinhole press, which is the whole factory reset.

Recovery: an ATT error 0x05, 0x08, 0x0c or 0x0f on the enabling measurement updates or the start write means the bond on one side no longer matches the other. Forget the cuff on the phone, press the pinhole, reconnect.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Properties Description 00001810-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Blood Pressure Service Standard SIG service plus one vendor characteristic 00002a35-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Blood Pressure Measurement notify, indicate (not from a GATT dump) The SIG profile specifies indications (CCCD 02 00); the open Android port writes 01 00 (notifications) and receives records, so notifications work. Enable whichever the cuff's GATT declares 583cb5b3-875d-40ed-9098-c39eb0c1983d QardioArm control write Two-byte command, first byte f1 0000180f-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Battery Service Standard; "when the cuff exposes it" 00002a19-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Battery Level read 0–100 %; LibreArm blocks a start at ≤ 10 %

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Written to 583cb5b3-875d-40ed-9098-c39eb0c1983d:

Bytes Meaning f1 01 Start measurement — the cuff inflates and streams 0x2a35 records f1 02 Cancel measurement — stops inflating, releases pressure

No reply comes back on the control characteristic; the response to a start is the stream of measurement records.

docs.title: Blood Pressure Measurement record (0x2a35)
docs.text:
The standard SIG layout, little-endian, no vendor quirk:

Offset Length Field 0 1 Flags: bit0 unit (0 mmHg, 1 kPa); bit1 timestamp; bit2 pulse; bit3 user ID; bit4 measurement status; bits 5–7 reserved 1 2 Systolic, SFLOAT 3 2 Diastolic, SFLOAT 5 2 Mean arterial pressure, SFLOAT 7 7 Timestamp (year uint16 LE, month, day, hour, minute, second) — if bit1 … 2 Pulse rate, SFLOAT, bpm — if bit2 … 1 User ID (255 = unknown) — if bit3 … 2 Measurement status, uint16 LE: bit0 body movement, bit1 cuff loose, bit2 irregular pulse, bits 3–4 pulse range, bit5 position — if bit4

SFLOAT: low 12 bits two's-complement mantissa, high 4 bits two's-complement exponent, value = mantissa × 10^exponent. Mantissas 0x07ff (NaN), 0x0800 (NRes), 0x07fe (+INF), 0x0802 (−INF) and 0x0801 (reserved) carry no value. kPa × 7.500617 = mmHg.

Records arrive while the cuff inflates and deflates. A record is a result only when systolic and diastolic both decode finite and above zero with systolic greater than diastolic; both clients debounce 1.5 s after the last measurement update and keep that record. Worked example: 04 78 00 50 00 5f 00 48 00 = mmHg, pulse present: 120 / 80, MAP 95, pulse 72.

Which optional fields the cuff actually sets has not been published, which is why pulse is documented but not bound as an entity. One captured record would settle it.

scripts/test_qardio_arm_spec.py transcribes the SFLOAT rule and the record walk from the standard library and holds the spec's worked examples to them.

docs.title: Firmware update
docs.text:
The vendor Android app bundles a Nordic legacy DFU client, but nothing ties it to the cuff rather than the QardioBase scale or QardioCore patch the same app served, and neither open client finds a DFU service on the cuff. The spec declares a firmware_update feature at verification: hypothesis with no entry command, so a GATT explorer knows to leave 00001530-1212-efde-1523-785feabcd123 alone if it ever appears. No new image will ever ship.

See device-specs/devices/qardio-arm.yaml for the full machine-readable spec.

docs.title: Qianghe "HappyLighting" (Triones / QHM) BLE LED Strip Controller
docs.text: Status: Complete (app-analysis based; no hardware capture in this project) Protocol: BLE (GATT) Manufacturer: Shenzhen Qianghe Technology Co., Ltd. (qh-tek.com) Manufacturer Status: Active (protocol closed; reverse engineered from the app)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Cheap BLE RGB(W) LED strip controllers driven by the vendor HappyLighting app (Android com.qh.Happylight, iOS id1145694075, Huawei AppGallery C104507761). The reference instance is the AliExpress 3256812708626256 4×72-LED USB car interior strip kit: four rigid 5050 RGB bars on an inline "LED LAMP" controller whose QR code resolves to the HappyLighting download portal — that QR decode is what ties the hardware to the app.

This is the Triones / HappyLighting / QHM family — not Tuya, and not the ELK-BLEDOM (duoCo) family covered by the elk-bledom-led-strip spec; the packet formats are unrelated. The family is natively supported by Home Assistant's led_ble integration.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number None marked; "LED LAMP" / "LED Controller" inline box LEDs 4× rigid 5050 RGB bars, 18 LEDs each (72 total), USB 5V Chipset Unknown Radio BLE FCC ID Unknown

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
No provisioning — the controller advertises when powered and takes writes from any central with no pairing or account. See Initial Device Setup; the machine-readable spec mirrors this in device.setup.

Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Advertised name Dream# / Dream~ / Dream= / QLAMP / QHM* / Triones~ Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (from decompiled app; not replayed against hardware)

Factory reset: no credential or pairing state exists to clear, and no dedicated reset procedure was found in the app. Power-cycling returns the controller to its default state. Confidence: low.

Rebinding to a new controller: trivial — there is no bonding or owner binding; any central in range can connect and take control.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
Two GATT layouts exist; the app picks by which service the unit exposes. Which layout a given controller revision uses is unconfirmed — try 0xFFD5/0xFFD9 first.

UUID Name Description 0xFFD5 Qianghe command service Current app builds write commands here 0xFFD9 Write Command frames (write / write-without-response) 0xFFE0 Qianghe legacy service Older controller revisions 0xFFE1 Write Same command frames as 0xFFD9 0xFFE2 Notify Status replies (legacy layout)

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Frames are short fixed literals: no length prefix, no checksum, no sequence byte. Each write is a complete command.

docs.title: Command: Power on/off
docs.text:
Request:

Offset Length Description 0 1 0xCC opcode 1 1 0x23 = on, 0x24 = off 2 1 0x33 trailer

So power on = CC 23 33, off = CC 24 33.

docs.title: Command: Static colour
docs.text:
Request (56 R G B W F0 AA):

Offset Length Description 0 1 0x56 opcode (0x57 … 0x75 variant on a second app code path) 1 1 Red (0–255) 2 1 Green (0–255) 3 1 Blue (0–255) 4 1 White channel; app scales it with brightness on RGBW hardware (0 on RGB-only) 5 1 0xF0 6 1 0xAA trailer

docs.title: Command: Effect mode
docs.text:
Request (BB <mode> <speed> 44):

Offset Length Description 0 1 0xBB opcode 1 1 Mode index (app's effect list; full table not extracted) 2 1 Speed (0–255) 3 1 0x44 trailer

docs.title: Command: Status query
docs.text:
Request: EF 01 77

Response: notification (0xFFE2 on the legacy layout); the app parses state fields from byte offsets 3–9 of the value. Per-field semantics are unverified.

docs.title: Command: Mic/music sensitivity
docs.text: Fixed literal 69 00 00 F0 96 observed on the 0xFFD5/0xFFD9 layout; which byte carries the sensitivity value was not established.

docs.title: Cloud Dependency
docs.text: None. BLE-local only: the app works with no account and no internet, and the decompiled tree contains no OTA or firmware-download URLs (only qh-tek.com privacy/about pages). Ad/analytics SDKs are bundled but not functionally required.

docs.title: Qingping / ClearGrass Sensors (stock BLE broadcasts)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (source-derived; untested on hardware here) Protocol: BLE service data 0xFDCD, receive-only Manufacturer: Qingping / ClearGrass Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Many Qingping and ClearGrass sensors broadcast current readings in stock BLE advertisements. A client can receive them without connecting, pairing, an account, a hub or the vendor cloud. The maintained qingping-ble parser and its anonymized fixtures provide the protocol evidence; this project did not scan or configure a physical sensor.

This page covers stock 0xFDCD service data only. It does not cover PVVX custom firmware, MiBeacon, BTHome, LoRaWAN products, or a GATT history and configuration connection.

Unauthenticated broadcasts

The documented format has no sender authentication or replay protection. Validate packet lengths, retain unknown values as unavailable, and do not use one reading as the sole input to a medical alarm, safety interlock or high-confidence occupancy decision.

docs.title: Supported model identifiers
docs.text:
The second byte of the service-data value selects the model. Unknown IDs must remain unknown rather than being assigned to a look-alike product.

Type byte Model 0x01, 0x07 CGG1 0x04 CGH1 Door/Window Sensor 0x09 CGP1W 0x0c CGD1 Alarm Clock 0x0e, 0x24 CGDN1 Air Monitor Lite 0x0f CGM1 Lee Guitars Thermo-Hygrometer 0x10 CGDK2 Temp & RH Monitor Lite 0x12 CGPR1 Motion & Light 0x15 CGF1W Temp RH Pro E 0x16 CGG1 Temp RH M 0x18 CGP23W Temp & RH Monitor Pro 0x1e CGC1 BT Clock Lite 0x26 CGP23W Temp RH Baro Pro S 0x33, 0x5d CGP22C CO2 Temp RH 0x4f CGG3 Temp RH M 0x52, 0x62 CGR1PC Indoor Environment Monitor

The parser recognizes more models than Home Assistant's published support list. Parser support is not physical verification: CGDK2, CGR1PC and CGP23W Pro S still need captures on actual hardware.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No, for passive current readings Method ble_direct: scan service data, without connecting Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (maintained parser and fixtures; not replayed here)

The historical Qingping Air app, current Qingping apps, optional Bluetooth gateway, display settings and history synchronization are separate surfaces. None is needed for this receive-only protocol.

Factory reset: no family-wide procedure is established. The archived CGG1 guide says its reset erases locally recorded data and releases app pairing. That is a destructive model-specific owner operation, not something a passive client needs or should trigger. Do not generalize it to the other models.

Rebinding: there is no passive-client bond or network membership to move. Resume scanning. Recovering an app/history pairing is outside this document.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none for advertisement reception Bonding none Confidence medium

The frames themselves contain no pairing proof or sender authentication. A separate GATT configuration or history surface may have different security; it is not covered here.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
Read service data associated with full UUID 0000fdcd-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb. The offsets below begin at the service-data value, after the UUID.

Offset Size Meaning 0 1 Header/flags; bit 6 (0x40) marks an event packet 1 1 Device type from the model table 2 6 Address-like bytes; not used by the parser to prove identity or select a model 8 1 First TLV type 9 1 First TLV payload length 10 length First TLV payload; further type-length-value records follow

Require the complete header and each complete TLV before decoding. Skip an unknown or truncated TLV without inventing values or discarding valid earlier TLVs. All multibyte integers are little-endian.

docs.title: TLV map
docs.text:
TLV Length Decode 0x01 4 Signed int16 temperature × 0.1 °C, then uint16 relative humidity × 0.1 % 0x02 1 Battery percent; 0xff means externally powered and is displayed as 100, not measured battery capacity 0x04 1 Door/open true for 0 and 2; left-open/problem true only for 2 0x07 2 Unsigned pressure × 0.1 mbar 0x08 4 Motion byte, low uint16 illuminance, high uint8 illuminance; on event packets update motion only 0x09 4 Unsigned uint32 illuminance in lux 0x11 1 Ambient-light boolean 0x12 4 PM2.5 and PM10, each uint16 in µg/m³ 0x13 2 CO₂, uint16 ppm 0x15 2 VOC index, uint16, unitless; exact range unresolved 0x18 2 Static hardware capability bitmap, not CO₂ and not a sensor output 0x19 1 Sound pressure in dB 0x0f 1 Packet ID, metadata rather than a measurement

For non-event TLV 0x08, calculate illuminance as:

uint16_le(payload[1:3]) + (payload[3] << 16)

On an event packet, ignore those three light bytes and retain the previous illuminance. For every other omitted measurement, also retain the previous value rather than replacing it with zero.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
08 10 00 00 00 00 00 00   01 04 1c 01 af 02   02 01 64

The address-like bytes are zero placeholders. Model 0x10 is CGDK2. TLV 0x01 carries 0x011c = 28.4 °C and 0x02af = 68.7 % RH; TLV 0x02 reports 100 % battery.

scripts/test_qingping_stock_ble_spec.py independently walks the documented envelope and TLVs. It also checks signed temperature, 24-bit illuminance, truncation, the event-packet rule, and that capability TLV 0x18 never becomes CO₂.

docs.title: Out of scope and remaining questions
docs.text:
History, alarms, names, display content, settings and firmware updates need a separate documented interface. The remaining header bits, model-specific event variants and VOC range are unresolved. Physical captures are still needed for the newer parser mappings.

See device-specs/devices/qingping-stock-ble.yaml for the complete machine-readable model and TLV maps.

docs.title: Quicklynks BM2 Battery Monitor
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (source-derived; untested on hardware here) Protocol: BLE GATT and passive advertisements Manufacturer: Quicklynks Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The BM2 / Battery Monitor 2 can report voltage, percentage and status locally without an account or cloud. Two public clients establish an active FFF4 notification format and two advertisement generations. This project did not connect to a physical BM2 or validate electrical accuracy.

This spec is BM2-only. Do not apply it to BM6 or assume other battery monitors share its protocol. History, configuration, chemistry selection, cranking/charging-test history, firmware and alarm writes are outside its read-only scope.

docs.title: Initial Setup and Pairing
docs.text:
No provisioning, account, pairing key or application credential is needed. Advertised-name leads are Battery Monitor, Li Battery Monitor and ZX-1689; the active service is 0000fff0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb.

No genuine BM2 manual or factory-reset procedure was found. There is no passive-client state to reset; reconnect or resume scanning to recover a client.

The protocol uses a published shared AES key and zero IV. These are wire-format constants, not owner credentials, secure pairing or sender authentication.

docs.title: Active FFF4 telemetry
docs.text:
1. Discover 0000fff4-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb and subscribe.
  2. Wait for a fresh notification without writing FFF3.

  3. Require exactly 16 ciphertext bytes and decrypt AES-128-CBC with:

  4. Key: 6c656167656e64fffe31383832343636

  5. IV: 00000000000000000000000000000000

  6. Require plaintext type 0xf5, then decode:

Offset Meaning 0 Packet type f5 1–2 Big-endian packed word: voltage = (word >> 4) / 100 V; status = word & 0x0f 3 Battery percentage, 0–100 4 onward No additional read-only telemetry established

Status values are 0 Critical, 1 Low, 2 Normal, 4 Charging and 8 Floating. Other values are unknown. The reference charging flag is status ≥ 4, but retain the raw status rather than treating that flag as a complete state model.

Active validation accepts 5.0–20.0 V and 0–100 %. These are client sanity bounds, not verified electrical ratings. Missing FFF4 is incompatible; a timeout is inconclusive. Always stop notifications and disconnect afterward, including on failure.

Constructed vector:

Plaintext:  f5 50 82 50 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
Ciphertext: cd 9d a1 bf c3 eb 13 1c 59 90 df 26 5d 06 4d c4

It represents 12.88 V, 80 % and Normal.

docs.title: Enhanced
docs.text:
A 14-byte manufacturer body is preceded by its two-byte manufacturer ID in little-endian order, reconstructing one encrypted 16-byte block. Decrypt it and read voltage as big-endian uint16 / 100 at bytes 6–7 and percentage at byte 8. Status is unavailable.

The example in the YAML uses manufacturer ID 43248 and body aa0a2e42b2a68aafdd2e23559079, reconstructing ciphertext f0a8aa0a2e42b2a68aafdd2e23559079. Its plaintext is 00000000000005085000000000000000: 12.88 V and 80 %. The manufacturer ID was derived from the ciphertext's first two bytes, not chosen arbitrarily.

docs.title: Legacy
docs.text:
Company ID 0x004c carries a 23-byte body:

Offset Meaning 0–17 Fixed prefix 0215655f83caae16a10a702e31f30d58dd82 18–19 Major bytes, no established telemetry meaning 20–21 Minor bytes, no established telemetry meaning 22 Battery percentage, 0–100

Voltage and status are unavailable. Do not invent values from major/minor. When enhanced data is followed by legacy data, refresh percentage but retain enhanced voltage/generation and clear status.

docs.title: Freshness and limits
docs.text:
Prefer a fresh FFF4 notification. Use the latest valid advertisement only if active access fails or no connectable path exists. If neither path supplies valid data, report unavailable rather than a healthy default. Timestamp cached advertisements and expose staleness; the upstream cache has no demonstrated expiry.

scripts/test_quicklynks_bm2_spec.py independently decrypts the constructed vectors, checks packed fields and both advertisement generations, and rejects malformed values. These checks do not prove firmware coverage, electrical accuracy or safe installation.

See device-specs/devices/quicklynks-bm2.yaml for the complete machine-readable formats and evidence limits.
