docs.title: Sengled Wi-Fi Smart Bulbs
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (unverified) Protocol: WiFi (UDP 9080 JSON; MQTT over TLS once re-pointed at your own broker) Manufacturer: Sengled Manufacturer Status: Unsupported — cloud failing since June 2025, Alexa skill removed by Amazon on 1 August 2025

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Sengled's Wi-Fi bulbs (the "Smart Wi-Fi LED" A19/BR30 family: W11-N13, W21-N13, W31-N15, W31-N11, W12-N15, W21-U23 and kin) join the home 2.4 GHz network directly and were driven through Sengled's cloud. That cloud went down for most of a week from about 18 June 2025, kept dropping through July, and on 1 August 2025 Amazon pulled the Sengled Alexa skill for "prolonged outages" Sengled had not fixed. Trade press reported unpaid staff and an unresponsive company. The bulbs still work at the wall switch, and two local paths survive:

  • UDP JSON on port 9080. Every bulb on Wi-Fi answers {"func": "...", "param": {...}} datagrams with no authentication — on/off, brightness, RGB, colour temperature, a state read that doubles as the discovery broadcast. A bulb paired with the app years ago still answers.
  • Your own MQTT broker. During Wi-Fi provisioning the bulb is handed two HTTP base URLs it treats as "the cloud"; it asks one of them where its MQTT broker is. Give it URLs on your LAN, answer two small JSON requests, run a TLS MQTT broker, and the bulb publishes to wifielement/<MAC>/status and takes commands on wifielement/<MAC>/update exactly as it did for Sengled.

Not covered: Sengled's Zigbee bulbs (Element, Z01-/E11-/E12-) and Bluetooth-mesh bulbs (B11-) are different radios and protocols. OTA flashing to Tasmota/ESPHome/WLED is possible on the ESP8266 models (W31-N15, W31-N11, W21-U23) via the same firmware-URL command and is noted, not specified.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes (a bulb already on Wi-Fi needs nothing for UDP control) Method softap_udp — the bulb's setup AP, UDP 9080 at the bulb's fixed AP address Setup AP Sengled_Wi-Fi Bulb_XXXXXX, open Passphrase protection device_encrypted — RC4 under a fixed, public key, then base64; treat as plaintext Confidence medium (two open-source implementations have run it; this project has not)

The route: stand up a stand-in cloud on the LAN — an HTTP server answering POST /life2/device/accessCloud.json and GET /jbalancer/new/bimqtt ({"protocal":"mqtt","host":"<broker>","port":8883}), and a TLS 1.2 MQTT broker that allows anonymous clients and offers ALPN x-amzn-mqtt-ca. Reset the bulb, join its AP, then over UDP 9080: startConfigRequest (returns the MAC), optionally scanWifiRequest/getAPListRequest, startConfigRequest again (payload.result true), one RC4+base64 setParamsRequest carrying the SSID, passphrase and the two base URLs, then endConfigRequest. The bulb joins, hits both HTTP endpoints within about 180 s, connects to the broker as <MAC>@wifielement and starts publishing. The Sengled Home app route still exists but depends on Sengled's cloud.

Factory reset: from on, switch the bulb off and on five times quickly; it flashes three times, blinks twice, and the setup AP appears (support.com's guide and the SengledTools README; one retailer guide says ten cycles — not replayed here). factory_reset over UDP and reset over MQTT do the same on a reachable bulb.

Rebinding to a new network: no in-place rewrite; reset and provision again. A new broker address under the same CA needs only a reissued server certificate — the bulb re-reads /bimqtt on every boot.

docs.title: UDP 9080
docs.text:
Request {"func": "<name>", "param": {...}}; reply {"func": "<name>", "result": {"ret": 0, "msg": "...", ...}} (ret 1 = error). 3 s timeout, no retries, no checksum.

func param Notes set_device_switch switch 0/1 power set_device_brightness / get_device_brightness brightness 0–100 percent set_device_color red,green,blue 0–255 RGB engine; colour bulbs set_device_colortemp colorTemperature 1–100 warm→cool; Kelvin ends unmeasured (2000–6500 or 2700–6500) set_device_pwm r,g,b,w 0–100 volatile channel drive search_devices — mac, ip, version, MN, R/G/B/W {freq,value}; broadcast it to discover get_software_version, get_device_mac, reboot — factory_reset, set_factory_mode, update_led_firmware {ota_url} — advanced

Power is on when any channel reports freq 0; W.value > 0 means the white engine is active; a white-only bulb's reply has no R/G/B keys.

docs.title: MQTT (after re-pointing)
docs.text: Payloads are JSON arrays of {"dn": "<MAC>", "type": "...", "value": "<string>", "time": <epoch ms>}. Publish to wifielement/<MAC>/update: switch "0"/"1", brightness "0"–"100", color "R:G:B", colorTemperature "0"–"100" (sent with switch "1"), reset, update <url>. Subscribe to wifielement/<MAC>/status (full set on connect, then deltas: switch, brightness, color, colorTemperature, colorMode, typeCode, identifyNO, supportAttributes, version, ip, deviceRssi…), /consumption, /consumptionTime, and wifielement/c/status for the connect announcement.

docs.title: Provisioning cipher
docs.text:
RC4 keyed with the 52 ASCII bytes of MTlCaWppbmdTaGFuZ2hhaVdpU2VuZ2xlZEZpMjBBQUJBU0U2NA== (not base64-decoded), no IV, over the compact JSON of the whole setParamsRequest; the base64 of the ciphertext is the datagram. scripts/test_sengled_wifi_bulb_spec.py holds the spec's vectors.

See device-specs/devices/sengled-wifi-bulb.yaml for the full spec.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
See Shining Mask for full command table — protocol is identical. Key commands:

Command Plaintext bytes Description Set brightness [0x06, 'L','I',0x47,0x48,'T', level] Set LED brightness Set speed [0x06, 'S','P','E','E',0x44, speed] Set scroll/animation speed Select animation [0x05, 'A',0x35,'I',0x34, index] Play built-in animation Select image [0x05, 'I',0x34,'A',0x47, index] Show built-in image Set FG color [0x06, 'F','C', flag, R, G, B] Set text foreground color Set BG color [0x06, 'B','C', flag, R, G, B] Set text background color Enter DIY mode [0x06, 'S',0x34,'V','E','W', 1] Single-frame DIY drawing Exit DIY (save) [0x06, 'S',0x34,'V','E','W', 2] Save and exit DIY Play DIY [0x04, 'P','L','A','Y'] Play saved DIY animation

docs.title: Data Transfer Protocol
docs.text:
1. DATS → device on WRITE1: [0x09, 0x44,'A','T','S', len_hi, len_lo, datalen_hi, datalen_lo, type]
  2. Device responds DATSOK on notify
  3. Send data frames on WRITE2: [payload_len+1, frame_index, ...data] (18 or 98 bytes per frame)
  4. Device responds REOK per frame
  5. DATCP → device on WRITE1: [0x05, 0x44,'A','T','C','P']
  6. Device responds DATCPOK

docs.title: Silk'n Infinity / Silk'n 7
docs.text: Status: Complete (static analysis; not yet hardware-verified) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Home Skinovations (Silk'n) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
IPL can permanently damage skin and eyes

This is an intense-pulsed-light hair-removal handset (a home-pulsed-light (HPL) handset). Improper use can cause permanent skin burns, blistering, discolouration or scarring, and serious eye injury. Patch-test first, match the intensity to your skin tone (IPL is unsafe on the darkest skin tones), never treat broken, tanned, tattooed or moled skin, and keep it away from the eyes. This project ships an experimental, unaffiliated third-party client — the manufacturer's own instructions govern.

  • Manufacturer safety guidance: https://www.manualslib.com/manual/2132171/Home-Skinovations-Silk-N-Infinity.html
  • Archived copy (web.archive.org), if the page above is offline: https://web.archive.org/web/20260831005752/https://www.manualslib.com/manual/2132171/Home-Skinovations-Silk-N-Infinity.html

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Home IPL (intense pulsed light) hair-removal devices: the Infinity family (advertising as Infinity or SilknV_F) and the newer Silk'n 7 (advertising as Silkn7_App). Recovered by static analysis of the companion app Hair Removal – Silk'n (com.ewavemobile.silkn) v6.1 (versionCode 38), 2026-08. Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/silkn-infinity.yaml.

The headline: the device works fully without the app, and the BLE protocol is unauthenticated — no pairing, no bonding, no challenge, no paywall. The app counts flashes via notifications, shows device errors, polls the skin-color sensor, and has exactly one write: an opt-in lock. The app itself is account-centric (a blocking no-network dialogue at startup, login before the main screen), but none of that reaches the hardware — a cloud shutdown strands the app, not the device.

The app cannot fire flashes or set intensity — no write path exists to anything but the lock. Energy levels are physical-button only, so a replacement client is telemetry-plus-lock, exactly like the vendor's.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number Infinity family (Infinity, SilknV_F), Silk'n 7 (Silkn7_App) Chipset Unknown Radio BLE FCC ID Not established

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
None — the device needs no provisioning and works standalone out of the box. See Initial Device Setup; mirrored into device.setup in the spec.

Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct (scan, connect, subscribe — nothing else) Setup AP / advertised name Infinity, SilknV_F, or Silkn7_App (exact match) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (static analysis of the app's BLE layer, not replayed)

Factory reset: unknown whether one exists. The app contains no reset function and no write path to the on-device treatment counters; if a reset exists at all it is an undocumented physical button procedure. In practice there is almost nothing to reset: the lock clears with one documented write, and the counters are cosmetic history, not an adoption barrier.

Rebinding to a new phone/client: trivial — no bond is stored on either side, so a new client simply scans and connects. The only residue a previous app install can leave is the opt-in lock: if the old client locked the device on disconnect, write 30 30 (Released + Unlocked) to the lock characteristic once and move on.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
None. See Pairing, Bonding and Unpairing; mirrored into device.pairing.

Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none (open GATT on a bare connection) Bonding none (nothing stored on either side) PIN source not_applicable One central at a time Unknown One bond at a time No (no bonds exist) Confidence medium (static analysis, not yet confirmed on hardware)

Entering pairing mode: not applicable — the device advertises and accepts connections whenever powered.

Unpairing: not applicable — there is no bond to drop. Adopting a second-hand unit costs nothing but the optional lock-clearing write above.

Recovery: the worst case is the vendor app holding the connection in the background — close it (or power-cycle the device) and connect again.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
One custom primary service with five synthetic characteristics sharing the 12345678-9012-3456-7890-1234567890xx prefix, plus standard DIS.

Client integration: protocol_handler: ipl_silkn selects the mobile lock-state check and conditional Released + Unlocked write. Intensity remains a physical control; the client must not invent an energy-level write.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 720411ac-adfe-2015-0820-835742ad3835 Silk'n Hair Removal Service The whole application surface 0000180a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Device Information (standard) Serial number string 0x2A25

docs.title: Characteristics (Hair Removal Service)
docs.text: UUID suffix Name Access Payload …9011 TreatmentDynamicInformation read + notify 20-byte frame, one per pulse (layout below) …9022 DeviceErrors read + notify 5 × u8 error codes (range ~10–70: HV, temp, fan, ignition, color-sensor calibration, stuck buttons, checksum, micro-current) …9033 LockUnlockDevice read + write 2 bytes — the only writable characteristic …9044 DeviceIO read 1 byte: bit7 = trigger pressed, bit6 = function button …9055 ColorMeasurements read 7 × u16: raw RGB + threshold RGB (+1 unknown), polled every 20 pulses; endianness unconfirmed

docs.title: TreatmentDynamicInformation (20 bytes, notify per pulse)
docs.text:
Two layouts, selected by the advertised name the client connected to — keep the scan-result name, not just the address.

Infinity / SilknV_F — big-endian:

Offset Length Type Description 0 1 u8 opcode (1 = per-pulse event; 0 likely a status snapshot, unconfirmed) 1 4 u32 BE max_pulses (lamp/cartridge lifetime capacity) 5 4 u32 BE total_counter (lifetime flashes fired) 9 1 u8 current_level (set by the physical button, never over BLE) 10–18 5 × 2 u16 BE per-level counters, levels 1–5

Silkn7_App — little-endian variant: same header fields, little-endian, with the per-level counters omitted from the payload; the app increments its own per-level tallies on each opcode==1 notification, and a replacement client must do the same. Byte 19 is unused/unknown in both layouts.

docs.title: Command: release_and_unlock (write to …9033)
docs.text: 30 30 — mode Released + state Unlocked. Clears the app-managed lock and sets the mode that keeps it cleared; a never-paired device ships in this state. This is the one write a replacement client should issue on first connect if the device reads back Locked.

docs.title: Command: lock (write to …9033)
docs.text:
31 31 — mode Lock + state Locked: what the app writes between sessions when the user enabled lock mode (it unlocks from its treatment-start screen and re-locks on disconnect). A local-control client has no reason to send it.

Read layout of …9033: byte 0 = mode (0x30 Released / 0x31 Lock), byte 1 = state (0x30 Unlocked / 0x31 Locked). The lock is advisory and app-managed, not a security feature — any client can clear it with a single unauthenticated write.

docs.title: Cloud
docs.text: Not required, and never on the device path. The phone app talks to https://ws.silknglobal.com/ (REST: signup/login, treatments CRUD, pair-device telemetry, per-pulse data upload, malfunction reports) and gates its main screen behind an account — but the pair-device call is telemetry only and the hardware never contacts any of it. Data that leaves the device: per-pulse treatment data, malfunction reports, and account identity — all app-side, all optional once you stop using the vendor app.

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text: • Static analysis (decompile) of the Android companion app — no hardware, no capture yet. One HCI snoop of a treatment session would close the remaining gaps: opcode values beyond 1, the Silkn7_App frame on-air, the ColorMeasurements endianness, and the exact DeviceErrors code table.

docs.title: SmartDawn Smart Lights
docs.text: Status: In Progress Protocol: BLE (Wi-Fi/UDP variants on the platform) Manufacturer: Hangzhou Daniao Technology Co., Ltd (SmartDawn / Minetom store brand) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: SmartDawn (smartdawn.com) sells addressable-RGB holiday lighting — RGBIC permanent outdoor string lights, icicle/net/curtain lights, meteor-shower tubes, cone trees — controlled by the "SmartDawn" app. The products are white-label builds of Hangzhou Daniao Technology's pixel-light platform (the same stack as Daniao's SuperPix and legacy SmartPixel apps). This page documents the local BLE command protocol, reconstructed from a decompile of the official Android app (v1.2.4) and its bundled H5 JavaScript — no cloud or account is needed for local control.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number JY25CUT-series curtain lights; HL1123 firecracker light; unnumbered string/icicle/net/meteor SKUs Chipset Unknown (FCC ID unresolved — internals not yet identified) Radio BLE (Wi-Fi on some Daniao-platform SKUs; which SmartDawn models include it is unverified) FCC ID Unresolved; manuals hosted on fccid.io (see References)

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No (BLE models) Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name DN-prefixed BLE name, 6-8 chars; Wi-Fi SKUs would expose AP DN?????? (password 00000000) Passphrase protection not_applicable (BLE) Confidence medium (from app code, not a live capture)

Power the lights and they advertise immediately. Connect, subscribe to the DDP and BIN notify characteristics, raise MTU, and send M_TIME_SYNC — then commands flow. No pairing or authentication on the command path.

Factory reset: the protocol has M_FACTORY_RESET (mt=2598) and M_REBOOT (mt=2599) commands (low confidence — from app code). The controller also has a physical mode button: press to switch effects, hold-and-release to turn off (per the FCC manual). No bonding state exists to clear.

Rebinding to a new network: BLE control is network-independent. Wi-Fi provisioning (Wi-Fi SKUs only) is re-done in place via the app's AP-mode flow; nothing depends on the old network.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: Discovery: advertised local name is 6–8 chars starting with DN (case-insensitive), plus the custom service UUID below; a 14-byte manufacturer-data record carries firmware version, factory id, product type, pixel width/height, group, vendor and run-mode flags.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 00000074-1972-1925-3022-077119514e44 Daniao DDP Service Sole service; holds all channels below 01020074-...-077119514e44 DDP Write Command writes (fragmented DDP/DNX packets) 01010074-...-077119514e44 DDP Notify Command responses, state pushes 02020074-...-077119514e44 BIN Write Bulk uploads (effects, animations, layouts) 02010074-...-077119514e44 BIN Notify Bulk-channel responses/progress 27923001-2072-...-077119514e44 Uploader Firmware upload (OTA flow)

(All characteristic UUIDs except the Uploader share the 1972-1925-3022-077119514e44 base; the Uploader's second group is 2072 — confirmed in BleUtils5 and SuperPix's BleUtils3.)

docs.title: Transport framing
docs.text:
Every logical packet is split into BLE writes of at most the negotiated payload MTU (app requests ATT MTU 512; payload = MTU − 3, fallback 20), each prefixed with a 4-byte fragment header:

Offset Length Description 0 1 Message serial (u8, per logical packet) 1 1 Total fragment count 2 1 Fragments remaining after this one (down to 0) 3 1 Channel tag: 0x00 on DDP; on BIN a buffer type — 1=TUTU_DOODLE, 2=TUTU_ERASE, 4=TUTU_RESTORE, 16=MUSIC_BIN 4 MTU−4 Payload chunk

Writes use WRITE_TYPE_NO_RESPONSE (BleUtils5 sets write type 2).

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Commands are protobuf messages under a 20-byte extended (DNX) header:

Offset Length Description 0 1 0xF0 (flag nibble 0xF, version 0) 1 1 from-role; app hardcodes 0x04 (gateway) 2 2 sn (u16 BE) 4 2 total length (u16 BE) 6 2 mt — message type (u16 BE) 8 4 cid (u32 BE, 0 from app) 12 2 osn (u16 BE) 14 1 rcode (0) 15 1 ts (random u8) 16 2 csum (u16 BE, app sends 0) 18 2 zeros 20 n optional protobuf payload (default type SimpleMessage {i1,i2,s1,s2,i3,i4})

Core message types (full table in the YAML spec):

mt Command Payload 2504 M_TIME_SYNC TimeSync 2507 / 2508 playlist loop / single play none 2509 M_SET_BRIGHTNESS SimpleMessage 2514 / 2515 power on / off none 2523 M_SET_PLAYSPEED SimpleMessage 2598 / 2599 factory reset / reboot none 2601 / 2603 / 2628 palette / color mode / color ext protobuf 2604 / 2605 / 2606 play next / prev / specific effect effect ref for 2606 2611 / 2612 music mode start / stop – 2650 / 2651 device-mic music mode start / stop none 2701 / 2702 doodle (live pixel session) start / end SimpleMessage 237 M_DEV_SHOW_PIXEL (single-pixel preview) SimpleMessage 2104 get running status none 2901–2933 install/remove effects, apps, animations, layouts; firmware update –

Inbound highlights: M_DEVICE_INFO_NOTIFY (mt=2103, hardware/ports/fwVer/ effects/width/height), M_POWER_STATUS_NOTIFY (2105), M_PLAY_INFO_NOTIFY (2610).

docs.title: Image / animation frames (pixel push)
docs.text:
Confirmed live path (v1.2.4): the app's draw / photo-to-light modes push pixels over the BIN channel, not the DDP channel. M_DOODLE_START (mt=2701, SimpleMessage {i1:1, i2:1}) opens the session; the canvas is then sent as buffer arrays whose fragment-header tag byte is TUTU_DOODLE (1) for incremental strokes or TUTU_RESTORE (4) for a full-canvas redraw (TUTU_ERASE = 2 clears). The buffer payload is a palette-indexed raster chunked at ~200 bytes: a 3-byte header [x][y][colorCount ≤ 16], the RGB palette (3 bytes/colour), then per-pixel palette indices. M_DOODLE_END (mt=2702) closes the session; M_DOODLE_SCROLL (mt=2715) scrolls it. M_DEV_SHOW_PIXEL (mt=237) previews single pixels while drawing. Music mode either starts the controller's own mic (M_START_DEVICE_MIC, mt=2650) or, for phone-mic mode, computes FFT on the phone and drives effect selection.

Dormant encoder: every Daniao H5 bundle checked (SmartDawn 1.2.4, SuperPix 4.4.1, legacy SmartPixels) also ships mkOrginDdp, an encoder for standard DDP DISPLAY packets (datatype 0x01, flag 0xE1, offset-ordered fragments into a raster buffer) — but it has no call sites in any of them. Treat DISPLAY-packet streaming as a legacy/dormant capability until an on-air capture shows it in use; likewise the "PUSH flag latches the frame" convention is inference from the header semantics, not confirmed.

Stored designs (pictures, text, animations): persist over the Uploader characteristic as "DN" AMX microapp containers (UploadRequest.type=3, no path), confirmed by on-air captures (smartdawn_longer2.pcapng frames 6214–6252 is a complete animation save: type=3, size=4096, packetnum=9). The device answers on DDP Notify (M_UPLOAD_START_RESPONSE mt=2931, M_UPLOAD_COMPLETE mt=2934); wait for the completion before M_PLAY_EFFECT (2606) — playing an uncommitted cid is a silent no-op. The vendor app refreshes M_EFFECT_LIST (2904) between completion and play. The M_START_INSTALL_ANIMATION / M_INSTALL_ANIMATION_PACKET / M_END_INSTALL_ANIMATION (mt 2918–2920) messages from p2p.proto were never observed on the wire and are presumed a legacy/alternate flow; .eff (type=0 + path) uploads serve CDN catalogue effects only.

Machine-readable capability: the YAML spec declares features: [image_upload] (rgb888, device-reported resolution) plus stored_upload (container_format: daniao_amx, file_type: 3, play_command: play_effect, response_characteristic) and protocol_handler: "daniao_ddp" for clients that implement the fragment framing + packet encoders. Per-model resolution (width × height) comes from the manufacturer-data record and M_DEVICE_INFO_NOTIFY (mt=2103).

docs.text: Same DDP framing over UDP port 4048; devices announce presence to app UDP port 14040; AP-mode provisioning per the SmartPixel manual (DN?????? / i5g* hotspot, password 00000000, WPA/OPEN only). Unverified which SmartDawn SKUs ship Wi-Fi.

docs.title: SmartThings Hub v2
docs.text: Status: Local discovery and service map documented Protocol: WiFi (mDNS + SmartThings/Edge/Matter local services) Manufacturer: Samsung SmartThings Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SmartThings Hub v2 advertises local SmartThings, Edge driver, and Matter controller services. The primary stable identity is TXT id from _smartthings._tcp. Every local endpoint it serves is gated behind a cloud-issued Samsung bearer token, so this project identifies the hub and stops there.

Running Home Assistant? Use LocalThings for your Samsung appliances

If this hub is on your network, the Samsung appliances on the same SmartThings account probably are too — and those can leave the cloud today. LocalThings is a Home Assistant integration (HACS, domain localthings) that controls Samsung washers, dryers, refrigerators, air conditioners, ovens, dishwashers and more straight over your LAN, with no Samsung account. It needs Samsung's servers once, without logging in, for the first appliance, and never again.

Open LocalThings in HACS · then add an appliance by its IP address.

LocalThings does not drive the hub itself, or the Zigbee and Z-Wave devices paired to it. Those stay on the hub, or move to a local coordinator (ZHA, Zigbee2MQTT, Z-Wave JS) — see Keeping devices alive.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text: Browse _smartthings._tcp.local. first. _smartthings-hedge._tcp.local. on port 8766 is the Edge driver HTTPS service, and _matter._tcp.local. advertises the hub's Matter controller node.

docs.title: Local Services
docs.text:
Service Port TXT Description _smartthings._tcp.local. 8081 type=hubv2, id=... Primary hub service _smartthings-hedge._tcp.local. 8766 feat=ctrl Edge driver HTTPS (bearer token) _matter._tcp.local. 49722 T=6 Matter controller (not a bridge)

Observed hostname: hubv2-0d052a80000000001.local

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/smartthings-hub-v2.yaml

docs.title: Home Assistant
docs.text:
Integration Path Covers LocalThings (HACS, localthings) Local — OCF over CoAP/DTLS to each appliance; HTTPS on TCP 8888 for 2018–2022 units Samsung SmartThings-compatible appliances. Recommended. Core SmartThings Cloud — SmartThings API Everything on the account, hub children included, while the cloud lasts

LocalThings is built on the smartthings-local Python library, the starting point for a client that is not Home Assistant.

docs.title: Snapmaker U1 Multi-Color 3D Printer
docs.text: Status: Complete (read/monitor path hardware-verified 2026-08-14; write/print and secure-MQTT documented from the vendor's open-sourced forks) Protocol: WiFi (Moonraker HTTP REST + JSON-RPC WebSocket on port 80) Manufacturer: Snapmaker (Shenzhen Snapmaker Technologies) Manufacturer Status: Active — cloud-independent local control; firmware is open source

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Snapmaker U1 is a 2025/2026 CoreXY four-toolhead multi-color FDM printer. Unlike Snapmaker's earlier SACP/HTTP-token machines, the U1 runs a stock-shaped Klipper + Moonraker + Fluidd stack (Snapmaker's own GPL forks, open-sourced 2026-03-30) on embedded Linux. Local control is therefore ordinary Moonraker — and on stock firmware the REST/WebSocket API on port 80 is reachable unauthenticated on the LAN (all RFC-1918 ranges are in Moonraker's trusted_clients). No cloud, no account, no pairing for local monitoring or control.

Verified live 2026-08-14: a real U1 (Moonraker host "lava", firmware 1.5.1.2, Klipper ready) answered /printer/info, /server/info, /printer/objects/list (showing all four toolheads extruder..extruder3) and /printer/objects/query (bed 27 °C, a completed print on the bed) with no API key.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Type CoreXY FDM, 4 independent toolheads (4-color) Compute Embedded Linux (Buildroot 2024.02), internal user lava Firmware Klipper (motion) + Moonraker (API) + Fluidd (UI), Snapmaker GPL forks Discovery mDNS _snapmaker._tcp.local. (TXT ip/sn/device_name/link_mode)

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No (for local control of a networked unit) Method Join Wi-Fi at the touchscreen; then Moonraker on port 80 Passphrase protection device_encrypted (Wi-Fi creds entered on-device) Confidence high (verified live; matches ha-snapmaker-u1)

Important: the mDNS answer advertises port 1884 (the plain-MQTT LAN broker), not the HTTP port. Ignore it and use 80 (upload falls back to 8080).

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
Standard Moonraker: HTTP REST + JSON-RPC-2.0-over-WebSocket (ws://<ip>/websocket).

Purpose Endpoint Identity / readiness GET /printer/info, GET /server/info Object list (4 toolheads) GET /printer/objects/list Telemetry GET /printer/objects/query?heater_bed&extruder&print_stats&display_status Live telemetry stream printer.objects.subscribe over WebSocket Files GET /server/files/list Upload / print POST /server/files/upload (multipart), POST /printer/print/{start,pause,resume,cancel} — advanced, moves a heated printer G-code POST /printer/gcode/script — advanced

A separate on-device secure-MQTT channel (plain 1884 / mTLS 8883, topics {SN}/request|response|notification, touchscreen-approved cert pairing with default access code 12345678) mirrors the same JSON-RPC API — used by Snapmaker Orca and the mobile app. It is not required for the local HTTP path.

docs.title: SolarEdge Inverters (Modbus TCP / SunSpec)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (from public sources; not replayed against hardware) Protocol: Wi-Fi/LAN: Modbus TCP on port 1502 (SetApp inverters) or 502 (older display inverters), SunSpec register map Manufacturer: SolarEdge Technologies Manufacturer Status: Active. Cloud Monitoring API V1 reported retired at the start of November 2026

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SolarEdge grid-tied PV inverters (HD-Wave single phase, three phase, Synergy three phase, Energy Hub and StorEdge) carry a local Modbus TCP server that speaks SunSpec. It needs no account, no cloud and no app once it is switched on, and it is the path SolarEdge itself documents for third-party monitoring.

Two things make it the durable local path now:

  • Community reports say SolarEdge retires its cloud Monitoring API V1 at the start of November 2026 (1 or 3 November, depending on the source) in favour of an OAuth-based V2.
  • Home Assistant 2026.10 removed its "SolarEdge Local" integration, which used the inverter's undocumented web API that newer firmware closes, and added a core SolarEdge Modbus integration built on this protocol.

One client at a time: SolarEdge's technical note says the Modbus TCP server accepts a single connection and session. A second poller (another home-automation system, a datalogger, two integrations each opening their own socket) is refused or starves the first. Use one client, or put a Modbus proxy in front of the inverter.

Security: Modbus TCP has no authentication and no encryption. Keep the port on a trusted LAN segment and never forward it to the internet.

Control registers: the power-limit, export-limit and storage registers change what a grid-connected inverter produces and exports. Export limits are often part of the grid connection agreement, and persistent settings are stored in flash meant for occasional writes. They are documented in the spec but flagged advanced.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Models SetApp inverters (all SunSpec-capable); display (LCD) inverters with CPU firmware 3.xxxx or later Network Ethernet (the vendor-documented path for Modbus TCP); built-in or plug-in Wi-Fi on many models Modbus over Wi-Fi Works today per Home Assistant and binsentsu; SolarEdge may drop it in a future firmware Also RS485 Modbus RTU (115200 8N1 default), not covered here

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes: Modbus TCP is off from the factory Method device_ui: SetApp or the inverter display Port 1502 (SetApp), 502 (display inverters); changeable Unit id 1 for the inverter on the network Discovery mDNS _solaredge-modbus._tcp.local. with a MODBUS_ID TXT key (as Home Assistant reads it), or by address Passphrase protection not_applicable (no credentials) Confidence medium (vendor technical note plus open-source clients)

SetApp inverters: in SetApp, Commissioning > Site Communication > Modbus TCP > Enable; the port menu shows 1502. Home Assistant's page and binsentsu's README say the same page is reachable without the app by flipping the inverter's red P switch briefly (under five seconds) to start its commissioning Wi-Fi access point and opening the address the inverter shows.

Display (LCD) inverters: enter the setup menu as the installation guide describes, then Communication > LAN Conf > Modbus TCP. The display shows the server state: Init, Ready, Connected or Failed (with Disconnected, Gateway Ping Failed or No IP as the reason).

Then connect to the port and read 69 registers from 40000 with unit id 1: the first two must be SunS (0x53756E53).

Factory reset: no procedure found. The power-control registers have their own restore-defaults command (write 1 to 0xF101), which returns them to the country defaults.

Rebinding to a new network: in place, from SetApp or the display. The Modbus setting survives an address change; key the inverter on its serial number (registers 40052-40067) to follow it.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
Property Value Pairing required No Security mode none One client at a time Yes, per SolarEdge's note Confidence medium

There is nothing to pair. The connection drops after 2 minutes without a request; poll at least that often to keep it.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
Standard Modbus TCP: a 7-byte MBAP header (transaction id, protocol id 0, length of what follows, unit id) then the PDU, all big-endian, no CRC.

Function Use 0x03 Read Holding Registers All monitoring data 0x06 Write Single Register Active power limit (0xF001), commit (0xF100), restore defaults (0xF101) 0x10 Write Multiple Registers 32-bit control values (two registers written together)

Errors come back with bit 7 set on the function code and one exception code. Both community integrations report that some firmware stays silent on unsupported registers instead, so a client should treat a timeout on an optional block as "not present".

docs.title: SunSpec register map (zero-based addresses)
docs.text:
Address Block Contents 40000 Marker SunS 40002 Common model (id 1, length 65) Manufacturer, model, firmware version, serial, unit id 40069 Inverter model (101 / 102 / 103, length 50) AC current, voltages, power, frequency, VA, var, PF, lifetime energy, DC current/voltage/power, heat-sink temperature, status, vendor status 40121 Multiple MPPT model 160 (Synergy only) Per-unit DC current, voltage, power, temperature 40121 / 40295 / 40469 Meters 1-3 (common block, then model 201-204) Current, voltage, frequency, power, VA, var, PF, import/export energy, events. +50 or +70 on Synergy inverters

Every reading is an integer multiplied by 10 to the power of a signed scale-factor register next to it (2071 with SF -2 is 20.71). SunSpec 32-bit values are high word first; unsupported registers read 0x8000 (int16), 0xFFFF (uint16) or 0 (energy accumulators).

Inverter status (40107): 1 off, 2 sleeping (night), 3 starting, 4 producing, 5 producing curtailed, 6 shutting down, 7 fault, 8 standby.

docs.title: Control registers (advanced)
docs.text:
From SolarEdge's 2017 power-control note, implemented by both Home Assistant integrations. They act only after AdvancedPwrControlEn (0xF142) is 1 and ReactivePwrConfig (0xF104) is 4 (RRCR), followed by a commit (0xF100). Their 32-bit and float values are sent low word first, unlike SunSpec.

Register Meaning 0xF001 Active power limit, 0-100 % of rated power. Not saved; lost on restart 0xF100 / 0xF101 Commit settings / restore defaults (write 1; read back a result code) 0xE000 Export control mode (bit field) 0xE002 Export site limit, float32 W 0xE004 on StorEdge battery control

scripts/test_solaredge_modbus_tcp_spec.py rebuilds every example frame in the spec from the MBAP rule and decodes the example replies with their scale factors.

See device-specs/devices/solaredge-modbus-tcp.yaml for the full spec.

docs.title: Sony Bravia TVs — IRCC-IP and REST API
docs.text: Status: Documented from Sony's official references and pybravia/Home Assistant; not replayed against hardware here Protocol: WiFi (SSDP + HTTP on port 80; SOAP and JSON-RPC-style POSTs) Manufacturer: Sony Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Bravia TVs from 2013 onward (including the FW-BZ professional displays) expose two local control surfaces on port 80:

  • IRCC-IP — SOAP POSTs to /sony/IRCC, one base64 remote-key code per call. The wire sibling of the infrared remote: every button press is an X_SendIRCC action carrying an IRCCCode.
  • The Bravia REST API ("Scalar Web API") — POSTs to /sony/<service> (system, avContent, appControl, audio, guide, ...) with a JSON-RPC-flavoured body {"method", "params": [...], "id", "version"}. Covers identity, power, volume, input switching, app launching and content listing.

Both surfaces are off until the user enables IP control on the TV, and both require authentication once enabled.

Transport gap: every request here is a POST with a body (SOAP envelope or JSON document) plus an auth header (X-Auth-PSK or the pairing cookie). The reference app today sends GET/POST with an empty body and no per-device headers. A client must implement SOAP with arguments plus a per-device auth header (the IRCC keys) and JSON-body POSTs with the same header (the REST surface) — neither is yet supported by the reference app. The machine-readable spec therefore declares the IRCC keys as transport: "soap" commands and catalogues the REST methods in http_endpoints only.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
SSDP M-SEARCH to 239.255.255.250:1900 with either search target:

  • urn:schemas-sony-com:service:ScalarWebAPI:1 — the REST API. LOCATION points at /sony/webapi/ssdp/dd.xml, whose X_ScalarWebAPI_ServiceList names every REST service and its base URL (resolve ports from here rather than assuming 80).
  • urn:dial-multiscreen-org:service:dial:1 — DIAL second-screen discovery (YouTube/Netflix pairing). The response's Application-URL header is the DIAL REST base; app icons are served under /DIAL/icon/. DIAL is unauthenticated but offers no power/key/volume control.

Identity (serial, MAC, model, user name) is not in either descriptor — fetch it from the REST API once authenticated:

POST /sony/system
{"method": "getSystemInformation", "params": [], "id": 1, "version": "1.0"}

→ serial (primary key), macAddr (secondary), name (display), model.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Enable on the TV first: Settings > Network & Internet > Remote device settings > Control remotely = On (older models: Settings > Network > Home Network Setup > IP Control). Then one of:

  • Pre-shared key (recommended by Home Assistant): set Remote device settings > IP control > Pre-Shared Key; the client sends X-Auth-PSK: <key> on every request, SOAP and REST alike. No handshake, no expiry.
  • PIN pairing: POST actRegister to /sony/accessControl with HTTP Basic auth (empty username, password 0000) to make the TV show a PIN, then repeat with the shown PIN as the Basic-auth password. Success returns Set-Cookie: auth=...; send that cookie on every later request. Note the TV's Set-Cookie spelling is not RFC-compliant — strict cookie jars silently drop it (pybravia issue #1). A TV that refuses to show a new PIN still has the old client registered: remove it via Settings > Network > Remote device settings > Deregister remote device.

Unauthenticated calls on a locked TV answer 401/403; a TV in standby answers control calls with the error string "not power-on".

docs.title: IRCC-IP (remote keys)
docs.text:
POST /sony/IRCC
Content-Type: text/xml; charset=UTF-8
SOAPACTION: "urn:schemas-sony-com:service:IRCC:1#X_SendIRCC"
X-Auth-PSK: <key>

<s:Envelope ...><s:Body>
  <u:X_SendIRCC xmlns:u="urn:schemas-sony-com:service:IRCC:1">
    <IRCCCode>AAAAAQAAAAEAAABgAw==</IRCCCode>   <!-- Home -->
  </u:X_SendIRCC></s:Body></s:Envelope>

Success is a bare 200; there is no per-key feedback. Quirks worth copying from pybravia rather than rediscovering:

  • Case: /sony/IRCC on most models, /sony/ircc on some — the wrong case answers 404; probe and swap.
  • Idle drop: after ~13 idle minutes the first command is silently ignored; send an empty-code wake-up first.
  • Code authority: the TV's own getRemoteControllerInfo REST call returns its exact key table and wins over any static list. Sony's published pro-display table and the widely-copied community table disagree on some keys (Left/Right, Prev).

The spec's commands block carries the full published table — power, navigation, digits 0-9, transport, volume/channel, colour keys, HDMI 1-4 — plus consumer-set codes from pybravia/community sources (PowerOn, PowerOff, Exit, Rewind, Forward, EPG), each labelled by source.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
Service Method Purpose /sony/guide getSupportedApiInfo Per-device inventory of services/methods/versions (authLevel none — call first) /sony/system getSystemInformation Identity: model, serial, macAddr, name /sony/system getPowerStatus / setPowerStatus Power state read/write /sony/system getRemoteControllerInfo This model's IRCC key table /sony/system requestReboot Recovery when the REST service freezes /sony/audio getVolumeInformation Per-target volume/mute (0-100) /sony/audio setAudioVolume / setAudioMute Volume as "N"/"+N"/"-N"; mute needs read-then-invert /sony/avContent getPlayingContentInfo What's on (input or tuner programme; blind inside Android apps) /sony/avContent getCurrentExternalInputsStatus Input list with extInput:hdmi?port=N URIs /sony/avContent setPlayContent Switch input/channel by URI — Bravia's input switching /sony/appControl getApplicationList Installed apps: title, uri, icon /sony/appControl setActiveApp Launch an app by its URI /sony/appControl setTextForm Type into the on-screen keyboard /sony/accessControl actRegister PIN pairing (see Authentication)

Power on (from network standby only): WoL magic packet (needs the TV's Remote Start setting), setPowerStatus {"status": true}, or the IRCC PowerOn code — pybravia tries all three.

Known instability: the REST surface is served by the TV's WebApiCore system app, which freezes on long uptimes. Recovery is a full TV reboot (hold Power on the remote > Restart, or requestReboot) or clearing WebApiCore's data under Settings > Apps.

docs.title: Control surface in the spec
docs.text:
entities declares the remote as button entities in remote-layout order (power, navigation, digits, transport, volume/channel, colour keys, HDMI inputs), each bound to one IRCC soap command. Three sensor entities (Power Status, Now Playing, Volume) bind REST reads via state_endpoint/state_command, and an Application select binds getApplicationList — the sensors and select are declared with their transport gap in their notes and become live once the app can send JSON bodies with auth headers.

A stateful Power switch entity binds turn_on/turn_off to the discrete IRCC codes and toggle to the one key every set carries, with the getPowerStatus read as its state (Spec Evolution P13) — the standby error string not power-on on any other call is that reading saying "standby", not a failure.

Machine-readable spec: device-specs/devices/sony-bravia.yaml

docs.title: SP105E Magic LED Pixel Controller
docs.text: Status: Complete (static analysis — not yet driven against hardware) Protocol: BLE Manufacturer: Sperll-era firmware family; sold under BTF-LIGHTING, ALITOVE, Super Bright LEDs and other brands Manufacturer Status: Unsupported

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The SP105E is a generic Bluetooth SPI pixel ("dream color") controller sold with addressable LED strips under dozens of brand names. It is driven by the Magic-LED app (com.vengean.magicled), and the good news is unusual for this catalogue: the app is fully local — no account, no cloud service, no OTA mechanism, no analytics. The only thing standing between you and permanent local control was the undocumented BLE protocol, which is now recovered in full: command frame, complete opcode map, handshake, status layout, and the 27-IC driver table.

The protocol was recovered by clean-room static analysis of Magic-LED v2.2.1. The byte formats and opcodes the app sends are exact; what still needs a live capture is flagged under Open Questions.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number SP105E (advertised BLE name is exactly SP105E) Chipset Unknown BLE module (HM-10-style serial-port profile; no vendor SDK fingerprints) Radio BLE 4.x Output SPI data for addressable pixel strips Supported LED ICs 27 drivers: SM16703, TM1804, UCS1903, WS2811, WS2801, SK6812 (+RGBW), LPD6803, LPD8806, APA102/APA105, TM1814/TM1914/TM1913, P9813, INK1003, DMX512, P943S/P9411-P9414, TX1812/TX1813, GS8206/GS8208, SK9822 Power DC 5–24 V (per retail listings)

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct Setup AP / advertised name SP105E (exact) Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence medium (from app analysis; not yet run against hardware)

Power the controller, scan for the exact advertised name SP105E, connect, enable notifications on 0xFFE1, run the handshake (below), then query status. There is no account, no pairing PIN and no credential exchange.

Factory reset: there is no documented reset and nothing credential-like to clear — the device bonds to nothing. The opcode table contains a defined-but-never-sent clear command (0x0F) that is the likely reset-to-defaults, but its behaviour is unverified; do not rely on it yet. Whether the strip configuration (IC type, RGB order, pixel count) survives a power cycle is also unknown. The practical remedy for "won't connect" is a power cycle: the controller holds a single BLE connection, and a nearby phone still connected to it will block you.

Rebinding to a new controller: just connect from the new one — nothing ties the device to an owner or network. Disconnect (or forget) the old phone first, since a client that auto-reconnects will hold the single available link.

docs.title: BLE Services
docs.text: UUID Name Description 0000ffe0-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb SP105E Control Service Serial-port profile 0000ffe1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Control Commands (write) + replies (notify)

docs.title: Command frame
docs.text:
Every command is exactly 5 bytes written to 0xFFE1. No length prefix, no checksum.

Offset Length Description 0 1 Header 0x38 (ASCII 8) 1–3 3 Parameters p0..p2 (big-endian where multi-byte); unused slots are filler — the app sends random bytes avoiding 0x38/0x83, 0x00 is fine 4 1 Opcode

docs.title: Handshake
docs.text:
After connecting, send check_device with three arbitrary bytes r0 r1 r2 (none of them 0x38 or 0x83):

38 r0 r1 r2 D5

The device replies within ~5 s with exactly 8 bytes 00 01 02 03 04 05 06 KEY where:

KEY = ((r2 >> 5) & 0x07) | ((r0 << 1) & 0x53) | r1

Only after a correct reply will the vendor app send further commands. This is an obfuscation-grade challenge, not encryption — the formula above is complete.

docs.title: Status reply
docs.text:
get_info returns an 8-byte notification; any 8-byte notification is parsed as this block:

Offset Length Description 0 1 Power (1 = on, 0 = off) 1 1 Current mode (1–200 effect index; static/auto modes' report value unverified) 2 1 Speed (range unverified, commonly 1–31) 3 1 Brightness (range unverified, commonly 1–255) 4 1 IC type index (0–26) 5 1 RGB order index (0–5) 6–7 2 Pixel count, big-endian uint16

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Filler bytes shown as 00.

Command Bytes Description Power toggle 38 00 00 00 AA Toggles output — no discrete on/off exists; read status byte 0 first Get status 38 00 00 00 10 Returns the 8-byte status block Auto cycle 38 00 00 00 06 Cycle through effect modes automatically Jump to mode 38 MM 00 00 2C Dynamic effect 1–200 (wraps 200 → 1); modes are numeric, the app has no names Static red / green / blue 38 00 00 00 12 / 18 / 36 Static presets Static white / warm white 38 00 00 00 3B / 56 Static presets Solid color 38 RR GG BB 1E Custom static RGB Speed up / down 38 00 00 00 03 / 09 Relative steps — no absolute setter Brightness up / down 38 00 00 00 2A / 28 Relative steps — read status for the current value Set pixel count 38 HI LO 00 2D Big-endian uint16 Set RGB order 38 NN 00 00 3C Index 0–5 into [RGB, RBG, GRB, GBR, BRG, BGR] Set IC type 38 NN 00 00 1C Index 0–26 into the IC table (see Hardware)

Defined but never sent by this app version (behaviour unverified): mode up 0x17, mode down 0x05, remote pairing 0x1D, clear 0x0F.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text: Pace commands at one per ~200 ms, retry a failed write once after 200 ms, and allow up to 5 s for the handshake reply — that is what the vendor app does, and the controller is a low-end MCU.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Signal Meaning Local name exactly SP105E This device — use this command set Service 0000ffe0-… present SP105E or an SP107E/SP110E sibling — discriminate by name

The SP107E/SP110E family (spec) shares the 0xFFE0 service but advertises different names and speaks a 4-byte opcode set with no 0x38 header.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
• Speed/brightness accepted ranges (step to the limits and read status back).
  • Whether IC type / RGB order / pixel count persist across power cycles.
  • Behaviour of the four never-sent opcodes — clear (0x0F) is the probable factory reset.
  • Whether device→app frames carry an 0x83 header (inferred from the app's filler avoidance; only 8-byte replies are actually parsed).
  • What the status mode byte reports while a static or auto mode is active.

docs.text:

  • [ ] HCI snoop of connect + command pass (pending)

docs.title: SPOTLED LED Panels
docs.text: Status: Minimally verified, plus official-app multi-frame capture Protocol: BLE (legacy FF20 protocol; reported OTA and PIXELY extensions) Manufacturer: Host No.4 Technology (Chengdu) Co., Ltd. / generic OEM Manufacturer Status: Unsupported

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SPOTLED drives full-colour and monochrome LED matrix hats, badges, backpack skins, chest panels and flexible signs under many reseller names. It includes the Lunchbox / LEDs 2 RAVE 4 Dream Skin 2.0 and early 3.0. Recent DreamPanel v3 boards instead use iLEDColor, an incompatible protocol.

SPOTLED 1.9.4 (2023) is the last release on Android and iOS. Local BLE control does not depend on its account or cloud. PIXELY GLOW is a reseller-suggested alternative; its reported v2/v3 extensions are not interchangeable with the capture-proven legacy protocol below.

docs.title: Discovery and pairing
docs.text:
Known name prefixes are LBXDRMSKIN_LED_ and SpotLED_. FF20 is useful when advertised but can be absent from short advertisements. One tested panel also advertised 00001812-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb and company 0x05D6; do not match every HID-over-GATT device on 0x1812. Confirm FF20/FF21/FF22 after connecting.

Pairing is not required, but it is not true that pairing never happens:

  • Bondless community clients work without a PIN or persistent bond.
  • The official app initiates legacy Just Works pairing.
  • The captured panel selects No Bonding, no MITM and no LTK distribution; the phone then enables encryption for that connection.

This is transient, unauthenticated pairing—not a durable owner credential. Close the old central before reconnecting; power-cycle only for connection recovery, not as a claimed factory wipe.

docs.title: Bootstrap
docs.text:
1. Connect and negotiate MTU; discover FF21/FF22 under FF20.
  2. Enable FF21 notifications through the GATT client. If writing the CCCD directly, discover it and use the standard 01 00, not bytes written to FF21 itself.
  3. Send Version 04 10 00 00, DisplayInfo 04 12 00 00 and BufferSize 04 14 00 00, awaiting response types 17, 19 and 21.
  4. Optionally query animation/text capability with 04 1a 00 00 (response 27).

The official app's fuller order is version → display → capability → playlist/object queries → receive capacity. The three queries above are sufficient for this documented upload path. Notifications are not ATT read-back responses.

docs.title: Response layouts
docs.text:
Query responses 17, 19, 21 and 27 begin [length][type][serial_be16][status], with payload from byte 5 and success status zero.

Response Full bytes Fields after the common query header Version (17) 15 hardware type u16 BE, hardware version u32 BE, firmware version u32 BE DisplayInfo (19) 13 width u16 BE, height u16 BE, colour type u8, advertised frames u8, brightness u8, font count u8 BufferSize (21) 9 receive capacity u32 BE Animation/text capability (27) 9 animation frame capacity u16 BE, character capacity u16 BE

Newer capability responses may append a length-gated u32 storage size at byte 9; that extension is reported, not present in the captured base response.

Transfer replies use two other layouts. Captured type-2 start and type-4 finish acknowledgements are seven bytes: [length][type][serial_be16][status][command_type_be16]. Require status zero and matching serial and command type. ContinueSending type 255 instead is ten bytes: [length][type][serial_be16][command_type_be16][resume_offset_be32]. It has no status byte; match its response type, serial and command type, then use the offset at byte 6 rather than applying either status-bearing layout. PauseSending type 254 is separate and was not captured.

Newer DisplayInfo responses may append a length-gated light-state byte. The tested geometry was 96×16, colour type 255, advertised frame count 20, brightness 100 and receive capacity 7280 bytes; none is a universal constant.

Colour types recovered statically are 16 = 1-bit mono, 128 = RGB332, 238 = RGB565 and 255 = RGB888. Type 49 selects the older RGB888 lattice record 6. Only RGB888/type-96 is capture-confirmed.

docs.title: BLE services
docs.text:
UUID Role Properties / confidence 0000ff20-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Legacy display service Confirmed 0000ff21-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Commands/responses Write without response, notify; confirmed 0000ff22-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb Bulk display data Write without response; confirmed 0000ff10-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb OTA service Reported, not exercised 0000ff11-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb OTA instructions Write/notify; reported 0000ff12-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb OTA data Write/notify; reported

Legacy FF21 frames are [u8 length][u8 command_id][u16_be serial] [u16_be command_type][u32_be command_length]. Fixed queries use only the first four bytes. The command channel has no checksum; do not add another framing layer. Vendor serial counters wrap at 255 despite wider wire fields.

docs.title: Data records and checksum
docs.text:
FF22 legacy payloads have a 15-byte header: big-endian header length 15, command 0x8004, serial, content length and checksum. Records follow as [u32_be length][u16_be type][fields][checksum].

Type Meaning 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 Colour / character / character string / word stock 6 / 7 / 8 / 9 Lattice frame / time / effect / speed 10 / 11 / 13 Number bar / animation / font glyph 14 Brightness, 0–100 15 Screen mode (value + two padding bytes): normal, upside-down, mirror, both 96 Dynamic colour frame: width, height, depth, bitmap

Effects are 0 none, 1 up, 2 down, 3 left, 4 right, 5 stack, 6 expand, 7 laser. The checksum sums the covered bytes; if the sum exceeds 0xff, negate with (~sum)+1 and keep the low byte. A smaller sum is emitted unchanged.

docs.title: Multi-frame animation container
docs.text:
The captured animation is not three bare frame records. Its record order is:

  1. FrameAnimation, 9 bytes: length, type 11, u16 BE frame count, checksum.
  2. That many DynamicColorFrame records. Each has length, type 96, u16 BE width and height, u8 depth, the bitmap and checksum. RGB888 pixels are R,G,B per pixel, left to right then top to bottom. Record length is 12 + width * height * (depth / 8); a 96×16 RGB888 frame is 4620 bytes.
  3. Time, 10 bytes: length, type 7, u8 time type, u16 BE milliseconds, checksum. The capture uses type 0 and 200 ms.
  4. SpecialEffects, 8 bytes: length, type 8, one effect byte, checksum.

Thus three 96×16 frames have 9 + 3 * 4620 + 10 + 8 = 13887 bytes of records; the separate 15-byte data header brings the payload to 13902 bytes. The spec's synthetic_three_frame_vector uses solid red, green and blue frames and has SHA-256 b5ea06e26a8327c98d799fd9c5df1d7587ec828b006010e9010fd61e0f53d5d6. scripts/test_spotled_led_panel.py builds and parses that complete payload, including every checksum and the 7280-byte receive-window split.

docs.title: Upload flow control
docs.text:
1. Send SendingDataStart and require type 2 with status zero and matching serial and command type.
  2. Serialize the complete payload once, then slice it into raw writes no larger than MTU − 3. Do not add a length or checksum to each ATT chunk.
  3. Pace writes and respond to the device. The official app chose 182-byte writes after negotiating MTU 512; negotiated MTU alone does not select the application's chunk size.
  4. ContinueSending type 255 carries the command type at bytes 4–5 and the offset to resume from at bytes 6–9. Use that offset, not the client's cursor, and do not apply either status-bearing response layout.
  5. Send SendingDataFinish and require type 4 with status zero and matching serial and command type, not type 2. PauseSending type 254 alone does not diagnose MTU.

The official capture paused after exactly 7280 data bytes and resumed both 13902-byte three-frame transfers successfully.

docs.title: What the new capture proves
docs.text:
A supplied 2026-11-10 official-app capture contains seven reconstructed data transactions, including font/text records, a one-frame RGB888 image and two three-frame RGB888 animations. All declared lengths and checksums validate and all finish responses are successful. Decoded 96×16 frames match camera images, including RGB channel order. Each RGB888 frame record is 4620 bytes.

This resolves the older invisible-static-upload and three-frame capability questions. Earlier custom-client three/eight-frame attempts failed, so their serialization difference still needs investigation; the advertised 20-frame field is not a proven arbitrary transfer limit. Other geometries, monochrome/RGB332/RGB565, settings writes and factory reset remain open.

docs.title: OTA and PIXELY GLOW boundaries
docs.text:
Static app analysis identifies FF10/FF11/FF12 and this OTA sequence:

  1. Command 80 presents whole-image CRC-16 (poly 0x1021, init zero, MSB-first) and a u24 big-endian image length.
  2. Command 81 obtains the acknowledgement window.
  3. Command 82 streams image blocks on FF12 with per-window ACKs.
  4. Command 83 asks whether the update completed.

OTA command IDs are little-endian 16-bit values. Metadata comes from the vendor API, but no OTA session, image-signature policy, exact-model compatibility or interrupted recovery was captured. Do not replay an image from this documentary sequence alone.

PIXELY GLOW retains the legacy path on the captured panel and includes separate protocol v2/v3 framing and request IDs. Those static extensions are recorded in the YAML under protocol_details.pixely_glow_extensions; they need their own advertisement-gated captures and must not be sent to every SPOTLED unit.

docs.title: Setup, reset and rebinding
docs.text: No account or network provisioning is needed. Scan, connect, subscribe and query. Rebinding is a fresh connection from another controller after closing the old one; no persistent LTK bond was established in the capture. No factory reset is established, and power-cycling is not claimed to erase content.

docs.title: Logitech Squeezebox (SlimProto)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (unverified — from Lyrion/Logitech Media Server docs) Protocol: WiFi (TCP) Manufacturer: Slim Devices / Logitech (server now community-run as Lyrion) Manufacturer Status: Abandoned — hardware line discontinued 2012, cloud shut; server continues as the GPL Lyrion Music Server

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Squeezebox network music players (Classic, Boom, Transporter, Radio, Touch) never needed the vendor cloud: a player connects to a local music server and streams from it. Logitech dropped the hardware in 2012 and later killed mysqueezebox.com, but the server lives on as the community Lyrion Music Server (GPL) — so the hardware keeps working as long as a server runs.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
Two protocols. SlimProto (TCP 3483) is the player↔server control channel: the player connects out, the server pushes strm/audg/grfe and the player answers HELO/STAT; audio is pulled over HTTP from the server (port 9000). The control API — a line CLI on TCP 9090 and the equivalent JSON-RPC over HTTP (POST /jsonrpc.js on port 9000) — is how an app drives playback, addressing a player by its MAC. Discovery is a UDP 3483 broadcast.

See device-specs/devices/squeezebox-slimproto.yaml for the framing, the HELO/ strm fields and the JSON-RPC commands.

docs.title: Synology DiskStation NAS (identify-only)
docs.text: Status: Identify-only (discovery signature from public reverse-engineering; untested — no hardware) Protocol: findhostd (UDP 9999) — Synology Assistant discovery Manufacturer: Synology Inc. Manufacturer Status: Active — recognised and linked to DSM, not driven here

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Synology DiskStation/RackStation NAS units run DSM and are found on the local segment by Synology Assistant and the web-based find.synology.com finder, which talk to the on-device findhostd service over UDP 9999. This app identifies the NAS — shows a NAS pictogram and deep-links to DSM — rather than driving DSM (its web UI and APIs are fully capable and out of scope as home infrastructure).

docs.title: Discovery Summary
docs.text:
• findhostd, UDP 9999 (also 9997/9998). Synology Assistant sends a broadcast query; findhostd answers with a broadcast + a unicast reply.
  • Packet framing begins with an 8-byte magic ending in ASCII SYNO (53 59 4E 4F): plaintext 12 34 56 78 53 59 4E 4F, encrypted 12 34 55 66 53 59 4E 4F. This magic is Synology-specific, so a reply carrying it is an unambiguous identification.
  • Payload after the magic is TLV records carrying MAC, serial, model and hostname. Stable key: MAC/serial. Display: hostname.
  • findhostd answers a solicitation (it does not beacon). The spec ships no probe_hex — the exact valid query TLV is not in our captures, so we do not publish unverified probe bytes; a consumer listens for broadcast replies or sends a valid Assistant query.

Admin: DSM at https://<ip>:5001/ (HTTPS default) or http://<ip>:5000/ (HTTP default). Both are DSM defaults and commonly reconfigured.

docs.title: ThermoPro TP357 / TP358 / TP359 / TP393 Hygrometers
docs.text: Status: Complete (parser-library-derived; connected mode from single-project RE) Protocol: BLE (passive advertisements; connected history on TP357/TP357S) Manufacturer: ThermoPro (Adsmart) Manufacturer Status: Active

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Small battery BLE temperature/humidity sensors broadcasting readings in advertisement manufacturer data — no connection needed for live values. Covers the TP35x/TP39x family: TP357, TP357S, TP358, TP358S, TP359, TP393, TP397. TempSpike BBQ probes (TP96x/TP97x) are a different family — see spec device-specs/devices/thermopro-tempspike-bbq.yaml. The TP357S additionally has a connected GATT history mode documented by pytp357s; the original TP357 has a different one (pasky/tp357).

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Property Value Model Number TP357(S), TP358(S), TP359, TP393, TP397 Radio BLE (legacy advertising, connectable) Advertised name TP357 (2142) style — model + last two MAC bytes in hex Battery 1× AAA (TP357), ~6 months

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required No Method ble_direct (passive scan) Setup AP / advertised name TP35* / TP39* Passphrase protection not_applicable Confidence high for passive decode (capture-pinned parser), medium for connected mode

Factory reset: none documented and none needed — no credentials or bindings on the device. Note a battery pull appears to clear the stored history buffer (pasky/tp357).

Rebinding: in place. Broadcast-only for live data; the connected history mode requires no pairing, just a per-session datetime-sync write (TP357S).

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text: Advertisement quirk: like Inkbird's IBS-TH, there is no real company ID — byte 1 of the temperature sits in the company-ID high byte, so every reading surfaces under a different "manufacturer id" (clusters like 0xF1C2, 0xEEC2). Match on the advertised name, never on a company id.

docs.title: Manufacturer data (6 bytes; 7 on TP357S)
docs.text:
Offset Length Description 0 1 Per-unit prefix (0xC2 common, 0x82 seen) 1 2 Temperature, s16 LE, /10 °C (f1 00 → 24.1 °C) 3 1 Humidity, uint8 % 4 1 Battery, low 2 bits: 0→1 %, 1→50 %, 2→100 % 5 1-2 0x2C (6-byte models); 2-byte tail 0b 01 on TP357S

FF FF FF in the temp/humidity bytes is an invalid-reading sentinel — drop the packet. Example frame 82 f1 00 1d 02 2c → 24.1 °C, 29 %, battery full.

docs.title: BLE Services (TP357S connected mode)
docs.text:
UUID Name Description 00010203-0405-0607-0809-0a0b0c0d1910 Data service Fixed across units; Nordic DFU 0xFE59 also present ...2b11 Command write 0xa5 datetime sync (required each connection), then 0xcccc-framed history commands ...2b10 Response notify Live 0xc2 frames + streamed history ending in 66 66

Session: enable notify → write a5 YY MM DD HH MM SS DOW CS (CS = sum & 0xFF) → device replies with a live c2 reading then a5 01 13 5a → send the three history commands (~200 ms apart; third carries the wanted record count as u16 LE) → reassemble notifications between cc cc and 66 66 → records are temp×10 s16 LE + humidity triplets, most-recent-first, 1-minute steps. Counts above 28800 (~20 days) are silently ignored — that is presumably the buffer. The original (non-S) TP357 instead uses opcodes 0xa6/0xa7/0xa8 (year/week/day) — a different protocol, see pasky/tp357.

docs.title: TiVo Network Remote (DVRs and Minis)
docs.text: Status: Spec Available (unverified) Protocol: LAN (TCP 31339, ASCII lines) Manufacturer: TiVo (Xperi) Manufacturer Status: Unsupported — hardware sales ended 1 October 2025

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: TiVo stopped selling DVRs on 1 October 2025, leaving a large fleet of Series 3, Premiere, Roamio, Bolt and Edge boxes and Minis. Each one has a local remote socket that needs no account: with Network Remote Control enabled it takes plain-text commands on TCP 31339 that press remote buttons, jump to screens and tune channels, and it reports the channel back as text.

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Property Value Setup required Yes — enable Network Remote Control (off by default) Method device_ui Discovery mDNS _tivo-remote._tcp (only while enabled); legacy TiVoConnect beacon on UDP/TCP 2190 Passphrase protection not_applicable — the socket has no authentication Confidence medium

Enabling: TiVo Central, Messages & Settings, Settings, then Remote, CableCARD & Devices, then Network Remote Control, Enabled. On Virgin Media boxes: Help & Settings, Settings, Devices.

Factory reset: Help, then Restart or Reset — never needed for this protocol, and it turns the setting back off.

docs.title: Protocol Summary
docs.text:
One command per line, CR-terminated. One client at a time: connect, act, disconnect. Pause 100–200 ms between commands.

Command Meaning IRCODE <key> Press a remote button (UP, SELECT, TIVO, PLAY, NUM0…) KEYBOARD <key> Type a key (Premiere and later; TiVo publishes no minimum software) TELEPORT TIVO\|LIVETV\|GUIDE\|NOWPLAYING Jump to a screen SETCH <n> / SETCH <major> <minor> Tune (must be on Live TV) FORCECH <n> Tune, cancelling a recording if needed Reply Meaning CH_STATUS 0702 LOCAL Current channel; sent on connect (whether later changes are pushed is undocumented) CH_FAILED NO_LIVE Not on Live TV; also RECORDING, MISSING_CHANNEL, MALFORMED_CHANNEL, INVALID_CHANNEL LIVETV_READY, INVALID_COMMAND, COMMAND_TIMEOUT Informational; COMMAND_TIMEOUT is harmless

TiVo's own protocol PDF is gone from tivo.com (a 2008 edition survives in the Internet Archive, unread here); the facts come from the openHAB binding and McBrine's Network Remote, which agree. Whether a Mini accepts SETCH is unknown.

See device-specs/devices/tivo-network-remote.yaml for the full spec.

docs.title: TP-Link Kasa Smart Plug
docs.text: Status: Verified on legacy Kasa hardware; bulb, plug and power-strip switching manually confirmed Protocol: WiFi (JSON over TCP/UDP port 9999, XOR-autokey cipher) Manufacturer: TP-Link Manufacturer Status: Active (company alive; the local protocol is what's endangered)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Kasa-era TP-Link smart plugs — HS100 (switching) and HS110 (switching + energy monitoring), plus the same-protocol HS103/HS105 and KP105/KP115 — speak a plaintext local protocol on TCP port 9999: JSON commands wrapped in a trivial XOR "autokey" cipher, with no authentication. softScheck reverse-engineered it in 2016, and python-kasa — which backs Home Assistant's tplink integration — has implemented it ever since.

Control is entirely LAN-local: block the plug from the internet at the router and everything here still works.

Live discovery and get_sysinfo were exercised in August 2026 across KP200, HS210, HS300, KL430 and EP40 hardware. On 2026-11-08 a maintainer manually confirmed normal switching and state readback for a Kasa bulb, a single-outlet plug and a child outlet on a power strip. KL430 light-strip commands were verified separately. Provisioning, energy readings, scheduling and cloud operations are not covered by that manual confirmation.

The local protocol is being retired

TP-Link the company is alive, so this is manufacturer_status: active; what is endangered is the protocol. HS100 hardware v4 on firmware 1.1.0 (~2020) closed port 9999, and newer hardware (EP25, KP125M, the whole Tapo line) moved to the encrypted KLAP/AES protocol with cloud-tied credentials — out of scope here. Keep a working unit offline from vendor firmware updates to preserve the API.

No authentication on a mains relay

The relay is mains-rated (13–16 A depending on region) and the protocol has no authentication of any kind, so anything on the LAN can toggle the load. Segment the device accordingly.

docs.title: The cipher (XOR autokey)
docs.text:
Every payload — control and discovery alike — is obfuscated with a running XOR:

  • Encrypt: start key = 0xAB; for each plaintext byte p, emit c = key XOR p, then set key = c.
  • Decrypt: start key = 0xAB; for each ciphertext byte c, emit p = key XOR c, then set key = c.

So after the first byte the key is the previous ciphertext byte. This is obfuscation, not security — there is no secret. Reproducible test vectors (hex) live in the machine-readable spec and are asserted by scripts/test_kasa_spec.py:

Plaintext Ciphertext 00 00 00 ab ab ab 01 02 03 aa a8 ab {"system":{"get_sysinfo":null}} d0f281f88bff9af7d5ef94b6d1b4c09fec95e68fe187e8caf09eeb87eb96eb

docs.title: Framing
docs.text: Transport Framing TCP (control) 4-byte big-endian length prefix (encrypted-payload length, prefix excluded) + XOR-encrypted JSON. Replies use the same framing. UDP (discovery) A single datagram of the XOR-encrypted JSON, no length prefix.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text: Broadcast the XOR-encoded {"system":{"get_sysinfo":null}} to 255.255.255.255:9999. Every Kasa-protocol device on the segment answers with a unicast datagram carrying its full get_sysinfo — alias, model, feature, deviceId, mac, rssi and relay_state. deviceId is the stable identity; alias is the user-facing name; model and feature are what a client matches to decide which entities this unit actually has (see Energy monitoring).

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: JSON Meaning {"system":{"get_sysinfo":null}} Device info + current relay_state (0/1). The state poll and the discovery probe. {"system":{"set_relay_state":{"state":1}}} Turn the outlet on. {"system":{"set_relay_state":{"state":0}}} Turn the outlet off. {"emeter":{"get_realtime":null}} Metering models only (HS110, KP115) — instantaneous voltage/current/power/total. The state poll for the energy sensors below. netif.set_stainfo Provisioning: join the plug to a Wi-Fi network.

docs.title: Energy monitoring (HS110, KP115)
docs.text:
The meter is modelled as four sensor entities in the machine-readable spec — Voltage (V), Current (A), Power (W) and Total Consumption (kWh) — all polled with emeter.get_realtime. The reply nests under {"emeter":{"get_realtime":{...}}}.

Only some of the family has the hardware. The HS110 and KP115 meter; the HS100/HS103/HS105/KP105 do not, and answer this command with an error rather than a reading. The four sensors are scoped in the spec with variants: ["HS110", "KP115"], matched against the device.variants table, so a client can drop them instead of drawing four tiles that are permanently unavailable. Match get_sysinfo's model against a variant's model_prefix as a prefix — the reply is "HS110(US)", region suffix and all. Better still, get_sysinfo answers a colon-separated feature list: "ENE" in it means this unit has the meter, which is the check python-kasa's has_emeter makes and the one that stays correct when a new model ships.

And the field names vary by hardware revision. Current firmware reports voltage/current/power/total as floats already in V/A/W/kWh; HS110 hardware v1 reports voltage_mv/current_ma/power_mw/total_wh in milli-units instead. This is a rename, not just a scaling — on hw v1 the modern keys are absent, so a client resolving the primary path finds nothing at all. Each sensor therefore carries a state_mapping.value_fallback naming the legacy path and the factor (0.001) that brings it back to the entity's unit: try the primary, fall back only when that key is missing. That is what python-kasa's EmeterStatus does, and both code paths exist in the vendor app (see the spec's evidence block).

docs.title: Setup (adopting a reset plug)
docs.text:
A factory-fresh or reset plug hosts an open AP named TP-LINK_Smart Plug_XXXX and speaks the same port-9999 protocol on it. Joining it to the home Wi-Fi needs no cloud account: send netif.set_stainfo with the target SSID, passphrase and key type over the local protocol (this is what kasa wifi join does in python-kasa). The passphrase rides inside the same XOR obfuscation, so it is effectively plaintext — the open setup AP is the only transport protection. Not replayed against hardware here; full steps live in device.setup in the machine-readable spec.

Factory reset: with the plug powered, press and hold its physical button for about 5 seconds until the LED blinks rapidly. This clears Wi-Fi credentials, the alias and any schedules, returning the plug to its setup-AP state. A short press just toggles the relay.

docs.title: Power strips
docs.text: Power strips (HS300 / KP200 / KP303 / EP40) report a children array in get_sysinfo and address each outlet by wrapping a command in {"context":{"child_ids":["<deviceId>0N"]}}. This spec handles them: the instanced "Outlets" switch enumerates the children, and relay_on_child / relay_off_child scope the write. A single-relay plug reports no children, so the plain "Outlet" switch covers it.

docs.title: Keeping it off the internet
docs.text:
The local protocol needs no cloud; the reason to cut the cloud off is that a firmware update is how HS100 hardware v4 lost port 9999. The spec's cloud.egress lists what the device phones and what blocking each name costs:

  • Update images come from download.tplinkcloud.com over plain HTTP — block it to stop updates while keeping off-LAN control through the app.
  • The cloud link is n-devs.tplinkcloud.com on current firmware (devs.tplinkcloud.com, TCP 50443, on 2016-era units). Ask the unit which: {"cnCloud":{"get_info":null}} returns it as server (bulbs: the smartlife.iot.common.cloud module). Some 2023 builds rejoin Wi-Fi every ten minutes when this is blocked; unbind first, while it is still online — {"cnCloud":{"unbind":null}} fails with err_code -24 once the cloud is unreachable. That stopped the loop for one owner, though not on every unit.
  • Time comes from pool.ntp.org and time.nist.gov. Redirect them to a LAN NTP server rather than blocking them: schedules run on the device's clock, which has no battery backup.

Ready-made lists for Pi-hole, AdGuard Home, dnsmasq, Unbound, RouterOS and RPZ, and the full walk-through, are in Blocking Vendor Updates and the Cloud.
