The catalogue has grown well past those counts since, and some candidates below have been specced in the meantime — iRobot Roomba and the June Oven both ship specs now, and each section says so inline. Before spending money on a candidate here, check device-specs/devices/ and targets/ for it first. The reasoning about why a device is worth doing survives; the "nobody has done this" half does not age.

Newer survey: Missing Devices (2026-09)

A fresh gap survey from 2026-09-23 was checked against the full catalogue of 203 specs. It lists what on this page has since been done, carries the rest forward, and adds about 200 candidates this page never looked at, each verified against the repo and against its sources. Start there when you are choosing what to spec next. Use this page for its hardware prices and its reasoning about filters.

This page answers two questions at once:

  1. What should we document next? Devices whose vendor cloud is dead or dying, where enough public protocol work already exists to write a clean-room spec.
  2. What does the verification hardware cost? Every candidate carries a real listing price, so a spec can be confirmed against hardware instead of staying a paper exercise.

Prices are snapshots, not quotes

All prices are eBay US listings observed on 2026-07-30, sorted by lowest total price (item + shipping). They move constantly, and the cheapest listing is often "parts only" — the notes say which. Re-check before buying. Amazon was not surveyed programmatically (it returns 503 to automated fetches); Amazon prices for the new-hardware items in Tier 3 and Tier 6 are generally within a few dollars of the eBay figures.

Clean-room discipline still applies

A public reverse-engineering write-up is a reference, not a licence to copy. Follow Clean-room Rules: cite the source, re-derive the protocol, and never lift code or vendor assets into a spec.

docs.title: Vendor-risk classification (A / B / C)
docs.text:
The device tiers below sort candidates by technical fit. This axis is orthogonal: it sorts by how urgently the vendor relationship is failing the owner, which is what decides whether a spec is a rescue or just a nicety.

  • A — already subscription-gated or abandoned. The cloud is off, the app is paywalled, or the company is in bankruptcy. Owners are hurting now. A spec is a rescue.
  • B — likely to land in A. Going-concern warnings, a parent company folding related lines, a subscription on new models that will spread to old, or a track record of doing exactly this. Documenting ahead of the shutdown means the spec exists before owners need it.
  • C — unlikely to be abandoned, but still worthwhile purely for local-first independence: one fewer cloud account, one fewer app, one less thing that phones home. Lower urgency, real value.

Each candidate below carries an [A], [B] or [C] tag. The at-risk device groups section near the end is organised entirely around this axis and collects the groups surfaced specifically by scanning for subscription and shutdown risk.

docs.title: What this repo should actually spend effort on
docs.text:
Three filters decide whether a candidate is our work, applied in order. All three must pass — the third is the one that usually settles it:

  1. Can it be saved locally at all? If the device only ever talks to the vendor cloud with no LAN path (Cosori/VeSync, and — on the evidence — June), then no amount of RE gives local control; you'd be building a self-hosted cloud replacement. Those are parked in No local path, not worked now.
  2. Does the user's phone speak to the device's own radio, or must they add hardware? This is the one that matters most for the sibling Flutter BLE app. Many "local" solutions are really an ESP32 bridge wired or soldered into the device — that's a different product, not a phone-native protocol. We want specs a phone app can implement to talk to the device's existing radio directly, the same path the vendor app uses. Anything whose only route is "add an ESP32" (Neato's serial pads, a keypad-only desk's pass-through dongle) fails this filter, however cheap.
  3. Is the protocol written down cleanly anywhere, or does it only live inside client code? A maintained HA/ESPHome integration is a client, not a spec — but if it already documents the wire format well (Roomba via dorita980, RuuviTag, TTLock), re-specifying adds little. The differentiated work is protocols that exist only as source code or scattered forum posts: those are where a clean, implementation-independent spec is the thing nobody else has written.

The sweet spot is cheap + phone-direct + protocol-unwritten, on either radio — a short list of undocumented BLE gadgets (the Qingping frame, blind motors, Bluetooth-equipped desks) and LAN-controllable Wi-Fi devices (WiZ lights, AVRs) the phone can drive with no added hardware. Expensive, cloud-only, or ESP-bridge-only candidates are kept but clearly marked as heavier or parked.

docs.title: Tier 1 — Orphaned by the vendor (highest mission fit)
docs.text:
Every device in this tier is risk class [A] — orphaned or subscription-gated by definition; that is what "Tier 1" means. The A/B/C tags matter more in the lower tiers and in the at-risk groups section, where fit and urgency diverge.

These are the devices the project exists for: hardware that still works but whose cloud has been switched off.

docs.title: 1. Spotify Car Thing
docs.text:
Transport USB (serial/ADB), Bluetooth Status Bricked by vendor — killed 2024-12-09; Spotify issued refunds Public RE err4o4/spotify-car-thing-reverse-engineering, iFixit custom-firmware guide, Nocturne replacement firmware (2026) Cheap unit $40 used (no cable, auction) — $68 open-box, typical range $54–$75

The bootloader is unlocked-able and the community already has feature-parity firmware. What is missing is a written protocol/interface spec: the USB control surface, the display bus, and the dial/button event encoding. Good first Tier-1 target because the device is inert without documentation.

docs.title: 2. Neato Botvac Connected (D3/D4/D5/D6/D7)
docs.text:
Transport Wi-Fi (cloud, now dead) + internal UART serial console Status Cloud shut down 2025 by Vorwerk; app control and scheduling gone Public RE pybotvac (Nucleo cloud API, RE by Lars Brillert), RobertSundling/neato-botvac, neato-connected ESP32-on-UART approach Cheap unit $99.99 used complete D5. Parts/spares $3–$15

The interesting half is the local serial command set on the robot's RX/TX pads — that is what survives the cloud shutdown, and it is only documented as scattered forum posts. Vorwerk explicitly refused to release the cloud API, so this is the canonical "documentation is the only rescue" case. Most expensive Tier-1 buy; worth one unit.

docs.title: 3. Logitech Harmony Hub
docs.text:
Transport Wi-Fi LAN — local WebSocket API + (restored) XMPP Status Product line discontinued; local API was removed in firmware 4.15.206, then restored in 4.15.250 as officially-unsupported Public RE JordanMartin/harmonyhub-api, maddox/harmony-api Cheap unit $9.99 used hub-only — $10–$18 is the normal band

Cheapest Tier-1 hardware by a wide margin, and the precedent matters: a vendor removed a local API and public pressure got it back. A spec pins that down so the next firmware change cannot quietly take it away again. Slots naturally into the existing WiFi Devices cluster alongside roku-ecp and hue-bridge.

docs.title: 4. Bose SoundTouch
docs.text:
Transport Wi-Fi LAN — local HTTP/XML API, plus Bluetooth/AirPlay Status Cloud ended 2026-05-06 (extended from 2026-02-18). Bose shipped a final offline-capable app and published the API Public reference Bose SoundTouch end-of-life page, SoundTouchPlus HA component Cheap unit $29.97–$50 parts-only SoundTouch 10; ~$60–$70 for a tested working unit

Note this one needs documentation, not reverse engineering — Bose released the specs. That makes it the fastest spec on this page to write and the easiest to verify, and it is a useful contrast case in the docs: the vendor did the right thing on the way out.

docs.title: 5. Insteon Hub 2245-222
docs.text:
Transport Wi-Fi/Ethernet LAN HTTP API; Insteon powerline + 915 MHz dual-mesh Status Cloud died abruptly in 2022 when SmartLabs folded (later revived by a user group) Public reference Insteon's own published developer guides; pyinsteon, insteon-terminal Cheap unit $14.88–$22 used hub; $9.99 parts-only

Two protocol layers worth separate specs: the hub's local HTTP interface and the underlying Insteon message format over the PLM serial link. The dual-band powerline mesh is a transport the repo has no coverage of at all.

docs.title: 6. Nest Learning Thermostat, 1st & 2nd generation
docs.text:
Transport Wi-Fi (Weave/TLS, port 9243) Status Support ended October 2025 after 14 years Public RE Fragmentary. No complete public local protocol map located Cheap unit ~$22.95 tested working; $15.90 unit-only, $10 parts-only

Listed for reach, not for readiness — a very large installed base went dark at once. Be honest about the state: the local Weave interface is authenticated and not publicly mapped, so this is a research target, not a spec that can be drafted from existing sources. Buy one only if someone intends to do the capture work.

docs.title: Tier 2 — Cheap BLE sensors that extend families we already cover
docs.text:
Low cost, low risk, and each one broadens an existing spec cluster rather than starting a new one. All risk class [C] — these vendors are fine; the value is local-first sensor reads with no app. (RuuviTag is barely even that: the vendor publishes the format, so it's cooperative rather than a rescue.)

Device Why Public RE Cheap unit Govee H5074 / H5179 Extends the existing govee-h5075-thermo.yaml to the rest of the family Theengs decoder H5074, H5179 $15 + $5 ship; $17.81–$22 typical RuuviTag Vendor publishes its RAWv2 advertisement format — a reference-quality passive-advertisement spec Theengs RuuviTag RAWv2 $27.95 open box; $29.95 new; Pro $64 BLE TPMS sensors Fits the OBD-II / vehicle cluster; passive advertisement decode, no pairing Theengs decoder TPMS support $19.98 for 4 (≈$5/sensor), new Qingping CGG1 / CGDK2 Xiaomi-adjacent; sends both MiBeacon and an undocumented Qingping format — the Qingping format is the gap Theengs / ble_monitor by brand No eBay listings found 2026-07-30; source from AliExpress (~$10–15)

The Qingping second format is the most interesting item in this tier: it is a documented absence — decoders support MiBeacon from these sensors and explicitly do not support the Qingping frames.

docs.title: Tier 3 — Battery, solar and energy (a transport family the repo lacks)
docs.text: The repo had only enphase-envoy in this space at survey time — it now also has enphase-iqbattery-ble and bluetti-power-station — and this is still the best-documented and cheapest-to-buy category surveyed.

docs.title: JK-BMS / JBD (Xiaoxiang) / Daly BMS — BLE + UART
docs.text:
Public RE syssi/esphome-jk-bms, syssi/esphome-jbd-bms, fl4p/batmon-ha, patman15/BMS_BLE-HA Cheap unit JK BMS from $6.35 (4S entry) new; JBD BLE module $12.35–$13 new; Daly BLE/UART module ~$21 new

Cheapest new hardware on this entire page, three vendors share one problem space, and the protocols are already mapped in maintained implementations. Highest specs-per-dollar of anything surveyed. Each vendor deserves its own spec; a shared "BMS BLE patterns" protocol page would mirror the existing obd2-common.md.

docs.title: Victron Instant Readout — BLE advertisement
docs.text:
Public RE keshavdv/victron-ble, felixwatts/victron_ble, Olen/VictronConnect Cheap unit $38.88–$39.10 new Smart Battery Sense

Victron publishes its extra-manufacturer-data layout, and the community decoders fill the rest. Encrypted advertisements with a per-device key — a pattern nothing in the repo currently documents.

docs.title: Renogy BT-1 / BT-2 — BLE-to-Modbus bridge
docs.text:
Public RE cyrils/renogy-bt; also covered by BMS_BLE-HA Cheap unit $19.95 new; $19.99 open box

A BLE wrapper around Modbus registers — worth documenting as a transport pattern, since the same trick shows up across solar and inverter gear.

docs.title: Tier 4 — Locks and actuators
docs.text:
Device Transport Public RE Cheap unit TTLock locks BLE Fusseldieb/ttlock-reverse-engineering — packet framing documented down to CRC8/MAXIM and the 0d 0a tail; ttlock-sdk-js, ha-ttlock-ble Lock bodies from $28.50 (cabinet/NFC); full door locks $34+; G2 gateway $18 Tuya BLE (Fingerbot etc.) BLE redphx/python-tuya-ble, ShonP40/Tuya-BLE, BillyNate/esphome-tuya-ble Fingerbot from $8.99 new

TTLock is the strongest lock candidate: the framing is already published, the lock name encodes the MAC in reverse byte order (a nice discovery signal for the spec's discovery block), and it complements the existing nuki-smart-lock and switchbot-ble specs.

Tuya BLE is a platform, not a device — one spec covering the DP (datapoint) framing and session key exchange would unlock hundreds of cheap devices at once. Best leverage-per-spec on the page. Note the honest catch: the local key normally comes from a one-time cloud enrolment, and that dependency belongs in the spec.

docs.title: Tier 5 — Mobility (extends the existing e-bike/scooter cluster)
docs.text:
Device Transport Public RE Cheap unit Xiaomi M365 / Ninebot BLE serial with register map CamiAlfa/M365-BLE-PROTOCOL (protocol notes + register spreadsheet), m365py, macbury/m365 BLE dashboard board $18.78–$22.99 new — no need to buy a whole scooter to bench-test Votol EM series controllers CAN bus + BLE programming dongle bananu7/votol, Ming2k8-Coder/VotolAIO, Endless Sphere protocol threads $25–$28.72 new (LanDe EM25–EM150S / EM150-2 class)

The M365 dashboard-board trick is the useful find here: the BLE module is sold separately for under $23, so the protocol can be exercised on a bench supply. Votol pairs directly with the existing fardriver-controller.yaml and would give the repo a second CAN-based controller alongside the OBD-II references.

docs.title: Tier 6 — Wi-Fi and BLE commodity gear
docs.text:
Device Transport Public RE Cheap unit Zengge / Magic Home / LEDnetWF Wi-Fi binary + BLE flux_led (Wi-Fi, protocol RE'd from captures), 8none1/zengge_lednetwf (BLE), vikstrous/zengge-lightcontrol, HA led_ble $1.99–$5 new controller TP-Link Kasa Wi-Fi LAN, TCP/9999 XOR-obfuscated JSON python-kasa $6.74 used HS103; ~$1.50/plug in used multipacks Electronic shelf labels (Solum ZBS243) 802.15.4 + BLE OpenEPaperLink — SoC reverse engineered by dmitry.gr, unencrypted Zigbee-like packets ~$4.90/tag (Solum Newton Lite 20-pack, $97.99); 2.2" single $62.50

Zengge is the highest-volume LED family the repo does not cover, and it is the cheapest hardware surveyed — dual-stack (Wi-Fi and BLE) with firmware revisions that shift the framing, which is exactly the kind of variation a written spec is good at capturing. It sits right next to the existing elk-bledom-led-strip and coolledx-led-sign specs.

On the ESL listings: the Solum lots are the OpenEPaperLink-compatible ones. The much cheaper Altierre lots (50 tags for $80.75, ≈$1.62/tag) are a different, unmapped proprietary system — cheap, but they are a research target, not a quick spec.

docs.title: Tier 7 — Kitchen BLE (cheap, but the vendors are still alive)
docs.text:
Documentable and inexpensive; lower mission fit because nothing here is abandoned. Extends inkbird-bbq-thermometer, ibbq-meat-thermo, thermopro-tempspike-bbq and chef-iq-sense. Mostly risk class [C], but Anova (its own section below) is the cautionary tale for the whole tier — a subscription arrived on a "still alive" kitchen vendor, which nudges the rest of this group toward [B] on a long horizon.

Device Public RE Cheap unit Vendor status Weber / iDevices iGrill 2, mini, v3 1mckenna/esp32_iGrill, fransakeson/ESP32_iGrill, pilot1981/weber-igrill-integration-HA $17.99 used iGrill 2 App still updated (v4.9.1, Jan 2025) — not abandoned MEATER / MEATER+ nathanfaber/meaterble $19.99 open-box MEATER+ Active Fellow Stagg EKG+ / EKG Pro tlyakhov/fellow-stagg-ekg-plus, calvinmclean/stagg-ekg-plus, breiflabb/ekg-pro-ble-lib $44 EKG Pro (parts-only); working units higher Active Anova See the dedicated section below — three protocol generations $9.99 used circulator Active, but app is now paywalled for new accounts

The Stagg is the most technically interesting single device here: BLE serial-port service 0x1820 / characteristic 0x2A80, 0xEFDD frame separator, and a magic init sequence the kettle requires before it will talk — a clean worked example for the BLE patterns page.

docs.title: Anova kitchen gear — three protocol generations
docs.text: Anova earns its own section: it is not one device but three distinct protocol families, two of which the vendor documents publicly, and the cheapest hardware on this page that has a first-party protocol reference.

docs.title: Vendor status — the nuance that matters
docs.text:
Date What happened Jul 2024 Anova announced it would cut remote connectivity for the original Bluetooth and Bluetooth+ cookers on 2025-09-28, with a 50%-off trade-up that expired 2024-08-01 2024-08-21 App went subscription: $1.99/mo or $9.99/yr. Accounts created before this date are grandfathered free. Account creation, previously optional, became mandatory 2025-01-16 Anova rescinded the shutdown: "we will continue to support all versions of our products indefinitely"

So Anova is not an abandoned vendor — credit where due, they reversed the shutdown. The reason it still belongs here is the interaction between the grandfather clause and the used market: a $10 circulator bought on eBay today is being paired with a new account, which is not grandfathered. The hardware outlives the entitlement. A local spec is what makes second-hand Anova gear usable without a subscription — which is the same rescue as a dead cloud, arriving by a different route.

docs.title: Generation 1 — original Precision Cooker (2014, "Anova PC"), 800W BT / 900W Wi-Fi
docs.text:
Transport BLE — a single service with a single characteristic carrying both TX and RX Encoding ASCII strings terminated with \r; responses arrive as notifications, possibly chunked across several Vendor docs A2/A3 protocol overview — covers the 800W BT-only and 900W Wi-Fi variants Public RE Aldaviva/SousVide (+ its Communication Protocol wiki, tested against a 2014 PC 1.0), pyanova, jshridha/anovamaster, openHAB binding Cheap unit $9.99 untested 900W · $20.00 working 800W (BIN) · $25.99–$33.49 tested/excellent

The easiest spec on this page to write and verify: line-oriented ASCII over one characteristic, two independent descriptions to cross-check (vendor docs and a community RE with a protocol wiki), and $10–$20 hardware. Note the quirk worth capturing — one characteristic for both directions is unusual enough that naive GATT clients get it wrong.

docs.title: Generation 2 — Nano and Mini (2018+)
docs.text:
Transport BLE — service 0e140000-0af1-4582-a242-773e63054c68, three characteristics: TX, RX, ASYNC (unsolicited status) Encoding [Domain byte][Message type byte][optional protobuf payload], COBS-encoded to strip zero bytes, zero-byte terminator, then chunked for the BLE MTU Vendor docs Nano overview; separate pages for Mini and A2/A3 Cheap unit $14.99 Nano (Wi-Fi+BT) · $25 Nano BT-only · $19.95 Mini AN300-US00 (BIN) · $28 Mini open-box

The most valuable of the three for the repo. COBS framing appears nowhere in device-specs/ today — protobuf does (admore-light-bar, vector-robot) but consistent-overhead byte stuffing does not, and it is a recurring pattern in BLE protocols that need a clean packet delimiter. A separate ASYNC notification channel is also worth documenting as a pattern. First-party UUIDs and encoding means the spec can be written with high confidence and then confirmed against $15 hardware.

Correction, 2026-09-23: the Mini is a different protocol

Only the Nano uses the service, COBS and protobuf framing above. The Mini has its own BLE service (910772a8-a5e7-49a7-bc6d-701e9a783a5c) and sends JSON payloads Base64-encoded, one characteristic per function (vendor docs). That makes two specs, or one family spec with two clearly separate profiles.

docs.title: Generation 3 — Wi-Fi devices and the Precision Oven
docs.text:
Transport WebSocket, real-time messaging Auth Personal access token, generated in the app under More → Developer → Generate Personal Access Token Vendor docs Wi-Fi implementation example — covers both Precision Cookers and Precision Ovens, with an official Python CLI reference implementation Public RE bogd/anova-oven-api (documents the oven API), awgneo/anova-homeassistant (local WebSocket control), andr83/hacs-anova-oven, kmdm/hass_anova_cooker Cheap unit Oven: $50 parts-only · $300–$400 faulty · $783–$850 working/new. Wi-Fi circulator: $25.99

Superseded by the correction below: Gen 3 has no local path, so neither unit is worth buying for a spec. Do the Wi-Fi circulator here, not the oven. The oven is the one genuinely expensive item surveyed, and several 1.0 listings report the same "temperature runaway" fault — poor value as a verification unit when the same WebSocket API can be exercised on a $26 Wi-Fi cooker.

Correction, 2026-09-23: this WebSocket is a cloud endpoint

The Generation 3 WebSocket is served by Anova's cloud (wss://devices.anovaculinary.io, per bogd/anova-oven-api), not by the device on the LAN. That puts Generation 3 in No local path until someone shows a LAN endpoint. The awgneo/anova-homeassistant link in the table above no longer resolves.

Worth flagging honestly: a token minted through the vendor app is a cloud dependency, and here the transport is the cloud as well. The spec should say so plainly and record what happens to an already-issued token if the account lapses — that is the question a subscription-era owner actually needs answered, and it is exactly the kind of thing that goes unrecorded until the answer stops mattering.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Two specs, roughly $35 of hardware:

  1. anova-precision-cooker.yaml — Gen 1 ASCII/BLE, verified on a $20 unit. Fastest to land, two independent references.
  2. anova-precision-cooker-nano.yaml — Gen 2 COBS+protobuf/BLE, verified on a $15 Nano. Brings a new framing pattern into the repo.

Skip Gen 3 entirely, circulator and oven alike: its WebSocket is a cloud endpoint (see the correction above), so no hardware buys an in-scope local spec.

docs.title: At-risk device groups (subscription and abandonment watch)
docs.text: This section is the result of scanning specifically for groups of devices likely to be abandoned or to have a subscription bolted on — the failure modes the project exists to pre-empt. It is organised by the A/B/C axis, not by transport, because here the timing of the vendor's decision is the point. Prices are eBay US, observed 2026-07-30 unless noted.

docs.title: Group A — already abandoned or subscription-gated
docs.text: The urgent ones. Owners are already losing function or paying for what they used to own.

docs.title: iRobot Roomba (900 / 960 / 980 / i / e series)
docs.text:
Risk A — iRobot filed Chapter 11 on 2025-12-15 and is being taken private by Picea Robotics; a March 2025 going-concern warning preceded it Transport Wi-Fi LAN — local command channel, no cloud required Public RE koalazak/dorita980 (900/960/980/i7/e5/690 and more), koalazak/rest980 (local REST wrapper) Cheap unit $32.50 Wi-Fi robot w/ dock · $40–$70 for a tested 980

Done — device-specs/devices/irobot-roomba.yaml

This one was acted on after the survey and the spec ships, including a dated field test of the discovery probe. What is left here is hardware verification of the rest of the command set, not a fresh write-up.

The strongest single A-group find, and the reason it was picked up first. A ~50-million-device installed base whose maker is in bankruptcy, and the local protocol already mapped in a mature, widely-forked library that talks straight to the robot over the LAN. The spec largely wrote itself from dorita980, and $33 hardware verifies it. This is the canonical case the project was built for.

docs.title: Eight Sleep Pod (Pod 2 / Pod 3)
docs.text:
Risk A — core features (Autopilot, temperature scheduling, sleep tracking) were retroactively moved behind a mandatory ~$25/mo subscription; the device also needs the internet to change temperature, so an AWS outage left beds stuck Transport Local network — the community firmware replaces the cloud-facing dac process and talks to the Pod's microcontrollers directly Public RE LiamSnow/opensleep (full open firmware), bobobo1618/ninesleep, throwaway31265/free-sleep, freesleep-notes, ZeroSleep root-access writeup Cheap unit Pod 3 hub $60 parts/repair; working cover+hub sets $579+

Unusually mature liberation ecosystem — there is already complete open firmware, so a spec here is documentation of a solved problem, high-confidence and high-value. The catch is hardware cost: the cover is expensive, and the cheap listings are hub-only. Document from the existing firmware; buy a $60 hub if bench verification is needed.

docs.title: Snoo Smart Sleeper (Happiest Baby)
docs.text:
Risk A — in July 2024 Happiest Baby paywalled features that shipped free (weaning/"sleepytime", car-ride mode) behind $20/mo; buyers before 2024-07-15 grandfathered, so the used market is squarely affected Transport Cloud API + PubNub messaging (not local today) Public RE rado0x54/pysnoo, DanPatten/pysnoo2, swar/homeassistant-snoo-smart-bassinet Cheap unit $399 used bassinet (a $1,695 device new)

Textbook subscription bait-and-switch, and the same grandfather-clause trap as Anova: a used Snoo pairs to a new account that isn't grandfathered. Honesty flag — the public work is all cloud-API RE via PubNub; nobody has a local channel yet. So this is a cloud-protocol spec (how to talk to the Snoo backend without the paywalled app), not a local rescue, and the spec must say so. Lower priority than the local-capable A devices.

docs.title: June Oven (Weber)
docs.text:
Risk A — Weber will shut down all June connected services on 2026-09-22; remote control and the in-oven camera die with the servers. A change.org petition is asking Weber to open-source the app Transport Wi-Fi / cloud-only — the app appears to reach the oven only through Weber's hosted service, with no local LAN control path Public RE Minimal — no complete local protocol map located; the petition exists precisely because owners have no fallback Cheap unit $60 parts-only; working Gen3 units $950

Partly acted on — device-specs/devices/june-oven.yaml

A spec and a target stub exist, recording the cloud-only finding rather than a local protocol; docs/devices/june-oven-lan-recon.md and scripts/june_discover.py cover the recon. The open work is the capture-before-shutdown investigation described below, not a first write-up.

The honest revision: June has no confirmed local path, so it belongs with the no-local-path group — a clean RE likely yields "impersonate the June cloud," not "control the oven on the LAN," and that is a self-hosted-server project, not a spec. Its one genuinely useful, time-boxed action is capturing app↔cloud traffic before 2026-09-22 while the servers still answer — that window does not reopen. Don't buy a $950 oven for it; capture from an owner's unit if one surfaces.

docs.title: Echelon Connect bikes / fitness gear
docs.text:
Risk A — a July 2025 firmware update forced a server connection; offline, resistance and metrics are disabled, and a $40/mo plan is needed for more than basics Transport BLE (the machine's own sensor/resistance channel) Public RE Legally blocked. A working jailbreak won a $20k Fulu Foundation bounty but cannot be released — DMCA §1201. See 404 Media, TechSpot Cheap unit Parts only in this survey; complete bikes not surfaced in the sorted results

Included as a documented non-starter, deliberately. The protocol is understood by at least one developer, but the legal situation makes a public spec a §1201 problem in a way the rest of this page is not — most candidates here rest on freely-published RE, whereas Echelon's is under a bounty NDA. Flag it, watch it, and let a right-to-repair exemption or the older pre-update-firmware BLE profile be the opening before spending effort. This is the clearest example of why the legal note at the top of the page matters.

docs.title: Group B — likely to land in A
docs.text:
Not gated yet, but the signals are there: a subscription on new models that will creep to old, a parent company shedding related lines, or a history of exactly this move.

Device group Why B Public RE Cheap unit Owlet Smart Sock Baby vitals behind an app + cloud (Ayla Networks); FDA history already forced one product change, and vitals-as-a-service is the obvious paywall puco/owlet-api, ryanbdclark/pyowletapi, mbevand/owlet_monitor Base station $10–$18 Nanit / cloud baby cams Live view and history increasingly subscription-tied; no vendor RTSP, so local viewing already needs a proxy gregory-m/nanit (local restream proxy) Varies; not surveyed Furbo / Petcube pet cameras Newer Furbo models require a paid plan just to activate; AI alerts and history already paywalled — the direction of travel is clear Community integrations exist; protocol not fully mapped Not surveyed (new models subscription-locked) Tonal Movement library, training modes and Apple Watch link are subscription-locked today; hardware is inert without it — one bad quarter from an Echelon-style enforcement None public located Not surveyed

Owlet is the actionable one: the Ayla Networks cloud API is well-documented by three independent projects, base stations are $10, and it slots beside the sensor specs the repo already carries. The rest are watch-list — record the signal now so the work is scoped when the paywall lands.

docs.title: Group C — unlikely to be abandoned, but worth it for local-first
docs.text:
These vendors are healthy; the value is purely fewer clouds and fewer apps.

Device group Why still worth it Public RE Cheap unit Wyze Cam (v2 / v3 / Pan) Vendor pulled the official RTSP firmware and pushes cloud/AI plans; local streaming already needs community help mrlt8/docker-wyze-bridge, thingino firmware, openmiko, wyzecam PyPI $4.65–$12 camera TP-Link Kasa Healthy vendor, but a fully local TCP/9999 JSON protocol already exists — trivial spec, zero cloud python-kasa $6.74 (already in Tier 6) Tile trackers Life360 keeps nudging Premium, but basic BLE find still works; a passive-advertisement spec removes the app entirely BLE advertisement decoders Low; not surveyed Zengge / Magic Home LED Active vendor, but local BLE/Wi-Fi control is fully mapped — no reason to route $2 LED controllers through a cloud flux_led (already in Tier 6) $1.99 (already in Tier 6)

Wyze is the standout C: cameras are almost free on the used market, the vendor keeps trimming local features, and there is a deep community firmware base (Thingino, OpenMiko) plus a local Python library. Not abandoned, but the direction is unmistakable and the hardware is disposable-cheap.

docs.title: At-risk groups — buy list
docs.text:
Device Risk Cheapest observed Public RE ready? Wyze Cam v3 / Pan C $4.65 Yes (bridge + firmware) iRobot Roomba 980 A $32.50 Yes (dorita980) Owlet base station B $10.00 Yes (3 projects) Eight Sleep Pod 3 hub A $60.00 (parts) Yes (opensleep) June Oven A $60.00 (parts) No — capture before 2026-09-22 Snoo bassinet A $399.00 Cloud-only RE Echelon bike A — Blocked (DMCA)

Reading this section against the effort filter: Roomba and Wyze are the highest-urgency items here, but their protocols are already mapped and documented — so for us they are link-and-setup-guide, not spec work (see Already liberated elsewhere). Owlet (B) is the cheap pre-emptive pick where a written spec still has value, because the cloud API is only encoded in three scattered projects.

docs.title: Undocumented local BLE (protocol lives only in client code)
docs.text:
This is the sweet spot the effort filter points at: devices that are cheap, driven entirely over local BLE by the phone's own radio (no ESP32, no soldering, no controller swap), and whose protocol has been figured out but only exists inside a client — never written as an implementation-independent spec. Writing that spec is exactly what the Flutter app needs, and none of these need an expensive unit to verify.

All three are risk class [C] on the vendor axis (the makers are fine) but top of the list on the effort axis. The Hardware column is the decider: "phone only" means a phone app talks straight to the device, the same path the vendor app uses.

Device Hardware to add Protocol state Public RE (code-only) Cheap unit Qingping CGG1 / CGDK2 thermo-hygrometer None — phone passively listens to advertisements Undocumented — Theengs/ble_monitor decode the MiBeacon frames but explicitly not the Qingping-format frames these also emit ble_monitor by brand ~$10–14 AliExpress (no eBay listings 2026-07-30) AM43 / A-OK blind & shade motors None — the motor is the BLE peripheral; the phone connects to it directly (homebridge-am43 confirms host-BLE, no ESP) RE'd, but the frame format lives in code, not prose buxtronix/am43 (ESP is optional, for MQTT), homebridge-am43-blinds, openHAB AM43 binding $30 open-box motor; $39 typical Jiecang / Uplift / Desky desks — BT-equipped only None if the desk has the factory BLE receiver (JCP35N-BLT); the vendor app already drives it over BLE. Keypad-only desks need an ESP dongle — out of scope Clean F1 F1 … 7E framing with opcode/len/checksum — documented only in blog posts and sketches SitStand writeup, graiz/sitstand, tzermias/deskctl receiver box $25 open-box

Notes that make these good spec targets, not just good devices:

  • Qingping is a documented hole, not a guess — the decoders tell you exactly which frames they refuse, so the spec has a precise, testable scope. It slots straight beside the existing xiaomi-lywsd03mmc MiBeacon work, and it's the purest phone-direct case on the page: no connection at all, just advertisement decode.
  • AM43 has a one-client-at-a-time quirk (the app and any controller can't both be connected) that belongs in the spec's connection notes — the kind of operational detail that only survives if it's written down.
  • Desks share one BLE profile across many resellers (Uplift, Desky, Assmann, Jiecang OEM) that carry the receiver box, so a single spec covers a whole shelf of hardware — the same leverage the SPOTLED and CoolLEDX specs give the repo. Scope the spec to the BLE receiver, and say plainly that keypad-only desks are an ESP-bridge job we don't cover.

Also phone-direct BLE, but pricier hardware: Acaia / Felicita / Bookoo coffee scales. The protocol is a genuine gap — it lives only in pyacaia and AcaiaArduinoBLE code, the phone talks BLE straight to the scale, and it's a popular niche. The catch is cost: the RE'd scales run $95+ (Bookoo SC-mini $95, Acaia $100+), so it's a good spec for someone who already owns one, not a cheap bench buy.

Recommended first specs: Qingping and AM43 — both are pure phone-direct (no added hardware at all), cheap, and unwritten. The BT-equipped desk is a strong third, scoped to units with the factory receiver.

docs.title: Undocumented local Wi-Fi (LAN-controllable, phone-direct)
docs.text:
The Wi-Fi sibling of the section above, held to the same three filters — the phone reaches the device on the LAN (UDP/TCP/HTTP), no cloud, no added hardware, and the protocol is unwritten. The repo already carries LAN specs of exactly this shape (lifx-z UDP, wemo-devices SOAP, roku-ecp), so these slot in as siblings rather than a new category.

The trap here is filter #1: most "smart Wi-Fi" gear is cloud-only and has no LAN path at all (see No local path). The winners are the few that expose a genuine local API the vendor app itself uses on-network.

Device Local transport Hardware to add Protocol state Public RE Cheap unit WiZ (Philips) lights UDP :38899 JSON, no auth, UDP-broadcast discovery None — phone sends JSON straight to the bulb No official spec — protocol only in pywizlight and blog posts pywizlight, wiz-hack, CLI writeup $7.99 open-box bulb Denon / Marantz AVRs Telnet + an undocumented HTTP API; single connection None — phone talks to the receiver directly Telnet is semi-known; the HTTP API is undocumented (the real gap) HA denonavr, openHAB denonmarantz $15–30 used networked AVR Govee Wi-Fi (LAN-API models) UDP multicast 4001/4002, control :4003 None (must toggle LAN API on in the app) Partly documented — Govee's own "LAN API 101" + govee2mqtt LAN.md wez/govee-lan-hass $9.99 Wi-Fi bulb Ecowitt GW1000/GW1100 weather gateway HTTP /get_livedata_info JSON on the LAN None — phone/HTTP polls the gateway Undocumented — this JSON endpoint isn't in Ecowitt's docs (their published protocol is a separate TCP one) ecowitt_local, gw1000-http $22.99 open-box gateway Daikin Wi-Fi AC (BRP069A/B) HTTP REST on :80, no auth None — phone hits the module directly Older API community-documented; the firmware-2.8+ /dsiot/multireq JSON is under-documented (newest C4x modules are cloud-only — see below) daimik local-API docs, ael-code/daikin-control, pydaikin adapter $130 (or built into the unit) Yamaha AVRs (YNCA) Telnet :50000 text protocol None — phone talks to the receiver Semi-gap — YNCA is less documented than MusicCast's leaked YXC spec mvdwetering/yamaha_ynca $20–40 used networked AVR

Notes:

  • WiZ is the standout — the LAN equivalent of Qingping. Unauthenticated UDP+JSON, $8 hardware, one of the most common budget bulbs sold, and no vendor spec exists. It sits right next to lifx-z and would be one of the fastest, most reusable Wi-Fi specs on the page.
  • Ecowitt is the second cheap standout: a $23 gateway with an undocumented local JSON endpoint, and a whole weather-sensor category the repo doesn't touch. The vendor documents a TCP protocol but not this HTTP one — a precise, testable hole like Qingping.
  • Daikin opens HVAC — a big, high-value category — over a no-auth local HTTP API. Two honest caveats: the newest BRP069C4x modules are cloud-only (parked below), and the standalone adapter is ~$130, so this is best done by someone who already owns a Daikin, not bought to bench.
  • Denon/Marantz and Yamaha YNCA together stake out AV receivers. Scope Denon to its undocumented HTTP API (telnet is semi-covered by vendor PDFs); YNCA is the lighter-documented Yamaha equivalent. Cheap used, just bulky.
  • Govee LAN extends the repo's existing Govee BLE specs (govee-h5075, -h5080, -h6001) to Wi-Fi, but it's only partly a gap since Govee published a LAN primer — worth doing for family completeness, lower novelty.

Already local but already written → link, don't spec: a surprising number of LAN protocols are already cleanly documented, so they go straight to the link registry rather than becoming spec work:

  • Yeelight — TCP :55443 JSON-RPC, but Yeelight published an Inter-Operation Spec.
  • Venstar thermostats — a vendor-published local REST API.
  • Onkyo / Pioneer eISCP — commands come from an official Excel spec (parsed into YAML). Documented.
  • Vizio SmartCast TVs — the community already maintains full API docs (token-paired, port 7345).
  • LG webOS TVs — the local websocket protocol is well-mapped (aiowebostv).
  • PurpleAir — local sensor JSON is community-documented.

These are the WiFi analogue of the Roomba/dorita980 case: real local control, but re-specifying would just duplicate an existing written protocol.

docs.title: No local path (cloud-only architecture)
docs.text:
Parked, deliberately. These devices only ever talk to the vendor cloud — there is no LAN control path to reverse-engineer, so RE yields at best a self-hosted replacement of the vendor's servers, not local control of the device. That is a materially bigger project than a protocol spec, and it is not what we're taking on right now.

Device Why it's here Shutdown / gate June Oven App reaches the oven only through Weber's hosted service; no confirmed local path Services off 2026-09-22 Cosori / VeSync air fryers Control is the VeSync cloud API with cloud token auth; no local network control Vendor active, fully cloud-bound Snoo (cloud-RE only) RE exists but via the Snoo backend + PubNub, not a local channel Paywalled July 2024 Traeger WiFire WiFi path relays through the vendor socket (the BLE-capable grills are the exception) Vendor active Daikin BRP069C4x (newest modules) Unlike the BRP069A/B, the current-gen module is cloud-only — no local API. Buy the older module or a unit with it Vendor active

docs.title: If we ever come back to these
docs.text:
Two lighter-weight ideas were floated and are worth recording — both are future work, not now:

  • Reclaim the domain on shutdown. When a vendor turns off and lets its service domain lapse (June's, say), re-registering it and standing up a minimal look-alike endpoint could let already-configured devices keep working. Depends entirely on the device not pinning TLS certs and on the domain actually dropping — neither guaranteed, and it carries real operational and trust burden.
  • Local DNS redirect. Rather than owning the public domain, point the device at a self-hosted endpoint from the user's own network — e.g. a DNS override on their Home Assistant / Pi-hole box that maps the vendor host to a local replacement server. Per-user setup, but no domain race and no cert-pinning fight if the device tolerates it.

Both need the same prerequisite: capturing the cloud protocol while the servers are still up. For June specifically that means before 2026-09-22. Until we decide to build a replacement server, the only cheap insurance is that capture — everything past it is the heavier lift we're choosing not to start.

docs.title: Already liberated elsewhere (link, don't spec)
docs.text:
Lower priority by design: a maintained tool already gives local control and documents the protocol well enough that a fresh spec would just compete with it — exactly the pywemo situation the README describes. The useful contribution here is a pointer (and maybe a setup guide or video), not a YAML.

Device Use this Local? iRobot Roomba (900/i/e/j) dorita980 / roombapy + HA native Yes (LAN) TP-Link Kasa python-kasa + HA Yes (TCP/9999) Zengge / Magic Home flux_led + HA led_ble Yes JK / JBD / Victron esphome-jk-bms, victron-ble Yes (BLE) Wyze Cam docker-wyze-bridge, thingino Yes Logitech Harmony Hub harmonyhub-api + HA native Yes (WS) Neato Botvac (serial) OpenNeato, botvac-wifi Yes (UART) Eight Sleep Pod opensleep firmware Yes (post-flash) Husqvarna Automower automower-ble Yes (BLE) Yeelight python-yeelight; vendor Inter-Op Spec Yes (TCP :55443) Venstar thermostats vendor local REST API + HA native Yes (HTTP)

Neato is the honest edge case: its protocol isn't cleanly written, but every route (OpenNeato, botvac-wifi) solders an ESP32 onto the robot's serial pads — there is no radio the phone can reach, so it fails the phone-direct filter and stays here rather than graduating to a spec candidate. If a device here turns out to be protocol-unwritten and phone-reachable, that one can graduate up; Neato can't.

docs.title: Considered and deprioritised
docs.text:
Recording these so the same ground is not re-covered.

Device Why not now Sena / Cardo intercoms DFU images are signed and flash extraction needs hardware modification; no usable public protocol map. High effort, low odds. Chamberlain / LiftMaster Security+ 2.0 ratgdo already solves it properly with a wired board, and the rolling-code serial protocol is obfuscated. Document only if we can add something ratgdo has not. Logitech POP buttons Bricked in 2025 with two weeks' notice, but the hardware is a thin bridge-dependent button — little protocol surface to liberate. Broadlink RM4 python-broadlink covers it and eBay results were all accessories; no clean price signal. Low priority. Wink / Lowe's Iris hubs Iris hubs stopped working in 2019, and Wink is the archetypal [A] cautionary tale — a "no monthly fees" hub that imposed a mandatory $5/mo in 2020 with one week's notice, then suffered multi-day outages. But no local protocol documentation surfaced in this survey, so a spec would need ground-up research. Cited in the write-up as why the B watch-list exists more than as a candidate. June Oven Moved to No local path: [A] urgency (2026-09-22 shutdown) but cloud-only, so it's a capture-before-shutdown investigation, not a local spec.

docs.title: Consolidated buy list
docs.text:
Ordered by cost. Every price is the cheapest listing observed on 2026-07-30; "parts" flags a listing sold as non-functional.

Device Cheapest observed Condition Tier Zengge / Magic Home LED controller $1.99 New 6 JK-BMS (4S entry) $6.35 New 3 TP-Link Kasa HS103 $6.74 Used 6 WiZ (Philips) smart bulb $7.99 Open box WiFi gap Tuya Fingerbot $8.99 New 4 Govee Wi-Fi bulb (LAN-API) $9.99 New WiFi gap Qingping CGG1 / CGDK2 ~$10–14 (AliExpress) New BLE gap Denon / Marantz networked AVR $15–30 Used WiFi gap Yamaha AVR (YNCA) $20–40 Used WiFi gap Ecowitt GW1100 weather gateway $22.99 Open box WiFi gap Standing-desk BLE controller $25.00 Open box BLE gap AM43 / A-OK blind motor $30.00 Open box BLE gap Acaia / Bookoo BLE coffee scale $95+ New BLE gap (pricey) Daikin BRP069A/B Wi-Fi adapter $130 (or built-in) New WiFi gap (pricey) Anova Precision Cooker, original BT $9.99 (untested) / $20.00 working Used Anova Logitech Harmony Hub $9.99 Used 1 JBD / Xiaoxiang BLE module $12.35 New 3 Insteon Hub 2245-222 $14.88 Used 1 Anova Precision Cooker Nano $14.99 Used Anova Govee H5074-class thermo-hygrometer $15.00 + ship New 2 Weber iGrill 2 $17.99 Used 7 Xiaomi M365 BLE dashboard board $18.78 New 5 MEATER+ $19.99 Open box 7 Renogy BT-1 $19.95 New 3 BLE TPMS, set of 4 $19.98 New 2 Daly BMS BLE/UART module ~$21 New 3 Nest Learning Thermostat gen 2 $22.95 Used, tested 1 Votol EM controller $25.00 New 5 RuuviTag $27.95 Open box 2 TTLock cabinet/NFC lock $28.50 New 4 Bose SoundTouch 10 $29.97 (parts) / ~$60 working Mixed 1 Victron Smart Battery Sense $38.88 New 3 Spotify Car Thing $40.00 Used 1 Fellow Stagg EKG Pro $44.00 Parts 7 Solum ESL tags (20-pack) $97.99 (~$4.90/tag) New 6 Neato Botvac D5 $99.99 Used, complete 1

A Tier-1-plus-Tier-3 starter basket — Harmony Hub, Insteon Hub, Car Thing, JK-BMS, JBD module, Renogy BT-1, Victron Smart Battery Sense — comes to roughly $160 and covers five protocol families the repo has no spec for.

docs.title: Suggested order of work
docs.text:
Re-ordered against the effort filter — phone-direct + protocol-unwritten first, not raw urgency. Already-liberated urgent devices (Roomba, Wyze, BMS, Zengge) drop off to the link registry; anything whose only route is an added ESP32 (Neato serial, keypad-only desks) is excluded from spec work by the phone-direct filter.

  1. Qingping CGG1 / CGDK2 frame — ~$12, zero added hardware (passive advertisement listen), a precisely-scoped documented hole next to the existing MiBeacon work. The cleanest phone-direct spec on the page.
  2. AM43 / A-OK blind motors — $30, phone talks BLE straight to the motor (confirmed, no ESP); the one-client quirk is worth writing down.
  3. WiZ lights — $8, unauthenticated UDP+JSON on the LAN, no vendor spec, sibling to lifx-z. The Wi-Fi twin of Qingping and just as clean.
  4. Ecowitt GW1100 — $23, an undocumented local JSON endpoint, opens the weather-sensor category. Precise, testable hole.
  5. BT-equipped standing desks — $25 receiver, phone-direct for units with the factory BLE box, one framed profile across many resellers. Scope to the receiver; keypad-only desks are out.
  6. Denon / Marantz (+ Yamaha YNCA) — the AV-receiver category; scope Denon to its undocumented HTTP API, YNCA is the lighter Yamaha equivalent. Cheap used hardware.
  7. Spotify Car Thing — $40, high-profile orphan with no protocol spec anywhere. Not BLE (USB/host), but it liberates the device itself rather than adding hardware, so it passes the spirit of the filter.
  8. Insteon PLM / powerline message format — $15 hub; the hub HTTP layer is phone-reachable and the powerline layer is a transport the repo has zero coverage of.
  9. Anova Gen 1 and Gen 2 — ~$35, vendor-documented, phone-direct BLE; Gen 2 brings COBS framing into the repo.

Higher-value but pricier hardware (do if you already own one): Daikin BRP069A/B local HTTP (HVAC category, ~$130 adapter) and Acaia/Bookoo BLE coffee scales (protocol gap, $95+).

Time-boxed, separate track: capture June Oven cloud traffic before 2026-09-22 if a unit is reachable — the only cheap action on the parked no-local-path group.

Not spec work (link, don't build): point owners of Roomba, Wyze, Kasa, Zengge, BMS, Harmony, Eight Sleep and Automower at the existing tools. Neato belongs here too — its only route is an ESP on the serial pads, so it's a hardware-mod to link to, not a phone-native spec to write. Where you want to add value, record a setup guide or video — the schema's helpful_videos field is built for exactly that.

Time-boxed exception: capture June Oven app/API traffic before its 2026-09-22 shutdown if any owner's unit is reachable — that window does not reopen, unlike everything else here.

Pre-emptive [B] pick: Owlet Smart Sock — $10 hardware, three independent RE projects, documents a vitals cloud API before the obvious paywall lands.

docs.title: Missing Devices — September 2026 Survey
docs.text:
Survey date: 2026-09-23. Every candidate below was checked against the catalogue as it stood that day: 203 validated specs in device-specs/devices/, about 270 unvalidated write-ups in research-notes/, 69 target stubs in targets/, and the drafts in new_devices/.

A dated survey, not a live view

Like Candidate Devices & Hardware Sourcing, this page is a snapshot. Specs land every week. Before starting on anything here, grep device-specs/devices/, research-notes/ and targets/ for it. Vendor status moves too: a shutdown date given here can slip, get reversed (Anova did exactly that), or arrive early.

Progress against this list, and new finds since it was written, are logged week by week in Weekly Device Sweeps. Done so far from Do these next: #1 Instant Pot, #2 AM43, #3 JuiceBox, #5 Sengled, #7 Yummly,

This page answers one question: which locally-controllable devices does the catalogue still lack, and which of them should be written up next? It follows the older candidates survey, which was checked against 69 specs. Much of that list has since been done, and it was organised around seven technical tiers plus watch lists rather than a sweep of every device category. This survey starts again from the full catalogue.

docs.title: 6 BiSecur, #8 LIVISI, #11 AirPort ACP, #12 Philips air purifiers, #15
docs.text: Drobo, #16 Kano wand, #17 TiVo, #18 Hot Wheels id, #19 TRÅDFRI gateway, #22 Insteon Hub, #23 Furby Connect, #24 Nissan Leaf; from the category tables: Orbit B-hyve, the Elgato classic-HTTP family, SolarEdge (as Modbus TCP, not the SetApp web API), Qingping, Eurotronic Comet Blue, Big Ass Fans, RadonEye, Anova, Weber iGrill, Acaia, Furbo (identify-only), Boosted, Lippert OneControl (incomplete) and InMotion; from Graduate these research notes: QardioArm, Insteon Hub, Boosted Boards, Joule, Hestan Cue.

docs.title: How the list was built
docs.text:
1. Sweep. Eleven independent searches, one per angle: orphaned and bricked hardware, subscription-gated hardware, lighting and hubs, climate and outdoor, energy, security, AV, health and wearables, kitchen/maker/robots, mobility, and network gear. One more angle mined the device lists of the open-source local-control ecosystems (Home Assistant local integrations, Theengs, Gadgetbridge, openHAB, Homebridge) for devices whose protocol lives only in that code.
  2. Coverage check. Every candidate was grepped against the repo. Anything a validated spec already covers was dropped, including devices covered by family and platform specs (tuya-generic-device, xiaomi-miio, bthome-v2, ftms-fitness-machine-service, govee-rgbic-light's LAN API, and so on). Candidates with only a research note were kept and marked.
  3. Adversarial fact-check. Each candidate was checked on the web against its cited sources: do they exist, and do they describe this device's protocol? Vendor-status claims (shutdowns, bankruptcies, subscriptions) need a source. Claims resting only on a community project's README say so. Two premises failed outright and are left out: Spinn and Scout Alarm are still trading.
  4. Completeness passes. Two critic rounds asked what was still missing. A final targeted pass covered well-known names the sweep had skipped (Anova, iGrill, Shelly, and the cloud-only orphans in Parked).

The result: 242 devices and families the catalogue does not cover. That is 157 ready to spec from public work, 36 research targets, 30 already documented well elsewhere (link them), 14 with no local path, 4 waiting on a Bluetooth Classic value in the schema, and 1 held back on safety grounds. The 25 research notes worth graduating are listed at the end.

No prices this time. The older page's eBay snapshots are still the best starting point for hardware cost.

docs.title: Reading the tables
docs.text:
• Risk uses the older page's A / B / C vendor-risk classes. A: already abandoned, bricked or subscription-gated. B: likely to become A. C: a healthy vendor, where the value is local-first independence.
  • P1–P5 is priority against the repo's three filters. P5 usually means an A/B device with a genuine local path that the phone reaches directly, whose protocol lives only in client code. A C device whose vendor gates local use behind a cloud login (EcoFlow) can also rate P5. P1 is a nicety.
  • Effort: S is one sitting from public sources. M needs real consolidation or a capture. L is a large message catalogue, encryption, or several protocol generations.
  • Local path ends with phone-direct when the phone talks to the device's own radio or LAN endpoint, the same path the vendor app uses. Needs a host/bridge means a LAN server, a plug-in dongle or an always-on listener, not a soldered ESP32: anything that needs soldering was scored down or parked. Protocol is the state of the public write-up: code-only (lives in a client's source; the most valuable to spec), community-documented, vendor-documented or undocumented.
  • Research target means a local path is likely, but the public RE is too thin to draft a spec without captures. July list marks a device that was already on the older candidates page and still has no spec.

docs.title: Since the July survey
docs.text:
Done since 2026-07-30, and no longer candidates: WiZ, Denon AVR, TTLock, Victron Instant Readout, Renogy BT, JBD / Xiaoxiang BMS, Bose SoundTouch, Logitech Harmony Hub, TP-Link Kasa (tplink-kasa-smart-plug.yaml), Magic Home / Zengge, RuuviTag, Xiaomi M365, Yeelight, LG webOS, PurpleAir, Vizio SmartCast, iRobot Roomba, Wyze, ratgdo, June Oven and Chamberlain Security+. The Govee LAN API is in govee-rgbic-light, and the H5074/H5179 family is in govee-h5075-thermo.

Still missing from the July list, and carried forward below with a July list tag: AM43 blind motors, Insteon and Echelon (old firmware only) in Do these next, and in the tables BLE standing desks, Broadlink RM4, Fellow Stagg, MEATER, Spotify Car Thing, Neato, Nest gen 1/2, Owlet, the Tuya BLE Fingerbot, JK-BMS, Daly BMS, Husqvarna Automower, Yamaha YNCA and Votol. Onkyo eISCP and Eight Sleep stay link-only, and the Solum shelf labels move to link-only; Snoo and Traeger stay parked.

docs.title: Do these next
docs.text:
The 27 that best fit the project: every one is a spec-ready P5, or an orphaned (A) P4 with a local path and enough public work to draft from. They are ordered by priority, then risk, then effort. Most are phone-direct. The exceptions say what else is needed: a LAN listener for JuiceBox, and a plug-in OBD dongle for the Nissan Leaf.

  1. Instant Pot Smart Bluetooth (IP-Smart 6 qt) — [A] · effort S. The official Instant Pot Smart Bluetooth app has been withdrawn and the vendor went through Chapter 11, so nothing official can drive these cookers. The phone-direct protocol is simple: BLE GATT services 0xDAB0 for control, 0xDAB2 for telemetry, 0xDAA0 for time and 0xDAC0 for recipes, with 20-byte frames. It is written down in a single README of a 0-star repo, so a validated spec is what keeps it alive, and it fits the Flutter app with no extra hardware. Commands start pressure cooking remotely, so require attended use. Sources: openpot replacement app README

  2. AM43 / A-OK / Zemismart BLE blind motors (Blind Engine) — [A] · effort S · July list. The Blind Engine app is no longer on Google Play, so AM43, A-OK and Zemismart motors depend on third-party code, and homebridge-am43-blinds has been archived since September 2025. The phone talks straight to the motor's BLE GATT service with no hub or cloud: framed commands move, stop and set position, and notifications return battery, position and light level. No source describes the frame format in prose, so the spec is the missing piece. Exclude Tuya AM43 variants, note the one-client limit, and establish whether travel limits can be set over BLE. Sources: A-OK AM43 Python BLE control · buxtronix AM43 ESP32 library

  3. Enel X JuiceBox EV charger (JuiceBox 32/40/48) — [A] · effort M. Enel X Way North America shut down on 2024-10-11, leaving JuiceBox owners unable to change settings such as charge current. The charger sends UDP telemetry (ports 8042/8043/8047) to a configurable server, and owners can re-point that target over the telnet console on port 2000, through a DNS override or by masquerading the traffic. A LAN host, including a phone, can then read telemetry and set the current. The protocol lives only in juicepassproxy's code and a thin wiki. The spec must cap current at the wiring maximum and describe the Nov 2024 encrypted-UDP split. Sources: JuiceboxRescueWiki: how communication works · JuiceboxRescueWiki: console commands

  4. VanMoof S3 / X3 e-bike (plus legacy S2/X2 and earlier) — [A] · effort M. VanMoof went bankrupt in July 2023 and was bought by Lavoie, but every S3/X3 still depends on a per-bike encryption key and user key ID that only the vendor's account API ever issued. With the key exported once, the phone controls lock, lights, bell, assist levels, alarm and battery over local BLE with no cloud. The protocol exists only in client code (VanMoofKit, pymoof). A written spec plus an offline-key workflow keeps the bikes usable. Whether the API still serves keys is unknown, and the spec must leave out speed-limit and region changes. Sources: VanMoofKit Swift client and exporter · pymoof Python BLE client

  5. Sengled Wi-Fi smart bulbs — [A] · effort M. Sengled's cloud has failed repeatedly since June 2025 and Amazon removed the Alexa skill on 2025-08-01, but the Wi-Fi bulbs still answer JSON commands over LAN UDP port 9080 for on/off, brightness and colour. A phone can send these directly once a bulb is on the owner's Wi-Fi, and the setup flow can re-pair bulbs to a user-owned MQTT broker. The protocol exists only in SengledTools' code. The spec should cover the UDP commands, the provisioning handshake and the MQTT topics. OTA flashing to Tasmota works only on WF863 models, and the Zigbee bulbs are unaffected. Sources: SengledTools local control and re-pair · Sengled local server add-on

  6. Hörmann BiSecur Gateway — [A] · effort M. The BiSecur Gateway is Hörmann's LAN hub for garage-door and gate operators. A community README reports official support ended around the end of 2023 or beginning of 2024, and Hörmann declined to publish the protocol. The phone app talks to it on the LAN: UDP broadcast discovery on port 4001, then hex-ASCII frames over TCP 4000 with a login token and one client at a time. bisdk/sdk already sketches the frame layout, so the spec consolidates command semantics, error codes and session handling. Caveat: frames embed gateway MACs, so every capture must be placeholdered. Sources: bisdk/sdk protocol and frame layout · halacs/BiSecur SDK, EOL notes

  7. Yummly Smart Thermometer (Mastrad Meatit white-label) — [A] · effort M. The Yummly thermometer lost its app when Whirlpool took Yummly offline in December 2024 (the RE repo gives 2024-12-18). The probe still works locally: the phone talks BLE GATT to the T1 or T3 base, completes a rotating challenge handshake, then reads TLV frames with bit-rotation obfuscation carrying core and ambient temperature, battery and signal strength. The only write-up is a single-commit repository, so a clean spec would make it durable. Mark the XW3 generation (T3 + P3) as protocol-mapped but untested, and treat the Mastrad white-label names as unconfirmed. Sources: yummly-thermometer protocol docs

  8. LIVISI SmartHome (ex RWE / innogy) SHC 1 / SHC 2 — [A] · effort M. LIVISI SmartHome, sold since the RWE and innogy days, has a large German installed base, and the vendor website no longer resolves. The Local SmartHome API, launched around October 2022, may now be the only way to run the controllers; it survives only in openHAB, Home Assistant and Python clients. The path is plain LAN: HTTP on 8080 plus a WebSocket event stream, unencrypted, once Local SmartHome is enabled on recent firmware. It mirrors the already-specced devolo case. Main caveat: the auth flow, cloud shutdown date and any insolvency are still unsourced, and the SHC 1 and SHC 2 dialects differ. Sources: openHAB LIVISI binding · planbnet/livisi Python library

  9. Fossil Hybrid HR / Gen 6 Hybrid (Skagen, Citizen CZ, Q) — [A] · effort L. Fossil has left the smartwatch business and is restructuring, yet Hybrid HR and Gen 6 Hybrid watches cannot be set up without a 16-byte per-watch key that only Fossil's cloud issues. The phone-direct BLE protocol, covering key-authenticated sessions, encrypted file transfer, notifications, activity sync and watch-app install, exists only in Gadgetbridge, Hybridge and small RE repos. No key-server shutdown date has been announced, which makes this time-sensitive. Gadgetbridge is AGPL, so derive facts rather than code, and describe key retrieval only as an owner exporting their own watch's key. Sources: Gadgetbridge Fossil device page · Gadgetbridge Fossil Hybrid internals

  10. Sleep Number SleepIQ beds, BLE pump and base control — [A] · effort L. Sleep Number filed Chapter 11 on 2026-06-12, and a community project already reports cloud endpoints failing and forced account migration. Phones can talk BLE GATT directly to the bed's controller for firmness, base position and lighting, but that path exists only in recent Home Assistant code. There are two protocol families: request/response MCR on older beds, and Fuzion on 360 beds, which needs bonding and authentication first. Base motion carries a pinch and entrapment hazard, so the spec must require a user present. Clean-room: the community work says MCR was found by decompiling the vendor app, so take wire-level facts only. Sources: trooperthorn Sleep Number HA integration · ha-adjustable-bed PR #579 (Fuzion, MCR)

  11. Apple AirPort Extreme / Time Capsule / Express (ACP) — [A] · effort L. Apple discontinued the AirPort Extreme and Time Capsule in April 2018, and the management protocol, ACP on TCP 5009, is known only from two community codebases, one archived in 2022. The local path is fully cloud-free: property get/set, reboot, feature detection and logs, with SRP authentication and an encrypted session. A spec would let the app stand in for Apple's ageing AirPort Utility on any platform. Effort is large because of the property encoding and catalogue. The spec must recommend SRP over the weak legacy auth and leave out the firmware decryption and flashing material both repos contain. Sources: node-acp (port 5009, SRP) · airpyrt-tools Python ACP client

  12. Philips Wi-Fi air purifiers and humidifiers — [B] · effort M. A large installed base of Philips purifiers and humidifiers, phone-direct, with a local protocol that exists only in client code, and firmware updates that are removing local access on some models. The local path is encrypted CoAP over UDP to the unit with no account, as implemented by aioairctrl; the oldest units use HTTP or plain CoAP. Scope the first spec to the encrypted-CoAP generation, list the FUSION cloud-relay models as parked, and record which firmware still allows local control. Port 5683 and AES-128-CBC still need confirming from code. Sources: aioairctrl encrypted CoAP library · philips-airpurifier-coap models and caveat

  13. GE Cync / C by GE lights, plugs and switches — [B] · effort L. GE Cync has a very large US installed base, and GE Lighting has stopped making the original C by GE bulbs. The phone joins the Telink BLE mesh directly with AES-encrypted opcodes, as the vendor app does, but the protocol is split across four client code bases. Mesh credentials must be exported from the Cync cloud once, so the spec should say what happens when that export is gone. Wi-Fi models need a LAN server and DNS override; keep them separate. A shared Telink-mesh spec could cover AwoX/EGLO. Sources: cync2mqtt Telink BLE mesh · cync-lan cloud impersonation (TLS)

  14. EcoFlow power stations and home-energy devices (BLE) — [C] · effort L. EcoFlow's app demands a server login even over Bluetooth, and the main reverse-engineering repo, ef-ble-reverse, was archived on 2026-09-16, so a written spec would preserve a protocol that now lives only in code. The phone talks to the unit directly: an ECDH key exchange, then AES-128-encrypted frames carrying protobuf (V3 devices) or a legacy binary payload (V2, such as Wave 2). After a one-time account User ID lookup it runs fully offline. Caveat: that repo derived its schemas by decompiling the app, so field meanings must be restated in the spec's own words. Sources: ef-ble-reverse protocol RE · ESP32-Ecoflow-BLE handshake notes

  15. Drobo NAS status daemon (FS / 5N / 5N2 / B810n) — [A] · effort S. Drobo's parent was liquidated in 2023 and its Dashboard software is unsupported, but owners still run BeyondRAID arrays whose drive health is visible only through an undocumented status socket. On TCP port 5000 the NAS pushes a 16-byte 'DRINASD' header and an XML status document every 10-20 seconds, with no authentication, so a phone on the LAN can read it directly. Community notes and a wiki page cover the format, making this a small spec. It should stay read-only, handle the three header-magic variants, and paraphrase rather than copy the daemon's internal command names. Sources: drobo-nas-protocol notes · DroboPorts wiki: NASD XML format

  16. Kano Harry Potter Coding Kit Wand — [A] · effort S. Kano Computing went into administration on 2023-06-06, leaving the Harry Potter wand with an insolvent vendor. The wand talks BLE GATT straight to the phone with no cloud: three custom services (info, IO, sensor) share a 64a7… UUID base, alongside a Nordic DFU service. The map is confirmed on a Hackaday log, but the button, vibration, LED and 9-axis stream semantics are scattered across hobby clients. A small spec makes the wand a gesture-input device for the app. Spell recognition runs on the host, so it stays out of scope. Sources: Kano Wand Hack GATT map · kano_wand Python client

  17. TiVo DVRs and Minis (Series 3+): network remote, Mind RPC — [A] · effort S. TiVo left hardware manufacturing on 2025-10-01 and now sells only monthly service, but a large fleet of Series 3 and later boxes remains. Once the owner enables Network Remote Control, each box accepts an unauthenticated text remote on TCP 31339 and announces itself over mDNS or legacy port-2190 beacons. That protocol survives only as an old forum post and scattered clients, so a small phone-direct spec is quick to write. Mind RPC on Series 4+ can follow later; it needs a TiVo-issued certificate, which must never be shipped or quoted. Sources: tivoremote network remote client · kmttg wiki: remote control RPC

  18. Hot Wheels id Smart Track Race Portal (FXB53) — [A] · effort S. Mattel's Hot Wheels id app was discontinued on 2024-01-01 according to the community project, leaving the Race Portal (FXB53) without official software. The portal is phone-direct: it advertises HWiD over BLE and exposes three services for authentication, data and control, then reports each car's NFC UID, serial and NDEF records along with float32 speed and lap events. One small repository already has a PROTOCOL.md, so a clean spec mainly adds durability. Cite the retirement date as community-sourced, and describe the car-ID structure without copying Mattel's ID tables. Sources: hotwheels-portal BLE protocol

  19. IKEA TRÅDFRI Gateway E1526 (CoAP over DTLS-PSK) — [A] · effort M. IKEA stopped adding features to the TRÅDFRI gateway in April 2024 in favour of DIRIGERA (security firmware continued into 2026; see the 2026-10-18 sweep), leaving a very widely owned Zigbee gateway frozen. It works fully locally: coaps on UDP 5684, a PSK obtained from the label's security code, and GET/PUT on LwM2M/IPSO resources for devices, groups and scenes. A good prose reference exists, so the value is consolidation: fixtures, the pairing state machine and the object-ID tables, in the same shape as osram-lightify-gateway. The main risk is the phone side, since Flutter/Dart DTLS 1.2 PSK support is thin. Sources: TRÅDFRI CoAP docs (glenndehaan) · Debugging CoAPS with TRÅDFRI gateway

  20. Oura Ring Gen3 and Ring 4, BLE sync protocol — [A] · effort M. Oura gates detailed data behind a paid membership, yet the ring itself speaks BLE GATT directly to the phone. After an AES-128 nonce exchange under a 16-byte per-ring key, a client can read battery, live heart rate, SpO2 and the history-event stream with no Oura account. Public RE from 2025-26 is spread across open_oura, its forks and ringverse, so a clean-room consolidation would help owners of used rings or lapsed memberships. Carry only wire facts, no app internals or scoring models, and label health fields non-clinical. Sources: open_oura Rust toolkit · ringverse Oura Ring 4 BLE

  21. Echelon Connect bikes and Stride (pre-July-2025 firmware) — [A] · effort M · July list. Echelon's July 2025 firmware made bikes wait for a server authentication challenge before streaming metrics over BLE, which ended offline use and broke third-party apps. Bikes and treadmills still on older firmware speak a plain phone-direct BLE profile for cadence, resistance, power and speed, already public in QZ's GPL drivers. A spec keeps un-updated and second-hand machines usable without a subscription. Because of DMCA §1201, it must cover only the pre-update profile and say nothing about meeting or bypassing the new challenge. Sources: QZ issue #62: Echelon BLE log · QZ Equipment Compatibility wiki

  22. Insteon Hub 2245-222 (v2) / 2242-222 (v1) — [A] · effort M · July list. Insteon's servers went down without notice in mid-April 2022, but hubs kept running offline with their local API intact. Hub v2 (2245) takes raw PLM commands over HTTP on port 25105 with Basic auth from the hub label and returns replies through a 200-character circular buffer that must be polled about twice a second; Hub v1 (2242) uses a different transport on port 9761. The repo already has an unvalidated research note. Link the vendor PLM guide rather than restating it, spec the Hub v2 wrapper and buffer semantics, and placeholder hub credentials. Sources: KRKeegan Hub2 technical inspection · Home Assistant Insteon integration

  23. Hasbro Furby Connect (2016) — [A] · effort M. Furby Connect lost its companion app when Hasbro dropped support (quoted from the PyFluff README; no date given). Control is phone-direct over BLE GATT: a Nordic SoC fronts the GeneralPlus main MCU and accepts commands for actions, antenna LED colour, mood and LCD backlight, sends joystick, tickle and accelerometer notifications, and takes DLC uploads for eye animations and audio. bluefluff already has a doc folder, so the work is consolidating it with the modern Python port into one spec. Document the DLC container format only, never the content of Hasbro's own DLC files. Sources: bluefluff protocol docs · PyFluff Python control library

  24. Nissan Leaf (ZE0 / AZE0 / ZE1) battery data over OBD-II — [A] · effort M. Nissan shut down NissanConnect EV in the UK and Europe on 30 March 2026 for pre-2019 Leafs, so owners there have lost the cloud telematics path. Battery state of charge, state of health and capacity can still be read locally: a phone talks to a plug-in BLE ELM327-class OBD-II adapter and sends diagnostic polls such as the LBC query 0x79B with its response on 0x7BB. Public CAN spreadsheets and DBC files already exist, so the spec's value is a clean decode write-up on the repo's OBD, UDS and ISO-TP layers. Keep it strictly read-only, with separate tables for each generation. Sources: Leaf CAN spreadsheet and DBCs · nissan-leaf-obd-ble integration

  25. Slingbox place-shifters (240/350/500/M1/M2/Solo/Pro/Pro-HD) — [A] · effort L. Sling Media shut its servers down on 2022-11-09, and the SlingPlayer app went with them. The boxes still accept direct LAN connections: Slinger re-implements the client, sends IR remote codes, sets resolution and re-serves the video. Its README lists the IR codes and resolutions, but the handshake, auth and stream framing exist only in code. A spec would let a phone app talk to the box directly. The open questions are recovering the admin password after the shutdown and several chipset generations. Stream obfuscation touches pay-TV content, so cipher details need a DMCA 1201 review first. Sources: Slinger local Slingbox server · Wikipedia: Slingbox

  26. Anki / DDL Cozmo robot — [A] · effort L. Cozmo's behaviour engine runs on the phone, and the app comes from Digital Dream Labs, which the Pennsylvania Attorney General sued in 2024. The phone joins the robot's own access point and speaks a UDP protocol on port 5551 with selective-repeat ARQ framing. pycozmo's docs describe the transport clearly, but every message definition sits only in generated code, so the message layer is code-only. A first spec should cover transport, handshake and the core drive, lift, head, display and audio messages. Do not draw on cozmo-stack, which was built from decompiled vendor material. Sources: pycozmo protocol doc · pycozmo Python client

docs.title: Everything else worth a spec, by category
docs.text: Every other spec-ready device and research target, grouped by what the device is. Within each table the order is priority, then spec-ready before research target, then risk. The Caveat line is the one thing the verification pass says a spec author must not get wrong. Read it before starting.

docs.title: Energy, solar and EV charging
docs.text: Device and vendor status Risk Local path Why a spec, and the catch Effort Public work Wallbox Pulsar Plus and Pulsar MAX EV chargers (BLE)Wallbox's FY2025 20-F warns that failing to complete its restructuring or equity raise threatens its going concern. B · P4 BLE GATT, 'EaE'-framed JSON: lock, current, status, untested start/stop. Plus and MAX differ; firmware 6.11.26+ adds SMP pairing and a PIN.phone-direct; protocol code-only A best-selling European home charger from a vendor with a formal going-concern warning; the phone-direct BLE path is documented only in code.Caveat: Settable current stays within the installer-configured maximum; document no way to raise hardware limits or change installer settings. M wallbox-ble HA component · HA Community: Wallbox BLE gateway Anker SOLIX power stations and Solarbank (BLE)Vendor active; Anker's official Modbus TCP integration covers home products (Solarbank Max, XE, E5000 Pro) but not C- or F-series stations. C · P4 BLE GATT without pairing: telemetry (battery, AC/DC power, temperature, expansion packs) and control of outputs, timers, light bar, display. Not simultaneous with Wi-Fi.phone-direct; protocol code-only Huge-selling portable stations whose BLE protocol exists only in SolixBLE (code-only); Anker's official local API skips them. Link, don't spec, for Solarbank.Caveat: Frame encryption or per-session key exchange is unconfirmed; check SolixBLE code before sizing. BLE and Wi-Fi cannot be used together. M SolixBLE library · HaSolixBLE integration · Anker official Modbus TCP integration GoodWe inverters (UDP 8899 / Modbus TCP)No shutdown or subscription evidence; inverters on older ARM firmware may need a vendor upgrade to respond. (unverified) C · P4 UDP 8899 to the Wi-Fi/LAN dongle (proprietary AA55 and Modbus-over-UDP), or Modbus TCP 502 on the V2.0 LAN+WiFi dongle.phone-direct; protocol code-only Large inverter family (ET, EH, BT, ES, DT and more, plus GE white-label) whose UDP protocol is described only in library code (code-only), despite native HA support.Caveat: Unverified that the vendor apps use this path; EMS-mode and export-limit writes affect grid behaviour, so scope them carefully. M goodwe Python library · GoodWe HA custom component Hoymiles DTU and HMS-W Wi-Fi microinvertersVendor active; firmware v01.x requires encrypted communication, and polling faster than about 32 s may disable cloud functions. (community-sourced) C · P4 Protobuf over LAN TCP to the stand-alone or HMS-W built-in DTU: real-time data, alarms, power limit, on/off. Firmware v01.x adds per-device encryption.phone-direct; protocol code-only HMS-W-2T is Europe's default balcony-solar inverter, Wi-Fi only; the stock DTU's protobuf and encryption exist only in hoymiles-wifi code. OpenDTU fails phone-direct.Caveat: Warn that repeated power-limit writes wear inverter EEPROM; document the minimum poll interval. The TCP port must come from the code. M hoymiles-wifi protobuf library · ha-hoymiles-wifi integration Jackery Explorer power stations (BLE)Vendor active; the official HA integration covers SolarVault3 over local MQTT only. The Explorer BLE protocol is undocumented. C · P4 Phone-direct BLE, no account: RC4 frames on most models, AES-128-CBC on HP3600, E1500V2 and 'box' units; responses CRC-16 checked.phone-direct; protocol code-only Top-3 power station brand absent from the repo; the BLE crypto lives only in one young project (code-only). Phone-direct and account-free.Caveat: Key combines the advertised serial, a device GUID and a static salt; weigh DMCA 1201 before publishing the salt; confirm against a second implementation. M private_jack local BLE · Jackery official HA integration LiTime / Redodo / Power Queen Bluetooth LiFePO4 batteriesBrands appear active as Amazon and direct sellers; no shutdown or subscription found (unverified). C · P4 Phone-direct BLE GATT: write a status request, parse notifications for voltage, current, SOC, temperature, cells. Proven from a phone browser via Web Bluetooth.phone-direct; protocol code-only Common drop-in 12 V LiFePO4 packs sharing one BMS that is not JBD, JK or Daly; the protocol lives only in scattered client code.Caveat: Each client was tested on only one or two packs; mark model coverage per pack. Read-only telemetry is enough. S litime-bluetooth-battery Web Bluetooth client · litime-ble Python library · BMS_BLE-HA (Redodo BMS) Sungrow inverters via WiNet-S dongleVendor active; Sungrow disabled direct Modbus requests on WiNet-S dongles. Whether later firmware restored port 502 is unverified. (community-sourced) C · P4 WebSocket plus HTTP API on the WiNet-S dongle over the LAN or its setup access point, returning Modbus register data; login with username and password.phone-direct; protocol code-only A top-3 global inverter vendor closed its documented Modbus path; the replacement WebSocket API is spread across Python, Go and Rust clients (code-only).Caveat: The Sungrow-Inverter repo holds vendor datasheets and manuals: cite by URL, copy nothing. Unverified whether the vendor app uses this API.
